To me, this game is simply a stain on Sid Meier's name. I can't imagine he had any interest in the project, and it feels like the producers simply pinned his arms to the desk until he signed over permission to use his name for a overly-glossed project that probably didn't take them very long to develop.
This game tries to 'feel' a bit like Master of Orion, but it fails to deliver in pretty much every category. I played it for two days and finished it on epic size. Every planet, faction and technology is the same, no random events happened, there are a short list of "missions" for every uncolonied planet which are all very much the same. It is to MoO what Empire At War was to Supremacy: take a good concept, cut it down to its most bare elements, and slap a price on it.
There's almost no diplomacy, not in the sense that you feel there is real politics taking place as happens with Sid Meier's civilisation games - the AI is neither bold to attack nor is scared of you when you're powerful. Alliances are empty. The game feels as though it has no soul to the purpose but to play through the simple rules, you are fully aware you're just clicking to interact with a simple ruleset, no immersion in actually "being a part" of a story, not even on sandbox level.
The graphics "are nice" but feels like pretty paint on something so simple and simply boring. The game forces you to watch ships explode in its terrible animation (which is, flashes here and there, while the camera shakes galore, focusing on the ship with no choice, then it disappears, this animation when repeated actually made me a bit ill) so, when you take out 5 ships with one torpedo (which is pretty necessary to get through the game without spending too long in the boring battles) you just check your phone while you wait for it to go all "oh look shaky screen in space, isn't space cool??" No. It's not cool.
This is the space-4X equivalent of Farmville. It's only worth getting if you need to keep your son quiet in the evenings, but even then, in my opinion, it's also a waste of his time.

Recomended but not at full price
The game its self is fairly fun but be mindful of your expectations.
Think of this as a mobile friendly snack not a full on civ game or even a full on game of any type. Gameplay is simple, easy to pick up and prety easy to master to and thats not bad if you go at this thinking ... casual time sink in the civ beyond earth theme ... because thats what it is and that fills a nice nitch honistly.
Thus far I have had 0 luck with any integration between civ beyond earth and starships but honistly I dont care about that aspect.
Ship/Fleet building is very simple really its just a matter of adding more to your current set while technologies are simply making what you have a bit stronger/more efficent.
Battles come in a handfull of flavors, kill everything, avoid death, and goaly e.g. keep enemy away from this. It fits well given the scope of the game; remimber its not a 4hr play session your getting out of it, think casual time sink.
Visualy its expected, would be nice if the PC version had a bit more to it but honistly at this scale I would rather have more lore and story than eye candy. The lore is light I had hoped for a bit more there and that would have been a nice easy tie-in to the 'main game' if you will but its not a deal breaker.
If we compare this to what I feel are similar games, not in play style but in purpose I would compare this to say Fallout Shelter.
In that case it doesn't have as much to do as Fallout Shelter does, wont hold you as long likely but it does play faster and for a casual game thats a positive I think.
Price point wise, I wouldn't recomend it at full price unless you just have spare cash laying about. That said I have paid that much for lesser games and been happy enough. Taking the purly numbers point of view I will likely play this game a few more hours and if we see any more expansions to the 'main game' it will likely see me return now and then. If I dont log another hour im getting about an hour of play for 3.33€ not bad but not as efficent other options out there.
I would like to see more games like this, e.g. smaller more casual 'side dish' like games to our fav big games but not at the expence of the main product. They fit well in a buisy schedule, add a little extra to IPs your a fan of and if the devs can manage to keep the price point down and find interesting tie-ins to the main game then all the more better.
Honistly I wouldn't want the game to become bigger or more involved, adding a bit more lore or what ever is appropreate for your IP fans to chew on in the main game it supports would be key I think. For civ (and me specificly) that would be a bit more detail on tech, history, etc. perhaps some screens or concept art I can find/unlock what have you. As for the gameplay its self I think its plenty deep and just right on the complexity side all be it a bit easy on the difficulty aspect for what it is.

Easily one of the most fun, fluid, and weird platformers around. If you could condense "Wheeeeeeeeeee" down and give it a physical form, it would be this game.

TL;DR - 9/10 - Most fun 2D platformer I've played in a long time. Buy now.
My pro list is shorter than my con list by a long shot, but only because I'm hard from loving this game. My pros make up 95% of what I experienced in all of my playtime, so most of my cons are just silly gripes.
Pros:
-Movement and platforming is incredibly fast, smooth and fun.
-Combat is satisfying and fluid.
-Soundtrack and graphics blend very well together to create a very nice aesthetic.
-There's a good sense of challenge, nothing cheap that I noticed.
-No noticable bugs or preformance issues on Intel HD 630. This game is modern but a breeze to run on lower end hardware.
Cons:
-As soon as the ink pen's shooting is introduced and the enemy variation changes, combat and shooting based puzzles halt the sense of speed and momentum that came with the fast paced platforming beforehand.
-Checkpoint system is invisible and occasionally it didn't seem like I deserved to go back to the beginning of the room.
-Environment and music varation is lacking. Every challenge room has the same visual style and the same song, same goes for almost every other area in the game.
-Some features are absent in some levels: Hooks appear in the first and last levels only, the shell only appeared in the first level, and you find no NPCs in the Basement (Besides your sister), Ascent, or Volcano. I found with only a few in the Plains, and couldn't interact with any in the area with the tents just outside the Bathtub.
-The ink enemy type selection is extremely small.
-This installment is missing features from previous ones (swimming, snail golf, green squiggles that were worth 5, etc). You won't notice this if this is your first game in the series.
-Grinding in a platformer (more on this later).
-Beating the final boss reset my lives counter from 11 to 3 :(
-The bosses are the weakest point IMO. They were short and sweet, but I can't help but noticed the missed opportunity with the new gimmicks (red/yellow rails, pen surfing). They were platformer based, but didn't incorporate momentum or physics, just combat.
-Didn't care for the story at all. The only time I felt anything was talking to an NPC in the Plains who was having a rough time.
Compared to the previous games in the series, this is the game to play if you want the best controls. However, it's very clear that this game will either see a massive update, or an "Episode 2" DLC. This game is short. At the time of writing, I'm 3 hours in and I've completed all the hidden challenge levels that unlock cosmetics, but I'm still working my way through all the upgrades. I'm replaying levels to max out the upgrades. I'm grinding in a platformer. It isn't THAT bad since this game is so fun, but I feel it still should not be there.
Another huge reason why this will get a huge update or DLC is that the Bathtub floors are void of features. There's a floor with 3 arcade cabinets. This is the 4th game in the series and the first on Steam, so it makes sense that there would be plans to port the first 3 games over in the new engine and have them playable there. But since I haven't technically beat the game 100%, I may not have unlocked everything yet.
Yeah, I know, it sounds bad when I focus on the negatives, but again. The bad is only 10% of what I experienced.
9/10. Both as a sequel and a standalone game, it's a blast to play and is worth the price tag. It's not perfect by any means, and I am waiting eagerly for any next installment. But as much as I love the series nostalgically, I can't get lost in this game and its world for its length and minor design issues (AKA me being picky).
P.S.: Anyone know when the health and combat upgrades cap out?

The Collider is a very short but immensely satisfying reflex game. You basically have to pass through obstacles without crashing while constantly increasing speed at a fixed rate. It's quite casual in the sense that you don't have to finish speed 100 to 1300 in one sitting. You can readjust the starting speed whenever you unlock a new one (which makes for quick and painless achievements). My only complaint with the game is that I somehow lost progress after reaching 1200. I tried to record the last stretch on Fraps and I'm not sure what happened during that time to trigger it. Thankfully, you can easily re-climb back to 1300 by using extra lives that cost coins. For all of you achievement hunters, don't use extra lives if you're trying to get the no-crash achievements. Whenever you crash, just go back to main menu and replay at the desired speed.
4/5. Very affordable and I definitely recommend it.

Its time to move the couch in front of the 70" TV,  get the box fans out, place strategically around the tv, turn on full blast, and play 'The Collider'. Don't forget the snacks as you're going to be playing for a while until you beat it. Yes, 'The Collider' has that essential element to it, that challenges you to beat it. It's a very simple but frustrating game. and forces you to play it until you have beaten it ! Its simple fun, and it apparently messes with time and space, as before you know it, you have either beaten it in an hour, and gotten another perfect game to show off on your profile, or you have spent most of the day in front of it, wandering why you can't quite make the last couple of achievements. The collider isn't very original, essentially a simplified 'Race The Sun', or perhaps 'AaAaAA!!! - A Reckless Disregard for Gravity' ... it isn't really that well done ...not many options, variety, or backing music but it works. The game is simply coded to consist of a narrow light tunnel which is constructed to give the impression of motion, with occasional twists and turns, obstacles are introduced which consist of disks with holes of varying shape and size blocking said tunnel, occasionally rotate through which you have to navigate. It has 13 levels which once beaten can be used as a starting point to continue in your efforts to complete the game. These save points make it easier to beat and greatly simplifies the pursuit of the 'perfect game'.  Its all about not blinking, turning up the mouse sensitivity, drinking coffee and getting those reflexes sharpened.... if you're like me and really really _REALLY_ old, its going to be really hard....and you will be writing reviews just to get a break! But if you're not out of elementary school you should be done in an hour. Don't think about it, buy this game, don't even waste time looking for a coupon on the forums... buy it now, play it now. You will enjoy.

Man, i don't know. I have mixed feelings about recommend this or not. Let's start the Review:
Red Faction 2 when compared to its predecessor, is a disappointment. Despite maintaining certain foundations established in the first part, mainly due to technical issues.
PROS :
- LOTS of weapons (with primary and secondary shot system for each one as in the first part).
- The shooting mechanics makes some intense gunfights fun.
- Sections where you drive vehicles are well made ​​and are quite fun.
- Apart from the primary mission objectives, the game have hidden secondary objectives for each map, which when completed, will give you bonus points.
- Karma system that varies the ending of the game (Accomplish the primary and secondary objectives provides you of good Karma, while doing bad actions like killing innocent civilians, will give you bad Karma).
CONS :
- Generic story.
- Easily forgettable characters.
- Clearly this is a PS2 port (You can easily notice it viewing the avaliable options, not to mention the graphics).
- Enemies and allies AI is doubtful.
- There are sections where enemies respawn infinitely until you pass a certain point.
- Exploration of the maps is practically non-existent (compared to the first game).
- The Geo-Mod technology is implemented despite being not quite exploited.
- Ridiculously short (the campaing last 5-6 hours).
If you can get past the fact that this is a direct port of a PS2 game, and you value the game for what it is (a short, mindless, linear first person shooter focused only in killing whatever you have in front) you may like it, if you want something deeper, you won't find it here.
Note: Played it on Windows XP - SP3

Sequel to the Red Fraction series. This was rushed to meet THQ's deadlines resulting in a rushed development of this game and some of massive plotholes that werent answered from the first game. The overrule of Ultor by EDF (Earth Defense Force) after Red Faction 1 has resulted saved Parker and Eos.
Enter Alias, the explosives expert. Alias was employed by the SSF (Sopot Special Forces) to steal the Ultor blueprints which allowed for super-soldier research, a nanotechology then things go horribly wrong, research turns up poor results. Results are mutant beings coupled with psionic powers. 5 members survive the experiments, Alias, Shrike and Tangier join the Red Faction, who were previously exposed to the experimentations set their objective to assassinate Sopot, a despot scumbag who runs the Commonwealth and was responsible for stealing and utilizing the nanotechnology that Ultor created.
Gunplay is simply point and shoot without recoil control, no distinct pattern spraying. Flat, boring and not really entertaining. Mostly all the weapons include little imagination put into their design and feel generic. The pistols remain obsolete throughout the game, even as an emergency sidearm.
The game features Jason Statham as Shiek, which is in itself, quite surprising. He provides a cheesy radio banter but comical relief. The game supports full 1080p without modding, in comparison to other ports which fail to deliver even on the mark of HD resolution this is very impressive for a game it's age.
Art-style and thematic structure is quite unique in concept. Soviet Union parallels and themes/motifs of revolution and uprising make most of the charm of the game. Sound effects in some regard are improved, a tiny bit more crisp and varied and the atmosphere gloomy and dystopian.
A morality system, which was kept in Red Faction Guerilla.
Dated graphics that have aged like an elephant's wrinkly arsé, modelling quality aside, the texturing is extremely dull, consists of shades of brown with a layer of fog for bad measure, probably to mask pop-up:

Horrible implementation of the health system. I personally did not appreciate removing the "medics" from the first game which added to the tension of finding a way to replenish health whenever there was no medical pickups which added to the challenge and Sci-Fi horror atmosphere of Red Faction. Crappy level design - excessively boxxy, enclosed areas with hardly any breathing space, lacklustre vehicle sections.
Previous weapons from the first installment with new skins slapped on front, rather than acting like new weapons, you simply have the same weapons. AI is braindead and fires unrealistically upon the wrong targets (which I might add, your teammates are invincible and thus recieve the most hits in regard) making the game fairly easy to progress unless you have it on hard then it becomes worse, all the enemies focus purely upon you if you fire once. No online mode, especially for the fact the first game had this, working with plugins is INSULTING to PC and console gamers as a whole!
Destruction is heavily nerfed and reacts unrealistically. No smoke or dust dissipates from the explosion, simply fragmenting the walls or other destructibles as if by magic. Level design is basic and very linear, as in, lacks the complexity seen in previous games in terms of being able to make alternate routes to outflank an enemy are not allowed by GeoMod 2.0.
Unlikable characters with the character development of a Kardashian.
Graphically, it is - for the most part - satisfactory but the lack of particle effects and poor use of draw distance fog destroys my immersion and suspense of disbelief of being in a dystopian world. Animations are very static and robotic. Texturing and modelling is flat colour-wise and it appears not effort was put into some parts of the environment. Destruction is heavily downgraded to the point it becomes a novelty or a gimmick not exactly the novel - make your own way here and there ideal. To compensate, secrets lie ahead from destroying walls. Well played in that aspect but still not enough as to merit it on that quality alone.
The plot is sub-standard and laughably simplistic. Case in point, assassinating the antagonist is revealed to be least treacharous of the cast, instead your leader is THE antagonist. Reason is mainly because of a Deus Ex Machina cliché, the Nanocell - an asspull in the story and the culimation of research that created the cast in the first place was powerful enough to create an army that Sopot/RedFaction would not be able to handle is somehow better in the hands of a militia with very little prior scientific knowledge of the NanoCell technology in the previous hands of Ultor. Molov subsequently not only betrays the only help he has but the story also fails to be self-aware of the consequences of betrayal.
This twist would make M. Night wet his panties, it retains not a single iota of consistency or explanation for this betrayal only in the late game is it hinted the 'Super Soldier' concept which would allow him to dominate the world and thus you are left wondering what the point of the game was; kill almost everyone or grab the technology?
Red Faction II is a major disappoinment. Though some thanks can be given for the fact it gave rise to a far more superior sequel, Red Faction: Guerilla. Not worth the purchase like Armageddon. It seems Volition has the curse of making every second game their worst one but third one their best.

A crafting game in which you will never punch a tree or heft a pickaxe against a rockface. Instead it puts you in an RTS: you want resources, you better go take them from the AI-controlled factions, either by conquering resource point areas and putting automated drilling platforms on them, or just ripping their ships apart as salvage. You, know: fun.
The game is still under very active development, which is a mixed blessing. Replacing custom cannons with CRAM cannons, and making the drag model more realistic, made the game more fun, but you need to be prepared for a ship that was awesome yesterday to need rework to be effective tomorrow. Nick, the developer, *is* good at making sure they still load in and do best-effort conversions, so you can tweak rather than rebuild from start---important, given building a good battleship can take you a weekend's play.
Nick is pretty active on the forum. He tends to pick up serious bug reports pretty quick, but there's the risk that as always the fanbase constantly pressures for more difficulty, more complexity (without actually introducing more intersting decisions), more dilution of a design just to have more everything. Such is early access.
Philosophically, this is a nerd game. It doesn't have difficulty levels: it has a pair of difficulty sliders that control different scaling factors. If you want the AI to stop throwing the controls to full lock every time it's a fraction off-course, you'd better learn to start tuning a PID controller. You can control some things with Lua, although not as thorougly as I'd like yet---you can't *quite* replace the stock AI with it. Lua missiles are currently as gods to their lesser, built-in-guidance bretheren. You don't *need* to do any of this, and there's a lot of effort put into getting you going with simpler subsets, but this is game that's not shy about giving you parameters to tune.
It's ugly, and the dirty, rusty, outlined art-style can make it hard to identify blocks at first. The UI is pure programmer, weirdly positioned buttons and the occasional bizzare workflow (like having to manually save workshop items to disk). The physical nature of battles can make it pretty attractive in motion, though, missiles streaking through the air as a ship rips in half from a huge ammo explosion.
The build tools are pretty good. It's got arbitrary symmetry and plane-fills, saveable prefab regions and subobjects, and the recommended keyboard-based mode is pretty slick once you've got used to it. Ships themselves are instanceable in the strategy game proper, and remember how they used to be before they were damaged, so repair is automatic once enabled even if they were completely destroyed. This is not a game about manual labour; this is a game about designing machines of war and using them to conquer the world.
Seriously, though. You'll lose a weekend doing combat trials on that battleship.

Shame on the developers for advertising this game as a 'racing' game, this piece of trash shares absolutely no similarity between any of the existing good racing games both in terms of mechanics and competitiveness. If you like to have the outcome of your game be based on your skill level, look elsewhere as this game cheats so blatantly that it renders this game absolutely unplayable.
Just about every major gameplay aspect of the game is pointless in terms of competitive racing.
-Drifting? Pointless. There is no effective way of recovering from a drift and it does nothing to help you as it slows you down to an incredible level.
-Unlocking cars? Pointless. For every new car, your opponent AI automatically gets a car that is at least two level above yours, so whatever car you bring into a race makes no difference whatsoever as you will always automatically be in a disadvantage. (Every opponent car, regardless of model, will have a better acceleration and top speed than you do)
-Powerplay? Pointless. Each time you wreck an opponent car, they receive a huge acceleration bonus as well as speed bonus, making them able to catch up to you within the matter of seconds.
-Taking the lead? Pointless. I have seen cars that literally spawn right in front of me right before the finish line, so you can be in first place and two seconds away from the finish line and still end up in fifth as you see four other cars spawn right next to you and zoom past the finish line.
How such a fantastic idea of a video game came up with such a poor level of execution is beyond me.

While a little less accomplished than the Family Secrets entry, this is still a wonderfully atmospheric and reasonably satisfying hidden object/puzzle game. It's thin on story compared to the aforementioned title - you basically just go through a series of slightly exotic "other worlds" to enable the finale - and the ending holds a significance which its scant content fails to live up to, but for the right price it's a good buy for genre fans.

This game is the sequel to "House of 1000 Doors: Family Secrets."  You don't necessarily need to play through that one first to understand this one, but I would highly recommend it.
The gameplay is similar to its predecessor, and involves:
1. Item-based puzzles (find objects, then use them to solve tasks).
Compared to the first game, "Palm of Zoroaster" does a much better job of streamlining your puzzle solution objects.  It drastically reduced the rate of item redundancy, and it also paced the items properly, so that most of the time you are only lugging around things that are germane to the puzzles at hand.
2. Traditional hidden object screens.  As with "Family Secrets," these take the form of "junk with no coherent theme, scattered across a location." (Seriously, why are there always children's toys mixed in with priceless antiques and vegetables?)  The puzzles were a good challenge level, incorporating two-part objects (i.e. pitcher + glass = "glass of water"), cached objects (stowed in drawers or chests), and click-to-zoom areas.  The objects were well drawn, well delineated, and clearly labeled.
3. Bonus hidden "beyond" objects that appear in the background art and slowly morph back and forth between two different images. There are 46 total to find in the main game (approximately one per screen, including some detail screens).  There is no incentive to collect these other than personal pride, and the locations are included in the game's built-in comprehensive strategy guide.
4. A handful of easy mini-games (rotating discs, swapping tiles, matching, etc.) that unlock new objects or open new paths.  I liked all the mini-games in the main mission, but I actually skipped one in the bonus content because it was just too tedious (and I pride myself on never skipping anything in a casual game).
The music and character designs are pretty much recycled from the first game, which makes sense, but all of the background art and puzzles are new.
I liked the story of this game better.  It was more coherent, and the plot was a bit less dark, centering around the history of a single cursed object instead of around cursed objects + unfortunate accidents + witchcraft + mediums and psy powers + your maligned grandmother.  I also thought the locations were more interesting (even though they were stereotypical, rather than accurate, representations of those places).
One nit-picky thing that bothered me was the tone of the portals.  In the first game it was clear that the portals led to a dream-like world where ghosts were trapped in the moment of their tragedy.  In this game I was unsure at first whether I was in a dream world created by the house, whether I was in the actual past, or whether I was in the present day.  This was mostly due to the letters and journal entries, but there was also an odd mash-up of anachronistic items in each location.  The confusion didn't really affect my overall understanding of the plot or my ultimate enjoyment of the game, but it did momentarily break the immersive experience.
The voice-acting was also bothersome.
Some things this game did that the first game didn't:
- There is now a map that not only shows you where you have actions available, but allows you to instantly teleport to any screen in the game.  This is a great feature to eliminate backtracking, or to give you a nudge in the right direction if you are stuck.
- They added an "expert" difficulty that has a slower hint recharge rate and eliminates the "interactive area" sparkles.
- They reused HOGs from the main game in the bonus content. (Booooo. Lazy.)
Overall, I enjoyed the art, the story, and the adventure game elements better than "Family Secrets," and I liked the new map feature, but the HOG puzzles and mini-games weren't quite as solid, and the bonus content felt rushed and superfluous.
I would rate the game a 7.5/10

I'm going through my second playthrough now under Prince Of Darkness difficulty, and figured I'd write a bit of a review about the game itself.
First off, I would have to agree with some people who have posted "not recommended" reviews on the game for a few reasons:  The primary being that the game itself feels entirely too short for it's own good.  In comparison to LoS1 where levels are abundant and the scenery constantly changing as you progress, LoS2 seems to rehash the same areas, in a similar fashion to that of Dragon Age 2.  You spend more time running through the same areas and just gives off a feeling of redundancy throughout the course of the game.  Sure, the areas are pretty huge, but when you need to run through the same areas repeatedly to progress it's more of an annoyance than anything.
Groups of enemies seem to perfectly chain their "undodgeable" attacks to seemingly no end.  I'm up for a challenge, but when you're surrounded by a whole group of enemies it's extremtly annoying to constantly be chained from special to special.  Then again, I suppose that's how the NPCs feel so bit of karma I suppose.
The stealth sections truly are a bit annoying.  I understand that they're trying to incorporate a bit more than your run of the mill hack and slash, but there aren't multiple ways to approach them or to resolve them.  Not to mention that if you're spotted, you can pretty much expect to just restart from checkpoint; rarely is there a chance to regroup without taking massive damage.
On to the good, as this overall is a recommendation for the game.  Overall, I have to say that I did quite enjoy the storyline, and being able to play as Alucard really gave me some flashbacks to some of the greatest games in the canon.  [Spoilers] The surprise appearance of another Belmont was quite good as well!
The combat system, while much has been leveraged from the first game I quite enjoyed, even if it was a bit repetitive.  There seems to be quite a large focus on countering in this game as opposed to its predecessor, which I don't mind personally.  The new abilities are quite interesting as well, and the upgrade/mastery system keeps you trying to use new attacks against the same enemies you encounter.
All in all, I wouldn't agree with the Metascore rating as it does seem a bit low.  Sequels are always tough and when you have a title as solid as LoS1, it's hard to not play second fiddle.  Anyone who is a fan of the series I would think would like the game, and overall it's a good playthrough with the added Kleidos challenges.

Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 is a solid entry for the series, delivering an intense, visually adventure. I liked the first one and I like this one too, the game is pretty good, but not perfect. The graphics, animation, voice acting, details are amazing, storytelling is not obvious and thrilling. However even gameplay is pretty the same to the previous Lords of Shadows, but it provides us with some new interesting gameplay mechanics like an ability to become a fog or the ability to freeze opponents.

So, I actually liked it a lot more than I expected. The overall impression of it everywhere seemed to be very negative (regardless of what you think about metacritic, 58/100 doesn't exactly inspire confidence), but I ended up liking it quite a bit.
The combat is fun, even though it sometimes feel like the enemies have too many unblockacle moves, so instead of sync blocking you are dodging maybe more than I would prefer. Still, Dracula is nimble and there are enough new moves doled out every now and then to keep things interesting all the way through. Void and Chaos powers replace the light and dark magic from the first game, but more in name than function. You still get orbs from keeping your combat focus going, in order to fill out those magic meters, and one of them is more powerful and the other one is less, but heals with every hit landed. It's essentially the same system as the first LoS, but some very minor differences. Probably the biggest difference with combat is not even directly related to combat, but it's the free camera. And they handle it well, the combat camera is smart most of the time (unlike say, the camera in MGRR), and doesn't get in the way. All the finishers take too long though, I get it, you are Dracula, but suck that blood a little faster, thanks. But overall, good stuff.
Presentation is probably the most uneven thing in the entire package. Environments and locations can be gorgeous, but they can also be ♥♥♥♥ing boring. Boring sewers and industrial plants, but also gorgeous gothic (or something) architecture and fantastic vistas. Dracula seems incredibly tiny in this world too. The grand scale of everything works well in the non-industrial setting, big majectic doors and windows etc, but in the industrial setting it just looks comical. Music is the same, Araujo does some good work with some tracks, but others are just a big meeh. I remember reading an interview from him where he says that he didn't really have a lot of freedom in the end, that he had tried to approach the music from other angles but was told that it needed to be more cinematic. Some of it works, some of it doesn't. The story is really really dumb, somewhat poorly written, but it does its job of pushing you towards your next objective.
The worst part are the sections where they probably thought that they should add some variety in the gameplay design or something. Obviously the much talked stealth stuff is one part of that. They have absolutely no place in this game, they are just poor. But they are also really easy and short, so I'm not sure how the press was so badly hung up on them. Yes, they suck♥♥♥♥♥ but it takes like 2 minutes to go through. The elevator action section is dumb as well, again, not because it's hard or anything, but a timed switch to restore power in order to use an elevator is not fun. And I imagine the director had played Uncharted and told that we need something like that, heart pounding set pieces. The results are absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥ There's one section where the floor falls under you, push forward and push A for awesome. The entire train section is hot garbage, but especially the part where you dodge the roof lights or whatever. And then there's the QTE's, which you can turn off from the settings. If you played LoS, you'll probably remember that most boss fights had some easy quicktime event sequences in them, sometimes in the middle or in the end, and usually if you failed the boss would gain a little health back, rinse and repeat until you were quick and timely enough. That's still here, but if you turn them off, it will just play that whole section as if you were successful. And I very much recommend it. What does it tell you about this hot feature that they added an option to just disable them?
The game is very linear, but it has a hint of that non-linearity with all the secrets you can find. That speaks to me in some primal level and I can just get lost in the world, just running around and looking behind every corner and such to find everything. It just speaks to me man. Of course I would recommend you do this only after you get all your powers back, can't get them all without all your powers. There's also some combat challenges, and I played through couple tiers of them... but didn't bother with the rest. It gets into a little more complicated stuff than I have patience for (you can only hit this dude while he is frozen, while simultaneously killing smaller dudes every 20 seconds etc etc). For me it takes the fun out of it.
So overall, I'd say my experience with the game is positive. I paid ~20$ for it and I'd say it's worth at least that if not more.

TL;DR: Postal is best enjoyed for its unique and sickening atmosphere and themes, and not for its rather barebones gameplay.
Postal is a one of a kind game, even with contemporaries such as Hatred. Few other pieces of media have the ability to fascinate purely through subject matter and tone with little more backing it up. The closest thing I could compare Postal’s tone to is Silent Hill, with their decrepit towns, hellish imagery, and hugely uncomfortable music. The moment that set the game apart for me however was during a loading screen, one where bodies were strewn across a grime filled alley as somber yet harsh drones played in the background. This wasn’t the result of a creature, the manifestations of someone’s subconscious, or even forced self-defense. No, all of this was because of me. All the horror in Postal is created by the player and, and no other game has created such a guttural feeling of disgust in me, not even the aforementioned Silent Hill games.
It isn’t a perfect atmosphere however, and many little things broke the tension for me. Much of the Dude’s dialogue just seemed out of place and overly enthusiastic. One could argue that’s the point, because clearly the man isn’t right in the head, but for me it made everything feel less serious. Many of the NPC’s share this issue, where many of the lines are simply funny given their predicament. My personal favorite stupid line is when some people yells “PRICK!” after taking any damage, and then proceeds to stutter that same word as they’re shot repeatedly. The sentry turrets also seem out of place, as well as the napalm and rocket launcher models which just look silly.
The worst offenders of atmosphere breaking however are most of the extra levels after the Air Force Base. Most feature vibrant colors, clean streets, and some additional Dude lines that seem more akin to Postal 2. I’d actually suggest only playing the original levels because of this, as it felt odd having built up all this tension through the levels, beating the Air Force Base which really should be the final level, and then being thrown into a convenience store.
To me, the gameplay in Postal is secondary to its atmosphere. There isn’t really much to say about combat other than a few unique things it does, most notably it’s fire spreading system which is a blast to see in motion and would became a series staple. For the most part however, it’s a fairly simple isometric shooter that doesn’t really change itself up much, meaning its short length works in its favor.
Lastly, the ending: arguably the most controversial part of the game. It comes in two parts, and both are pretty much just cutscenes. The first cutscene can be interpreted a couple ways, but is honestly not too much to write home about after the initial “WTF” factor wears off. The devs themselves have said that the reason they changed the ending in Redux is because this cutscene lost its shock value. The second cutscene ties everything together though, and makes a clear statement on the themes of the game and leaves the player with plenty of questions to ask themself about.
Not many other pieces of media deal with mass shootings and the psyche of a killer, and if you really want to experience a unique and entertainingly disgusting atmosphere that has a semblance of relevance in modern society, you can’t get much better than Postal.

Soldier Front 2 is without a doubt the best F2P FPS experience i've ever come across. This game manages to not only outdo its (very) dated predecessor but also remain a viable option in todays overpopulated shooter scene. Everything from the animations, guns, and gameplay very closely mimics its big brother Call of Duty, and does a damn good job at delivering the same experience without paying every year for a new edition (map packs included). A pleasantly surprising free game, Soldier Front 2 doesn't really try anything new, but it plays well for Generic Modern FPS #174.
A mesh between CoD and CS, where you can successfully run and gun like a fool if you wish, but against a skilled player you'll lose to headshots everytime. Game modes consist of classic modes like Team Deathmatch, Sabotage (pretty much classic CS game mode), Corp Battles (clan battles) and a survival based mode vs aliens.  The game is not pay to win if you're decent at shooters, the payed guns are only marginally better than the free ones,  and there's a wide selection of perfectly viable free guns anyway (in fact one of the most popular guns is one of the default starter guns).
Cons would be that the UI feels very cluttered and confusing at first, and the game does push store items in your face often, but there's pretty much no reason to buy anything from there excpt cosmetics.

I wouldn't actually recommend this game. Let me explain.
If you're lazy, there's now unique escapes. I'll get into more detail on this later, though.
Combat is literally just hit and run. You can also block, which makes it easier, I guess. Yet again, more detail later.
There's now actual doctors, not just some guy who hangs around in the infirmary talking about how everyone who ends up there pretty much died. More detail later.
Graphics are better, I guess. You know the drill.
And you also know the drill for the hidden compartment, letting you hide contraband in your desk safely.
I guess solitary isn't as bad, but... I don't have to say it, do I?
Lockdown is definitely a plus for me, I guess. Instead of guards looking around and a timer to escape, it's now an entire team looking for you, and only a timer for the lockdown to end. More detail.
The security level is a thing I won't go into more detail with. It's perfect as it is.
The contraband system is now, contraband doesn't get dropped into the void, but instead into a little contraband desk. I won't go into more detail, it's brilliant, especially with unique escapes needing hard to find items that are contraband.
Being a fan of the original Escapists, I don't like the new and improved graphics. Wouldn't call this a bad thing, because not everyone started at the Escapists 1.
Also being a fan of the original Escapists, I do like that you can still mold keys and knock guards out with the hot chocolate. There is also a stun gun now, which I like.
The unique escapes do feel more like an easy way to just skip a prison. The Escapists 1 was fun because it didn't have unique escapes (the Jungle Compund doesn't count, that was the only way to escape) and had prison takeovers as the only other escape option.
Combat is now just easier. Combat in the Escapists 1 PC was just having the better nunchucks bought for $12 and the best plated inmate outfit. Combat in the Escapists 1 Console was similiar to the 2 combat, I guess, but didn't have the same feel.
The doctors actually made the game harder. Considering how the last ones were about how easy the game was, this may seem strange to complain, but you waste valuable time being carried by a doctor unlike just waking up at the same time you got knocked out, and inmates or guards don't wake up anymore, no, they get carried away, pretty fast considering how far they are from the infirmary.
The hidden compartment is great, I guess, but really decreases the demand for secret contraband tunnels. I mean, while we're on the subject, it seems you don't get searched really often. Beat up a couple of people for money, activate many contraband detectors, they think "no, no, he's lost all his contraband, he doesn't need a search!"
Solitary. It's easier. You should know this by now... anyways, instead of having 3 days in solitary after being found escaping or having contraband, you only have a real life minute, which you can shorten to like, 10 seconds by peeling potatoes. Plus, in the original Escapists, if you were sent to solitary, your entire escape plan would be ruined, which is pretty much a basic for any prison.
Lockdown doesn't have the feel of "you've been busted, it's time to escape, once and for all" anymore, and more like "you better hide in a tunnel or in a vent. the dogs are after you. they will find you. and they will kill you." Sure, the SWAT team is after you, but 2 people with metal batons? Only 2? I mean, the only way you can escape in a Escapists 2 lockdown is either a blocked entrance to an escape route only accessible by vents/tunnels, or by digging out.
Dogs are completely annoying and overpowered. Dogs are invincible, portable contraband detectors. They know where you are, 24/7. Went in through the vents? Too bad, they can smell through the vents. Went through a tunnel? Too bad, they can smell through a tunnel. Went in by walking? Too bad, you won't even reach where you're going. Also, have any contraband on you? Say goodbye to your contraband, they can smell anything. Nails, foil, plastic keys, you name it. Gone.
You either read the whole thing or you're illiterate and can't read. Either way, here's an overview.
The Escapists 2 focuses heavily on making the game easier, with the only real "hard" part being the doctors and dogs. There's a lot of things like solitary, lockdowns, shakedowns, escapes and contraband hiding being made easier that really makes the game way too easy. If you've never played any Escapists game, start with whatever one you'd like, but I'd recommend the original, The Escapists 1.

Before purchasing this game, I took the time to read reviews made by others, and nearly did not purchase it. I've been a fan of Sid Meier's games since the original Civilization, this and a sale price prompted me to make the acquisition of Starships. Boy, am I glad I made this purchase! It's Civ-like enough to make me happy, but at its core, Starships is a turn-based tactical combat simulator.
I've read complaints that it doesn't play like Civ - which is good since it is not a Civ-type of game. It's distantly connected to Civilization Beyond Earth (which also worked for me because it inspired me to play that game again). That connection  primarily gave the designer's a ready-made universe so they did not have to spend time creating one. The designers also made cross-game connections - so playing one, can unlock items in the other.
The Civ-like aspect comes from planets that you influence to join your federation. Think of a planet as if it were a city in a regular Civ game - it provides your basic resources; however, your resources are key to your success. The game does an excellent job of demonstrating the principle of scarcity - having one thing means not having something else. This drives your decisions regarding where to send your fleet of Starships and how to best allocate your resources. I found the simplicity of growing/managing your federation ample for this game's purpose. For those seeking a greater likeness to Civ, I can understand their disappointment, but need to point out that the game's name is Starships.
Starships is about using your fleet of starships to explore and grow your federation - frequently this involves combat. As such, Starships shines as  more of a turn-based tactical combat sim, and it is on this basis that I recommend this game.
Also, you can easily FINISH a game of Starships in one sitting - unlike most Civ games which require an investment in time to complete (at least the way I play them). This makes it perfect for killing just a little time....
If you enjoy learning through experience (i.e. trial and error) give the game a try and see what happens. The more you play it, the better your grasp on the game's mechanics. For those not interested in trial and error, I strongly recommend  reading through a guide. I found several on the Steam Community for Starships - one of which I forwarded to friends so that could take a peek at what Starships might have in store for them (Welcome to Starships: A Reference Guide by thecrazyscotsman).

There is no more boring running around. The titular house serves only as a nexus between the four distinct paintings/levels, all featuring their own new ghost story that eventually form a larger plot. What that plot is can be a good question though, since the game lacks an ending, it just stops after the last artefact. And no, the bonus chapter won’t help either, although it reveals a few interesting secrets on its own.

After playing through House of 1000 Doors - Family Secrets, I was a little concerned about how enjoyable this game was going to be.  (I wasn't even sure if I was playing them in the proper order, chronologically.)  However, this worked out perfectly.
Almost all the Interface annoyances I had with the first game were resolved by UI changes in this sequel.  (i.e. MAP feature made it feel less like I was constantly backtracking. I've played Contract Wars for some years now, I'll acknowledge Hired Ops as a different game, but it won't stop me from comparing the two.
For starters, this game is in early access to its obiously going to have a few problems. A few common ones are like internet connection, the server will throw you into an in-progress game where unlike Contract Wars, you wont be able to choose the server with the best latency to your region. This does have some serious implications for people like me who live the 'Land Down Under.' I know the devs pretty much address that they are testing their servers at the moment, but I truly hope they don't just stop there.
Another problem I've noticed is the night levels. Yes I understand that you're supposed to use the NV for them, but seriously, nighttime is so dark it really doesnt feel realistic anymore. Unless in this future world the moon was blown up by Russian/US militants, it would be useful and immersive to feature one to light up the world.
A possible future problem that most if not all competitive FPS games suffer from, is cheaters. Contract Wars sure had a lot of them. That was really the only beef I had with that game. This game will need the VAC system implemented as soon as possible, even simply as a deterrent.
This one doesn't really bother me much, but the jumping physics suck. True, it didn't really stray from the old Contract Wars mechanic, but unless your feet needed to wind up like a spring every time to jump, it isn't really realistic.
And climbing. This game needs to have a form of climbing. I dont want to keep on trying to jump onto trains in vain.
Now for some things I do like.
-The new reload pausing as your run feature feels nice, even if its there to your annoyance.
-They replaced the Tier 1 KAC with the much better M4A1. (Sorry TD :)
-Meta levels actually have more of a precence now and function as the new 'premium currency' so no more Pay2Win.
-Tactically sound and slower pace than CSGO.
-Awesome graphics.
-good, not best, gun variety.
-Realistic.
To sum up:
-Lag, needs fixing.
-Night, being more like you blackscreened.
-Possible hacking.
-Jumping sucks. (still)
-Climbing, needs to be implemented. (Even if only at select areas)
-great graphics.
-Immersive.
-Potential to surpass the original Contract Wars in terms of gameplay.
-SV98 still is awesome.
-Needs a bigger map to use the above on.
-Great game
-At $10 this game is a steal.
Totally recommend this game.

If Red Faction doesn't take place on Mars, is it really Red Faction?
I guess the "Red" in Red Faction this time comes from the obvious Communist era tones in the artwork and "for the people" storyline. Red Faction 2 doesn't take place on Mars. It doesn't have a whole lot to do with the first game at all, really, and that's okay with me. I love/hate Red Faction. I hate it because the AI was awful, the geo-mod was not entirely impressive or overly useful, and the levels were linear and sparsely decorated. It felt like a crap Half-Life. I did, however, enjoy the couple of vehicle sequences and, for some reason, feel compelled to play through the game every now and then, if just to remind myself how much it sucks.
Here's what Red Faction 2 does right; more vehicle sequences (the battle mech is particularly fun), better graphics and effects (like rain), and a more interesting story with love and betrayal. The AI still amounts to running around or standing stark still while being shot in the face. The levels are still super linear, and particularly short. Geo-mod provides some neat effects sometimes but I don't think I tore down a single building.
The biggest flaws Red Faction 2 has are one particularly painful boss fight, and the game is very short. The one boss fight takes place in a cathedral, where snipers respawn in the balconies, and zombies respawn on the ground floor, and between those two you have to find time to whittle down a human size boss's lifebar from halfway across a large room. It is not fun. And the whole game, respawns and all, took me less than three hours to complete. That's Kane & Lynch 2 short.
But, it is an improvement over Red Faction, even if that's not saying much because Red Faction is pretty awful.

The Final Boss:
[no spoiler] If I were to give one reason to play this game, it would be to challenge your gamer skills against the final boss (easy mode doesn't count!) HOLY COW BALLS, RFII has one of the hardest final bosses I have ever played against. Palms sweaty, pants full of spaghetti, and mom crying in the bathroom, I will never forget that day I had to face one of the toughest opponents in gaming history.
Other than that, this game is mediocre, probably worth it if it goes on sale for under $5.

The Good:
-Vehicle sections.
-Destructible environments.
The Bad:
-No skippable cutscenes.
-Ridiculously difficult final boss in comparison to the rest of the game's difficulty.
-Terrible voice-over/dialog.
Terrible game, shouldn't be part of a great franchise.

Let me start this off with that the most played game I have on Steam is Planetside 2 and I've had it for 3-4 years and played it on and off for long period of time. That now said, I've managed to get to 100 hours within the first month of me getting this game and am currently at the 200+ mark which is nearing itself closer to being Planetside 2 which as a gamer I've played quite a bit of. That in itself should tell you how awesome this game is.
Either way lets really start this off. Have you even wanted to play a game like minecraft but had more moving parts and gizmos that aren't just pistons or buggy/poorly implemented mods? Guess what From the Depths is what you are looking for. The resource system is different than minecraft in that you have stored resoures of a few types such as metal, natural (wooden), crystals and etc. Which can be used to craft together different types of crafts ranged from a death laser barg to even space ships with orbital ordinance, or even maybe you like fluffy sheeps that happen to swim to the enemy and may or may not swing a hammer causing massive damage like some users have made. Hell the game normally has an angry chicken flying craft with cannons and missles.
Are you creative? Well you really can't get bored with this game because the limit is how much you can think of building or if you aren't creative guess what. There is a massive sharing of things called blueprints which are other players or your own crafts. You don't need to build a good ship when someone else has already done it for you, or maybe you wanna build a better one than them!
You can play this game in so many ways its silly. You can just sit in the designer making what ever you want. Maybe you wanna face off other players which you can do in multiplayer which is still in development and comes with its slew of problems but most are minor or not even noticable. You know what I hate. Games that give me only a single player experience but let me have a useless companion follow me around or even force said uselss companion on me, guess what From the Depths doesn't do. Limit you to just having useless companions but also useless friends too! Unless you happen to be the useless one but either way you can game either by yourself or play the FULL game with a friend or even play a community made world.
The only issue this game has currently is the UI needs some work and the game can be too much for new players at the start, its a very deep game and its not gonna hold your hand too well. Anyone who gets this game, I recommend you try to make it through the first 10-20 hours of gameplay before you give up. This is around the time things click and you can start making awesome crafts. That may seem like a long time to play the game but it flew by for me and many others I've talked to about the starting of the game online with.
Oh and if you are worried about it being abandoned. The dev 'Nick Smart' does regular updates and recently expended the staff to more than just himself. He works very hard on this game and is very vocal with the community on the games own webpage. Every update seems to bring new and better candy.

Sound effects are a real letdown - when placing or removing large numbers of objects the 'holodeck' sound gets irritating, and the character's walking sounds are an incredibly obnoxious array of clanking noises as if carrying hundreds of frying pans.
Claiming new types of objects has the worst sound effect of all, and is slow, because the menu is downloaded over the internet (or at least run through a browser).
Most content in the game is downloaded from the internet, and virtually all objects display content through a browser - be prepared for loading times when interacting with things, and less-than smooth webpage loading.
Ultimately a fun concept, which holds together relatively well - lots of potential and lots of room for improvement. Not recommended now, but maybe worth a look when it's fully released.

Well, this is a pretty big dissapointment.
I first played "Fancy Pants" back in 2009 with "World 1" on
. It was my first ever flash game and I thought the game was perfect back in the day. Great controls, great music and great level design. Then "World 2" came out and it was a huge improvement over the original. Even better controls, more levels, and an actual story (well kinda). After that "World 3" came out and it was even bigger and better than "World 2". A real storyline, better level aesthetics, a brand new weapon (pencil), new challenge rooms. Overall the original trilogy was perfect and if you want to know what's the best way to experience it, go buy "Fancy Pants Adventure", it has Remixed "World 1", "World 2" and "World 3", more levels, over 130+ customizations and more modes. So why am I saying all this? Because after 5 year long hiatus we finally got "World 4" and sadly, "World 4" or "Super Fancy Pants Adventure" is just ok. It's not great, it's not bad, it's just okay...
Pro's:
- The controls are better than ever. they're much smoother and much more refined than in the previous games.
- New gimmicks like ink riding, grinding, ink shooting are actually really fun.
- New challenges are great. They're fast, they test your reflexes and most importantly - they're not boring.
Con's:
- The game is really really short. Like I beated it in 1.2 hours, how is it even possible that "World 4" is shorter than "World 3"? What did Brad say in the description of the game -- "So many levels! - 56 brand new levels of parkour platforming". More like 6 levels of platforming and 56 screen transitions. I think that is what he meant.
- Do you remember all the old enemies like spiders, mices and bats? Well say goodbye to them because they only appear for one level, after that we're introduced to the new enemies - "Ink monsters". You can no longer slide or jump at them since you'll get hurt now. Instead the only way you can kill them is with the new weapon - the pen (which permanently replaces the old pencil). Which means you have to always stop just to destroy them and clear the path which is slow and tedious.
- Where are the level themes? Back in previous games you had underground lair, islands, forests, pirate ship. In "World 4", you have only 2 level themes, and it's pirate forest and a volcano. Everything else is just a bunch of colorful platforms and blocks, like in some places it looks even more bland than "World 1". Brad also added the new layer mechanic in which you'll be jumping from one layer to another using springs and portals which sounds cool and it is. BUT sometimes (and sometimes means 90% of the time) the layers are either poorly rendered, created in a really low resolution, or have intense artifacting which makes them look really ugly.
- The soundtrack is ok. In some moments it sounded good while in other cases it sounded like something you would hear in college ads. Also, no returning music except the pirate ship theme, but really who cares?
- Where's the content, no really where is it? "20+ items"? "Fancy Pants Adventure" had 130+ items. Only hats and pants, but where are all the patterns for pants from "World 1 Remix"? Where is the weapon customization? Where's the skateboard gimmick? Where's the day/night mechanic? Where's is the remixed "World 1", "World 2" and "World 3"? Where's the multiplayer, "Fancy Box", the level editor, the hub-world like every single "Fancy Pants" game, the racing mini-game, the "Smash Bros" - like mode? Where is it?!
In the end, "Super Fancy Pants Adventure" is a good platformer, but not a good "Fancy Pants" game. I suggest you either wait for a pricedrop, or wait until Brad will add more content to it, and I sure hope he will, because this game has a lot of potential.

I loved playing the Fancy Pants games all those years ago. It was such a fun sonic-esque game, with very fluid gameplay and smooth, fully-functioning mechanics. Once Super Fancy Pants Adventure on Steam, I was pretty hyped for a while. I picked it up several days ago, and it was just as I had remembered it being. It was fun, fast, and challenging when it needed to be. Now that I've finished it, I have a bunch of stuff to talk about, so let's get right into it.
THE GOOD:
- Smooth gameplay - Everything is smooth as butter. The combat is responsive and very fun to do. The platforming/parkour is even better, being able to run and jump with little to no quirks, any mistakes that happen are on you and you alone, not the game, nor the physics.
- Level Design - Every single level in here is beautifully crafted to emphasize speed and fluidity. Most levels consist solely on platforms and curved pathways, which synergizes incredibly with the fluid movement system. The scenery itself, however, is only okay at best (in my opinion)
- Boss Fights - Honestly, I was having a hard time finding out if I should keep this as a positive, all because one specific boss seemed so out of place and not very entertaining. However, I had a ton of fun with the other bosses, the final one in particular was my favorite. So, I'll keep this as a good, rather than a meh. At least the boss I don't like can be beat quickly...
The Bad:
- The Length - Unfortunately, this is the biggest reason why I'm not recommending this game. I wasn't expecting something too long, especially considering the flash games could easily be beaten in under an hour. However, for the $10 price point that they're asking for, I'm having a hard time justifying the fact that it only takes 2 hours to beat the game. Maybe 2 and a half if you're getting every single collectible.
- The Price - Yeah, I'm kind've complaining about the price twice now, and I can already hear people saying "$10 isn't that bad, it could have been $20", and yeah, they'd be right, but I'm still having a hard time believing that $10 for 2 hours of gameplay is justifiable.
- Mechanic Introduction - So before I go into this, I should probably tack on that I haven't really played any Fancy Pants games past 2, but I have seen some gameplay on the third addition, and I can see some of the mechanics that have been brought over to this game (i.e. the actual combat instead of just jumping on things and kicking them). Top it off with all the new mechanics that were added, everything kind've fits in well. You'll get most of what you're able to do within the first or second lands, but aside from the basic stuff from the tutorials in the beginning of the game, you're not really told what you CAN do. It's only until they're arbitrarily forcing you to do a certain action to progress (and then never use that mechanic again) that they remind you that you had X ability all along.
CONCLUSION:
I wanted to like this game, and in some aspects, I definitely do. It's a really fun game to run and jump around in, and I can kick some♥♥♥♥♥here and there too. However, the game's too short. There's only such a small amount of time to get used to everything, and by the time you've done that, it's over. You don't get too much of a chance to play around with some mechanics, and there's a few that are only really used once or twice (sometimes more if you count some challenge rooms, but most of them rely on the basic movements). If there were more content, or at LEAST a level editor, I would be able to recommend this game. But where it's sitting now, it's fun, yeah, but it's not worth the money.
TL;DR:
If you don't mind the dissapointingly short 2 hour playtime, then consider this review a recommendation. If you want more bang for your buck, just get Sonic Mania or something

AdVenture Communist. When my gaze first fell upon this game, it was a euphoric feeling. "more great content streaming straight from the teat of hyper hippo." i thought to my self. But alas, T'was not the case in the slightest. early game is pretty fun and enthralling, but as the game progresses you tend to notice a bit of a misbalance. I have put a (somewhat) substantial amount of time into this game, and in my time have figured out that it would take a stupid amout of time to "finish" this game. From what I can tell, there are 2 major bottlenecks, and each one restricts progression too much on its own. The first is the Comrade system. Basically, you need comrades in order to upgrade any one thing. The problem with this, is that you need far more than what is supplied to you. after my 60ish hours of playing, i have only gotten it to 89 per second, and to really progress in this game at all, you would need thousands to tens of thousands a second. To put this in perspective, i did the math: I get 89 comrades per second, the max is somewhere around 500. At my current rate of comrade production (89 per second) it would take 13582260000000000 years to get a hospital, the top tier medicine upgrade. so yeah, needs some rebalancing. The second major bottle neck is in the weapons and medicine. In the other three categories, each different thing you buy produces more of the previous thing you bought (hives make plantations which make collectives which make communes which make farmers), making growth (somewhat) exponential. This is not the case with weapons and medicine. The only things that the upgrades you buy make is weapons and medicine respectively. also, the math in some cases makes literally no sense at all. to get a field hospial you need to spend 10,000,000 ambulances. a field hospital only gets you 1.85+10 while not even 250,000 ambulances gets you 5.92E+12, which is already over 100 times what a field hospital gets you. overall, fun game, but for it to actually be playable past a certain point, it needs a serious rebalance.
and just to let you know, i use an auto clicker that clicks 100 times a second, so its not like i'm trying to be legitimate in any way.
TLDR: decent game, but dont expect to progress very far, needs an insane amount of rebalancing to be worth investing even one tenth of the amount of time i have into it

Fantastic game!   It absolutely lived up to all of my expectations, including the DLC.  It ended, for the most part, exactly how I would have wanted.  It is sad that Mercury Steam will most likely never work with the Lords of Shadow series again, but the story is at least complete and was well done from start to finish.  What more could a fan of great story-telling ask for?
It does have some problems here and there, but if you are interested in it due to being a Lords of Shadow fan then your money will be well spent, since you are most likely here for the series' most accomplished attribute, it's lovingly crafted tale.  Otherwise, I suggest doing some more research on it, or maybe even trying the first two games (Don't forget Mirror of Fate) to see if the story grabs you.
Either way, my final opinion on this game is that it is a finely polished piece of software that has phenomenal storytelling and an extremely well implemented combat system.  It suffers slightly from some odd gameplay design choices here and there that might be a bit off-putting to some, but this game did not get the attention, nor respect, that it truly deserved.  Hopefully, Mercury Steam will craft something in the future that is not so much the "diamond in the rough" that this game, and it's predecessors, ended up being.  Maybe something with a bit more mainstream appeal, i suppose?  I hope only the best for their future after having finished the Lords of Shadow series and am tentatively awaiting news of their next project.

I'm going to try not to dissolve into a puddle of tears and hyperbole while describing my love for this game. But I flippin' love this game! First, I'll just get out of the way the fact that I waited 10 years for it to come out. I played Dreamfall when it came out on XBox and was devastated that it ended the way it did with no new development in sight. The world building was rich, I love playing as Zoe, and the story was great. Solid writing, fantastic voice acting, and a female protagonist with agency. I'm a long time PC adventure gamer, and I felt like I'd been waiting for this game all my life. I went back and played The Longest Journey and loved that too. Then I played Dreamfall again just to appreciate how well the fleshed out the world, and how aware you are of the passage of time and it's affect on both places and people. There was also always wonderful diversity in the characters, and I don't just mean the magical races. This series was hitting all the right spots for me.
When they announced the Kickstarted for Chapters, I flipped my♥♥♥♥♥♥ I couldn't back it fast enough. But of course I was on the edge of my seat, wondering if it would be worth the wait? What if I waited all this time and it was a total disappointment?
Having finished Book 3, I can say emphatically that this game is excellent. Zoe has deepened as a character. The changes that have happened in the world between games have deep impact. This game is taking on huge themes - militarization and fascism, racism, politics, revolution. But it all feels very personal as you get to know the characters living through all this. My heart has broken over the people and places that have been wiped away by the conflicts (no spoilers, but there are some deaths that happened between games that I found profoundly tragic). With all this going on, I'm delighted that the quirky, meta, snarky sense of humor that has run through this series has remained. It feels well balanced, and never takes itself too seriously, which I really enjoy. Especially when they make nods to previous PC adventure games, or lampshade a particularly obvious trope.
TL;DR if you like PC adventure games ala Monkey Island and old Sierra stuff, but you want something a little deeper and more conscious (cheesy as that sounds, I mean it) you have to check out this series. Start from the beginning and work your way through. You will be rewarded for your exploration. It's just lovely.

I like this game. It is essentially a paid (and arguably better) version of the F2P browser FPS called "Contract Wars", albeit with a better framerate and textures. If you've played that and liked it, you'll find this one just as enjoyable, even with the $9.99 price tag. However, there are a few things that need some attention in order to make this game better.
Typical FPS fare in terms of gameplay, motion, etc. However, be prepared for heavy visual and recoil kick, especially when you have no attachments on your weapon of choice. It goes for "realism" with the recoil, and truthfully I have no qualms with it.
The game also features small-medium sized maps (total of 5) with day and night variants.
Hired Ops does have a currency system. You start with a pistol and 5,000 credits, enough to buy you any of the available weapons in the first tier. You can earn these credits quite easily through gameplay. There also is an unlockable system for both attachments and the game's progression system, offering different things such as increasing armor strength, reload speed, proficiency in certain weapon types, etc. The skill tree is larger than I expected for an Early Access game.
I never experienced any frame drops that others seem to have had, after reading some of the reviews myself. Perhaps this is either a failure on the developers for optimizing for a wider range of builds, or perhaps the fault of the buyers who's setups can't handle this game's graphics. I really don't know if it is either.
Anyway, the game does look good; VERY good for an Early Access game. Nice use of lense flare, motion blur, and shadows.
The nighttime maps can either be really fun or furiously annoying, as it is, well, too damn dark to see anyone. I get it: it is in the middle of the night, but most of the time, especially on the larger maps, you'll get killed from seemingly nowhere. This is honestly really subjective, as others have told me the night maps are interesting and allows for a slower, more careful play style.
Furthermore, the amount of weapons (at the time of writing) is quite small, only offerring 2 Tiers (I think roughly 40 guns) in total. Of course, this is subject to change, as the game is in Early Access, but I found that the lack of weaponry at launch was a tad bit disappointing.
I give Hired Ops an 8/10. Perhaps I'm baised towards it after playing its counterpart Contract Wars, but I found it quite enjoyable. If you're really unsure of buying this game, play Contract Wars as a "test run", as both experiences are similar. I prefer Hired Ops for its unlocked framerate and better graphical potential when compared to its in-browser counterpart.

After giving Castlevania Lords of Shadow 1 a glowing review, it really pains me to give this a thumbs down.  I was really hopeful that this sequel would follow in its footsteps as a worthy successor. Unfortunately this game is marred by a clunky camera system, weird game mechanics that don't always work right and an irritating save/checkpoint system that punishes you heavily for failure by making you repeat the same sequences and boss fights over and over again until you get them exactly right.
By contrast, the first game's checkpoint system was much better in saving your progress (even during boss fight stages) and all the artifacts and items you picked up you kept after you got them. If you died at a particular place, you would just restart at that place with all of your previous progress saved. Not here, you're forced to proceed a great deal further in most instances in order for everything to be saved. Make a mistake and you're going all the way back to the beginning of the sequence or fight. It's just frustrating and not fun.
The story is just OK. Nothing that really draws you in and connects you to its ficitional world like the first one. The levels take place in a bizarre alternating transition between the past and present which makes the game feel like a cross between its gothic horror roots and the futuristic setting of Doom 3. In the modern levels Dracula will be operating elevators, powering modern machinery and battling mechanized bad guys that are equipped machine guns, grenade launchers and electronic counter measures, it just feels out of place. The main characters aren't as memorable nor do they stir up the same level of emotion as Lords of Shadow 1.
It's also much harder to go back to previous levels and pick up many of the artifacts you'll need to make your character strong enough to face the tougher enemies in the late game after you unlock the special powers required to get to them. There isn't an individual level selection system like the first game. Instead you have to select a previous location and then find a special room which allows you to teleport to an area of the that location where you think you might have left something behind. It takes way more time to do and just means more repetition of the same convoluted areas over and over.
I'd say it's worth picking up only on sale and only if you're a fan of the first one (having completed it) and Mirror of Fate and have an interest in the story. That's alot of ands. It's an Adventure game in the classic tradition; heavy on the story, light on the gameplay, point and click. It's got all that and for a while it's actually pretty interesting. However, there aren't really any puzzles in the game, it's more errand running to move the story along - which is fine if you like the ambiance.
One problem is the way developers sought to slow players progression. Repeatedly, the game will tell you a general goal ("get into X" or "find a Y") and then nothing. Only 30 minutes later (or after checking a FAQ) do you find that the innocuous flavor NPC on a side street ACTUALLY has a new interaction that, when used in the right place, allows you to progress. Nothing will hint that this, you're just expected to click everything again to find it.
What got me to uninstall this game though was the hamfisted moral choice-consequence system. Spoilers -- but there's a segment where you're given a choice to Torture or Blackmail a person. Despite the illusion of choice; TORTURE is considered CORRECT. If you don't torture a certain NPC, people will die and then blame you. They will then explain to you how torture is more reliable than blackmail / interrogation. (screenshot:
)
I don't care if there's supposed to be some long-haul lesson about complex morality; torture is always wrong and I can't recommend any media that argues otherwise.
