In my opinion, my favorite game ever created would have to be The Longest Journey. I believe not only did it have one of the best and intriguing stories of any video game, it was a "thinking person's" game. It was beautifully crafted, fully detailed, featured superb voice acting, and contained challenging puzzle-gameplay. TLJ not only gave us one of the coolest female heroines, April Ryan, but created an entire world to get sucked up in. Most movies getting pumped out today do not have half the creativity that TLJ did.
Dreamfall, the sequel, was an amazing game as well, though not without its faults (horrible combat system for one), that brought the loveable Zoe Castillo character into the limelight. Now we have Dreamfall Chapters, the continuation of the Zoe character arc and world.
Dreamfall Chapters is one of the best games I have played in years. I am a fan of adventure games and they seem to be taking off in episodic, choice-making formats. I have played quite a number of them, and have to say that Dreamfall Chapters is about the only game where your choices do matter and have drastic effect on the gameplay. Even though Telltale and DONTNOD have made some incredible games, Red Thread is about the only company to truly master a choice making format in my honest opinion.
As far as Dreamfall Chapters itself, there is nothing lazy about how this game is crafted. Just like The Longest Journey, Dreamfall Chapters is meticulously detailed and meaningful. As the books progress, the puzzles do go up in difficulty, but still not quite near the challenge that The Longest Journey provided.
I ultimately feel that Dreamfall Chapters provides the best aspects of both games. I can't wait for Book 4!
I can only find two cons:
1) Does this really have to end after Book 5? I think I speak for a lot of old Funcom and now Red Thread fans by saying "we want more!"
2) There is no set release date or official announcement for The Longest Journey home. It would be a dark era of gaming if TLJH does not get made, as it is what started it all and deserves a proper sequel and possible closing for April Ryan's story.
Zoë's butt gets me harder than Nirgali steel.

Chapters is certainly a logical continuation of The Longest Journey. All the effort and love that's gone into bringing the world to life would be hard to miss. The shamelessly colourful storybook artwork is as great as ever at setting the atmosphere. It seems nice to have some closure after Dreamfall's abrupt cliffhanger. I felt a slight giddyness starting the game up for the first time.
But it doesn't take long for it to get back to the old tricks. The puzzles are simple but tedious, usually taking you on pointless jogs from one edge of the map to the other, or relying on you to catch that one hint buried in the awkward and long-winded dialogue. Other times it's just about finding the exactly right sequence of messed-up dream logic so you can do the bleeding obvious. All business as usual to those who played adventure games in the 90s, but unfortunately the world has moved on and the design feels decidedly out of place with the otherwise very decent production values.
All in all, I'm not sure that I can honestly recommend buying Dreamfall Chapters unless you have a high tolerance for frustration or a positive outlook on the previous parts in the series. Maybe grab it from a sale, and take the experience as it is, and you may find yourself enjoying the good parts.

There's times that I come across a game that I just loved, but really cannot recommend to others. Usually it comes down to just one thing in the game that is a complete deal breaker. Sadly, for me, Super Fancy Pants Adventure falls under that category.
So, why the red, angry thumbs down? Quite simply, it comes down to game length. Yes, I had a lot of fun with the game; it played well, for the most part, and I can see a lot of love was given to the title. However, there just isn't much content there. I beat two bosses within the first 30 minutes of the game, which made me wonder just how much I had left. Based on what others have said, and a bit of digging on my part, I'm pretty much through the campaign already at the 77 minute mark. Granted, that's not finding all the secrets and unlocking all of the skills. So there's still a couple of hours left, but even four hours isn't that much for this price range. Unless you're really into the Fancy Pants series itself, it's just not worth it at this point.
Perhaps, if the promised additional content comes out then it will be worth picking up, or when it's on sale. But, but it stands right now... I just don't fancy it.

From the Depths feels to me like Kerbal Space Program meets Mount and Blade. Like KSP, you have super-creative, nearly limitless vehicle design and physics-based gameplay. Like M&B, there are huge epic battles and a sandbox-style campaign where you can conquer your enemies and take over their holdings and such.
You can make motorboats, sailboats, planes, tanks, spaceships, submarines, aircraft carriers, helicopters, towers, fortresses, or whatever you want. You can arm them with infrared missiles, laser guided missiles, railguns, explosive shells, old-school cannons, or even a ram. And then you can send them out to fight enemies and see how they perform.
This is in a great state for early access. I consider it a totally complete game experience already. It's a little rough around the edges and there are some skeletal features not quite developed yet, but it is definitely continuing to be developed and new stuff is released all the time.
The Good:

Super Fancy Pants Adventure is a great experience for gamers who love clean and rewarding platforming that doesn't take itself too seriously. Challenges that reward you with cosmetics to make your pants as fancy as ever populate almost every level with challenges that will test your platforming skills. The story is a little lacking, but Mario has never been critiqued on his stories in games so it can be overlooked here. If you ever played the earlier iterations of The Fancy Pants games, or are new to the series, I would definitely recommend picking this game up!

But, hello. It's Fancy Pants. What more is there to say?

First off, all these people ranting about te game being unplayable and stuff, talking about how great their pc is, lower your settings.

The game is playable at medium settings even on a gaming rig a few years old.

Look at Verdun, also an unity game, in the beginning i allways run lower graphics and fps, nowadays the game looks amazing and runs pretty sweet.
First the good stuff:
-Nice graphics and effects, of course there are games with way better graphics, but for the type of  game these are pretty good.
-Gameplay, it's fun, the way it plays is just right and the extra options they put in are an nice addition.
Don't expect revolutionairy changes from Contract Wars, it's basicly the same game where you have to pay for now.
-Customization, there is a lot to unlock and customize, frome your weapons to skills to your avatar.
I like that you can change everything, making an game your own is something i allways enjoy.
-Damage system, at first you are gonna hate it... Really, you are gonna be raging about how you get killed over and over again and you never see those guys.
After a while you'll find out how to play this game and that is where the fun starts, you can drop enemies pretty fast.
Now the stuff that is mediocre or needs improvement:
-Controls, they are clunky, very clunky, i was used to this because i played Contract Wars before.
But for the stand alone they need to fix this and make it a lot tighter. Also inputs are not registered regularly, which means dying sometimes bebause you wanted to bring up your sights and it register giving the enemy time to spot and shoot you.
-Sound, not bad but shallow, there is little immersion, tho sound direction is pretty good like footsteps and such.
-Level design, invisible walls and getting stuck on nothing is common. Although this could be an Unity thing as other Unity shoots have the same problem.
The bad:
-too few maps, especially with team deathmatch, whicht is my favorite, there is only 1 map in TDM which has 2 versions: day and night.
This needs to change fast! Otherwise i forsee a lot of people stopping or refunding Hired Ops.
-Optimization, needs not more explanation
-no server browser of friend system, if they want people to enjoy the game more they need to let them play with friends.
I'll probably think of more things along the way and i will add those when i come across them.
For now, i do recommend this game, because i do thing the developer will put a lot of work in the issues and make more content.
See it as an investment for an game that will become good and enjoyable in the next few months.

What is Anarchy Arcade? Well to put it simply it's a modified Source Engine virtual desktop that allows you to create and simulate your own arcade or theatre experience using virtually any kind of media.
There are 8 (as of this writing) maps which you can unlock and play, each with their own distinct taste where you can build your own custom arcade using a large variety of cabinets and a few props. There is a slight meta-game in unlocking new maps, cabinets, and props through various simple means.
You can link any media on your PC or on the internet, and use images and videos to provide cabinet marquees and screen images. A convenient website allows you look up most games and movies and automatically downloads images and information for all but the most obscure or indie titles. Steam games are automatically loaded into your library making it easy to place them as arcade cabinets in-game.
While no-doubt the concept of a virtual desktop may be lost on some, there is a very pleasing sensibility of being able to craft your own arcade from your PC games and arrange them by whatever categorization you choose, and even give them fitting cabinets (racing cabinets for racing sims, shooting cabinets for FPS, etc.) The props while currently limited do allow you to spice up the maps a bit with some creative planning.
In addition to arcade cabinets you can also spawn TVs, Photo frames, CDs, and Tablets to display your movie, tv, or music collection, or hotlink a video from youtube or other streaming sites.
Multiplayer is an interesting feature but only works well if you hotlink all media from the internet, otherwise a lot of "broken link" screens will be displayed, but it is a fun way to have a little youtube field trip with your friends.
For people like me whose media library of games and movies grows rather large, a program like this is a nice visual browser to help you pick a good game or movie to watch that you might otherwise skip over in a long list.
At any rate, the asking price can't be beat, it's definitely a fun diversion! 8/10

so this definitely an interesting game, and its surprisingly functional, especially for early access.
first and foremost, if you enjoy collecting things, and displaying things, and you always felt that digital copies of things made them harder if not impossible to display, like you would physical games in their box, then this program should peak your interest.
it's built off the Source engine and is compatible with most things related to the source engine. adding new maps, models and other addons is easy enough as it is, just drop the zip filein the addon folder in the anarchy arcade directory, and AA does the rest when you boot it up.
you can also set it up to work with tf2, counter strike, and most other source games using the main menu. thanks to this, i was able to turn cs_office into my own personal arcade.
thats probably the most important feature in this game. is the fact that it gives you the ability to make your own "Namco museum" style arcade, it's the closest thing to giving the media on your hard drive it's own physical form.
i have my NES and SNES games mixed in with my steam games, all with their own unique graphics on every cabinet, and theres plenty of cabinets to choose from, especially once you start unlocking some, (although i think the unlocking system is pointless as it stands now, besides being a loose tutorial).
it's easy to use your own graphics, or graphics from the internet to decorate your cabinets and your chosen environment.
the video tutorials which can be watched in game, show you how easy it is to customize everything, and get youtube videos working as attractors to your cabinets.
now here's what's wrong with this game.
it's not much of a game.
at least not yet.
multiplayer is somewhat pointless, when it takes about an hour to download a server for the first time, and in order to use any of their content, you'd have to have the same content. which i can understand the reason for this, but it does make it a little boring if you're trying to join any old server off the steam browser, (which there aren't many of yet.) youll just end up looking at youtube videos, and looking around at all the neat stuff in their arcade, not likely playing too much of it though. but, i could see this still being pretty cool between two or three friends who share a lot of the same games or content. and i imagine there's still plenty of things to be added, and there will probably be more things to do server side. like i'm sure the source engine could support some faux mechanical games like ski-ball, or air hockey.
also, even though it's on the source engine, they took out most of the typical environment editing tools, like the phys gun, now i know this isn't trying to be a garry's mod clone, but i sure would like a way to clean up most of the props and filing cabinets laying around in my cs_office arcade.

The port itself, when it runs, runs well with the right mods (4K texture support, stable FPS fix, cel shading outlines), but when it works, it works. The problem is the game will work fine for the first 10 or so hours, and after that, it will refuse to load. I've tried uninstalling it and reinstalling it, verifying cache integrity, and it won't work. I don't recommend this to anyone, thank goodness I only spent 5 bucks on it when it was 75% off, no way would I recommend paying full price for this rushed port.
Edit: I figured out the source of the problem, the game can be very finnicky about how admin rights are used (in the properties settings), and uninstalling and reinstalling the TOS Fix gets around it.  Keeping a close eye, but yeah. Updating it to barely "recommended" for now.

1997 was one heck of a year, we had everything from the sequel to a major arcade game (rampage, and its sequel rampage world tour) epic tales that took our emotions and ate up time like Final Fantasy 7, and even galactic adventures as we try to uncover every nook and cranny in Starfox 64. But, and make no mistake, Postal deffinately made it mark among these other big titles from 1997
Whether or not the game has held up graphically (that can be up to debate and vary from person to person) what makes the game wonderous is that, despite being morbid, its crazy, off the wall mindless fun, and not only did it set standards for other twin stick shooters or bring the genre into the spotlight, but its controversy (both understandable but a bit overreactive imo) showed that your game doesn't have to be "normal" to be fun, don't get me wrong, the game is grim, but I have a feeling if it weren't for Postal, games like Hotline Miami or Dead Space wouldn't be around, Postal essentially "broke the barrier" about how far you can push the envelope with grim concepts or horror games, despite Postal not being a horror game in itself
The thing that makes me most happy however is that Running with Scissors (RWS for short) is very in touch with their community, and you know a game company cares when they go as far as to make an update to a game from over 20 years ago. The better controls are wonderous and make it much less like a tank simulator, and it makes the original more accessible for those that want to experience the "OG" game
It also adds the Japanese exclusive areas as playable bonuses, which harness back to the "expansion pack" days and extend replay value
Yes, Postal Redux is out, and it does have online and better graphics and multiplayer, but just as how FF7 is getting a remake, that doesn't degrade the original one bit or the fans liking to Final Fantasy 7, despite it not aging well. The same approach can be "added" to Postal 1
In short, Postal one might be a step back, but this review isn't built on nostalgia (as I was born in 1996) its more a reason why you should get the game, because of its significance, fixes, care RWS puts into it to this day, and because of its impact. Does it have problems, yes, is it the best game ever or for everyone? no. But what it is is one of the games that turned gaming into what it is today
NOTE/EDIT-RWS, if you read this, PLZ add the areas from the Russian  postal game/postal expansion or whatever it was, I would strongly enjoy that extra content and I think it would be an awesome way to expand this old game and add replay value

This game is almost the perfect balance of right and wrong game design.
The Good: The hack and slash gameplay is incredibly fun. The leveling system for your weapons actually requires you to try out different combos in order to max out and get points to make the weapon stronger, which encourages trying new attack patterns and not using the same, one effective combo over and over again (*cough* God of War *cough*). The character models are very detailed and the voice acting is pretty spot on. Not to mention the level design is absolutely gorgeous when you're in the castle. The bosses have memorable designs and battles. And I loved the open world to explore that wasn't of the MetroidVania design.
The Bad: Despite the game throwing hordes of different looking enemies at you, they oddly enough don't feel too varied. The game constantly shifts back and forth betwen the modern city evironment and Dracula's castle, but it feels kinda hectic and you almost never do anything in the city; Kinda like they just didn't have much planned out for it. The story is actually pretty awful and does an almost complete nose dive in the last hour or so and ends with one of the weakest plot resolutions I think I've seen in a long time, even though everything up to that point in the writing feels pretty sturdy; Almost as if the writer just stopped caring when the game was almost finished. And the stealth sections are absolutely terrible. They're the kind where you only have ONE way to go about getting through each section and it never changes EVER. The game designed one specific enemy for you to encounter during this sections which kill you easily. This is explained by Zobek saying you're too weak to fight them. If you're familiar with old vampire lore, you know they can take different animal shapes, typically being of the night time variety (wolves, bats, etc.) but the game only lets you change into one animal, being rats. But both these points really fall through at the end when you're pretty much a full strength Dracula and you're still having to sneak past these things disguised as rats.
I don't really know if I'd recomend this or not. I mean, I did enjoy the game for the most part. But if you're wanting to play this because you enjoyed the last one as I did and really wanted to see how things would end for Gabriel, all I can say is, without giving any spoilers, I couldn't have felt like I got a bigger slap in the face. But if you don't care about the story and want to play a beautiful game with some of the best hack and slash I've seen in a while, I say try.

I played the first Lords of Shadow and I enjoyed it. As for this one, I would say it's better in some areas and worse in others.
COMBAT: Compared to the first, it feels like they really smoothed out the combat in terms of how you move around and perform moves. some difficulties become clearer when it comes to one mechanic though: the way some enemies block in this game. When some enemies are blocking, they stop your combo and deflect your attack and zero damage is done. This can get really annoying when there are multiple enemies and you are attacking one that is open, but the one right next to the first is blocking. it will stop your combo. This makes engagements with multiple blocking enemies really annoying unless you are really good with your chaos energy (it's like the shadow energy from the first game and it breaks through shield and armor). Multiple skeletons are the most annoying thing in this game... That said, thankfully those kinds of enemies don't show up terribly often, and combat can still be very fun now that it's smoothed out.
STORY: Sadly, I would have to say the story in this game is inferior to the first overall. There is no longer an opening narration to each stage like their was in the first because of the way they made the map somewhat open world (I'll get into that further down). There are also seems to be less moments of significant plot progression throughout the game; a lot of times it feels as if you go a great distance just to get a small snippet of story. That said, one of the things that brought me back toward liking the game more were the story moments (they pick up more once you get a bit further) when you see the way Gabriel changes based on his interaction with the other characters. Some of them were very moving. Still, overall there just doesn't seem to be as much story as there was in the first game, and for Patrick Stewart in particular, it almost seems like a waste of his talent.
VISUALS: For the most part, I'm going to say that this game's visuals are gorgeous. Very pretty and detailed environments. Not a lot of more vibrant environments like the first game, but they are still very detailed and pretty, especially when the game's graphics are turned up. However, i did say "for the most part" because some of the more industrial areas that you explore in the game, particularly the areas with a lot of pipes and wires going along the walls and cielings, are very dull and start to feel repetitive really quickly.
MAP SYSTEM: I think they had a good idea when they started this game to give it a more open world feel, but ultimately the traveling around the map gets very tedious, especially when you are backtracking to find all the hidden upgrades, and again in the more industrial areas, it becomes easy to get lost and start traveling in circles when you are looking for certain areas.
OVERALL I would say Lords of Shadow 2 is a decent game that you will enjoy for its beauty and decent combat system if you have the patience for the map and sometimes tedious battles with annoying enemies, but I would buy it when the price lowers. Also, if you have a choice, play the first Lords of Shadow before you play the second, it will make your experience with the second. The story will of course make more sense and be more enjoyable.

Out of all the vehicle building games around I played a lot of (Space Engineers, Empyirion Galactic Survival, Starmade) I have to say, this one is my favorite.
You can do so much!
At the time I wrote this review, you could do: Ships, Hydrofoils, Hovercrafts(Well, technically. But there's no hovercraft skirt parts right now, just thrusters and propellers), Submarines(those are a bit trickier to get working AI wise), Aircrafts, Airships, Spacecrafts, Helicopters(Those are tricky to make too), and they just added land vehicles(Still rough around the edges, and not very usable in combat, but some fun can be had with those already).
Or, you can get creative and just abuse the physic engine to make weird contraptions :B
The game relies mainly on AI to control the vehicles/structures you build in the game. The AI is still a bit wonky, especially path finding and collision avoidance, but its possible to minimize the problems using long range weapons and spreading your ships around in formations. However, it'll always find a way to use whatever you give it..
Another nice thing is that, your creation can be controlled in battle using a strategic map view, which makes things much easier.
Manual controls are available, but, right now they're very limited, convoluted, and not very practical for anything that's more than a simple basic ship. And even then, there's some weirdness with it. However, I'm pretty sure the devs are definitely going to fix those in a way or another before release.
The build mode is probably one of my favorite part of this game. I'm talking about Keyboard mode. Its really efficient and handy most of the time. Most people seems to say it has a high learning curve, but personally I figure it out under 2 hours, after watching the video tutorial. And I usually have issues with different control schemes in games. (Actually, the vehicle steering controls are more confusing than this tbh)
Sure its a bit intimidating at first, but try messing around with it, not building anything serious. Your first ship will probably be a complete piece of junk that keeps sinking on its own, or capsizing but try watching getting started tutorial videos by Irelan gaming for example, you'll understand a lot better how to make things work. Or you can also just spawn ships/vehicles from the campaign and take them apart and see how they managed to make them float/fly/etc and work.
One thing I love particularly here is the way you can customize almost every system you build with attachements and extensions. Nearly all systems are multi-blocks. And not just in a quantitative way, like Starmade for example(AKA more blocks == more powerful) Building large systems without powerful enough support systems to back them up will yield a pretty innefective system. It'll still work, but you could do better use of your space.
For instance, you can build a huge engine, but it'll drink so much fuel at mid and low RPMs compared to several smaller engines that turn on and off to meet demands that you'll get a very fuel hungry design with a very weak spot. And well, there's also overheating to take into account, but its pretty manageable, even though radiators are pretty shoddy right now.
Of course, you can do that with way more things than just engines! Weapons systems, propellers, etc.. And probably more in the future. You can build canons from the magazine to the tip of the barrels. You assemble each parts together to get the best out of the space you have, while making sure a single shell won't find a way to hit your magazines and blow everything up! And you can customize your shells, build gauss canons, add timed/proximity detonation and a lot more!
The recent weapon and armor rebalance did a pretty solid job at balancing out the game. AKA you can't sink a big floating metal castle ship armored with 2 to 5m of armor, with an army of tiny ships with 20mm chainloaded AP guns anymore :P
Some things are still a bit overpowered though, and some things definitely need some work. Namely UI, engine and power mechanics, shields, player weapons, land vehicles, space vehicles and the physics involved with going to space.
But, from what the devs teased, there's a lot of great improvements coming soon. And even in this state, the game is a ton of fun. Playing the campaign and designing your ships, or refitting any enemy ships you manage to capture, sending massive fleets against an enemy's forces is already tons of fun IMO.
The devs are overall doing amazing work with this game! They listen to feedback, keeps asking questions and mentioning what they're working on in the forums, and release patches and content regularly. (During early access at least)

From the Depths is a physics based sandbox game that has taken up a ton of my time. On the surface it looks like another one of those Minecraft clones we all see floating about but with boats. It's a block building game, right? There are tons of those out there.
But FtD is different. This game is quite complex and in-depth. So much so that I am glad I got in when I did way back when because with all the new features and complexity that have been added I'm not sure I would've enjoyed it as much. That is this game's biggest downside. The learning curve is quite steep. I have over 500 hours in this game and I still learn a thing or two every now and then.
The only thing limiting what you can build, for the most part, is your imagination. If you want to build a four-legged Godzilla that fires missiles from its claws and lasers from its eyes, you can. And you are not limited to just sea based vessels despite the name. Planes, spacecraft, tanks, and submarines are all possible and viable.
The developer is hard at work at this game and has been ever since I started playing. The amount of updates and the rate that they come out at is more than satisfactory. It's not the fastest updating game, but this is not a title you have to worry about the developer walking away from.
All in all, FtD is a very fun game with literally hundreds of hours of potential. My library of games on Steam is not insubstantial and includes more than a few AAA titles, yet this is the game I've put the most hours in to. It's very easy to sit down, start building a ship, and then look up and three hours have passed. So if you've always wanted to build, sail, and fight a vehicle of war in a fairly well balanced, physics based sandbox, this is the game for you!

This is a good game. It is a adventure (not exactly the old point and click) in a 3d environment. It presents a great story (so far I have played 3 of5 episodes) and follows the events of the last game however I do think that the gameplay itself could be better.
Graphics 7.5/10 - Do not get me wrong, these are very good graphics however they are not truly optimized. In a 270x even if it does not stay at 99% usage, I have to disable anti-aliasing to get over 30 fps. Using far higher settings I can get 45-50 fps in Mordor with the same hardware. There are also strange lighting effects with weird results. If the graphics in this game were optimized, I would have given it one more point.
Sound 8.5/10 - The music is good and there are voiceover gems . Shitbot is hillarious.
Story 10/10 - I love the story and its intrigue. Lots of unexplained misteries. True choices and consequences (better than telltale).
Gameplay 7/10 - Although I love the story, sometimes I wonder why the developers opted to construct the gameplay the way they did. It feels awkard sometimes. Some tasks are just random and almost no clue is given. Navigating on the open world is tedious and there is a lot of backtracking. You do not carry a map, which is only available in selected places.
Overall 8.5/10 - If you enjoy adventures, liked the The Longest Journey, or like a great mistery story, I recommend this game to you. It is a very good game indeed. A few of the design choices are awkard however they do not take away the charm the story offers.

This game is similar to those virtual reality arcade games from the late 90's: horrible, sticky controls, graphics all over the spectrum, and a game design that won't let you escape.
When I bought this game in febuary of 2015, the reviews praised this game, and there was not one downvote on the whole site.
I was aprehensive at the Disney Logo appearing upon booting up the game, because they did a very good job of not letting that slip on the store page.
it just went downhill from there.
the game immidiately throws you into a tutorial without further explination. as it teaches you to drive, it rattles off the game's interpretation on a tired, cliche plot. (Smash T.V , anyone?)
an additional note; the game's default key mapping uses the arrow keys, which i find horrid. not only that, but it also disables the mouse. good luck learning how to navigate the 80 billion menus with your puny little arrow keys.
anyway, so it takes you around the track at least twice. my indifinitiveness is based on the fact that i did not complete the tutorial. the game called for a key i did not have access to, and so i had to abort the tutorial. good thing you CAN NEVER GO BACK TO IT AGAIN.
So, once I left the tutorial, I was greeted with a menu that is cut-and-pasted out of Ridge Racer. Now, I dont know which came out first, but considering the impression R Racer had left on me, my confidince in the game was dropping like Seattle's Space Needle in level 2. But I'm getting ahead of myself.
The game comes with this 'revolutionary' autosave feature, that can identify when something has changed or not. not very well, i might add. the autosave means that you get 0 feedback from the menus, which resulted in me having to restart the first race 4 times to get my key mapping saved.
when you enter the race (after 4 or 5 more menus, at least), you get a few vehicle options. a muscle car with poor acceleration, a truck with poor acceleration, or a lamborghini bootleg thats faster than hell but is made out of balsa wood. you can guerentee getting destroyed at least 3 times on the first lap.
as soon as you start the race (two more menus later), something becomes painfully obvious. three-second cutscenes are the latest, greatest thing (or thats what the developers thought). This game has these tiny cut scenes everywhere, and they rapidly begin to get old. but thats not the irritating thing. You cant skip these Random-camera-angle anthologies. instead, pushing 'enter' or 'space' will bring up the pause menu. that means instead of skipping some pointless Replay, you may restart the race, or even exit to the main menu unintentionally.
So you say to yourself; "ok. i can put up with annoying game design. but how is the control?"
think of it this way:
every car is a mercedes
If you have never driven a mercedes, all i am saying is the car control is as floaty as a cheap balloon puppy from a B- list clown. you slide all over the place when you drive, so much so that its actually a mechanic. I've been fascinated with space ever since I was a young kid reading astronomy books about quasars and black holes. Even the celestial bodies in our tiny corner of the universe invite mystery and awe. Are there other species? Other dimensions?
Starbound holds out the promise of space exploration, but never quite delivers. It is hindered by stale design, poor combat, and a linear story that feels forced rather than inspired.
Everything in the game feels derivative rather than creative. All the playable races come across as genetic cousins of humanity, rather than something truly alien. Even on the “alien” worlds you’re treated to prosaic forms such as trees with eyeballs, like some young child’s Halloween costume with the occasional tentacle stapled on.
Perhaps I was unlucky, but the procedural generation of worlds had me arriving at the same series of structures time and again. There’s no variety. You begin to see the same templates too quickly, and that drains the mystery. The star map might go on forever, but you feel no desire to click a distant star. Exploring the Starbound universe feels like exploring the polka dotted wallpaper of a 1970’s diner.
Similarly, much of the story involved scanning objects from various races over and over again. It didn’t matter if you had scanned those items before you received a mission—you had to go through each race’s individual artifacts again, often traveling to locations you’ve already been to just to pass the scanner over some tapestry or book on a planet you’d already fully explored.
Combat is tedious. I’m less sympathetic to complaints about weapon selection—every game with a large variety of weapons eventually reduces to a handful that are best in class or superior for particular zones or battles—but once I found the highest tier rocket launcher, I never looked back. Two or three shots on any of the ubiquitous bunny-cantaloupe-pellet-monsters, and they were dead.
NPCs are shells with no depth, either standing around or offering fetch quests of dubious value. True, Terraria’s simplistic, understated style operated in a somewhat similar fashion, but it still managed characterization through clever naming and useful, persistent NPCs.
This ties into base building. In a game like Terraria, you feel some measure of attachment to the NPCs, and building a base that houses them is rewarding on both aesthetic and practical grounds. You could theme housing to match a character’s background and interests. In Starbound, the few times I did start to build a base, I wondered what the point of it all was. Why not just use the player’s starship instead? Though perhaps here I betray a desire for the functional over the aesthetic.
I’ve also had a recurring graphical error where something like half my screen renders slower than the other. It makes the game difficult to play—more so that my eyes begin to hurt than interfering with what little challenge the enemies offer. Tinkering with vertical sync, resolution, refresh rates, etc., haven’t resolved it, and it seems like other players deal with the same issue. It wasn’t a deal-breaker for me, but it almost was, and I can certainly imagine it would be for some people.
I think on what this game could have been, and so it is with some reluctance that I must give a negative rating.

This game is extremely well designed with regard to longevity of playability. Reading other reviews shows me that people are generally missing the point of the way the game is set up. The upgrades available for your first three categories of resources are obtainable simply by generating enough of the preceding upgrade, and the last two resource categories' upgrades are obtained by unlocking daily rewards that add to the resources or upgrades of which you've already obtained at least one. The first few hours of play are clicking like mad to generate enough resources to begin passively generating them, but following that, patience is required. Daily rewards are offered for clicking the resource buttons, which is where in my opinion the genius lies. You play for a few minutes a day, stacking your daily rewards that advance your game state. The potential exists to play endlessly.
Initially I was against the idea of the comrades limiting how quickly you can advance, as it limited how much I could actually play at a given time and it was completely contrary to the previous iteration of the game. However, I found that the comrades are a key ingredient in devising strategy, as in what expenditure would be the most time efficient and profitable. The daily rewards include a large fraction of any resource of which you have at least one, meaning that if you save your comrades rather than spend them, you could multiply them significantly with a bit of luck. That also goes for the upgrades of your weapons and medicine: lose a bit of resource generation by spending them for upgrades in return for the ability to raise the growth ceiling. Of course, you may not get the multiplier in the daily rewards for that particular resource or upgrade, so it may just be time wasted in that your stockpiled resources aren't generating you more. It's a perfect risk-versus-reward model.
My criticisms lie exclusively with the Experiments tab. The math for the State multipliers is questionable, as the more expensive upgrades are less efficient. It sort of feels like a trap for the less scrutinous players. And the math for the auto clicker upgrade is simply incorrect, if the visual flashes of the clicker upgrade bar are a proper indication of an increase in your resource pool. By spending 250 scientists (10 purchases of the auto clicker), your clicker upgrade bar should be flickering about 100 times a second. My experience in game has not reflected this.
To those players expecting the sequel of AdVenture Capitalist to be a flashy new clone of the original, it is not. They're different games with different growth structures, play styles, and strategies. AdCap's strategy was significantly more straight forward: Buy whatever you can as soon as you can. Stockpiled money is wasted money. AdCom has an entirely different philosophy. It's still laden with the humor of Hyper Hippo, which makes the game a very flavorful and enjoyable experience when you hit milestones.
Overall I'd give the game in its current state about 8.5/10, points deducted for general lack of clarity and unintuitiveness of the experiments tab and what I perceive to be mistakes therein.

Please disregard the "thumbs down" for now. I don't mean it so harshly. I'm sorry ToS, forgive me. :(
So I only recommend this game if you really like JRPGs, have played every quality JRPG out there, and you must play something else to hold you over until some other, higher-quality JRPG comes out. This game has an average story, with almost entirely bland characters, a dated mechanics and gameplay, and a decent soundtrack. It's by no means terrible. I've encountered no glitches and I had fun during my 100ish hours playthrough+post-game (I played this on gamecube console a year ago). But I wanted to wait a while before I wrote a review. I've reflected on my time invested in ToS. I've also played a bit of Tales of Berseria, and I have changed my stance on this game from "an above-average JRPG, but nothing too special" to "Yeah, I mean, it's alright, certainly nothing special. I just think there are like, I don't know, maybefifty other things that would be more fulfilling than playing ToS. Want to experience a great story? Read Infinite Jest or The Metamorphosis,  play Undertale or Xenoblade Chronicles, or watch Your Lie in April. Want a fun experience? Watch Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood,  Made in Abyss, or Assassination Classroom or read Infinite Jest. Want to experience aesthetically pleasing art? Read Lolita or play Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons or Journey.
Just a quick note on the story, I gagged at how poorly written an executed this story is. I burst out laughing at how blatent the foreshadowing is, and how poorly developed the themes of friendship are. Antagonists and enemies, with the exception of Kratos (see, I said spoilers) and Mithos are all just unambiguously bad.The one part I will praise is how ToS deals with discrimination.
My point is ToS is is no way bad. Yet it fails to justify the 60-80+ hour investment. It's mediocre in terms of fun, story, or aestetic appeal. In fact, it's just another  "meh" JRPG. There is an abundance of other media that would so what ToS does better, either in terms of the components of the story (art, music, gameplay, etc.), or as a whole. Xenoblade Chronicles is a better game in every aspect.

Sid Meier's Starships (SMS) is NOT Civ-in-Space, as many people hoped, but rather, it's as if "Heroes of Might and Magic" (HOMM) had a baby with "Strange Adventures in Infinite Space" and transplanted into Sid Meier's CIV: Beyond Earth universe. It somewhat resembles the Civ Series in that it involves growing star systems, managing resources, and has multiple victory conditions including tech, diplomancy, population, and so on, but all the parameters are either preset or simplified into "levels" rather than micro-management choices that delighted Civ fans. And rather than building as many units as you want, you have to make do with a single fleet (which can be a swarm of smaller ships, or a few uber powerful ones) that you must continually upgrade as needed. As a result, it's a bit of "neither fish nor fowl". It's not as complex as Civilization series (certainly not that this price point) yet it's deeper than most games at this price level.
SMS limits you to a single fleet, which started at 2 corvettes, but as you continued to upgrade them they became larger, stronger, more heavily armed, more heavily shielded and armored, faster, better sensors and/or stealth, even more fighter bays. You can also add ships if you can afford to do so. Prices go up as component ratings go up. And given the various fields you can upgrade, you can customize the ships to fit almost any strategy. Enjoy hit and run? Long range torpedo attack under stealth? Long range laser bombardment? Sending fighters to pick apart the enemy? You can do it in this game.
SMS starts you off with one world, and as you move your fleet you will discover more systems, each of which will have a mission for you. Could be as simple as fleet action (where you need to destroy the other fleet) to hold on for five turns, to escape in 5 turns, and so on. Each world also produce resources (energy, food, metal, science, etc.) which can then be spent on planet upgrades, ship upgrades, research, and so on. Each planet upgrade, much like the city structures in Civ, have tangible production benefits. Perform enough missions at a system and you can pull that planet into your sphere of influence.
SMS lets you interact with other political entities as you find them, and they, much like civilizations in Civ, will greet, threaten, cajole, sign treaties, and more.
SMS lets you setup various map conditions from tiny to huge in size, different starting positions and tech levels, and more. Even the win condition can vary, as you can go for domination, or get wonders, science, diplomacy, and other victories.
You can only have one fleet, whcih is why this game drew a comparison with the Heroes of Might and Magic (HOMM) series, where the hero with his stack of creatures move around the map, to various action points on the map to do combat with either defenders of a castle or other important locations. As one conquers each castle one also needs to spend $$$ on the castle as improvements, much like in SMS one must buy planetary population or planetary improvements.
If there's combat, then your units will do combat on a hex-map of the system where there are various wormholes, asteroids (small and large), planets, and other structures, as your ship(s) will fire lasers, plasma cannons, and/or torpedoes at the enemy ships, as well as send out fighter wings to conducting harassing or direct attacks. Whoever left standing is the winner, but depending on damage suffered it can be a pyrrhic victory. The idea generally is put yourself where your fleet can concentrate fire on one enemy ship while staying out of range or firing arc of others by hiding behind asteroids and/or planets.
Graphics are "fine", as it's sci-fi-y look but quite clear and concise. The map scrolling takes a little getting useto as there is no free rotation (there is, but it snaps back into place as you release the mouse) and there is no edge scroll or keyboard scroll which surprised me somewhat. OTOH, the ships, the protagonist of the game, are interesting as everything you add has an immediate visual effect. Ships get longer, bulkier, with visible weapons and other modules added, and what was a wimpy corvette will eventually morph into a full battleship, and you'll visually see the differences.
All in all, SMS is NOT Civ-in-Space, though it has a similar feel, but it's far more related to HOMM or Infinite Space series than Civ. As long as you keep that in mind, enjoy the strategy-lite game.

Pros:
- Extremely smooth platforming! I mean it.
- The combat system is pretty good, with Fancy Pants man being able to stomp and slide through enemies with his own platforming abilities before finishing them off with a selection of his pencil attacks.
- The customisation is great, with the player being able to choose a multitude of pants and hats to wear
- Throughout the game the player recieves upgrades to his pencil, first upgrading it to a fountain pen, then to the ability to use new attacks like dashing, spinning around like a buzz saw, and shooting ink from it like a machine gun among others.
- The art style is very unique. It may looks bland, but it fits in with the whole theme of the game being set in a cartoon world.
- The bosses require thinking in order to defeat them, unlike just running around slicing at their faces.
- There are a ton of challenges in the game that start out relatively simple, but near the end get HARD. Not just from the amount of enemies, but in the changes in direction and speed you need to make, sometimes in mid air, and the reflexes you need. They are also pretty hard to find and get to, meaning you need to explore every part of the world and leave no stone unturned!
- Great music that never gets boring! I especially liked the music in Squiggleville Plains.
- The developer spends a lot of time squashing out the bugs in recent updates!
Cons:
- Short. Like really, really short. The game is about 1-2 hours long, and some of the levels are about an entire screen long. Plus, at the end of the final boss fight, (SPOILER ALERT), you're given a "To be continued..." with not even anything to answer why you've been fighting those ink blob thingos the whole time. I'm hoping that the developer Brad Borne is going to add the rest of the story in a future update and not post it as another game.
- The enemy design cuts back to ink blobs about 30 minutes into the game and that's how it stays. There's no explanation on what happened to the spiders and ninjas you've been fighting for the past few levels, and the ink blobs can't be stomped on or slided into, which turns the mid-air parkour fighting style you've been doing into a simple game of spam the attack button.
- The game doesn't tell you what to do at the start of the game (In case your wondering the controls are arrow keys and A and S to jump and attack respectively.) I only knew that because I played the original games on the developer's website.
- There isn't a menu. Every time you start the game it launches straight in. It's not really a con but I was a tad bit annoyed that you can't select level from a menu or choose to restart the level like in earlier games. About 3/4 in you get a map to go through earlier worlds, but it's not the same since you can't choose the exact place and find the challenge rooms you missed easily, although the map does tell you in which world you missed them.
Overall though, I enjoyed the game but I think that it feels like an early access game since there's no ending to it, and things like a menu and a tutorial are missing from it. Hopefully these will be changed in future updates but for now, I'd give this game about 8/10.

I'm going to outright list a few things here before I review unless you're THAT guy who wants to scroll to the bottom for a TL;DR, I'll put one at the bottom, you lazy person you. First off:
1. I am a huge fan of the Fancy Pants Series
2. I finished the game all the way to completion
3. I hadn't played the game in a long time
Super Fancy Pants Adventires is a fun and exciting game to play, and it is something I think anyone from all ages can enjoy. The best way I can some it up is that it's a momentum platformer game, with Hack and Slash elements that build off of what was experienced at the end of Fancy Pants 3. Yes I said Fancy Pants 3, there are a lot of games out there already, and I recommend checking them out. The game isn't that long once you get the mechanics down, it's a very simple combo system, but the game adds new things throughout your playthrough that make it more interesting. There are hidden easter eggs, and challenges that allow you to collect fancy hats and pants. The challenges are designed to teach you about certain tricks when platforming, or attacking, which I think is pretty cool.
I also want to say, from what I've seen of my playthrough, I don't think this is an entire game, as some parts of the map seem incomplete, or some things look like they are designed to be interacted with, but were never made to, mechanics wise, I think it's really worth it, as people can have fun for hours on end, even in a smaller area that the maps provide, as running through again, isn't boring, as once you have all the abillites, you can find new ways to make your way around the map, and sometimes find challenges you couldn't see before.
TL;DR
It's a fun platformer, if albeit a bit short, I do think more content is going to be added at a later date though, which has got me excited for what's in store for the rest of the game. If you want to wait for more, then that's fine I totally understand that, but I do want to say that the gameplay is really worth it, even if the game isn't that long.

There are no levels, checkpoints, objectives (at least none that I found) - anything to really give you a sense of accomplishment.

A friend purchased this game for me years and ago. It wasn't long before I gave into furstration and gave up. Years later I revisted the game, determined and looking for a good time simply because a friend was playing through it for the first time and talking about all the interesting aspects.
I soon found myself lost in a world of frustrating satisfaction, a world I became so quickly immersed in after years of searching for a game to get lost in...it was right under my nose this whole time. In short, I could literally write a book of a review on what made Dark Souls a difficult, but ultimately satisfying journey. It's been a long time since I felt attached to an adventure as I had this one. Literally the only game to date where I make my character into a complete joke (because I've yet to see a satisfying looking Dark Souls 1 character), but then falling in love with the idea of said character due to the journey he battles.
Long live Frog Mayne, long live Dark Souls.

*Foreword: While this game just recently made its way here, I have been playing for years now, for a couple hundreds of hours at least, so my "hrs on record" is a little off.
This is an arcade racing game where you have to drift/draft/jump in order to get your bar filled up so you can trigger power plays. Power plays basically trigger explosions in front of you to take out your opponents. (The explosions will harm you as well if you time them poorly.) As this is a racing game, the aim is almost always to cross the finish line first.
Power plays have two levels. Level 1 power plays range from simple explosions (like dropping explosive barrels on your opponents) to blowing up gas stations, planes, etc. With level 2 power plays you can blow up a bridge/dam/ship/road, or make an airplane crash land on the track and so forth. Some Level 2 power plays are also route changers which destroy part of the track thus opening up a whole new (usually faster) section while blocking the old one.
The more I played, the more I realized that this game is all about timing. It really makes a difference when you trigger the various explosions or when you make that explosive barrel drop. There are also simple power plays, where you open up a door temporarily to take a shortcut. The ones behind you can get a free ride through as long as they are close enough, but once the door closes, the rest of them attempting to get through will crash.
The various cars feel very different. Some of them start to drift easier, some are harder to blow up, some fills up the bar faster, etc. There are a couple of game modes too, but not all of them are playable in multiplayer.
My biggest "problem" with this game is that there are only 11 tracks. But it has a Split/Screen mode which is a rare treat nowadays. I already had countless hours of fun playing with my friends side by side. Not that I would get tired of it any time soon, but honestly, a track editor would make this game ageless.
All in all, it is insanely fun trying to avoid crashing when something just blew up near you sending your car drifting sideways while looking for the perfect moment to trigger a power play in order to beat your opponents to the finish line.

Like many of the people here, I played this game back when it was on the Gamecube. And BOY did I play that thing to death... it was easily my go-to RPG (that and KotOR, but hey, gotta give some love to the PC). So when they announced the game was being put on Steam, I just about flipped my lid in excitement. Then it came out and everyone was up in arms about the frame drop and other issues, and since my old computer could not even open the game, let alone run it, I had to pass it up. However, it died and I was able to procure a new one, and immediately bought this game.
I have to be blunt, this plays FAR better than it did on the PS3 - I really can't tell any difference between this and the Gamecube version (text aside) because it plays just as smoothly on it. I even put the graphics settings on the highest settings possible and didn't experience any issues. Maybe it's just because the game was patched at some point between then and now (I haven't seen any news since March/April) but this has far too many 'not recommended'  settings. And my computer is just an average one; the components are not top-of-the-line, nor did they cost an arm and a leg. Now all I need is a Gamecube controller adapter... XD
The game has all of the content of not just the GC/PS2 but the additions of the ToSC release for the PS3, including the unlockable costumes that reference other games in the series. Lloyd and Genis, for example, get the outfits of Guy and Luke, respectively, from Tales of the Abyss. The mechanics work exactly the same as they did in the GC version, which can be a bit jarring if you're used to the mechanics from the more recent games - this game does not have a 'free run' mode that allows you to circle around your enemies. Even back when I had both this and Abyss, I'd find myself trying to free-run but not being able to, but that didn't diminish my enjoyment of the game.
In short, if you can at least meet the minimum requirements for the game, I highly recommend picking up this classic. There's a reason it stands alongside the likes of Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door, Metroid Prime, and The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess as the best games of the Gamecube.

"Tales" series is less well known than Final Fantasy, but I've always liked it a bit more. And Tales of Symphonia is my favorite one (though arguably Vesperia might be better in many ways).
The story, and characters, are every JRPG cliché ever condensed into one game. But clichés aren't a bad thing in and of itself, there's a reason they exist, reason for them to be, well clichés. Symphonia executes all of them so well, you barely realize they're there. It's like you're watching the best 90's anime ever made. Think Lethal Weapon and buddycop clichés.
Normal JRPGs have the screen shatter, music start blasting, and you're moved into turn based combat. From the beginning, Tales did something different, you're moved into real time combat, with fighting game style moves. Think Soul Calibur or whatever. You have your team of four people, each with their own very specific gameplay. You control one of them, usually the main character Lloyd (heaviest hitter + decent mobility + second most HP + most moves). The gameplay is really satisfying even when it sometimes might get repetitive.
It's a world that pulls you in. Characters that you love more and more. Open field that opens just the right amounts for you to explore more and more. It's MWAHHH, it's perfect.
This PC port is honestly kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥though, even if elevated by the game itself. It's from the Play Station 2 version, the worse version (even though it has some additional content). It should have been made the best of both worlds, GameCube version with PS2's added outfits etc. The fighting UI and everything is just better on GC. There's a bunch of other changes that should have been made as well; 30fps doesn't bother me, 16:9 1080p with humongous UI elements blocking half the screen do.
BUT. If you do not own any other version, please try this one. It's worth whatever dollaridoos it is, even at full price.

Review -- SoldierFront 2 is a free to play game developed by the South Korean developer Dragonfly and published by Aeria games. This game, in my opinion, combines elements from Counter-Strike and those of arcade shooters such as Call of Duty. This game features 5 game channel -- Newbie, Open, Competitive, Xanthid, and Hero Mode. Newbie is for all players under the rank of 47. Open is for everyone, although the skill based is definitely higher than that of the Newbie channel. Competitve is mostly for corps (clan) battles, but also has a corps recruting channel to try to get new corps members. Xanthid mode reminds me of the Zombies mode from Black Ops, but it is different and quite fun. It has two modes, Survival and Defense. Survival is wave after wave after wave with now defensive barriers to help you. Survive 30 wave and win. Defense has you protecting a node from wave of xanthids. Easy mode -- defend against 15 waves, Normal mode -- defend against 20 waves. Now, it also has a Hard mode and Hell mode which can be unlocked, but I have yet to do so. The last mode, and the cetainly most interestin mode, is Hero mode. Hero mode is essentially a League of Legends or Dota 2 game, but in first person. It can be a 3v3 (recomended), 4v4, or 5v5. Players and team xanthids have to destroy enimy turrets and thier node, while protecting their own.
This game also features a very good shop. You rank up to unloack the weapons, and use SP (in game currency) to buy them. Now, if you want to, you can pay real money for AP. AP can get you a very limited amount of items straight up. Only 3 weapons are available for AP. You can get a VIP cupon to get better looking items of ones you can get with SP. To get the good items, you have to take a chance. You buy 1, 6, or 12 lottery tickets, and you can get either a really good gun, or some crap. The good items have a small chance of actually getting. Now, there are also some lottery tickets you can get with SP, and you can have a chance to get some weapons that rival those that you have to pay real money for.
I highly recomend this game, and since it's free, there is no reason you shouldn't at least give it a try. :D

OutDrive, in one way, is an amazing achievement, and DENVER has a lot to be proud of with their creation. I mean that. The screenshots simply do not do this game any level of justice, as there's actually a lot of varied scenary to keep things fresh and thus never feels like the "empty sunset highway" some people have voiced concern over before buying. The combination of audio/visual elements delivers THE best 80's/neon/VHS/vaporwave experience I've ever seen in a video game, hands down.There is so much attention put into everything, from the tastefully low polygon count on most of the assets, to the bloom that glows softly off of the neon and the post-processing filter across the screen, it all ensures that this game feels like a 3D interactive vaporwave poster art. As a work of art, it's meticulously crafted and feels SO good to play for the first few minutes.
Alas, the art style is not the aforementioned achievement displayed in this product, because it's just ripping off of the upcoming Kickstarter-funded game Power Drive 2000. Seriously, look up some screenshots and try not to feel insulted on behalf of PD2k's developers. Even if you're someone who's really into the whole vaporwave/vhs aesthetic, this game is not worth the price of admission as it's just a petty clone/cashgrab feeding itself off of the Power Drive hype. I want to make it clear that I do not hate this game for not being Power Drive, because I had no idea what Power Drive was until after I  played this game and read some of the user reviews. I have zero attachment to that project, and my opinion is not in comparison to that game, but how the game stands on its own merit in a world where it was actually an original idea.
The problem with OutDrive is that, beyond stimulating your eyes and ears, there is NOTHING left. At its most basic level, the game mechanics are actually quite good, which makes it even more confusing that nothing interesting was done with them. Driting around sharper turns is fun, hitting the ramp between roadblocks is fun, balancing speed with trying not to overheat keeps you engaged as you drive. And yet, absolutely none of these things provide you with any real challenge. My FIRST run in the game lasted 28 minutes and the only reason I stopped was because I was BORED, not because I failed. Despite having a meter that forces you to go fast but not too fast, I spun out, came to a COMPLETE halt, hit the (unlimited) boost, and was back on my way without penalty. It's borderline insulting.
There are so many great ideas here that just don't do anything meaningful. If you're driving through a city (which looks ♥♥♥♥ing SICK, by the way) you may have to dodge cross-traffic or some of the lanes may have a car driving alongside you. It would have been so easy to use this as an opportunity to challenge the players environmental awareness as they have to watch the road ahead of them, and dodge the cars beside them, and yet these other cars are separated by wide distance, predictable, and easily avoided. Likewise, there is a helicopter that shows up once in a while to fire bullets at you, which literally just bounce off your car when you do get hit, there is no consequence for this whatsoever. Sometimes, the chopper will try missiles instead, which hit the road ahead of you, bringing up chunks of pavement that you may crash into if you're not careful. While these missiles are the hardest part of the game, they are by no means a threat, considering even if you get hit by a big slab of the road and find yourself turned 180 degrees, all you have to do is quickly press that boost, turn around, and you're on your way before your speed meter ever reaches the bottom.
If you want to jam out to some downtempo 80's-esque electronic synth music while dining on a visual feast, go for it, but do not expect the game to challenge you in any way. It's an endless runner that somehow screwed up the most necessary part of the genre: losing. And that's one hell of an achievement to be proud of.
Could be good with some work but very bare bones and dull at the moment.

As an avid fan of the Castlevania series, I will say most of the 3D entries have been mostly mediocre.  Some had good ideas marred by poor controls (N64 games) while others had tedious gameplay with excellent music and atmosphere (Lament of Innocence and Curse of Darkness).
Then 2010 rolled around and Lords of Shadow came out.  Another 3D Castlevania that I had zero expectations for but still an almost forced obligation to try...and it blew me away.  Amazing graphics, gripping story, phenomenal soundtrack, varied enemy encounters, huge boss fights, and a simple on the surface but surprisingly deep combat system in the vein of God of War (this doesn't have to be an insult, people) gave a shockingly well rounded package that earned the game some high sales and critical praise the series hadn't seen in a long time.  It had its faults, namely a camera that couldn't be controlled and a somewhat slow beginning, but the series seemed to be headed in a positive direction.
A few years later we got Mirror of Fate, a sort of in-betweener entry to bind the stories of LOS1 and LOS2.  It also marked a return to the side-scrolling roots with flashes of SOTN style gameplay.  The story was interesting but markedly less central compared to LOS.  Still, the gameplay was mostly interesting, a little different, and again had a wonderful score.
With the announcement of certain features like a seamless world and a controlled camera, LOS2 had a lot to live up to.  For the most part it delivers, though it definitely has its flaws.  Rather than continue on with the paragraphs at length, I'll make some easy to peruse pros and cons lists.
PROS:
-The story is still well told and interesting, voice actors all nail their roles (specifically Robert Carlyle and Jason Isaacs).
-The soundtrack is still amazing.
-Gameplay remains mostly unchanged, though there is less emphasis on puzzle solving.
-Good length, around 15-20 hours depending on how much secret hunting you engage in.
-Lots of neat references to classic entries.
-Dracula's castle offers some cool, varied areas.
-Weapon mastery/skill tree system rewards experimentation and discourages 'spamming.'
CONS:
-Seamless world exploration is hurt by an incredibly weak map system.  Opening the map in the menu only lets you see a very small portion of the area you are in, and you can't cycle between them.  There are also a scant number of teleportation rooms, making backtracking quite painful.
-Difficulty seemed all over the place.  I found most bosses very easy and generally struggled more with the regular enemy encounters.
-The modern city you explore has that Gothic Castlevania feel to it, but unfortunately most of the areas are hard to differentiate.
-Ending is rather abrupt and anti-climactic.
As for the now infamous 'stealth' sections, I can safely say they have been completely overblown in just about every review.  Yes, they are by no means a good part of the game.  However they are very simple and account for less than 45 minutes or so of game time.  Don't let that be what sways your heart on the game.
Although it has a few questionable design choices, for the most part I can give a positive recommendation for LOS2.  Arguably one of the best facets of the series is that each game brings something different to the table.  LOS was about the closest we've gotten to a (fun) 3D classic Castlevania, Mirror of Fate was more along the lines of a 2D SOTN/Circle of the Moon type game, and LOS2 was an attempt to merge the two.  None of them are perfect, but the series hasn't been this interesting in over a decade.  I look forward to whatever Mercury Steam does next, and we will see what future Castlevanias have in store for us.

Orcs Must Die 2 continues right where 1 left off. The much-awaited multiplayer experience is here, but this review will be from a single-player standpoint.
To start with, you get to pick between the Warmage and the Sorceress. Both have their strengths and weaknesses, but the Warmage simply feels easier to play with due to his superior health, superior tar trap, and arguably superior weapon. The Sorceress is better for charming single, large targets though, and her acid trap does more damage than the Warmage's Arrow Trap.
Gameplay is more or less the same. If you played OMD1, this will all be familiar. The Elementalist girls are gone, which is a shame. This change means that you have less options to adjust to your enemies in the middle of a level. Fortunately any upgrades you purchased prior to battle can be reset at no cost. Autoballistae are now considered guardians, which means you can no longer spam them. I was sad about that as well.
Amazingly they made the Gnolls more irritating. They seem to have more HP, run faster (both probably untrue, but it feels like it), and can now slow you upon hitting you, making escape impossible. A whole pack of them, especially in Endless mode (see below), will ruin your day.
I'm rather disappointed that the campaign is so short. The first game took maybe 15-20 hours to complete, and had a good progression. OMD2 instead took me a mere 10 hours on normal difficulty. Granted, I already knew the basics of the game, but this was far shorter than I expected. DLC's extend the game's length a bit, but they contain no story segments, and thus you are basically playing for skulls (the game's peristent currency) and variety. Note that you'll have to play through Campaign again with another character if you want stuff unlocked on both characters.
Endless mode is interesting. Waves come indefinitely and keep getting tougher until you can no longer handle it, much like Survival mode in other types of games. This mode by far is the biggest time-sink, though you are rewarded with plenty of skulls to compensate.
If you like the first game and want a way to play it with friends, then OMD2 is the way to go. Overall it's an acceptable game. I still recommend the first game though.

I enjoy The Escapists and I enjoyed the sequel. I'm not the greatest at the game, though. I only beat the first 3 prisons in the first game and decided to stop on the fourth. I am finally calling it quits on the third prison in this one. Why?
I understand that players are better and want harder prisons, but what about players that aren't as good? I don't like thinking I only get half of a game because I hit a threshold and the game just becomes frustrating.
The game's bugs aside (I never had a problem with bugs or glitches) I have one MAJOR COMPLAINT, and this is the sole reason I'm not playing more of this game:
Saving is no longer done at the beginning of each morning and instead auto-saves throughout the day.
Why is this such a problem? I had all my tools and everything perfectly set up. I left my cell using a red key and before I could even get to the wall I was about to cut through for my escape I was spotted. Why? light (spotlights, lamp lights, any light) is instant lockdown EVEN IN A GUARD OUTFIT.
I Then lost all my sturdy tools, my red key, my weapon, and about 6 hours of progress.
THEN IT AUTO-SAVES? Oh, so if you lose your tools on a failed attempt you are ♥♥♥♥ed. Instead of doing a 15 minute day for a second attempt now you have to do all your progress up to that point again.
There is no manual saving either. It's not even an option. ♥♥♥♥ the developers if they thought this was a good design choice.
I understand that good players of the game will argue "that just makes it more rewarding when you get out. It awards not getting caught over and over again," but when was escaping in the first Escapists NOT rewarding? Why did it have to be changed this way? And you still had to go through the whole day before you could attempt your escape again. Was waiting 15 minutes not a big enough punishment for getting caught?
Horrible design choice, and I do NOT recommend this game because of the "improved" save feature. Unless you like losing everything when you get caught even once.
I still like the game a lot and it's a great game. The new mobile prisons are interesting and all the unique escapes gives a lot more replayability.
A shame that there's a huge deal-breaker for me. I would have loved to play it with a friend with the new multiplayer. When it's fixed, that is.

what isn't necessarily a bad idea is unfortunately crippled by poor execution. locked at 30fps and crashing on resolution change, I searched for a fix for my resolution crash, but I mostly found a large amount of people complaining that the game crashes on start for them. there have been no patches released to fix either of these issues. infact, no patches have been released at all! small gripe, but alt tabbing out also crashes the game.
the AI has a -really- bad case of rubberbanding. they're given cars that are generally a tier above what you're currently given and so you have to use the "powerplay" feature (where you attempt to use the enviornment against the other racers) to try and level the playing field. it's neat, but also annoying when the all-too-common sight of 1-3 cars end up with a 6 second lead ahead of everyone else and your attempts to catch up with them are met with you being ♥♥♥♥ed with by the other racers behind you at every opportunity given to them. if you use a powerplay on someone far away, it'll zoom in to show you their car explode. during this time, you're vulnerable and can't see your car. multiple times now I've destroyed someone and had my car plow into a wall helplessly as the camera zoomed in on someone elses blown up vehicle.
some of the event types really could use some revision, such as the avoiding helicopter missile barrages mode and the time trial mode. a mode where you have to avoid helicopter attacks and get bonuses depending on how long you can continue avoiding missiles is a neat concept, but when you're put on a single lane and the helicopter is firing 4 missiles horizontally across said lane with no way to avoid it, the gamemode quickly loses appeal. one of your 3 lives is gone and your combo is lost because the game gave you no way to avoid what it tossed at you. the time trial mode is brought down by the fact that you have to deal with powerplays being thrown at you during them. it usually gives you either a drifty car or one with poor handling for these events and so getting a good time on them will probably consist of trial and error where you hit a powerplay you couldn't have avoided (unless you knew it was coming, but sometimes it puts you on an entirely new map where you have no way of expecting some of the things it throws at you), exploding, restarting, and seeing how far you get the next time before another powerplay destroys you before your vehicle has a chance to move out of the way.
the sound is depressingly low quality and your graphics options are limited to simply "low", "medium", "high", and "very high" with no way to customize them beyond that. even on very high, it really shows that the game is a ps3 port as the graphics are very much last generation. all these problems with the game are a damn shame because it really is a game that had a lot of potential. instead, it manages to be considerably worse than even ridge racer unbounded, which I was still able to enjoy despite all of its flaws. split/second? not so much. the flaws are too many and shine too bright for me to enjoy it for any real length of time.
the menus are messy and lacking. for example, if you want to look at the new car you got and change its paintjob or even just exit the game after completing an event, that means restarting the race, pausing, and returning to the main menu because there is no option to just return to the main menu after completing an event. admittedly the load times aren't that bad, but it's just absurd to have to go through such steps to do something so basic.
I'd recommend this game for $10 at the -absolute- most. anything above that is really not worth it. it's frustrating, blatantly unfair at times, outdated looking, and generally unpleasant as a racing game. don't expect multiplayer either if that's your thing as the mp servers have been shut down. your only hope of mp is using a third party program to connect to friends over lan. on the bright side, if the bright lights from explosions are highly amusing to you, then this may very well be worth the price to you.
ps: who even puts unskippable cutscenes in a racing game? yeesh.
