Note: This review is for Book One to Three
I recommend this game to anyone who's into beautifully crafted stories and characters, and who enjoys diving into a detailed, fantastic world once in a while. DFC does everything right on these parts. I fell in love again with some characters I've been missing since TLJ Dreamfall and I'm thrilled to finally learn about the countless complex mysteries of both worlds, Stark and Arcadia. The only major downside at this point is that you have to wait quite a bit for the next Book. And the one after that. And the... ugh. This is an exercise in patience.
Some more detailed notes/impressions:
- DFC is not an Action Adventure. It's not fast-paced. You don't run around guns blazing or jumping from roof to roof. Thankfully you also don't have to endure wacky stealth sequences anymore, or actively punch the bad guys on the nose (like in the predecessor). What you do is solving puzzles, exploring, making decisions, and watching a lot of cutscenes and dialogue while the story unfolds and things get complicated. If the latter's your thing, this game is for you.
- The tone swings between drama, suspense, and sometimes totally unexpected comedy. It's all there. There's a lot of lighthearted stuff going on while drama and mystery keep you hooked at the same time. Great mix.
- The game starts out quite slow, linear, and even depressing in Book One. Personally I came to a point when I got pretty bored. Just play through the first 2-3 hours and there's a good chance you'll get into it. Book Two and Three became real page-turners quickly. Book Three especially.
- While I enjoyed most of the puzzles, this game also made me pull out my hair from time to time. Excessively running around in a fairly big open world just because you've overlooked that one darn item that isn't even hinted at isn't always fun. Oh well. There have to be these parts in any game, I guess.
- KB+M controls sometimes feel a bit clunky. I have to get accustomed to them anew every time a new book is released.
- DFC has a keen eye on diversity and tries to be as inclusive as possible. This is a good thing.
Conclusion: Great game with minor flaws. Recommended for everyone who's all about story and characters!

Oh dear.
I'm a huge fan of the first two games, warts and all.
Dreamfall: The Longest Journey left the series on a cliff-hanger.  After just completing book three of Dreamfall Chapters I feel like I'm still waiting for the game to really start answering questions left over from the last game; to begin working towards a satisfying conclusion.
Gameplay, (what little there is) is stale and uninteresting. The Kian character is dull and uninteresting. The Zoe character, while I like playing as her, is a totally different construct from the second game. Not only does she not even resemble the same character in the looks department but her attitude and speech patterns are different as well.
Casually Discarding Damien Cavanaugh the way they  did in Book One was actually really annoying and felt like a betrayal actually.
On the plus side Mira and shitbot are really entertaining. I just wish this game felt more energetic, like it had purpose and was leading us somewhere cool and interesting instead of wasting my time with pointless uninteresting errands.
What is the link between Waticorp/dreamnet and the Azadi's White Tower in Arcadia?
Why did Zoe say at the end of TLF: Dreamfall that Reza couldn't be trusted?
What happened to April Ryan? How does she survive (And she does survive as evidenced at the end of TLJ) being stabbed and falling to a dark watery grave?
And for the love of the balance, will we ever see Wonkers again?!
If you were expecting any of these questions to be answered in books 1-3 you will be left feeling very sorely disappointed.
In a way, I can't help drawing a comparison with this game and the writing of the Star Wars Prequels. Nothing really happened in the first two movies, everything was squished into Revenge of the Sith. Is that what's going to happen here? Will we begin to get some meaty story in Book 4 or worse book 5?
This game so far just feels like a wasted opportunity to me. I'm hanging in there, but only because I've already pre brought the season pass.

*** UPDATE through Book 5 - SPOILER-FREE ***
Finished the game!  Final verdict:  The team at Red Thread Games delivered on all fronts.  As an original Kickstarter backer, I don't see how this final product could have been better than my expectations way back then.  I'm ready for them to go back and remaster the first two now, after some well-deserved rest...
The technical issues were ironed out over time, the choice system actually mattered (in good ways) and most importantly, the story began in The Longest Journey and continued in Dreamfall concluded meaningfully.  Rich depth was added throughout and made returning and new characters more interesting and complex.
*** ORIGINAL REVIEW - SPOILER-FREE   ***  (through book 3)
For those who have played The Longest Journey AND Dreamfall, this is a must-play.
It's hard to write a comprehensive review for a game that is not finished, but I applaud the work that has gone into the game so far and the responsiveness of Red Thread Games (RTG).  As an immediate Kickstarter backer, very excited for a conclusion to the trilogy, I was initially disappointed with Chapters.  It wasn't clear from the outset when you are making critical choices, and I wish there was an easier way to replay specific scenarios instead of entire chapters to see the branching impact on the story.   Book 1 started strong, 2 slumped a bit for my taste, and 3 kicked it off again with major plot developments.
The story overall is a familiar continuation to Dreamfall, which itself was a strong thematic sequel to The Longest Journey (TLJ), one of the best adventure games of all time.  Dreamfall was plagued with some questionable technical decisions in gameplay, and unfortunately, that extends into Dreamfall Chapters.  The game is pretty in still shots, but runs horribly on many PCs.  I've been fortunate - running a Core i5 with a recent midrange GeForce, it runs acceptably.  It has gotten better since the launch of Book 1 and may be dramatically better by the end of Book 5.
I've heard that RTG is getting a lot of bad press after book 3, but it was my absolute favorite so far.   It seriously advanced the story beyond 1 and 2, and was also in many ways a return to form of the original Dreamfall and TLJ.   It is much better than the overly-long book 2 that feels padded with fetch quests and spends too much time in Propast, the dystopian future city that has a lot of atmosphere and yet manages to be boring beyond a few memorable characters.  I much prefer time spent in Marcuria, although I would like to see more of Arcadia overall.  Sometimes the downside to making a modern game is the sheer amount of work to pull of any new environment -- this makes me wonder if we will ever truly see an updated version of TLJ due to the insanely larger scale of that game.
** SPOILERS BELOW **  (through book 3)
I want more magic!  I hope that Zoe in Marcuria/Arcadia is used beyond where she was in book 3 as a stranger in a strange land.  She's been there before, and I'm sure she can be of use to the resistance.
I wish Kian had shared about the purpose of the pipes and tower (maybe he did, but it wasn't discussed on camera) so that Zoe can go to the magical hub under the city (from previous games) and we can hear more of her story.
I really don't care if Kian is gay, the writers can do what they want with that, but I'm disappointed that he has the potential for two love interests and the player can't choose either to pursue.  Yes, my Kian kissed Anna.  And her revelations at the end of Book 3 were good at establishing her character.   Enu is much more interesting overall, but is likely too young for Kian anyway.
I'm very excited to see Ge'en finally, and am crossing my fingers that Captain Nebevay (TLJ) survived the Chaos Storm and will be there!
I'm not giving up on April Ryan either.  Ragnar seemed pretty certain she was dead, but Dreamfall Chapters has already established that dreams can be used to shape reality.  It's a longshot that she'll return, but Saga's story recap of TLJ through her illustrations drove home that the authors want us to remember April.
Must play!!

Poor Mans latino Max Payne.
El Matador is a third person shooter which takes place in Colombia. You play as Victor a DEA agent sent to Colombia to fight the crime on drugs.
The story is as plain and by the numbers as it seems. It hits all cop movie cliches and twists them in it's favor and it actually makes El Matador into a very charming game.
As stated in the title the game is a massive Max Payne rip off. The gameplay is a very clear rip off of Max Payne. Everything from Bullet time jumping and dodging bullets comes back in this game, so if you played Max Payne you know what you can expect out of this game.
El Matador is also full of bugs and glitches throughout. The game is rather old (10 years old if you're wondering) and it really shows it age. The textures pop in frequently, the character models look dead and the lip syncing is absolutely hilarious at some moments. The voice acting is also really really bad which adds to the charm.
The shooting is rather stiff and cover proves rather useless so what you mostly want to do is keep running and jumping so you can avoid gunfire.
The game is also rather short. There's only 6 chapters in the game and it takes 2 hours to finish all of it. After the first initial playthrough there is no replay value. For this game however being short actually helped it out a lot as the game is rather clumsy and the longer it went on the more flaws appeared.
The game is also kind of difficult. In a lot of the stages you fight in very open areas and you actually don't understand where some of the gunfire is coming from.
The game also has one of the worst endings I have ever seen, so don't get your hopes up for an amazing explosion filled finale.
In the end do I recommend El Matador ? Weirdly enough yes. It's cheap and provides you a solid 2 hours of blasting Colombian cartels in the face.
Final Rating:
7/10
Pros:
+ Pretty Fun
+ Hilarious Cop cliches do wonders for the story
Cons:
- Graphics are horrendous and so is the voice acting
- Rather stiff gunplay mechanics
- Terrible Ending

In a F2P FPS, it's all about balance and mechanics.  While weapons seem somewhat well-balanced, the core mechanics of this Modern Warfare lookalike are kind of, well, bad.
Movement feels similar to Modern Warfare, with a smoother feeling hop.  Unfortunately, that hop is a tool too often used in firefights.  I found myself shooting at several hopping targets in all game modes.
A headshot is crippling, a 1-2 shot kill (depending on the wep ofc), yet the limbs and torso can absorb half a clip.
All the automatic weapons feel the same- little recoil with weird ballistics.  It's like an unpolished BF3 projectile pewpewing, so it seems like your rounds aren't hitting.
Snipers rule most maps.  This is a problem with a lot of these F2P FPS's.  No scope sway, no accuracy penalty for moving.  Snipers do lots of jump shots, as well.  They seem to ALWAYS have the advantage.  While playing with the AWP, my performance was much less mediocre than with an M4 in Sabatoge (classic plant the bomb mode) and in TDMs.
I suppose it's worth a try, as some people like those A/D spamming games.

So first of all I didn't play the Castlevania series before which means I don't know anything about the GBA/Nintendo etc games.
I bought Darksiders -which was in a bundle- and I realy fell in love with the game. Afterwards I got Darksiders 2 and after I finished it aswell I started to search for games which are alike. Someone told me about Castlevania: Lords of Shadows.
So I started with Castlevania:LoS (Ultimate Edition) and it was one of the best expiriences I've ever had. The atmosphere, the fights, the mechanics (light/darkness) and the insanelly good music made this game a 9/10 for me. When I finished the game and closed the client I got an announcement by Steam about Castlevania:LoS2 and I was soooooooooo happy.
I immediatelly bought it and when it was released, I immediatelly started it.
The 1st thing was the "Tutorial" which was epic as♥♥♥♥♥♥ One of the greatest things in my opinion is the new usage of Light and Darkness which is splitt in new weapons (Sword/Gauntlet). I really liked the character development and how much the characters in the game actually changed.
I'll be honest. After I played for about 1 hour I was really disappointed about the game. It didn't feel like the 1st LoS and something was missing. I felt that the story was really flat and -maybe- it was the new location which I felt were not fitting the game. And I stopped playing it.
After some time passed I started the game again and realized it was the worst mistake ever to stop playing it.
#######################SPOILER###########################
It's amazing! I love how the game changes all the time. The timetravel and the changes in the locations are amazing. The story of the 1st LoS and LoS2 combine themself very well and makes a lot of sense. The story of LoS2 feels very flat but after I reach a certain point in the game my opinion changed completely. It pretty much change the whole point of view.
One of my favourite parts is still the music in this game which fits perfectly.
About the gameplay it's really simple to explain. The people who played the 1st LoS won't find many differences. You can still  find containers to increase your life/light/darkness. The 1st difference lies within the skilltree. While you still purchase new combos with the points you gain, your skills level aswell if you use them and you can compile them in your weapon which makes the weapon stronger. This change is really good in my opinion because it was one of the flaws in LoS. The skilltree didn't seem to be important and you didn't really need to unlock the combos becuase you could beat the game with the stadart attack. Now there is at least a reason to use different attacks.
A new feature I really appreciate are the challenges which are a small sidekick. You get different challenges where you need to kill enemies within a certain time of do other things.
One of the facts that every LoS1 players will love is the camera which you can move completely freely.
What else can I add. The bossfights are still really good and the finishing moves are still epic as♥♥♥♥♥♥ the enemys use undodgeable moves more often which makes the fights a bit harder while the overall gameplay didn't change that much from LoS1.
I will say it this way: If you liked the 1st LoS and enjoyed it you will like the 1nd one aswell. Give it some time and don't drop it after an hour like me. Play it and see how well it develops.
My rating: 8 /10

This game is extremely well designed with regard to longevity of playability. Reading other reviews shows me that people are generally missing the point of the way the game is set up. The upgrades available for your first three categories of resources are obtainable simply by generating enough of the preceding upgrade, and the last two resource categories' upgrades are obtained by unlocking daily rewards that add to the resources or upgrades of which you've already obtained at least one. The first few hours of play are clicking like mad to generate enough resources to begin passively generating them, but following that, patience is required. Daily rewards are offered for clicking the resource buttons, which is where in my opinion the genius lies. You play for a few minutes a day, stacking your daily rewards that advance your game state. The potential exists to play endlessly.
Initially I was against the idea of the comrades limiting how quickly you can advance, as it limited how much I could actually play at a given time and it was completely contrary to the previous iteration of the game. However, I found that the comrades are a key ingredient in devising strategy, as in what expenditure would be the most time efficient and profitable. The daily rewards include a large fraction of any resource of which you have at least one, meaning that if you save your comrades rather than spend them, you could multiply them significantly with a bit of luck. That also goes for the upgrades of your weapons and medicine: lose a bit of resource generation by spending them for upgrades in return for the ability to raise the growth ceiling. Of course, you may not get the multiplier in the daily rewards for that particular resource or upgrade, so it may just be time wasted in that your stockpiled resources aren't generating you more. It's a perfect risk-versus-reward model.
My criticisms lie exclusively with the Experiments tab. The math for the State multipliers is questionable, as the more expensive upgrades are less efficient. It sort of feels like a trap for the less scrutinous players. And the math for the auto clicker upgrade is simply incorrect, if the visual flashes of the clicker upgrade bar are a proper indication of an increase in your resource pool. By spending 250 scientists (10 purchases of the auto clicker), your clicker upgrade bar should be flickering about 100 times a second. My experience in game has not reflected this.

Overall I'd give the game in its current state about 8.5/10, points deducted for general lack of clarity and unintuitiveness of the experiments tab and what I perceive to be mistakes therein.

Hyper Hippo is probably most well known by its game AdVenture Capitalist. Hyper Hippo opened up a beta for its upcoming sequel to the well-known game called AdVenture Communist. AdVenture Capitalist was known for being an idle clicker game. Basically, you’d click on the business until you could “hire” a manager, which would keep the business going without you even having to touch the business. The managers would even collect money for you when you exited the game. When you would return, it’d say, “Welcome back Capitalist! You were offline for [insert amount of hours]: [insert amount of minutes]: [insert amount of seconds]. You earned [insert amount of money] on Earth while you were gone. Now get in there and maximize those profits, you job creator!” And you’d click the button that says, “Dandy!” For example, say I was gone for one week, two days, fifteen hours, thirty-six minutes, and twenty seconds and while I was gone, I made one hundred and fifty million dollars. It would read, “Welcome back Capitalist! You were offline for 231:36:20. You earned $150 million on Earth while you were gone. Now get in there and maximize those profits, you job creator!”
With AdVenture Communist, the idea is that communism is WAY different than capitalism. With AdVenture Communist, your “managers” will only earn you a certain amount of a certain item. For example, say I had one hundred and seventy five farmers (managers for potatoes). This means that when the countdown was over, I’d only get about 175 potatoes. Plus, if you wanted to get one manager for the land property, you would have to use seven farmers to make one manager for land.
In my opinion, AdVenture Communist tries too hard to be different from AdVenture Capitalist. We understand that communism is different from capitalism and that AdVenture Communist would have to be different from AdVenture Capitalist, but it’s too different. Many fans of AdVenture Communist liked how simple it was to learn how to play. I believe if AdVenture Communist was to stay the way it is, many of Hyper Hippo’s fans from AdVenture Capitalist will leave. They will not accept AdVenture Communist because of how different it is compared to the original.
So the big question is: Is AdVenture Communist a sequel or something completely different? The way to answer that question is to ask another: What exactly IS a sequel? The definition of a sequel is a published, broadcast, or recorded work that continues the story or develops the theme of an earlier one. Does AdVenture Communist continue the story of AdVenture Capitalist? In a way, yes, but only because we still are out to get the maximum profit. Does AdVenture Communist develop the theme of AdVenture Capitalist? Yes, but in a way that changes the overall feel of the game.

My brother and I love this game and I would personally rate it as one of the best co-op experiences I have had in years, since probably Killing Floor.
The hectic and engaging orc killing features a fun but somewhat flakey physics engine that often sees your enemies helplessly and hliariously tumbling across the screen, off edges, and being turn into a gibby mush on giant meat grinders. Enemies are, however, surprisingly varied and some of them really put up a decent fight and pose significant threat, especially in the higher difficulty levels.
Gameplay is simple and easy to learn yet offers great customization options through use of a kind of levelling system based on the amount of skulls you have collected throughout the campaign. Skulls can be used to purchase improved skills and traps and have a large impact on the effectiveness of your character and the way you play. Respeccing after every match becomes compulsive but luckily it is free and can be done an unlimited amount of times. I highly recommend staying away from FAQs on this one, finding out your favourite set ups on your own is definitely half the fun.
Finally, perfomance is great even on lower spec PCs, but expect a little frame drop if playing on mid-range gaming laptops in big fights. Controls are precise, easy to configure and arena-shooter-responsive. Controlling this game just feels great.
Single player is effective but certainly somewhat lacking. Really, this game is designed from the ground up to be completed by 2 players, and for 2 player co-op, I personally don't know of anything better. If you do, please let me know in the comments!

I've played Demon Soul, Dark Souls, and Dark Souls 2.... so far.  Dark Souls is definitely my favorite of them for one reason alone: The Map.  It is rare to find such a beautifully designed map in any game now adays.  The game also subtly forces you to learn it by going down one path and then returning to the central hub through a locked door or passage way you couldn't access from before.  You can't warp between bonfires until you are through 75% of the game and it only adds to the expeince.  It makes you dread looking around the next corner knowing there could be a tough enemy that may kill you, but you need to press on to make it to the next bonfire.  Dark Souls 2 gives the ability to warp between bonfires immediately and I felt like although beautiful it never captures the feeling of Dark Souls simply because you just warp from one seemingly non-connected setting to the next.  These games are all tough, but reward patience and practice.  It is usually panic that kills me and not some broken/unfair mechanic.  Enjoy.

The Escapists 2 is the sequel to the hit pixel-graphic prison escape game released in 2015, by Mouldy Toof Studios and Team 17.
If you've played The Escapists then the setting and core gameplay of this sequel will be familiar to you already, and you can probably just skim over most of this review. For anyone else, The Escapists put you in charge of a prison inmate and gave you a series of 'sandbox' prisons to inhabit and from which you had to try to escape. The Escapists 2 retains the same basic idea.
Whereas The Escapists made use of reasonably well-made pixel graphics, this sequel improves upon them immensely; everything looks so much nicer in full-screen HD resolutions now! The characters appear much more cartoon-like, though, which may not appeal to fans of the blockier graphics from the first game.
Characters have a lot of personality. When you start a level you can customise (or randomise) the appearance of the cons and guards in the prison, and as you play you unlock further customisation options as well. These don't make any difference to the gameplay, but they're still a nice reward. Animations are good, too, though there isn't a huge amount of variation in them.
The core game includes 10 different prisons, which vary vastly in appearance as well as setting and escape methods. Most floors and walls are destructible, and there's a huge array of crafting components, weapons, crafted objects, and other general scenery objects lying around, some of which are movable. The detail is good, given the graphical style.
Graphics options are limited to vsync, resolution, windowed / full screen, blur, and a detail level for shadows. I haven't had any graphical glitches or performance issues.
The soundtrack to the game sounds to me like a 90s midi festival, with tracks in many different styles: the title music is a sort of sneaky heist number, while the credits are a western theme. In-game there are a few different background tracks that play depending on the situation. It's not the sort of thing I'd choose to listen to normally, but it suits the game well and has a consistent overall sound.
Sound effects are appropriate to the action. They are volume-normalised properly and well produced. Nothing stands out as being exceptional here, but I also have no complaints about any of the sound.
There are no voices.
The basic gameplay is extremely similar to The Escapists, though it has been refined and expanded significantly. You're dropped in a prison as a new inmate, told to stick to the rigid time-based schedule each day, and then left to your own devices, dreaming of escape. You can ignore the schedule entirely, but that's a sure-fire way to getting caught and placed in solitary confinement. So you have to be clever, ensuring the guards see you at each location designated by the schedule, while you plot your escape, collect the items you need, and craft your jail-breaking tools!
When I first loaded up the game I was impressed by the presentation and structure. Where The Escapists seemed like it had grown from a prototype that had never been abandoned for the real thing, The Escapists 2 oozes high production values everywhere: fancy intro, nice menu interface, well-implemented Steam integration, mostly excellent grammar, and an overall game structure that, while being somewhat traditional in its reward-based progression, is familiar and well thought out. This sense of refinement continues into the game itself.
There's an in-game menu help section with screenshots and plenty of information, as well as a short tutorial level -- Precinct 17 -- set with a funny story told from the perspective of its protagonist, in order to introduce you to the game's basics. And then each of the 10 included prisons provides you with a scripted camera pan across important points in the prison as the warden shows you around your new home. And oh, what a lovely minimap, expandable to full screen and scrollable. Hooray!
The interface is slightly more complicated than the first game, but also more user friendly. I got lost very easily in The Escapists and felt as though I didn't really know what I was doing, often getting blasted by the guards when I didn't even realise I was doing anything wrong. This game doesn't give me that same feeling and, usually, if I get caught by the guards it's because I did something stupid.
It feels more interactive than the first game, too, with plenty of items to find and craft, more quests to undertake for other inmates, and plenty of opportunity to get creative with your escape plans. You can move some objects around and hide contraband in a special section in your desk, away from guards' prying eyes. Each prison does have two or three 'unique escapes' that reward you a key and an achievement for escaping the level in a certain way. Collect enough keys and you unlock the later, more difficult prisons.
And finally, there's up-to-four-player multiplayer, with some escape methods only available if you have friends to help you out. Though I'm generally not that keen on multiplayer games, the developers have done an excellent job of integrating it into the game style, though a planning interface would be great to enable some more-detailed escape plots to be organised in game. Just be aware that, as with basically any multiplayer game these days, there are griefers here, too.
Security levels and lockdowns seem to make more sense now, too, though I don't understand why guards will sometimes intervene in an inmate brawl and sometimes just walk past, seemingly oblivious to what's going on around them. The guard dogs are ridiculously good, too; they can sniff out a stolen key no matter where you hide it!
The game still involves a lot of grinding. In order to craft what you need to escape, you have to either find or buy various components. And that involves either money, from favours for other inmates or getting a job, or luck in finding what you need scattered around. Inmate desk contents seem to refresh randomly quite often, making this less frustrating than it could be, but I've wasted a fair bit of time just wandering around searching for that elusive toothpaste, duct tape, or file. Stamina is still a pain, too. It's too easy to lose and too slow to gain, so you need to make sure you carry around stamina-recovering items if you plan on doing any hard work.
I've only encountered two obvious bugs, where some of my contraband items and equipment morphed into different items in my desk or when I was knocked out. I'm not sure why it happened and it was only temporary, but still weird.
Pros:
+ Improves on the first game in basically every way
+ Great sense of humour
+ Much higher production values than the first game
+ Multiplayer that's well thought out and integrated
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- Grindy
- Dogs are a bit over-the-top
- Occasional bugs
This comment might raise the ire of die-hard fans of the first game, but to me The Escapists 2 is what the original game should have been. The graphics are better, the controls are better, and the gameplay just seems to make so much more sense. And it has multiplayer to boot! While the first game was a very creative setting for a crafting-based sandbox game, The Escapists 2 is necessarily a bit old-hat in that regard, but it is a much better game. There are many hours of fun to be had here, though quite a lot of them will be rather grindy.

This is a simple, straightforward, fun game with nice UI controls, nice graphics, no bugs, etc.  You have a fleet, you move it to planets, you fight various types of battles, you win the hearts and minds of the local planetarians, they join your Federation, and you move on to the next system rinse and repeat until all of the free systems are taken.  Then you duke it out with the other expanding empires.
Once you conquer a planet, you build cities and upgrades on your planet (each system only has one planet, so again, it is very easy and fast to manage your planets).  You build wonders.  You invest in research (a very simple science tree of maybe 10-12 categories which increase your ship powers.  You can buy and sell a few commodities like science, metal, fuel, and food, all of which are needed though to build cities, ships, upgrades, etc.
Building ships is the fantastic part.  It is dead simple.  You use metal to add points to your defenses (hull and shields), engine, weapons, hangers, tubes, sensors and stealth, and that is about it.  You can upgrade your ships to super dreadnaughts, or create lots of smaller ships to swarm the enemy.  You can add fighter bays and launch fighters.  You can add long range lazer weapons or short range kenetic weapons that do a lot of damage up close.  You can also add torpedo tubes.  At first I didn't like them, now they are my go-to weapon. It is with some regret that I, partially through Book 3, must advise people not to buy this game.
Dreamfall Chapters is, frankly, not good enough. It's not smart enough, it's not pretty enough, it's not fun enough, and it's certainly not compelling enough.
Which is a shame, because it could have been. Parts of it are good. Parts of it made me enjoy it, even enjoy it far more, or far differently than I normally enjoy major titles from major companies.
The central problem is that the game is too in love with its own setting, and its writing tries to brush off its shortcomings with supposedly clever wit to paper over the fundamental lack of actual emotion in much of the character writing. This essentially manifests in the game being worse the more serious it gets, which means each Book is a steady slide towards worse and worse writing.
Kian's half of the story exemplifies this the best, and most all the faults to be found in Zoë's story can be found first with his.
Firstly, his behaviour and personality is completely inappropriate to the tone of his supposed story. A member of a resistance, a traitor to his own, hunted by his former allies. Yet he and the resistance gallivante about in a bar outside the slum which is frequented also by the soldiers of the occupying force! Much of his dialogue consists of the same witticisms that Zoë is fond of sprouting. He can even come to appear laidback. And then the moment a more important scene occurs, all this characterization is cast aside for some nebulous serious personality that seems largely unconnected with his general behaviour.
What is worse, Kian's wit is rarely funny, and the gallery of rogues - really, three other characters in total - is distinctly unimpressive, and sadly one-note.
The resistance proper seems to be driven exclusively by the actions of three individuals and one urchin boy, and their grand plan is nowhere to be seen.
What, then, is there to invest in? For what reason might one care about Kian and the resistance?
I cannot answer that question, because to my mind, there is nothing. All that seemed like it might have been worthwhile turned vacuous and meaningless the more it was dwelt on.
But Zoë, then. What of her? Is there at least some merit to her story?
Some, yes. Fundamentally, Zoë, almost solely from breaking mildly with convention, and from her archetypical pluck, manages to hold on to some coherent characterization. But it doesn't seem able to last. The pressures of the plot are driving her into a role that the writing cannot sustain, and her coherence and integrity seems to dissolve as she reacts in the same blandly determined manner to any sort of challenge or setback.
And in the end, the core plot itself is simply not interesting enough to sustain the game on its own.

This review is updated up to Book Five.
Basically, playing this game is like watching a film that stops every five minutes, and continues only after you walk around your house three times. Even though saying that, books four and five have MAJOR improvements compared to the first three, and are more streamlined and less running around randomly.
5/10
Even a story game should stick to what it knows. This game is heavily based on the worlds of the two previous games, TLJ and Dreamfall, but the new story is unlike them at all, and this game tries to be many things it isn't: It tries to be a Telltale game by including a choice every second, and it tries to be Game of Thrones by including so many war-politics, both which only hinders the game.
The fourth and fifth books tried to change things, and felt much more like the original Dreamfall (which is still light-years below TLJ). It's an improvement, even if it might be too little and too late, but let's face it, no graphics, sound or story can save a game from horrible gameplay.
The worst things about the original Dreamfall was how much backtracking, walking and running we had to suffer. There are no fighting scenes this time, which is a good thing, but the long and tedious runnings are still here, not to mention an unrelated action scene here and there with Kian, and these hold the game back from turning into the beautiful masterpiece that The Longest Journey was.
The game is long not because of its content, but because of how much time is wasted by reaching from point A to point B, and only after you find out where point B is, and it is SO hard to find out where to go, even if you know the name of the place. Like I said at the beginning, playing this game is like watching a film that stops every five minutes, and continues only after you walk around your house three times. Although, again, this is true mostly to the first three books.
I had bad Kickstarter decisions, but this is the worst of them all by far. I did find the ending of the game quite satisfying in giving a complete conclusion to many open threads and characters in the whole series, and the final scene placed a smile on my face, but too little and too late. During most of this journey I was screaming "I don't care about Kian! Go back to Zoe and let me play the game!" and I would have rather watched a let's play of it on Youtube.

In 1997 (and to this day) this game meant a lot to me. Having been a huge fan of similarly violent games the years prior (Quarantine, Dark Seed, I Have No Mouth And I Must Scream, Harvester, Grand Theft Auto 1 and later releases like Hooligans Storm Over Europe (2002)) this was a real milestone for my gaming life and for gaming in general.
It has one of the darkest and most brooding soundtracks, ambient for gameplay and industrial noisescapes for level loadings / back story sections. It has an execute button which was I believe a first for its time. And considering games were out that pushed the boundaries of gore and ethnics like Soldier of Fortune 2, it wasn't as if Postal was the only dark game out there.
A million times better than modern imitators like 'Hatred', the original Postal was testament to a time when the US was more than a little f'd up. In years before its release there was the Oklahoma City bombing, years of Unabomber attacks, Ruby Ridge standoff/murder, Waco seige and more similar events around the world (Port Arthur) - this game was just (in my mind) a reactionary artwork reflecting on the gun-crazy society of the USA as well as the beginning of the many spree and massacre killings that were to take place regularly since its release.
While Postal 2 was the high point of the series, without Postal there would be no Postal 2.
Highly recommend for anyone interested in the history of gaming or great games in general. For fans of isometric shooters.

I'm not the most obsessive gamer. I have trouble getting invested in RPGs, I like games that're fast, hardcore, and mindless. Doom is a great example of a game I'll play endlessly, something I'll sink my teeth into with gusto. Hell, I'll play Tetris for hours on end, just because it's the kind of game I can zone out while playing. And then, there's Postal.
Postal is special. Postal is ugly, tasteless, and ♥♥♥♥ed up. It's the story of a man, the Postal Dude, going insane and suffering from inner demons of a most vile and hateful breed. He is the ultimate misanthrope. He's going to destroy the world. And he hates you.
Postal is the game in which the player is dropped into the darkness, the twisted and psychological nightmare the Postal Dude descends into. The gameplay is that of a twin-stick shooter, and players are thrust into an isometric gauntlet of violence. Shoot 'em all down, that's the goal. Kill enough hostiles and move on to the next area. It's a brutal, simple premise, built upon the simple phrase of 'going postal,' of becoming so uncontrollably and absolutely enraged that turning to malevolence and destruction is the only way to go.
Now let me be clear, as much as I love this game, I don't condone violence. I'll sing praises of how much I enjoy this game, but I believe that this game, like say Manhunt, isn't trying to make the massacre fun or entertaining. No, Postal is more than aware of what it is. Postal's psycho-horror presentation and grindhouse atmosphere drives the underlying darkness Postal presents to us. The violence is played straight, and the executions one can perform are heralded by a foreboding tone of dissonant music. Nothing here is played for laughs, like in Postal 2 and it's DLC Paradise Lost, or even in the abysmal Postal III. No, the original Postal presents it's morbid premise as dark and nihilistic as it needs to be.
Don't worry, the game is fun. Despite the idiosyncratic controls, it can be a lot of hardcore action. If it wasn't for the modifiable controls, which are quite liberal with how you can tweak them to your liking, this game would be far more frustrating. Fortunately, the easy-to-tweak controls, a difficulty you can change on the fly, and a game length that makes for a solid few hours of action. The graphics remind me of an exploitation film production: grimy, unrefined, but oddly fitting. There's a solid arsenal of weaponry to choose from, making for lots of variety within the confines of the simple gameplay and objectives. There's an absurd, almost ghastly sense of humour here, demonstrated in the diabolical blurbs of the Postal Dude sprawled in red lettering across the loading screens. One can almost laugh in abject horror at just what the hell they're looking at.
Twenty years, in less than a month from when this is written and posted, will have gone by since Postal was originally unleashed onto PCs in 1997. To this day, it still feels dangerous to play Postal, to get sucked into the madness that Running With Scissors had crafted all the way back then. Postal could have only existed in a pre-Columbine world. And weirdly enough, not even Hatred could come as close as Postal did to being both a dangerous thrill and a deeply flawed, but still enjoyable, game.
I can't recommend this cult classic enough.

I liked the first and enjoyed this one even more, it's not anywhere as bad as reviews made it out to be but it's still pretty flawed. The combat is good but 80% of the moves you can buy you'll never use since the basic ones are good enough and there's no point in using anything else. The infamous stealth sections act as replacement for the puzzles from LOS1 (of which there are a grand total of 2 this time around) and are very short, few and far between - I don't really remember more than a handful during the entire 13 hour campaign - but at the same time add nothing to the game, they're just "there." If there's one thing I genuinely liked then it was the semi-open world which is very similar to the Batman Arkham series in that you head down a linear path but there's plenty of optional areas with collectibles/upgrades.
The storyline is nothing special, and the ending itself is very underwhelming considering it was supposed to be the last installment in the franchise. During the last 2 hours the plot quickly rushes to the end as if developers ran out of time, having you repeat a very simple puzzle 3 times in between a series of cutscenes then fighting two final bosses in a row with nothing else in between.
If they had cleaned up the combat system, gotten rid of the stealth sections, fixed the pacing issues at the end and put more thought into the storyline it could've been great, but in the end it's only slightly above average.

The aesthetics of the game are spot on 80s.  Everything is bright blue and purple neon--even the car model used is the quintessentially 80s DeLorean DMC-12. And the music is perfect period synth-pop, excellently composed.
The "story" is as follows. You're some kind of wheelman for some shady people and the S goes down. Your girl takes a bullet for your sorry butt and somehow (it's not really explained how this works) you connect your car's engine to your girlfriend's heart, which apparently keeps her heart beating. You drive for as long as possible until you foul up. You foul up, the girl dies and the stage ends.  There is no end stage--you go until you can't go any further, then try again to go farther. There really isn't much to this game.
The controls are awkward and not customizable, and there is no gamepad support as of this writing (2/23/16).
You boost to go faster (by holding LShift) and you'll need to be boosting most of the time. Being off boost means the meter that follows your car drops. Dropping too low (to the left) means your girl starts to die--her heart slows down, the music distorts and everything goes gray.  Going too far to the right makes the car overheat (which isn't doing your dying girlfriend any favors either). Roadblocks, jumps and attack choppers will all attempt to slow you down on the endless winding road.
As I said, the controls are awkward.   WASD to control the car, arrows to control the camera (you will almost never need to use these) LShift to boost and Space to drift.  The WASD controls mean your pinky is left to the boost button, and as I said before you'll be on boost more than you're off. This gets really tiring after a few minutes and it's needlessly awkward.
The game is unsubstantial and could use some extremely basic additions (like gamepad support, or even the ability to remap controls).  I can't recommend this game at full price. In fact even for what I paid ($1.79) I'm not sure if it's worth the money.

It was 2011, and one of my friends had told me about a browser game called 'Fancy Pants'. He said it was a really great game that he found on Miniclip, and so I soon gave it a try and enjoyed it heaps. I also played the sequel on Miniclip, enjoying that throughly. A year later, I discovered the iOS version which added a whole new world as well as the previous two for a solid $3 or $4. The amount of enjoyment and time I got out of it was well worth it, and I recently redownloaded it on my new phone and have 100%ed each world again, bringing back some nostalgia. I soon found out that a new Fancy Pants game was coming out on Steam, and I was pretty excited. However, I can't say that Super Fancy Pants Adventure really lived up to my expectations.
Overall, I sort of enjoyed Super Fancy Pants Adventure. It was a fun addition to the series and has some of the smoothest and fast-paced gameplay the series has ever had. However, it is bogged down by an overexpensive price tag (even $10 is too much imo) in relation to its lack of content, somewhat repetitive nature and ending which left me feeling deceived, to a degree.
As stated, the gameplay is super fun, if the levels do feel a bit samey. I dislike the way that the pencil and pen are real jpegs in game as it takes away from the style I feel, but that's just a minor gripe. However, in other places when it comes to game design and graphics, it just is not very good. I was playing in fullscreen and you can somewhat tell this is not the game's native resolution. I remember in particular there was one run which looked like something you could run up, but was instead something you had to continously jump up. Why? There is also not much indication of platforms that you can actually move through and the consistency of walls for jumping off is lacking. Some other aspects of design are just flat out lazy, like when you increase your health bar and instead of continuing the pattern or colour, it would just be white next to the colour you've chosen. How did this make it to the final product?
I could sort of get past all this though, if it weren't for it being grossly overpriced for a game that is, at most, 2 hours worth of largely unsatisfying content. The levels don't have the same charm and persona as previous games, particularly World 3 imo. Not only this, but the ending was legit fighting a dark Fancy Pants then falling into a white abyss and then the words 'To be continued..." show up on screen. I felt cheated. Also, do NOT believe there are 57 levels. There are 57 sections of levels, but all the indiviudal areas are what I actually consider levels, and there is only 7 or 8 of these. They are all pretty samey but still fun to travel through due to the great gameplay, but still, World 3 had 13 or 14 levels and were infinitely more varied and interesting. I hope more comes as free DLC, because I won't be paying full price for another game if this is the level of content we will get.
I wouldn't say the game is without value necessarily, but its value certainly does not surpass $5. The iOS version of Fancy Pants Adventures had more content, not only including a slew of original levels, but also bundling in Worlds 1 and 2, and the best part was that you didn't even have to spend $5. I almost wish the game were just that tad bit shorter so I could've refunded it.
Apparently there's some Fancy Key you can buy on Brad's website that gives you access to a bunch of Fancy Pants content that's yet to come. Why was this not advertised elsewhere? The one that's $5 includes a World 1 remix and future access to all other Fancy Pants games. Why is this one $10 then?
(It's important to note I didn't do EVERY single challenge but I still did quite a few. Still, not everyone is going to intently do the challenges and they will finish it even quicker. You could probably speedrun this very quickly.)

This game has a lot of pros, and one con. I'm gonna start with that one con: It's short. Like, really short. I blew through it in a couple hours. Granted, there are quite a few optional challenge rooms, many of which I missed, but still, I can't imagine it taking more than 3 or 4 hours to fully exhaust the content on offer if you know what you're doing.
BUT, having said that, it's an incredibly fun game that I'm most certainly going to be revisiting over the years. It's got an excellent sense of inertia and momentum to the movement, it's not so much platforming as it is 2D parkour. The game isn't about landing pixel-perfect jumps, it's about managing and directing your momentum in order to get where you need to go. Additionally, the game is beautifully hand-animated; some of the assets don't scale exceptionally to higher resolutions, but the cozy yet polished art direction more than makes up for some technically lacking textures.
When you combine the movement physics, the lovely, rolling level design, and the beatiful animation, the result is a game which flows beautifully and just feels incredibly smooth and fun to play, and this is only helped by the fact that it runs at a silky 60fps.
That's without even getting into some of the special mechanics that are unlocked over the course of the game, all of which are pretty well-realized and complement the core moveset. In particular, I like the pen-riding sections, which are sort of a microcosm of the swooshing, looping, momentum-heavy gameplay.
This is just an excellent game, the mechanics more than make up for the somewhat lacking length, and I think that your moveset lends it quite a lot of replayability due to just how sheerly, viscerally GOOD everything feels on a fundamental level.
Granted, a good chunk of enjoyment for me also came from nostalgia for the expreiences of playing the early FPA games on various flash portals, but this is definitely a game which lives up to the nostalgia rather than being carried by it.
I highly recommend buying this game. It's definitely worth the ten dollars.

If you don't want to read this boring a** review, then I'll say this, it's okay for a PC version, but I would rather have the console version to have a better experince. But the game itself is great if you enjoy a pure arcade expeince. So for the main portion of this game I'll give it a recommend.
After playing this game four years since its release, I've really got my money's worth because of the excitement that this game provides. But first let me say that this will be mostly based on my review on the console (which I played the game mostly on).
Okay so how should I say about this game: Micheal Bay explsions (the good kind!), crazy crashes, on edge races, and drifting everywhere! This game provdies a great orginal arcade experince to the racing genre by using the enviroment as your weapon. Exploding taxi cars to a falling cargo plane, this game provides an on edge experince that puts you on your toes, watching for the enviroment that may crush your chance at winning. There's a great varity of obstacles that you can use to crash your oppenents to gain that first spot position. Even though after a while that you'll immediately remember what objects that will be used by your opponents, the fun factor is about stragatizing your moves, or powerplays. Powerplays are basicly your main mechanic of triggering the enviroment around you to stop your opponents from pulling away. With the blue bars representing the small powerplays that are mostly scattered around the tracks. And you have your red bars which triggers the more drastic or "epic" powerplays which will most likely wreck your opponents. These powerplays are fairly balanced which you can aviod by memorizing their actions when being acitvated. The objects that you can use your powerplay on has a nice unique features based on what enviroment is being raced on.
The tracks in this game are decent to say the best. Some have a good balance of alternative routes, but there are some routes that can completely waste a considerable amount of time, expically with shortcuts. But at the same time with shortcuts (which are used by powerplays), the game is trying to teach you again to stratagize your powerplays bars so that you can be prepared whenever you come across one.
Back to the track design, the tracks in the game can be both fun and fustrating, based on your vehicle of choice and playstyle. Tracks like Downtown or Power Plant can be a bit fun and annoying at the same time because of the tight corners, but can be mastered with throttle control and again the vehicle of choice. Whereas tracks like Dry Docks will rely more of vehicles with higher speed and a bit less corner efficiancy.
The vehicles in the game are decent to say the less in terms of being competitive. I feel that the majority of the cars in the game aren't that useful to drive because of their drifting capabilities. There are some that drifts out really wide and doesn't grip that well with the road and there are those that can grip around corners like it's on rails. But that doesn't goes to say that those that grip that well while drifting are bad. The Goliath and the Titan, which are trucks, are mostly useful for tracks that isn't technical and rely more on straights.
The handling in this game is a bit weird. You can't simply do a smooth turn in a long hander turn of a chicane because of the dramatic loss of speed as compared to the tapping on the analog stick. So wheel users, I wouldn't even bother.... But the pro about the handling is that each car has its own handling characteristic, so every exeprince with a different car would be different than the other, which is great for a arcade game.
Comparing the AI's to the PC port and the console port, it's better in a sense that the AI's are compeitive, but at the same time, the rubberbanding is a bit ridiculous in the PC port which makes it fustrating to get 1st in all races.
How do I think of the PC port as compared to the console overall? Honeslty, it sucks. There's a couple of things that may turn PC players away from this game: One is the frames are capped to 30fps, which to some is immersive breaking, but personally for me I don't really mind that much. Second is the icons for the Xbox controller isn't there......at all. I'm literally shocked to see that Blackrock (which went defunt) or Disney Interactive didn't even add controller support for the PC port. The graphic options isn't there either, just the basic quality options. So if you want to turn off AA or lower the shadows, that AIN'T happenin'. Some of the sounds in this game are muffled, which is weird. From what I've heard, the multiplayer is dead, unless you use a third party software or program. And oh yeah, there's no DLC for this port either, which made me a bit disappointed.
Overally, I'm a bit neutral about this port, the basic's in this game isn't that different with the console port, which I'm glad, but I wish that they gave the PC version more support to make it equally enjoyable.

Put simply, this is the best game on Steam if you wanna build something neat. The basic individual mechanics of construction and combat are incredibly simple, but to be able to put those principles into practice is a never-ending learning experience. The interface is, frankly, pretty ugly, but only because it sacrifices form for function. The construction controls are highly customizable; I found the default setup quite intuitive but I've seen plenty of people say they didn't like the defaults. The in-game tutorials are passable and a good amount of the necessary information is easily accessible at any time through the build menu. Honestly, your worst enemy will be the user interface for a good long while, but once you've put a little bit of time into the game it becomes a non-issue. More than any other game though, From The Depths lets you create anything you want as long as you're willing to put in a couple hours of learning.
The actual gameplay is split up into a variety of different cross-genre styles. In the standard campaigns you're handling both the strategic and tactical aspects of the conflict. Fans of more realistic large-scale strategy games can turn on realistic supply management, where you'll need to be able to set up and protect supply lines to replenish your forces on campaign. If you're looking for something less micro-intensive you can simply set resources to global, allowing all your forces to draw from your faction's resources directly rather than requiring supply infrastructure.
The actual combat can be amazing. The battles can involve dozens of ships/aircraft/etc. but the ability to speed up and slow down time lets you keep control over what would otherwise be an unmanageable mess.
There are definitely some problems. Mainly, in my opinion, the poor UI and lackluster optimization. If your computer is at the lower end of its specs, you may want to wait for another round of polishing. The devs don't communicate with the playerbase as much as I'd like, but they do have their own official forum where they make semi-regular appearances. Updates are slow but the game is certainly more than functional in its current state. There are multiple campaigns that are playable, ranging from realistic WWII scenarios to sci-fi alien invasion type campaigns.
What makes this game better than any similar contender is the sheer amount of freedom you have in your choices. Every bullet, every weapon, every vehicle, every fleet, they can all be built, altered, and remade into whatever you want.
Other games tend to give you a small selection of assets and force you to play mix and match until you can make something kind of okay. Empyrion hands you a massive tool kit, mutters some vague instructions, and lets you sink or swim (mostly sink) on your own.
No game on the market today gives you anywhere near as much meaningful control over the things you build. Other games and devs would do well to learn from it. (But seriously, the UI is awful. You need like six hands if you want to fly a plane yourself instead of programming an AI to do it.)

I always did think the original Escapists was fun, but it got dull after awhile. There were also some limiting mechanics (only being able to save at bedtime was especially infuriating), but overall it was a good game.

While the character modofication isn't as quite as open-ended as I would have hoped (the hair is the worst offender here: there are limited hairstyles and only four/five main hair colors to choose from), but it gets the job done very well.

Anyway, my verdict? Buy it. If you don't enjoy the "escaping" part (but why wouldn't you), you can sit and look at the stupid but funny dialogue all day. "OH MY!!! WHAT ON EARTH IS THAT!?!?"

As far as turn-based strategy games go, Starships is okay. It isn't very complex, but it is an enjoyable little game. Sure, there are a lot better space-based conqure-the-planets-and-build-and-empire games out there, but if you don't want to spend a lot of time in the details of allocating planetary resources, managing planetary defenses, dealing with multiple fleets, yada, yada, yada... then this game is for you. Otherwise, it's a nice break from those other sorts of games.
Positives:
* Turn-based tactical combat is intuitive and rather straigh-forward
* Building and customization of your fleet is straightforward
* Resource development and trade isn't overly complex
* Wonders add an interesting twist making resource allocation decisions interesting early on
* Multiple ways to win
* (Very) loose integration with Sid Meyer's Civilization: Beyond Earth
Negatives:
* Winning is a sudden surprise that ends the game... suddenly
* Not a lot of depth to the game
* AI in combat gets predictable after a few games
* Not Steam Workshop compatible...
All in all, its just a fun little game that's worth purchasing when it is on sale.

Ah, Tales of Symphonia. One of the most beloved games in the series with its rich story about a young country boy named Lloyd Irving, who ends all racism....
This game is one of my all-time favorites. It means a lot to me; it was my first game in the series, and I've been in Tales H*ck™ ever since. I had played it on my gamecube two years ago, and I had been in love ever since. Naturally, I was more than happy to play it on PC after hearing that all the bugs have been fixed and the game was playable enough, and my friend was nice enough to buy it for me, and I enjoyed it even more the second time I played it. Just.... this game is so important to me.
Just.... what's not to love about Tales of Symphonia? You've got the idiot country bumpkin raised by a dwarf, a sassy little kid who has some of the most powerful spells later on in the game and his older sister who will heal you while geeking out over ruins, a clumsy ninja, a Chosen one who loves dogs, another Chosen who's more than just a flirt/gag character.... the list goes on, and the character development is STRONG. Lloyd goes from being kind of an idiot to a strong leader who doesn't just sit there and watch while others are suffering, Genis starts trusting humans more, etc....
The combat system, while lackluster compared to the more recent tales games is fun and not like your typical turn-based JRPG combat.... and unison attacks were a nice touch; I enjoyed figuring out which artes triggered those. My only problems with the system would be the lack of free run and the fact that you practically have to bend over backwards to use mystic artes since you can't activate Over Limit yourself and with some you have to be almost dead....
The story was probably my favorite part about the game; it goes from the simple "protect the Chosen one and save your dying world" to "There's another world and we have to try to save both of them!" to "Let's try to save both worlds while also ending racism altogether and give everybody an equal chance to live!". It's just.... god, I love this game way too much.
The only problems I really have with this port are the fact that some of the dialogue was screwy; for example I was in a cutscene in Altamira where
I can't recall if that's happened in any other cutscenes, but this is the first one that came to mind for me.
My other problem was that my controller didn't seem to be compatible despite it working with Zestiria and Berseria, which left me having to use my keyboard, and that was a pain during the Temple of Lightning since I kept falling in the dark rooms and had to hold down shift while moving to make sure I didn't fall the next few times.
All in all, there's so many reasons to love this game, and so many reasons to buy it.
If you're new to Tales, this is definitely a good game to start out with~

Anarchy Arcade has the potential to be incredible but so far I have found that it doesn't provide the experience you would expect or want.
Imagine an arcade filled with YOUR games. YOU can post pictures of you all over the walls, YOU can make gigantic YouTube TV's, YOU can make bunches of cabinets that open your Steam games, YOU can make a cool tablet hooked up to Spotify, so you can have background noise as you watch YouTube, sit in chairs, make cabinets, and more. Sounds fun, right? That also kinda sounds like what this game says it is, right? That's where Anarchy Arcade loses me.
I start off in a prebuilt arcade in an incredibly small enviroment called the Apartment. It's odd, because I wanted creative freedom, but I guess since it unlocked the next level that was okay.
I went to the next level, the house. I immediately started placing a poster of my icon, and then it hit me: For being a game focusing on creativity, it makes things too limiting to bother.
Let's stop with the story and get the elements of the game out of the way:
*Everything is a shortcut. Doesn't matter if it's a website or an image, they act and behave (and are referred to) as shortcuts.
*Creating shortcuts is an incredibly annoying task. You have to navigate through menus and lists to find what you need, and
the game doesn't include a tutorial on this.
*The game does not allow for you to have more than one shortcut open at a time, making it impossible to have (for instance) music streaming and cabinet placing going on concurrently.
*Instead of using Steam in-game's browser, they use a special browser with horrible resolution and speed, that lags like crazy.
*Enviroments are limiting to creativity.
*To access most things you will want, you need to acquire points. However, in a game about YOUR arcade, it's something that will limit you so much that you will not want to bother.
*Props cannot be interacted with much, i.e you cannot sit in chairs.
and many more limitations.
I also found issues like framerate drops (especially while using web browsers in cabinets), things being too technically advanced, and finally just an overall sense of half-baked software and user experience.
To the developers. This game seems like it shouldn't be done in the Source engine, which I can assume is the reason for all of the technical limitations like concurrently running cabinets and resolutions. I also think that this game should take better advantage of what shortcuts you choose, making it easier for the user to use. Finally, I think you should expand these concepts and make it revolving around creativity, not making it revolve around points and stuff like that. It should be a creative game, since it really isn't a game at all but a customizable launcher.
My overall review of Anarchy Arcade is a 2/10. I love the concept, but the execution needs major TLC. And for that reason, I cannot recommend this title.

This game has great potential and I'd really want to like it, but it has many problems. The game is full of annoying puzzles, pointless erands, flat/unwitty dialogue and you don't really get anything good until after second half of episode three. To get this point, you need to suffer through roughly 10 hours of boringness. The last two episodes do have better storytelling and final episode does resolve the open issues from the original Dreamfall. Still, as a whole, the game is very mixed bag and I can't help but to feel unsatisfied after playing it.
Problems (detailed list):
1) Most of the puzzles are about finding right place to click and then clicking them in right order. Often you have good idea what you're supposed to do, but just can't find any way to do it. It's easy to miss interaction points and the game often hides them until you have completed all previous steps.
2) Uninteresting characters, flat dialoque and everything is boring and monotone. I mean adventure games should be fun, witty or at least somehow exciting. This game just isn't. Last episodes are little bit better in this regard, but first episodes are just horrible.
3) Filler content (lots of it). I can't help but to feel that some of the puzzles/tasks are there just strech the playing time. The episodic format is probably partly to blame. Each episode needs to be have decent length even if storywise the episode could be shorter.
4) Uninteresting story. I kind of expected this game to pick up where the original Dreamfall left. Well... it doesn't. Original story isn't really resolved until in final episode (to lesser extent also in Episode 4). Instead we get boring relationship crap, boring rebels/magical stuff (which although has it's moments, we don't really care about) and other new stuff that is more or less irrelevant to bigger story.
5) Character animations are just bad. Nothing quite ruins your character driven story like characters who look like they are some weird robots without any human emotion. I mean the original Dreamfall had better character animations frigging 10 years ago.
6) Game is resource heavy (even after engine updates). I have two years old mid-price laptop, which runs similar 3D games pretty nicely. This game had parts which where barely playable.

El Matador is a Third Person shooter set in Colombia and centered around taking down a powerful cartel know as La Valedora. You play as a DEA special agent called Victor who quickly earns the nickname “El Matador” due to his effectiveness and ruthlessness on the field. Victor is more of an executioner than anything and will make no attempts to arrest anyone or secure any drugs. Pretty much all you will be doing throughout the game is killing from start to end. There are hardly any moments when your life is not at risk but without a decent storyline that may get old fast for some people. Countless hordes of goons will try to take you down and luckily they are fairly fun to fight. What separates Vincent from his peers is that he used to love the movie 'The Matrix' in high school and has somehow gained the power to dramatically leap through the air in slow motion. It is a useful move for a quick retreat when you are surrounded though there is a limit to how many times you can use it.
Your ability to slow time will deplete as you use it and depletes even further if you kill a enemy during it's effect. Killing an enemy normally refills your slow-mo bar shown at the top of the screen. You will be able to toggle slow-mo on and off at will, whether you are standing or crouching and it lasts a long time. I have never had it run out and this ability can easily turn the game into a cakewalk if overused. Without it the game would be quite challenging as enemies are surprisingly good at finding cover and are excellent shots. To add to that, Victor is no superhero, he may have the ability to slow time but he is quite fragile. Taking gunfire will quickly burn through your health and while this game does have regenerating health, you can not rely on it. You gain about one hit-point out of 100 every 30 seconds so you will be there a long time if you want to be healed. Health kits are your only real option to patch yourself up and they can be found in many places like hanging on walls, resting on desks or by opening random cabinets.
Armor can also be found and greatly increases the amount of damage you can take before biting the dirt. These are much rarer than health kits and  will not affect your movement  in anyway. You will frequently be accompanied by heavily equipped police officers, that also appear to wear body armor but in reality they are all appearance. They are pretty much near useless and will die if an enemy so much as sneezes in their direction. I say nearly useless, since it does help to reveal where the enemy is when they get shot and they do drop some valuable rifle ammo when killed. So your allies are walking piggy banks for the most part. Your enemies on the other hand are  highly skilled and hyper alert to everything around them. It will be impossible to go unnoticed and you will be gunned down quickly if you are out in the open. There is no cover system in the game, though you will definitely still want to find some cover via crouching. I quite liked the need for cover, it kept the game from feeling like a pure action game and added some tension as you pop out  of cover, while diving near your enemies in slow motion, guns blazing glory.
Speaking of guns there are quite a few of them in the game and you will be able to carry all of them at once. You can't carry much ammo and many of them share the same ammo type, so it does force you to be careful with your shots. Annoyingly enough after every mission, they will take all your guns away and will send you back in with nothing but basic gear, making you scavenge more ammo and gear all over again. It makes sense that the police force wouldn't allow you to keep random weapons you got from a raid, but in a game where you are pretty much a space wizard, it just feels like pointless busy work. Most guns are too inaccurate and under-powered to be useful in any sense, so you will want to mainly stick to rifles or even a pistol over your shotgun. In enemy hands they are pinpoint accurate, frustratingly enough. Dual wielding is pretty pointless due to inaccuracy and low ammo supply. Some weapons have alternate firing modes like being able to set it to full auto or single shots, which is a cool feature that allows more options to take down your foes. Bullets even ricochet off of some surfaces and are still capable of killing either you or your enemies. That feature isn't used much but it was a neat gimmick.
Glass also has a neat physics systems that allow them to break part by part in gunfights and it just looks awesome to see the aftermath of a battle in a setting full of glass. Your typical explosive barrels are also present but they take way too long to go off and will give your enemy plenty of time to kill you. Simply shooting him is far less trouble. Enemies dress in casual clothes most of the time and all fight pretty much the same way regardless of the weapon they have. An enemy with a shotgun will fire at you from a very far distance while a enemy with a pistol will try to rush you, it can be odd at times but nothing major. Bosses are the exact same as normal enemies and have no different patterns, the only difference being they have much more health and never feel satisfying to fight. They usually appear in the end of a mission and have no sense of importance. The missions end really abruptly, you will kill a boss and that very second you will be teleported somewhere else with no idea as to what just happened. They have no sense of flow and you will be at a loss as to what you are doing now and why. It has no sense of progression or upping the ante, the first mission felt the exact same as the last but in a different environment.
The story is so bad that it would have been better if they didn't even try. There are multiple other characters in the police force, but having just finished the game, I couldn't for the life of me tell you the name of any character other than your own or anything about them. They are just there for the sake of it and add absolutely nothing to the plot or the events. I don't even know what I accomplished throughout the game. The ending was the worst I have ever seen, in any form of media, to top it off. El Matador would have benefited from just being a bunch of levels with no story, honestly. All it served to do was confuse the player, conveniently take away your weapons every mission and break up the action for some pointless banter. To make matters worse the voice acting is horrible and the Hispanic accents they were going for, are terrible as well. It could have been used to their advantage if they had made this into a cheesy, tongue in cheek kind of game, but nope, this game is dead serious in it's “narrative”. Environments themselves haven't aged too badly and it does inject quite a bit of color at times, which is a nice change of pace from the missions were you are in typical warehouses or sewers.
Now here is the thing that will likely annoy or even ruin the game for some players. POSTAL 1 is the first game in what would soon to follow one of the most controversial (and arguably greatest) series of all time. Released in 1997, it allows you to take control of a man nicknamed as the "Postal Dude", in which he goes on a violent rampage throughout the state of Arizona, eventually making his way to the Air Force Base. What happens next, I'll let you figure out on your own.
It's a very dark and violent game. If the "games you should never play in front of anybody ever" list ever existed, this game would definitely be up there at the very top. You're required to kill the HOSTILES in every level, not civilians. Civilians will run around in the levels, and you have a choice of shooting them or not. It's your choice. Wanna shoot all the civilians and hostiles? Go ahead. Only the hostiles? Sure. However, when you shoot these people, your kills usually aren't that clean. Most of the time, the people you shoot will drop to the ground and cling onto whatever life they have left. And yes, you do have the option of executing them.
The game features a pretty diverse range of weapons, ranging from a simple M4A1 (at least, that's what I think it is) rifle, a shotgun, and crazy weapons like a napalm launcher and a rocket launcher that can both shoot seeking and regular missiles. There is also a range of grenades as well, featuring regular hand grenades, molotovs, and things that aren't even grenades like landmines.
A couple complaints I have with this game (so far) is that the aiming isn't that good. You can use the arrow keys to aim and automatically shoot at something. Unlike in POSTAL Redux, there is no mouse aiming, so you'll probably have to get used to aiming with a keyboard. Also, unlike in POSTAL Redux, there's no indicator showing you how much health an enemy/civilian has. This isn't that much of an issue, since most enemies will drop to the ground in a couple of shots regardless. On the bright side, the source code has been released, so somebody should probably work on that if they have the chance.
Overall, it's a pretty interesting game that strays from the mainstream and does a great job at making a dark, isometric shooter a good experience. If I was able to rate this game, I'd say it would be around 7/10. You should check it out when it goes on sale.
