As a huge fan of Lords of Shadow 1, I sadly find myself rather disappointed in the sequel.  It seems like every change they made to the gameplay is for the worse.
First let's talk about the much lamented stealth sections.  They truly and unequivocally suck.  They are relatively infrequent and certainly not insurmountable, but they simply are not entertaining, often annoying if not outright frustrating, and aren't even logically consistent with the rest of the game. One moment you're ripping the heart out of a monster the size of a building, the next you're hiding from two grunts with guns. I can not fathom the developer's reasoning behind their inclusion to the game.  Who played Lords of Shadow 1 and thought "You know what would make this game better? Insta-fail stealth segments!"
Then there's the combat.  I found the combat in Lords of Shadow 1 quite satisfying even it could be simple at times.  It seems they wanted to up the challenge here, but they did so by making the enemies get staggered less, attack at a much faster rate, and having more attack you simultaneously. The problem with this is not that it makes the game too hard, but you need to guard or dodge so frequently that you rarely have time to execute anything more than the most basic attack combo.  Several of the more powerful attacks have such long windups or leave you open so long that they're nearly useless.  As a result, I'm finding the combat to be less varied and far more tedious than the first game.  Too much time is spent dodging and not rattling off impressive combos.
There are also little bits of level design that make me wonder at what point the developers stopped asking whether it was fun in favor of just coming up with tasks for the player to do (much like the stealth sections).  For example there are several timed switches where you'll hit a switch to open a door, and as you get close to the door several enemies will appear.  Spend time fighting the enemies (and likely you'll have to) and you won't make the door in time.  So you walk back to the switch, hit it again and this time you can cross the area unmolested.  It's the most egregious form of repetition to pad playtime and makes no sense in a game that's sufficiently long regardless.  It's the kind of thing that makes you feel like the designer isn't respecting you as a player.
If that wasn't enough, even the camera is disappointing.  Some reviewers whined about the fixed cameras of the first game, when the problem was just a few bad angles.  They switched to a controllable behind the back camera here, and while it's perfectly functional, the game has lost the epic vistas and panning shots of the first game that you only get with fixed (or more accurately: not player controlled) camera angles.  As a result, despite environment design that feels roughly on par with LoS1, the game has lost much of the grand feeling of it's predecessor.
Now on the plus side, everything that doesn't have to do with the mechanics of the game are at least as good as the original.  The art design and aesthetics are great even if you don't get to appreciate them as much with the narrow camera.  The characters and cinematics are absurd, but in a way that feels fitting and not like it's trying too hard - though it can get close at times.
Taken by itself, the game isn't awful, I still found it reasonably entertaining on the whole.  It's just that everything about how it plays feels worse than the original and it's especially disappointing to see so many mistakes made by the developer after the success they had with original.

Split/Second is, hands down, my favorite racing game ever and one of my all-time best games.  I bought this game for both the PC and the PS3 even before it came to Steam and I played the hell out of both versions.  This is a great game that any racing fan should play at least once and is also a great entry game for those wishing to check out the genre.
The premise of this game is, frankly, not very original but sets up the game nicely.  You are a contestant on the new explosive racing show Split/Second.  During the course of the "season" you will have to compete in races to advance to the next "episode."  Finishing higher in events will get you more points and will allow you to progress further in the season.  Each episode is capped off by an Elite Race, a race around the track against Split/Second's best drivers.  Beat each episode to win the season championship.  Like I said, not very original but it gets the job done.
The gameplay is very simple.  You race around a track, drift around the corners and use power-ups to destroy your opponants.  However, the center piece of this game is that it doesn't use traditional power-ups like those in Mario Kart or Blur.  Instead, you attain energy through drifts, drafts, and air-time.  Once you have enough, you can activate power-plays on the track, which usually involve destroying parts of the track to crush your rivals.  Filling up your energy all the way will allow you activate the biggest power plays on the track and will also allow you to change the track's route (if the track has a route changer).  Racing hard while effectively using your power plays are essential if you want to win the season championship.
In addition to the races, there are also several other types of events.  The first one is Elimination.  It's similar to the race, but there aren't any set laps.  Instead, a there is a timer that counts down.  When the timer reaches zero, the last place car is eliminated from the race.  Survive all eliminations to win.
The second event is the Air Strike, where a helicopter shoots missles at you and you have to dodge the missle waves in order to gain points.  The longer you last, the harder the waves become to dodge.  Gain the most points to win the event.
A variant of the Air Strike event is the Air Revenge, which is kind of like a boss fight.  Instead of getting points for dodging missles, you get power-play energy in addition to the energy you get from drifts and jumps.  You can then use the energy to reflect the missiles back at the helicopter.  Down the helicopter in the shortest amount of time to win.
The final event is by far my favorite: Survival.  Here, semis are driving around a track while dropping bombs in front of you in order to kill you.  As you stay alive and pass these trucks, you gain points.  Passing several trucks in a row without dying will increase your score multiplyer.  Get the highest score to win the event.  I have sunk hours on end trying to beat my own high scores, so I think you'll get alot out of this mode.
On the down side, this game's graphics are pretty standard.  It looks okay, but if you're more accustomed to the realistic racing games like Forza then you'll definately notice the difference.  There are also some glitches and hitbox issues that, while not game-breaking, can lead to outburts of rage over what the heck just happened.  Sometimes, though, the glitches can be entertaining in their own right (like getting killed by an explosion and restarting a hundred feet in the air).  These issues, however, are very infrequent and most likely won't dampen you experience.
[EDIT] As for the controls, there isn't a manual shifting option, which I don't mind but some might be a bit miffed that this wasn't included.  Also, the initial key set-up is a bit weird.  You drive using the arrow keys and use the right control and right shift buttons to activate power plays.  I assume this was done so that a second player could use the WASD area of the keyboard when doing split-screen.  Thankfully, this is easily remediated since all inputs can be remapped in the Options menu, but it's still a bit jarring when you first start.
So those are the basics of Split/Second.  It is very simplistic but very addictive.  There's also a bit more to the game than what I mentioned, but I'll leave you to discover those on your own if you wish to pursue this game.  Score: 8/10

If you like Minecraft, Robocraft or any of those types of building games then this is probably a game you would enjoy. Building is similar to both, with more options and different types of blocks available. I have several hundred hours on both Robocraft and Minecraft, but prefer this game in terms of creativity and open endedness. There are no blocks to unlock, credits to earn, and all features are available from the onset. In the campaign, building is limited by resources, which you gather in zones or by defeating enemies. In sandbox mode, building is unlimited and design generated there can  be built in the campaign. Since it is still in alpha stage, changes are continually coming out and not all in game features have been implemented. It is primarily single player, and the campaign mode works but again as an alpha, it can change as updates come out which can be pretty frequent as the developer is VERY active.
The world it takes place on is mostly water and the game's focus is primarily water based ship building and combat, however aircraft, submarines, balloon craft and, to a limited extent, even spacecraft are possible. Land based craft are in the works and ground based structures are possible. There is currently 4 types of weapons available: projectile (cannons, machine guns, electromagnetic gauss), missiles, energy based (lasers and particle cannons) and simple types like rams and drills. Most have different parts to make them configurable for different effects and potency.
The only downside to this game is the learning curve is VERY steep for some of the more in depth or advanced functions and the enemy can be very difficult in the later stages of the campaign and the multiplayer aspect is limited. Fortunately, the game difficulty can be tweaked and the campaign is optional. You can just build in sandbox mode and pit your designs against each other (or the built in designs) if you choose. The Steam Workshop also has very many designs from the community (many are exceptional and are even in the game itself) and the user interface is very easy to use and vehicles and structures are  easy to install and can be used in the campaign or sandbox.
I have not experimented with multiplayer at all, so I can't  comment on what it entails or how well it functions.
Overall this is a fun builder type game in which I have spent over 2000 hours on and continually come back to. I highly recommend it.

This game has great potential and I'd really want to like it, but it has many problems. The game is full of annoying puzzles, pointless erands, flat/unwitty dialogue and you don't really get anything good until after second half of episode three. To get this point, you need to suffer through roughly 10 hours of boringness. The last two episodes do have better storytelling and final episode does resolve the open issues from the original Dreamfall. Still, as a whole, the game is very mixed bag and I can't help but to feel unsatisfied after playing it.
Problems (detailed list):
1) Most of the puzzles are about finding right place to click and then clicking them in right order. Often you have good idea what you're supposed to do, but just can't find any way to do it. It's easy to miss interaction points and the game often hides them until you have completed all previous steps.
2) Uninteresting characters, flat dialoque and everything is boring and monotone. I mean adventure games should be fun, witty or at least somehow exciting. This game just isn't. Last episodes are little bit better in this regard, but first episodes are just horrible.
3) Filler content (lots of it). I can't help but to feel that some of the puzzles/tasks are there just strech the playing time. The episodic format is probably partly to blame. Each episode needs to be have decent length even if storywise the episode could be shorter.
4) Uninteresting story. I kind of expected this game to pick up where the original Dreamfall left. Well... it doesn't. Original story isn't really resolved until in final episode (to lesser extent also in Episode 4). Instead we get boring relationship crap, boring rebels/magical stuff (which although has it's moments, we don't really care about) and other new stuff that is more or less irrelevant to bigger story.
5) Character animations are just bad. Nothing quite ruins your character driven story like characters who look like they are some weird robots without any human emotion. I mean the original Dreamfall had better character animations frigging 10 years ago.
6) Game is resource heavy (even after engine updates). I have two years old mid-price laptop, which runs similar 3D games pretty nicely. This game had parts which where barely playable.

El Matador is one of those games that's launched too late to cash in on a trend, and are too average to stand out among the other shooters, so it ended up being a bit of... meh.
The setup is simple... Victor Corbett, DEA, after prologue mission (where he gets to shoot up a night club alongside Mexican Federal Police to catch a bad guy) is being sent to Colombia where he, was assigned by Colombia National Police chief to "observe" a local drug meeting. When his observation post was hit by RPG, he fought his way out and went on the exterminate multiple drug barons, with a bit of help on the local side... but as you can guess, there's going to be a huge betrayl at the end... who's the real bad guy, and who's just a pawn?
The short of it is you're basically lead through a rat run of bad guys here and there, and you'll get to exterminate them with extreme prejudice using variety of weapons, from twin pistols, to pistol with scope, twin SMGs, to various assault rifles (some with scope), sniper rifle, even grenade launcher, RPG, and LMG (light machine gun).
This is an old-school shooter with no autoheal. You have to find first-aid kits and armor to keep going. And there's no nav pointer either. You figure out which way you need to go, and it's usually pretty obvious. If not, explore a little.
Apparently Corbett racked up such a body count after that first mission in Colombia someone bestowed "El Matador" callsign on him, thus the game title.
Production values are not bad for its time, and there are a lot of things to shoot up, and enemies are upgraded thus. You start with common thugs, and by the end you're looking at virtually enemy commandos. But the game mechanics doesn't change much... Single-path rat-runs. Periodic boss or mini-boss battles.
Graphics are not too bad given this game is more than 5 years old. Sound is... tolerable. This game at first gave me horrible skipping sound, and this was apparently a RealTek problem that disabling some unused ports SPDIF and such cleared it right up.
I doubt this is any good for modern players, though. I'll recommend it, but remember, it may not suit your tastes.
All in all, this is a retro game. if you miss this sort of shooter, buy it, and play it. Don't expect realistic plot or physics or that sort of thing (this guy was carrying about 6 pistols, 4 SMGs, about 6 assault rifles, 3 shotguns, and a LMG and/or more by the end... Hahahahaha. Yes, that's oldschool for you.

Split/Second is, hands down, my favorite racing game ever and one of my all-time best games.  I bought this game for both the PC and the PS3 even before it came to Steam and I played the hell out of both versions.  This is a great game that any racing fan should play at least once and is also a great entry game for those wishing to check out the genre.
The premise of this game is, frankly, not very original but sets up the game nicely.  You are a contestant on the new explosive racing show Split/Second.  During the course of the "season" you will have to compete in races to advance to the next "episode."  Finishing higher in events will get you more points and will allow you to progress further in the season.  Each episode is capped off by an Elite Race, a race around the track against Split/Second's best drivers.  Beat each episode to win the season championship.  Like I said, not very original but it gets the job done.
The gameplay is very simple.  You race around a track, drift around the corners and use power-ups to destroy your opponants.  However, the center piece of this game is that it doesn't use traditional power-ups like those in Mario Kart or Blur.  Instead, you attain energy through drifts, drafts, and air-time.  Once you have enough, you can activate power-plays on the track, which usually involve destroying parts of the track to crush your rivals.  Filling up your energy all the way will allow you activate the biggest power plays on the track and will also allow you to change the track's route (if the track has a route changer).  Racing hard while effectively using your power plays are essential if you want to win the season championship.
In addition to the races, there are also several other types of events.  The first one is Elimination.  It's similar to the race, but there aren't any set laps.  Instead, a there is a timer that counts down.  When the timer reaches zero, the last place car is eliminated from the race.  Survive all eliminations to win.
The second event is the Air Strike, where a helicopter shoots missles at you and you have to dodge the missle waves in order to gain points.  The longer you last, the harder the waves become to dodge.  Gain the most points to win the event.
A variant of the Air Strike event is the Air Revenge, which is kind of like a boss fight.  Instead of getting points for dodging missles, you get power-play energy in addition to the energy you get from drifts and jumps.  You can then use the energy to reflect the missiles back at the helicopter.  Down the helicopter in the shortest amount of time to win.
The final event is by far my favorite: Survival.  Here, semis are driving around a track while dropping bombs in front of you in order to kill you.  As you stay alive and pass these trucks, you gain points.  Passing several trucks in a row without dying will increase your score multiplyer.  Get the highest score to win the event.  I have sunk hours on end trying to beat my own high scores, so I think you'll get alot out of this mode.
On the down side, this game's graphics are pretty standard.  It looks okay, but if you're more accustomed to the realistic racing games like Forza then you'll definately notice the difference.  There are also some glitches and hitbox issues that, while not game-breaking, can lead to outburts of rage over what the heck just happened.  Sometimes, though, the glitches can be entertaining in their own right (like getting killed by an explosion and restarting a hundred feet in the air).  These issues, however, are very infrequent and most likely won't dampen you experience.
[EDIT] As for the controls, there isn't a manual shifting option, which I don't mind but some might be a bit miffed that this wasn't included.  Also, the initial key set-up is a bit weird.  You drive using the arrow keys and use the right control and right shift buttons to activate power plays.  I assume this was done so that a second player could use the WASD area of the keyboard when doing split-screen.  Thankfully, this is easily remediated since all inputs can be remapped in the Options menu, but it's still a bit jarring when you first start.
So those are the basics of Split/Second.  It is very simplistic but very addictive.  There's also a bit more to the game than what I mentioned, but I'll leave you to discover those on your own if you wish to pursue this game.  Score: 8/10

There are some quirks here and there, like you have to press "F1" to get to the next level, you can't load a savefile from within a level, no proper mouse support to control the reticle (you can move your mouse from left to right to rotate the reticle around your character, simmilar to how wolfenstein 3D works, but top-down though it's not really a problem cause you can walk with wsad and shoot with arrows, you get used it after the first level).
Overall however, the game is really fun, even today, and I do recommend you buy it and play for yourself.

The bad: That's pretty much else. Not to mention there are a few bugs that might be found here and there and sometimes if you don't make the arcade to function properly the way you want it, you might have to rewatch the totourals over and over again to make sure you got it right the first time.

-Core flaw (of personal opinion): Very tiring and steep learning curve with the build interface, I would say thats its biggest flaw. Example: theres an 'align block with camera' button, but not a rotate button? Or if they do its very hidden, so again, deep (lol) learning curve.
You can always find guides on youtube for ship building / button layout, etc. But for example: I purchased this game some time in 2015 and had a blast with it, trying to relearn the controls again after remembering the several sessions I spent trying to memorize things so it didn't take me an eternity to build the simplist of things really sort of just 'turned me off' again from playing, my feelings on its flaws aside and how they discouraged me from re-learning at the present moment aside!
------------------------------------------
It's a very 'deep' voxel based game, not quite as hands on as minecraft, you dont collect your resources by hand. The process is some thing of harvesting resources from visable fields in the ocean / using the remains of your enemies. The game does offer missions, multiplayer, a few different campaigns. If you lack ideas you can grab almost anything conceaved on the workshop, no one seems to be shy about sharing their vessels, terrible or not some times. The campaigns sort of turn into an RTS of sorts pretty quickly, as you manage AI fleets and build / repair / arm said vessels with autorepair parts once you can afford them / build repair AI vehicles / Add guns, missiles, torpedoes, etc.
-Build anything from 'Space Ships' (I'm not sure if you could call it space, look into that if its a selling point to you*) to old timey galleys to submarines to helicopters to zeplin airships, Aircraft carriers, aircraft carrier subs, sub carrier subs, space ship carrier subs?- the sky is sort of the limit along with your imagination (hence the title) and it can seem a bit primitive, users have come up with some very creative content and shared in the workshop to help 'put wind in your sails' for creative ideas of your own.
-Battles can become very exciting, and you can witness your dreams get ripped to shreds, luckily you can save blueprints of your works in progress pretty much any time you like before hand so yeah, you'll learn to save often. I would say having your creation fight other AI craft and win or lose can be quite satisfying and challanging especially at first. Combat can be done manually (manual turret aim, etc) or have AI do 50% - 100% (shoot, or shoot & drive) depending on how you've designed your ships, again because its a voxel game using odd blocks to represent ideas of ship componenets, there is a learning curve even on how AI works on a boat, unless its been changed you must add certain AI controller blocks to work with other AI blocks, its not quite as complicated as it sounds but does take a bit of reading and guide sloothing. That being said, because of its complexity with parts it will allow users to create very cool and unusual concept vehicles.
-Bugs and crashing, it's at a minimal if any, and if memory serves me correct earlier versions were relitively bug and crash free, though again if I remember correctly from the peroid I played when I purchased, it did not include multiplayer of any sort less sharing vessels, so I cannot speak for the potential bugginess of the MP aspects of the game.
DO I recommend this for you?:
--------------------------------
If you enjoy playing creator mode more so in minecraft for the end results of aesthetics or loved tekkit because of the layers of complexity from new blocks it added and how they worked together, and you can learn a 'new way of building' with some keys that almost seem to have purpose behind their strangeness after you remember/figure out why, then yes I do recommend this title to you, especially if you're a fan of naval combat.

Gametime: 16hrs - Story Mode/DLC finished.
This game has been an absolute blast, now I'm onto the Revelations DLC and the challenges in the main game (possibly New Game+ too!)
Having finished the story mode, I can confirm this game is brilliant in some ways but also has its downsides.
The combat system is fantastic, as a fan of the Devil May Cry series I have to say that even in comparison to my favourite games it is an absolute scorcher of an achievement. The graphics are gorgeous, and the characters are comical in some places but also keep their dark, evil, sorrowful or otherwise just plain crazy characteristics. Boss fights, what can I say? Easily some of the most fun I've had (the fight against the corrupt Toy Makers is probably my favourite, that character as well had my emotions sparking). The addition of camera control is great, only fixed in certain places unlike the original that was pretty much fixed the entire way through. The voice acting yet again is incredible, and although the story isn't as good as the first game it still gets you grinning, frowning and eager to hear more.
I found the game unfortunately to be quite short, it took me just over two days to complete the story mode, but then again most modern games lack a lengthy story mode (this game DOES have challenges including an arena of some sort that I'm yet to try). The stealth sections are a bit of a hinderance also...but, people who say they ruin the game are just making mountains out of mole hills. Yes, they're a bit frustrating but they're few and far between and don't set the overall theme of the game. An added challenge isn't always a bad thing, this time it was just a bit unwanted. The environments aren't as gothic or pretty as the first game, but the modern day setting isn't necessarily a bad thing and the story gets you to grips with the sorrow and anger Dracula is forced to put up with.
The DLC is great, playing as Dracula's son is a blast. He doesn't feel as OP as his Father, but still packs a mighty swing with that sword.
I would definitely recommend getting a gamepad for this game...mainly because as a (until recently) keyboard user, I found myself COMPLETELY unable to navigate the menus in the travel book as my key binds for some reason wouldn't respond! That was very annoying, but then again it's a console game brought to the PC so I suppose there's some room for improvement and alteration.
My only other sort of let-down is the replayability, if you complete the game on one difficulty and want to play through again, you have to either select New Game+ in which you HAVE to play the hardest difficulty, or delete your current save game...or not, I found out this morning that you can change the difficulty setting in the options menu, MY BAD! That's cleared that up, still, replayability is definitely better on the first game.
I would absolutely recommend getting this, if you loved the first one and are expecting this to be the same then you'll be disappointed...but then again, what's the point in paying 29.99 for a sequel that feels EXACTLY the same as the first?

Let me first say that I am a huge fan of the first two games, the Longest Journey and the Longest Journey: Dreamfall. They are my favorite games of all time and I have played through them several times. If you expect this sequel to be anything like the first two, like I did, then you will be sorely disappointed.
I played the Longest Journey and the Longest Journey: Dreamfall because of the compelling and interesting storyline, the gorgeous scenery and because I grew attached to the characters themselves. They are the type of games that let you escape into a dazzling and mysterious world with interesting characters that you can't get enough of.
Dreamfall Chapters started out pretty well in the very beginning of Book 1, but as the game progressed it very quickly became obvious that the developers of the game wanted to shove their political views down your throat. The political agenda became very clear. For example, Zoë is engaged in a political campaign helping a socialist party, Zoë has a Marxist best friend and then every other girl in the street is walking around with hijab on.
I did not buy this game to play "Politics Simulator 2015" or "Baby Simulator" (if you played this game you will know what I'm talking about).
Dreamfall Chapters is otherwise visually gorgeous, but it lacks gameplay,story and puzzles. It also lacks clues to lead you to the next point.
Let me also point out that the dialogue is a lot of times vulgar and forced. They manage to squeeze in profanity where it's not needed. Dropping the f-bomb and saying sh*t several times in a single sentence does not make good or "cool" dialogue. It seems like they are using profanity as filler to make up for a poor script. The Longest Journey and Dreamfall are not known for vulgar dialogue and it is not something that needed to be added.
The developers have turned a fantastic game series into something bland and stereotypical with political propaganda. Zoë has become someone I don't recognize, doing and saying things that don't fit her personality as I know her from the Longest Journey: Dreamfall. I am also sad about April Ryan.
I won't recommend this game to fans of the series, but I will likely continue with Book 3 because I invested time in the other chapters and want to see if there is some hope on the horizon. I doubt it though.
I will replay the original games but not this one.
Summary:
+Visually gorgeous
+Zoës updated model is beautiful (except her new haircut in book 3).
-Blatant political agenda
-Lacks story
-Lacks gameplay
-Lacks puzzles
-Poor and forced dialogue
-Vulgar language
-Short chapters

Book 3 left my mouth agape. It was VERY short. I have no further comments as my opinion have not changed for the better.

It is a successor to a series I never played, but the previous games are on steam for the interested people.
"Dreamfall Chapters" is a game which heavily features lore & choice rather then (fps) action.
You do not get to fight or sprint around like mad.
Instead you walk/run around, talking a lot to people, looking at the world & try to solve puzzles as 'a normal person' would. Conversation choices & actions feature
in this.
The game in essence tells a story and you get to make various choices during the game on how it progresses. These can be small or big choices like lying to someone, or reacting to situations in certain ways.
If you like lore, choices and a lot of ingame discussions this is the game for you. If you like mindless action, you might as well stop reading here.
Another big point is simply this.. female protagonist.
Most games either have a male protagonist or, incase of a female one, sexualise her.
As roughly half the gamers out there are female, its nice to see more games which also include a female protagonist.
Note that NOT all chapters of the game are released YET. (again, indie company.)
While some question this choice it means they already get a income in sales on the chapters which are released, to keep making the new chapters.
This makes sure the chapters we already have are NOT RUSHED.
Not rushing a game release is rare in these days.
While not, per se, up to par with triple A games, the graphics do look rather stunning. The occasional glitch can occur, but ive seen those in games of any 'quality'.
Considering even that this game is made by a small indie developer who even had to kickstart it, I would say we very much get more than expected.
The game has its own style, which works well for the story in question.
The main 2 characters tend to change looks and clothes depending on situation (and chapter), further adding to some realism.
I personally did not experience any fps issues. (but of course your mileage may vary)
ACTUALLY with further testing it seems on my i7 970 + GTX 770, my fps on the 'awesome' setting is averaging around 30-45. I just do not notice due to gsync)
The game has good music, nice voiceacting and plenty of ambient sounds to make you feel at home, or better said in the world.
It is at times however hard to hear voice from music and ambient. Some tweaking in your settings may help against this.
I left subtitles on to make sure I did not miss any words in sentences, as the default config can make that happen. Other noises then the voices talking can drown out the convo at times.
So some minor tweaks needed on what is otherwise good music and sound. (on a 2.0 speaker & headset setup. I did not test more speakers)
Controls are fine and work well for the game IF you account for one big thing.
For MANY functions its NOT HOLD KEY but CLICK KEY. There, if you are used to games where you hold keys I just saved you a headache.
While functions like movement and running require you to HOLD they key, function like using and opening the RADIAL MENU requires you to CLICK and not hold.
If you hold the (mouse)key the radial menu will open and do... nothing. You are supposed to click it open and then click on the option you want to perform.
This method of control is absolutely no problem in playing the game as long as you know that its click.

At times, I really like playing Dreamfall Chapters, while at other times, I'd rather claw my own eyes out. Only two choices here - (Recommend) Yes or No. I have to choose No, because the drawbacks below outnumber and outweigh the benefits.
+ The basic "choice and consequence" mechanism and different story paths are the meat and potatoes in this genre, even though the consequence part seems minimal so far into the story.
+ Some likable characters, such as Mira and Shitbot.
+ The male protagonist is interesting and could use more screen time.
- The large areas are like labyrinths and a total ♥♥♥♥♥ to navigate, even with the laughable "running" speed. The maps are completely useless.
- The amount of running back and forth, all over and over again, is totally out of control.
- The dialogue is almost impossible to hear at some points, while it's crystal clear in others. Even if you turn down the ambient noise and music volume, the main character's mumbling from the bottom of a metallic barrell is impossible to hear over the maddening, repeating cries of street vendors. How could they screw this up this badly???
- Endless, pointless dialogue between playable chapters that goes from nowhere to nowhere.
- Completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ political theme. The story forces the player character to do campaign work for the developers' favourite political ideology - one that has been in steady decline everywhere for several years now but is supposed to be on top again 200 years into the future. The alternatives? Marxists and fascists. 200 years into the future. I mean, seriously???
- The female protagonist is a wimp and the infantile story needs a spine, while the writers need to lay off the weed.
- The graphics engine looks less than spectacular, but makes the cooling fans in the graphics card whine at full speed.
If you enjoy adventure, I'd really recommend giving Dreamfall Chapters a try.

I am not a fan of the adventure time tv series but I bought this game because it was cheap as ♥♥♥♥ and it looked like a Zelda clone, and not having the latest Nintendo consoles makes me always miss Zelda.
The game really is a big love letter to Zelda, specifically A Link to the Past - for example, the first boss directly resembles the Armos Knights. There are lots of other little callbacks to Zelda, some specifically designed to mess with a Zelda player's expectations. But a game like this can't be carried on references alone, and despite being a licensed game its quite adequate.
With this game Wayforward delivers dungeons that could fit right into a Zelda game, with an aesthetic change. These are the highlights of the experience - these dungeons avoid the simple, linear layouts of the worst Zelda dungeons (and of many bad Zelda clones). However, there is a distinct lack of difficult puzzles (though I imagine this has to do with being a licensed game for a cartoon).
The dungeons may be pretty good, but that's just part of the game, and the rest of the game isn't as interesting. Its not that the Overworld lacks things to do, but so many of those things are just collection sidequests, like Kinstone Pieces or Secret Seashells from the Zelda games. Almost everything else to do in the overworld is required by the story. And the overworld itself is just kind of boring. Its small and it lacks a sense of scale or grandeur. You climb no mountains, swim in no lakes, and traverse no deserts. The overworld is effectively just four variants of "forest area".
There are other issues besides the overworld. There's a lack of story. The story and writing that's there is geared toward Adventure Time fans as far as I can tell. The game has a tendency to crash during loading screens. And really there's just a lack of interesting ideas in the game. It goes a bit too far in trying to be a tribute and ends up doing nothing unique of its own.
Do I recommend this game?
Probably not. Its not that its really bad, its just that there are other similar games that you could be playing instead.
If you have a Nintendo console and there's any Zelda you haven't yet completed, that's probably more worth your time.
If you don't and need a Zelda fix, you could try a better and more unique Zelda clone like Oceanhorn, Anodyne, Darksiders, or Shantae and the Pirate's Curse
Really I'd only recommend this game if you've already played all those games or if you're a fan of the show. Or if its the only one you can afford for some weird reason.

So I'm just going to list out the Pro's and Con's
Pros
- There is a lot of good dialogue, Hard to follow at first but It includes lots of references to Japanese culture and there was even some funny references that are easy to miss(There was a Ghous Busters Reference!)
- You don't have to constantly grind
- This game is generally cheap (I got it for 50cents), Well worth the 7-9 hours of gameplay you can get out of it, and if you don't like it there are trading cards that at the moment are worth 8-10 cents so you would essentially only be out 25 cents if you really didn't like the game
Cons
-The controls are a bit irritating, you can use the mouse but it's much easier to just play with your right hand on Shift, Z, and X and your left on the arrow keys because the WASD keys don't do anything.
- Game ends on a black screen and the save doesn't even carry over to the next game
- No progress tracking
- Some things are way overpowered, For examples Later in the game fighting Takumi's they have a sonic wave or blast that can confuse your entire party so they solely hit your people and it lasts at least three turns, effectively killing your party if the wave hits them all. There s also a Destruction scroll that you can buy for 2000 currency and it takes 90% of your enemies health (works on all bosses so it will make you win a hard boss in about two turns after using the scroll)

If you like Tower Defense games but are sick of waiting for each wave..this game is for you. Being able to not only be strategic with traps but have the control over fighting the waves of orcs yourself truly makes this game a must buy for tower defense fans!

As much as i like the game and want to write a positive review, it's simply impossible...
I played a 7 hour session with a friend on coop, and well... No positive feedback of it. Game kept crashing between us, throwing host forth and back. Though as host it seemed to crash way less than the connected people. The coop does not save AT ALL, meaning that if first both crashed, or we had game breaking situations (not being able to pick up items, loot desks, take quests, etc.), we could not restart as we would be sent back to day 1 with no progress.
With the game advertising as a game with multiplayer and coop, this is definetly not a complete product and should not be sold as such. If you intend to buy this for coop purposes, I'd suggest saving your time and money as its only frustration to get from here. Close to no fun in the games current state.
TL;DR
-Game crashes a lot (even more for connected people on coop)
-Game breaking glitches that prevents looting and interaction
-No auto saves on Coop, if all dc's, you start at day 1 again
Save your money for now, not worth its current price at a stage like this.

The game, or concept (as the devs call it) is okay. I've thought a lot about whether I want to give a thumb up or down and I'm not happy with either option. I got it for 1,79€ which might be okay if you really like it. But I have to admit that I'm quite disappointed.
As it stands the game doesn't deliver a reason to be played.
As other reviews already said - it totally lacks in content und optimization. And I thought about what I feel it's missing:
Firstly, it definitely needs more settings. An adjustable camera - it's really hard to see what's coming on the road. Even if it would be like in Trackmania with 3 different positions to choose from.
Audio sliders for not only the music, but also the car noises and SFX would be awesome.
The game definitely needs graphic options. I just played for 20 minutes but now I've got a huge headache from those horizontal lines and all the different lights everywhere. Please give us an options menu with ways to enable and disable all the different visual effects used. This is literally the first game I've played that game me a headache just because of the visuals.
And a menu with a tracklist where you can listen/preview the tracks and disable/enable them for the game. Maybe even add support for own music or spotify/soundcloud. maybe give us an adjustable RNG - like how many events (roadblocks etc.) occur and such.
It's just "Hey, you can drive as long as you want - or can. Look at the street (or the blue bar beneath the car) and enjoy the music (if it suits your taste)."
Reasons for playing could include achievements, multiple play modes, maybe even a small storymode. driving through different parts of the country with levels getting harder. and a happy ending where you are actually able to save the girl.
just quick ideas for another play mode: relaxation mode, where the girl can't die and you just drive and boost the way you want.
The game could also get Steam Workshop support. Player-made mods would be awesome. More car models, different scenery textures, other modifiers.
This game has so much potential that just screams to be used!
Please make it happen!
P.s.: Nothing happened to me after 8 minutes. Not even after 16. Scamaz.

This game is actually a better game compared to an empty game like No Man's Sky, which is receiving updates but it's a far inferior game in contrast to Starbound. Starbound was an appealing game for me, I like the visuals and the 64bit-ish style to it, It a lot of times reminded me of another game that I love Terraria, maybe a more updated version of the game. By the way this game has a absolutely beautiful soundtrack. Every song in the OST is good. There is also a lot of versatility in the game, with crafting and exploring planets even though some of them are the same because it's procedurely generated. The planets each all have uniquely cool looking animals to fight. And villages to explore, with merchants that can trade items to you. And Base Building is SO versatile in this game, I spent my first 15 hours gathering materials for my base.
The storyline for this game is overall okay, I thought it was fine. The Ruin is a cool final boss to fight. But one of the bosses that might have disappointed me the most was Big Ape, this Apex dictator that was set up to be a huge threat but then we find out that he's just a hologram and you fight his head.
The RNG loot system in this game is good, a lot of the armors and the weapons look really cool. They have a lot of meticulous detail put into them.
However with the multiplayer aspect, it creates a lot of lag with generating the world. I received constant crashes when I wanted to play with friends. Multiplayer is just unoptimized but it can receive updates and become more playable. But for now unless you're modding the game it isn't that playable. And it's not because of my Network I checked that several times.
Speaking of modding, Nexus offers a ton of mods that are cool. After beating the game 3 or 4 times and just playing through it I started modding the game through Nexus. The steam workshop also offers some good mods that I like, like Frackin' Universe which is like a completely new expansion that adds new planets, guns and armor! It's amazing how expansive this mod is.
Overall, I would recommend at least trying this game it is a fine space game.

I loved the first Castlevania LoS. I was really excited the moment they shown the first trailer for the sequal over two years ago that I was highly anticipating this next installment.  When the reviews started coming out for the sequal I was upset what they were saying when I had high hopes for this game.  The negative comments seem to over embelish the quality of the game that it would get a D minus rating over issues such as the stealth portion, a shallow ending, and boring environments.  After playing this game I thought whoever was playing this game seem to be as bad as the critics, reviewing movies in that they are blind to what is an actual great movie when the majority movie going public seems to love the movie.  This game my fellow gamers is a great quality game.  Gone the fixed camera angels, you now have a free camera you can manipulate around the character to get a better view of Dracula and his environment.  The environment is breathtaking, The amount of work and detail that went into Dracula's castle and Castlevania City makes you take a moment to study the detail and architecture. The environment also reminds me they were trying a Castlevania SOTN where the city and castle are connected to each other. The gameplay is very smooth especially the combat portion. Gone are the Combat Cross, light and shadow magic systems in place are the Shadow Whip, Void Sword, and Chaos Claws.  My favorite weapon is Chaos Claws simply because it reminds me of using Hercules Gauntlets in God of War.  But interchanging between weapons is a fluid motion you can make awesome combos.  If I had to make any complaints about this game is the story.  It didn't feel fulfilling (ie character development)  especially the end.    I was disappointed with the last boss Satan. It would have been nice to fight him head on vice using (SPOILER ALERT) someone close to Dracula. Also I wish the ending had an epilogue like the first one. It sort of left a question mark on Dracula's fate.  Like I said the grips that people had of this game is minor.  The stealth system was interesting idea but in some place poorly executed. Like when Dracula is already powerful why does he need to avoid Satan's Elite Armored brutes? Some of the stealth puzzles can prove irritating for some people have to start over and over again namely sneaking past Pan's brother.  But after observing other players in how they pass him it became quite easy and a little scarey lol.  This is great game which I highly recommend if your fan of this genre or God Of War type games.  Additionally I am re-playing this game again. This is one of those games I hope they make a movie out of this game use this plot for the story.

At times, I really like playing Dreamfall Chapters, while at other times, I'd rather claw my own eyes out. Only two choices here - (Recommend) Yes or No. I have to choose No, because the drawbacks below outnumber and outweigh the benefits.
+ The basic "choice and consequence" mechanism and different story paths are the meat and potatoes in this genre, even though the consequence part seems minimal so far into the story.
+ Some likable characters, such as Mira and Shitbot.
+ The male protagonist is interesting and could use more screen time.
- The large areas are like labyrinths and a total ♥♥♥♥♥ to navigate, even with the laughable "running" speed. The maps are completely useless.
- The amount of running back and forth, all over and over again, is totally out of control.
- The dialogue is almost impossible to hear at some points, while it's crystal clear in others. Even if you turn down the ambient noise and music volume, the main character's mumbling from the bottom of a metallic barrell is impossible to hear over the maddening, repeating cries of street vendors. How could they screw this up this badly???
- Endless, pointless dialogue between playable chapters that goes from nowhere to nowhere.
- Completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ political theme. The story forces the player character to do campaign work for the developers' favourite political ideology - one that has been in steady decline everywhere for several years now but is supposed to be on top again 200 years into the future. The alternatives? Marxists and fascists. 200 years into the future. I mean, seriously???
- The female protagonist is a wimp and the infantile story needs a spine, while the writers need to lay off the weed.
- The graphics engine looks less than spectacular, but makes the cooling fans in the graphics card whine at full speed.
If you enjoy adventure, I'd really recommend giving Dreamfall Chapters a try.

UPDATE AFTER FINISHING BOOK 5:
Not a bad game overall, but greatly disconnected from The Longest Journey, sadly. Even from Dreamfall, but to a lesser degree.
Sadly, the developer is encouraging fans to post preferably positive reviews in order to boost up sales. I loved the prequels as much as I'm dissapointed with what this game has become. For the game itself, the development process, *the developer's attitude*, the change of publishing format from what was originally stated in the kickstarter, and I can go on, and on, and on.

Friend, do not give up at the start. If you are looking for an impressive hook, it fails completely at it. Do you recall Zoë? If you do not, many things in this segment will confuse and potentially upset you, as they did me. I took the time, after understanding just about nothing, to play Dreamfall:TLJ. I had played the original eons before, sparking my interest in this little thing, but I never got around to playing its sequel. To get a good grasp of Zoë's story, I'm afraid you need to. And if you have played the game, as I did, it will still frustrate you, as it should.
Dreamfall: TLJ is perhaps the greatest example of blueballs I have ever seen immortalized in video games. The first half of the story establishes the character and the story, the next fourth sets the stage for the climax, and then... the final fourth of the game shows you just how horrifically rushed the game was. We rush through so much character development, so much of the climax (we effectively end on it), and the denouement is nonexistent: perhaps one story thread finds an actual resolution in the game, while many--such as Zoë's depression and feelings of aimlessness--are left open in the air. Completely unanswered, without so much as an indication of left or right.
Here is where Chapters enters in and leads us on our journey. We meet Zoë again, and we expect the same old girl. And we do get it, in terms of the voice acting: the delivery of the lines is close, as well as her actual diction. She sounds like the same character, and certainly seems to see the world similar to her earlier version. Of course, she also suddenly has MAGIC DREAM POWERS to give the player something to do through our first chapter... because it, in itself, spends a lot of time TELLING US the resolutions to last game's questions. The dream sequence is not too terrible of an offender, beyond that it introduces us to a 'past Zoë' that never existed. Perhaps there were dialogue paths in the predecessor that I missed, but at no point was she a conceited, self-absorbed ♥♥♥♥♥. I'm not really sure why the first chapter ends with us 'accepting' this old Zoë that was just have to accept exists. Maybe she was a jerk before she quite her studies. Maybe the developers totally weren't trying to introduce some canned drama to the mix of an otherwise completely boring chapter.
Kian Alvane is the other focal character of the game, and he is something of a tabula rasa. Let's be real, for a second: his character was an expense they just had to let go of in D:TLJ. All of his development was clearly supposed to come in the rising action and climax of the game where YOU KNOW WHO gets the spear, but it is so horribly rushed and his character shifts his ideologies so radically and so unrealistically... does a word of what he said in that game matter? The only thing of real importance would maybe be his affection for YOU KNOW WHO, but in this game he has deer girl. So really, nothing again. Here's the thing, though: this is good. In fact, this is great. Not at all understanding who Kian was from the predecessor did not really impact his story in the least, and I was so much more drawn in by it than Zoë's. Kian's story, in the first and the second book, is comprised of many different tropes all strung together in the unique canon of TLJ. It is, however, done -well-. The characters are fun and interesting, and though Kian is a fairly predictable character, that does not really matter. Honestly, his voice actor carries the role. The dilemmas he is put into are interesting, and the character's responses feel believable. Unfortunately, the first chapter rushes you into this dilemmas and spoon-feeds you tension, giving you only a few points at which to get a feel for the world or for however you would prefer to play Kian. While I was much more interested in his story than Zoë's at this point in the game (and playing D:TLJ does not change this), I still found it incredibly boring and insultingly similar to the telltale games formula. And there's no escaping this: every time you see 'CHARACTER WILL REMEMBER YOUR ACTIONS' flash atop the screen, you should be mildly frustrated at how horribly lazy that approach is.
That is, of course, until the final chapter of book one. Its introduction is fairly bad, I will admit. A cutscene that would make metal gear solid rolls across, that TELLS THE PLAYER DIRECTLY THE ANSWER TO ALL OF THOSE PLOTHOOKS THAT WERE LEFT HANGING. This enraged me so much that I put the game down for a couple days--it is downright lazy storytelling. Zoë speaks to a counselor about what's happened to her, what she recalls, and what she does not recall--as well as the effect of her lengthy coma on her personal life and beliefs. Honestly, the consequences of that are fairly interesting--especially how her relationship with her father becomes more muddled (and this is one of the few instances where playing the earlier game changes something's impact). The problem is that we see none of them, and we are told absolutely every last one of them. Her therapist's office is also terribly boring, really emphasizing just how incredibly boring all of the talking angles are: someone stands in perspective, their head sometimes moving to 3/4ths as their eyes move around randomly. Sometimes they show emotion, but honestly the voice acting carries this♥♥♥♥♥♥ So. Hard. Think Bioware level of 'model behaves awkwardly,' and tone it down just a little and you're here.
This all changes the instant you talk with the doctor or head out onto the street, and I mean this to the depths of my heart. The dialogue with the doctor is fun, believable, and Zoë's thoughts, presented to you before you make a decision, are honestly entertaining. The worldbuilding of Stark is incredibly visual, with a definite cyberpunk aesethetic revealed. And when the characters are used as tools to further the worldbuilding--describing, for example, the role of the EYE--it's done in a completely believable way. The characters are not looking at the camera and winking with a grin; they're living out their days. You are allowed to roam around a city's section and get acquainted for yourself with the nuances of the future. Given how closely the game modelled the incredibly restrictive and boring TTG model to this point, this caught me completely off-guard. And I almost had a heart attack when my seemingly inconsequential choices--you know, beyond the incredibly tacky YOUR CHOICE HERE WILL MATTER sign--actually altered the way that the plot progressed. This is perhaps what won me over the most at this point. Little details have considerable impacts. Yes, the direction of the overarching story does not change, but the stuff inbetween is altered. Characters take notice of your actions, and there are consequences in how they regard you. They also have different value systems--some prefer being lied to, while the others enjoy a brutal, hard truth. It's a refreshing touch to a genre that increasingly takes every effort not to create branching dialogue trees. My one complaint with the Stark sections is the journal: it tells you important things about what's going on in Zoë's life, and while they are interesting... they are also not really in line with Zoë. It's pretty obvious that somehow April Ryan is writing your notes, because they're written in the same eccentric way. April's diary in TLJ made sense and fit her character; Zoë's sortof sticks out like a sore thumb.
Book two really won me over. Chapter 3, that last bit with Zoë, showed me potential: cool worldbuilding and realistic dialogue. When we start book three, we start with Kian. And this is really all I need to talk about: Kian's shot at a nonlinear environment. It's great. Characters are tropes, but excellently done tropes. I am out of space. Give this game time, and you will not be disappointed. It has flaws, but  weather the storm and you can be sure to be entertained by your choices' consequences.

Boy, oh boy, do I LOVE this game!
If you loved the Choose Your Own Adventure books as a kid, this game is for you! Dreamfall Chapters is the third in a series of games (including The Longest Journey and Dreamfall The Longest Journey). After playing and really liking the first two games, I was excited to try this latest addition to the trilogy.
The graphics of this game are so beautiful, and the story is so compelling, playing truly takes you into another world. You really end up caring about the characters in the game (you play as two different people, switching as the game goes on). Buy it, play it, love it!

It would be hard to describe this game without pointing at any top down Zelda like because it has every aspect of the kind. Though where games like Ittle dew would be more puzzle focus, this one is more about action and collectibles.
Basically you control Finn, who's been sent by PB to investigate the royal governance shenanigans of the nameless kingdom. But as you arrive, you realise that you have to find back a bunch of princesses by beating dungeons and bad guys.
You will quickly be left on an overworld map to explore and will find a lot of minigames hut with some challenges to complete, caves to wander, stuff to collect and merchants to trade with. All of that will be populated with a lot of characters from the show, all having their little catch phrase that will steal a smile from you, as they all have concerns and, eventually, side tasks to offer in their own personnal ways.
But worry not, for Jake is here to support you, and will take the role of a Shield or a couple of other 'handy' tools like a grab or a slap to pick up items, hit enemis or interract with switches to unlock parts of certain dungeons.
Just like any other zelda, Finn's progression will be tied to the items and collectibles he will get through the game.
You will have a set of hearts to symbolize your lifepoints, that can be upgraded by collecting heart quarters, a sword and an inventory that will soon fill up with a lot of consumable items you can bind to buttons to use during the game.
Some of them will be like, bombs that can breach through walls, a boomerang to stun enemies and bring items back at you, a grapling of some sort, plastic bags that serve as bottle to keep items you can grab... You have a gauntlet and keys and boss keys, dungeons maps to find, chests, compasses... Well, the usual you expect from a top down Zelda game.
Truth is, while it clearly uses all of the codes from that type of games, some of the mecanics, while not being necessarly fresh like the grab or gauntlet, will be cleverly used in each dungeons and path that you unlock later on. Every key items gained leads to new places you'll be able to access and so on.
There's also tint of derision and self awareness in certain aspect of the game, like when you can throw items to a fairy pool to upgrade them and decide to throw Jake. Or the way some npcs will conveniently notice that they are just doing the regular tropes of that kind of games. All in all it gives a nice feeling of things being fun and, sometimes downright silly, just like the early seasons of the show. Though, if you expect some sort of lore building, revelations or plot twist of the actual serie, you won't find anything here for the plot is more a pretext to justify the exploration gameplay.
Technically, it runs okay on a regular computer (with a few fps drops on a few zones), though it is clearly calibrated to play with a controler. So screw your mouse and keyboard.
Some of the mecanics works well, you won't be unfairly stuck because some items refuses to work the way it was intended to be, at least. Only exception, i'd say, would be Jake's shield; for i realised that it was kind of hard to use in tense situations and not so much efficient. To be more precise, you have to hold LT to raise it in the direction you are facing, but you can't rotate your character afterward, which makes blocking tough since you have to face the projectiles and raise. A setting like in Zelda 3, where the shield was passive and triggered while facing the right direction, would have worked better.Or like, if you were able to reorientate Finn or just, move slowly when shield is raised so i can have more control over it.
The top down camera in 3D background with 2D characters, projectiles and enemies makes certain actions or situations hard to gauge, perform or dodge too. It happens that you get hit by a bullet or an AoE while thinking you were out of range or, like, under an enemy when actually not.
You will also encounter a bunch of crashes on the overworld here and there, especially on the north west zones past the second dungeon, for some reasons. So i'd recommand to save your game often.
So... Is the game worth playing ? Well, if you like the show and top down RPGs, i'd say yes. The lore is pretty well rendered, there is a lot of references to episodes of the serie everywhere, either being items or backgrounds, npcs or quests. A bunch of secrets to find, an item delivery side quest that is comon to every zelda, dungeons are okay and the end is kind of fun, actually.
Every npcs you'll encounter will be voice acted by the actual actors from the show (except for Treetrunk, which is really, really sad !). It's well enough written to excuse some unpolished stability here and there. But the core mecanic already made its proof so you won't be badly surprised.
Though you have to keep in mind that the game is short, like, really short. I spent 10 hours to complete everything, from storyline to hidden items. If you rush it you can probably finish it in only 4 or 5.

Pros:
+Art style
+Multiplayer pretty enjoyable
+Gameplay is certainly fun but can have bad moments
+Active devs
+Honestly haven't experienced any crashes or bugs (see cons)
Cons:
-Various QOL changes needed to not make the game a pain at some points
-Needs a prison creator like the first (I believe this will eventually be added... like the first)
-Gameplay can get frustrating sometimes

So what's the difference between this game and the first? Well there is a few.
Firstly the prisons will have different ways to escape them in that, you will have the original way of just getting to edge of the board and you will escape, however you will also have others ways to esape by using certain items in a certain area. To me this is a great way to either plan a quick and easy route for those who want to try out all the prsions the game has to offer (or for those who want to speed run), but it's also great for those who want to plan out a escape route like they did in the first game. (I will also add that you will get a key for clearing the level in a different way. The more keys you get the more levels you unlock).
Secondly the prisons are not as harsh as they could be seen in the first game. What I mean is that if a guard saw a hole, you would automatic be thrown into solidarity and everything would reset. This would mean most of the time you have to start all over again or just reload the game file. In this game if they do see a hole or a chipped wall, they will not target you personally (unless they see you digging or chipping). Rather the prison security become more harsher and will fix the problem area. They will come with attack dogs and if these dogs smell contraband on you they will attack you. So in some ways the prison will get harder if you make mistakes, but at the same time it doesn't feel as harsh as it did in the first game (this could be seen both a good or bad thing).
I will also add they have levels which have to escape in one day. These levels are more different than your standard levels. You collect items, you make tools and you try to hide from the guards and escape. These levels are more for those times you just want a quick game without planning too much.
As for multiplayer, I haven't played with others at this time, however there have been problems with that side of the game (which I believe have been fixed).
However there have been some bugs which need to be fixed (for example if you take a bed sheet they will not replace that sheet meaning that if you lose a lot of bed sheets, you could be running into problem when crafting certain items). UPDATE: This has been fixed.
Overall I really like this game and I hope to see some new features over time. But again there are some bugs which do need to be fixed, other than that, I'm happy with what this game has provided.

It's hard to click yes on recommended.  I more... do not NOT recommend it.
As infinity people have said before me, the game currently has 5 tiers.  I only just started playing a few weeks or even singular week back, so I'm not aware of any time when progress wasn't constrained.
Tiers 1-3 are recursive, as the capitalists would say.  They feed into themselves as you go, pretty typical AdCap fare.
On the side of all this, you generate... bodies.  Not in a "you're in a planet with a surplus of potatoes" kind of way which would lead to a massive population explosion while there was excessive copulation and no starvation, but in a "you've passed this milestone so now you make 2 more comrades per second" kind of way.
This is disconcerting- I generate 3e14 potatoes a second, while generating about 50 people.  thats 300000000000000 potatoes, if i counted my zeroes right, for every 50 humans.   Divided, that's 6000000000000 potatoes each.  At a potato a day, that's 16438356164.38 years worth of potatoes.  Go ahead and eat 100 potatoes per day and knock the decimal forward two places.  You're still probably good.
Goofy communist life math about how they have some 16 billion potatoes to barter in their lifetime, each, per annum, that's not the killer.
The final two tiers do not self feed.  So you need to wait for the arbitrary-tron to generate enough bodies to upgrade these zones... forever.
I don't see a lot of zoning in this game.  It's possible that communist utopia is your only goal and restricting the limits on your final two tiers gives the game longevity... but I don't play clickers for forced restrictions.  I want bigger numbers, all the time.  Not waiting for 1000 comrades to spawn so I can hire one tier one ammo, so that I can get to 10,000 (i'm guessing here) of those to make 1 tier two upgrade... the thought of making a second upgrade literally gives me nausea.
So long winded whinge aside-  here's a bit of pro.  They do encourage actual clicking, daily.  A lot of clickers to date seem to lose an integral interaction factor once you hit a certain point, and you're more just leveling stuff because you reset.  Here, there is a reward system that encourages you to actually want to "play", as it were, at least for a bit.  I think this is a significant development, and want to encourage it.  Game development not being my current career path, and hyperhippo not being my current employer, I'm not instantly sure how this could be integrated into the "older" system.
All of that said, I think if nothing else it's worth diving into this game.  This is still EA, and free, and if they do knock out all of the kinks, you'll likely be happy you had a head start.
And if they don't, the worst thing that happened is you started up a clicker and never came back.  You're already playing a clicker game, it's not like you don't have free time!

This game is actually a better game compared to an empty game like No Man's Sky, which is receiving updates but it's a far inferior game in contrast to Starbound. Starbound was an appealing game for me, I like the visuals and the 64bit-ish style to it, It a lot of times reminded me of another game that I love Terraria, maybe a more updated version of the game. By the way this game has a absolutely beautiful soundtrack. Every song in the OST is good. There is also a lot of versatility in the game, with crafting and exploring planets even though some of them are the same because it's procedurely generated. The planets each all have uniquely cool looking animals to fight. And villages to explore, with merchants that can trade items to you. And Base Building is SO versatile in this game, I spent my first 15 hours gathering materials for my base.
The storyline for this game is overall okay, I thought it was fine. The Ruin is a cool final boss to fight. But one of the bosses that might have disappointed me the most was Big Ape, this Apex dictator that was set up to be a huge threat but then we find out that he's just a hologram and you fight his head.
The RNG loot system in this game is good, a lot of the armors and the weapons look really cool. They have a lot of meticulous detail put into them.
However with the multiplayer aspect, it creates a lot of lag with generating the world. I received constant crashes when I wanted to play with friends. Multiplayer is just unoptimized but it can receive updates and become more playable. But for now unless you're modding the game it isn't that playable. And it's not because of my Network I checked that several times.
Speaking of modding, Nexus offers a ton of mods that are cool. After beating the game 3 or 4 times and just playing through it I started modding the game through Nexus. The steam workshop also offers some good mods that I like, like Frackin' Universe which is like a completely new expansion that adds new planets, guns and armor! It's amazing how expansive this mod is.
Overall, I would recommend at least trying this game it is a fine space game.

As the sequel to Castlevania: Lords of Shadow, one of the most memorable games of 2010 I played. This game holds up very well and takes advantage of the modern setting it takes place in pretty well.
That said, it does have flaws, but the main thing is you are not getting a buggy game. I found no bugs, glitches, or problems while playing.
The stealth elements could have been handled better, considering Konami funded this you would think they have *someone* who knows a thing or two about that.
But for what it is worth, the few instances of stealth were handled better than I thought they could have been. I did not find myself confused too easily by some of the stealth sections. But they were, at first, problematic due to the fact that they seemed forced rather than a natural progression of things.
That aside the artwork for the game is awesome, yes, the modern city sections of Castlevania seem out of place. But that is not a flaw to me. Dracula's castle is not Castlevania. The city which is named as such, was built on and around Dracula's castle. So the design changes from running around a beautiful old castle and its environments. To an open city that looks nice, but is not as nice as the castle, is not such a bad thing.
I am not going to obsess over art direction when I want a game's story to make sense. And the story only makes complete sense once you are near the end of the game. At first I thought it was poor writing. But I suspect it was a bit of Play Mirror of Fate to get the full story/purchase our DLC.
Yes, I honestly feel that with the announcement of DLC. I think they *may* have cut story content just for the DLC. But everything comes together towards the end of the main game anyway.
The bosses are fun, the exploration is fun, generally speaking if you are on the fence about this and you played the original. You will LIKE the sequel. I personally love it, and love the way the game came together in the end in my opinion.

The only slightly redeeming factors are some of the story/gameplay elements. The dialogue wheel is excellent, and choices have decent impacts. It just feels like a complete chore most of the time and you'll likely be forced to Google the answer to many puzzles due to how time-consuming they are.
Get any of the Telltale or Dontnod games* instead. Although they may have fewer consequences to your actions, they at least respect your time, gets to the point, are well optimized, have decent controls/camera; and most importantly, provide enjoyable stories with interesting characters whom you learn about through their actions and voluntary dialogue. Unlike Dreamfall Chapters or Syberia 3 (which has the same problems).
* Such as Life is Strange, Walking Dead, Tales from the Borderlands, Wolf Among Us, Game of Thrones, Guardians of the Galaxy, Minecraft Story Mode, Batman, etc.

Based on the video, images, and reviews, I honestly thought I would love this game.
Ha, NOPE!
Almost 60-minutes in and I am literally pulling my hair our ranting about this game to my boyfriend.  Not only is it extremely linear, but it is mind-numbing.  I have learned absolutely nothing about the game nor the characters.  All I do know is that it's very one-way.  Do this.  Do this.  Do this.  DON'T THINK ABOUT EXPLORING--It's not happening!  Or at least it hasn't yet.
Oh and tutorials?  What are is this thing you speak of?  They don't exist.  I have no idea what I'm doing to the point where I, in frustration, button mash with the hopes of magically clicking on or doing the right thing.
Seriously though, it doesn't explain how to interact with the world.  Yes, in theory, it's straightforward.  But in reality?  It's harder than it looks.  For example, right off the bat, someone is falling.  There's no tutorial to show you how to use your powers.  There's nothing that says, "HEY, LOOK AT HER AND CLICK A!"  No, that would make too sense.  It would rather have you frantically look around for a stick, rope, ladder--whatever to save this falling person's life.  Sadly, no such thing exists so you just feel like you've failed the world.
When you eventually realize that A is the only button worth using (assuming you're using an Xbox controller), you think to yourself, "God, I'm dumb."  No, you're really not.  The game really just wants to make you figure everything out on your own.  Which is fine and dandy but... no.  I want to have fun.  Not throw my controller across the room because I failed to save the falling woman 20 times!  Yes, 20 times.  I swear, if we weren't in dreamworld, she would be dead.
Mechanics aside, the main character is annoying.  WHY DO YOU USE THE SAME LINE 100 TIMES?!  Like, yes, we get it.  The dream machine is bad.  CAN YOU BE ORIGINAL!?  How old are you?  5?  Because you honestly sound 5.  Not only that, but she's extremely judgmental.  And, from the sounds of it, she's saved the world before.  SO WHY IS SHE BEING SO EDGY?!  Like, ooooh, the world is calling upon you to save them again.  Better be salty as f--- so everyone knows I'm really just a teenage girl who's useless.
Long rant aside, I do not recommend this game.  Only buy it if it's like... $1.99.  Not worth a penny more.  So glad Steam decide to do this return policy.  I'm definitely getting my money back.
/END RANT/

Also, quick note. I'm not saying the people who wrote these bad reviews are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, because they also make valid points in their reviews and i'm sure most of them enjoy the game just as much as i do.

If you're looking for a civilizations game in space, this isn't it. You might enjoy Galactic Civilizations if that is what you're looking for. This game is based in the same universe as Sid Meier's Civilizations but the mechanics are much simpler.
Story:
It's based upon a future almost immediately proceeding Civilizations: Beyond Earth. You are just beginning to foray into the galaxy with the ability to travel faster than light, thus enabling interstellar commerce. Your goal is to win via military might, cultural or diplomatic prowess, economic finesse, population sustainance, or scientific transcendence.
Mechanics:
Basically you build up a fleet of ships and upgrade them to fill roles you want them to fill. You then use this fleet to win the loyalty of other planets in the galaxy. It's turned based, so once your fleet has exhausted it's resources you will pass the turn to the other players or AI's. The combat is very reminiscent of civilization, but more tactical. It throws in objectives and obstacles and environment hazards. Your ships will have certain abilities based on the upgrades you outfit them with. They can range from Carriers, Battleships, Destroyers, or Corvettes. You start with a corvette, then outfit it with heavier weapons, better sensors, faster engines, stealth, or fighter bays.
When you have influence on a planet, they contribute resources to your pool and you may build improvements on them, such as increased metal production, or science, energy, or even building a wonder to boost your fleet.
Conclusion:
It's a fun game! Not quite as in depth as Civ 5 or BE, but Sid Meier did well with providing us a new game for the universe. I recommend it.
