This is my first time playing a Tales game and I found myself enjoying many aspects of Tales of Symphonia and sometimes downright hating portions of the game.
Combat is often fun and complex, rarely devolving into a boring attack button mash. Dungeon design is also another thing that this game excels at. Dungeon puzzles are interesting and always sastifying to solve. However, one dungeon in particular the Tower of Darkness is an exercise in frustration, so be warned.
Visually, the game's chibi models and city backgrounds are good to look at. However, dungeon and overworld backgrounds are drab and lifeless. The overworld model for monsters were just black tadpoles and frogs which I found to be disappointing.  Unfortunately, there are only 4 or 5 animated cutscenes in the game which is a shame because they are always great to watch.
Story wise, the narrative tends to become a convoluted mess and drags on. I want to love the characters that I am playing but the leads of the game feels underdeveloped and often present themselves as 1-dimensional stereotypes.
Another major gripe that I have with the game is how poorly done the vast majority of the side quests are. Most side quests are very simple travel here and talk to this guy missions with often paltry or zero rewards. Only a few side quests have some story to enjoy. Side quest progress are also not tracked in game(except for the treasure and monster hunt quests) and unless you are reading a complete guide, you will likely miss several side quests.
Overall, I did find myself enjoying the game despite several fundamental problems I had with the game.  I would only recommend this game to anyone willing to bear a lifeless story and drab visuals for a good rpg experience.

This is one of the most interesting games I have ever played. I've never seen a game with RTS elements where you could build custom units to pit into the battlefield. Not only that, they only explode when ammo racked and not when they just get destroyed. Units take damage by blocks and it's not much of a hassle when it comes to replacing them. If you're a fan of commanding an army of vehicles of your own creation, or just want to simulate some awesome epic battles, get this game!

This game is allows for a very diverse play style, though mostly based around an RTS field of commands. If you've ever wanted to have a military simulator that allows for hand crafted units, you should take a look at From the Depths. Even if you don't end up playing a campaign. You can still have fun learning the ways of creating formidable warships or even aircraft and ground vehicles.
As a person who owns a shoddy laptop (a 32 bit windows 7 with 2.98GBs usable RAM and an Intel i5 m480@2.67ghz), I find this game runs relatively well, especially at low resolutions. Although I have problems running large craft, I still find my experience enjoyable.
One thing to note about this game is it's learning curve, so if you do buy it, check out the tutorials (at the time of writing this, it's in the top left region of the main menu).
And finally, before buying this game, I highly recommend watching videos of people playing this game (like Enter Elysium for example). It may allow for a better understanding of how the game works.

Exit 2 Directions is the sequel to the original Exit puzzler game. The concept of this game is the exact same one as the first, you start by controlling different coloured marbles and the objective is to get those marbles onto the correct corresponding coloured panels. The difficulty compared to the first Exit game has most definitely increased and this is the type of game where you really have to use your head to think or risk your marbles being destroyed!
There is an element of pressure while playing this game due to the time limit, the clock starts ticking as soon as you click on your first marble. You also only get a finite amount of lives and if you use up all your lives.. well it's back to level 1 with you! This may seem daunting to the casual player, thankfully though there is an easy mode which completely disregards these features allowing you to play in a much more relaxed way. Additionally if you want to play in an even more time pressured manner there is also a pro mode which decreases the amount of time you have to complete each level!
So what could use improvements? This is of course a very minor thing but i think the menu could be set out a little neater as it looks a little bit messy and at a quick first glance it's hard to tell where to look. I would also love to see a little bit more variety in the soundtracks as i only came across a few different tracks while playing. Most of the soundtracks are quiet and relaxing which doesn't really suit the atmosphere of the game unless you are playing on easy. A change in beat would be a welcome addition.
Overall i think Exit 2 directions is a fun game that everyone can participate in even if you think you might not be very good at puzzle games. For how much content you get with this game i also believe that the price is quite fair.

EXIT 2 - Directions:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
It’s all about placing coloured marbles onto their own coloured squares. The question is, how well do your marbles work? As it’s been some time since I played the original game, it took me a while to put my marbles back together. To be honest with you, during the original game my brain took an un-scheduled vacation.  This time, though, I had it covered. Locks all around my head to keep my brain in, and my marbles are going to help me to solve all the puzzles of EXIT 2 - Directions.
EXIT 2 – Directions is a well-designed puzzle game where you have to clear each level by placing a coloured marble on the respective coloured square.
As you roll on the main menu, you’ll have to select a level of difficulty; casual, normal or pro. In the casual mode, you can take all the time you want to clear a level. In the normal mode, you’ll be given five lives and you’ll have to clear a level within a specific time frame, which is usually around one and a half minutes. The pro mode will provide you with one life and most of the levels must be cleared within thirty seconds.
After selecting your mode of difficulty, you can either choose to play the campaign or the survival mode. The survival mode will be accessible after you successfully clear all five chapters on the campaign mode. Each chapter has ten stages to clear and let me tell you, it’s going to be a brain work out!
In regards to the gameplay, the layout hasn’t changed from the first game. You’ll be presented with a small map with either one or four marbles to place in their respective squares. However, you need to be careful how you proceed. This spring thingy will send your marbles back from whence they came! Make sure your marbles don’t touch the bombs, and use the directional (left, right, up and down) tiles with ease as they might send your marbles to an explosive end.
Graphically, the game looks good and the control are easy to use.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good Graphics
-	50 levels to clear
-	Fun and challenging
-	Good price point
-	Great replay-ability
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No trading cards
-	Can be frustrating
A great puzzle game to have on your game list. Beware, you could lose your marbles!

Lords of shadow 2 is a mess, I mean, it's a good mess, but it's still a mess.
first off, imagine the flat, 2d hallways of symphony of the night, got that in your head? good, now imagine the verticality of those hallways replaced with nothing, they just remove the ascending branching paths, the descending branching paths, and leave you with 1 big hallway that leads into rooms that leads into other smaller hallways that have either health upgrades or lore scrolls.
Imagine, if you will, a limited but extremely faithful translation of SoTN's Metroidvania adapted into a game that's more of a stylish hack'n slash than an rpg, imagine that everything about this proposed symphony of the night successor checked all the right boxes, but did literally only that.
Exploration and backtracking? yes. Good gameplay with nuisance enemies that attack you as you entert certain rooms? check. upgrade system and weapon leveling that's meant to sorta be those rpg elements from SoTN? big ol' check.
Let me explain something to you, this game FEELS like symphony of the night translated into a 3d format, it feels right, it feels sooo ♥♥♥♥ing good. but once the upgrades are all found and the lore stuff is all found, half the game basically vanishes forever. once you play it that first time and explore and get everything, the magic is mostly gone, it still feels right, but the SoTN feeling diminishes when you have all your upgrades'
LoS2 is by no means a bad game or even a bad metroidvania (it's a good one when it does its job) but it suffers from the ever prevailing "Not enough time" syndrome that most AAA games undergo.
The stuff that made LoS1 great is here, that magic system we all love is here, the combat is just as fun if not moreso than ever (I honestly feel it hit its peak) however there are some....err....problems with the story.
Basically by MoF we got our reasoning for dracula's madness, dracula could no longer trust his humanity or the people he loved when he found out his wife hid his son away, dracula suffered from a complete mental breakdown and went on a genocidal rampage with the percieved "death" of his son at the end of the game. with his motivations out of the way, the plot doesn't have anything else to tell, he's dracula now, we saw how he became a vamp in los1 and we saw how he became a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in MoF, there was nowhere else for the plot to go but....back.
Back to the good guy he used to be, the problem is, that's not an easy transition.
with alucard "alive" drac no longer has any reason to be a genocidal maniac, his rampage from MoF is largely over and shortly after his return he begins incorporating mankind into his ranks, subjugating villages and resuming his original goals of "Kill the brotherhood because they threaten the world" but his....rampage from before still hit him pretty hard, he got a good, hard look at just how bad he could be and this only gave him cause to further isolate himself from the world.
with the return of dracula and castlevania, he pushed the brotherhood into an ever-narrowing corner for 500 years, leading to the desperate siege in the intro.
once he defeated them, he has literally nothing left to do. his other two objects of revenge are out of reach, he's got nothing left. he doesn't even have his "son" as alucard actively wants to kill his old man because, again, genocidal rampage from MoF, that's a big deal.
he wakes up and has to go get his powers, and it's with the castle that the game fumbles its narrative. Basically the "dream castle" dracula experiences is a real world that's shaped by his memories ( I had to ask the devs and this is what they told me) it's a curse he's afflicted by, a sort of test. it's based on his castle and self-perceptions, it has real grounding and the events he experiences there have real parallels to his very obscure history. there was an agreus he fought once, there was a toymaker he met, there was a conversation with four stray brotherhood soldiers who invaded his castle. but all this is one big test of his newfound desire for redemption, that's the point of the dream castle, it's his redemption test, the castle even has its own, twisted version of him as he percieves himself "Inner dracula"
the problem is the game doesn't outline this or even act as if things have stakes, it keeps silent and dracula seems to follow dream logic whenever he's there. it's confusing as hell and not really well told.
the ending of the game is just that, it ends, no ifs, ands or buts. congrats, revenge is had, has dracula redeemed himself? honestly it ceases to matter, drac had a past, but with this incredibly ironic twist dracula must enter his own castle and defeat his darker self to find redemption, but really, it's dracula burying his past, stepping all over it and moving on. so what if he comitted mass genocide?♥♥♥♥♥♥happens, so what if his family hates him? they'll get over it. (they actually do in this game) ultimately, the message conveyed here is that "we all make mistakes, and no matter the magnitude a mistake is still a mistake, once made it can't be unmade, best to move on and not dwell on it and try to do better the next time."
the end of the game gives a neutral tone, it's not positive or negative, it shrugs and says "make up your own damned ending." is he good? bad? it doesn't matter, he got everything he wanted, his son forgave him, he killed satan and put zobek firmly in his place, brotherhood's dead and the belmonts will never bother him again. he has options now, he can die if he wants, he can rule the world, he can continue protecting it, he has choices, but we don't get to see what choices he makes now because we're not supposed to.
the biggest flaw in gameplay to me is the removal of puzzles for "stealth" the stealth sections are awful, no two ways about it, I vastly prefer the puzzles to the stealth stuff. it's just a bram stoker's dracula reference, complete with the ability to dissolve into a pile of rats (which is visually identical to the scene from the film)
Deep down inside, lords of shadow respects and adores the franchise it came from, it pays homage to its roots as often as it can (inner drac's boss theme reuses "the tragic prince" and "nothing to lose", james rolf reference, older classicvania callbacks are scattered throughout the game) this is a reboot done right. it told its tale, it brought it to a conclusion. the end. congrats, you have just witnessed the complete construction of castlevania's main antagonist, thoroughly explained. hell, he even has powers like his classic counterpart, he can use his own version of demonic meggiddo and spams fireballs that can outright kill lesser enemies in one hit, they went all out for his combat.
also, and this is important, this game has a lot of over the top action sequences in it, I vaguely recall dracula riding a rocket at one point.
do i suggest you get this? damned right i do. it's a solid 8/10 it's the SoTN of the lords of shadow franchise, while not quite as amazing, it's good enough.

The best part about this game is the audio, and to punish the player by pulling them out of the amazing soundtrack they were listening to only because they drifted incorrectly is a terrible mechanic. If they can rework that single problem, I wouldn't mind holding my WASD/space keys down for an hour on this neon lit road towards the neon sun. OutDrive doesn't have controller support  yet, and the game's resolution is a bit hard to get right. I hope that the developers intend to fix this soon because I would love to play this game often.
Although I didn't live through the 80's, it definitely has that vibe, and if you enjoyed Hotline Miami, you'll enjoy this game. OutDrive has a lot of potential, and it's a must buy for the current price. The soundtrack itself is worth much more than that, and so are the aesthetics. I can't wait to see how much the game will improve over the course of this year.

This game has such a bad rep, because people see the name Sid Meier and assume 'Alpha Centauri 2!!!' You're wrong. It's a sci fi spinoff from Civilization: Beyond Earth.
The galactic conquest and expansion side of the game plays in a similar fashion to the Civ games, albeit a very simplified version of Civ. The tech tree consists of 8 or 9 different fields of research, which can be upgraded from 0 to 8. Planets you conquer can have cities added to them, as well as a number of structures built to improve planetary resource income. These structures again go up to level 8, although there does not seem to be a limit on how many cities you can have.
Each planet also has the possibility of being able to build a Wonder. Unlike the Civ games, these Wonders do not increase income or resources, but instead have a direct impact on your fleet.
The fleet is the main part of the game. As with everything else, upgrading it is simple. There are a number of different options depending on what you want your ship to be good at, and the upgrades go up to level 8. You can also have up to 8 ships in your fleet.
Space missions and encounters are the main part of the game. To bring new planets into your Empire, you need to do missions for them. They may limit you to a single ship for the mission, or you can take your entire fleet. Missions range from escape, to protect a colony ship, to defend from pirates, or capture an escaping fugitive.
These missions take place in a fairly large area of space. The planet in question forms the centre of the map, and the mission takes place around it.  They are fun, easy to learn, and mistakes are rarely fatal (not at the normal difficulty levels anyways).
One last touch I did like was when I was going for a domination victory. I defeated one race, leaving only two left on the map. Both of our Empires were pretty big, having split the galaxy almost down the middle. The next turn, I got a message from the NPC controlling the enemy faction, saying "There's just the two of us left. It's been nice having peace with you for all these years, but what do you say we now find out which of us has the best Empire?" Very friendly-like declaration of war. It's not about the conflict. It's about the honour.

I loved the flawed but beautiful original ("Tales of Phantasia") on SNES.  Tales of Symphonia has all of the same flaws, but practically none of the charm or interest.
The 3-D models are dated now, of course, but they're not terrible. Still, I'd prefer the old 16-bit sprites to this incarnation.  The music is okay, but the best tunes are repurposed from the original.  The sound effects and voice acting are adequate, although the voice acting is only for special cutscenes and battle--and hearing Genis utter the same sentence over and over again to cast the same spell can get tiresome pretty quick. The rest of the time it's text, which I don't mind.  But the lack of a click-thru ability makes even dialigue a chore sometimes.
Speaking of a tiresome chore, I spent 60 hours finishing this game: the first few waiting for the game to pick up, and the last 20 just to finish te damn thing, thinking that the end was in sight. I started out as my usual completionist self, trying to steal from every monster and find every treasure, but it didn't take long before I just wanted it to be over.  The characters are two-dimensional, the dialogue is stilted, the plot is justand excuse to go to the next location, the "philosophy" and moralizing are superficial, the puzzles are simplistic timewasters, and the battle system has a whole lot of options that are no more efficient than constant attacks and healing. Bosses rarely have elemental weaknesses--even the Summon Spirits are simply strong against the element they represent (not weak to the opposing element).  The systems for learning different skills is opaque, and I certainly couldn't be bothered "studying" for a boring class which was certain to have an easy final exam.
And it WAS easy. By the end, I had lost interest in finding treasures, rare weapons, or even my favorite summon spirit from the original, Maxwell.  I started avoiding all fights in the final dungeons, so I was not levelled up. And I simply strode in and brute-forced the final boss.
And honestly, all I felt at the end was relief. I was done.  My 60-hour study in boredom was over.  Don't make the same mistake I did.
TL;DR: This game is not worth the time spent playing it, much less the money to buy it (I got moy copy on sale for less than $5.)

UPDATE: My initial review was written approx. 30 hours into the game, which is about the halfway point, and I've now completed it. My opinion about the first half of the game is the same as it was, so I'm keeping my original review below. However, I thought that 'Tales of Symphonia' improved considerably in the second half as the story began to improve and there were more things to do, particularly at the point that would have been the second disc on the GameCube original (which is maybe less than a quarter of the game). I don't think it's a fantastic RPG by today's standards, or compared to many contemporary and older RPGs that are still wonderful, but I can definitely see why this game is so loved, especially for the time when quite a lot of it would have been very novel (particularly to the Western audience). The story, while generic and dull for much of the first half, becomes quite deep and interesting as it progresses. I don't think that the battle system hasn't dated at all, and the soundtrack, voice acting, and art style are all still great. But I do think that the game is unnecessarily long and requires far too much perseverance before it pays off.
I'm going to recommend this game, but only to people who like old J-RPGs and who are willing to invest a lot of time into it.
ORIGINAL: I think many of the reviewers here are recommending this game through rose-tinted glasses. Like most of the others here, I had fond memories of the original GameCube version, but I realise now that I should have left my memories intact. ‘Tales of Symphonia’ has simply not aged well at all. The story isn’t nearly as “epic” and “deep” as I remember, the dungeons are tedious and seemed designed to frustrate, the puzzles are obscure, and the save point system is annoying.
From the looks of the guide (which I ended up using because I’d been wasting too many hours of my life trying to figure out those obscure puzzles), I’m only about half way into the game after about 30 hours. This game is massive, but not because it has a particularly engaging story or immersive world, but just for the sake of being long. Clearly gamers had a lot more patience back in 2003 to grind and go through identical dungeon after identical dungeon (I know I did, but I was 18 years old, living with my parents, and working in a games shop when this was released in Europe, so all I had was time). Some people might argue that’s a negative sign of the times that gamers don’t have that kind of patience anymore, and I wouldn’t necessarily disagree. But I can’t possibly recommend this game to anyone in 2017, especially when there are classic J-RPGs that have dated far better than this.

This is at true adventure game and a continuation of the Longest Journey and Dreamfall.  Dreamfall Chapters again follows Zoe Castillo, a young woman who first appeared in Dreamfall being asked to find and save April Ryan, the main character  from the first game, the Longest Journey.  Dreamfall Chapter's furthers Zoe's particular part in the adventure in helping to determine the fate of the balance between the two worlds of magic and science, Stark and Arcadia.  If you like mysteries, don't mind fantasy or sci-fi and like agnozing over decisions that may affect your own fate as well as the overall fate of the world, this game is for you.
To continue,  I wholly recommend this to people who like TellTale style games, as this game uses the similar mechanic of "choose your own adventure."  If you have not ever seen one of these type of tales, which started out in books, it's a format where your actions can lead to different paths or at least a different experience in the overall plot, can flesh out what and who characters are and give you at a deeper understanding of the environment, the story and it's meaning,  and give you a better sense of actually participating in the adventure.  You can actually feel and understand Zoe and Kian's decisions and agonize over them, and worry about what kind of effect this is going to have on the character and the worlds.  Is it going to get them killed? Is this decision later on down the line going to make the end result of the story actually change?
The game development team is on the third book in several chapters, and the gameplay is over 10 hours already for $20.00.  That's less than the price of two movie tickets in my state , and there will only be more to come.  With that $20.00 you get to immerse yourself in another world, feel the environment and participate in it, make decisions that may or may not affect your life and well being, as well as the world around you.   Some decisions are quite small and some very large.   Some small decisions actually lead to larger consequences .  You get to participate in an overall mystery and experience more than one world in the combination of fantasy, sci-fi, mystery and ordinary things that are part of life.
This game is not for everyone, but neither is any game that you can possibly buy out there.  Some people don't like shooters, some don't like strategy, or side-scrollers, and some people don't like adventure games.  Some people think adventure games should only come in one format and involve tons of mind-breaking puzzles.  Some people don't like certain content.  In the the end, to me It's just like some people preferring hockey over football or baseball.  It's up to you whether you like this game or not.  I can only say in the end though that I really enjoy it and it was worth every penny  spent on it for me.  These adventures are truly different and you can never quite be sure what is going on.
I hope that this review was helpful, and I hope that Red Thread Games can continue making adventures in the future that are like this.

Thus far Dreamfall Chapters is a thoroughly enjoyable adventure title with a choice and consequence style gameplay and stunning visuals. The story telling in this and the previous games are second to none, with the developers going to great lengths to provide a strong history and back story to the characters and worlds they have created. This series really draws you in, and the choice and consequence element to this game ensures that the player truly feels involved with the actions of the protagonists.
The Story telling in Dreamfall Chapters is wonderfully enhanced by the quality of the visual representation of two unique worlds, and a solid soundtrack.
I highly recommend this game to everyone, but the players who will get the most out of this title are Adventurers who enjoy playing games driven by an original and compelling plot, involving genuinely likeable and relatable characters!
Although the series is not complete, this game sets the stage for an intense crescendo of an incredible journey.
I can only hope people enjoy playing this as much as I am.

When I first saw the reviews come out for this game I was a little worried, though I did really enjoy the first Lords of Shadow a few years back. Bought the game anyway and surprise, it's the reviewers being crap at games and reviewing again.
LoS2 is, like LoS1, a game that takes the best parts of various action games like God of War and it works out great as a result. Dracula is a great choice for a protagonist and is made a much better character than his main Castlevania counterpart in both abilities and personality. The story isn't too weak either, it's there, it does the job so you can't complain either.
A lot of complains were aimed towards the stealth sections in the game, sure this seems like an odd decision but it works, and despite what reviewers say, it's not as inhumanly hard or excessive as they say. There's probably 5 stealth sections overall, they're all incredibly brief and are there to act as a bit of variety to prevent fatigue from constant fighting smaller enemies. Although it is easy to see why reviewers proclaimed the stealth section involving Agreus as the scourge of gaming, it requires you to use multiple skills you have gained so far, but the game doesn't tell you. Thinking is too hard for reviewers after all.
Overall, Lords of Shadow 2 is a solid game and definitely deserved a better reception than what it got.

Imagine Space Engineers with worse graphics, and a far better set of features, set on an Earth-like planet (Neter). You have much more control over everything (from custom-building your engine to building your entire ship around a giant gun if you so choose) but there's also a steeper learning curve due to the wide range of features. If the in-game tutorials aren't enough, just ask on the discussion forums and you'll get a quick answer at most times of day.
From the Depths is centered around two things
If you don't find it compelling to have the chance to custom build the best combined fleet of ships, submarines, aircraft (whether propellled by jets, balloon, or propellers), and then sending in your fleet to fight as per specific set of commands you and the AI mainframe will give it, this probably isn't the game for you.
I'll explain the campaign, but first I want to talk about what From the Depths has that really sets it apart:
-A unique keyboard-based build mode (in addition to the mouse-based mode of building common to games like Space Engineers.) It's impossible to explain in words, but I find it more efficient in most cases. Don't worry, there is a symmetry mode. It'll take you an hour to get used to this, the time investment will pay off in the long-run, the only downside is you'll be wondering why every other game like this doesn't offer the same system. Also, make sure you don't build your ship backwards, the in-game tutorial will explain this, don't skip it.
-Four unique offensive weapon systems, all customizable. Also, your AI (if properly set up) can use all of these effectively, don't worry about trying to pinpoint the lasers your guided missiles will follow far into the horizon. I'll try to explain each in-game system briefly (the in-game tutorial will give much more detail):
Honorable mention would be drills and rams, both of which can be used to ram other ships, and some people create some rapidly spinning versions mounted on the front for a large boost to the damage- but I don't really bother.
For defensive systems, you can use shields which, at steeper angles, reflect incoming cannon shells, flares as mentioned before can distract incoming missiles, and of course you can stack heavy metal armor for protecting against anything that gets through. Do not forget to put some surge protection from EMP around things like your AI mainframe.
Engines are fully customizable- I won't explain it in detail, but the way you design your cylinders/exhaust/carburators/injectors/etc. allows you to compromise between fuel efficiency, performance, and so on. Jet engines also come in a small standard size which takes up 1 block, or a large customizable jet which has parts that are 3 wide x 3 high x 1 long, and you can stack these parts to make an engine as powerful as it is thirsty for fuel.
Now, why does any of this matter? Because of the creativity the massive set of tools allows, my overview of what you can do in the game is far from exhaustive. If you want to create a giant, inexplicably airborne floating metal death cube, you can do it, and you've got about half a dozen different ways to make sure it doesn't fall to the ground, or you can make much more realistic design of fighter craft, you can try to design a fleet around a set of workhorse medium cruisers with a few pieces thrown in, or, alternatively, gamble the whole battle on one giant metal ship which has a huge engine, is shielded from all angles, and has several systems designed to fight submarines, aircraft big and small, defeat missiles, and of course destroy large enemy ships threatening you from several kilometers away. IF you really want, you can design your ship around a massive railgun which fires shells at several kilometers per hour, and an engine which can hopefully power it- sort of like an A10, except it floats and is intended to fire through entire ships- also, make sure to use hollowpoint heads on railguns, they impart the entire kinetic force of the shell travelling at 3km/second to the point of impact.
Now, again, if you're only interested in seeing these ships blow up, and you don't want to tweak them yourself, you're better off not buying the game and instead just watching a nicely edited video someone else has made where they below up the ships for you.

Written as of Release 1.947, 19 April, 2016.
This game is one I've been addicted to for months now. I may not have the hours to show it, as I play a fair amount offline, but the experience is definitely here. I'll have a quick summary. Would I recommend From The Depths to someone who is willing to learn and values gaining experience through trial and error? Yes. Would I recommend it to someone who just wants a simple game that's easy to get into and you can easily become a powerful god in? Absolutely not.
Well, why would I recommend this to the first type of people? Well, it's a hard game. I'm not going to lie. This game will slam your face in the ground many times. But the ones who learn from things like that will thrive off of what they learned from that. They'll get back up, dust themselves off, and fix the problem before heading back in. A fair amount of knowledge is useful in From The Depths. Simple physics, some mathematics, advanced problem solving, etc. But even people who don't know those can easily excel with the will to learn from mistakes. Your ship keeps flipping over? Well, time to make sure the center of mass sits lower in the vehicle. Basic problem solving can soothe the rage I see in others.
But what about the second group, Dim? As I said, it's a hard game. Not everything will just pop right up to you. I first started playing this before the new tutorial additions, and let me tell you, it was hard. 90% of what I know came from reverse engineering, experimentation, and watching others. But now there's a much better tutorial system that even helped me with some things. I can say if you instantly want to be a god at building things, this will never be the game for you. No amount of tutorials will ever make it so. You have to be able to not get frustrated at every little thing and be able to problem solve. It takes time.
Now some people complain about the "horrible" UI. Well, yes, it's extremely simple and definitely not pretty. But it gets the job done. There are a few things that I'd say are difficult to figure out, but once you get it, it's second nature. I will admittedly say the multiplayer is lackluster. It's originally what I got the game for, to play with friends. But now they're working on it. It's an Early Access game after all. There will be issues. There are quite a few other little issues, but everything is subject to change since I first typed this. No game is perfect. I will say the learning curve was rough, but the game must have some addictive drug in it after you get the hang of what to do.
Pros:
Amazing building capabilities
Smart AI systems (usually)
Infinite combinations of gun systems
Highly reactive physics
Superb combat effects (shell impacts, pieces flying off, etc.)
Amazingly rewarding for the ones who persist
Great graphics (for a Voxel game)
Cons:
Harsh learning curve
Poor optimization
Poor multiplayer
Small glitches (shouldn't be much of a problem, however)
Overall:
8/10. Amazing game in my opinion, but it has flaws. Worth the buy for those willing to invest some time into it.

You know the drill with this one already, so let’s not waste any time and sink our teeth into this one.
I – Story [5/10]
Orcs Must Die! 2 is a third-person tower defense game from Robot Entertainment and is the sequel to Orcs Must Die! The story starts a few days after the closing events of OMD! and begins with the Sorceress hiding from the Mob in the Dead World. A mysterious Rift opens beside her and she goes through it, finding herself face to face with the Hero. After the Rift was closed and the Mob could no longer enter the human world, the Hero retired from being a War Mage and became a miner. But, with more and more Rifts opening up, he can no longer sit idle. He and the Sorceress decide to cross through a Rift and back into the Dead World. In the Dead World, it is revealed that the Hero’s and the Sorceress’ former master (believed to be dead in OMD!) is not dead and has been opening Rifts from the Dead World in order to restore the magic and save the human world.
Spoiler Alert: After the Hero and the Sorceress close the final Rift, magic is fully returned to the world. The Master has disappeared and the Hero claims that he and the Sorceress will always be guarding the Fortress from the Mob.
The story itself was quite rudimentary and somewhat predictable. I didn’t quite like it as much as the first game and, to be perfectly honest, I was a bit let down.
II – UI [10/10]
The user interface was practically the same as OMD!, but my complaints about the clunky menus had been assuaged. In fact, the HUD even improved. Trap and equipment icons were much smaller and allowed for a more expansive view of the screen. Much to my dismay, I still continued to press the “Ready” button by accident long before I was ready.
III – Gameplay [10/10]
Everything I loved about the gameplay in OMD! was completely present in Orcs Must Die! 2. Some levels seemed a bit less free form and permitted less strategy due to a lack of open space, but it didn’t make too much of an impact on the game. Third-person mode was still great; both in and out of combat.
The option to play as a different character was a nice change of pace. Instead of only playing as the Hero, players could now choose to play as the Sorceress. Not only could I kill as many orcs as I wanted, I could use the Sorceress’ Wand of Domination to make orcs kill other orcs for me. In what world could that not be a grand idea? In addition to this incredibly useful ability, the Sorceress has a different set of basic traps than the Hero and, while similar in function, allowed for vastly different strategies.
OMD!2 also added in the capability for co-op which, I can imagine, is spectacularly good fun. Some of the maps even seemed as though they were designed specifically for two people. While that proved difficult at times going through with only one person, it wasn’t all that bad.
IV – Content [10/10]
Once again Orcs Must Die! 2, like it’s predecessor, pulled out all the stops when it came to content. Without purchasing any additional DLC, the game has a couple dozen maps (plus ten bonus maps if you own the original OMD!), over 20 types of enemies; some new and some old, over 50 traps, weapons, and minions to arm yourself with, over 200 upgrades to weapons and equipment, along with unlockable costumes for both characters. Good Lord that was a long sentence. Sorry about that.
Again, you can purchase DLC for OMD!2 and add in even more content to the game. There is enough here to keep you happily slaying orcs for hours upon end.
V – Visual [9/10]
I was a big fan of the graphics in OMD! and the same can be said for Orcs Must Die! 2. However, there was little to no change in the visuals from the original installment. While this isn’t necessarily a bad thing, it’s not necessarily a good thing either. I still love the art style and the environments, but I had hoped to see something new brought to the table.
VI – Audio [10/10]
The music was, once more, fantastic. The game’s constant mayhem is backed up by an extremely solid soundtrack. There will be blood, oh yes, but there will also be some kick♥♥♥♥♥tunes to go along with it. Additionally, voice acting was also top notch for our second foray into the wonderful world of Orcs Must Die!
VII – Overall [9/10]
Overall, Orcs Must Die! 2 does the original justice and even improves upon in certain areas. It’s a great game and a worthy addition to any collection.

Wow... Very rarely have I finished a game with such bittersweet feelings. Fulfilled at the accomplishment, but deeply saddened that the journey was over. Not since Baldur's Gate or FFVII have I felt this way, and that's made playing this game so worthwhile.
The best part about the whole game was... well, it's hard to say. A combination of the story, the characters, the depth of the world and the sheer number of things to do make this game feel huge. It was quite challenging at times, especially the bosses. It's also got a poor tutorial, as in the game barely tells you how most of the mechanics work. As a result, you'll get a lot more into the game more quickly if you research the mechanics a bit first. I had to resort to using a walkthrough a couple of times to even attempt some of the gigantic sidequests in the game - not too different from FFVII.
The characters and voice acting are great, and their personalities and pasts are gradually revealed throughout the progression, made by many lines of dialogue, though most are not voiced. Despite this, I found every party member memorable and deep, and I doubt I'll forget them anytime soon. And don't be fooled by the cartoonish anime style, this game can dark and violent, and deeply emotional, and is all the more engrossing because of it.
The story was OK, but it was really the characters, and the villains, that really invested me in the story. The intricate plotlines that all link together with each character was also great and what pulled me into the world/worlds.
The combat is also very deep and rich for a JRPG. There's actual timed blocking, countering, area effect spells, and an intricate skill system. However, like I mentioned, it takes a lot of effort to learn all the ins and outs without some sort of reference.
The music's pretty decent, and fits with the themes and the worlds, but nothing too mind-blowing to the point of me buying the soundtrack.
The anime style movies were great but I wish there were more of them actually in the game. I guess I should be thankful, though, since I hadn't seen anime style cutscences used this well in an RPG... ever.
Overall, one the most memorable RPGs I have played in years. Just goes to show that somewhat dated games can easily outshine all the soulless cash grabs of today's games with a little heart and care put into the game.

Well, after some prolonged and frustrating problems I eventually got this game to run, and I must say that as a Sid Meier linked game my expectations were high.  The man is a genius.  However, things had been tempered by reading some mixed reviews and the annoyance of actually getting it to run.
When I got the game to play I found it to be pretty much what the reviews had described.  There are several levels of difficulty, 3 different player factions to choose from and each has I think 8 different leaders to choose from, and their skills have a direct impact on your play.
The map is basic but pleasing on the eye.  Combat is simple, easy to learn and again fairly nice to watch.  The diplomacy is very limited, but seems to function as intended.
However, and it's a big HOWEVER, all is not well in my spiral arms of space.  The gameplay is repetative, to the point were the desire to play "just one more game" eveporates fast.  This is a new experience for me with a Sid game.  Combat, at the heart of the game, is so basic it can be painful.  I have repeatedly seen the AI bring a fleet that should have had me struggling just to survive get crushed as it makes one moronic choice after another.  Another thing I can't say I like is that so far every time I conquer a homeworld of a rival I inherit their entire empire.  While that might work on a National lever (and I doubt even then), it seems a bit lame in this sort of game.  It also makes achieving an outright win over a mighty rival possible in 1 combat.  Wonders are fun, but get a powerful 1 early and your enemies are doomed.
Fun? Yes.  Limited replayability?  Also yes.

I first played this game only a few years ago. However, I did know about this game's controversies before then. When I learned that Postal 1 was coming out on Steam, I had to try it.
Postal 1 is much less humorous than Postal 2, focusing more on disturbing violence. Not only do you go on a shooting rampage, but your victims' screams and moans sound a lot more agonizing than in other games. Despite this, I didn't think the game was "trying too hard" to be shocking. The shocking, disturbing parts of the game don't feel like filler, and fit into the overall feel of the game.
Also, the game can be pretty challenging; it's not just a mindless killing spree game. The people who shoot back can be difficult to deal with, especially when there's a lot of them and they use explosives. You'll have to make use of your wide arsenal of weapons and use cover wisely.
Postal 1 was updated a while back to support Xbox 360 controllers. This makes the game so much easier to control; you don't have to stick to the tank controls the game used to only have.
This game is violent, shocking, and disturbing (especially for 1997), but it's done well, and it's a shining example of what you can do with art. RWS wasn't afraid to put their vision out, and I'm glad that they did.

I love both TLJ and Dreamfall: TLJ and have been waiting for the follow-up for a very very long time. Dreamfall Chapters, like its predecessor, is a heavily narrative-driven game. If you like games like The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, Heavy Rain, and Beyond: Two Souls like I do, I believe you are going to enjoy Dreamfall Chapters.
All the endearing trademarks of the TLJ franchise are also back: funny, witty dialogue, interesting characters, exotic locales, fascinating but mind boggling mysteries :P, great soundtrack, and fantastic voice acting. I also love the new internal monologue game mechanic. It allows you to weigh conversation options in a more organic way because you get to literally hear what Zoey or Kian is thinking.  The choice and consequence mechanic is also pretty intriguing and adds replay value. Book 1 starts out slow but I actually love the pacing. It gives you time to get acquainted with Zoey and, to a lesser extent, Kian and their present situations. Book 2 moves into more traditional adventure gaming territory with more quests and puzzles. The story in Book 2 also picks up considerably and ends with an unexpected and surprising "bang".
One gripe is that the game is really taking its time reintroducing our favorite characters from past games. The good news is that we'll be seeing Crow in Book 3. Another gripe of mine is that fairly prominent characters from the previous game seem to have been unceremoniously written off. After 8 or so years of waiting, that was a bummer :(. I am hoping that there will be lots of surprises in store for us in the last 3 chapters.
All in all, if story matters to you, then I highly recommend Dreamfall Chapters. It's also a bitter sweet end to the Longest Journey series.
Just like most good movies it takes some time to get to know the characters, but its well worth the "slow" start. Great game.

Dreamfall Chapters is the direct continuation of the critically acclaimed adventure games The Longest Journey and its sequel Dreamfall: The Longest Journey, both published by Funcom. In a rare case of trademark Heaven on Earth, Red Thread game, a game company consisting mainly of some of the key people from the previous games in the series (such as the writers) have been allowed to borrow the rights to the series.
Dreamfall Chapters plays very much like an improved version of Dreamfall. The good parts have been amplified and iterated upon, whereas the less than stellar elements of its predecessor have been toned down or eliminated entirely.
It is very much a game driven by its narrative, it has more puzzles then the first Dreamfall, but nothing like in The Longest Journey. This is a game that should be played for it's story, characters and worldbuilding rather than its gameplay, so if that doesn't sound appealing to you, this is most likely not a game you would appreciate.
So far, I have not been disappointed with the first two episodes.

Dreamfall Chapters is a new episodic instalment on the TLJ series, and a direct sequel to Dreamfall: The Longest Journey.

Quick summary: Reasonable Zelda Clone that while has charm and is faithful to its source material suffers from poor communication and player feedback regarding objectives and puzzles, clunky controls, lack luster pickups/powerups and finally no autosave with a tendancy to crash after cut scenes potentially losing hours of play time.
6.5/10 Was not worth the £30 price tag, current price is aceptable.
In Depth Below:
First of all let me say I am a big fan of both Adventure Time and The Legend of Zelda Series and when I saw this game I was rather excited as this seemed like the ideal formula for an adventure time game and if a sequal is released with the issues in this game addressed it could be a real hit.
Now I'll go over the following areas in depth, Story/Theme, Controls/Game Mechanics, Graphics/Sound though it should be noted there may be overlape at times.
Story/Theme
Adventure Time: The Secret of The Nameless Kingdom strongest point is its loyalty to it source material, the games plot could easily be made into a two or three part episode and be well recieved and its newly introduced characters all have the charm and strangeness one would expect from Adventure Time.
Nearly all the monsters can be recognised from the show (however theres no real reasoning or theme why they are in a location and are often recoloured and resused elsewhere with more hitpoints) and there is no shortage of cameos from major and minor characters, all of which are voiced and have perfectly written in character lines, this been said there is not nearly enough character interaction between them with each only having a handful of lines. Another minor issue is that unless you are very familar with the series many of these cameos will be unrecognisable and having a small character journal which unlocks a paragraph about each character you meet would of been a nice addition.
Outside of cutscenes Finn is the only one who speaks at least in the early periods of the game (I confess I have not completed it due to crashing issues after the second dungeon), these short lines are spoken each time Finn picks up an item or treasure with 4-5 lines of alternative dialogue for each. While these didn't bother me so much as I naturally phased them out I do know players who would be driven crazy by this over the first hour so this is just a warning for those who have little tolerance for such things.
This also highlights another issue which is the lack of banter or comments by character to the enviroments or bosses as you go through the game, this feels like a real wasted oppertunity and unfortuately means theres little to distract from the lackluster gameplay that is the core of the game.
While there are side quests in the game they are of "Find Item A give to Person A collect item from person A give to Person B" which is typical of top down adventures, the only trouble been the location of these characters are not marked on your map and are often in tedious to travel to locations.
Controls/Game Mechanics
As basic controls go the game is passable, if you have played any of the gameboy Legend of Zelda games you'll feel pretty much at home however in spite of this you'll find traveling and combat becomes a chore.
First of all Finn seems to move slightly too slow which combined with the large amount of travel, exploration and fetch quests in the game begins to grow frustrating, also there are numberous stairs and cave entrances/exits which you need to traverse and unless you are exactly in the centre of them you just walk against them rather than up/down/through them which often leaves you open to been struck if your just passing through an area trying to avoid combat this can be a further problem when moving up or down stairs. Due to this been an animation you cannot attack or stop but this often lead to cheap hits from monsters gathered at the top or bottom, while there seems to be an slight invisible barrier to try and prevent this this doesn't work very well and actually causes issues with any block pushing puzzles that require you to push it near a door.
These movement issues begin to also affect combat as well with many monsters been able to out pace you in general or with sudden bursts of speed making you get hit (as any monster touching you harms you) or miss a swing often as unlike Link Finn requires to stand still to attack with his sword which again slows down gameplay.
The sword is your main weapon throughout the game as Finn and has seeming extremely short range but with reasonable power with some monsters dying in a single blow but with some taking up to 4-5 hits by the second dungeon, I say seemingly short range as the hit box for the blade (or in fact anything in the game is rather difficult to judge) combined with a slightly too slow swing animation and the inability to move when attacking means you'll be getting much closer than I suspect you need to and as such take damage more often than you would normally.
The sword can not be swung diagonal so if your moving diagonal and need to attack you will swing in the direction closest to the angle you are moving.

Even hitting a monster can actually do more harm than good in most cases as it knocks away and with most monsters possessing range attacks and you'll often get hit just as your moving in to finish them off. The ideal way to avoid this is to obtain the boomerang stand in which like the Legend of Zelda series paralyzes monsters briefly if you hit them (and can be thrown diagonal) and then go in swinging.
You also get a ranged attack yourself by the second dungeon but you again need to stand still when using it, its slow to fire, it does less damage than the sword, if you miss you have to wait until it strikes a wall or goes its full screen travel distance before you can fire again which means its only good as a utility item in most cases.
Your main defense other than hopefully moving out the way of the monsters far faster attacks is a shield which bluntly borders on useless, Like the sword it can only be used in the main four directions it is also extremely picky about positioning and will only block attacks that are central on Finn, a few pixels either way and you'll get hit. Its inconsistent about exactly which attacks it will block for example it will block a monster thats running at you with a blade knocking it back but if a monster just walks into you it won't stop them and when using it to push spiky objects you can suddenly slip past its perfect blocking spot and be damaged.
With these issues combined with the fact that monsters respawn the moment you re-enter an area you'll quickly start trying to avoid unnecessary combat unless you need money, this brings us to the next few points the shops and baggies..
Baggies are small plastic bags and these are essentially glass jars from the Legend of Zelda game but you use them for even more, they are your potion bottle, your bomb bag, your monster catcher, I'm at the second dungeon and I've already found eight items that can go in them, however they are as rare as hell and you'll often need a spare one to get through a dungeons puzzles so as a result all the healing items which you can collect (which are lost if you don't have a free bag btw) or buy you won't be using them even if they weren't stupidly high prices. You see Legend of Zelda has multiple different values of Zenny and Zenny chests littered everywhere Adventure Time you get coins in values of 1 sparsely (3-6 a screen if lucky) on average and chests are rare often giving you trail mix or one of the other healling item components (which you also have to pay to create). To be fair the most expensive thing I have bought was 200 coins but  the combination of low coins, little bag space and high prices means I rarely go near a shop.
Opps I've hit my word count so Graphics/Sound: Music forgetable Graphics pixelated sprites from earlier game.

Some spoilers ahead:
Finishing Lords of Shadow 2 left me with a bitter aftertaste.
From the very beginning of the game, you will be forced into stealth missions, evading generic vat-grown monstrosities in high-tech labs. The game's combat system, one of it's greatest strengths, is mercilessly defenestrated here, and as you find yourself sneaking behind an invulnerable guard for the fifth time, you start to wonder at what point it was that you stopped having fun.
But then you cross over into a castle area, and the familiar atmosphere coupled with the excellent swordplay (whipplay?) makes the game seem like a worthy sequel once again. The combat is fast and fluid, with the accelerated orb gain (compared to the first game) playing a great part in that. The platforming is much more forgiving, although the inclusion of (even more) platform highlighting was really not needed.
As soon as the game manages to realize you're having fun, however, you encounter the acolytes of Satan. These unfortunate excuses for characters that seem to have been created by pulling edgy tropes from a hat will casually wipe the floor with you - that is, until you use a clever trick to defeat them. Unfortunately, this is a sign of things to come, as well as one of my biggest issues with the game. You are Dracula, the Prince of Darkness. You've ruled this Earth from the shadows for centures, while Satan cowered from you ever since his last defeat. Well, it sure doesn't feel like it, since you'll spend most of your time in LoS2 running away from large fights and powerful enemies. Gabriel Belmont feels no more powerful than he was in the first game - weaker, in fact, due to the fact that you start the game with no skills or abilities.
Still, I went on with the game, hoping that the story would make it worthwhile. I cleaved my way through research facilities and desolated city streets, castle ramparts and dungeons. The narration was served to me in droplets, as if the whole story was an afterthought - an idea that I haven't quite managed to fully dismiss. Eventually, after maybe 12 hours of gameplay, the story started going somewhere. A major revelation was shown, and it had me genuinely interested.
Then it abruptly ended. There was a boss dull boss fight, set on an epic stage only to serve as a distraction from its lazy design (I'll use this opportunity to coin the term "forced epic"). It was over, Dracula said a cheesy one-liner and the credits rolled. That was it. The cluttered mess that the story had become turned into a Gordian knot not even Dracula's Void sword could sever, and it seemed like the developers didn't even bother trying. No shocking twists after the credits, not this time, only a lingering feeling of disappointment. There's a certain sense of irony that the only distinct feeling this game managed to evoke in me, that of sadness, was not over Gabriel's fate, but rather over the missed potential that this game had once held.
Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 is a game as empty as its protagonist's soul. Avoid it, especially if you were a fan of the original.

Starcrawlers is a fun dungeon crawler with procedurally generated dungeons and turn based combat. The game is absolutely loaded with personality and I've found myself smiling on more than one occasion. Though I haven't finished the game at the time of writing this, I'm drawn in by the story and the writing. Be prepared to make decisions that will effect your playthough.
The game is divided into both story driven and side dungeons. The story driven dungeons have large handcrafted sections loaded with secrets and the occasional puzzle section. The puzzles themselves aren’t overly challenging and the game frequently provides you with alternatives if puzzles aren’t your thing. The side dungeons are entirely procedurally generated, so far I haven't really had any issues with them. I suppose if you grind them over and over again they will get repetitive, but so far for every story dungeon I've only had to run one side dungeon. Let's be real here though, if you're not a fan of procedural generation, than this is probably not for you.
You'll start the game, but creating your first crawler from one of the eight classes in the game. Don't worry, overtime you'll be able to hire more crawlers to bring with you on your adventures. But you can only ever bring four crawlers with you to any given dungeon. Each class has it's own strengths, weaknesses, gear restrictions and a unique skill tree with twenty-one skills that each have three levels. The crawlers you bring with you also provide unique opportunities to resolve situations during the game. Need to reprogram an AI to get passed a section? Well needless to say the hacker will make that a breeze.
Unfortunately, it's not an entirely bug free experience and in particular there is a nasty crash bug that rears it's ugly head from time to time. Because of this, I wouldn't recommend playing it in “Ironmode”. The devs are aware and working to resolve the issue. So far I am really enjoying my time with Starcrawlers and recommend it if you're looking for a game in this genre.

Negative review boils down to a matter of personal taste. EDIT: It's really frustrating to be negative here, since my first reaction to this game was "If I didn't have to work to support a family, this is the kind of game I'd like to be writing myself."
Some notes:
Finicky equipment optimization games for a single character can be fun.
Coarse-grained equipment optimization for a large party can be fun.
This game seems to have the worst of both worlds: equipment selection making a 1 or 2% difference, across a large spectrum of items and 8 characters. The UI isn't well-set-up for managing this, whether knowing which character should conisder a piece of equipment or managing the backpack, the stash, and the characters not currently deployed on missions. There's a constant flow of green items, and hardly any of higher rarity - which seems reasonable, but between the inherent complexity and the sci-fi naming it means I'm automatically selling off 95% of loot because it's too much of a pain to seriously consider it even for the subset of character classes I'm currently deploying - which, according to some reviews, is suboptimal.
EDIT: Oh, it's worse than that. The indication of which "level" a piece of equipment is is in very small type buried in the lower-middle of the description. So some of those level 7 greens I've been discarding far outperform my level 1 blues; my party is starting to be undergeared.
Combat feels slow; not sure how much of this is poor class choice, poor skill choice, or just the lengthy animations. EDIT: Reading online guides for party composition helps, but that it's necessary is a bit frustrating. Or maybe it's just that I chose the background option that gave me a rare weapon, which left me overpowered for the first couple of levels?
Presence of collectable cubes and hidden stashes feels like it's meant to encourage exploring, but pixel♥♥♥♥♥ing is slow and frustrating.
I'd love to walk know the story, but don't currently have the patience on normal difficulty.

I've enjoyed what I have played of this game.
First of, a warning.
It's a Unity3D game, so it suffers from ALL the same core issues every other Unity3D game suffers from.
The Game will launch on your secondary screen, at the wrong resolution, and will run like absolute garbage while gobbling up an unreasonable amount of resources.
I don't care what anyone says, the main menu alone should not need 2.5GB of RAM and run nearly 3 CPU cores full throttle.
Also, a recently published version (1.0.3?) introduced some issues due to the halloween event, like the game crashing after a mission and costing you an hour or more's dungeon crawling.
It also leaves the cursor horribly offset in permanent free-look mode, which makes it incredibly difficult to pick up cred-sticks.
If you can stomach that, we actually have a genuinely good dungeon crawler, with some sweet music and some lovely art design.
The dungeon crawling itself takes place on a grid, but you have a free camera, and you're expected to use it.
If you tried to use a more static camera and rotate with just A D keys, you'll miss out on a lot of objects strewn about the floor, and make it difficult to find hotspots and terminals, as you'll find many on diagonals.
Many things also don't hint that you can interact with them, so click on ANYTHING suspicious - you'll learn this in the tutorial as that is how you gain access to the secret area there.
Movement is generally turn based - you take a step, your enemies take a step, etc.
There are however some realtime parts to it, for example search lights you have to dodge aboard the colony ship you go to early on.
Combat is lovingly animated - I'm not sure if they're 3D, but they're all full of vigour and bounce about and throw things at you - I'm pretty used to low budget crawlers which basically just give you a static sprite.
Each character have some abilities (with passives) they can use each turn, and the ability then typically goes into a 2-5 turn cooldown.
What abilities you have, and how they work differ wildly by class.
For example your main melee unit, the cyberninja, their attacks add combo points onto a target, which are points needed to use their abilities (period) and make them more effective.
A Void psyker, who will probably be your main mage type class, needs to balance generating void energy via their abilities, and using  up this energy,
Turns jumps between your characters and the enemy, based on an entropy system they have called Time Points.
All actions have a time cost associated with it, and the igher the cost, the further back into the queue you go.
If you've played Final Fantasy X, it's like that, except there's no speed stat to restore the entropy faster.
Otherwise, combat is quite straight forward, with enough twists to be interesting and set it apart.
It also initiates as soon as you're adjacent to a mob, so there's no manuevering around them like you can in Etrian Odyssey.
As far as the character system goes, I need to experiment with it more.
But basically each class has 3 specialisations you can spend your points on, and you get access to more abilities (up to 7) in each as you've spent more points in each.
At a glance I do wish there were more skill synergies between characters,
Most cases are covered ie. we have the melee fighter that follows up his allies' strikes, a hacker that disables enemies for easy attacks, or buffs the party, and a nasty robot that can draw most of the aggro and damage, and so on.
But a large number of the skills and abilities are focused on dealing damage without much of a twist beyond maybe tweaking the hit chance and crit chance bit.
With that said, as I have recently been playing Etrian Odyssey, I must say that love how transparent this game is with how your abilities work in comparison. It really helps you plan your character, and avoid skills that aren't quite right for you.

This game is rage.  Pure, undiluted rage injected straight into your brain through your eyeballs.  Oh sure, LUFTRAUSERS may
simple, with its pixelated design and basic flight controls, but don't be fooled.  This is a tough-as-nails aerial arcade shooter that will make you punch your screen if you have even the slightest bit of a temper.  And you will love it for this.
So this is an aerial arcade shooter where you fly around the area, shoot the baddies, and try (fruitlessly) to not die as you rack up the high score.  The difference here is that this displays on a 2D plain, which makes it more like a top-down arcade shooter than anything else.  The controls are also made simpler because of this design - you only need the arrow keys to fly and the "X" bottom to shoot.  There are no secondary weapons, special abilities, or fancy flying tricks to help you - you just focus on flying and shooting.  Which is all you can do without being driven insane.
As you play the game, you earn experience and complete challenges to unlock new add-ons.  These are broken down into three categories: weapon, armor, and engine.  Each add-on changes the way your plane operates, and with a little effort you can adjust your play style to fully optiize each element when you enter combat.  My one issue here is that the way some items are balanced (and dependant on the way you play), it feels like there's not enough benefit to outweigh the detriments.  This is only probematic when trying to accomplish specific challenges - you'll feel like your alomst playing with a penalty, instead of with exciting new equipmment.
Normally I would leave the enemies out of a review like this, but because they are integral to my main criticisms I'm going to talk about them.  There are both air-based abd sea-based enemies.  These include:
Killed enemies a worth set point values that add to your high score.  More difficult enemies are worth more points, and as you shoot them down they add to your combo muliplier (max = x20).  Stop killing enemies for long enough, and your multiplier resets.  Easy enough, right?
Well, as you play a round, more and more enemies fill the area, and sometimes this results in overwhelming encounters.  I get that it's randomized, but I still maintain that having 4 Aces and 2 battleships firing at you at once is a little unfair.  Better combatant progression, so that you always feel on the verge of being overwhelmed but never turning impossible would be appreciated.  At the very least, limit the amount of heavy-duty enemies on the screen at one time so there's always a slim (if next-to-impossible) chance of survival.
Thankfully, LUFTRAUSERS always give you sense of accomplishment after playing each round (most of the time), which gives you that "Just One More" mentality that makes in so addictive.  "Maybe this time I'll kill that battleship." "Next time, that Ace is MINE."  You get the idea.  Even with all my complaints listed, this sense makes the game absolutely worth the strife.
This game looks and sounds absolutely stunning.  Kozilek's techno-facsist marches fit the wartime theme perfectly - like WWII translated into digital form.  Same for the pixel artwork, even if it makes the cartoonish character models seem a little over-exaggerated.  You can also change the color themes, though I find the original is always the best.
LUFTRAUSERS tests your patience.  You'l be thrown from the elation of victory to the agony of death, and back and forth over and over, to the point where you'll start to wonder if you're going crazy.  Don't get me wrong - overall it's very enjoyable.  Just don't expect war to play fair.

Quite a good block-based building game. Although the game's genre is focused on naval battles, you can build ground vehicles if you so wish. You can create various weaponry for different roles: Flak cannons for your battleships; CRAM cannons for your artillery; or LUA-guided missiles for Air-to-Air, Air-to-Ground or vice-versa. There are wheel blocks for land-based vehicles, but they are highly neglected, and I hope they are worked on soon; as you can create some stunning tanks with various shell types that will surely catch the interests of many War Thunder players, such as myself.
Pros:
A vast selection of parts ranging from lightweight metal alloys and ERA armour to LUA script for AI mainframes and various cannon types for both beginners and professionals.
Stable multiplayer capability, although some bugs should be ironed out, such as the lack of Prefabs and host-only barrel-number selection for advanced cannons.
Cons:
You need a good graphics card to run this game over 30 fps at 1080p. I had around 15 on 720p with my old GT 620 (came with my prebuilt computer), now I get 60fps on 1080p at high.
All-in-all a fun build game for Land, Air, and Naval vehicles.

As an avid gamer and an older redneck, I have always found Sid Meier's games to be great for hours of entertainment in each gaming session. So, when given the chance to purchase Beyond Earth in a discounted bundle with Starships, I jumped at the chance. Sometimes, you really do get what you pay for.
Let's start with overall appearance. Starships uses some rather simplistic graphics, but is more than adequate for the type of gameplay intended. There is nothing overly special graphically speaking. Personally, I find how the camera follows the player's shots to the point of impact in space battles to be the most exciting part of the game from a graphic standpoint. And, yes, just as many players have pointed out, the overall appearance of the game gives the impression of something you would normally find designed for iOS, Android, or a tablet.
Now, to game setup and user friendliness. Game setup is extremely simplistic in that you have just the most basic of choices. Options are nothing more than if you prefer a windowed screen and game volume. Setting up an actual game, again, you have VERY limited choices which barely covers the basic criteria for what a turn based strategy game should consist of. Map size, number of opponents, affinity(your chosen race's galactic outlook), player's race/leader, and victory conditions. The last being a subject of what has become quite a heated debate in many forums across the Net, but more on that in a moment. Let's break each of the previously mentioned choices down.
The choice of map sizes range from the typical small map to what the game considers gigantic. The choices are fairly accurate to the stated size with gigantic being just a tad bit smaller than the name would imply. Just your basic "how big of a game do you want to play?"
Choice of number of opponents is rather self explanatory with 4 being default.
Then we come to affinity as well as the player's choice of leader as the two choices are rather intertwined. There are three choices for affinity: Supremacy, Harmony, and Purity. If you are unfamiliar with Beyond Earth, affinity can be simply summed up as how the player has decided to approach the progression and evolution of the human race. Supremacy embraces technology giving way to augmentations and upgrades of the human existence. Harmony denotes a desire to be a productive and well balanced race among many in the Universe. Purity is a choice to maintain the normal progression of the human race while embracing those qualities that make a human, well...human. In the game, you choose one of the three affinities then choose your leader from the given options. No matter which affinity you choose, the same leaders are available. And as you can guess, the choice of affinity/leader each has their own particular pros and cons.
Now we come to aspect of gameplay that has caused so much "ruckus" in so many forums across the Net: victory conditions. To start, the choice of victory conditions seems simple enough with each being what you would typically find in any strategy game be it real-time or turn-based. Choices like Domination(controlling the majority of the known galaxy) to Science along with familiar choices like Time, Population, and so on. Are you asking yourself "so what's the the big deal" yet? As it turns out, the choice of victory conditions ONLY applies to the human player and not any of the A.I. players in the game. Each A.I. player chooses it's own victory terms from the given choices. Example: A human player may choose Domination to which the player is required to decisively rule the majority of the galaxy whereas the A.I. player may choose the Wonder victory conditions which requires the A.I. player to complete a certain number of wonders to attain victory. The human player is not made privy to the A.I. player's choice of victory conditions. Now you can start to understand why this type of gameplay has been the source of much aggravation for many players. A human player can choose a strategy that requires a long term outlook such as the tried-and-true "build up, build up, and attack" only to lose the game a few dozen turns in due to the A.I. player building a quick ten wonders. When asked as to why gameplay is like this, the developers stated they wished to add a challenge. Challenge or insurmountable source of aggravation? You be the judge.
Finally, the overall impression of Starships. The game really seems to be nothing more than a "dumbed down" and cloned version of Galactic Empires with certain aspects of Sins of a Solar Empire incorporated in. And I must say, a rather bad clone at that. Starships has it's moments, but no portion of the game really stands out. Gameplay is entertaining only for a short time then becomes repetitive. Graphics and sound are less than what many would consider average. The only positive Starships has is it's rather easy to use and simple User Interface. Between the victory conditions "glitch" and numerous reported bugs that seem to cause fatal crashes before gameplay even begins, Starships seems destined to boldly go where no game has gone before: making a negative stain on the otherwise legendary career of Sid Meier.
Score:
Using a 0 to 5 scoring system, I give this game 1.5.
Wait for Starships to become a rather heavily discounted game before purchasing. And even then, don't part with more than $5 plus be ready for only a moment's entertainment.
