Before you even read this, note the kneejerk and attempted bullying in some of the 'developer responses.' That should tell you all you need to know. Ragnar has fallen so far, I don't even understand how it could've happened.
This is going to be long, as I want you to understand, to see if you'll agree with me about this game.
I'm not regularly critical about games, I like games, and I wanted to like this game. It began with The Longest Journey, which to me was a legendary affair, it still is. I remember so much about it, how it touched my imagination and inspired wanderlust. I recall much -- from the flying creatures that passed down stories in their own tongue, to the awakening of Venice. I approached it with wide-eyed wonder, it spoke to both the child and the adult in me.
So it was with that wonder I looked onward. I recall, again, at the time when friends and I chittered excitedly about Dreamfall. What would it hold? We wanted to think that our Ragnar would be brave enough, bold enough, to let the barrier between worlds fall. And that the dragons themselves may realise their error, and allow this to pass. And what would follow? An amazing epic about the trials and tribulations of two worlds colliding, perhaps with chaos taken to the brink and then to become better than either had ever been.
Dreamfall wasn't that. That was fine. It was okay. It was a little overwrought with awkward drama and unnecessary bouts of ennui to be edgy, but it was... all right. Of all the things it might have been, it wasn't memorable. It didn't leave a mark on me the way The Longest Journey did. It felt like Ragnar had left the child by the wayside, picking up an angsty teenager instead. One with dyed hair and a gruff attitude, a shallow, one-dimensional creature that was so desperate to be edgy, to be cool. The wonder had died. It was an intrigue, but it wasn't amazing.
I'd hoped that Ragnar would turn to the child's wonder again. No such luck. The teenager was running rampant now, lots of new hormones as puberty set in. Rage against the machine, man! Stick it to the man, man! And it's a little embarrassing. The teenager holds the reigns, believing that ham-fisted writing, that beating you over the head with cheesy, kludged attempts at emotional manipulation, and overdone twists in an effort to be clever, and unnecessary amounts of Dark & Edgy...
Now, you may play Dreamfall Chapters and disagree with me. Keep playing.
The first episode is okay. It is merely okay, much like Dreamfall which preceded it. It's okay. It's not going to stir your spirit, it's not going to ease your soulsickness, awaken your wonder, or give you that pleasant sensation that runs down your spine as your jaw falls agape in appreciation for just how much raw creativity a person can have. The Longest Journey could do that. This won't. But that's not a crime, Something can be just okay. And being just okay may not be quite worth the lack of a recommendation. Okay is fine, right?
Well, then the second episode hits. Ragnar gets bored and leaves the teenager at the typewriter. Suffice it to say? This goes about as well as you'd expect it to, and it ends about as well as you'd expect it to. It's trashy, embarrassing, silly, and edgy. It's the sort of thing you see when a teenager writes a fan-fiction about their favourite TV show, except they try to make it dark by having people die and/or suffer. You have to feel my pain, man! Do you feel my pain? DO YOU???? Do. You. Feel. My. Pain?!?
Embarrassing.
I felt genuinely awkward. I was worried someone would see me playing it. And this isn't a good thing. After the first episode, I was expecting better. I wanted better. I thought... okay, Ragnar is hitting his stride. The Longest Journey took a little bit to get off the ground, it had a slow start. Perhaps this does too? And that's about as far as my faith went. For all intents and purposes, I think it's fair to call Ragnar a one-trick pony. He had one trick -- The Longest Journey -- and he's been riding that wave ever since. Preying on nostalgia in the hopes that no one will notice that he's unable to actually write anything decent any more.
He shouldn't have let his inner child grow up into that obnoxious teenager. He really shouldn't.
And the thing is is that I can no longer trust him, nor can you. He hasn't written anything really good since The Longest Journey, I'm not sure why I was expecting him to start now. I gave him a chance. This was his last chance. If you're an intelligent, well read person with an appreciation for literature, this is so bad it'll make you want to go and find a corner to curl up foetal in. You'll want it to stop being so very bad. It doesn't stop being so very bad. It continues being so very bad until you can't take it any more and you crack. It's really very bad, then, yes. Very bad. In fact, at the risk of sounding like Sewer Urchin, I'd say it's very, very bad. Yeah.
So bad. I need to stop writing those words, but I can't. Good grief. I've been exposed to an angsty teenager and I want to point you in a different direction so you won't have to sit awkwardly through what I did.
Okay. Okay. I think I have what I need. There's a character in there who fires quick and fast ableist slurs at the mentally disabled. So edgy! The writer felt that that was necessary in order to create a shock response. It was exploitative, cheap, nasty, and as ham fisted as anything else in Chapters is what it was. If he'd had a black person being attacked by someone flinging ethnic slurs, he'd never have gone through with it. He played it safe, he chose a group who're regularly victimised and chose to pick on them. Sounds edgy, doesn't it? Picking on the easiest group like a giant yellow-bellied coward, I mean? He could only have sunk lower if his target had been furries.
What, exactly, happened to you, Ragnar? I mean, what?? How do you go from The Longest Journey to... this pile of drivelling brain rot? Christ. So... don't buy this. Move on. Forget it exists. Just forget it exists. Go and play The Longest Journey again. You don't need this much angsty teenager in your life. You really don't. Off you go.

This episodic series is nothing like other episodic games out there right now. Open worlds to explore, largely varying outcomes to decisions, and an expansive and deep lore world. You can have a completely different life for Zoe depending on decisions you make as her. Small choices you make can have consequences that change the world around you in ways you didn't expect.
The first "book"/episode is a bit slow in terms of story beats. But book 2 brings all the set up together. The characters are flawed in realistic ways. They have relationships that are not perfect in ways that are relatable. The art direction of this game is really solid, and will stand the test of time in the future. It's not cutting edge graphics, by there is a definite beauty to the models and levels.
If you're the type of gamer who wants their "decisions to matter", this is definitely the game for you.

Dracula is back and this time, it's worth it.
Castlevania Lords of Shadow 2 is one of the few decent 3D castlevania's, with Dracula's character being dark and even cruel at times.
I enjoyed the combat, though the decision to include the blood-whip as a primary weapon was headscratching, why not use a different weapon?
Regardless, it has a bestiary which is interesting and plenty of in-game lore to read th rough if you enjoy that.
The game has however some flaws: the biggest being the forced stealth segments. These can range from creative to asinine, and they get progressively less fun, forcing the question of: Why does Dracula have to sneak around? it's Dracula!
The storyline can be silly at times and I would've preffered the timeline to stay in the past, in Castlevania. However the decision to include the present was confusing as it neglects the most interesting part: Dracula in the present. The social implications of this would be amazing, yet it's completely ignored. I feel this was a wasted opportunity.
That being said, at the end of the day this is easily the strongest entry into the 'Lords of Shadow' stable, but I'd only recommend it for diehard fans.

If you like sci fi, turn based rpgs and dungeon crawling then this game is an obvious choice for you.
The game has everything you would want from a sci fi game. Arrogant hackers, sturdy engineers, tough soldiers, creepy spellcasters that draw their power from a parallel universe(?) and........cyberninjas. If that's not enough to make you go buy the game now then i don't know what will. Although the game may feel intimidating at first, if you keep at it and learn its secrets you will fall in love with it.
The pros
1. Every class feels like the class should.
Usually games (especially ones that feature ninjas) just change numbers to make a class (a ninja would have more dodge, a soldier more hp) but their skills would more or less remain the same (attack that bleeds, attack that burns etc). In this game however each class is UNIQUE, in all caps. And again, i have to say, the class FEELS like it should.
I will only talk for the ninja here to give you an example. A ninja can play around with the order of the characters and the class' skills make use of that order in a way i haven't seen before (seriously, i've never seen the way the ninja plays in any other game of this genre). You will get to kick, slash and bounce off enemies while orchestrating combo attacks with your teammates. And i've only talked about one class, and one skill tree of that class.
2. Every class is completely different and plays completely differently.
I had to put this up as a second point since it's not only that each class feels like what it should, but also that it's separated. And I haven't even seen three of the classes yet. The classes' trees also play a role outside combat (for example a hacker's tree can hack normal machines, but another tree can hack through corrupt, malfunctioning ones). And it's up to you to decide what works best.
3. Secrets and puzzles that aren't obvious
Most dungeon crawlers feature the wall button. This one doesn't have that. You may have to find a loose panel (no, you can't distinguish it from other panels through the graphics), or solve a puzzle that doesn't have an obvious solution. I'm not saying anything more because spoilers
4. Music and sound effects
When you play a game with just the right music to immerse you or just the right sound effects to make you feel like you're doing what you're supposed to be doing (for example throwing a grenade), it really makes a difference. It's neither exaggerated nor generic, it's just what it should be.
5. Graphics
So obviously this is an indie game. However its graphics will surprise you. I was really expecting much less for its team (2 people?) and its price. It's always great when you get much much more.
6. Ng+
So the game features a level cap (i hate level caps, but the chars would feel really overpowered without it) however the game has ng+ that raises that cap. I don't know if you can max out all trees but you really don't need to.
7. Politics?
Well, kinda. The missions you do have an impact on how the factions see you (and there are many factions). Megacorps, just one type of factions, feature more than 8 (maybe 16?) different factions, each with its own goals and rewards. So for example one corp may get you to steal something from another corp with the obvious results. You can go to your codex to read what each faction does, wants, or rewards and play for those ones, or you can just play according to your wallet. The game, when it comes to politics, feels as chaotic as a sci fi should feel. And it's great.
The cons
1. No auto combat
You will find yourself against easy low-level foes many times, and unfortunately you can't go auto on them. I don't know why, but i think that's because there really aren't any generic skills, it all has to do what what the player does with them i guess. But there should at least be an auto-combat where everyone will just fire their basic attacks.
2. Very little explanation of what's happening or what some words mean
I started with the ninja and as i was selecting the background i was introduced to a word i had no idea what it meant. Then, at a loading screen, it was explained to me, after i was level 5 or something.
Also, the number of factions is really overwhelming and you have to go back and forth through your codex to see what the faction is. I would prefer it if you could just click on the factions name without having to change screens.
Some items are missing their explanations. For example, are consumables valid for one fight? For an entire mission? Are "loot" objects meant to be sold or will i need them later? etc
3. Backpack
Your backpack space is limited and doesn't change (it's the same if you're one char or if you're four). Medkits and consumables actually take space in your backpack. So if you want to have 2 medkits per char, this means you will have a permanent lock on 8 slots in your backpack. There's also no auto-sorting (which would come in handy if you read point 4)
4. Item levels
God i hate this. You may have exactly the same item, but since it's a different level, one of them is superior. So basically the items' comparison is chaotic, since you not only have to compare the item's abilities but also its level. They countered this by making it so that you get items according to your char's level, but that's just not doing it for me. I want specific items not procgen. This also means there's not an auto-equip or "optimize" option, which makes it hell to look through all the different items with tiny impovements and details. I wish more work was done in this area, so that the epic item really felt like an epic item (like it has some history). Now it really feels random.
However, i personally feel the pros outmatch the cons in this game. Even if the cons are things i hate, i'm having much fun with this game.
Anyway i'll stop this review now since it was meant to be shorter. Just go and buy it and you'll not regret it.

From the Depths has been one of the most rewarding games I have ever played. It is rewarding because there is a lot of complex aspects of the game that take time to learn, but once you learn them, you kind of feel like the master of the universe. Seriously, when you build a ship that only uses 1000 blocks, and that 1000 block ship can take out a 7000 block monster ship, you will sit back and make those two ships fight over and over and you will be just as excited the 100th time you duel them as you were the first time.
My most favorite thing about the game is that it is such blank canvas. You can create and design your war death machines any way you would like. The sky is the limit (well actually space is the limit, yes you can build space craft). SO many possibilities. My style is typically extremely fast small craft with only one large weapon mounted to them, think of my ships and aircraft as fast gun carriers. But that is just one of thousands of possibilities. Some people like to re-create EVE Online ships. Some folks like to build battleships that are so huge it takes them weeks to do so. I love to just download other people's designs and have a look at all the crazy things people come up with. I always come away with new cool ideas to integrate into my designs when I do this.
So, the learning curve. Yep, it’s there, and it’s steep. It is not impassable though. Like other games in this genre you will have to put in a little work in order to learn it. Post questions on the forums (fantastic community there by the way), watch Youtube videos, have a look at the wiki...those kinds of things. The in-game tutorials are getting better and better, so you may not have to do quite so much homework as you did a year ago.
If you are reading this, then you must at least like building games or sandbox games. If that describes you, then this is definitely the game for you.

(This is an Early Access game, review written on 4/8/16)
From the Depths is an engineering game where you construct naval ships, aircraft, subs, and structures to shoot at and conquer other ships, aircraft, subs, and structures.  This is done mostly in first-person although there are map overview RTS aspects as well.
From the Depths has a lot of, well, depth to its building.  Every aspect of your air/water craft is constructed of essentially minecraft blocks.  Even fuctional aspects, like the engines or weaponry, are contructed of special blocks.  There are several weapon types to build, including two types of naval cannon, missiles and torpedoes, and even lasers, each with relative checks and balances.  There is a ton of customization when it comes to building your fleet, but there is also a big learning curve.  I feel this curve is not insurmountable though.
There is a strategic campaign where you fight and defeat 8 unique factions for world domination or something.  The forces featured are largely designed by the community.  The campaign can be fairly challenging for a newer player, but it can get very unbalanced later on, as you get an over abundance of resources.
While Early Access titles are typically very dubious in value, I find From the Depths trustworthy.  The dev is fairly active on the official forums, and often informs us on what he is working on.  I've owned this game for about six months, and multiple major updates with big features have been released.
Overall, From the Depths is a complex but nonetheless fun and intriguing game in the build-stuff-out-of-blocks genre.

As a fan of the series, I am disappointed to write that I have been less than thrilled by Dreamfall Chapters. Apart from the obvious bugs and other problems following the first chapter's launch, the overall feeling of the game remains unpolished and, in some areas, downright sloppy. While the environments, character models, and animations are visually stunning, there are several moments throughout the first two chapters that weren't given the attention they deserved. For instance, there are many dialogue sequences throughout the game that feel unnatural or devote camera focus solely to a single character. It's possible that this is because the developers did not have enough time to fully animate the other characters in the conversation. This sort of oversight removes the player from the immersion they would otherwise feel while living through each character. In summary, the game looks great but feels tragically rushed. The complete lack of challenging puzzles makes the game feel more like a piece of interactive fiction than it's adventure-oriented predecessors. I would still (cautiously) recommend this title to any fan of the previous games.

Good music, artwork and decent atmosphere.   It was entertaining, I enjoyed exploring the various locations, and the developers were careful to avoid needless tedium.  But, it doesn't feel like a finished product.  The tried-and-true plot device of background information in the form letters left behind by various characters is employed, but beyond that there is no worthwhile  information or descriptions on anything other than quest items and objects, and even that is really light.   There are spirits wandering about the game that you can interact with, but they'll only give you one or two lines of information and that's it.  Some are critical in advancing the game, but even then the dialog goes something like  "I did X for you", to which the reply is "Thanks! Now here's the next place you need to go."
As such, the letters themselves offer the most complete picture of what's going on in the game.  Because of this, it feels less like playing a game and more like turning pages in a book.  There just isn't that much payoff in the gameplay.  Beyond the letters, the plot definitely could use a lot more work.  The game tries to set itself up as a treatise on the nature of evil, which had promise.  But then, the game just felt like it ended suddenly as if someone said "Never mind, let's wrap this up".
I don't dislike the game enough to give it a "no" on a recommendation.  But, I definitely would not pay full price and would suggest to hold off purchase until a >75% off sale.

A decent adventure puzzle game with more classic horror puzzle gameplay and relatively unique mechanics. Although it looks and handles like a Unity indie game it's quite satisfying and creative for what it is. With a relatively strong lore and atmosphere backing it.
One of the biggest disappointments of the game are the ghosts, which are one of the initial most gripping concepts of the game. The ghosts seldom ever say anything interesting or pertinent to anything, they could not be there at all and it would make little difference. Often, there isn't even any reason for them to be where they are. There's little signs that a human died or even may have died in the place where the ghost is, they're just in this place to fluff up the gameplay.
The game has an abundance of quirky, cosmetic achievements players get for examining certain things. They only serve to detract from the immersion especially when the game has so many achievement pop ups just for progressing at all. There is also an abundance of juvenille references in the game which also kill immersion and respect.
The main enemies are terrible. Little boney insect things. Uncreative, uninteresting. And what's worse, the game actually has a cool looking and threatening enemy appear at one point. But apparently it's a one time thing. That enemy is only used for one scene, afterwards it's just boney insect things that are the threat. The ending of the confrontation with the finale villain is also overly dismissive and rushed.
There is also no horror. The world is soft macabre, but not horror. It does manage to balance the gameplay itself quite well save for one part where it forces the player to run back and forth around the map for something.
It's a fun game with a decent length. The price is high compared to other game genres which give players way more playtime for almost the same price, but for an adventure game it's not too bad. It's an experience that feels good to come out of.

Lords of Shadow 2 continues where Lords of Shadow left off, almost literally, with an aged Dracula awakening during modern times, weakened and missing his memories from the past thousand years or so. Soon, Zobek comes to Dracula and informs him that Satan is preparing to return. Zobek offers Dracula eternal rest in return for destroying Satan’s acolytes, thus preventing Satan return. With the two coming to an agreement, Dracula sets out to recover his full power and prevent the return of Satan.
As one of its strongest aspects, Lords of Shadow 2 expands on the excellent combat system from the original Lords of Shadow. Many of Dracula’s combat moves are very similar to those used in LoS, this time with a vampiric twist. Instead of the Combat Cross Dracula wields whips made from his own demonic blood. Instead of the light and chaos magic from the first game, Dracula has the Void Sword and Chaos Claws. The Void Sword can restore Dracula’s health with each successive hit, while the Chaos Claws increase the Dracula’s combat strength. Similar to the magic system from LoS, both the Void Sword and the Chaos Cross have their own pool of magic which can be restored by chaining combos, which drops magic orbs.
Chaining combos is not as easy as it sounds however, as even the weakest enemies have ranged attacks, as well as strong unblockable attacks. Thankfully, Dracula’s dodge and parry will mostly keep the player safe as long as they are mindful of enemy patterns. Lords of Shadow 2, like Lords of Shadow before it, shows the player no mercy when they fail to dodge or parry an attack. In fact, even with some of the weakest enemies, a failed dodge can mean getting hit by a string of unblockable attacks until the enemies combos are over. This can lead to a somewhat abrupt death if the player does not manage to restore Dracula’s health immediately.
Combat does feel more forgiving in Lords of Shadow 2 this time around, however. For one, checkpoints are more frequent and areas before large fights generally have an artifacts which allow Dracula to recharge his health and magic before heading into the fray. Helping to make things easier this time, secondary combat items such as daggers no longer require collection and instead recharge after a few seconds. There are also a host of consumable items in LoS2 that do everything from restore health and make attacks stronger to slow down time and give unlimited magic. These items make the difficulty curve in Lords of Shadow 2 feel more manageable, despite its sometimes unforgiving combat.
Unfortunately, the game is not always about its fantastic combat system. Sometimes, the game slows to a crawl as Dracula is forced to use stealth to proceed. These segments see Dracula using some of his abilities such as possession, rat transformation, and bat swarm to progress. At first, the stealth segments make sense as Dracula is weak and needs to possess either scientists or cyborgs to progress. As Dracula recovers his powers however, it becomes unclear why he is forced to sneak about. Dracula can destroy one of Satan’s acolytes but is unfit to face a simple cyborg? It makes little sense.
One particular stealth segment towards the middle of the game is particularly frustrating. Dracula is forced to sneak about a maze full of dry leaves as a boss actively hunts for him. If the boss hears Dracula step on the leaves, the boss finds Dracula and forces him back to the start of the maze, taking a portion of the player’s health. This is made worse by the boss actively pursuing Dracula regardless of the noise made, sending Dracula back to the start if he simply comes into line of sight. The segment is made all the more insulting since Dracula and the said boss fight almost immediately following the maze. What was the point of the maze at all? Why did Dracula run if he could simply stand and fight?
Some of the frustrations involved with Lords of Shadows 2 also stem from what should have been its greatest strength: the open world. Without spoiling too much, the game basically revolved around two semi-open worlds: the city and Dracula’s castle. The game looks beautiful and the levels are mostly well designed, but the navigation map struggles to keep up. Sometimes the player is left with nothing more than a vague arrow pointing somewhere off-screen. I found myself several times wandering in circles only to discover a small ledge I strained to see or a far off switch I was supposed to hit with a dagger. These moments can be frustrating, and may be played off as exploration/puzzles but mostly just feel like poor design.
In regards to puzzles, LoS2 is a little bit disappointing. While the volume of puzzles seems to have increased significantly from the previous entries, the quality seems to have gone down. Most of the puzzles boil down to pull this switch/use that power. Rarely do the puzzles reach the height of those in the original Lords of Shadow, if at all.
That’s not to say the game doesn’t have its inspired moments though. Part way into the game, Dracula unlocks optional arena style challenges where the player can put Dracula’s powers to the test. These can be a lot of fun and test the player’s skill by doing such things as banning the use of a specific power or setting a time limit to kill enemies.
There are also moments where the game shines creatively such as a first person feeding segment, some clever sliding puzzles, and an interactive play. Equally enjoyable are several segments in the game where Dracula fights with a companion at his side. Dracula may be required to work with his companion to platform past obstacles or to solve puzzles, which really feels great. These moments are too few and far between, unfortunately.
On the more positive end of things, the boss fights in Lords of Shadow 2 are actually an improvement on Lords of Shadow and seems to take a page from Mirror of Fate. The fights feel more epic, with larger bosses, and fewer quick time events.  The QTE are mostly limited to escape animations but are sometimes used for boss finishers. Wisely, Mercury Stream has provided checkpoints before boss finishers which makes the QTE less frustrating. Wiser still, you can turn off QTE entirely if you so choose. With boss fights less reliant on QTE, the game flows a lot better, and it gives the player more of a sense of involvement during boss fights.
As someone who actually enjoys the Lords of Shadow universe, I felt slightly let down by its supposed conclusion. While the ending was satisfying enough, it felt a bit abrupt and unexpected. The story also pays almost no attention to the events of Lords of Shadow, only vaguely referring to the game’s events. Instead, the game focuses more on events from Mirror of Fate. This combined with the sudden demise of some key characters and a lack of explanation regarding how the player comes to arrive at Dracula’s castle, make the story feel unrealized at times. This is further compounded by an ending that doesn’t necessarily feel appropriate for the series, especially given the general direction of the entire game’s story and portrayal of Dracula throughout.
As the player progresses through Lords of Shadow 2, they see Dracula coming to terms with the monster that he has become - how becoming Dracula has affected him, his family, and the world around him. Unfortunately, that character progression just doesn’t live up to the ultimate ending, leaving loose ends right at the moment that it seemed everything was going to be tied up.
Overall, Lords of Shadow 2 was an enjoyable experience despite some questionable gameplay additions and a lackluster ending. There’s a lot of content to Lords of Shadow 2 and a lot of fun to be had, including a New Game+ mode. Hopefully the upcoming Alucard DLC just ties up some of the loose ends that LoS2 left unraveled.

It's a big improvement of the first game. No doubt about that. Also I would love to like this game but it's decent at best. I'm pretty sure they made it as irritating as they could. I'm going to list the MAJOR grievances I have with this game.
EXAMPLE: At one point in the game, you have to ride an elevator. So you kill a bunch of enemies and go to the elevator to find out it has no power. Then you go back to the entrance and start the generator. All enemies respawn and you kill them again. When you're finally at the elevator there's still no power since the generator has a timer >: ( So back to the entrance again and start the generator AGAIN! Then back to the elavator a final third time. Frustrates me to no end.
The game constantly pulls this sort of thing.
EXAMPLE: You see a powerup just out of reach. You move through the entire area of jumping puzzles and climbing to get to the top. That's where the way to the powerup is found and you have to jump down all the way to the beginning to get it.
Unnecessary and long cutscenes is also gravely irritating. I love cutscenes when they tell story and fill a purpose.
When you fast travel you get a 15 sec cutscene when he "opens" the device, a second cutscene (10 sec) when he enters, and a third (10 sec) when he exits. That is not fast. When you enter the shop there is a annoying cutscene every time.
To be fair though you can skip the cutscenes by entering the pause menu and selecting skip cutscene but that is also slow and annoying.
Oh! I broke my keybord in half in pure rage recently when playing the challenges in this game. You don't get full health or magic between tries. You don't even get back the levels of hp and mp you had when you entered the challenge if you retry. And the goals in the challenges are not set to be fun. They are set to be as irritating as (un)humanly possible.
And the chupacabra character. I seriously want to punch the creator of that guy. I'm dead serious.
Other than that it's a pretty decent game. Combat is mostly fun and the whole idea with the castle(won't say more) was actually great. The lore is a good read and the existance of dodo birds is a great relief for any perfectionist. Also the freedom to run around the city and castle however you want (after you've unlocked the area) is a welcome change in the series.
Oh! Also the story is pretty bad.

After a little more than 15 hours of a rather painful experience, I've finally managed to plough through the boredom, frustration and dismay, feeling a great and lasting sadness when the credits finally rolled over, putting an end the whole agony.
A calamitous art direction:  Bland and repetitive backdrops (sewers, laboratory, castle, then more sewers), poor choice of a de-saturated almost monochromatic color palette (everything seems to be just another variation of grey), botched facial 3D renders (the characters' faces look like plastic with absolutely no emotional range, Dracula's face is particularly bad and almost laughable), uninspired character design (Nergal is just some random bald dude and Satan looks like a gym bro on steroids).
Incoherent game design:  Ridiculous mandatory and aggravating stealth (the 'Agreus' sequence is already famous all across internet, and that's not even talking about Dracula being forced to transform into a rat to avoid security guards that are stronger than Satan), exploration ruined by a archaic game structure and sub-par plat-forming (the wolf game mechanic breaks the rhythm and the climbing is either unclear or too easy with the pointers).
Mediocre sound design:  The only thing worth listening to is Dracula's theme at the title screen and a couple of action themes during the prologue, the rest being forgettable (compared to the first Lords of Shadow, this is a major let down), and the voice actors seem to be reading their lines more than they are giving it any kind of emotional depth (Robert Carlyle, Patrick Stewart and Richard Madden, shame on you ! You guys were so much better in previous games !).
A decent plot, completely destroyed by the worst appalling ending I've ever witnessed in a triple A game.  The story is actually interesting if you've completed both the first Lords of Shadow and Mirror of Fate (otherwise, don't even bother), but the grand finale and the game's ending is so embarrassingly insulting, it's actually a league of its own.
Combat mechanics are half-way decent, since it's basically a dumbed-down version of the first game (the game is much easier, thanks to a larger Synchronized Block window and an overpowered evade move, which knocks down and interrupts enemies), but let's not delude ourselves any longer and call this game what it is: shameful.
Objectively, it's not the worst piece of gaming♥♥♥♥♥♥this century, but unfortunately the first Lords of Shadow which was published 3 years before this sequel, is just way better in every possible way (yes, even the fixed camera which actually provided some cinematic flair).  As a fan of the first Lords of Shadow and having always argued about Mirror of Fate's qualities (still waiting for it on Steam), Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 has been such a disappointment it has made me depressed, disgusted and hateful.  And I don't play video games to be depressed, disgusted and hateful.  You have been warned.

From the depths is a fantastic idea with lot of potential that you can already experience in the Early Access.
In this game you build a ship or aircraft (or a combination of both) using a combination of blocks (think minecraft) that you then use in a Campaign map to destroy other crafts, or in single event battles against others.
The crucial element of this game is that each element of the build (engine, guns, missiles, hull) is itself built by blocks, that, depending on what you want to optimise, requires non-trivial choices of configurations. This reasoning applies to everything:
* hulls: material and structure affects: attrition in water/air, area of exposure, weight vs armour.
* guns: length of gun barrel, shell exit velocity, shell composition, reload time, barrel cool-out time, affects effectiveness of the shell on target, size, area of exposure to enemy fire.
* missiles, mines and grenades, torpedo (pins, Infra-red detection, warhead size, etc.)
* engine (cylinders, turbo-chargers, exhausts, etc.).
For example, an engine can be built to be very heavy and efficient (in fuel consumption), but can also be lighter and less efficient, or optimised for low-RPM, or for high-RPM, and this depends solely on the blocks you choose, and how they are positioned in relation to each other.
Finally, the combination of each of these pieces then makes the craft itself suitable for some things (e.g. a bomber, a battleship), but very unsuitable for others (a fighter, a submarine), and is therefore the combination of different designs that leads to total victory.
Ah, and, of course, you then actually drive/fly the thing, or put an AI doing it for yourself. And there are a lot of other things (resources management and logistics, strategy and tactics in campaign), that I will not even touch here to simplify...

This is one of those "I really wanted to like this game" situations.  It is a good game but here is my list of grievances:
The combat is very very basic; some skills apply effects (stun, charm) and the rest apply damage (+/-).
There are hidden stats.  If I have 100% accuracy vs. mob how does it miss or dodge?
There are unexplained combat systems: Energy, physical, fire etc. but guess what! usually you have no clue what.
Hidden doors! Yay! But once you know what to look for you just scan area for that one thing.
Real possibilities for making friends/enemies with different corps but they are all available even if they hate you.

I've had this game since early access and it just keeps getting better. It's still got a few bugs here and there but nothing game breaking. The combat can be a bit dull and repetitive and I think the regular difficulty is too easy, but it has got a good in depth character building system that impacts both your combat abilities and your overworld interaction. For example, if you use a hacker and upgrade one of his three skill trees then he'll be better suited to hacking particular objects during exploration.
I think the reputation system is good too, although my one niggle would be that it's so much easier to lose rep than it is to gain rep. For example, I was doing a mission for one of the corps in their own offices (so no negative relation for doing the mission) and I found a terminal. It gave me the option to try to hack in and find out where my objective was. I thought, hey, sure, they won't mind since it helps with my objective, right? Wrong. I failed the hack, security bot fight was easy but then I get -15 rep. The mission was worth +1 rep... If you add in the auctionable loot then I made a net rep of -6 or so, just because of one terminal interaction that didn't make sense. (To be fair, perhaps that one is a bug... It usually makes it clear when you'll lose rep for doing something and it's usually when you steal info from a specific terminal or if you steal valuable company specific items to auction afterward.) Still, the difference in gaining and losing rep is immence. So my tactic just ended up being to pick one poor company that I'd target relentlessly for everyone else. They start sending in super difficult enemies but since the combat system is pretty easy (if you set up your party right) it actually made it about the normal difficulty you'd expect.
All in all though, it's a great game. The characters are well written, you feel like you get enough choices to accurately play the kind of character you want to play and the depth of the universe is apparent. If you like grinding for the ultimate endgame then this is the game for you, haha.

Star Crawlers, is a turn based  dungeon crawler rpg  that had alot of potential to be good. the soundtracks are enjoyable, the dialogue for some npcs and characters is well thought out delivered and interesting, the lore of the world the different factions the different conflicts is all entertaining and fun to watch and somtimes your choices will have huge consquences or great rewards. everything that you could want from a space faring game is right here and for the most part it starts out enjoyable till you play a certain amount of hours and realize the game is actually very hollow and shallow.
lets get down to the reasons I say this shall we? the game is fun, for the first few hours you start out witha tutorial which you can manually skip once you complete it your first time where you are then introudced to the bar tender and then introduced to the hub world where you will buy supplies from the npcs for your missions, buy weapons upgrade talk of rumours and open different sub mission plots. so far so good. Your first mission will be to board a abandoned spacestation  for a faction where your job is to recover a blacksuit case with top secret information on some workers of a certain company that the company wishes to have to stop a cordinated worker protest which could end up costing them  a great deal of money and the revealing of one of the few secrets they wish to keep.
you'll go through this job acquire the suitcase be given 4 different options and depending on class and background one additional choice will pop up mostly revolving around the two central choices of whether or not  help the worker union or B turn the  information back to the big company for big money. you'll also do a part of this mission where after doing all this you'll run into your first boss enemy a giant alien robot who is malfunctioning and has a big gun that deals a little bit of damage. you'll beat him easily unless on a fairly challenging difficulty and continue on with the quest till finished with it and obtaining your rewards.
this is the first mission and its fun this it the true starting point of the game where you will soon be able to after taking this quest begin doing more missions. if you're playing on non perma death mode good because if you die you won;t have to go through this whole process again.. if you're on perma death however.. well we will talk about that in a bit.
after completing this quest more missions will pop up you'll have some money to hire some  party members  or fix the malfunctioning robot to be a part of your team and they will help quite a bit at the start of this game. you'll have some more missions that become avalible which after ocmpleting will unlock another story quest for you to do that you should not take on yet instead go grind a bit till you are the appropiate level and tackle it eventually. if you die on normal mode congrats you lost some of your party members but your items and everything you had kept will be fine.if you die on perma death mode however.. well congratulations YOU GET TO GO THROUGH THAT WHOOOLE ENITRE MISSION SET UP to get to that part..AGAIN and lose everything.
this, is when the game starts to get annoying. if you don't know what im talking about then make another save file load it up and play the game on permadeath mode. now i know what some of you are thinking "thats the point of a roguelike game you die you restart." which yes you are correct that is the point of a dungeon crawler and roguelike.. but what is not the point is everytime you die everything changes.. maps are completely different lay outs of dungeons are different new oppertunities present themselves... that is the not case here for starcrawlers if you die on permadeath  you'll go through the same phase, the same begining over..and over..and over again again. you'll do the same quest and mission progression listen to the same soundtracks and go through the same levels only this time with a  different layout but fighting basically the same enemies doing a faction quest or non faction quest grinding for exp searching for itms and then you will do basiclaly the same thing on another ship based level like the last one only with varying mobs.. and you will do this till the storyline quest pops up and goes "heeey go do thiiiis!" ..as linearly.. as linear can be.

This is a pretty good game.  I've been on a dungeon crawler kick recently and this fit the bill.  Not many (if any?) sci-fi type blobbers around, so it was unique in that way.  The various character classes are cool and have some interesting abilities.  Loot is certainly plentiful and if you constantly do red(hard) missions you'll be loaded up with purples constantly.  Don't let the "hard" rating of missions scare you, with the right character balance you still pretty much steam roll anything but boss mobs...and they aren't that much harder to deal with.  The randomly generated missions start to feel a little grindy toward the end of the game but the story created missions were really good.  I would have liked to see more puzzles and secrets, as they are a staple of blobber games.  I think my team of Smuggler, Hacker, Soldier, and Void Psyker worked a little too well together because I barely lost any hit points on the final fight! If you like blobbers and sci-fi, pick this one up and enjoy!

So this game got me hooked and I LOVE IT... however...
I have found like many others apparently that there are some major flaws which I am compelled to point out.  It looks like I'm going to find all sorts of nifty ways to use my character classes.  I mean, the way the dialog and story line is written out, it's exciting and fun how your team interacts with each other and the world, how you gain and lose reputation.  It's a fun juggling romp which makes you feel connected to actual entities in space, which not a lot of games are so fluent in creating.  I love the setting, I love the relationship of the corporations and how every class has been written in with their own personalities.
Atmospherically and contextually, and other big words, Starcrawlers is so easy to sink into.  The classes are a great blend of sci-fi persona with both traditional and original concepts.  I think the Psykers are very cool yin and yang ideas.  All together this game looks to be amazingly well rounded, and it is a blast to start getting your toes wet in the crawl.
Then hours later, unfortunately you start to realize things aren't making sense.  As I have progressed, I start looking at these skill trees up and down and going, "What the hell?".  The abilities are all just about doing the same thing, damage this way, damage that way, but hardly any of them make a difference.  I hate to say this, but they are all just different spellings of doing the same thing.  Doing damage with different presentations.
There seems to be somewhat strong identities from class to class, but I'm not seeing how they're being used to their full potential.  For instance, the Cyberninja has the ability "Ambush", which is on the 1st tree, 2nd tier, and takes advantage of enemies who are BLINDED.  That's great!  So look around and see what other abilities cause BLIND....  Uhhh.. ok I see one... It's the "Shadowfall" ability that's on the 3rd tree, 5th tier?!
So I'd have to master tree 3 before I could strategically use a very young branch from another.  With that kind of logic (or lack there of) that practically forces me to focus on tree 3 before anything else, which in this is example is merely something considerably minor.. right?
Well... maybe that's not so much of a big deal.  Maybe it's a matter of finding skills that cause BLINDNESS from other classes.  That would be cool!  That would really make the cohesion of the team work together!  Let's see... nope.. nope.. nope AH, Void Psyker!  He/She has some tricks for that.  Great...  But that's it?  Seriously, of my whole team (discluding Soldier and Engineer thus far) I only see one or two classes that barely utilize this debuff.  It's not just that, there seems to be a lack of noticeable relation to each other.  As if they're just put there as a decal.
Now looking at all these other conditions like Dazed, Charmed, Confused, Stunned... and VULNERABLE... whatever the hell that means?  You see what I'm getting at? These buffs and debuffs, to me, appear aimlessly scattered around.  You look through it all and you find a HUGE lack of correlation between skills.  The Smuggler is a prime example of this with its traps.  Just random outcomes and no follow through.  What does the Smuggler do, or for that matter, any other class or weapon, that can take advantage of these effects?
But maybe I'm barking up the wrong "tree". (pun intended) What about the elements? Besides debuffs, you have an array of "elemental" damage types, (Fire, Force, Nanite, Void, Corrosion... am I missing any?) but what difference do they make besides a name? How am I gonna know what I'm guarding against or, like others have mentioned, what makes one armor or shield more useful than another?  It's not completely without effect, fire burns, and corrosion melts armor I guess, and maybe the others have their own nature, but hell if I know?  THERE IS NOTHING, NO GUIDE, NOT EVEN A PROPER WIKI that is going to explain any of this to you.
I would say it's all just random, but I can't because I don't know.  Many of these trees, from top to bottom, have nothing to offer that consist of any strategy.  It's just damaging, straightforward and no kind of tandem to speak of.  Some skills make other skills obsolete and pointless.  Just previous lame versions you trade out.  And mixing two trees is just as sterile.  Using the Smuggler as an example again, he/she has a trap mine that damages all or most enemies once triggered... well, in the Gunslinger tree there's "Trick Shot", and what does it do?  Damages up to three targets, which, most of the time, that's the magic enemy number.  They both use the damage type of your weapon.  If you want to spend all day trying to figure out what makes those two any different, or reason as to why you're "building" a character in any form or fashion, you're going to get ridiculously frustrated.  It's pointless... that's my point.
It's all broken, or never assembled really.
The only part of this game that I have found any strategy with at all is TIMING, and it's one repeated pattern. Simply put, BUFF allies and infect enemies with Hacker, let everyone else unleash their "skills" (multi-colored damage output) and when you want to really laugh at them, pull another Hacker trick by speeding up a teammate. and he gets to cut in line.  This works great when you time your timing, (LOL) and you pull one member in for a finisher.
That's my next subject... The Cyberninja and Prototype overkill.  Want to make sure you always have the upper hand?  "Acid Rain" and "Overcharge" are ridiculous trump cards.  That's all I'll say about that.
So I think that's all I need to say for my 2 cents.  I'm gonna thumbs down this game.  I hope that it will encourage the developers to think about putting as much thought into the mechanics as they have into the world.  I love the atmosphere and I love the just about everything this game presents except for this big stump.  It just seems unfinished.  I don't quite understand the high rating of this game unless they were made in the first 6 hours of playing.  It's such a beautiful game with so many enticing elements.  I think people must have the same idea as I had, that you're adventuring and exploring and finding gear, and maybe you're not sure about how it all fits together yet, but that's part of the adventure is finding out later.  Well... I'm sorry to say this but there's a major disappointment ahead.  The only thing to figure out is how many times you'll pay to reset all your ability points before realizing you're not working with a full bag of tricks.
This is what bugs me, again, the elements are there but are not being used!  So because I actually DO believe in this game.. I mean.. I'm ready for the REAL VERSION.. whether that be a complete overhaul update (which would be nice) or STARCRAWLERS 2 (which should happen anyway) ...I'm going to give some suggestions to the Juggernaut team.
PLEASE, finish the combat system.  All it would take is a little TLC.  Make the skills stand out.  Give the crawlers abilities that work in conjunction with each other so you can really use the timing of your crew in different ways.  I'm sure this was the goal in the first place, but I know what happened... the engineer for the skill system and stats mechanics was abducted by space worms as you were nearing the end of the kickstarter campaign... these things happen.
Look at this crappy review by me and... understand I represent the common, and not all that successful of a gamer ...consider the outline of what I and others have identified about your product and take some pride in your creation!  I can shamelessly give this game a thumbs up in my heart.  It's got the soul of something that could be the foundation of a continuing epic.
Anyway, I'm going to keep going at it, maybe I'll figure a little more out and get to the end of the story.  Maybe.. be nice to come back to it working right. -J

I know that it may seem unwise to judge a game before it is fully released, but I felt it to be a kind of duty to say: so far it is going great! "Dreamfall: Chapters" masterfully develops the beautiful story started in "TLJ" and "TLJ: Dreamfall," keeping the same unique atmosphere and quality. It is really worth it to spare a minute and experience one of the biggest adventures you might take part in on your computer.

There are two very engaging plot structures at play in this game; a mystery construction of pipes in the magical realm and an epic political/corporate conspiracy in the technological one, and the desire to see where these went (coupled with some fond memories of The Longest Journey) was what kept me playing. And then it ended quite suddenly, without any form of denouement or resolution, which is solely the reason for my 'not recommended' -- the feeling that stuck with me as the credits rolled being "was that it?". The nature of episodic content is to string you out as long as possible so I wasn't expecting everything to be laid out in front of me, but I was expecting something.
There are also a bunch of design decisions that didn't sit well with me. Zoe (one of the main protagonists) is an incredibly well rounded, emotional, likeable, believable character with some fantastic dialogue, and playing as her is fun, rewarding, and easily the high point of the game, and it's worth playing for this alone (though was it really necessary to see her in her underwear so prominently? Just because it was in the first game doesn't mean you've got to put it in the sequel). However, it causes a rather jarring discontinuity when you're presented the muscly hunk of the second protagonist Kian, who is as generic as they come and has all the personality and humour of a plank of wood with a serious face painted on it. If they were trying to make a point about the opposing nature of the two main characters then it is poorly made, as the opposite of an interesting character does not need to be a boring one. Playing as Kian was a deeply tedious experience.
There are only two main environments (one per character) and while they look pretty nice at first, they're less appealing after the fifth time trudging through them, and it's a far cry from the feeling of adventure and discovery in the previous games. At one point a bunch of paths in the technological overworld get closed off, which serves no point other than to be annoying as you can still get everywhere, you just need to take an even longer route. The magical world's equivalent to this is to feature the most epically terrible stealth puzzle the world has ever seen -- something which the designers attempt to hang a lantern on with a 'so you thought there wouldn't be stealth, but there is and you suck at it' achievement, which is a joke in somewhat poor taste considering how badly the puzzle is designed, and how completely unecesscary it is.
Sadly it's not the only bit of questionable design. There's a big thing about how your choices shape the story, but the choices you're presented with are so highly ambiguous that you might as well flip a coin for them, and then you're told in big letters THIS WAS IMPORTANT. THIS PERSON WILL REMEMBER. What, so all the other stuff I've been doing isn't important? The rest of my interactions are forgettable? The mechanic appears to be that these choices shift the gameplay in some manner, but they can't shift it too much as the story has to follow the same overall arc, so it comes across as kind of pointless. All it means is that you're guaranteed to be denied some content -- some of the walkthroughs I looked at referred to puzzles and sections that I never got to see. Adventure games don't have a terribly high replay value, so all this achieved was making me feel that I'd missed out. The choices feel very unsatisfying, and I think it's because they're trying to make them shape the story rather than the character. In Mass Effect (which I consider to be the gold standard for choice-based gameplay) the choices you make have little to no impact on the main story, but they have a massive effect on how you view your character, and while they may have had minor gameplay implications you didn't feel that you'd missed out on anything, but that's a roleplaying game where the development of your character is important to you. Here there aren't any roleplaying elements, and the choices you're forced to make don't develop your character in any way as the game will rationalise them so that the character you've been given remains consistent.
And then there are bits where the illusion of choice comes crashing down -- there's one bit where you have to chase after a character, but you're not in time to catch them. Only this is in an overworld, so you have the option of buggering off somewhere else. It's okay, they'll wait for you. You can even work your way around and approach them from the front -- but the game then begins its cutscene with you running up behind them.
There are some profoundly interminable cutscenes, invariably of people talking to each other - I was playing on a laptop and there were several times where the screensaver kicked in due to the lack of input, which made me wonder a bit if the creators would have preferred to make a film. It's also distinctly tonally inconsistent. Sometimes it's lighthearted and funny, sometimes it's serious and drab and sometimes there are bits that make me think 'really? was that entirely necessary?'.
There are some interesting moments, and it's possible that once it's complete I'll revisit it with a different opinion, but as it stands I don't feel it a story worth the time it takes to tell.

Rescue Team 5 continues right where the previous game left off. The lack of story is still a sore point, but the level design and the refined time-manager gameplay work together well.
After Rescue Team 4 went back to the roots of the series by removing everything that was not part of the core gameplay, this follow-up chose the “expansion disk” route by putting most of its focus on the level design.
Time management games are always similar: we get a few workers who gather some resources to remove obstacles and build production buildings (plus to save some helpless citizens here, since we are playing as rescue workers, after all). This simple formula needs interesting level layouts to keep the player away from boredom, and this is where Rescue Team 5 shines throughout all of its 50 stages. It eliminates most of the downtime by always providing something to do. Even the levels are a bit unpredictable thanks to a new mechanic that lets us build, demolish, and rebuild production buildings.
This is a double-edged sword, as timed mode can quickly turn into frantic trial and error, but relaxed mode suddenly has a certain strategic aspect that elevates Rescue Team 5 above many of its competitors. If only there were some kind of story to go with it, RT5 could have been a must-have among time management fans—still, as it is, the game provides ample fun for those who like these games for their mechanics.

This is very much the kind of game which either becomes a cult classic a few years down the line, or simply gets forgotten. It's not really anything like Civilisation at all, there's very little "city" (planet) management, and the research gameplay is relaxed to put it mildly. It's really just a turn-based-tactics spaceship battle game with some persistence elements.
Those of you who are old enough, I'd like to take you on a brief journey through time. Back to when UFO: Enemy Unknown/XCOM: UFO Defense was new. Remember how the geoscape felt tacked on, like it was providing the minimum amount of glue to get you to the next battle? It's exactly the same here. Replace soldiers and aliens with space ships and, well, other space ships and you'd have something very close to Sid Meier's Starships. That sounds kind of like a compliment, doesn't it? Well, not entirely. The look and feel of the game would really sit quite well in the mid-late 90s (compare Total Annihilation), and frankly the pared-down Civ-like engine for outside of battle is less polished even than XCOM was in its day.
In addition to that, and perhaps in some ways as a consequence, the difficulty seems to be miscalibrated. I put it on "normal" (from the default "easy"??) for the first try at playing, and really got straight through to winning the game with pretty trivial ease - maybe 3 battles lost - and that's without ever learning half the interface or discovering where the last faction was. I'd speculate that players who have a reasonable sense of where to put there upgrade points would find it painfully easy on any but the higher difficulties.
Thankfully, the actual turn-based battling is pretty enjoyable, and the ship customisation works well. Good for a pick-up-and-play, assuming that you have a couple of hours to spare, and perhaps a worthy antidote to too much Civ.

I would not regard this strongly as a horror game. Given how much of the game involves talking to ghosts (many of whom are disfigured), it unsurprisingly is a little dark with (no shortage of) murder in its story. A couple of monsters have an element of jump-scare factor when they attack for the first time, but it wears off into irritation. Initially the atmosphere made me uneasy, but after a while I relaxed as it became apparent there wasn't much concern of nasty surprises. Some of the time as she examines some of the items in the mansion Elena seems to be enjoying herself. More adorable than scary at times really.
So it's not trying very hard to scare the player, which can be good or bad depending how you feel about the jumpscare-fests some games that do try are.
Regarding the issues I've found most noticeable, at least once the game has become unresponsive and the menu screen consistently has been slow to appear. How much of this is down to my own computer's limitations is unknown.
I'm not sure why, but one puzzle involves setting a clock to a particular time. For a while I struggled with only getting it half a milimetre away from 'on the dot', only to seemingly accidentally have 'four minutes to' be accepted by the game as the solution (as opposed to what was very clearly said by the hint-giver). I've seen a video where someone managed to get it on the dot, so it's not a consistent issue.
It's pretty short (a handful of hours), which I think is for the better. Most of the game roughly follows a fairly simple pattern of exploring and backtracking to find objects or what they're needed for. So the shortness partly helps in that it means there aren't too many places to check if you've forgotten what needs a particular item. Then something tries to kill you once an area is complete. There are puzzles in the game, but they aren't designed to be all that difficult. I only missed one of the notes that tell the story, but from looking at the achievements there were optional hidden things I missed.
There are details I found likeable, such as the moment of blurring as you 'switch forms'. There is also a painting which markedly differs in appearance depending which form you're in (it's in the guest house). Although I found the gameplay irritating during the final chapter (there are four in total), the chapter was a pleasant surprise in a number of ways to me, which helped in the positivity of my final impression.
The soundtrack was okay and the art style quite nice, but overall I feel like the focus was on story and gameplay. I enjoyed picking up notes and reading about the experiences of the characters. Although it's not immensely intriguing, this together with the snippets from some of the random ghosts and examining objects give the world flavour and (un/)life. The idea of helping spirits of the dead find peace is something that appeals to me, so that's one aspect of the story I like. The explanation for the origins of the monsters and the malice infecting the place is also a decently interesting one.
It's more the puzzles that give the gameplay variation. Although I found it a touch tedious at times, the methods of progress overall aren't complicated. A highlight is the mechanic of possessing objects to move them (like a vase or a table), which I find a fun idea.
So.
-Not much in the way of horror
-Decent gameplay but would become repetitive if the game were much longer
-Expect backtracking
-Puzzles aren't very complicated
-Story isn't stunning but isn't bland
-Some nice ideas

Let's get this out of the way: this is clearly an indie title so it doesn't have AAA production values. That said, it's a very nicely done adventure game.
One thing I love is that the plot seem rich and well done, with the gameplay written to fit it rather than some wonky game concept with a plot thinly stretched over it. I was quite pleasantly surprised how well the plot was tied together. Granted, you play as a teenage girl so there is some awkwardness there in diary entries that felt a bit clunky to this middle-aged man, but I'm pretty sure I'm not the target audience.
The game itself is a side-scrolling adventure with *very* slight horror elements - and I felt they were well done.
On the downside, I play with a controller and this isn't the most controller-friendly game. Problem 1: it is absolutely impossible to change the game resolution with a controller. You can bring up a menu to choose the resolution, but once you do, you're stuck. If you're streaming the game to your TV (as I am), it means a trip into the other room to un-stick yourself.
Similarly, you can only navigate up and down in the menus with the dpad on your controller - the sticks will not cut it.
Finally, all the in-game prompts show up as keystrokes, not buttons, so I had to experiment a bit with pressing buttons to figure out that "[E]" to bring up my inventory was the yellow Y on my Xbox 360 controller.
That said, the controller issues were not game-breaking by any stretch, once I sorted out the game resolution business.
The game is not terribly long - maybe 3 or so hours. There's not much replayability either, but that's to be expected.
The only other complaint I have is the cutscene artwork. This is where the game really looks its budget. The in-game graphics seem well-done and I love the presentation of the mansion, but the cutscene artwork is not up to the same level, and it's disappointing given that the rest of the game is solid.
All told, this is a good game with a few drawbacks. I'd rate it a solid 3 out of 5 if you set your indie expectations accordingly.

If you're reading this review, you've probably played the original Castlevania: Lords of Shadow. If not, go check out that game first before you buy LoS 2, since this game relies VERY heavily on the backstory from the original LoS.
For those of you who have played the original LoS and finished the game, your next question is probably going to be: how does LoS 2 compare to the original?
I was a very big fan of the original LoS, and my review of that game gave it a 9 on 10, with high praise for its beautiful landscapes and art direction, for its incredible musical soundtrack, its professional voice acting, and for its ambition in telling the origin story of Castlevania. I felt its weak points were the holes in the story that sometimes just didn't make any sense, and the odd puzzles that forced you into a puzzle menu to play the associated minigame.
LoS 2 retains all of the things that I felt made LoS a wonderful work of art, and also retains the higher resolution graphic textures that are unique to the PC version. It still runs easily at 120 fps for those who are using 120hz monitors and want to lock the VSync to the refresh. No screen tearing, no artifacts, just beauty. But be sure to disable the motion blur in the graphic settings (setting it to LOW is 100% disabled).
The game looks stunning, the backdrops and scenery are jaw-dropping, the animation is superb and flows like water. New weapons in the game have their own detailed animations and combos, and open up a whole new God of War-like variation to weapon variety that wasn't present in the first LoS. The music is modernized but retains the original LoS theme throughout many of the compositions, keeping true to the original soundtrack (the composer is the same as the original LoS, so he knows exactly how to bring back variations on the old tunes).
If you were a fan of the original, then I strongly recommend buying this game. In my opinion, this game is as good as the original, if not better in a number of ways. It isn't just a brand new story slapped on top of the old one, but rather it builds entirely on the story from the first LoS and gives it a full tribute in everything that it does. It is a very worthy sequel to the original game.
As a final score, I give Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 a rating of 9 on 10.  The only reason it did not score a 10 on 10 was due to the introduction of a new stealth mechanic that wasn't entirely fleshed out enough. Thankfully it isn't used that frequently, but it can get frustrating when you're in the mood to kick♥♥♥♥♥and you're forced into a medicore stealth mode.
I'd also like to thank Mercurysteam and Konami for releasing this game on PC, and for releasing it at the same time as their Console launches! They have shown us PC gamers a great deal of respect. Thank you!

Castlevania: Lord of Shadows 2 is a sequel to the well recieved but amoung some circles oft trashed "Lord of Shadows." Which blended God of War/Devil May Cry style gameplay with the original Castlevania actiony dark fantasy romp through monster land. I won't give away the ending to that game as some jerks do in even mentioning this game, but you probably already know. If you have not played Lord of Shadows, playing it first is an absolute necessity, and it's also a superior game to this one in my opinion.
That said, in my opinion, contrary to the many reviews that are probably due to people not getting paid enough to give the usual IGN "9.5/10 it's ok" kind of review, I found this game a great experience, for many many reasons, since I always like to leave the reader with a positive taste in their mouth if I reccomend this game, (which I do), Then I'll start with the things this game gets wrong once I briefly summarize what it's about.
Lord of Shadows 2 has you playing as a newly awakened Dracula after a brief and extremely handholdy tutorial (which will be especially tedious if you played the tutorial), Where he defends his castle from the Forces of The Brotherhood of light. These events take place after Lord of Shadows, and Mirror of Fate (which still needs a port, get on it Konami) And you can read the rest of this in the game summary above on the steam page.
The gameplay is a blend of the 3D actiony combat and beat em up that Devil May Cry and God of War pioneered and refined also seen in Lord of Shadows, it is similar enough to that game that it doesnt feel brand brand new, but still new enough to not feel rehashy. It also features platforming and Uncharted and God of War brand climbing sections. And some stealth sections. You explore Dracula's castle, both in the quasi-otherdimensional quasi-memory quasi-past, and the modern day city Castlevania which was built over the ruins of Dracula's castle and it's quite cool how they overlap.
Now, lets get to the negative bits. The stealth in this game is awful and unnessecary, There was a way this could've been done, which would involve Dracula stalking his prey and feeding, but the mighty Prince of Darkness running away from rejects in red from Legacy of Kain: Blood Omen 2 on steroids as rats was just ugh. But this can be forgiven as it is mostly just puzzles. The worst one is a particularly aggravating section of stealth against a giant monster satyr that you fight immediately afterward, and is a *COMPLETE* Pushover. It's ridiculous how easy it is to beat this guy after you were cowering in fear in the most difficult stealth section of the game.
Another thing that bothered me is how utterly uninspired and generic the soundtrack is. It's beautifully written and scored but it's utterly forgettable and generic. there is maybe one, possibly two pieces on the whole soundtrack I remember at all, and they were variations on something from the previous game. This is forgivable for most games, But not Castlevania a series which has always had an extremely memorable soundtrack.
Another odd thing is how arbitrary the things you can climb on and things you cant seem to be, giving a linearity that's even more irritating, but It's a standard of the genre so it is not so bothersome. I dislike how few platforming sections there are, honest platforming and it lacks puzzles compared to the first one.
And one last flaw I noticed, was how much I hate enemies that require a certain power to defeat, though thankfully those enemies are either rare or this can be gotten around by clever gameplay. In addition, nto enough moves interrupt enemies for long enough making it too easy to be overwhelmed in situations you shouldn't be, and there simply isnt a large enough variety of enemies compared to the first game.
Now onto the positives.
The Art Direction of this game and it's implementation is breathtakig, it's simply magnificent. And is definately the strongest points  of it. The animation is fantastic, the atmosphere is gorgeous and captures castlevania to a T, while reminding me of Devil May Cry, and Vampire: The Masquerade, this all creates a neo-gothic feel that perfectly suits this game.
The Combat is very good, and very polished. A skilled player can defeat most enemies completely untouched while keeping an very strong level of  challenge. the only drawback of the combat is the lack of stunlocks hits on groups of enemies causes far too much interruption, but this can be argued adds to the challenge, and I am a bit inclined to agree. The game feel is a bit light, but otherwise the sound of the fighting. I particularly like how it is a better Devil May Cry than the latest DMC game, and still retains all of the castlevania feel.
The Characters are all excellent, and the story is beautifully told, and has much pathos even if it's a touch predictable. All in all, it fits together in a really excellent way and creates an atmospheric, fun, rich experience, if a touch too short. It starts with a whimper and ends with a bang. Many great boss fights and difficult enemies, and no shortage of action.
To sum up, Castlevania Lord of Shadows 2 deserves is an excellently designed and executed game with a haunting and engaging story, a rich atmosphere, a fairly deep and well done combat system and plenty of gameplay and is well worth the money.
Visuals 9/10- Excellent art design and execution, well done animations, Rich, beautiful enviroments and atmosphere.
Sound 7/10- forgettable if well done soundtrack holds back what otherwise is an excellently voiced experience with quality foley .
Gameplay 7/10- Lack of enemy variety, with some flaws to an excellent combat system as well as lack of platforming, combined with not enough puzzles for my liking hold back slightly what is an extremely fun experience, the tedious stealth sections at times could've been an improvement were they better executed and designed but otherwise it is another black mark lowering it's score
