Having been pleasantly surprised by just how good the orginal lords of shadows was, it's fair to say that my expectations for its  sequel were fairly high and nearly four years  later, we have lords of shadow 2 and with it, two questions which roughly translate to: "Is this game a worthy sequel to the orginal" and "should I buy it? In answer to the first question, my answer would be, for the most part, yes it is. The reason why I say for the most part is because while I think that los2 is a genuinely good game, I feel that it falls just short of matching the greatness of the orginal. The main reason why I think this is, is because los2 is a game of two halves.
On the one half you have the exploration of draculas castle, which to say the least is huge and the medieval gothic  architecture as well as the unique characters and enemies that inhabit the prince of darkness's home. For me, this is where the game truly shines as it is this part of the game that seems to embody both the aesthetics and quality of the first game.
The other half of this game involves navigating through a modern day setting, which I'm afraid to say is where this game falters. The main reason for this is because while the modern envioments are competently enough designed from a gameplay perspective, they lack any kind of personality and uniqueness of their own to make them memorable or even particularly interesting enough to warrent further exploration beyond the main game. Indeed, aside from the boss battles that take place in these locations and the stealth sections (The latter of which I actually quite enjoyed, contrary to popular opinion!) I found most of my time spent in the modern setting to be fairly forgettable,  especially when compared to the parts that take place in Draculas castle, and ultimately hold the game back from being truly on par with the first game.
In answer to the second question as to whether the game is worth buying, my answer would be that if you enjoyed the original los then I defiantly believe that this game is worth buying. If you've never played the original but like God Of War style hack and slah games then I would also recomend this title as being a worthy purchase. In short, I would say that if you liked the original los then the odds are that you'll probably like this game as well. In conclusion, If I had to give the first game a score out of ten, then I would probably give it an 8. With this game, I feel that a 7 would be more appropriate.

Did you like the first game in this series? Well, you might find this one annoying then.
The first major problem is that unlike the first game, this one is much shorter. You can beat it in about 6-8 hours. That's a decent run time, but then you realize there is nothing else. The game even feels like less is going on, even when a lot of stuff is happening. And not in a good way.
The story is this:
Gabriel Belmont is Dracula. He wants to die. Because being Dracula is really rough. Now it's the future, and he wakes up. Death shows up and tells Dracula that if they defeat Satan together, than Dracula can have a weapon that will give him eternal rest. Dracula agrees, and it's off to hunt down three of Satan's kids to save the world.
Seems like a simple story, right? Well, it kinda isn't. Dracula ends up world hopping from time to time. This means he travels between two totally different world maps. A city, and a castle. The castle is a highly detailed and very pretty wonderland. It's well designed, tons of interesting enemies, and great atmosphere. The castle areas are the best enviornments in the game. Unfortunetly, the castle areas are also home to the worst bits of story. You mostly spend time running around, talking to characters from related to the lore. This also includes Dracula's dead wife and son, who ask you to preform fetch quests for them. At the end, you fight Dracula's inner evil, and the castle section is dead forever. No more use out that.
The city on the other hand is the worst. Everything is grey and looks alike. All the good will of the castle and it's varied enviornments is sucked away by the fact that Dracula can't jump over a fence. Running around the city area is difficult too, as the layout is poor and often trying to cram too much into too little space. I got lost a great number of times just trying to go back the way I came because they force you to take different routes all the time. The enemies are mutated humans who somehow manage to be able to block your strongest attacks by using a shotgun as a shield. The other enemies are humans in mech suits, which are easily amongst the most annoying since they fly outside your range and have high damage dealing guns. They even come equiped with shields to block the attacks that do land.
But the City part is where all the story happens. All the important, interesting, story details go on in the city. But the boss battles suffer even then. Boss fights in the city are single stage moments with more cutscene than combat, in comparison to the more interesting and BETTER boss fights found at the castle. Clearly there was a conflict during development.
The game seems split most of the time actually. It feels like there was a great deal of splits amongst the developers, as some stuff feels a lot less fleshed out. Especially since the ending is flat and awful. Nothing feels resolved, and I guess this was done so that you would still be able to free roam through the city and pick up the collectables you missed.
And now, for something that some may be a bit confused by. But the game needed more Quick Time Events. OR at least a better allocation of those QTEs. Let me explain. The bosses are completely void of quick time events. But, there is still a quick time event to open a door. The QTEs for the bosses was deemed LESS important than the QTEs to open the door. It just seems odd to me. And in a way makes the ability to turn off QTEs utterly pointless since there aren't enough to justify the option.
The combat is better though. The gameplay has been improved. But oddly enough, the difficulty has raised quite a lot. But not in the good way. Instead of making the enemies more interesting to fight, they no longer stagger, have more health, and tend to swarm. Most have shields that require a three hit combo from your chaos guantlets. The chaos guantlets are really slow, have poor range, drain magic, and the enemies tend to dodge after the second hit, so the third hit rarely hits. And that's if you even manage to get a full combo off since the enemies attack so often you spend most of your time dodging instead of attacking. The game even brings in enemies later in the game who summon more enemies, and have unblockable attacks.
The game isn't bad. But is a sad sequel to the first Lords of Shadow.

Saw some interesting videos about the game and decided to give it a try.
The game strongly suggests that you complete a series of tutorials that are intended to teach you the various aspects of the game. This is smart, since it would be kind to call the building controls clumsy, and they have a steep learning curve to gain any level of control. This is not helped by the tutorials and tooltips insisting on telling you the default control mappings and not using any re-mappings you may have done.
I was a bit surprised at how fast the tutorial ramped up the difficulty, with a very early tutorial "Muddy Waters" giving you a very short time to repair a ship hull and build an engine before enemy ships blow your ship apart. I'm sure this is a trivial task for someone who has played the game for months and is an old hand at using the clumsy building controls to make numerous ships, but having only about 10 minutes to fight the controls to build anything is quite the challenge only a few tutorials in.
Just two examples of clumsly build controls:
1) Placing and motion are relative to the camera, not an absolute coordinate system. So as you try and find a camera angle where you can see what you are doing in cramped locations your control direction keeps changing with respect to trying to place blocks on the ship.
2) The cursor keeps moving toward/away from the camera every time you place or remove a block (depending if you right or left click). So if I'm trying to place blocks horizontally I have to keep re-adjusting the place cursor back to the row I'm working on.
I'm sure with enough time I could get used to how it behaved, except for the fact that you do not get an opportunity and are thrown into the timed build mission long before you have a chance to get used to the controls. It is literally the second time you build anything, and the first time was a "place the block I tell you here" sandbox mission.
The alpha nature of the game is very evident in the help/tutorial sections: spelling errors, sentences that just sort of trail off and missing words are just some of the more obvious. I've also encountered strange graphical glitches like the water surface vanishing; sometimes it is there and looks nice and other times not.
TL;DR The game shows some promise, but give it a pass until it gets out of alpha unless you like torturing yourself.

I'm thinking this game might have benefited from a story with some missions that had a purpose for generating certain enemies - i.e. fighting through squadrons to get to a battleship or blimp for instance. I had never even heard of this series until they ran the kickstarter for Dreamfall Chapters, but it caught my attention. I now own all the games in the series and love them. The only problem I have and it seems to be a common issue is that the game isn't optimized properly. Or so that is what I keep hearing. Personally the game runs fantastic for me on my pc at high settings, but for only 30 minutes or so. After that the framerate drops significantly. I can stop the game and restart and the problem is fixed. Sometimes I even have to logout out of my pc account. Trying to lower the settings does absolutely nothing. I am sure that Red Thread will address this situation at some point. It doesnt make the game unplayable and it is well worth this small inconvenience. It is a treat for the eyes and ears. The graphics wont blow everyone away but the art style really catches the eye. The story for all of these games is probably the best I have encountered in the video game industry and the voice acting from game to game is consistent as well. I think only one major character has a different voice actor in Dreamfall Chapters and it is a vast improvement. (I am a little biased due to the fact that this actor voiced one of my all time favorite video game characters of all time;  Sir Hawke, the Champion of Kirkwall. All in all this game is amazing so far and I am sure books 3-5 will be just as amazing, and I for one cant wait for them to drop. I give it a 9/10 only for the fact that the gameplay is a little soft. Even though its predecessor was lauded for its horrible stealth and combat mechanics, at least it had them.  There is no combat (so far) and there was one instance where you have to avoid a guard by making sure he is pointing in the oppsite direction. If he catches you then it places you outside a gate 20 feet from where you were. And you actually get an achievment for the quest called "And you thought there wouldnt be stealth." Despite these minor flaws the game has me hungering for more and I cant wait to see how it all ends.

I simply loved 'Legend of Grimrock' and when I saw 'StarCrawlers' in my 'suggested feed', I just had to check it out, and I'm VERY glad that I did. Just like 'Legend of Grimrock', StarCrawlers is a turn-based, squad-based dungeon crawler, set in a futuristic age where you explore different ships, or star-bases to complete different missions and to collect any loot you find along the way... whilst overcoming the many different foes who are trying to kill you. The quest-system involves getting missions from a 'bulletin board' and then completing it, but different quests increases (or decreases) reputation with the different 'corporations' in the game, which means if you favor one corporation over the other too much, you'll soon be hated (and hunted) by one corporation, while being adored and admired by another (which gives you certain rewards at certain reputation milestones). Apart from that, there's tonnes of random loot, many different weapon types and a bunch of different classes who are all unique, which allows you to build a squad of space-explorers to take on every mission, whom gain strength and experience with every new mission. There's also a skill tree for every character, with 3 different paths for every class, which allows you to play with every class differently. Overall I'd rate StarCrawlers as being on-par (if not slightly above) 'Legend of Grimrock', and at the end of the day StarCrawlers will have bigger appeal to those that prefer a futuristic setting, instead of a 'old-timey' setting like Grimrock. StarCrawlers is WELL worth the $20 it asks and you'll be able to get well over 40hours of fun gameplay out of it and that's not even including the replayability of multiple playthroughs.

This is a very short game, only 5 levels. At 1 hour I finished each stage on normal difficulty. The art is also somewhat lackluster, the ship is downright boring which is a cardinal sin for a space shooter. The game is saved, however, by interesting mechanics and a hilarious satirical narrative between missions. I picked up this game for half-price at $2 and consider it worth the investment.
The mechanics are pretty fun. Use your shield to block all enemy attacks (but not enemies themselves), but you must meter your usage so you don't run out when you need it. Using your shield also powers up your attack, so there's parts when you'll want to use some of your shield power to take out extra enemies (assuming you're going for a high score). The shields go up at the same time you power your attack, so there's not a trade-off between using your power for shield or using your power to power-up your attacks, which may have been more interesting.
There are three types of attacks, a spread shot (for lots of small enemies), which will spread more when powered up, a tracer beam (for larger enemies and bosses), which will do more damage when powered up, and a lightning attack that will do massive damage but has a separate gague that needs to be filled by killing enemies.
More game time can be had by playing on higher difficulties and chasing a high score for the leaderboards.

I'm thoroughly enjoying this game.  I think it needs some variety, but despite that, I'm really enjoying the class skills, faction system, and story.  I just made a big choice in the game's story that hit really hard; I loaded my old save and I'm carefully reconsidering how I want to handle the matter.  Excellent.  When a game has me really thinking about my choice because of story reasons, instead of mechanical reasons, then it's doing a good job.
Playing Darkest Dungeon taught me a lot of gamer skills that were useful here, and this game is much easier than DD.  Healing is uncommon and ineffective compared to a lot of RPGs (which treat a full party heal during a quest or a battle as a given).  Instead you should be using disables like Stun and Confuse, and occasional buffs, to mitigate damage to your team, because that damage is not easily healed until you can return to town.  When you launch on a mission, you need to carefully manage your fights so that they don't cost you too much.
I'm at the point now where Hard and Very Hard missions aren't really a serious threat, as long as I don't do something foolish.  I have died a couple times and had to load a save because I did something foolish.
If this game is ever expanded upon, I'd like to see a lot more variety in the art assets, enemies, even types of environments.  Feels kinda samey after not too many hours.  But it's been a decent enough ride so far, I'm satisfied with my current run of 47 hours.  As a kickstarter of the game, I was hopeful but didn't expect much because of how many kickstarters have disappointed me.  Despite some rough edges, this game did not disappoint.

is a fun time-management game where you control workers who have to clear paths, rescue people and animals as well as build buildings in order to clear each level. Each level offers different combinations of goals to achieve which require strategy and good allocation of time to accomplish. This game is a great casual game to play when you want to relax and kill some time, there are enough levels to keep you busy for hours. There isn’t a story, however, which isn’t a big issue in this type of game.
The game plays very well, you point and click to direct your workers to complete a task. Tasks range from clearing debris to fixing gas stations and, of course, rescuing people. Things start off simple at first: clear the roads and save people as well as build buildings. Other elements are added as you play, including police officers who stop thieves and doctors who can heal wounded civilians. Helicopters, boats, trains and other vehicles get added as well to help rescue people and animals. One part of the strategy element is figuring who to save first, what to build first and where to focus your efforts first.
Another strategy element is managing resources. You need money to pay the police and doctors, you need food to fuel your workers, so on and so forth. Choosing which buildings to build and demolish can make or break a level. While the game gives the option to play the game timed or very casually, without managing your resources correctly you can still easily get stuck and have to start a level over again. One feature I liked is that you can demolish buildings if you make a mistake building them or you don’t need the resource they provide anymore.
The artwork in the game is colorful and eye-catching, even though some elements are tiny to fit on the game map there is still plenty of attention to detail. The music in the game is a bit basic but not annoying to the ears, there are also sound effects as well. Police sirens, construction sounds and many other beeps and boops. While there isn’t much in the way of voice acting, civilians will say “thank you” when rescued, cats meow and dogs bark and my personal favorite the police and firefighters say “I’m on my way” when you deploy them in voice I found rather humorous.
+ The game is very cheap.
+ Offers a good amount of gameplay for the price, at least three to four hours worth.
+ Overall presentation looks good.
+ I enjoyed being able to rescue people and animals, a game with cats is always a plus.
+ Can play the game with timed levels to challenge yourself or play casually with no time limit.
+ It has trading cards.
- Levels can get repetitive, best if played in short bursts.
- Some levels can be a bit easy.
I’ve played other games of this type and this one is one of my favorites. It’s a fun experience but I really enjoyed playing the hero and helping people. All the tasks you must complete to finish a level make sense and help reach the end goal. I recommend this game to fans of casual play or for those that just want to change up things and relax.
8/10

I like to build stuff. I like to blow stuff up.
This game lets me do this in a spectacular way.
This game lets you design your own vehicles of destruction, and the choice is yours if you want to unleash them on your friends in multiplayer, or on the AI factions in the campaign.
When you first start this game up and try to build something awesome, you will most likely fail. DON'T GIVE UP! Keep trying to improve on your designs, and eventually you will have built some incredible crafts that you can be proud of. It takes some time to learn the mechanics, but when you do learn them you will come to love this game. The recently added tutorials will help you to get started, and I insist that you give them a go early on to get a good grip on what to do, and what not to do.

Create ships, planes with and without wings, space stations and ships, submarines, buildings, and newly added land vehicles, only limited by the strength of your PC!  Jump into the designer mode to realize your internal warlord, then spawn in any enemy to learn how its made! Learn, build, and destroy to your hearts content until your forces are strong enough to contend with the denizens of Neter, then subjegate them all in open campaign.  The community is very supportive, and the Devs are open, funny, and active on the forums.  there are tournaments, contests, RP players, replica builders, and scientists to welcome you.  Make sure you have a day off after you buy it, you'll need it!

When I played this as a kid, I remember easily spending a hundred hours on the game and loving it. Playing it again today, the nostalgia factor is a sizable part of my enjoyment.
There are a few sidequests, but most of the ones that exist to help you get to know certain characters can be made unavailable when you progress past a certain point in the story, which sucks, because they are extremely easy to miss, but there are plenty of other forms of non-plot character development to be had.
The dialogue can be pretty irritatingly bad and cringe-worthy at times, and whoever wrote the game has no idea what subtlety is, so if you're not too busy playing with your fidget spinner you will see every plot twist coming from a mile away.
The battle system is really simple. There's even a feature where you can put everyone on auto and watch your entire group run around like a bunch of ferociously incompetent chickens with their heads cut off(I don't particularly like that this exists, but I guess I could understand how some people would).
The Exspheres/exskills system really sucks, and you'll probably have to look up a guide if you want to get any use out of it.
I know I've made it sound like I really hate this game so far, but it's a fun, lighthearted game and it's even enjoyable to laugh at the terrible writing. If you like JRPGs, it's worth a try. There are some lovely fully-2D-animated scenes. They are very few and far between, but still nice.

Take to the air and raus, Raus, RAUS!
This is a fairly simple little game, in which you pick up three parts of an aircraft: the nose, the hull and the tail, and then take to the air in an attempt to break your high score, complete sub-objectives and to see how long you can survive as the endless enemy onslaught piles on without mercy.
Aircaft, boats, ships, jets and zeppelins are all out to get you, and you will die over and over again, making for quick, bite-sized snippets of gameplay. It all leads to a rather wonderful 'one more run' -feeling.
The game opts for a stylized low-colour palette and simple, silhouette-based pixel art -style. The simplistic look of the game may turn some players away, as the game has something of a mobile-game look to it, but personally I found it quite pleasant to look at.
For the last piece of loveliness: music. Whichever pieces of aircraft you choose, whether it be the beam-spewing laserrauser or chainsaw-nosed, surface-skipping murder-machine, the music adapts, using different overlaind parts of the soundtrack to give you variations of the main theme song of the game. Marching boots and electronica combine for one of the more enjoyable, if short and simple, game soundtracks. The variation helps minimize the sense of repetition.
Luftrausers is not some great masterpiece or an epic journey, but it is a damn fun little game to waste a few hours on, and it remains as sone of my 'pick up to waste fifteen minutes' -games with ease.

Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 continues the story of Gabriel Belmont and his transformation into the dark lord; Dracula.
Upon starting the game you'll immediately be plunged into an epic battle as Dracula's castle is besieged by the Brotherhood of Light. During this time you'll be trained in the art of combat, mastering Dracula's three weapons as well as evasive maneuvers. The weapons vary and each of them fill a specialized role.
After the initial opening, you'll be unleashed into an open world with two dimensions to travel between, Dracula's Castle and a modern Gothic city built upon its ruins. The art direction and audio is phenomenal, featuring an amazing cast of voice actors; Robert Carlyle, Sir Patrick Stewart, and Jason Isaacs to name a few. The soundtrack is also really well done, fitting the mood of the game flawlessly. The environments are absolutely beautiful, allowing plenty of room for exploration while searching for the various upgrades, lore and abilities.
The story, when combined with the previous two entries is engaging and helps propel you through the 15 hour game, although the ending is a bit abrupt as well as disappointing. Veterans of the Hack n' Slash genre will want to begin on the harder difficulty as it's a bit simple when compared to games like Devil May Cry and Bayonetta. Between, fighting, exploring, puzzle solving, and platforming there's a lot of fun to be had.
While the stealth segments seem to be a major complaint for a lot of reviewers, they don’t detract from the overall game. I’ll admit that I was skeptical at first since stealth really has no business being in a Castlevania title, but they play out similarly to puzzles opposed to traditional stealth missions. They’re also few and far between.
The menu system is highly polished and will document every type of creature you fight against. It also acts to manage your upgrades and abilities as you level. Plenty of Lore and backstory is provided along the way from diaries as well.
While it'd be nice to have a triple A classic Symphony of the Night experience, LoS2 is great in its own way and playing as “The Dragon” with this new take on the legend is a blast. Don’t believe some of the critics, Lords of Shadow 2 is a must-play.

To be honest, I really enjoyed this game during.  I think the combat was well put together.  The story we really well done, IMO.
This is a tricky review though.  As I said, during the game it was fun.  On beating the game though, I did feel disappointed.  But let me break down some of the elements.
Stealth:  I feel the hate for these sections is misplaced.  The fact is, they are such a tiny part of the game, they might as well not even be there.  They can all be completed in no more than 10 minutes.  I also feel the whole transforming into the rat swarm was not neccesary at all.
Enemies:  Most enemies are very good.  They vary up their attacks, they dodge your attacks, and large groups of them can prove problematic.  Out of all the times I died, it was mostly to these situation.  At points you are under seige from large groups of small enemies, and then sometimes you are facing two or three very large hard to kill enemies.
As it should follow - Combat:  The combat I feel was excellent in this game.  It was as good as the combat in the first game, hands down.  They added this power up element which basically incentivizes changing attacks and weapons.  The dodge was much more responsive feeling in this game than the last game.  Accordingly, the timing for the charge moves of enemies is very much varied.  So there is no absolute time to block.  They also made it harder to syncronize block in this game.  It felt like you have less frames to hit the button in.  I noticed that some enemies hardly ever normal attack and almost always charge.  Those enemies ended up being the easiest though as their attacks tended to not be varied.
The World:  This is where the game has some failings.  It placed you in many small corridors and very few vistas.  In the first game you had lots of open and interesting areas to fight and puzzle your way through.  In this one lots of times it felt lackluster because of this failing.  The castle, as other reviews have stated, is awesome.  But it just feels like the castle is mostly optional.  You find Wolf portals between the worlds, but I found little reason to back to the castle and explore.
Environmental puzzles:  Almost non-existent.  It's a shame, iit was fun to try and get past timing puzzles and spike traps in the first game.  This game had none of that.  No timing puzzles, no spike traps, it just felt like you were walking forward a lot in this game with little to hinder your way... well little except finding a switch which was usually located in the same room.  I just didn't see the point of pulling a lever to open a door that was five feet away.
Extracurriculars: There was plenty of things in this game to collect.  But the back tracking isn't fun to me.  In the first game, the stage based design was awesome for this.  Go back, find the scrolls, collect the gem or the weapon upgrade, maybe do a the stage challenge while you are at it.  I loved the challenges in the first game, they were fun to try and complete.  This game didn't really have that.  They had some sort of challenges that I unlocked throughout the game, and the game managed to tell me about them about 700 times throughout the course of the game.  The funny part was, going through the pages of the Journal and menus... where the hell are they located?  I never figured it out, but I wan't inclined to backtrack and figure it out.
Pros that don't need explanation:
Music was awesome
Voice acting was awesome
Story was, for the most part, very good
Cons (many of these are personal cons and as such I know aren't objective or shared by many people):
Free Camera - I loved how the first one was with the locked camera.  The devs always put it in a good spot to show off the awesome world.  I feel that stepping away from that was a mistake.  The camera was downright annoying in some battles, and in other battles it didn't do a good job.
Open World:  As explained, I didn't enjoy this aspect.  I am a firm believer that not every game is automatically made better by an open world.  This one was definitely not.  Believe it or not, the world actually felt much smaller than the stage based world from the first game.  I think a good open world is truly awesome, but this unfortunately was not.  Also, in making it an open world that helped to deny my want to go back and find collectibles.
Overall Opinion:  I think this is a worthy game on a sale.  If you played and liked the combat from the first game, you are probably gonna love the combat in this one.  I also felt that the dev failed to deliver on a conclusion to the trilogy.  The ending was not a conclusion, but an outright attempt to further the series into yet another game, which disappoints me.  I am anxious to see what they do with DLC however.  There are rumors of an Alucard DLC, which I would be interested in playing.   If they did some sort of DLC that let you play as the other Belmont you meet in the game, that would also be fun.  If I had to give it a score, I would probably give it a 6/10.  This is not an objective review, I have explained what I personally did not like about it.
Edit:  At the time of writing my Steam timer shows 25 hours in game.. but I alt/tabbed out of the game to do something, realized I had to leave for work, and then left it on while I was at work by accident.  I really only put 15 hours or so into the game, so that was a disppointment.  The first one I put 29 actual hours into.
Edit2:  I did a "No" recommend.  But if you get it on sale and want to see how the story plays out, it's  a yes.

This game is not finished. It's pretty good technical quality for an early access game, but it's not finished and not early access. I wish I'd refunded it, because it's the kind of game where it really takes some time to explore it and understand what's wrong with it.
* Rebinding is missing for many key and all mouse binds.
* The control scheme is awkward, especially for combat.
* It's very easy to do actions with serious consequences completely by accident because of the awkward UI.
* The chat loses focus whenever any other UI does anything, and the hotbar seems to open or close at random, triggering that.
* Multiplayer can't pause.
* There is an overbearing chat filter that censors completely innocuous words for no reason, and is easily evaded by breaking up words. The word list will do nothing against many suggestions to kill oneself, but hey, at least the kids can't hear the words "butt" or "fudge". It cannot be disabled, either on a lobby or clientside basis.
* Tutorial menus pop up on every new save by default and as far as I know, cannot be disabled.
* All you need to do to get credit for a period of the day, like breakfast, is pop in once, even with no guards there. This completely devalues free time since every period of the day is essentially free time, and doesn't seem to change on higher security prisons.
* The stat-building minigames, while better than the first game, become an obnoxious grind on each prison, and some are still pure button spam. They're a formality to getting started, not something that actually matters in the general routine. Also, their UI design choices are odd, like the bar getting
when you need to press a key in some cases.
* The contentious issue of prisoners spawning with youtuber names was "solved" by reducing the rate at which they appear rather than making a config option for it, which made new people unhappy with it.
It's been hard to get any acknowledgement out of the devs on any problem that isn't clearly a bug or massively unpopular, like the apparent decision to make non-host players' items not save in co-op, mentioned below. This doesn't seem to be helped by their forum containing only a general discussion and bug reports, so game questions, suggestions, and multiplayer matchmaking are all piled together.
In general, these devs seem to be configuration-phobic, which is concerning, and it shows very badly in the game, and it seems like they didn't go early access merely to avoid the stigma of it.
Avoid this.
Original Review:
I got the escapists 2 close to launch and solely for co-op. Co-op was announced as soon as the game was. On release, non-host players' stats and items did not persist, at least for many people. This has apparently been patched now. However, this is a problem that was noted before the game was released (along with quite a few bugs) and wasn't fixed. A developer said this was a design decision, but as far as I know, there's been no clarification on whether that's really true or if so, why they made this baffling choice.
It's great that this big problem has been fixed, but it's one among many, they make multiplayer seem like an afterthought, which is odd because it was announced as early as the game was. Worst, my friend and I weren't sure about this one, so got it to try and possibly refund. In dealing with the problem that made co-op completely unplayable, we now have 0.6 hours left to give the game a real try in the only demo we have available to us short of pirating the game.
If players are going to be doing QA on your game to any significant extent, put it in early access. A chance to get interested fans or people willing to take a risk and make suggestions about something not quite finished (I might have been) to actually take a look at it first would've done this game good. But this was released without a core feature being even remotely acceptable.
As it is, unless you're only interested in single player, avoid this.

This is NOT a minecraft clone.  It stands alone as a brilliant game in a very different genre.  If you ever enjoyed building legos as a child, you need this game.  If you ever loved designing ships in Master of Orion, you need this game.  Imagine if you built something with legos, programmed it, and then it began shooting at other legos, built by other people.
The AI shines in this game.  I would never fire my own guns, though I have the option to, as the AI is simply a better shot.  Countless games that allow massive creative freedom lack any sort of 'challenge'.  Not so in FtD.  Enemy designs are hugely varied and hugely dangerous.  This game provides 4 singleplayer campaigns, resource limits and gathering, and multiple factions that can battle each other.  Designing a single turret can be very satisfying, and there is a lot of skill that goes into designing ships that are effective.
Did I mention that you can build submarines, planes, functional helicopters, and even spacecraft?  And your spacecraft can shoot at planetbased targets?
Now, the game is good, it's entirely worth the full cost, but it is alpha.  It's a very complete alpha, but there is clearly polishing still to do.  Optimization and balancing is needed, though the game is very playable and very fun currently.  Shield generators are OP at the moment, for example.  I am incredibly pleased to have bought this game, and I hope to see more people buying it, and a wonderful future for it.
The ships are both durable and fragile at times, with armor and materials playing a very realistic role.  Ships can be blown in half, but they can also take 10 minutes of solid pounding.  Everything is built into the game.  If a shell hits your ammo stores, it can gut the ship, or it can do very little if you designed to prevent a chain reaction.  Everything has tradeoffs.  The very AI that controls your ships is built on your ships, and pieces of it can be blown up.
Unlike most early access games, this game would be worth the price even if it there was never another update.  I would be very sad if that happened, but I wouldn't want a refund, because I'd still want to be playing the game.  I can give no higher praise.

I loved the combat then, and I still love it now. I died alot then becasue I didn't fuilly understand the tactics system, but now that I do, I find myself enjoying it more as an adult. TOS combat is quick, but tactical. Brutal, and forgiving. You work out the  best tactics for each boss and defeat them. Chaining combos together is always a delight as well when you're playing as Lloyd, and can actually pull off some impressive stuff.
Graphics are obviously dated, but that's to be expected of a game that initially came out on the gamecube, so no surprise there. Chracter design to me is very important. The design of your chracters can greatly impact how your story is percieved. Chracter design here is good. Nothing felt over the top, and chracters were deigned with an anime flair, but never felt like just that. What I mean is, tone done the anime trappings a bit, and you'd have chracters that wouldn't look out of place in a weestern RPG.
Soundwork is pretty good, but you'll hear tracks reused thorughout the entire game. I never minded much, but I can imagine it gets pretty annoying to some people. Weapons have sounds you'd expect, creatures have sounds you'd expect. It's nothing surprising, but It gets the job done. (Miss the original opening theme tho...)
I didn't go into much detail in this review, mostly because I want you to experience the game yourself. I can't reccomnded it enough now that ti's been patched and community fixes finalized. It saddens me, however, that we'll never get another Tales game with this combat style. I didn't play the newer two because their combat systems felt wayy too slow and clunky for me, among other reasons. But that's a different topic entirely. I sincerely hope that Tales of Vesperia gets a PC port someday, because Vesperia is even better hten Symphonia in the combat department.

One of the greats of the Tales of Franchise, a deeply engaging story that is definitely relatable to the real world. It's graphics and mechanics are a bit dated compared to modern tales games, and the voice acting is OK though quite not as immersive as newer titles.
The HD update is fantastic for those looking for nostagia in playing Symphonia again, or for Tales fans looking for something new. I would not reccomend this as an introduction for newer players, as the newest game Tales of Berseria is probably a much better introduction for the modern gamer.
It was a nice surprise unlocking PC exclusive costume\titles in newgame+ mode, and I'm curious to explore any other changes that might've been made.

This is a darn good RPG. Amazing characters, fun combat, and an interesting story. Though, be sure to have an FAQ on hand since some parts of the game can get needlessly cryptic as to what you have to do/where you have to go next for the main story.

Overall I would recommend this game, not without a couple of warnings though.
The game is fun to play and I'm sure to play it many more times... but there is also the first problem. It is a very short game. Personally I prefer the long drawn out building style or grand strategy games. This game can often be brought to conclusion (win or lose) in less than two hours, which for my personal taste is about two or three hundred hours too short ;) You are limited to one fleet which also makes it a bit too easy (no need to choose where precious resources are used)
The other problem that ties in with the above is that it then also tends to get quite redundant quite quickly (which does not mean it cannot still be fun! - I do have a lot of fun with it). There is a limited number of missions, which although randomized by the terrain do tend to be "always the same".  There is always a "Pirate Homeworld" and a "Marauder Homeworld". And since there tends to be very limited time you can't really get much into planing long detailed "reasearch paths", because the game will be over long before you reach your goal. Part of this can be alleviated by playing a domination game, but even then time will still be very limited.
So in conclusion:
Fun to play (thus the thumbs up).
But way too short.

TLDR: A good, almost great game.  If you can stand a little grinding, there's a nice dungeon crawl to be had.
Full disclosure: I backed this game on Kickstarter
Let's start with the good:
- Great art style.  Dark, but with a sense of humor
- Deep class trees with lots of synergies.  Not only between trees but also with your teammates.  A big part of the fun here is optimizing the builds of your team.
- Interesting cyberpunk meets Firefly story line.
- Lots of loot ala Diablo or Borderlands.  Sure, most of it's vendor trash but that's how these games work.
Now let's talk about the core weakness of this game: there's just not enough variety.  There's too few enemy types and too few tiles and tilesets.  It really needs about double the number in order for missions to not feel to samey.  I think this is the reason people complain about this game being so grindy.  It's not so much that there's too much fighting for too little XP, it's that you end up in the same fights in the same rooms over and over again.  For myself, I didn't feel the grind until 2-3 mission until the end.  That when you start needing to do a lot of side quests to get up to the level of the story quests and the lack of content really shows up.
If you can stand a some grind towards the end of the game, you'll definitely get your monies worth out of this one.

I didn't enjoy the game much, but I'd still recommend it to people liking grind and who don't mind very repetitive combat.
Starcrawlers is clearly a work of love by 2 developers fan of dungeon crawling ; however, they were obviously too ambitious : they wanted to create a feature level matching AAA games ; but with an Indie budget, it was just not possible without cutting corners everywhere, including on the gameplay which is a shame for an Indie game.
So they went for somewhat realistic environments (spaceship, offices, labs & mines), with many details (desk, cupboard, machinery, etc.), but everything seriously lacks quality as visually it feels we're back in 2005, or more likely on today mobiles (maybe a mobile port is planned?). And as they didn't have enough budget, it just gets horribly repetitive visually past a few hours in the game.
Exploration is really lacking which is a shame for a FPV dungeon crawler ; there's almost no puzzle nor secret, the progression in the levels is straightforward, you never can get lost, especially with the minimap always on the screen. There's very little thing of interest to discover or find in the whole game.
The strong point of the game is its combat system, with a timeline turn. For me it's very innovative but maybe it exists in some other game(s). So it's very close of a turn-based game, except each action takes a certain time, and thus you may have you next turn more or less early on the timeline depending of that.
The 8 available character classes are varied enough, and offer each 3 different skill trees that specialize in a certain aspect : damage against several targets or a single one, tanking, crowd control, damage over time, buff/debuff, etc. At 1st, they look super special and awesome. But once you understood them all, they are actually much simpler to apprehend, as like I just said, you can see each archetype in them. However, they are still leading to very complex effects/side effects/counter side effects that are very hard to apprehend, even with the combat log, as a single action can lead to dozen of actions in it, making it extremely cumbersome to follow exactly what's going on.
But despite that, the combats are actually pretty straightforward. Without mastering all the complex formulas, I have beaten the game in Challenge difficulty (which is the 3rd out of 4) almost without any actual challenge. And even worst, the combats are super repetitive : you have a limited number of possible abilities (5 + the normal) that you choose between all the unlocked abilities (around 5 to 7 per tree, and at end game you can unlock up to 2 trees). Often, abilities have to be used in a specific order (eg: attack to get combo points -> final strike to use combo points), so most of the times, you have very little choices and no hesitation about what ability to use.
Same for the target, not much thinking is required : most of the time, it's a no brainer as they are all the same. Sometimes, you have a spawner (which calls reinforcement), and a healer, so kill order is :
.
So after a few hours in, the combat became an awful chore for me, without any challenge. With a few exceptions :
- as there's almost no healing, especially at start of the game, it's a bit of an headache to understand if we're doing ok or not till we have actually successfully finished the current mission (you can fully heal at each mission end)
- around level 7, I noticed my team health was going down too fast, requiring too much use of the rare medikits ; I then changed my tank in my team (from Prototype to Soldier) and changed my AoE damage dealer (from Soldier to Engineer) and then I was ok for a long while
- once again, at level 27 (end game = lvl 30), I got huge health issue ; I then respec'ed 2 members of my team to get damage mitigation and small healing skills and then my team got totally invincible and could last forever even against the strongest enemies
- at level 28, I got an horrible boss
; my team was a bit low on damage output, so it was the most intense fight of the game, but it turned out well
The loot is random, in an identical way to many games based on grinding ; we often end up with useless loot which is rather frustrating, especially on the Epic & Legendary pieces, which are rare & extremely rare, and thus it's raging to see many ones wasted because their random stats don't match my team or aren't much useful.
So all in all, the difficulty of the game comes at 60% from the building of your team and their skill tree, 35% from getting correct loot ; as all skill damage scale with your weapon damage, if you don't get a correct weapon for a team member for too long, the difficulty will seriously ramp up ; and 5% during the actual combat.
The game is split between hand-made missions and random missions. The hand-made ones are good enough and offer a decent level of variety and challenges. At start of the game, you have to do something like 1 random mission between 2 hand-made ones to get the correct level to do it. Later on, the hand-made missions are more sparse and leveling up is slower so it requires 2 or even 3 boring & super repetitive random missions. It really feels like the devs hasted the end of development and couldn't handle to produce enough interesting hand-made missions. It's a pity because the game gets really better in these ones.
The game features as well a decent reputation system with many factions, although ultimately, it's really secondary, especially as the rewards I got from them were usually nearly insignificant.
The story of the game holds little interest and is ultimately disappointing. The story telling is correct but nothing more. The writing is however pretty decent and usually enjoyable, with a well dose of humor.
- Pretty original combat system, although ultimately too easy & lacking variations
- Pretty original and well-thought classes & skill trees, although ultimately being too simple & straightforward in their use
- Feels new, original & engaging for the first 6 hours
- Dev is listening to the community and might improve the game (at least he just did a nice update a few days ago! :) )
- Too much combats, too repetitive, and 99% of them don't have any real challenge

- The visuals look like the game was planned for mobiles : everything is simple, with low poly counts and lowres textures
- The environments feel varied for 5-6 hours, but after they get super repetitive as almost nothing new comes in sight

- You keep fighting cleaning and utility robots throwing plates and whatnot at your face for the first 10 hours of the game: unepic!
- Only 5 abilities + normal attack per team member, while a complete skill tree often have 6 or 7 abilities (and we end the game with 2 full skill trees)

- We regularly meet the
same set of enemies 3 or 4 times in a row

It looks good. It sounds good. It feels good.
So it's just a shame it doesn't actually play good. The short version is "randomness is not a game mechanic." The long version follows.
First, a description of how the game works: You've got a squad of four Crawlers(essentially space mercenaries), with a class, a bunch of stats and three skill trees each, as well as a bunch of equipment slots to pour stuff into. Each skill tree gives you more combat options(though you can only have five active skills readied at any given time, and they can only be switched out of combat), as well as contributing(ostensibly, we'll get to that), out-of-combat options for resolving issues.
You move through grid-based dungeons, collecting loot, battling bad guys and (in the main storyline missions) occasionally solving a puzzle of some sort. There's also some trap-disarming, but that's essentially always "notice the trap before you step in it, click it from a tile away, it goes away." Except when doing that also comes with a risk of setting off an alarm(sometimes these alarms result in an instant battle, other times, they seem to do nothing. The logic behind it escapes me. It may, like so many other things in the game, be completely random.). You also get to use some skills out of combat when interacting with stuff, but some skill lines I played through the entire game without getting to use, while others were regularly useful(for a given type of useful, even when essentially maxed out, their out-of-combat uses would regularly fail. And there's no indicator of what random chance you have of succeeding with these skills, so it's rolling in completely blind).
The good thing is that it always looks good, even if the area generation settles a bit more on "random mess" than "believable environment." Enemy sprites are great, effects look awesome, areas are excellently drawn. It also sounds good, great music by Ben Prunty(essentially what sold me on the game in the first place, I gotta admit), good effects. It's also well-written, like, there isn't a LOT of writing, but what there is, feels pretty solid and reasonable. It's a shame there isn't more of it, since there's a universe to flesh out there.
But the core of the game is the combat, and that's also where it comes apart. You line up against your enemies(they've got five spots to occupy, barring one or two gimmick battles that play a bit with that, shame more don't), while your guys are in some sort of nebulous, unspecified cluster on the other side of the battlefield. There's an init order, skills and actions cost TU's(Time Units) based on your weapon's TU use(all skills use a % of your weapon's TU cost), moving you along the initiative line, and some skills have different uses based on your location on said init line(in some cases being plain useless or downright harmful if used at the wrong point. So it's a good thing you have almost no control over your position in the init order, right? It's basically random whether these skills win you the fight or go unused.).
But everything in the battles is random. Everything. You're almost never gonna have a 100% chance to hit something or land a status effect(and even when you do, I've seen skills miss for no apparent reason). You have no idea what enemy skills do before they land(self-destructing enemy? Will it one-shot me or can I tank the hit? I have no idea until it actually goes off), and success is often down to whether the AI throws a cog or not(spend the first two turns buffing itself so I can stunlock it, or instantly summon in aid so I actually have a challenge? Completely random. Hit my highest HP guy or pummel the dude that's weak enough to kill in one hit? Completely random.). Even some skills are basically random, with what feels like an even chance of hitting everyone(your guys included), or just the enemies. The main battle in Starcrawlers is figuring out what skills are useless due to the random factors, and which ones you can actually rely on.
Even the final battle is super random and, to me, felt more down to where the init order started out(again, another random thing. Going into the same battle you can either lead init with all your guys, or be dead last with them all, for no apparent reason), and what units the AI felt like summoning into combat, than it was based on my decisions.
There's also the issue of drops. You're usually gonna be using skills instead of straight attacks(though a couple of useless abilities seem to presume the opposite, it feels like they didn't actually playtest and see what was useful or not...), but all skill power(damage, time unit use, sometimes even damage type) is based off of your weapons. So finding a high-tier drop can matter more to the difficulty than your skill loadout and what you do. I've had multiple missions be a breeze just because I lucked into a good drop early on.
Mind, you won't always know what your drops DO, because a lot of stats aren't really explained(maybe I just missed a tooltip or part of the tutorial, but what does "Maneuver" actually do? Nothing seems to explain it later on). Some maths is also nebulous, and occasionally some skills will do almost no damage compared to what they usually do, and shields in particular seem a bit random in their functionality.
Phew, that was quite an essay. Here's the tl;dr: The major issue is that Starcrawlers is too random, player actions matter less than random dice rolls all the way along, it was extremely rare that I felt like I had to do anything but the most obvious thing, and often when you're presented with a choice, the odds and mechanics involved are obfuscated from you(as in dungeoneering skill use).

Not without its faults, but still quite enjoyable.
After playing the full game. I certainly do not feel it deseved such low critic scores. Are there some issues, of course. But on the whole, I still had fun with it, and that's what it all boils down to. If you want some handy bullet points on the matter:
* Combat is very fluid, and there are a number of attacks and options at your disposal
* The Boss battles are the real showstoppers in terms of granduer and excitement, and are the high points of the game, and each one of them is unique.
* Platforming is also very fast and has definitely been streamlined from the original
* The Castle setting is simply beautiful and really makes the player want to explore it
* Game is super optimized and runs amazingly well on most machines. Played at 1080p with all settings maxed at a constant 60fps
* The musical score is just so well put together and a treat to listen to, fitting the action on screen perfectly
* The game starts off slow after the prologue, focusing a lot on the modern day section
* The modern day section is sadly lacking in terms of creativity and imagination. Was expecting something more unique from a modern day Satanic laboratory (especially compared to Frankenstein's Lab or the Toymakers Workshop from the previous games) for instance.
* Most time in the modern day is spent underground or in corridors, opposed to the more visually pleasing areas such as the Arts District.
* The Stealth sections needed more variety to be interesting, or should have been limited to just a few segments. Though they still only take a few minutes to do. Too much of a big deal was made about one stealth segment in particular, only because people forgot about the handy Mist ability.
* The ending is somewhat inconclusive and the final segment leading up to it lacks any real sense of build up.

This was my first Castlevania game so I went in not really knowing what to expect. First of all, the combat's fun, not played many hack'n'slash games and this made me wonder why, it's incredibly satisfying pulling off that perfect combo right after a successful synchronized block. Only real criticism I have of the combat is that there's not much of an incentive to try the special moves. When a game's this simple to beat and the enemies aren't overly difficult, nothing really forces you to have to pull off the special attacks, and you find yourself halfway through wondering if you're really getting the full experience because of your lack of variation in how you play combat-wise. Can't really comment on the exploration, as I've really no idea what makes someone want to explore a game world, some open worlds make you want to explore - some don't. I have no idea if it's to do with art style or hidden secrets, but I definitely wanted to explore the castle and find every secret there was to find, found myself spending hours just exploring different areas. Graphics-wise, this game looks amazing - found myself pressing F12 way more than I probably should have been, and I've changed my desktop to different screenshots about 5 times since I bought this game. The gothic architecture of the castle really gives the developers a chance to pull off some of the most stunning scenes, last-gen ports have never looked so good. Although I've never played the first LoS, I kinda felt myself wondering how great this game would be if it had the same setting, medieval Europe. I really dreaded the modern day parts of the game, the city was boring - everything looked the same, spent most of it hoping I'd see another castle sequence soon. Voice acting was great, can't really go wrong with a cast like Richard Madden, Robert Carlyle and Patrick Stewart, although when voice actors so famous play roles you can't help but see them as the actor as opposed to the character, because you've heard their voice so many times before. Characterisation wasn't the best, I wanted to see a Dracula that didn't start tearing up everytime he was reminded of his past, and he didn't really develop much throughout the story. Not going to go too into depth about stealth, all I'm going to say is that it was terrible and I'm glad it wasn't more prominent in the game. Story-wise, this game's brilliant, sometimes when the combat became a bit too repetitive and I was stuck in the city knowing I wouldn't see another medieval-esque area for a while, I was just hoping another cutscene would occur. The whole father-son dynamic between Trevor and Gabriel was really well-written and enjoyable to listen to, and although I complained about him being too emotional, I really liked the parts that Gabriel's human side showed in the scenes with his family. Boss fights were one of my favourite parts of the game, it was different every time and it forced you to adapt to the situation as opposed to just hitting and dodging, only criticism is that the dialogue during the fights could be improved as I heard the same line over 50 times when fighting some bosses. Can't really think of any other elements of the game to comment on. Overall I'd say this game is definitely worth getting - not got much replayability but the first playthrough is worth the money. Despite its many drawbacks like stealth and poor setting - the art style, voice acting, combat and story do more than enough to make up for it.

When in 2000 I played The Longest Journey I was blown away by it. Not by the graphics but by it’s story. It was so superbly told it was only later I realised the audio, voice acting and world in which it all took place, were beautiful also.
It took much to long before it’s follow-up, Dreamfall arrived. Somehow it was not what I was hoping for, but the story made it worthwhile.
And now finally the latest instalment of the Dreamfall saga arrived. And I have to say, the graphics are nice. Not the best there is, but after some time I saw the beauty of it. It’s about what’s there to see rather then what is missing. In other words, I got used to it and it made my fantasy render the world nicer than most games do because most important, atmosphere, so often overlooked,  is so much present.
Then there is the audio, most people tend to forget about it, hardly notice it, but in Dreamfall Chapters it so beautiful done. Take some time to listen to the great soundscapes, they mingle perfectly with the world surrounded by it, enrich it. And like in its predecessors voice acting is great. Zoë just wouldn’t be Zoë without that voice.
And then there is the story, in all honesty, it took me longer than expected to be struck by it. But once it did, it just didn’t let go. It’s (game) storytelling at its best; how I could only hope for all games should be told, but so few are.
So, for me, Dreamfall Chapters is in my top 3 of 2014 and after looking what games are still to come, most likely also in 2015.

This review is a work in progress as I have not completed Book Two.
This game is absolutely an amazing feat for the size and scope of their development team.  It is their life's passion having worked hard to reclaim the The Longest Journey/Dreamfall brand from it's original company did not want to further develop the title.  With the help of an amazing set of backers and crowdsourcing funds and support, Red Thread continued where Funcom left us off decades ago with the first two titles.  For many diehard fans, this series has represented a part of growing up.  This series was something I picked up years ago in an Electronics Boutique Games and haven't been able to put this game down since.  With the release of Dreamfall Chapters, many of us excitedly continue our adventures in Stark and Arcadia once more!
Pros:
- Beautiful Graphics; large cities and villages; Thoughtfully done cinematic sequences
- Innovative Dialogue System (very similar to Dragon Age: Inquisition or The Walking Dead, etc.)
- Rich story and character development
- The best of the best in voice acting
- Cinematic music that ties in the environment, action, and story all together
- Continuous development and active feedback from the developers
Cons:
- For the amount of effort gone into creating the size and scope of cities, I find the inability to interact with a large number of the people wandering around as well as the environment very disappointing.  Unless people are a part of a quest chain, the people walking around areas will just simply be decoration.  I understand that this is not too different when comparing this game to the preceding games in the series.  But, in prerendered, point and click environments, it  made sense to just walk by a bunch of people and stay focused on only the people that lended story development.  In a fully fleshed 3D world, gamers are expecting the ability to further interact with their environments.  Anything less just makes this or any game feel incredibly empty.
- If you can play on a game pad, you should.  I have played on the keyboard with several other MMOs and adventure games.  I find that the mouse camera controls very lacking.  You can make the adjustments to increase camera movement in game and in your operating system. However, it still takes me several swipes of the mouse to turn the camera around 180 degrees.
- Current content needs further time for optimization.  I am certain that developers are aware of this and will be working hard to smooth out Chapter 2.
Mix of Pros/Cons:
- This title is a lot slower to start than its predecessors.  For some, this is a plus.  Others may feel that things are too drawn out before any action happens.
- User interface is lacking in listing objectives and maps.  If you want to pull up a map to show you where to go or a quest finder, you'll have to rely on your surroundings to get you through.  However, players of the past games will know that relying on your environment intuitively to get information is the name of the game.
- Playing this game without having played the previous games is made possible through all the recap you get subjected to at the start of the game.  The makers of this game developed this game to make it stand on its own.  However, this game is a million times more enjoyable if you've already played the previous games.  I personally would find it harder to get attached to this game if I had not played the original two games.
Overall Review: I would recommend this game to people who enjoy heavily story driven adventures.  The experience is enhanced for those who have played the previous games though it's not necessary.  I imagine the makers of this game to be extreme perfectionists... and it shows!  But because of the size of the team and the constraints they have, I find that this game lacks the meatiness to be found in AAA titles.  I support indepdent franchises and am glad to see passionate developers making passionate games.  I currently have mixed feelings about this game and am waiting to hold out judgment till its finished.  The game has five parts with two released so far.  So, if you're looking for a game that's 40+ hours, I would say wait a little bit till several more parts are added.  My honest recommendation would be to play The Longest Journey and Dreamfall... and give this game some more time to further develop.

Much like it's 3D equivalent, 'Murdered: Soul Suspect', 'Whispering Willows' takes concepts of the paranormal investigation sub-genre and explores their effectiveness in the medium of narrative adventure gaming.
Arguably, 'Whispering Willows' succeeds better in this gamble because it displays far fewer plot holes. In particular, dabbling in the idea of astral projection gives the game a brevity all it's own. Similar to the possession abilities afforded to players in the 'Oddworld' series, Elena's astral projection abilities add extra depth to both the exploration and puzzle aspects of the game, while cementing it into the game's central plot by providing a host of spectral NPC's who keep the plot driving forward with a sandbox/RPG style 'quid-pro-quo' mission system.
The artistic style is amazingly detailed for a 2D game. The High Resolution graphics seem so smooth that they could easily pass for cell animation and make everything look sublime without that usual detraction between painted back ground and animated characters.
The only real issue comes from the fact that it isn't really that scary, which is a minor complaint even though fear IS supposed to be an integral part of the Horror genre. Similar non-violent exploration based third-person Horror games like 'SH: Shattered Memories' or 'Murdered: Soul Suspect' may be found wanting in comparison to 'Whispering Willows' on a number of areas but at least players could guarantee players that they would be periodically treated to the odd chase sequence or stealth trial. 'Whispering Willows' would have definitely benefitted from these elements and as such it is hoped that these elements could appear in a possible sequel. The game could also have benefitted from being longer but being a story-driven experience one can only expect so much in that regard.
All in all, 'Whispering Willows' is definitely worth playing and definitely worth downloading if you are a casual to moderate players, though hardcore gamers will likely be unfulfilled.

On a technical side there are a few flaws: The game only shows keyboard button-prompts even when using a controller and even though it will run fine in 4k, the 'cutscenes' don't seem to go above 1080p. The most frustrating thing was that the game crashed a few times while transitioning areas. Other than that the game mechanics seemed to work perfectly fine.
The sound design is the best thing about this game, it actually manages to create a somewhat immersive atmosphere.
After all is said and done, I did enjoy playing Whispering Willows. I would grade it 5.5/10, just a bit above average and I recommend picking it up on sale if you like a short, story-driven experience without many bells and whistles.

POSTAL Review - Raymond KT
Summary: We'd like to express our sincere thanks and gratitude to the Honorable Senator Liebermann of Connecticut for including POSTAL in his list of the three worst things in America. First place went to POSTAL, second place was Marylin Manson, and third place went to Calvin Klein underwear ads. *Not Joking that is what the summary was according to a website*
The selling point of Postal is still its best feature - unabashed anarchy and a willingness to go where other games haven't. The gameplay is average; really no new ground is broken, and at its core this is just arcade style action. But the fact remains that Postal has upped the ante as far as what is accepted in the mainstream gaming world. The lack of longevity in the single-player mode and the simplistic multiplayer options make Postal a moderately fun ride, at best. Postal rates a 64 for disappointing gameplay and general bad judgment in setting the game's focus on the shock value rather than on anything substantial or creative, and for wasting the obvious artistic talents of Postal's designers. Featuring inhumane, cold blooded killing and no purpose other than to lay waste to as many fellow human beings as possible, Postal truly stands in a zone of its own – a killing zone. A middle-of-the-road little action shooter -- nothing more, nothing less. It has enough charm to make it kind of fun, and enough senseless violence to leave an impression, but that's about it. The moaning and suffering of hit civilians can be quite disturbing in their realism, as are the fire effects and animations. While the graphics fail to evoke the surreal atmosphere that was intended, the sound plays its part superbly
I have no regrets.

From the Depths is perfect for people who want to build and test things for their own reasons and a lot less perfect for people who want a game with a clear objective or progression system.
Nothing new here for a sandbox game; people complaining that there isn't anything to do, just because they didn't go LOOKING for something to do, forgot to take a look at the tags under the description of the game. If you DO go looking for things to do, you'll find that there are, in fact, meaningful things to do with your creations, such as:
- Entering them into a tournament;
- Playing through the campaign using them;
- Playing through the story missions using them;
- Creating a custom campaign filled with them.
Not to mention the possibility of creating custom LUA AI code for the vehicles you make. There's potential for hundreds, no, thousands of hours of fun here. For only 20 euros at the time of writing, that's a much better deal than a thousand hours of film, a thousand hours of lecture/literature, a thousand hours of other games... you name it.
Of course, to get so much out of the game, you'll need to do some work yourself, too. Not only will you have to look for things to do (tournaments, custom campaigns, etc.), but you will also have to learn to play the game. I must warn you: learning to create all the possible vehicle types and making them work well took me a good 200 hours, if not more. This means you have to be prepared to learn. And by learning, I mean learning through trial and error.
The learning experience, however, is fun. That alone would be enough of a reason to recommend this game, but the best part of the game very definitely is this: building your creations, of whatever kind you choose*, for whatever purpose you choose**, at whatever time you choose: there's a great deal of freedom and a lot to do here.
*Submarines, boats, helicopters, airplanes, hovercraft, spacecraft, fortresses, hydrofoil surface-skimmers, completely unrealistic flying behemoths, land vehicles with jet engines because wheels don't work yet (update: now they do, but steering is complicated)...
**The campaign, story missions, custom campaigns, tournaments...

No. Just no.
While I appreciate the concept, this is all it is - a concept.
You will easily unlock 99% of the content within 3h (or even less) of playing the exact same content. So what's left? missions.
I realize that this is an early project of Vlambeer, so I'm writing this review for any future dev who might possibly read this and won't repeat the obnoxious bad decisions that were made here:
1. NO ♥♥♥♥ING RETRY BUTTON!!!
In a game that promotes multiple playthroughs in one sitting, you'd imagine this would be mandatory.
2. No consistent way of keeping up your combo multiplier by dealing with inconsistent spawn of large vs small enemies.
If the game decides to spawn a bunch of battleships, then expect NOTHING ELSE to spawn for a while until you'll deal with them. rip points, better hit that restart but--
3. Useless parts, for what reason do they exist?
We're talking about toothpick missiles with potato "homing" ability.
We're talking about "melee" body that can't sustain more than two bullets.
A "Gun" engine that begs you to put it out of its misery.
Spread shots that probably got spread damage as well.
4. Absurd missions:
Every piece of gear got its own related missions, some are fine, some require legit skill.
But we don't wanna talk about those, we wanna talk about the ones that straight up require an rng spawn based on probability of an enemy to spawn.
The lowest offender is the Blimp "boss", which spawns generally after hitting a certain difficulty level.
The greatest offender is a plane type with lower than 1% chance to appear, mind you that just killing it alone is challenging enough, so the general "strat" would be to use a nuke body and suicide when it spawns.
The only problem is that this mission can only be done with a randomized body, so you get 1/5 chance to get the desired plane body part with an additional sub 1% chance to get the spawn you need, so in other words - cancer.
All of the bs missions revolve around praying to rngesus to get the spawns you need in order to reach your goal.
Overall LUFTRAISERS is a decent game plagued with horrible decisions that were made to maintain its replay value.
I cannot support these decisions, and therefore will recommend to simply stay away.

Classic game, one of my all time favorites, and it mostly holds up.
Some elements, like the camera and unvoiced skits, show their age pretty quickly.  However if you stick to a melee character, the camera is only moderately annoying.
Nearly everything else about this game is incredible.  The voicework hits pretty well for the most part, the character design is incredible, the combat is fun, and easily varied, and can be quite challenging.  The game can take anywhere from 40 to 60 hours depending on how much of the side content you're doing, and there are seldom lulls in the plot.
The only other consideration would be that it starts a bit slowly, and doesn't really hit its stride until about 10 hours in.  That's not to say that the beginning is bad at all, but the complexity of the game and the depth of the plot doesn't really begin to reveal itself until you get pretty far in.
I've already beaten this game twice, but will definitely go back and beat again at some point.  There isn't a ton of immediate replay value, but the game does reward you if you've already beaten it with a bunch of new game + options that add replayability, especially if you've given yourself enough time to get fuzzy on the details of what happens in the game.

a Japanese role-playing game released for the Nintendo GameCube on August 29, 2003 in Japan. It was published by Namco and is the fifth core product of the Tales series. The game was localized and released in North America on July 13, 2004 and in Europe on November 19, 2004. In Japan, the game was ported for the PlayStation 2 with additional content and was released on September 22, 2004.
The game has been adapted into seven manga collections, two novel series, seven drama CDs, and an OVA anime series. A sequel entitled Tales of Symphonia: Dawn of the New World was released for the Wii in 2008. Tales of Symphonia and its sequel was collected as a PlayStation 3 high definition release in Tales of Symphonia Chronicles in 2013.A Steam version was released on February 2, 2016.
Lloyd Irving and his friend, Genis Sage accompany the chosen, Colette Brunel and her guardians, Raine Sage and Kratos Aurion on her journey of world regeneration. The purpose of the journey is to replenish Sylvarant with mana, a necessary energy to their survival.[NGC 1] The path of the journey consists of five temples which must be unsealed by Colette.
