I'll come right out and say this game isn't for everyone. As of right now, reviews are mixed. Some of the main cons cited for this game are the poorly responsive controls, clumsy movement and combat, and uninteresting level design. I have to agree that the game suffers from all of these issues. For a platformer, these problems are the kiss of death.
However, as far as platformers go, this one is rather easy and the poor controls and clumsy movement should not impede anyone too much. The level design isn't great; nothing is particularly challenging and puzzles can get boring quickly. It is not for you if you are looking for a challenging, highly polished, or well-designed platforming experience.
It's also somewhat buggy. The game has crashed on me a few times, bosses have glitched out, achievements didn't unlock when they should, certain pickups didn't spawn, and keys have disappeared. Because of the low difficulty and short levels, however, it is not that big of a deal to simply restart the level, although once, I did somehow lose a few levels worth of progress after a crash.  Ultimately, the bugginess is a minor nuisance and is easy to shrug off for the mere couple of hours it takes to play the game.
It is not an amazing game as far as any of the above goes. However, its main selling point is aesthetics/atmosphere. The graphics really are lovely, from the environment to the stained glass enemies. The music is primarily atmospheric and isn't bad. The voice acting in the intro kind of sucks (in his defense, I believe he is a non-native English speaker; in which case I think he did pretty decently), but this is the only voice acting in the game. The player animations are a little stiff, too. Still, it is very nice to look at, overall. You will probably find the enemies to be the most (perhaps only) memorable thing about this game.
Ultimately, I would recommend this game to anyone wanting 2-5 hours of casual gameplay. It is good for a leisurely, atmospheric stroll and a little sight-seeing of some unique enemy designs, if you don't mind clumsy controls and a bug every now and then. If you think you can enjoy it for its aesthetic appeal only, then I do recommend it.
Bottom line: Recommend for casual play and for those for whom aesthetics are enough. Not recommended for those wanting serious, challenging, or highly polished gameplay. Would say 6/10 overall, but maybe more if you fall into the former category.

Stained and Bleed (a much better game if you ask me) were some of the first games I voted for on Greenlight. I had previously played Bleed before when it was on Xbox Live Indie Games whereas Stained just looked interesting, which was all I really had to go on when I voted for it. Fast forward about a year when I discover I have a key for Stained when I bought it in a bundle. I install the game and as it turn out, Stained is a pretty bad game.
I'll list the Cons to keep things simple (this game doesn't actually have any Pros I can think of):
- Poor controls. This may be a subjective thing, but the jumping and attacking in this game are really bad. You either have too little or absolutely too much air control, which screws up some of the platforming. You can easily stun-lock enemies by continously hitting them and they can do the same to you
- Bad UI. The entire UI consists of a tiny healthbar in the corner and lines of text that sometimes show up at the bottom of the screen during boss fights.
- Poor controller support. I play with a Xbox 360 controller on my PC whenever I can, you can totally play Stained with one. What you can't do is actually finish the game with one. There are puzzles where you have to use the mouse to proceed and I came across a boss fight where a button on my controller didn't function properly but the keyboard key did.
- Buggy. The game will let you proceed without the proper power-ups making you unable to advance. The game will let you skip levels in the level select menu and then send you back several levels next time you enter the level select menu. There's several more that I can't quite remember. It's a mess.
It's unfortunate, I didn't have high hopes for this game but it's always a bummer when things turn out this way. I advise staying away from this game, even when/if it's on sale.

Now, if you liked the first Lords of Shadow, there is no reason not to like this second instalment. If, on the other hand, you are a fan of the old series (e.g: Symphony of the Night) then you probably didn't liked the first game and you shouldn't bother with this one. The name "Castlevania" is the only common ground between the old series and the reboot.
The story isn't memorable, but it is decent and it does its job. Also, the Castlevania series wasn't necessary about story. What you have in Lords of Shadows 1 and 2 is great pretext for an action game.
The artistic direction is more dark now and this is understandable since Gabriel turned into the evil Dracula. I am not a fan of the modern setting and I prefer the castle sections which look terrific.
The stealth part of the game does seem weird but it's not game breaking as it was stated by the critics. Blame it on a poor game design decision that doesn't quite blend in with the setting.
The gameplay is solid and the nice feature, called mastery, encourages you to use all the moves from your arsenal. Successfully using a skill in combat increases its mastery. Once it reaches 100%, you can improve your weapon by transfering the mastery of the skill.
A minimap has been added to help exploring and find secrets. The old life and magic gems are back in the form of pain boxes. You can still find more about the lore by reading the journals of the fallen soldiers of the Brotherhood.
You can and will return to previously visited areas.This is done better than the previous game, where you had to return to the map overview and select a completed level. Here you simply transition between areas. It's not sandbox, but there is a sense of continuity.
To sum it up, Lords of Shadow 2 is good action/combat game, with an excellent artistic direction, nice voice acting and a story that helps you move forward. It's not a classic but it never wanted to be one. Definitely this is not a terrible game as the game critics want you to believe for whatever reasons.

Most of the objectives are rather easy now with how extremely streamlined this game is, with population being at 51% (you can pump up the population of your planets infinitely with city upgrades) and conquest being the regular old "kill everyone", which is now by far the hardest objective to aim for what with population boosts from taking over enemy federations.
A lot of AI behaviors are locked off behind difficulty walls, so if you play normal or whatever you'll usually never see AI get aggressive enough to invade your homeworld. I kept digging looking for some sort of "rare" encounter, planet, etc, but it seems like no matter the difficulty or size you'll probably see most of everything.
I've definitely played worse strategy games, but I feel like the Sid Meier name gets affixed to titles that tend to have some depth. The tech tree too, is boiled down to it's barest essence, amounting to generic upgrades of wide areas of tech: "Better lasers", "better engines", etc.  The planet management too, is down to the essence: "Add city", "add more mines", "add more research stations"...
It's fun, in a casual-strategy-game kinda way.
If you're looking for something with a lot of depth, this isn't it.  But if you can get it cheap, and you want something that won't tax your brain too hard, this can be fun for a couple hours at a shot.

This review is a work in progress as I have not completed Book Two.
This game is absolutely an amazing feat for the size and scope of their development team.  It is their life's passion having worked hard to reclaim the The Longest Journey/Dreamfall brand from it's original company did not want to further develop the title.  With the help of an amazing set of backers and crowdsourcing funds and support, Red Thread continued where Funcom left us off decades ago with the first two titles.  For many diehard fans, this series has represented a part of growing up.  This series was something I picked up years ago in an Electronics Boutique Games and haven't been able to put this game down since.  With the release of Dreamfall Chapters, many of us excitedly continue our adventures in Stark and Arcadia once more!
Pros:
- Beautiful Graphics; large cities and villages; Thoughtfully done cinematic sequences
- Innovative Dialogue System (very similar to Dragon Age: Inquisition or The Walking Dead, etc.)
- Rich story and character development
- The best of the best in voice acting
- Cinematic music that ties in the environment, action, and story all together
- Continuous development and active feedback from the developers
Cons:
- For the amount of effort gone into creating the size and scope of cities, I find the inability to interact with a large number of the people wandering around as well as the environment very disappointing.  Unless people are a part of a quest chain, the people walking around areas will just simply be decoration.  I understand that this is not too different when comparing this game to the preceding games in the series.  But, in prerendered, point and click environments, it  made sense to just walk by a bunch of people and stay focused on only the people that lended story development.  In a fully fleshed 3D world, gamers are expecting the ability to further interact with their environments.  Anything less just makes this or any game feel incredibly empty.
- If you can play on a game pad, you should.  I have played on the keyboard with several other MMOs and adventure games.  I find that the mouse camera controls very lacking.  You can make the adjustments to increase camera movement in game and in your operating system. However, it still takes me several swipes of the mouse to turn the camera around 180 degrees.
- Current content needs further time for optimization.  I am certain that developers are aware of this and will be working hard to smooth out Chapter 2.
Mix of Pros/Cons:
- This title is a lot slower to start than its predecessors.  For some, this is a plus.  Others may feel that things are too drawn out before any action happens.
- User interface is lacking in listing objectives and maps.  If you want to pull up a map to show you where to go or a quest finder, you'll have to rely on your surroundings to get you through.  However, players of the past games will know that relying on your environment intuitively to get information is the name of the game.
- Playing this game without having played the previous games is made possible through all the recap you get subjected to at the start of the game.  The makers of this game developed this game to make it stand on its own.  However, this game is a million times more enjoyable if you've already played the previous games.  I personally would find it harder to get attached to this game if I had not played the original two games.
Overall Review: I would recommend this game to people who enjoy heavily story driven adventures.  The experience is enhanced for those who have played the previous games though it's not necessary.  I imagine the makers of this game to be extreme perfectionists... and it shows!  But because of the size of the team and the constraints they have, I find that this game lacks the meatiness to be found in AAA titles.  I support indepdent franchises and am glad to see passionate developers making passionate games.  I currently have mixed feelings about this game and am waiting to hold out judgment till its finished.  The game has five parts with two released so far.  So, if you're looking for a game that's 40+ hours, I would say wait a little bit till several more parts are added.  My honest recommendation would be to play The Longest Journey and Dreamfall... and give this game some more time to further develop.

For seasoned TLJ players, this is the game you've been waiting for, go play it. That's all.
If you have NOT played The Longest Journey and/or Dreamfall: TLJ, I highly recommend you do so. Playing the first 2 games will make this one much more relevant. I can see that it may not be necessary, but the depth of backstory that's apparent in Chapters will make it worthwhile. (For instance, new players will not get the full emotionally crushing blow when they meet the Mole. And WHO really IS Lady Alvane? Man I can't wait to find out.)
While the graphics are dated (especially for TLJ), much of the original game art consists of hand painted backgrounds, so it's still lovely to look at (especially parts of Arcadia and April's dreams). I re-play both games about once every 1-2 years, and they're still worth it. They're like being inside a particularly good fantasy/sci-fi novel. Every character is relevant, loveable (even the villains) and authentic.

It pains me to say this, but this game is nothing short of terrible. I've been a devout fan of the Longest Journey Saga for agest, and Dreamfall (the old one that is) sits tall and proud in my favourite games list. However, Dreamfall Chapters is a resounding disappointment. In essence, it's a mere TellTale Games clone (pick any of those to compare it to, they are all boring in my opinion). You get to play as a semi-depressed / fully apathetic Zoë Castillo, who aimlessly walks around a metropolis doing mundane chores, such as following a silly (and awfully unfunny) robot around. When it comes to dialogue, it's all about the TellTale system, aka you have a number of options to choose from and an unimmersive and unnecessary HUD tells you that "Character A will remember what you said". There is also a section where you get to play as Kian Alvane, with an improbable prison break with run off the mill, uninteresting puzzles to solve while climbing a tower to the exit. There is one thing I enjoyed, and that is the research that went behind the lore of the game. For instance, at some point Zoë starts talking about visiting North-Eastern Italy, specifically Trieste, and she goes on a tangent describing this city's sunny horizon. To summarise, Dreamfall Chapters is charmless, slow, mundane, and insipid. Again, I cannot stress enough how much I'd rather this game be great. Fact is it is not. I haven't finished the first chapter, and I don't think I'll be buying the next ones (edit: as pointed out in the comments, I was not aware that buying one of the chapters lands you all of them, Thanks eye). Now where did I put my Xbox copy... Ah here, let me pop that in for a second...
Are you into adventure games? Are you into games that think you are an adult? Are you into games with a refined, sometimes sarcastic humor? Then buy it, for the love of god!

I can however not recommend this game for a simple reason. The base game does not provide enough content to justify the price, the amount of orcs you'll be fighting is limited at best (personally I think boring amounts). However through mods a lot of things can be rectified and made fun, the amount of content is astonoshing and the various overpowered mods (both for the players and the orcs) make it much more fun and give it a lot more gametime.
Unfortunately the developers have rigged the game in such a way that adding even a single mod will prevent anything you do from being saved.
You heard me right, no saves, no unlocks will be remembered, no level progress, NOTHING.
Why? Well according to the devs it's to prevent people from installing "every unlock costs 0 gold"-mods and simply unlocking everything instantly. Personally I do not see the problem with that, some people prefer unlocking as they play, others prefer having everything from the start, and it certainly doesn't justify kicking mod support in the head for it.
Obviously, if you're the kind of person who doesn't mind lack of proper mod support, go ahead an buy it, you'll have a great time for a few hours.
If however, you're like me, you'll find this game is but a shell of what it can be with mods, and once you played with mods, you won't want to go back, but you'll be forced to go back because the game refused to safe otherwise.

I'll recommend this for those that want a nice little adventure game that lasts a few hours where you are solving some pretty straight forward and simple puzzles.
It is a ghost story, but I wouldn't really call it a horror game or even close.  It does have a slightly dark and creepy atmosphere, but I wouldn't call it scary at any point. I'd more place its horror level somewhere between Tim Burton's Corpse Bride and Coraline. So not for people that are into horror, more those that find darkness and ghost to be neat. Maybe those that just want a setting to be a tiny bit goth or emo.
The story is easy to follow, and you are able to get further backstory into several of the ghosts and their emotions when they were alive through notes that you find all over the mansion.
The puzzles were all very straight forward, and a lot of the npc in the world gives you hints on how to proceed. Which does make the game a bit easier, but also a bit more fun than the many adventure games that has absolutely silly solutions. The game also saves every time you pass into a new area, so you barely lose any progress if you get killed by
As for the main character herself... I didn't really feel like she was so important, and the focus felt much more on the ghosts and her father she is trying to save. After the game the only things I really can remember about her is
She seems to be the kind of protagonist that is supposed to be a mostly empty shell so the player can imagine themselves as her.
I felt the game was worth my time. It had a nice non-scary-ghostly atmosphere, a relaxing pace, and I only had to look up guides for some of the achievements, because the puzzles were all logical. I could see myself going back to replay it in a few months, if I just want to play an adventure game for a few hours one evening.

Whispering Willows is a 2D point-and-click adventure with fantastic graphics and a solid plot. It doesn't have puzzles so much as the ability to interact with the environment to keep moving the story forward. At only 3 hours to clear, it is also somewhat short. Even so, this game has a lot of charm, and clearly took a lot of effort and love to craft.

is an interactive short story that plays like an adventure game and has a little bit of puzzling thrown into the mix.
You play as Elena, who's looking for her father in and around the Willows Mansion. Elena has an amulet that enables her to take on some sort of ghost form, which allows her to talk to the dead, squeeze through narrow passageways and interact with objects like levers by possessing them.
You'll be exploring the mansion and its surroundings and you'll be gathering a few keys and other items that you need to advance your quest to find your father. Sometimes, you'll be running away from creepy creatures for a short while, too.
The graphics are cartoonish but easy on the eye. Throughout the whole game, the music and sound effects are subtle and add to the spooky atmosphere set by the haunted mansion and its unfolding story.
has 6 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 3 while running the game.
Most of the Steam Achievements are triggered automatically while going through the story, but there are a few missable achievements, too. 'Ultimate Pirate' made a nice simple overview of how to get those achievements. so if you want to be sure you get them all, check the 'Guides' section of the game.
tells a nice little short story. It's a fairly simple story, so don't expect too much of an in-depth plot or character development. As far as adventure games go,
is very accessible. That means it's pretty easy, so you will not find a mind-boggling challenge here. The puzzling is almost not worth mentioning: there are only two real puzzles and they aren't complex at all. You'll spend more time figuring out what the goal of the puzzles is than actually solving them. Now that you know
is a short, casual game, you'll also understand that the price tag of a tenner is too high. So I'll recommend it for what it is, but only when it's heavily discounted (66% or better).

Two to four hours of gameplay would be my estimate, depending on how fast or slow you take the game. For example if you skim through the various notes and diary entries you are likely to have a lesser experience. What is written in these pages are key to the story. There are a few tidbits from specific spectres that are vaguely important but most of them are not. For example there was a certain hidden creature behind vines that... I was disappointed to find actually brought absolutely nothing to the story. Since at the time I was searching for what the game wanted me to do.
There were several times I found myself lost on what to do as I failed to look in the spiritual mode in every single area. Since I had always believed that the glowing of the pendant or the little sparkles were meant to be indicators for the moments you needed to do this. At least one item is not indicated in this manner, if not more. As far as the few enemies that were included in various areas, I found myself irritated by the fact that occassionally they would spawn directly at entrances I had only barely gone through. Giving me not so much as a chance to run before I was caught unawares, and when you are in somewhere that you are trying to keep track of your coordinates... it's hard to do so when you find yourself more concerned over whether or not something random might spawn right on top of you. Even with the ability to respawn in relatively the same area. Then there was a small detail I found quite laughable... of there being windows far beneath where I imagine the surface of the mansion being, that allow in light.
Overall there was only one puzzle that was truly challenging enough that I almost looked up to see if there was a walkthrough. Apparently the mechanism was simply a lot more finicky than I thought it would be, making me second guess what I thought was the solution on multiple occassions before it finally decided to work.
Despite all of this, it was a story that had me tearing up on multiple occassions. It was not what I feel would have been an entirely original story line but the ability to talk to spirits and manipulate my surroundings made up for that. It left me constantly hoping there would in fact be more, but knowing by the count of notes that it would soon be brought to an end. The music and art truly are an enchanting combination. Although the animation of cutscenes could use a bit of work, they still do a fair job of depicting enough to get the story across. If they ever decided to make a sequel or additional content of some kind though..? I'd probably invest in it.

This is a heck of a game, but it might not be for everyone. It's a very particular blend of turn-based RPG, roguelike
Eye-of-the-Beholderesque dungeon-crawl, and Shadowrun. It borrows a lot of setting concepts heavily from both Shadowrun and Warhammer 40K, but blends them in a way that is satisfying even when you can still see things like the Void Psyker where the serial numbers haven't quite been filed off.
Star Crawlers' gameplay is a lot deeper than it seems, on almost every level. The game is heavily class-based, but there are a lot of classes to choose from for your party of four, all of them have unique ways of interacting with the various randomly generated dungeons (for example, the gameplay-unlockable hidden Prototype class can talk with hostile turrets or loafing loader-bots to get them to do what you want), and every class is packed with three distinct upgrade trees of abilities. All abilities have combat uses, and each ability tree has out-of-combat applications. By the end of the game, two of my party members (Malfunction Prototype and Bot Engineer) were merely very useful. The other two (Combination Ninja and Malware Hacker) were unstoppable gods of destruction.
Of course, that's just the combat mechanics. There's also fairly generous, low-churn loot drops, weapon upgrades, 360 degree free-look to allow you to search hidden overhead compartments and disable concealed traps, and a faction system that I all-but-ignored the entire game, only to discover its depth at the very end.
The faction system is probably one of the best parts of Star Crawlers, once you've dug into it. Every dungeon run is a posted listing, offered by one of a huge number of different corporations, each with its own distinct lore, personality, and feelings towards you. Completing a run for a corporation boosts their attitude towards you...and lowers the regard of whoever you did the run against. Between missions, you can call up any of the corporations for a chat, leading to side-quests, a separate bank of "Favor" currency for each corp, and various complications on your missions depending on who you've angered. I♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off a robotics corporation early on and, for the rest of the game, kept running into various flavors of automated assassins during my dungeon expeditions. On the other hand, I also promptly made friends with a cadre of space socialists, and after every other mission they had free rare-drop gear to give me.
The game's plot feels a little bare-bones at first, but it's surprisingly complex, with multiple viable paths and consequences that carry over between missions. There's not much by way of walkthroughs online, but all the game's puzzles are bonus objectives. I did not complete several of them, purely because I couldn't figure out how, but I still had a good time.
And to top it all off, the ending that I got--which I absolutely expected to be a "the GM screws you over no matter what you chose, because the universe is Orwellian and bleak"--did not follow my expectations at all. It allowed the universe to be complicated. It allowed the player characters to *survive*, which was more than I was hoping for in this genre.
Basically, I liked almost every aspect of Star Crawlers, and I will without hesitation pick up any expansions or sequels as soon as they surface.

I really wanted to like this game, but that didn't happen.
So what is good about this game:
It does what it says on the tin.
The artwork was ok, not bad, but nothing special either.
the writing is good.
The music is repetetive, but not bad
What I think was bad:
The combat, which is its main selling point combined with exploration.
The combat gets stale and repetetive really fast. Ramping dificulty spikes during a single mission is also not uncommon. I went from one-shotting groups of enemies in my turn, to having one, or multiple, characters of mine getting stunlocked and nearly killed by the next encountered group. Battle information and options are hidden from you during a fight or just plain lacking, the game could really stand to show you a hotbar with which options you have during a move. Almost every option in combat is constantly hidden from view (rightclick menu) which is unhelpfull and somewhat annoying. Want to access your inventory or run from a fight during combat but don't know/remember where the option is for that? Well though luck for you then.
Certain Battle animations are long and take forever, which would have been fine if they showed you a lot of different things, but alas they don't, which makes it feel that you are rewatching the same thing over and over again. Doubly annoying when your character(s) get stunned and kicked down the turn-que: it makes you feel powerless sitting their just waiting and then waiting some more while you see your characters health dropping...and dropping again. Losing turns is not what annoyed me, it was the constant waiting that comes along with it. Turn on fast animations.
The controls are clunky and take getting used to or just straight up remap them for exploration.
If you are not looking for a challenge but a nice cyberpunk story and grindy combat, then give it a try on 'story' difficulty.

Sadly, I'm completely baffled by the rave reviews here. Yes, the faction system is surprisingly deep, and yes, the classes are inventive. But that's about where it ends...
- The visuals are dated. No biggie.
- While the ambient sounds and effects are nice, the music is bad. YMMV, of course. Thankfully, it can be muted.
- The user interface is plain atrocious, going out of its way to hide important information. This is escpecially true during combat.
- Despite the interesting-on-paper class abilities, combat mostly involves spamming the same 2 or 3 abilities.
- Dungeons are basically a slog through repititious hordes of near-identical enemies.
- Dungeons are won or lost through attrition. Healing items are prohibitively expensive, and there is no 'healing' class in the cleric sense. The best you can get from an ability is a mild regeneration effect. This leads to bizarre situations where you will find find yourself low on health in the middle of a dungeon and have to think long and hard if you want to spend a medkit to heal a single character for about a quarter of their health or abort the mission - because the price for the medkit is higher than the reward you would get for completing the mission.
Unfortunately, the game is simply not fun. I cannot recommend it in good faith.

It looked interesting, like a 'Metroidvania' type platformer, but I hadn't had the money to throw at it before. Now that I did, I don't really regret buying it. The design of the game is rather charming, but it has some flaws to it.
First, the controls are a little unresponsive, making the first early boss ("Crystal Boss") a bit of a pain to time just right. Later on this dovetailed into some issues with platforming since the jump was a little "floaty" as it felt. However, the ability to just start a room over again if you die . . . infinitely, so it seems, makes it a little less annoying.
Secondly, there seems to be relatively few invincibility frames for you, so an enemy who spawns on top of you can easily kill you before you can kill it due to slow scythe swings. This becomes frustrating right about after the first boss.
Third, the voiceover in the beginning . . . there's something about the way it says some of the words, and how the sentences flow which feel off. It is minor, but I bring it up since it is the first thing which you hear and can grate a bit.
Lastly, there seems to be a few graphical glitches which occur now and then which necessitate reloading the game. It's another minor annoyance to stack onto the others.
I do recommend the game, especially with some of the issues with the release worked out. It's not a truly amazing game, but it is at least atmospheric.

Ugh. This is a technically-apt, dull German point and click adventure game with a nonsensical name.
The protagonist is a disgraced shrink tasked to get five catatonic patients to talk. Eventually there's a conspiracy revelation that you can see wading towards you a mile away.
The biggest unique trick in the game - getting into the minds of the patients - is playing back earlier pieces of conversation to advance with the patients. Unfortunately, it lacks finesse and quickly becomes repetitive and actually something of a guessing game, which isn't unusual for old-fashioned adventure games, I suppose.
You have plenty of situations where it's unclear how to proceed ("Why won't the game proceed? Oh, I needed to go have a drink!") and the finale just flat-out tests your memory by removing your journal and making you advance using said journal's information. That's just unforgivable.
The best thing about this game is that hitting spacebar will reveal all the hot spots in a screen. But really, that's not such a great tally of fine things.
Pass.

Thumbs-up with a footnote: if Steam allowed for a numerical rating system, I'd give this game 6/10.
Overclocked: A History of Violence is a point-and-click game in the 'film noir' style. Meaning that you find the rather mundane, every-day protagonist caught up (through no fault of his own) in a web of intrigue and danger. The setting is a mental institute, and the situation is five youngsters who were forcibly admitted after a violent episode. As it happens, the patients are often catatonic and suffer from amnesia. Your job is to investigate what happened to them, and this history is revealed through the fragmented accounts of the said patients. Through their eyes, you see a story-line that is torn-up both in chronology as well as between different perspectives.
Naturally, this kind of story-telling can be the recipe for either a fumbles mess or pure brilliance. Overclocked is neither, I must say. Though the plot is interesting enough to keep playing, it never really catches you off-guard and in the end, feels kind of anti-climatic. The game raises suspicions (there is more than enough fore-shadowing), and then simply confirms them. Keeping the plot going is often simply a matter of walking to the right location and adressing the right person. Together with the easy puzzles which allow for fairly little interaction (Overclocked is somewhere between a game and an interactive story), it never really manages to draw you in completely.
By no means a bad game, but simply one that never moves beyond the mere 'alright' or 'adequate'. Pacing, voice-acting, puzzles, graphics, plot twists... they are never really bad, and also never very good. Still, fans of the genre will probably not regret buying this game on sale.

The puzzles were logical and many had to do with what recordings to play to what patients in order to violate HIPAA-- and to unlock their memories which you then play as the patient tells the story. You then violate the before mentioned HIPAA laws and share these stories with other patients.
Really the main problem and where most of the negative votes come in I think is the storyline. The first act drags on and on. The developers could have shaved three hours off the beginning. I didn't think the game became suspensful until part Four, a good five or six hours into the game.
The pacing is very strange. So the first act covers part 1-3, act two is part 4 and act three is part 5. So it has a slow drawn out start and then things feel a bit rushed because of that. The memory sequences get smaller and smaller (I had the most fun outside the memory sequences anyway). Maybe the studio was on a time crunch but if this was a movie the pacing would drive me crazy and point and click games should feel like a story.
The ending is also strange and leaves a lot of loose threads and I feel the resolution with the wife makes zero sense. I won't say if it was a happy or sad ending but it should have been the opposite of what you get. I don't want to spoil the ending, as the game is good, but characters pop up out of no where and it just requires a big suspension of disbelief.

- Lots of technical issues

- Insanely convulted and nonsensical puzzles. And I know point&click games are known for this, but this drives it through the roof and puts it right up there with Cognition or so.
- The first chapter had an interesting hint system in the inner monologue of the characters. This seems gone from chapter 2 onwards, probably due to time constraints (played 4 chapters and 2-4 felt *very* rushed).
Now, don't get me wrong, like I said above it's not really terrible. Just disappointing, half-baked and really not worth the name, the price of the time.
There are *far* better point&click games with more than one interesting character and a sensible story out there.

Perhaps we will see some this in future updates.
Mostly I liked the game, but there was one aspect that got progressively more frustrating for me as the game went on.
The main character levels up after every mission, your companions only do so after the missions they complete with you. By about half way through, unless you use exactly the same team for every mission, the companions levels are starting to lag behind. The problem is the opponents' level  seems to be tied to the main character.  Thus, your companions often don't seem to have the firepower/stamina necessary to compete in some of the boss fights.
Another major gripe I have is that once you get past level 20 or so, no matter what "danger level" of side mission you select, there's always a boss fight which will push your party to the very limit.  I feel like there need to be more cakewalk and normal missions that are easier and allow you to level up some of your lesser companions.  I've had boss fights in which some or all of my companions (who were only 3 or 4 levels below me) went from full health to dead in one turn because one or more of the boss' henchmen were armed with a super-cannon of sorts or a self destruct sequence that I couldn't stop.  That's just not fun for me. I often feel like everything has to go just perfectly for me to win the boss fight. That's great for the higher level danger missions, but I think the lower level ones shouldn't be that tough.
Having said all that, I still think it's a great game and well worth the money.

To me, an RPG really only needs one thing to be truly great, and that is some degree of random generation. The first Diablo game from 1996 was the first game I played that had random dungeon generation, and I was instantly hooked.
Starbound takes this a few steps futher. The thrill of this game is largely derived from exploration. You travel from planet to planet in your spaceship, and every time you beam down to a new planet, the game randomly generates that planet for you; the environment, the plant/animal life, weather, etc. You can drill straight down to the planet's core, and you can walk all the way around the surface of it, and end up where you started. You will discover subterranian civilizations, and unspeakable monsters. There is also an element of space exploration, where you go out into asteroid fields and whatnot in your mech to explore pirate ships, asteroids, anomalies, etc.
Two-dimentional graphics, but nonetheless, totally addicting, and very fun. Recommended.

I'd this on my wishlist for a while, and grabbed it on discount. The game mechanics are rather simple: move around, collect notes and letters, help the ghosts by getting the items they want, occasionally use your spirit form to move levels/objects. It's a rather relaxing game other than the occasional times when you've to time your movements when escaping or avoiding the evils creatures.
The story makes for a rather riveting plot, slowly enfolding and telling both sides of the tales. One from Wortham, another from Flying Hawk, along with some stories from side characters. Not only that, there are ghosts around the areas that you can interact with to know more about their stories, fleshing out the background plot of the entire thing. The notes/letters are not revealed in order, so you only get snippets from different times, which makes it more fun when everything is put together to tell a story.
However, there isn't much replay value to this game, which can be done in a few hours, but I still recommend it. So if you can, grab this game at a discount and let yourself be told a story that is both engaging and saddening.

While everything about this game - the graphics, the music, the core gameplay - is great, it truly shines in customization.
You have complete control over how your plane works, but no combination is unbalanced. Want to make a ship that takes lots of damage and dishes out death? Go for it, but be aware that your ship might move slower and offer you less time to dodge. Want a plane that specializes in ramming through boats? I guess you can do that! A plane that hovers in the sky and spins around firing lasers and dropping bombs? Sure!
The myriad customization options keep me coming back to this game, whether it's to shoot up some baddies in my favorite armored death machine or if it's to try something new, like a ship that shoots ~10 bullets per second. Every run is as different as you want it to be.
As far as the core mechanics, everything about this game just
right. Things explode in satisfying ways, the controls are responsive if a bit (purposefully) unwieldy, and none of the options you can use for your plane will make you frustrated at how bad their disadvantages are. It is clear that the developers spent a lot of time fine-tuning things to make every run satisfying and fun.

Overclocked is a point and click adventure game from 2008, and a great example of how a good story cannot save a game. It has a decent, if predictable, plot and some excellent writing in spots. I won't spend much time summarizing the plot to avoid spoilers, it builds logically on the hook given above. It's predictable but well done, and would probably have made a good movie or novel or really anything other than a video game. The gimmick to the story is that it is told out of order through flashbacks by a group of mental patients, and from a storytelling perspective that is done well. The flashbacks build on each other and occasionally reveal different perspectives on events or answer questions raised by earlier flashbacks. What you wouldn't guess from the product summary is that the characterization is, within the limits of the terrible graphics and voice acting, surprisingly good at times. David McNamara, the player proxy and best match for a protagonist, is not a pleasant person, or the person he is initially presented as, and his character is revealed over the course of the game in a way that plays off the main plot. If the person who did the script for this game wrote a novel, I'd probably give it a look.
But none of that really matters, because the game part of this game is mostly, I'd say roughly 70-80% of what you do, is moving between five rooms with unmoving patients and playing sound clips to them in order to unlock a flashback section. The problem with this is that you have to do it over and over again, and in every case you've already heard everything you're playing back. This could have been a clever mechanic, but the poor signposting and the repetitive nature of the "puzzle" just kills the momenutm of the game unless you're using a walkthrough, and even then you spend far too much time jogging back and forth.
The flashback sections themselves are mostly alright. Those that have gameplay, a lot are only cutscenes, are typical point and click adventure game puzzles. Most of these are fine within the limits of the occasionally annoying camera system, and the occasional "stealth" puzzle that requires you to assume that someone turning their head slight becomes suddenly unable to see something that is still happening right in front of them.
If you like the idea of the story, and you can get it cheap, you may want to pick this up and go through it with a walkthrough, but otherwise you're better off finding a better point and click adventure elsewhere.

The premise is that you a\re a psychiatrist who is called on to investigate 5 unusual and possibly related cases in an isolated asylum on Staten Island. The background of your patients soon appears suspicicious and at the same time the main character has complications in his personal life that make things very difficult to handle.
The downside is that there aren't any real puzzles. You have an inventory much like a traditional point and click but any puzzles involving that are really easy.The game is somewhat artificially drawn out by the mechanic of interviewing patients- you need to play audio clips at your patients and the choice of clip and/or which patient you'e supposed to be interviewing at a particular time doesn't really make a lot of sense. So you end u wandering back and forth until something happens. It gets tedious after the second chapter of the game.
Fortunately the story, voice acting and graphics keep it interesting and enjoyable.
In short, an intriguing story with good acting and excellent atmosphere  only mildly hampered by a clunky mechanic.

I do not often write reviews for games on Steam. It is not something I am inclined to do, given that most games do not entertain me enough that I feel justified in preaching about their good points, nor do they manage to bore or antagonize me so much that I must tell the world of the evils of their binary code nightmare.
From The Depths is, as far as I can remember, the only game I have reviewed on Steam, and until something else as enrapturing floats along through the store, I am sure it will remain that way. The real joy of From the Depths is the engineering and building aspects. To take a concept, a simple outline of a deck shape, and then craft it over the course of several hours into a weapon of war is a joyous thing to those who love to tinker. Many hours I have spent refitting my various craft, the majority of them not spent in the grand strokes of deciding armament, propulsion, outline and armour. No, most of my time is frittered away testing. Endless testing, until I am absolutely satisfied, or completely frustrated at the performance of each system.
And once your many hours of tinkering, designing, hairpulling and testing are over, you finally decide to put your craft through a live fire test. Unless you have been playing for a very long time, it will inevitably fail, or perform far below expectations during the test, usuallly because of a minor error in the design, or an enemy suited to counter what defenses you have in place.
This is where From the Depths really differs from several 'Engineering' games. In From the Depths, I must consider bouyancy, drag on both the hull and superstructure, armour thickness from a variety of angles, armour spacing, and a myriad of other tiny details. It is in these minor details that the difference between a good and a great craft is made. Novel engineering is the name of the game, creating simple but efficient methods of doing things, testing out new ideas, scrapping bad ones, repurposing old ones. It is a game where my creativity matters far more than my ability to click on low resolution grass blocks.
On a closing point, I think that the truly stand out feature of From the Depths is the relatively realistic damage model. Ships do not simply have a HP bar which indicates it's relative closeness to a complete and sudden loss of all structural integrity. The granularity of the damage model allows for several real life armouring techniques to be used, and in the event that they fail, makes for lovely looking wreckage.
All in all, if you enjoy tinkering, building, or even just detailed damage modelling, then this is most definitely the game for you.

In conclusion, there are just so many things to tweak when building a vehicle, that the game just leaves me thinking after testing a vehicle: just gotta improve that thing to make it even better. And in the end i just realize: the previous vehicle was actually better... That being repeated multiple times gives the game a great replay value.
An EA title that is definetly worth the money (look at the playtime on reviews for extra proof). The game also gets updated at reasonable frequency, and seems completely bug free, but some features still need polishing.

There's the potential for a really good game here, but there are just some things that make it woefully inadequate and not quite worth your time.
There's definitely some good stuff here:
- The graphics and castle design, as well as some of the character, enemy and boss designs.
- The story, and hand-drawn 'story segments'.
- The platforming and puzzle elements
There's a lot of stuff that is just bad or half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
- The control. Character movement feels terrible and loose.
- Combat is dull and tedius.
- UI and terrible controller support. You can remap controller buttons, but not the directions. Play a platformer with a keyboard is difficult making a controller really preferred, and the absolute pain it is to get decent controls from the game is unfortunate. I ended up having to use JoyToKey to remap the controls to something decent. It shouldn't have been necessary.
- Unclear direction! There's a lot of trial and error required in finding out what you're supposed to do.
- Bugs!! I came across points where enemies that were essential (holding keys required to proceed) wouldn't spawn. I also lost some of my stained glass puzzle pieces between levels making it impossible for me to get certain power ups.
Other things frustrated me as well; the castle looks really awesome and has lots of little areas that make me want to explore. Most of this exploration however leads to the player dying and having to re-do the stage.
What this game really needed was some more play testing from random people in the gaming community. I feel like the developer is looking at their game through rose-tinted glasses which makes it very easy to ignore or put up with a lot of the game's shortcomings.
There's the potential for a good game here. The gimmick is interesting and the plot and graphics seem decent, but it needs a LOT more polish before it's something I can recommend you pay for. I'll likely pick it up again in a few months and see if any of things have improved.

It’s a fun, almost “casual” game in the genre. It’s something that be played while waiting for an appointment or during a lunch break. But I can see where other people would decry this one.
Most games like this are usually overbearing in its complexity, require a bit of micromanagement for everything, from upgrading colonies and structures, to specific types of research. But upgrades are a simple, one-button click and I love it. This game feels very intuitive. A playthrough or two and you’ve already gotten the gist and feel of it.
The combat sections are fun, although the “odds of success” part can get iffy. I’ve completed missions where my chances of success were in the low 40’s. Again, intuitive; once you know of what does what and how they can be useful it all starts to fit together. Torpedoes are to force the enemy out of cover, or try and take them out long-range and en mass. Fighters are heavy-hitters but are fragile. Asteroids are for cover, and so on.
No ability to name your ships. Considering that you’re entire success depends on your fleet, I thought that was an oversight. That lack of basic-level customization I hope would be corrected in a future patch.
I am hoping that this is a test platform of sorts for Firaxis: budget-level games, or just something that can be expanded later on with DLCs or something.

I had a good time overall. While it's pretty clear that this is one of the developer's first game releases, the core concept is interesting and the execution is commendable. The world is polished and detailed, each level is uniquely designed, and the enemies are varied and imaginative. If you're looking for an immersive action platformer, this is one of the better releases to come out of Greenlight.
On the flip side though, as I said before, the fact that this is one of the developer's early efforts is evident. As many people have mentioned, the controls are iffy, and some levels could do with a bit of clarity. Player death can be a hassle (although this is mitigated by a combat reward-based health system) and there is a scattering of minor glitches (though nothing game-breaking.)
But I'd consider it worth chugging through if you're a supporter of worthwhile indie content. With the half-hearted mediocrity that's been flooding Greenlight lately, this kind of thing should be encouraged to rise above the chaff.

I decided to edit my review so it's not just me praising the game. I have divided this review into 3 different sections. The main game, The prison creator, and the DLC. (I have recieved this product for free. It was a gift from my friend.)
My thoughts on the main game:
In my opinion, the main game of The Escapists 2 was amazing. I encountered a few glitches during the playthrough, but that's not a huge issue (due to recent patch notes and such). The graphics of this game have made a huge improvement, but they still stay in the style of the original Escapists. The lockdown feature made this game amazing for me. I remember in the first game if you didn't get the key in the guard's pocket in a certain amount of time, it would just give you a note basically saying "you didn't get rid of the key and they found out you took it. You lose all your stuff now! Too bad so sad!" and took all your stuff. Now with the lockdowns you actualy have a chance to hide the key mold if you mess up and not lose everything, even if you got caught. I love that you can escape the prison with secret missions instead of performing a perimeter escape. I rate the main game of the escapists 2 a 9/10.
My thoughts on the prison editor:
I'm not happy with the prison editor. In the original prison editor you could zone areas. Now in this one you can only use the preset builds. I wouldn't mind this if it weren't for one reason. You can't place items in a preset room, or remove a wall to place in another door. If you wanted to make a prison and compared this game to prison architect, you would buy prison architect. You can edit pre made rooms and you can play your prison. I like that the textures are fixed (on the escapists prison editor most of the tiles were missing textures for me). But that still doesn't do it much justice. The thing that annoys me about the prison editor in this version is that it has so much potential! I give it a 4/10 because they fixed problems with the original, but left out the features of the original editor that made it amazing.
My thoughts on the DLC:
The DLC did not dissapoint me this time around (at the time of writing this only the halloween and christmas prisons are available). I would feel empty with the DLC if it wasn't for the different cosmetics available for your character. The cosmetics included in the DLC maps just add an extra quality to the DLC that makes you not feel like you wasted 5 dollars for a prison that will take you less than a day to complete (if you're really good at the game). I would give the DLC aspect of this game a 7/10 because it is such a small part of the game, but an amazing one. I also like the fact that some DLC is free.
In conclusion, this game is great! I just wish some aspects of the game were better (mainly the prison editor). The prison editor was a let down in my mind because it has so much potential. If the devs see this, please add zoning (and the items to create those zones) into the prison editor! This game is great and I defenitely think it's worth the money.

Final word:
Since my initial first impressions post I have completed the game.
(optional let’s play footage conclusion)

You play as Elena, searching for her missing father in the abandoned mansion of the city's founder: Wortham Willow. Upon arriving, she quickly realizes that not everything is at it seems (wow, what a surprise): there's blood and skeletons everywhere, and she can see and comunicate with ghosts, for she is a descendant of a tribe of shamans. Unfortunatelly, there are also malevolent spirits that want to cause Elena harm. Finding text logs (no search required; they're usually in the way you have to go) is
to know more about Wortham and the story of the game, and the information is revealled slowly, untill you finally realize whats going on. Overall, it's interesting and makes you want to know more and more, but it's nothing revolutionary or new.
It's all drawn and animated frame-by-frame. The scenarios are nice and have a lot of detail to them, and it really gives a feel of abandon and danger, like something will pop out to scare you at any minute. The soundtrack is minimal and contribute to this as well. Elena's flowing hair when she's in astral form is awesome.
It's not good, but it's not frustrating either. There are not many movements in the first place, but somethings like climbing stairs and flying around in astral form could be done better. There's no difficulty; the puzzles are easy and the enemies (if you can even call then that) scarse. That's a problem, because the game manages to give a feeling of fear and dread, like something bad is going to happen, but after the beggining, nothing does. It's wasted potential. Also, you can beat it in 4 hours, tops.
It has an amusing mistery that's pretty well told, but the no replay value and short duration makes it only worth for players that enjoy a good story, and that bought it at a discount.
I love the story, I love the game play, and I love the graphics. I expected to like this title but instead loved this title to death!

Lets get this started
So, I very rarely write reviews. I think this is only my second one I have written. But something about StarCrawlers made me really want to write one. I think that is because I have rarely been as conflicted about a game as StarCrawlers. That is because, IMO, this a very good game that with a few tweaks could be great.
This review will be relatively long, so feel free to only read highlights.
Highlights:
The Good
-Excellent value for money, in terms of hours and contennt
-Very strong 8 classes, with genuine variety and choice in how one builds characters and party
-A surprisingly interesting plot and decisions choice, with at least 3 endings. (Only played through the first one)
-A deep faction system, which can be interesting to explore.
-Sometimes excellent turn based battles.
The Bad
- Later enemies tend to HP sponges, dragging out battle times for even random enemies, unless you get lucky with instant RNG kills
-Too much (this I think is subjective) RNG for many skills, particularly Void Psyker
-Certain skills are imbalanced both positively and negatively
-A lack of variety of common enemies.
The Frustrating
-The inventory and loot. Oh God, the inventory and loot.
-Very Poor explanations for important things, like weapon abilities, how to disable traps, reputation hits, etc
-A UI that take some getting used to, and is poorly explained.
-Only 5 active skills
The in-depth
So, as said Starcrawlers is, at its core, an excellent product, especially for the price. I originally backed it on kickstarter many years ago, tried it a bit in early access, and waited until it was complete to try it fully, as I normally do.
At first I was a bit put off by some things, like a UI that is simple but take some getting used (everything, including self heals involve clicking on enemies, weird key mapping, etc) but eventually I got it. I tested 7 classes (I just could not bring myself to try Smuggler, as I am not a random fan) and kept 6 around equal level until about halfway through the game, which takes significant grinding. I respected a couple times, tried combination, found a party I liked and went with it.
And for the most part, especially the mid game, I very much enjoyed myself. I liked trying skills, I liked how the void psycher went up and down in my opinion, while a respec of Hacker showed multiple ways the class could be good, and exploring the intricacies of combos, both within character skills and items and between the party. There is a good amount of complexity here, and despite what some reviewers have claimed, item choices and combo’s pick can make a huge difference.
I even liked the chance of random good items, fighting with different companies. It got even better when I discovered I could contact them and talk with people (which was not well explained at all). Even the random loot guy was interesting, as was auctioning items.
But certain things always bothered me
One was the absurdly small inventory: 40 total for the party, and 32 stash. This was widely insufficiently, especially since certain things make you keep items permanently if you want to advance. There was also no sort functions, no easy cross companions compares, and since mission often gave better loot, any degree of optimization required tedious comparison, upgrading (also poorly explained), and rethinking. Also, almost all loot was random, so it made getting good items for people a chore often. And the system for class unqiue....40+ hours and I got...one. But I have 30+ parts for them in my inventory....
Then too, as the game went on, the limit of 5 active skills became...weird. I kinda understand they developers want you to have to make hard choices, but it make leveling a lot less fun if you can’t even use your new skills.
Further on, enemies just gained massive hit pools, while rarely actively being hard. I ended up with ability on a character that random kills people, and when it worked, it was great, when not, battles dragged on with being really dangerous, though I did only play on challenger, and usually around my level. Bosses were great, but the individual mobs much less so.
And I found certain skills, even higher level ones, less useful then lower ones. Maybe in other builds might be work more, but some of ordering did seem weird.
Anyway, by the time I got to level 25+ I just wanted to finish, which was sad, because otherwise it was a good game. I just think, with a few tweaks, like expanding the inventory, redoing class unique, a better tutorial, giving more active skills, and fewer but harder enemies this could be a great game.
Still worth the money though, especially if they patch a few of those.

If you have any interest in the genre, you can't go wrong with this one.
All of that said, it is of course not a perfect game:
The levels can start to feel rather samey about a dozen hours in and the environments only rarely lose their brown-greyish tint.
While the balancing isn't bad, the different skill trees of the classes could use some work, as some skills seem far more powerful, while others are obviously lacking. On the upside, it challenges the player to think where to invest his points.
Also, do not expect the most deep combat and character simulation. The only thing you will invest points in are the skills. There are no attributes or feats.
Another point is that the game simply lags sometimes when a lot of things are going on in combat. Something that shouldn't happen on a higher-end rig such as mine.

Early Impression Review:
While many people are not aware what the term "blobber" means, this is the reimagining of the blobber (i.e. a group of people represented by a single icon, see: Bard's Tale, Wizardry, Might and Magic, etc).  I am blown away that this was created by a two-person team.  It is clever, quick with the WASD keys with mouse look, and looks really good.  The faction system seems so deep that it may alone be the long-term play value.  While some of the mission may be procedurally generated, there are more detailed missions that lead you along a story path.  The mix is fine; you'll want to do procedural missions for money, exp, goods, and faction rep.  The classes feel unique and the different paths work to create great syngergy with other class paths.
In-Xile better be looking at this before they go any futher with Bard's Tale IV.  This looks like a franchise with two highly skilled individuals.

Hello Crawler.
Feel free to accept any one of these randomly assigned mercenary jobs where you will dive into procedurally generated, grid-based dungeons, fight killer robots, giant giga-worms, and space pirates. Don't worry you're not alone, select a crew from many unique classes: Cthulhu tentacle spawning Void Psykers, hell-raining construct-a-bot Engineers, and virus-infecting kill-switching Hackers. What's that piece of junk in your hands? Be sure to replace it with one of the mass amounts of glorious EPIC loot awaiting you on your mission.
Oh and crawler, there's this "black market" thing — super rare loot — you didn't hear it from me.
Voidfox out.

All in all, I would definitely recommend it. :)

Postal is a bonafide classic. This was one of *the* games that we weren't allowed to play if we grew up in the 90's.  I thought I would never play this again, until I saw it here. At the time of this writing, I just got to The Mines, and the game plays better than it ever did before.
This is *not* a slapdash Steam retro release cash-grab. RWS did an excellent job, not only porting it to run without a hitch on modern operating systems with 16:9 aspect ratio, but adding controller support, cloud saves, and hilariously taboo achievements. You can tell RWS loves this game as much as the fans do.
I always felt like the series got too silly as it went on. Postal 1's atmosphere is gruesome and cruel. Postal Guy isn't a slapstick comedian peeing in people's mouths and shoving guns up the bums of cats - he is a terrifying serial killer, who sardonically mocks his victims as they beg for mercy. That is how I'll always remember him.
If the world ever makes you feel the urge to go on a murder spree, Postal is nothing short of therapeudic. It's also a lot cheaper than anger management classe.
Do yourself a favor, skip Hatred, and play the OG repugnant, abhorrent, disgusting masterpiece of video game violence for only a fraction of the price.
Many gamers might want to get Postal Redux in lieu of this, which is understandable given the added features. For those looking for a trip down memory lane, you can't go wrong with the true original.... for less than the price of a bag of potato chips.

18 hours on record, but it felt like a lot longer and I did barely any of the exploring. Lords of Shadow 2 is a fantastically composed game, with an enjoyable mix of platforming sections and combat, though the balance towards the platforming and forced stealth after the game's introduction is a bit skewed.
Combat feels incredibly meaty, and switching weapons mid combat is far more satisfying than the magic system from the previous game, really making combos feel heavy and devastating. Though there is a limited meter for each of the weapons, I found that I barely reached the bottom unless I was obsessing heavily over one. The one complaint is enemies with shields that need to be broken with the chaos claws, and whilst you can backflip over them, the mercenary soldiers seem to be able to rotate instantly, requiring the use of the claws more often than not. There is a plethora of abilities for each weapon, and unless you constantly back and forth between zones grinding enemies for xp, it is highly unlikely you will have unlocked them all by the game's end.
Boss battles are big and epic, featuring multiple phases, transitions and enjoyable visuals and backgrounds, the second fight with Volkova being one of the highlights of the game. Lords of Shadow 2 also ignores some of those awkward climbing bosses from the first game, with only a short climbing section featuring in the pentultimate encounter. Whilst it isn't always immediately obvious where to go, swarms of bats linger on ledges Dracula can jump on from the ground, whilst holding a button highlights the path you need to take.
The voice acting is superbly well delivered, Patrick Stewart as Zobek owns any scene he's in, and although Gabriel/Dracula's dialogue in the game's introduction is quite hammy, Robert Carlyle really hits his stride as the game's pace picks up, especially in the more emotional engagements with his family.
All in all I would recommend Lords of Shadow 2 if you're after a game that's going to last you a good long while, however one thing I would object to is marathoning it as fast as possible (as I did) as you'll find yourself getting burnt out and frustrated quickly.

Procyon is a very good indie 'shmup that fans of the genre should enjoy.
As a fan of these type of games, I judge them on 3 main factors. First is it's "uniqueness". One of my favorite shmups/bullet-hell games of all time is Ikaruga b/c of how it took a classic game formula and twisted it and made it something new to play.  This is probably one of Procyon's biggest drawbacks. There is not much to seperate it from other side-scrolling games of its ilk. This is not to say it's a bad game, on the contrary. It just doesn't do anything differently. The second factor is control. Games like these require tight and precise controls especially when the going gets hairy. Procyon has controlling down pat. I was able to jump right in and was able to pilot my ship and not once have I been disappointed by the controls. Thirdly, is fun-factor. Procyon is a fun game and has the right level of arcade challenge to keep me wanting to retry immediately when I fail. A good way to describe this game is a "meat and potatoes" shoot-em-up. I would have liked to seen more variety in weapons, but Im also not incredibly far into the game so that may change.
This game is definitely one that can be defined as "indie" in respect to looks alone. The design is very simple with ships not having a whole lot of pizazz or graphical oomph. I don't play these games to be wowed by graphics, so this is a minimal knock for me, but others that judge games purely on looks will probably not find much about Procyon. Lighting is well done and when there are a lot of enemies on screen with different colored beams going off its definitely eye candy. I also liked some of the stage backgrounds i.e. Empire City. Nothing extraordinary, but eye catching and adds to the level. Enemy design is mostly simple, and there's a particular enemy that looked to me like a Playstation controller. Whether this was intentional or not, I don't know, but its something that caught my eye.
A very strong aspect of the game is the soundtrack.  I find soundtracks in games like these to be more important than in other genres and Procyon's music to be excellent. A AAA developer would be happy to have this quality of a soundtrack in its game. The fact that it's in a shoot-em-up makes me very happy and will keep me playing.
Steamworks integration is very much appreciated. With card drops and achievements, this will add to the game's replayability. I love the fact it tracks high scores as well, as I consider this to be a staple of this genre.
All-in-all I recommend Procyon most especially to 'shmup fans. It's a classic side scroller and does pack a challenge as you go further on into the game. The music is awesome and adds to the gameplay experience.  I also think that it's $3.99 price point is pretty much right for a game like this.

I dig it, but of course, I bought it in a Beyond Earth/Starships bundle when both were also being offered on a Steam sale, so I paid $27 for both titles total.  Since BE runs $25 during a normal Steam sale, I ended up paying $2 for Starships - for $2, this game is AMAZING.  It's light...nothing at all like Civ or BE.
To me, to give a perspective/description to what the game feels like or what you should expect, you have to start with a baseline - for me, that's Civ 5 with all the DLCs/expansion packs.  If you start there, Civ 5 gives you tons of options and playstyles...then you simplify when you move to BE where you have a fairly young game with fewer options that still feels more or less like Civ 5 without any of the major DLC packs...then you move to something like "Pandora: First Contact" - a Civ-style 4x game that almost completely focuses on battles, and as such, has a lot of upgrade options for units, lots of unit variety, lots of fun attack graphics, but offers little in the way of multiple play styles...then finally, you get to Starships - a game that is *JUST* fighting.  Think of it as "Risk - Beyond Earth" or "Axis and Allies: year 3400AD Edition".  It's totally not a 4x game - it's just about claiming land, kicking spaceship♥♥♥♥♥ and buying new upgrades.  I think the game normally runs around $10, and by my math, I figure that I'm willing to spend roughly $0.50-$1/hour for a good game.  Well, since I spent $2 and have played for about 50 hours, I spent about a nickel per hour on this game.  I can live with that.  Even at $10, that'd still be less than a quater/hour.
Synopsis - if you want to shoot things in space, go for it.  If you want to play Civ 5, go do that instead.  If you want Civ 5 super space edition, wait another 2 years for Firaxis to release 2-3 BE DLC's and then buy it on a Steam sale.

Soldier Front 2 is overall a fun, fast paced action game with inspiration from games like Battlefield and Call of Duty.
Weapons
------------
Soldier Front 2's weapons feel powerful and heavy, such as in all good FPS games. Most guns are heavy hitters as a starter assault rifle or pistol does about 60%-70% damage PER SHOT! Sniping is respectably easier in Soldier Front 2 which allows many people to become the accurate damage dealers that they wish to become. Most weapons are purchasable through just playing the game and earning SP (The in-game currency). You can buy and funnel real-life currency into the game and that will obviously give you the edge over starter or beginner players, but I have on several occasions defeated and dominated players that have custom or bought weapons, So there is no worries if you cannot afford getting high powered expensive weapons.
Maps
--------
The maps within Soldier Front 2, have a certain something to be desired but offer a good gaming experience. Several maps are just "killhouses" such as "Dam" which allows enemy snipers on several occasions and several different vantage spots to camp senceless and pick off any clueless victims. There are better and bigger maps such as "Farm" and "Riverside" which is long range tactical 8v8 experience that leaves the player feeling happy with his/her progress and kills.
Customisation
----------------
There is a wide range of customisation options in Soldier Front 2 that lets the player become his/her own soldier and create his/her own character instead of being a randomly generated soldier in such games as Call of Duty. This lets the player feel as if he/she is the soldier instead of just being a name. Items such as Hats, Glasses, Helmets, Different force uniforms, Bandannas and masks really let you customise your soldier, many of these items are purchasable with SP and will only last 7 - 31 days depending on how much you spend on him/her.
Vehicles
----------
Sadly there is no drivable vehicles in Soldier Front 2 as the maps and gamemodes are based on "Deathmatch" settings and have no exploration rewards, Just kill, kill, kill for your experience.
Leveling
------------
Soldier Front has a very long and tedious leveling up system, I have personally clocked about 30 Hours into my character and he is only level 25. Expect a long and arduous journey but you will enjoy the ride.
Community
--------------
There is an in-game and in-lobby message system and a friend system that allows you to keep in contact and play with your comrades in arms, people are not very "sour", but occasionaly you will get a raging 12 year old telling you that you are a f****t because you killed him. His is evident in most FPS games and unfortunately happens here as well. Just stay friendly and they will be friendly back.
In summay Soldier Front 2 is the game to play for a frantic FPS multiplayer struggle, I have a 2Mb connection and play comfortably with a green ping at most times, some non-european servers have a touch of lag, but I am currently in Southern Africa. This game will leave you satisfied as it is completely free to play! Thumbs up!

Most negative reviews seem to focus on the issues with the port and not on the game itself, so here's the opinion of someone who's not wearing nostalgia goggles and genuinely did not enjoy the game:
Tales of Symphonia is a JRPG. As usual, you progress through the story fighting monsters, leveling up, learning new skills and acquiring better gear.
The element that stands out the most is the battle system, which the series is famous for.
It's very action oriented, you can move around freely (albeit in a 2.5D plane), jump, block attacks, chain combos and whatnot. It's important to note that you can only control one character at a time, while the others are controlled by the AI. You can configure their behavior to some extent but I found the options to be really really limited. As someone who enjoys the tactical aspect of things, I had a real hard time trying to assign specific roles to my characters, such as healing, tanking or just staying safe in general. Ultimately, all battles look like an all out brawl, with your party members doing stupid things and suiciding constantly, especially the magic users. Really frustrating, especially in boss battles.
Most of the time you'll just have to rely on brute forcing with the main character, spamming whatever combo does the most damage and hoping that it works out.
The game also does a very poor job of explaining its mechanics to the player. All you get is usually a pop up with some instructions and that's it. You know it's bad when you have to search the internet for some vital information. The interface is pretty confusing as well, for a long time I didn't even know you could play with other characters besides the protagonist. I still have no idea how to make a decent use of the cooking system.
I only have 7 hours on it, which I'm guessing is around 15% of the game, so I can't say much about the story, but from what I saw it wasn't bad, only a bit cliché, as you can expect.

I can see why it gets its praise, especially when it was first released, but the battle system and the feeling of complete LACK OF CONTROL killed it for me.
Now, if you don't mind grinding away on a lighthearted story, you might enjoy this.
