Whispering Willows is a mystery game, a 2D walking simulator. You play as Elena, a Native American girl who is searching for her vanished father in an enormous abandoned estate. Elena has no means of defending herself, her only unique ability being that she can use her father's amulet to astral project a spirit version of herself to talk to ghosts and solve puzzles.
Let's be concise here: the gameplay here is horrible. Absolute trash. Elena moves sloooowly but the game requires a lot of backtracking, a lot of "walk from Room 1 to Room 5, pull a lever, walk back to Room 1". She can only run in the outdoor hub area for absolutely no reason- what, is she afraid to scuff up the floor of a 200 year old catacomb?
The puzzles themselves range from primitive (find a locked door, send your ghost self through a peep hole, pull a lever, walk through the now-unlocked door.) to irritating (the garden section, which has many dead ends that all look exactly the same down to identical statues, comes to mind.)
There are "enemies" to dodge, mainly scorpions and tree monsters. If they come close to Elena, she dies and you get sent back to a checkpoint. The death animation is simply Elena falling to her knees and closing her eyes, and the monsters themselves lack any menace. They were just annoying to try to dodge.
But bad gameplay can be redeemed through good atmosphere and storytelling. The atmosphere is pretty good, I'll admit. The music is generic but creepy and fitting, I liked a lot of the audio, the lighting was excellent. It's not the most immersive game in the world but the atmosphere is assuredly the high point.
MODERATE SPOILERS FROM THIS POINT ON
I can't say the same for the writing, which is only slightly better than the gameplay. Elena is as flat and dull as a manhole cover. There are no interesting or likable NPC's. The only characters to get any personality are through the notes scattered throughout the maps. They tell the story of a group of sadistic and evil white men who came, slaughtered the peaceful and utopian natives (great attention is given to them murdering the children) and placing a curse on the land for decades to come. All the natives are one dimensional and shallow, pure beings of light and forgiveness. The game has lofty ideals of making Wortham, the owner of the estate, some sort of nuanced and tragic villain. Instead he just comes off as a Snidely Whiplash type figure, murdering his friends and consorting with dark magics. The game's story is a bundle of boring cliches, which is too bad because with such an open-ended set-up they could tell any story they want.
The feeling I have from Whispering Willows is "disappointment". An atmospheric mystery game with a female protagonist exploring a haunted mansion? Sign me the ♥♥♥♥ up. But the game delivers on almost none of the promises of its setting. That's too bad.

I've played this game for about eight hours so far, and I think I'm going to get a *ton* more playtime out of it. The gameplay is reminiscient of classic dungeon crawlers like Eye of the Beholder, and the procedurally generated dungeons and random loot drops make it addictive, satisfying and replayable. On top of that, this game has a very original skill system with a lot of creativity and ingenuity behind it. The complexity of the skills can be daunting at first, but its a small price to pay for the satisfaction of seeing your characters chain moves together to wreak havoc on a crowded screen of space bugs. Many of the skills have elements of chance and risk that make the combat unpredictable and exciting. The setting is familiar but well-executed and enjoyable- think Shadowrun meets Star Wars. The UI is polished and elegant, and the effects are definitely suitable.
That being said, the writing isn't all there and sometimes the humor misses a beat. A couple of the character classes look dorky as hell, if that matters to you. You'll find yourself fighting the same types of enemies again and again (although there can be pretty wide variation in how combats play out). Also, the robot who is supposed to say random haikus has a very small pool to choose from. :(
All in all, Star Crawlers does enough right to forgive its missteps. It shows that creativity and careful execution can breathe life into a genre two decades old. If you're a fan of dungeon crawls like me, the $20 price tag is definitely appropriate for the quality of the product you get: you'll find yourself wanting to play "just one more" mission again and again.

It would be a good game, if it had any depth at all.
The more I play it, the more it feels like I've seen everything it has to offer in the first 20 minutes or so. Sure, you'll be gaining levels, unlocking new skills, and advancing through the story, but the basic gameplay will stay the same. Here is what's wrong with StarCrawlers, in my opinion (compared to other dungeon crawlers, RPGs and turn-based games in general):
1) All battles are functionally the same, and there is no actual diversity between enemy compositions. While even in simpliest jRPGs you have to decide "do I want to focus the damage on opponent's damage dealer first, or spread the AOE damage to finish the battle faster, or disable the problematic enemy", etc, here there are dudes with slightly more hp and dudes with slightly less hp, and sometimes some enemies have some shields (which makes no difference at all for some of your party compositions). I do not expect each battle to be a truly unique puzzle, but surely there is no reason to repeat the same "3 identical Space Mites" battle 50 times in a row, over several different side-missions.
2) All the decisions in battle are trivial, regardless of your party (thanks to the ability to respec, I had a chance to try various builds). The most common enemy composition is "3-4 mobs of the same type", so it doesn't even matter what you are targeting. There is just one optimal sequence of actions that you discover in your 1st or 2nd battle with your group of choice, and you can stick to it in every battle. Surely you can bump the difficulty and make battles "harder" by tweaking some numbers in opponent's favor, but it won't actually force you to think about your actions. I don't even want to compare the strategic depth with games like Darkest Dungeon, because the StarCrawlers basically lacks the thing to compare.
3) Battles feel tedious, since they are not particularly thrilling, but are relatively long (even with quick animations turned on). A trivial battle where your opponent does ~0 damage to your entire party can take half a minute instead of a few seconds (like it should), there are dozens of battles like this, and each of them rewards you with almost nothing. At some point I had to unequip a weapon that does more DPS simply because its animation was longer (multiple slow-ish shots per enemy), and it made boring battles even more boring.
Some serious redesign is required to unlock this game's potential. Avoid it for now.

A great game for the first hours then it gets tedious.
Yes, i invested 40 hours into the game and liked the feeling of playing a cyperpunk Legend of Grimrock title, until i came to the sad conclusion i have to give it a negative recomendation based on lack of polish (both user interface and user experience), general info and limited diversity in explorable areas. Some very low res texturing and area layout (the offices) dont help to promote the game. Difficulty spikes and unbalanced difficulty dont help the casual gamer who just wants a title to relax inbetween more demanding titles.
Constant stutters after every patch forced me to redownload the game to fix it. First time loading a save would still cause stutters and prompt a restart of the game to bypass the issue.
Reached the last part of the game and realized that a specific party composition and playstyle is needed to overcome the last fighst, which are essentially a dps race against mobs with high health pools.
Healing is a chore since no dedicated classes exist.
Healing with items is slow, uneffective, slot consuming (in a limited slots inventory based game) and expensive to maintain.
Random regeneration is useless at higher levels.
RNG is brutal and can quickly turn a normal battle into a wipe.
Wipes mean loosing alot of time since autosaves are a joke and manual saves are a risky act if done near spotted enemies since they can outrun you. Saves done in the dungeon has to be named individually every time. No overwrites.
Since its a dungeon crawler it should reward exploration but after level 10 they randomly spawn high bosses with different mechanics, resists or buffs that can only be ovecome by certain clases with certain abilities, defacto negatinf the concept of choosing four characters and speccing them how you want. Some bosses are just huge health pools that become a foreshadowing of the endgame fights, effectively telling the player to go full dps or respecc. These bosses spawn during easy missions, missions meant to farm resources to later overcome the real challenges and if it happens while trying a new party and abilities its an almost guarenteed wipe.
Loot is generally unsatisfactory to collect and more a chore to manage on a limited inventory. RNG kindly makes sure you get gear for other classes you dont need. Extra items crafted after long grinds are useless. Usefulness of rare items is never explained.
The suggestion is to wait for a sale and in the meantime hope for more patches and general polish of this beautiful raw diamond of a game.

A pretty interesting take on the cRPG genre that is all about making space runs for money and reputation.
The best thing about this game is that all of the dungeons are all procedurally generated and no 2 will be mapped out the same way.  Things that could be clicked on before may not be clickable the next time you see the object or there may even be new found loot laying around.  The bad thing is that the objects repeat a lot throughout the dungeon and so it gets old fairly quickly.
There are 8 classes that play out very much differently from one another with 3 different experience trees.  Unfortunately they feel a lot like World of Warcraft and almost shamelessly takes some aspects from it.
Each class may also yield a special conversation or action that may prove useful or detrimental in your runs.  However many of these special actions or conversations are RNG based and because of this, you may miss out on something cool or interesting.
Reputation system that opens up different conversation bubbles and rewards.
The worst part about the game are the repetitive enemies.  From level 1 on up you will meet basically the same monsters but with more HP.  This is a huge letdown since the game is centered around the combat!
Loot drops aren't especially bad but at the same time it isn't good either.  They augment your stats and damage but there's really nothing special to lift up over your head with a squeal of enjoyment.
Overall a pretty good game that is extremely entertaining.  However after longer hours of play the fun will begin to drop off.

This review is written after having played almost three hours of gameplay with intent to play more. It's also important to note that this is written from the point of view of someone who has not played any of the Castlevania's before Lord of Shadow (The first one.)
Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 thrusts you into the role of Gabriel Belmont (otherwise known as Dracula) who is disturbed from his centuries of rest to once again battle Satan. The game stands well on it's own and I feel like someone who hasn't played the first game can still pick up this one and not be confused as to what is going on. However, I also feel like if someone were to have played the first one they will enjoy the story a lot more than if they didn't. (This is easily remedied by reading a wikipedia summary or watching the cutscenes of the first game on youtube.)
The gameplay is reminiscent of Devil May Cry, Ninja Gaiden and other stylish action fighters. You do combos against multiple enemies and emphasis is placed on avoiding attacks to survive. Even the normal mode feels difficult because there is just so much going on and it's easy to lose track of enemies that end up behind you. However, the combos you can upgrade into feel almost pointless when you can just mash your single target attack, dodge and come out victorious. However, it also does some things good by giving your weapons meaning. The Void Blade restores health through attacks and the Chaos claws deal extra damage to enemies. Dodging attacks is essential because in order to use these weapons you need to build up a combo meter which allows "blood orbs" to appear which gives power to the weapons.
Where Castlevania: LoS2 sets itself apart from Devil May Cry and Ninja Gaiden is in the platforming sections. With Devil May cry you time a bunch of jumps and with Ninja Gaiden you run across rooftops. With Castlevania it manages to execute a good platforming experience reminiscent of games like Prince of Persia. You'll scale up walls while under siege by enemies, time perfect jumps and use your abilities to reach hidden spots to power up Dracula.
I also think it's worthwhile to note that if you dislike Quick Time Events(QTE), there is an option to disable QTE's in the game menu. This is a huge step forward as a lot of gamers moan and gripe about having to "Press X to not die" and I hope to see this option more in the future in other games.
Overall, if you liked Ninja Gaiden or Devil May Cry you'll find a similarly enjoyable experience in Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2.

Postal is the ridiculous kind of game released in an era where activist groups thought Doom was a murder training device and mocks said activism with its wanton violence and campy humor. Each level is simply a free-for-all where you try to kill a percentage of hostiles and incidentally a few hundred innocent bystanders as well.
Gameplay-wise, Postal holds itself together very well. The controls on gamepad are quite fluid and the twin-stick style aiming system works good enough for a game made in 1997. The difficulty out of the box will probably be a bit too easy for most players and IMO the only way to really experience this game is on its maximum difficulty, where you will have to carefully plan your movement across each level to avoid a quick and surprising death. Since the viewable area is locked to an isometric perspective, and weapon ranges exceed the area from the player’s location, you will need to be very careful when moving up or down and zig-zagging across each level is an absolute must whenever possible. Enemies tend to be a bit spongey to bullets but go down in a single hit from incendiary or explosive weapons (and can kill you just as fast).
Postal’s graphical and audio shortcomings are typical for a game made in its time and haven’t aged particularly well but that’s to be expected. The levels also get repetitive after the 6th or 7th map and clearing them becomes more memorization than reflexes and skill. Yet for a retro game that you can easily get for less than a dollar these days, Postal still manages to squeeze out enough fun to make it worth picking up.

Sadly the finished product feels like a rushed attempt at trying to create something that could have been great but falls short in so many way and ultimately feels like a Civilization: Beyond Earth mini-game.
The game revolves around conquering planets with a single fleet of starships & engaging in repetitive battles that feature an uninspiring AI that can be easily defeated once you (quickly) discover a simple formulae for defeating opponents (You can quite easily hide your ships in cover and cripple the enemy with waves of torpedoes & fighters).
I don’t explicitly dislike Starships, however, there is very little replay value and almost no scope for variety in terms of how you play the game, due to the almost identical factions and simplistic victory conditions (I’ve found myself winning a population victory by accident on several occasions).
Although the game isn’t anywhere near as engaging as I hoped, it does have good touch support and is a pleasant enough game to play on a tablet when on the move or sitting in bed. As much as I hate taking the price into consideration, as I would have much rather paid three times as much for a far deeper experience, I do think that it’s a decent enough arcade game for killing time in short bursts.
In summary I’m going to (only just) recommend Starships based purely on the fact that it’s a cheap and cheerful game to pass an hour or so here-and-there, just don’t expect the same engaging experience that you might expect from other games in the franchise.

I was a fan since I played the Longest Journey back in 2002 (originally released in 2000) and I donated to the Kickstarter campaign for Dreamfall Chapters without regret.
If you are intrigued by this game start with the Longest Journey, then Dreamfall, then play Dreamfall Chapters.
The Longest Journey is one of those really special games that stays with you way after you're done playing.
I still remember reading Split Infinity  by Piers Anthony - and then to find a visualization of this in the Longest Journey and Dreamfall was so rewarding.
I look back on all that sci fi and fantasy that helped me grow up with great fondness.   I have a very deep resonance with this idea of bridging the two worlds and merging the two kinds of imagination.  It is only now that I am (much) older that I also understand how easy it is to lose your imagination - whether to intrusive technology or to ideological intolerance.
I think video games of this type still have a long evolution in front of them.

Many story based games struggle with pacing.  Dreamfall Chapters is no exception ... it is a healthy struggle.  We are just learning how to tell and participate in stories in a new way - immersive story based video games are maybe 30 years old.
I am very grateful that this work is being continued in Dreamfall and if there is another Kickstarter campaign to finish April Ryan's story - I'm in.

Your actions do have consequences to a point, so don't be afraid to experiment in your playthrough with answers and decisions you normally wouldn't choose. TL;DR. I like this game. I like it a lot. But it has flaws and a lot of those flaws spring from shallowness that comes from the fact that this is a reiteration of a flash game by the same name. It improved a lot upon the flash game, but at the same time is fully the prodigal son to it.
So, starting with what the flash game was:  You are launched as a little airplane from a submarine without help to fight endless waves of fighters, jets, boats, battleships, and submarines that progressively gets more difficult till eventually the surface of the water is 100% battleships and you are outrunning a death wall of shots from said battleships that will either kill you because you were in it for 0.001 seconds, or because it crashes your internet browser as a flash game trying to keep track of 10,000 projectiles at the same time and the graphical effects created when 1,000 of those hit a plane at the same time.
The beginning of this game, hour 0.0, goes as such:  You are launched as a little airplane from a submarine without help to fight endless waves of fighters, jets, boats, battleships, and submarines that progressively gets more difficult till eventually... oh, yeah, the premise is exactly the same. However, they mix it up in several ways. They are:
1) Your death doesn't come at the hand of 10,000,000 battleships, but one of the more advanced enemies that they have added to the game. They are:
So, because of this, the game at the point at which you die-die-die is definitely a lot better at running and a lot more entertaining. Dying to a fight in which you're fighting 4 aces trying to machine gun you down while two battleships try to kill you along with a blimp, five jets occasionally chasing you, and a dozen common fighters trying to take you down is a lot more fun than running from a wall of death.
2) Upgrades! While you start with the same fighter as you had in the flash, you gradually unlock new parts by completing challenges such as "Kill 50 enemies" or such, though a lot more complicated than that example. There are 5 main parts for weapons, chassis, and propulsion that all have their own challenges that will gradually grow more difficult until you have to make specially crafted builds out of the parts at hand to complete each one and all of the parts have their own special niches, often accented or challeged by their challenges.  Once you 100% the challenges in each respective part slot, you get a sixth end game weapon/chassis/propulsion system. Also, each respective build has its own unique name. My personal favorite is the "war turtle"-- there are 125 special builds in the main gameplay loop before the unlock of the super-special sixth slot, so good luck figuring out which one it is!
3) NG+/Hardcore mode! This game has a second mode that you unlock through playing--and will be the game mode for the final challenge for each weapon part-- that is honestly the hardest bullet hell experience I've ever had. It starts you off throwing every single enemy type at you--from the default enemies to multiple blimps-- at the same time as they upgrade all of them to ludicrous difficulty. Fighters shoot three bullets at once, battleships and aces shoot even more, jets leave trails of bullets in their wake, submarines absolutely spam missiles at you-- there's a reason one of the achievements for this game is to last through the first twenty seconds: it is bonkers.
4) The absolute least change is the alternative color schemes you unlock. You will spend 99% of your time in the classic colors introduced in the default game because the alternative color schemes are terribly design and range in experience from "I can't see anything", to "Ow, this is too bright and I now have a tension headache and a migrane simultaneously, thanks game", to "Ow, this is too bright, I now have a tension headache and a migrane simultaneously, I can't see anything, and it looks like I'm on the inside of a watermelon". Just stick to the creamy tan of paper folders and stark red of dried blood-- your performance in this bullet hell will both be better in most cases and will give you a lot less eye strain.
It is through these changes that they make the core game loop a lot more enveloping than the original flash game--but it still falls to the flaw of shallowness. You're still a fighter plane launched from a submarine to fight endless waves, and that's all you'll ever do. Though it has more variation than games of bullet hells with the endless survival premise, it still falls to the same usual flaws of those other ones and its predecessor flash game in that it gets repetitive. Some of the challenges are rediculously difficult, and one in particular is pretty close to broken. Hint: if you're using the bomber body and it tells you to "kill 30 enemies, never stop firing", use the laser-- that challenge is broken and nearing on uncompletable without using the laser. Though that challenge is pretty easy to some of the other ones that are just overall rediculously hard.  You will eventually get bored or tired of smashing your face into the wall when RNG ♥♥♥♥s you over with the overspecialized end-game builds.
If you like bullet hells and you like 2d, gravity-based dog-fighters, this game is fantastic. If you like bullet hells, give it a shot; it will give you a good challenge and is very satisfying as far as controls go. Definitely would recommend picking it up. If you need a demo of the game before you'll be sold on the premise, go play the flash game and then consider all that I've talked about in how they've updated it. This is also a loooot more polished than the flash game, of course.
Edit: I would like to also note that the way your plane controls is really quite unique and enjoyable, quite honestly like no other bullet hell.

I have mixed feelings about this game. I saw it during the summer sale, and decided to take a gamble. I'm not sure it totally paid off.
The art is great! During the gameplay, anyway. The cutscene art is not so good. And the animation is really hit and miss. Sometimes it feels like some frames of animation are missing. The music is atmospheric, and sets the mood. The story in the notes is intriguing, but the main story of Elena finding her dad is really basic and forgettable. And the ending could have been interesting, but it didn't really work.
The puzzles are also really easy. I only got stuck on one because I thought it was more complicated than it really was. And unfortunately, the movement speed is too slow. Add frequent backtracking, and it can get frustrating. Enemies were a minor nuisance at best. And they were disappointing, with only bugs and some demon hedge things.
I also had a few minor control issues. I played on an Xbox One gamepad, and it didn't always play nice. Down on the thumbstick didn't work on the menus, but other directions did. And down worked fine for ladders and such. Also, kind of frustrating that you have to stop moving the stick to open a door. There were also a few UI issues, namely with text going off screen or being obscured by other text. And the game gave me gamepad movement prompts and keyboard interaction prompts.
The bit in the crypt at the beginning was probably the best part of the whole game. You know, after you open the coffin and then that thing starts chasing you? It gave me really high hopes for the rest. But it doesn't fully embrace the horror atmosphere for the rest of the game. The ghosts are harmless, and again, very few (and kind of lame) enemies. And well, it's really short. I'm seeing most people say 3-4 hours, and I got through it in just over 2.
Still, I think this is a good way to burn through an afternoon. $10 might be a bit much, but I've paid more to see a movie. And I got it on sale, so that helps. I think that, overall, it's worth checking out if you can get it on sale.

LoS2 is a game that I found myself pretty hyped for. The downfall of this sequel, however, is that it doesn't even favorably stack up to its predecessor.
LoS2 has improved primary combat from the first game. The Void Sword and Chaos Claw mechanics feel distinctly unique from the main whip weapon, but unfortunately they do not really feel different from each other, except for the range of attacks and the focus on healing and damage. The Claws and the Sword have the same base combos as the whip, and while they offer more options once you learn the available skills, it still feels like the game is played largely the same regardless of which weapon you have equipped. The ability to dodge into enemies to interrupt some attacks, as well as dodging vertically or block from an aerial position, are welcome. It would still be nice for the dodge to have some window of invulnerability, for the cases where the camera is not being nice and you are unable to exactly avoid a tracking charge move or the like. Speaking of, the camera assist does seem to be helpful, but at the same time there are a few instances where I find myself needing to find the center of the room just so that I could get situated again with the camera and enemy placement.
Overall, the combat is the only real improvement that the sequel provides, and everything else changes for the worse. The story starts off really interesting, but nose dives quickly. Zobek is the game's instant chaperon, declaring to Dracula what needs to be done and why. This is kind of an instant turn off. The idea that Dracula has become an "errand boy" for a man who has deceived him in the past is a bit silly. Story threads seems half-baked, and some ideas are created and forgotten faster than the player anticipates. Early on the game focuses on an antidote subplot which drags further on into the story than it needs to, but the result of this is never really made known. Later plot threads involve putting an item back together, which of course is made up of various pieces held by various antagonists. The plot shifts back and forth from the modern day tasks set forth by Zobek and from emotionally declared tasks requested by Dracula's own desires. It's a bit vague but it's hard to be clear without spoiling things. The idea is that the shifting of gameplay between the City and the Castle is reflected in the story itself, and it is never really made clear which plot threads end up important and which don't.
The duality of the gameplay locations itself is a similar mess. Ignoring motivation or plot reasons, exploring the castle is pretty fun. The locales are pretty unique, ranging from a leaved garden, to a snowy tower, to a theatre and workshop and fire-lined deep halls and moonlit balconies. While the platforming is not terribly intricate, jumping and exploring paths between the castle sectors wasn't ever really boring, outside of the rooms that clearly act as loading areas. Too often does Dracula find himself in an "airlock" where he has to close off the path behind him and open that in front of him to continue on. While during the initial run through of a place, these parts aren't bad but are merely annoying. However, they make exploring after the fact a large chore. I found myself actually dreading shifting from one area to another if it meant passing through one of these airlocks, especially if I found I needed to run around and go through it again. Aside from those however, the castle is damn gorgeous and is generally a pleasure to visit.
The City, on the other hand, is a wreck. This doesn't just limit itself to the location itself, but also the way that it plays differently. First off, the locations of street level roads, parking garages, a church, a train station, industry hatches and factories... there's some variety but it just doesn't compare to the ornate castle areas. Most everything is drab, dark, and cramped. It's just boring. On its own this isn't something that is a deal breaker, but the fact that areas are often separated by underground hatches leading to cramped hallways and elevators and such, again, make exploring the areas after initially playing through them to simply not be very fun. Since the rewards for exploring visited areas is mostly limited to extensions to your health or magic bar, or perhaps background lore, these factors make backtracking around not the most appealing thing to undertake in the first place. Secondly, the enemy types found in these modern areas included demons with shotguns or grenades, as well as robot police type mechs. These enemies are not terrible, but having to avoid various manners of ranged attacks on awkward enemy types just make them not as fun to fight. The city area does have the spectre/wraith type enemies, which I do enjoy fighting, but it doesn't compare to the jailers, harpies, blood skeletons, brotherhood knights, and such of the castle areas.
The Boss fights of this game are spectacles, and while the motivation for fighting each of them is a bit silly, some of them are really well done. The boss designs are creative, fun to look at, and most importantly, fun to fight (generally). The boss fights do a fair job of mixing up how you are best to tackle them, including using ranged or aerial attacks, or using Void and Chaos power, as well as prioritizing positioning and reflexes. It's just unfortunate that one of the most interesting boss fights, the one you fight in the theater, ends up also being one of the easiest in the game. There is a challenge set of maps also available, but these feel so separate from the main game. Sure, you can "farm" experience through these, but you could just do that with enemies anywhere, and you don't have to skip a cutscene every time you want to enter the challenge area. I understand that for many players, the challenges being present for a sake of variety is plenty, but I would have liked some sort of exp bonus for each completed challenge as some sort of motivation for completing them during the main game. Aside from that, the challenges themselves are pretty interesting and some are fairly challenging. The limitations forced on the player for some of the later challenge rewards allow you to think of other ways to dispatch enemy types. For instance, a later challenge that required to freeze monsters readily taught me about the void power variant of the mist form, which normal gameplay might have never pushed me to attempt otherwise.
Final thing I want to touch on is the stealth. Outside of some admittedly shameful ineptitude from certain review sites when it comes to finishing the stealth sections, I will say that the reviews themselves are not wrong. They just seem unneeded, and they interrupt the pace of a game that needs all of the pacing consistency it can find. Even with the idea that the stealth sections are more like puzzles in the guise of stealth, they still feel manufactured and present just to be present; I think I would have preferred more Zelda-eqse puzzles like in the first game rather than avoid unkillable enemies as the immortal prince of darkness disguised as a rat. While puzzles can become an iterative process where you learn the patterns needed and slowly make progress to a solution, these stealth sections seem more like trail and error where you simply try out which combination of bat, rat, and possess needs to be done in what order in order to progress. The infamous stealth section in the garden area was the largest of the game, and while mechanically it wasn't much different from any of the numerous smaller stealth sections, it felt the most unneeded since the fight that it precedes make the whole section seem pointless.
The game is a decent run through, especially for fans of the initial Lords of Shadow, but for anyone waiting to jump in or wanting to be proven wrong about their opinion on this latest outing by MercurySteam, this game isn't going to make believers out of the doubters.

Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 is the latest in the Castlevania franchise. This title is a hack and slash action oriented game that is not for the faint of heart. Those who dislike blood and gore are likely to turn away from this game, however those who like blood guts and gore can go nuts. Fans of Castlevania will appreciate this game to a point, however those new to the series may find things a little confusing.
For starters, the control system in the game is very fluid for the most part. Abilities can be used at will depending on the situation at hand. Swapping between the 3 weapons you get in the game is very smooth, switching from one to the other and back again at the touch of a button while keeping a combo going. The combat in general is smooth, however there are minor things that can be very disheartening for newer players. Unblockable attacks can be overlooked given the amount of things going on in a heated battle at times. For example, fights with a lot of dirt, rubble, blood and enemies flying everywhere can sometimes (not always) block your view from unblockable attacks meaning you are going to get hit. And in a life or death situation this is very annoying.
The difficulty of the game varies between 4 difficulties, 3 of which are available from the outset. The 4th difficulty is unlocked by beating the game once. A veteran of games from series like Devil May Cry will not find the initial "hard mode" all that difficult. While it can be a challenge at times managing the players health and resources on hard, it isn't deathly hard. For newer players the easy and normal difficulties can provide their own challenge, but all in all things are very much dumbed down for ease of play.
Graphically, this game is incredible. The HD textures make everything within the environments stand out. From the tiniest pebble on the ground to the largest building in the distance, the developers have not skimped on anything. The whole game looks amazing from start to finish. The addition of several hundred pieces of concept art makes the whole look of things even better. The animations for every enemy, and every npc are very fuild, very good at depicting a certain realism about things.
The music in this game is also once again incredible with a few minor exceptions. Certain cutscenes have music that just doesn't fit at all. No emotion is felt from the music, no meaning. However that is just a few places. For the most part the music, and sounds in general are very well placed, very well composed and very well done overall. Voice acting is quite good, at times it's a bit questionable however again for the most part it fits, and is very well done by the actors including Robert Carlyle and Patrick Stewart.
Now. The major gripe I have with this game is the lack of direction throughout a lot of the games "open world" sections. Your minimap shows you the general direction on where to go, but a lot of the time you can spend a fair amount of time searching for the way to go. This could be a ledge to grapple, or a wall to walk around. For the most part things are easy to spot, but there were several times where I had to look around the area, after backtracking and re-entering the room just to find where to go next.
To conclude, I would give this game 8/10. It is a good solid game, well built and with a lot of nice features and well crafted gameplay. If you like hack and slash adventure games then this is a definite pick-up. 15 hours of solid gameplay minimum, well over 20 with NG+ and challenges, as well as the concept art collection. Those who know the Castlevania games of old may frown upon its story, but give it a shot and you'll like it.

For me, the “side-scrolling spaceship shooter” is a game genre that invokes an ambiguous response.
In one hand it offers addictive simplicity and nostalgia. In the other an absolute lack of narrative and gameplay conventions so well entrenched that it is almost impossible to distinguish any two examples of the genre from one another… also often little room for developing a strategy beyond mashing the attack button.
While obviously “retro” in many respects, Procyon is not a slavish tribute to early scrolling shooter games. Rather, the conventions have been bent for the players benefit.
The various modes and three tier difficulty setting allows the player as much, or as little, challenge as they desire. A ‘Practice Mode’, for example, allows a level to be played with unlimited lives, although this does not unlock the next level.
The graphics are also nice and 3D looking rather than “ironically” pixelated.
Lots of explosions and a large variety of alien spacecraft, all with different flight patterns and attacks.
The controls are simple and intuitive and the spaceship is highly mobile allowing you to dodge enemy attacks and move quickly around all over the screen. The weapon/shielding compromise system also gives you something to think about as expending your energy on supercharging your weapons leaves you unable to deflect attacks. Different enemies are also more or less vulnerable to the players two (or three if you count the lightening) weapons, so button mashing is not rewarded, “use ya noggin”.
What I particularly enjoyed were the cut scenes establishing a satire narrative between the levels.
It’s a short game (5 levels only), but it’s highly replay-able and considering that it only costs $3.00 or something its very good value for money.

Good fun shooter, it deserves a special mention for the great vertical display support. If you have a monitor which can be rotated the game will automatically adjust and switch from a horizontal to a vertical shmup.

Not sure when Shoot 'Em Ups became Shmups (sounds more like 'Schmucks' to me), but anyways perhaps the brevity is more appropriate for Procyon since it is very short at only 5 levels. For veteran Shoot 'Em Up players out there you might find Procyon less challenging than some of the brutal contenders currently on the market, but that's not to say that it is not an enjoyable experience.
Graphically, it looks sharp with high def effects & backdrops (no 8-bit look here) with sound effects & soundtrack holding strong too. Comes together very well. Controls are intuitive, allowing you to switch between your standard wide bullets to your concentrated beam weapon in an instant. The weapon & shield system implementation was one of the strong points for me. The weapons are linked into your shields and when combined offers a power-up damage to clear your path ahead. Beam weapon also arcs & bends which is a nice effect and allows you to still move around somewhat without loosing out on damaging your target.
For those that don't skip through the mini-story cutscenes there is also some humour to be had (worth watching through at least once).
On the negative side, I did find the boss fights a bit average; not bad but not really exciting either. Also an online co-op mode would have been awesome so I could play with friends around the world. With the duality in the weapons I could see online co-op being a lot of fun! Also, as I said earlier the game is very short. The 5 levels took me about 30 mins to complete first time through (and that was watching the cut-scenes!). Thankfully there is replayablity with higher difficulty levels in Attrition (5 lives + 1 per level completed) & Survival (1 life only!) to conquer.
For the price, overall quality & fun factor of this little title, this still gets a 'Thumbs Up' from me.

Once upon a time a frog
Croaked away in Bingle Bog
Every night from dusk to dawn
He croaked awn and awn and awn
Other creatures loathed his voice,
But, alas, they had no choice,
And the crass cacophony
Blared out from the sumac tree
At whose foot the frog each night
Minstrelled on till morning night
Neither stones nor prayers nor sticks.
Insults or complaints or bricks
Stilled the frogs determination
To display his heart's elation.
But one night a nightingale
In the moonlight cold and pale
Perched upon the sumac tree
Casting forth her melody
Dumbstruck sat the gaping frog
And the whole admiring bog
Stared towards the sumac, rapt,
And, when she had ended, clapped,
Ducks had swum and herons waded
To her as she serenaded
And a solitary loon
Wept, beneath the summer moon.
Toads and teals and tiddlers, captured
By her voice, cheered on, enraptured:
"Bravo! " "Too divine! " "Encore! "
So the nightingale once more,
Quite unused to such applause,
Sang till dawn without a pause.
Next night when the Nightingale
Shook her head and twitched her tail,
Closed an eye and fluffed a wing
And had cleared her throat to sing
She was startled by a croak.
"Sorry - was that you who spoke? "
She enquired when the frog
Hopped towards her from the bog.
"Yes," the frog replied. "You see,
I'm the frog who owns this tree
In this bog I've long been known
For my splendid baritone
And, of course, I wield my pen
For Bog Trumpet now and then"
"Did you… did you like my song? "
"Not too bad - but far too long.
The technique was fine of course,
But it lacked a certain force".
"Oh! " the nightingale confessed.
Greatly flattered and impressed
That a critic of such note
Had discussed her art and throat:
"I don't think the song's divine.
But - oh, well - at least it's mine".
"That's not much to boast about".
Said the heartless frog. "Without
Proper training such as I
- And few others can supply.
You'll remain a mere beginner.
But with me you'll be a winner"
"Dearest frog", the nightingale
Breathed: "This is a fairy tale -
And you are Mozart in disguise
Come to earth before my eyes".
"Well I charge a modest fee."
"Oh! " "But it won't hurt, you'll see"
Now the nightingale inspired,
Flushed with confidence, and fired
With both art and adoration,
Sang - and was a huge sensation.
Animals for miles around
Flocked towards the magic sound,
And the frog with great precision
Counted heads and charged admission.
Though next morning it was raining,
He began her vocal training.
"But I can't sing in this weather"
"Come my dear - we'll sing together.
Just put on your scarf and sash,
Koo-oh-ah! ko-ash! ko-ash! "
So the frog and nightingale
Journeyed up and down the scale
For six hours, till she was shivering
and her voice was hoarse and quivering.
Though subdued and sleep deprived,
In the night her throat revived,
And the sumac tree was bowed,
With a breathless, titled crowd:
Owl of Sandwich, Duck of Kent,
Mallard and Milady Trent,
Martin Cardinal Mephisto,
And the Coot of Monte Cristo,
Ladies with tiaras glittering
In the interval sat twittering -
And the frog observed them glitter
With a joy both sweet and bitter.
Every day the frog who'd sold her
Songs for silver tried to scold her:
"You must practice even longer
Till your voice, like mine grows stronger.
In the second song last night
You got nervous in mid-flight.
And, my dear, lay on more trills:
Audiences enjoy such frills.
You must make your public happier:
Give them something sharper snappier.
We must aim for better billings.
You still owe me sixty shillings."
Day by day the nightingale
Grew more sorrowful and pale.
Night on night her tired song
Zipped and trilled and bounced along,
Till the birds and beasts grew tired
At a voice so uninspired
And the ticket office gross
Crashed, and she grew more morose -
For her ears were now addicted
To applause quite unrestricted,
And to sing into the night
All alone gave no delight.
Now the frog puffed up with rage.
"Brainless bird - you're on the stage -
Use your wits and follow fashion.
Puff your lungs out with your passion."
Trembling, terrified to fail,
Blind with tears, the nightingale
Heard him out in silence, tried,
Puffed up, burst a vein, and died.
Said the frog: "I tried to teach her,
But she was a stupid creature -
Far too nervous, far too tense.
Far too prone to influence.
Well, poor bird - she should have known
That your song must be your own.
That's why I sing with panache:
"Koo-oh-ah! ko-ash! ko-ash! "
And the foghorn of the frog
Blared unrivalled through the bog.

After giving this game a second try (and playing for far longer) I'm changing my review - COMPLETELY.
Initially some of the controls of the game threw me off significantly compared to later entries like Tales of Vesperia (my entry into the series) - especially defending is pretty tricky. But setting movement to semi-automatic did make it easier & the battle system of the Tales series is fun and engaging & getting new moves is fun & adds extra variety into it.
I had read the manga before going into this and WOW, this is a much different experience - the manga totally cuts out huge chunks of content. The writing doesn't start off great, but it quickly gets better -a lot better. It's a cheesy story at parts, - but not a cringy one - and it's a cheesy story that KNOWS it's a cheesy story, which makes it so much better & enjoyable. While it has a fair amount of cheese in the writing, the storyline is also very interesting & good - and the characters & their development is where the Tales series really shine as they tackle many different issues both in main events and optional "skips" - many of pretty significant moral or emotional maturation issue. It is something that is really quite remarkable. The skits is actually a way of storytelling that I would say is an amazing part of the language of video games where we can do things in a much more impactful way than other media - something I do not say often.
On that note, I do have to put forth one strong critique. The skits are not voice acted. The voice acting talent is actually very good (as it is in Vesperia), but for some reason the English is not here. Not that I say the English - I had missed a few lines of dialogue in a in-game "cutscene" so I went on youtube to find it again & during the search I happened on some footage (taken from the PS3 version) from a skit - this was voice in Japanese. So it appears that the skits were originally voice, but for the localization into English they just didn't want to bother to do it. That's really damn awful.
All in all, it's an amazing game.

Great game. As expected of a game from the Tales Of franchise, the gameplay is a nice combination between comboes and strategy.
The only other Tales Of game I have played is Tales of Phantasia; To my surprise, it plays similarily (I was expecting the opposite since this one is 3D). You can move the character in three ways: moving toward the enemy, moving away from the enemy, and jumping toward/backward/in-place. Somehow, this 2D way of moving still works for this 3D fighting game since you can change which enemy you're targeting in the midst of battle.
After completing the game, I rate the combat system much better than Tales of Phantasia. For one, there's less infinite hitsun with the main character to kill bosses to death without giving them a chance to fight. Mages' abilities are learned one by one and soon you'll become used to using the right spell for any situation. Another contrast to Phantasia is that you can have multiple melee characters in your party. This means that you'll have to rely on how good the AI is at controlling these characters (seeing that you can only fully control one character at a time), but the AI turned out to be pretty good.
The difficulty curve of this game is a bit awkward. Know that I've only played this on the normal difficulty (I couldn't get past the first area in hard mode). I won't spoil any of the bosses, but I tended to find the earlier bosses harder (died alot to them) and then the endgame bosses became easy after upgrading EX skills and equipping your characters with end-game weapons. However, most bosses still have enough power to threaten a party wipe.
Lastly, I'll talk about the story and music. For a 50 hour game, the complexity of the main story was great and provided enough plot twists to keep it interesting. However, in its shadow lies some dirty ways of prolonging the story for very little reason. There are many places where it seems that the writers just wanted to make the story longer just to waste the player's time; I despised how the party had to go out of its way to save a few characters that would eventually become a part of the party themselves instead of doing their main objective: saving the world. I'm not saying that they should remove these characters, but their stories should have been an optional part.
Perhaps it was the lack of volume control in the options menu or my buzzing computer fan, but I found the music of Tales of Symphonia to be quite average. There are some great pieces here and there, but nothing amazing (except for Fighting of the Spirit. OHHHHHH YES.)
tl;dr/conclusion: All in all, I say it's a worthwhile buy if you enjoy JRPGs and can stand gamecube graphics (although the HD remaster makes some scenes look beautiful). Just don't expect this to be the best JRPG you've ever played and you will definitely find your money's worth.

This is a lengthy review, so scroll downf or a full report!
Having played this game a fair bit and getting up to level 26 in-game, I can say that this is well-worth the time and effort to play. I've played a large number of free to play shooters out there (nearly all of the most popular ones) and this one is the only one that can deliver on most bases successfully.
The biggest issue that seems to trouble most FPS games out there today (speaking FREE TO PLAY FPS games) are cash-shop imbalances, and currency gains.  Some games deliver on one, but lack on gameplay or maps, or somewhere else. At least that's what it feels like, Soldier Front 2's cash shop items are primarily cosmetic differences fromt heir normal counter parts. The stats on the weapons are listed and you can compare the regular weapons to the premium weapons, at most the differences are a different skin and occasionally a different optic which can also be obtained through buying the advanced version of each weapon through gameplay. It takes longer, but it is not game-breaking by ANY means. I myself, prefer good ol' iron sights as I'm sure plenty of others do as well.
On that topic, let me talk about the currency system. You start out with plenty enough to buy your first weapon, and maybe even a secondary weapon that are -permanent-. There's not that many weapons in the game compared to some other shooters out there, but it comes at the cost of all the weapons being relatively balanced and even with that in mind there is still a solid variety of weapons to choose from. The choice of the weapon you use is almost always dependant on your preference via aiming patterns, recoil, rate of fire, etc. Whatever suits your playstyle. The currency gains had me worried at first, though the following week I decided to give it another go and check out the weekly missions and all of my concerns were alleviated. On top of the traditional SP guage that fills up gradually as you play (some of you may remember from Soldier Front 1), the missions grant you these capsules which grant you items, currency, and different cosmetic things as well. You can win up to 1,000,000 SP from a single capsule. After playing for only a couple of hours, I was able to buy two different weapons and have SP left over.
A couple of things to note before you read the pros and cons, is that Soldier Front 2 does not offer weapon customization like other games may include such as Call of Duty, or A.v.A. or Combat Arms, instead it offers 5 slightly altered versions of the weapon you are using that you may purchase. For example, say you started with the AK-107, you will start with a basic version of the weapon. As you gain more kills with it, at certain intervals (75, 150, etc. as examples, not actual numbers) you will unlock AK-107 Version 2, which will be the same weapon with an increased rate of fire at the cost of some firepower. Later versions offer similar give and take versions, such as more fire power at the cost of rate of fire, or magazine size at the cost of weight as you get more kills with that weapon. While this does not seem as creative or fun as some other games, what you result in is a very balanced weapon progression system that ensures competitive gameplay across the board. I prefer the competitive nature of the game at the cost of pretty weapons, all day every day. If tinkering with guns is your thing, I would suggestion Blacklight: Retribution anyway.
The other thing to note is that headshots are REWARDED. The hitbox for the head in this game is NOTABLY smaller than in other shooters. This will be plainly obvious for you to see, but you are rewarded for taking those shots! Spraying into someone at a distance may cause your rounds to be scattered and it may feel like they're just super tanky and you can't do anything to take them down, but one shot to the head and they are gone. The difference is very noticeable, aiming for the head becomes a second nature while playing this game. What you're thinking might be "Oh well I always aim for the head, this means nothing!" and that's what I thought too, but because of the smaller hit box you will find yourself trying to squeeze those headshots in as much as possible. The feeling I get when playing this game is that I have to be very cautious with shot placement, none of that "3 shots in the leg woops you die!". This may or may not be appealing to some, while it doesn't exactly get any points for realism it gets huge points for competitive play.
Pros:
-Solid game play
-Varied game modes, including PvE content
-Very competitive
-Rewarding weekly missions/objectives
-NO requirements to join a "Corps" (clan/guild)
-Huge improvements over the first Soldier Front
-Balanced weapons
-Great currency earning rate, if you work for it
-Shares similarities with Call of Duty
Cons:
-Once you hit a certain k/d ratio, you will be kicked out of the newbie channel -permanently-
-Open channel may be discouraging at first, veterans and newer players alike
-No health regeneration
-You do have health points and armor points, like older FPS games such as Counter Strike. May not be appealing for some.
-Virtually no weapon customization, may turn some away
-Shares similarities with Call of Duty
I hope you took the time to read this review before you consider playing this game, and I hope that it helped paint a picture for some of you that may be trying it out for the first time! Keep in mind that I have played just about all of the popular free to play titles out there, I won't say all because that's a bit cocky and I'm sure I haven't. The titles I mention include Planetside 2, Combat Arms, A.v.A., Wolf Team, Counter Strike, Operation 7, Gunz, and several others.

From the Depths is a complex building game with quite a bit of a learning curve. However, putting in the time required to understand its intricacies will be rewarded, as the building system offers an enormous range of possibilities. The game includes variety of weapons and defensive systems, which need to be fed with ammunition and power, which are in turn produced by ammo factories and engines using materials and fuel, and all that combines with the game's detailed physics model to make tuning a vehicle into the perfect war machine a satisfying engineering challenge.
As regards to the game's Early Access status, I will say that, as of this writing, the game continues to be updated at a blistering pace despite having been perfectly playable for a long time already. The developer solicits feedback from the community frequently and communicates actively. Since the start of Early Access, the development team has been expanded using the funds gained from sales. The project hasn't yet exhausted its ambition, either, as more major additions to the game are still coming - to name a few, support for modders adding their own building blocks into the game is in the pipeline as of this writing, and a detailed detection and stealth system is being planned.

Best $20 you will ever spent. I have spent over 120 hours just on building viable ships for the campaign. That is more time than I spent on Fallout 4.  I have not even touched the campaign fully because I do not have all the vehicles I need to succeed. If you are a little OCD, you will be obsessed. There are 3 main downsides:
Balance is a little up in the air at this point of development. The ships that are your enemies are community made and take advantage of every exploit and imbalance currently present in the game so you will have to build at the highest possible level to make ships of equal size competitive.
Second, the AI requires quite a bit of tweeking to have them handle and fight effectively. If you plan to build anything more advanced than a ship, i.e. airships, spaceships, submarines etc. You will have a huge hurdle working with automated control blocks to have them works correctly.
Third, if you want to build a non-boat and have it be competitive at the higher block count, be prepared to spend 30+ hours just building a functional, beautiful vessel. You place blocks two at a time with mirroring and to create something of real substance, that is attractive, be prepared for a very, very steep learning curve. Just optimizing one cannon can mean 3+ hours of work. Luckily, there is support for prefabs that you can copy and paste onto the ship. As well, turrets can be copied and pasted as well, but learning the intricacies of making sure they rotate correctly, or are capped correctly, etc is a hurdle to learn.
In summation, I have to be very controversial and say that this is a game is on the level of something like Dwarf fortress in possible complexity.  You will have to place many hours to master it. Even after all the hours I have played, I am looking forward to unleashing my perfectly tuned creations on all of the factions of NETER.
Happy Hunting,

Star Crawlers is a first-person dungeon-crawling RPG with rogue-like elements and turn-based combat, set in an environment that is somewhat unusual for the genre, namely in a cyberpunk setting. The entire game, including story missions, takes place on a series of space ships and stations, to which we can get access through the main hub – kind of similarly to how Darkest Dungeon handles things, and the similarities, however faint they might be, don't end here.
Just like Darkest Dungeon, the game can be loosely divided into 2 sub-sections: the hub area, where you can hire new crawlers and upgrade your gear, as well as take new assignments, buy new equipment and auction off the rare things that you've found previously, manage your relations with numerous corporations, and progress the main story, which I'll talk about later.
The second section, that makes up most of the game, is actual "crawling" – heading to missions (either pre-programmed or randomly generated), fighting enemies and looting, and, in general, making use of all the resources you've spent upgrading your heroes.
Arguably the most important thing that you can do in between the missions is managing your heroes. There are at least 8 playable classes (7 available from the beginning) with 2 gender variations for each one, each one with a unique set of abilities, divided into 3 different upgrade trees (usually grouped by some sort of attribute), which lends each hero some degree of diversity and allows them to synergize with any other one. I am not sure if you can hire any of them more than once, since I don't really know how this game handles characters' deaths (haven't lost a single party member in 37 hours of playing), but they are definitely not as disposable as in aforementioned Darkest Dungeon.
Even though the roles are defined very loosely thanks to the different upgrade trees, every crawler has a set of specific uses on the battlefield (healing, control, debuffing, etc.) that should be taken into consideration when creating party compositions, since you can only send out 4 at a time.
Aside from having a different role in combat, every class also has a number of things they can do while exploring. Ran into a locked door? Let your Hacker deal with it. Found an impressive-looking gem? The Smuggler will know how to estimate its value and where to find a customer. Some of these require an ability check (with success chance depending on how much you have invested in a certain skill tree), while some just require that you have a character of a certain class in your party.
There are many more examples of such interactions, and even the most boring heroes (like, say, the Soldier) have something to do outside of combat,
in story missions, all of which consist of hand-designed puzzles and encounters. It's also worth noting that your party members can all take part in conversations (appropriately to their characters) and try to influence your decisions during the main quest.
Unlike most games of the genre, Star Crawlers actually has a main quest, giving the player a goal and a purpose for completing missions and finding better equipment, so that it's not just grinding for the sake of grinding. What makes it even better, this game has a non-linear story with a number of choices to make and a few major players to side with. The dialogue is pretty well-written (there is a typo every once in a while, but it's not a big deal) and captivating, the choices are meaningful (or seem to be so), and the story missions themselves are well-crafted, with (rather simple) puzzles to solve, secrets to find and bosses to defeat.
Another thing that can keep most rogue-like players going is loot. You can find a variety of different weapons and armor types, some of which are more suitable for certain classes, playstyles and party compositions, during both main and side missions. And upgrading your gear is absolutely crucial, since the enemies will become tougher as you level up, and most of your abilities scale with weapon damage. It is also worth noting that all at the start of combat you are taken out of the tile-based map and placed on a separate arena, so avoiding all enemy encounters is also not an option.
So, in the end, we have a pretty solid game in an unsusual setting, with a fun tactical combat, high replayability due to procedurally generated content and a non-linear story, interesting exploration thanks to character interactions, and an overall great and addicting gaming experience. If you are a cyberpunk fan or are just looking for a rogue-like to play, you should definitely give Star Crawlers a closer look.

The classes feel a lot more balanced, enemies in different areas feel a lot more distinct compared with EA, which did suffer a little from "same stats different model" that a lot of dungeon crawlers struggle with.
If i have to level a criticsism, it would be that a lot of the new systems are very poorly demo'ed by the tutorial now. As an example, hacking seems to have had a complete rip out and replace (no more thor freya and loki T.T) and the auction functionality completely confused me when the 2 tutorial items you can auction had no bidders. A simple text pop-up explaining the need for a hacker/autociphers, and how auctions work would be fantastic for both of these.
Finally, it is fantastic that this game will run on my potato of a laptop. I deeply appreciate the lack of "spec creep" that plagues some other early access games, rendering them unplayable to me after a while.
I am deeply excited to see what you guys do next!

It seems like this game hasn't gotten a lot of attention for some reason, and only a couple of hundred reviews for something that was in pre-release and now released seems very low for something this good.  I'm writing a review because it just seems like it's under-appreciated.  It's actually an excellent game.  The combat system feels polished, and has a good balance of complex mechanics without requiring spreadsheets and doing a bunch of math between each turn.  Standard difficulty isn't too easy, but it's not too hard either - as with most good RPGs, you can also adjust the difficulty level by grinding more between storyline missions.  Which is to say, you can continue with the storyline without much grinding for higher difficulty, or grind more and level way past where you need to be to continue the storyline and make it much easier.  This is good because if you get stuck, you can just go back and adjust some things or grind out some more exp/gear.
Gear and other drops use the now-common WoW/Borderlands color scheme - grey -> white -> green -> blue -> purple -> orange.  There's plenty to go around, and the likelihood of being underequipped seems pretty low, but you need to put at least a little bit of thought into your builds on standard difficulty setting.
There's a "reputation" system with a bunch of different factions that seems very coherent - if you decide to play an altruistic character, you'll probably have high rep with the citizens advocacy group, but not many others... if you go with a completely amoral character who just pulls down cash, you'll make friends with the corps who are paying you and enemies of the ones they're paying you to go after.  It all makes sense and works out pretty well, but you have to sometimes pay attention to it if you want to make the most of the system.
One thing I've noticed is that you can reset a lot of stuff by saving and reloading.  For example, when you check the jobs board, if none of the available jobs allow you to further your interests the way you want to, then you can pay some cash to wait for the next day and a new set of missions.  Or you can just save and reload from the title screen.  This also impacts terminals and other hack-ables.  There're a solid handful of things you can do with terminals but it seems like the game doesn't decide until you touch it, so if you save, attack the terminal, find it's not what you wanted, and then reload, you can try again and perhaps get the terminal you wanted it to be.  This obviously doesn't work with "iron man mode" which limits you to a single save file, auto-save only, and prevents you from retconning anything.  Some people like to play that way, I guess.  So if you don't want to be able to do this, there's your solution.
Anyhow, if you like RPGs in general, you'll probably enjoy this game.  I'd never heard of it prior to the release and it appearing on the steam store front page under new releases, but it's very much worth a look.

Pretty atmospheric dungeon crawler, the writing is good compared to a lot of diff. titles. You control a small band of mercs, doing missions for coin, looting escorting stealing killing stuff. Slowly gaining the love or hate of various factions. Eventually they pit against each other and you'll be nudged to take sides. The art and sounds are pretty good, basically reeking of shadowrun but with their own style. The combat/item systems are smooth, with high spd animations turned on combat feels like a breeze. It's got one of the best wheel-command UI i've ever seen. None of that JRPG up down A + B ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. You click and drag and its done. The dungeon crawling is like Etrian, but you can click things to interact like a puzzle game.
It's not a perfect game. It's got its kinks. Sometimes combat freezes and you'll have to load a save file that was two hours ago. Sometimes some characters, abilities get stuck and you'll have to load a save. But given that it's fun one can overlook these things. You can always head over to discussions and put in a bug report. The devs are very responsive.
I personally didn't like the overall power-balance. Some ability branches are useless to me so far (maybe on a second playthrough and enough levels will allow it to come together nicely). The item system is rng-ish. A hammer with good stats could be wasted if it didn't get good "Latent effects".
Overall, it's very good for its price and a very fun title coming into the dungeon crawler genre. It's atmospheric, witty dialogues, brisk combat will have hours and hours of fun for you.

"Dungeon crawler in space" already sounds good, but any fan of games like Legend of Grimrock and the battle screens in Child of Light, or really ALL point and click turn based rpgs, will be right at home here, and if you are a fan of sci-fi you'll be stoked about the premise and environments. I was very excited about this game - with a name like "Sid Meier" on it, and coming on the heels of Beyond Earth, I was hoping (Oh, how I was hoping) for Civilization in Space. Colonizing planets, building fleets, etc.
What this game has is far too simplistic. As far as I can tell you only get one fleet, and it's mostly doing "missions" at stars which are already colonized and winning their influence over to your federation. The combat might turn out to be interesting... but that's the most interesting thing the game has to offer. When they called it "Starships", they meant it - Starships, and just that. Maybe they should've called it "Starship Combat".
The plot is interesting, and there's a skeleton that could hold up a nice, robust game, but it's just not here. I've read reviews that indicate it seems like a tablet game that was just stuck onto PC, and I have to agree. We need more in a PC game, especially from a brand with the playability-and-depth we've come to expect from Sid Meier and Firaxis.
I still hold out hope that maybe an expansion - or a sequel? - will add some depth to this game. I only paid about $25 for both Beyond Earth and this game in a sale bundle, so I suppose I got my money's worth, but it doesn't feel like it.
I guess if I want my space-based empire-simulator, I should just fire up Master of Orion 2 from 1996; nobody has really done it that well since. (I think I still have my copy, actually...)

for individuals who are easily offended and question anyone's morality upon playing this game.
It's tough to decide how this game should be reviewed or even suggested to
curious if it's either a product of shock value or ironically an escape from reality to virtually descend into madness as the protagonist. There's many risks this game takes and a lot of it is deeply horrifying. The experience of portraying a fictionalized serial killer with little to zero likable traits or an explanation of his madness aside from creepy diary highlights is more alienating than exciting. It's as if the developer wanted audiences to truly experience being a heartless murderer while leaving slim reasonings why the seemingly corrupted society the protagonist lives in should perish.
The game deliberately descends into paths that would disgust and infuriate individuals that are struggling to cope with actual mass murders, loss of beloved ones from serial killers, or being the victim living their final moments facing their killer. There's certain sequences that are outright presented in ways that may appear uncanny or grotesque even the lowest denominator of society would have many questions about. It's an experience that tests your moral values with limited survival tactics, recycled stages, tedious difficulty settings, and moderately fulfilling replay value upon completion. Whether this game was intended to be a satire, or the ultimate test for an individual's personality traits, there's no doubt that it will forever be known as that classic arcade murder simulator that literally had more guts.
Even with all of the chaos, whether it'd be openly senseless or darkly comical, I only recommend this solely for its honesty.

Opening caveat:  I am not traditionally a person that plays Tower Defense games.  This is in fact my first one.
To get right to the point of it...I loved the game.  If the name wasn't a dead giveaway, the game has a silly, lighthearted tone to most of it that, when combined with the creative ways you can inflict mass orc genocide (some favorites being hurling them by the packs into bottomless chasms with a well timed gust of wind and launching them ragdoll-style for their afternoon lava bath), leads to plenty of destructive catharsis.
While you can play all the missions single player...the game is at its best (IMO) when played with a friend.  Many a map benefits heavily from having a second mind on hand to help combat the games challenges, and with co-op your individual action bar is halved so it emphasizes working and planning together.
The missions also reward player skill with the main currency of the game, skulls.  Doing things like beating a mission within a certain time limit...not letting anyone through your defenses...and even "hidden" bonuses like not using mana or not taking damage all reward you with additional skulls after the level.  If however you're not that great at pulling things off that way, levels can be farmed repeatedly for unlimited skulls so you aren't punished harshly.
In conclusion...recommended.  Get a friend...get some chips...and get killing.

Whispering Willows gets a big approval from me. I don't know about the other people that have played the game till now but the haunting music of the game really shoved horror under my skin. In this game you play as Elena. A young little girl that is looking for her missing father. You learn while playing the game that he disappeared when he was working at the Willows Mansion. As the game progresses, you'll need to find clues which will show you what happened with him and where he went exactly from there. While doing that, you'll get to do unspeakable things, like talking to ghosts, transforming yourself into one of them or even resolving a lot of puzzles.
The core concept of the game is that you're capable of leaving your body to another realm through the amulet which you've received from Elena's father. In which you can communicate with spirits, possess objects or even get scared of demons. The story it's very interesting as it’s one of the game’s strengths. And if you want to get the full access of it, you'll have to read all the notes that are scattered around the map. These notes are well-written and help bring the game to life. While there is nothing forcing the player to read the notes, to neglect them would be to skip the entire message of the game.
The game also does an interesting job at delving into the Native American folklore, which was interesting to see unfold through the course of the game.
- Support for Achievements and Trading Cards.
- Haunting music which fits to the game, creating an atmosphere and ambience that you would rarelly get from an adventure game. The sound is good too, there are some good ambient sounds in the environment. The game is not fully voiced but the character's groans and sounds work well within the game.
- Auto-saving system. You'll have all your progress saved everytime you enter a new room.
- Beautifully drawn artwork, I really like how hard they've worked on the design of the characters.
- Nice unique concept that will keep you tied to the game.
- If you're an achievement hunter, you'll love this one from the bottow of the heart. The achievements are easy to find and get a 100%, though some are hidden and might require you replay the game, but even so, it's a fun game to play.
- Around a few hours of delights.
- You will get to know some pretty interesting and macabre stories about the people who once used to live at the Willows Mansion.
- A lovely puzzle design that's not very challenging, I can promise you that you will not rage while playing this nice game.
- You have an awesome supernatural power!
- The graphics are very nice! Nice lighting effects matched with textured objects. Unique rooms, interesting sights, the style the game has it's definitely one of the best elements.
- No support for Steam Cloud.
- You don't have a map which can tell you where are you in the game. You'll find yourself lost and frustrated a couple of times if you're a scatterbrain like me.
- Slow movement that drags the game down, it feels a bit strange.
- There are enemies into the game, but they're so few and far between.
This is a great game for those who are into adventure games. And the game it's not even very challenging, you can relax while playing it and it has something for almost everyone within it's content. I cannot recommend it at it's full price due to the short length. You can actually finish it in less than 4 hours, but if you'll find it in a sale, don't think anymore about it, just purchase it. Whispering Willows blends elements of puzzle, visual novel, and point-and-click games which it's unique and satisfactory. While the gameplay may be a bit simple, the game compensates with the complex story and good artwork it has. Whispering Willows gets an 4.5/5 from me.
