Finished a run in 27 hours.
Pro:
- Well written, coherent branching plot with around a dozen story missions (maybe half a dozen different endings)
- All the classes play differently and have a bunch of interesting abilities that react with each other in interesting ways
- The reputation system is good, there's liasion officers for the megacorps you ally with and "we'll kill you!" spam from your enemies
- Exploring the different locations is fun and the various security measures and easy-to-miss loot keeps you on your toes
- UI is clear and easy to use
Con:
- There's only so many enemy types and combat encounters could benefit from being less common but harder (no 1-droid encounters at least in late game please)
- Even on Challenging combat can get way too easy with abilities that confuse, stun or taunt the enemies
I enjoyed my playthrough a lot and recommend the game, but anybody starting their first game should take a moment before to think before choosing the difficulty as that can't be changed afterwards.

Really an awesome, awesome game.  I picked up the title back in Early Access as it looked pretty cool and promised to have a Firefly meets Shadowrun feel to it.  For the cheap price, I got more than my money's worth out of it.
The combat is fun and strategic, and most classes can cover a few of the standard archetypes through clever utilization of abilities.  The different corporations that you can work for have a bit of depth to them (Not a novel, but for the playtime they each feel to them and benefits for working with them).  I was actually surprised at the story and world, for the genre, it was really well fleshed out.
My only minor gripes are that New Game+ is kind of a silly option, as levelling past the cap of 30 doesn't do too much for your character when you can only use a small pool of abilities at a time.  In addition, some of the later levels lack some of the fun interactions (secrets and puzzles) of the earlier missions, and become a lot more linear.
Bottom line, if you like the old Dungeon Crawls like Might & Magic, or if you want an RPG with some strategy that can be picked up and put down easily, this is a great add to your library.

Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 is an entertaining, 12+ hour long action game with a few issues holding it back from greatness. It's a shlocky, hamfisted and (in my mind) enjoyable story focused on Dracula and his bloody escapades around his palace in two different timelines.
While not wholly divergent enough from the play-book of the first Lords of Shadow to call it a Metroidvania, Lords of Shadow 2 (LoS2) makes an admirable attempt at creating a fully explorable world which requires backtracking to old nooks with new moves in your arsenal to claim some doodad for your growing inventory of glowing crystal assistance-thingies. It's all very obvious and not particularly exciting, but it does reward you for your time and attentiveness.
You won't really need those 'hidden' rewards unless you're playing on the upper difficulty echelons. The combat is instantly recognizeable if you've played the first game. This year's model does come with improvements, weapon switching on the fly similar to DmC: Devil May Cry replaces the blue glow/red glow for essentially the same status effect, but with new combos to learn. There's also a fully adjustable camera, which is a pleasant new necessity (given the level design). Like the first Lords of Shadow, LoS2 has a deeper combat system than you might give it credit for at first appearance, it'll grow on you, but it doesn't go as far as some contemporaries and on all but the highest difficulties you won't struggle in battle.
LoS2 has a few obvious issues. While there's some goofy and entertaining narrative chunks to push you forward early on, there's also some sluggish tutorialization. The two timelines are enjoyable, but the past clearly has the art design edge- with the present not really distinguishing itself nearly as much. You'll probably greet flashlights with a weary sigh as the signal in another easy, brainless stealth section that, conceptually, is used to break up the monotany of entertaining flashy combat and brisk level design. Yeah, great idea.
At the end of the day, Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 is a likeable sequel. It's self-aware, in many aspects, with fantastic options like 'Turn off QTEs' which I highly recommend, as well as boasting satisfying boss encounters. It unfortunately struggles with branching out and exploring new gameplay elements. The pacing could be tighter... But, that said, I had a lot of fun with it. There are some great sequences, great moments that play off of the crazy Castlevania Dracula power trip which make it easy to recommend to fans of the first game. When it's firing on all cylinders, it captures the essence of what so many people liked about the first.
It hits a lot more than it misses and is worth your time and money if you happened to enjoy the first. It runs great, looks great and is fun to play. While it didn't surpass my expectations, it met them.

Initially, definitely significant to mention is... *ahem*  F@CK NEGATIVE REVIEWS. Really now, many gaming magazines (see Edge #d0uche_detected) have underrated it... (4/10). Even "Octodad" or "The Banner Saga" got a higher score than LoS2... I can only assume that they were trying to elicit attention through these means... anyway --> TO THE POINT!
Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2, The Dragon Returns! :O \o/ Such a good game... but how come it has so many opponents this time, in contrary to its predecessor? lel.. Well, let's begin with the reasons I deem this game worthy of its money:
+ Gorgeous Graphics
+ Satisfying durance
+ Wide variety of actions, skills, collectibles, missions, enemies etc.
+ Very well contemplated and made plot (they have taken really good care of it), plus there is an awesome plot twist!
+ The combat mechanics (endless moves, powers and upgrades)
+ THE PROTAGONIST! Anyone who has played LoS 1, can definitely recall Gabriel being... uuhm... TOO QUITE! Honestly, he scarcely spoke, we knew almost nothing about him or his personality. Unlike that, this time, Gabriel (or what is left from that♥♥♥♥♥♥ starts to reveal who he really is, his character, his desires, and generally he now IS appropriate for a protagonist. (Moreover, his voice actor, Robert Carlyle, has done an undoubtly good job "incarnating" dracula)
+ Yup, MANY stunning bosses ^^
+ The soundtracks ;3 (♥♥♥♥♥yaeh)
....But, there is always the other side...
- A number of fans maintain that they face several problems (like the game can't start, or gets stuck at a certain point of the game). Also, in spite of the aforementionted problems, EVERYONE may face glitches (small or B I G ones)
- It could become monotonus at some point, especially when you get to roam the same area over and over again...
- The enviroments you play in... (yeah it's a whole new era, and yeah no more majestic forests etc., BUT, it is the plot that demands that! You are no longer Gabriel, but a creature of the night, you live in the 21st century, you can't move with the sunlight. The very game itself has "darkened". This is the reason some fans don't even consider this "negative" point at all, while others miss the old castlevania enviroments)
- Despite the fact that there are many boss battles, some of them end really quickly, and it is not that difficult to understand how to defeat them.
- There are TOO many (and a bit complicated) moves in the combat system, that you just don't have time to remember, use and make good use of them (some are just beautiful and expensive, nothing more, nothing less)
- The final boss battle... (relatively short and easy to cope with)
To sum up, this game has both various advantages and disadvantages. But I would still recommend you to purchase it, it is really stunning, fun, and worthy of your time. Yeah, it is true that there are some disturbing drawbacks, but the advantages still surpass them.

I bought this for my daughter and we played together, seeing it in the steam xmas sale. I'm not really sure who it is marketed at. As a hard core gamer, there was little to hold my interest (but then I didn't expect there to be) however it held my 7 year old daughters attention for a about 2 hours before she lost interest due to hard to reach items, collected cats disappearing for no obvious reason and ultimately boredom trying to find items.
The basic premise is a 3rd person cat "simulator" in which you search for fish icons, cat icons and bizarrely, a ninja lady with a golden fish which really makes no sense in the context of the game.
The graphics are reasonable, not sure if assets or not, but there are some strange inconsistencies like super shiney, realistic cars but then cat models with cartoon eyes that looks it's fur is wrapped in clingfilm with an odd shadowing effect. I'd forgive it if you didn't spend all of the time looking at the cat in game. Similarly, realistic rabbits yet a cartoon cactus that follows you around with an annoying boing boing noise. Funny for about 2 seconds and then simply annoying for the rest of the level. The overall presentation is nice.
The tutorial is confusing. After collecting the fishes, cats and ninja lady, there appears to be nothing else to do. The game needs to prompt you to go outside as the next objective to end the tutorial is out of sight and far from obvious for a child.
I assume the music is stock as I've heard at least 2 of the tracks on multiple youtube videos. Its not out of place in the game if you didn't know and not offensive.
Controls are clunky and clumsy (my daughter used Xbox 360 gamepad). There is no precision on the jumping and the trampoline items are luck rather than skill. Controls are perhaps the biggest bug bear and needs significant improvement.
The levels appear well designed at first, but don't have any obviously boundary limits, they just respawn you if you go outside of the limits. This frustrated the hell out of my daughter who wanted to go to the house accross the street in the 2nd map, but just kept respawning everytime we reached the middle of the road.  Also, the kittens cannot go underneath cars (whoever heard of cats NOT going under parked cars!)
Other bugs(?) which frustrated:
Kittens fell through the floor and got stuck in furniture, especially when respawning from a map limit.
Collected cats sometimes dissappeared for no obvious reason, with the count falling from 8 to 2 on level 2.
Cats on sledges in the first level were not responsive when either next to or on the sledge, it was not obvious if these were collectable or scenery.
Unreasonable delays on menus, game appears to freeze.
My daughter chose to call her cat "Banana Splits", the length of the name messed up menu buttons and disappeared off the title screen.
If the game was early access, I've give it a tentative thumbs up but as completed game, I cannot recommend due to the clumsy control, invisible map limits, buggy cat collection and ultimately, limited appeal. There is some stuff to like here, but a lot to improve.

I'm reviewing two games here. SiN, and SiN Episodes: Emergence. SiN comes with the latter, and Steam opens the Emergence review page regardless of which one I try to review. I'll comment on SiN first: It's not awful, but it's definitely not for me. I reached a vault door with two sentry guns that killed me, and I couldn't progress. I hadn't seen a vault code earlier, trying every combination possible didn't seem to work (though I was getting shot by two sentry guns while trying combos, so it's possible I goofed), and I'm fairly certain that I went through every door and other area in the level, and had found no codes or keys, despite being sure to look carefully at desk areas in particular, in case a key might be hidden there.
That was bothersome, but what was just as bad or worse were the graphics. You might think I'm spoiled by modern times, but I beg to differ. I would prefer this game have graphics like Doom 1992, Blake Stone, etc. The problem with these kinda-early 3D games was that everyone wanted their game fully 3D, even if it was ugly. Final Fantasy VII, I'm looking at you. That game is
. People will likely hate me for saying it, but I won't lie or be blinded by any kind of nostalgia. Just because 3D was there doesn't mean it was ready to be used by some developers just yet. The first Half-Life worked well enough with 3D, even if it was unattractive, but that's probably the only older 3D game I can think of before like...Aliens Vs Predator 2 came out, that had 3D graphics that I didn't find grotesque to look at. I just preferred the old Doom sprites' quality animation to the abominations that were early 3D graphics.
Secondly, with SiN Episodes: Emergence, I'm not going to choose not to recommend this game because the other episodes didn't come out. I'm going to not recommend it because it doesn't feel like a small game of its own. What do I mean by that? You may not like the Half-Life 2 Episodes, or the Telltale The Walking Dead episodes, or even the Telltale Sam & Max episodes, but look at them as an example of how to end something. Even if there's a cliffhanger, and even if the game was really short, it feels, at least to me, like a full, small game.
SiN Episode: Emergence, to me, at least, never felt like a full gaming experience that could stand on its own. Of course, this is purely subjective, but I could play through HL2 Episode 1, on its own, not play Episode 2, and feel like I got a full experience. Same with Episode 2, even with the kinda-cliffhanger ending. Sure, I'm a little butt-hurt that there's no Episode 3, but Episode 2 is pretty great. With this game, it ends, and I never once felt like I got a whole, small game, and I love short games since they don't monopolize my time.
To me, SiN Episodes: Emergence was unsatisfying for the most part, with only positive memories of the quasi-villain gal, Sinclare half-naked in a hot tub or something in a dream sequence I guess? You can look that up on YouTube if your curiosity gets the better of you. Also, I got stuck in the geometry of a short crate I touched near the very beginning of the game when fooling around for a few minutes just now, and died instantly. That's some shoddy design. I've completed the game on the disc version before Steam ever existed or right after its debut.

Like the Half Life Episodes, I'm going to not recommend this game on the fact alone that the episodes were not finished. But as for the game itself, the graphics are okay, not quite as good as Half Life Episodes.  The game takes a while to get going as well, there's a good 10-15 minutes it feels of exposition/running around before you finally get a gun in your hands, that sort of introduction doesn't really fly into today's game market I feel.
Gameplay wise, the player only has three guns with a primary and secondary mode in addition to a melee attack. This is admittedly very limited and the guns, being a pistol, shotgun and assault rifle are not particularly interesting.  The enemy variety is at times lacking with the bulk of the enemies being ordinary soldier guys of sometimes varying health with one of the three aforementioned weapons, in addition to that, we get some creepy crawly melee guys and some armored heavies.  In actuality the enemies do have some variety but most of the time it doesn't feel that way.  Gunplay is pretty solid, the guns are satisfying to use and the enemy animations when you take them out feel great.  They do try to add some new mechanics like, some noxious gas that gives you bullet time but I find it too fiddly to use. You'll also regain health mainly by medkits on the walls which can be refilled with medical-spray bottles, this works okay but can be fairly limiting and sometimes you have to search around for a refill.
I've played this through once years ago, and recently played through about 2/3rds of it again but gave up being on too high a difficulty. It does however highlight one of the problems with these older games is that sometimes you can find yourself in a difficult encounter and simply not have enough health to get through it. Oddly enough, this is the same problem that prevented me from finishing the original SiN as well.
So, on principle of not being a finished product (only one episode) I cannot recommend however if the price is right, knock yourself out.

Replaying this fills me with so much nostalgia.
Without contest the best RPG that was on the Gamecube, one of the best RPGs in general, one of the best Tales games, and one of the greatest games of all time.
So what makes Tales of Symphonia so worthy of these acclaims? Explaining that, unfortunately, spoils much about the story and what the Tales series in general is about. In short, imagine every JRPG ever, then imagine someone tearing everything about them all apart. Every stereotype about RPGs, from the character archetypes to their roles and premises eventually takes a turn on the chopping block, sometimes several. If the first ten or so hours feels like you're treading a very familiar ground if you've played ANY JRPG in the past 25 years... well, that's because it is. Don't let the bright colorful anime facade or the T-rating fool you. These games can get very dark while treading very complex and mature themes that most other games struggle to address; everything from racism, destiny, genocide, religion, idealism vs. cynicism, sacrifice, even what it means to be a hero. Once you get past the initial and mandatory buildup stage, the story is turned on its head, everything takes a turn for the dark, and you'll find yourself eager to play more to unfold more of the extremely rich story.
That is in essence what the Tales games are about, and Symphonia exemplifies everything the series stands for in one game that will take you upwards of 40-60 hours to play through, discounting New Game+ and the various sidequests and bonus bosses to beat, of which there are many, with a bit more added in the HD re-release that the Steam port is based off of. If you are a fan of anime, expect to find yourself saying "Hey it's that guy!" plenty of times throughout these games, with well known voice actors like Scott Menville (Robin from Teen Titans), Jennifer Hale (Femshep from Mass Effect among many, MANY others), Tara Strong (Twilight Sparkle from My Little Pony), Cam Clarke (Liquid Snake from Metal Gear Solid) and Crispin Freeman (Togusa from Ghost in the Shell) to name but a few from this game alone.
The downsides to this game mostly relate to its age. The combat system is about fourteen years old as of this review, with Symphonia being the fifth game of the now sixteen entry series and all of the improvements that came with it. The EX Skill system is a bit clunky and requires a LOT of experimentation and grinding entire playthroughs if you want to have the best EX Gem in all four slots for everyone and get 100% completion with all the titles, cooking recipes, figurines and a complete monster and item collection book. The skits, likewise, also suffer from Namco's old ambivalence towards localizing. The English skits are entirely unvoiced, but not the Japanese ones. On that note, the dubbing can be changed in-game, if you care about that sort of thing.
When it comes to the Steam release, it seems most of the problems that came from Namco releasing a rushed PC port have been resolved as of now. The biggest problem I end up having that isn't the 60 FPS debacle is when it comes to Colette's wings, which constantly shower particles in battle and chunk up my ancient computer, though this shouldn't be a problem for any computer from the past five years.
Symphonia is a must-have for any RPG library, and its release on Steam makes me eager to see if this sets a precedent for Namco to follow in Square-Enix's footsteps and start re-releasing all of their old Tales games onto Steam, particularly Abyss and Vesperia.

Postal is an isometric shooter with a horror-esque narrative developed by the infamous Running With Scissors and originally published by Ripcord Games in 1997. RWS were founded a year prior to Postal's release as a new company that would devote themselves to creating extreme and mature entertainment products, with some founding members having been previously employed at Riedel Software Productions, which focused on developing children's games. The Postal series has been panned by critics yet adored by fans for many years, with its dark satirical humor and graphic violence (contrary to the title, this is a series about seemingly unmotivated mass murder, not mail sorting). Postal was compared to Pulp Fiction by the late Bill Kunkel, veteran game journalist and game designer, as being just as much of a shock to video games as the Tarantino film was to the world of cinema. RWS definitely expected to attract some attention once the game's website went up but Vince Desi, CEO of 'the world's most dangerous software company' said the reaction to Postal and RWS had been overwhelming, sometimes funny, and even a little scary. The website
had drawn over 100k hits in less than a month, and while the numbers would be impressive for any new software-based site it's virtually unheard of for a game that was still in negotiations and not even available yet as a downloadable demo. Vince confessed losing his voice one week as he was on the phone constantly, talking to TV stations, magazines (both print and online) and all these incredibly interested users. 'Everybody wanted a Postal/RWS t-shirt' Vince reported, 'You don't see this much interest in games that are already on the shelves' he observed. 'Obviously, something about this product just hits a button with the public.' As for the response by the U.S. Postal Service and various media outlets, well, there's more to this fascinating history than I can fit in this review so if you're interested take a spin on the wayback machine.
The backstory according to
goes like this: Postal casts the user as a nameless surrogate character that is brought to the breaking point when his newly purchased home in the small desert community of Bisbee, Arizona is repossessed due to a trivial error in the escrow filing. However, when he comes to believe that the repossession is merely the tip of a demonic conspiracy intended to dominate humanity, he loses his sodding mind. The manual nor do the in-game intermissions between levels that consist of diaries and war journal entries by the Postal Dude (as he's been coined) himself ever state his personal background or what truly motivated him to go over the edge in the first place. But if the website is anything to go by, it definitely shows how satirical and over the top the game was always intended to be, despite the dark subject matter. Like Carmageddon, which might I add also came out that same year, in addition to the first entry in the Grand Theft Auto series. What a time to be alive as an adult gamer! What is speculated about the Postal Dude is that he's a tin foil-hatted paranoid delusional that thinks there's something in the air or water that's caused the population of this once peaceful fictional town of Paradise to turn into crazed killers.
The goal of the game is simple enough: kill or be killed. There's a percentage of hostiles killed on each level that must be reached in order to move onto the next scene. Hostiles consist largely of authority figures: sheriff, police, SWAT and eventually the military. Volunteers have also participated in the madness in the form of rocketeers, muscle-bound baldies and miners that throw explosives at you. And a bunch of weird turrets. Needless to say the cast is pretty 90's and rather cheesy at times, but that was probably the intention. It can cause a strange contrast between the unnervingly realistic portrayal of a mass shooting and the absurd things that happen throughout, like torching a marching band or ostrich farm. There's a number of defenseless civilians that populate most areas but these are never required to be killed in order to complete the level, only counting towards the population. There's a fair supply of health, Kevlar, weapon and ammo pickups littered throughout that will keep you going and even some minor secret areas. There's also an element of strategy to the gameplay, as enemies are often setup in defensive positions waiting for you to make a move and the whole guns blazing approach will not always suffice here. Plan your attack and divide and conquer or consider hitting the suicide key because it won't be much different if you just rush things.
Postal's world is unique looking, instead of 3D geometry with a limited set of textures the levels are all 2D backgrounds of highly detailed, painted scenes from an isometric camera angle (and sometimes a top-down perspective), which ensures every level doesn't look the same as the last. Low poly (very) 3D characters, weapons and objects are scattered about these scenes, complete with real-time lighting effects. An X-ray effect allows you to see through buildings you're behind, and there's a number of small details for things like spurting blood, bullet casings, and translucent fire and smoke effects and of course pools of blood that pile up quickly. Bodies also don't disappear, and people won't always succumb to their injuries, often dragging themselves across the ground leaving a trail of their life fluids while they moan and cry out in pain, quickly leading to some very macabre scenes of genocide. It's all very crude looking by today and it wasn't tipping any heads even back then either (well besides the violence), but for what they worked with as a small team they did a convincing enough job and managed to create an atmosphere, that to this day I still find very appealing. Incredibly disturbing and very raw in tone.
Weapons first consist of an unidentified assault rifle with unlimited ammo, a sawed off shotgun and some grenades and branch out to rocket launchers with heat-seeking missiles, a napalm launcher, flamethrower and the most deadly ballistics weapon in the game: the Spray Cannon, a fully automatic shotgun that turns even the most well armored foes to red swiss cheese. Throwables and more tactical options include Molotovs and three types of mine. You can also execute downed victims that are suffering and put them out of their misery with your machine gun or share the pain with others if you're on fire.
Visuals as stated earlier aren't pretty, but for what they are they capture a bleak look that I feel was kind of lost in the transition to more defined HD artwork in the Postal Redux released earlier this year. Loading screens have an acidic looking piece of abstract art that look like they'd burn your hand if you reached out and touched it, with eerily written dialogue by the Dude himself. Audio is a bit of a mixed bag admittedly, with some silly and often annoying voice-overs that play far too often, but everything else sounds pretty good, especially the screams. The voice for the Dude's 'demon' by Rick Hunter is well done and appropriately psychotic, but I wouldn't go about quoting his mean-spirited lines in public. The music, while limited and only playing on loading screens is very creepy and surreal, well composed and adds to the dark nature of the game excellently.
The downsides include the short length, antiquated controls, low quality visuals and some bizarre hit box detection at times. Grenades are hard to use properly and rocketeers can sometimes loop you in a neverending cycle of air time until you're out of their effective range, of which by then may be too late.
Postal's a flawed, underrated and sometimes truly scary game of the mid-to-late 90's before the world as we knew it changed post-Columbine. I recommend it to any open-minded action gamers. Just remember though, it's only a video game.

I was excited by the trailers and reviews for this game and was not disappointed in the slightest when I finally got to play it.
I've long been a fan of classic CRPG dungeon crawlers and Starcrawlers takes up that mantle proudly. The environments are fun to explore and create a great atmosphere, and they've gone a better than average job of making them feel like real places that have purpose.
The skill system is excellent. Each class feels very different than the others, and figuring out how to play them off of each other is a nice challenge.
The Diablo-like gear system does the job just as well here as it's ever done in Blizzard's games. You're rewarded for carefully choosing the right gear that works with your skills and party composition, and you're given plenty of options to work with so the decision isn't always straightforward.
Also I need to specifically call out how great the faction reputation system is because of the way it ties into many decisions that would otherwise be trivial. You're often offered rewards for the same objective by multiple parties offering different rewards and valuable loot always seems to upset someone. Instead of always ransacking the dungeon, sometimes you have to leave stuff behind to stay in an important faction's good graces.

I'm really enjoying Starcrawlers. I'm not super into dungeon crawlers but the futuristic setting drew me in. I like the simple, but immersive character creation. The graphics are cool and it's fun to explore the locations. There is a good bit of detail to the missions especially for procedurally generated dungeons. The puzzles are the right level of difficulty and add a nice bit of variety. The combat is fun and the classes all seem useful depending on playstyle. The thing that has really gotten me about this game is the writing and world building. The dialogue seems like it is out of a good sci-fi book. When I've had a special dialogue option as a result of my backstory, it's made my smuggler seem shady and smooth. Just like it should! Starcrawlers is a great example of a game that makes a well established genre feel fresh and fun again.

Whispering Willows gets a big thumbs up for me. I love the core gameplay mechanic that was chosen for the game. The mechanic is that you can press a button and your character transforms into a ghost-like form that enables you to get to places and solve puzzles that your full human form would otherwise be unable to do. Although it’s definitely not the first time that I have played a game that utilizes this form it fits the game like a glove here. It helps blend the puzzles and the story into a fascinating whole and ties the game together perfectly. This is aided by what Coke identified as a great atmosphere which I thoroughly agree with. The mood, ambience and everything that you would hope for an adventure horror game to be is at a high level.
The story itself is quite a reasonably told one. It’s one of the game’s strengths. It tells the story of a girl, Elena if you don’t change the name, who is on a journey to discover her missing father. In order to do so she will have to discover the many mysteries that haunt the Willows Mansion. The game starts relatively quickly which is a strong positive as it shows you receiving the amulet from her father which allows the core gameplay mechanic to come to life. I could delve into much deeper detail but I really don’t want to spoiler the game for you.
I would argue that the biggest problem with the game is the slow movement. I don’t understand why the developers made the decision for the character’s movement not to be smoother and quicker but it is what it is – arguably the games greatest problem. The other significant problem which can be argued either way is the lack of an in game map. I can understand that it was left out for exploration and perhaps even puzzle purposes but numerous times, particularly in the catacombs, I found myself lost and frustrated with where I had to go to get to where I was supposed to be. A map would have solved this issue. The puzzles themselves tend to be on the easier end of the difficulty scale and some will take issue with that as they may not feel that the game is rewarding enough. But given that we’re discussing a few relatively minor design choices to pick the game apart with I think that says a lot about the overall quality of the game. Though the sum of those negatives does add up, of course.
I recommend Whispering Willows for the adventure fans out there. The horror is on the lighter, less scarier side which adds to the game rather nicely. The game can be played from the early teens onward and there is something for almost everyone within the content.

Luftrausers was a pleasant surprise. I started out with almost no idea of what the game was except for a few screenshots and mentions that gave it high praise.
The relatively unintuitive controls for flying around ended up being a thrill and give just enough direct control to make it feel like you really are narrowly boosting in and out of swarms of enemy fights. The catchy music and brown stain palette do an amazing job of creating an ‘against all odds’/WW2 dogfight game feel that also complements the insanity the game can throw at you sometimes. Moving from blasting fighters while freefalling to boosting away from a mass of projectiles, waiting for your ship to repair, before you boost right back into the crowd feels exhilarating.
The customizations are interesting ways to keep you entertained while you complete mini-objectives but they can seem pretty useless if you already have a preferred setup for your plane. Since the arcade-like nature of the game prefers to have you improve your skill, none of the customizations are straight upgrades and all have downsides but it helps to keep the game interesting over the long run, especially as you find uniquely volatile combinations for beating certain enemies or mini-objectives.
That being said, the enemy variety gets old rather fast and you can experience what feels like a majority of the game in only a few hours. This feeling is amplified after running out of do-able mini-objectives (dang some of them are tough/rare). It’s the same handful of remixes and 5 or 6 enemy types every round, and I don’t get the feeling that things really change after defeating the blimp (which almost never appears).
Still, it’s a captivating game for the first couple hours and is something you’ll spend a lot of time revisiting.

Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 has polarized its' audience upon release: while the game is mostly well received by the gamers, it's has been a subject to negative criticism by the game media.
So is Lords of Shadow 2 a worthy sequel?
There has been some changes since the prequel, some for the worse and some for the better.
Lords of Shadow 2's core element is the combat which is very smooth and features a free movement camera. Gameplay wise the arcadish mission selection approach has been replaced by an open world with transitions from the present, modern age  to the medieval ages.
There's also a stealth mechanics introduced in the sequel, which is largely criticized by many people.
But is this new feature really THAT bad? I think not, while it certainly breaks the pace of the game, the number and difficulty of these segments are LOW, that it shouldn't bother many people. And certainly not a reason not to play the game because of these parts.
That being said, this game is a very solid and entertaining entry in the franchise, which also concludes the Lords of Shadow trilogy!
- Graphics are gorgeous, and performance wise the game is very well optimized!
- Soundtrack is excellent, and so is the voice acting!
- The game design also well done in Lords of Shadow 2. This includes the architecture, level, creature and boss designs.
- Combat is easier, than Lords of Shadow 1, but still very satisfying.
- Boss fights are easier than Lords of Shadow 1, but at the same time very entertainining.
- Platforming segments are more fluent this time.
- Lot's of content and collectibles providing huge replay value.
- Due to the newly introduced open world approach, the arcadish level selection feature is gone in Lords of Shadow 2. This means boss fights cannot be replayed, unless you start a new game!
- While the story is good, the story-telling is not so coherent as it was in the last game.
- Some characters weren't introduced properly (lack of screentime)
- Xbox button prompts, and console HUD. This wasn't an issue in the prequel, so there's no excuse here!
- The difficulty decreased signifantly in all aspects. This includes platforming, combat and boss fights as well.
- Puzzle elements were mostly removed from Lords of Shadow 2. It's a pity, the prequel had some nice puzzles.

A 1080p video review of Sid Meier's Starships:
Sid Meier's Starships is a recently released light-4X turn-based strategy game. It takes a stab at integrating FTL-like space exploration, Heroes of Might & Magic-style combat, and minimal 4X strategy elements... but is extremely lightweight in all regards. This PC version is a mobile port that's seen less than the bare minimum amount of effort put into it: 30fps limit, no fullscreen, no graphics options (not even resolutions!), UI designed for touch devices & small screens, and dated graphics even by mobile gaming standards. The gameplay proved interesting for a few campaigns, but quickly fell apart.
See the video review above for more details - and some visual examples of what I'm talking about.
If you'd like to play a lightweight 4X space strategy on the go... then you might like the mobile version.
There's nothing here that should appeal to PC gamers with an interest in the genre on PC.
Despite its low price point there are
superior alternatives at even lower price points:
4X strategy in space: Galactic Civilizations 2, Sins of a Solar Empire, Sword of the Stars, etc.
Space exploration: Faster Than Light, Space Rangers, etc.
120Hz - No
60 fps - No, it's limited to 30fps
Fullscreen - No
Borderless Window - Yes, but badly implemented
Graphics Options - None
Texture Quality - Low

A great game I highly reccomend if you have time and patience. The game is still in alpha so expect some problems like somewhat poor graphics and a lot of lag during big battles. Although the developer is working on these.
FTD is essentially a building game, mixed with an rts, and an fps. Because of this the game is immensely complex. The greatest complexity comes from the building process, which will take a lot of time to learn. You will need to learn to build hulls, ai's, cannons, missles, and engines. Each one of these has different rules that detirmine what parts can be connected to what section, and these rules will force you to make decisions about your ships design.  This will be espicially true when you play campaign where resources are limited. You can even use LUA scripting in the game to give your vehicles or missles custom behaviours.
Because of the ability to build what you want, the rts like gamepley is pretty interesting. Like modern battles from the depths battles are often detirmined by range and the ability to gain intelligence on enemy movements is crucial to success. The ability to download units from the steam workshop also makes it possible to play the game without needing to design a ton of vehicles.
If you've ever wanted to design your own weapons and take them into battle, then ftd is a great game for you. Just realize that this game gives you a ton of design options and a lot of the possible designs suck. This comes from the games balancing that usually forces you to choose between multiple factors especially how big your willing to go.

This is the best zombie apocalypse, survival-type base management game to be seen ever. This is the most enjoyable replay-able video game I have ever played in over 40 years of personal video gaming. The main mechanic of the game is 'group survivor management'. It's you the player, controlling and taking part in the life and story of initially two friends who find themselves in the midst of a 'plague driven' apocalypse. The story progresses and you inevitably meet up with other survivors. Though you can choose to not follow the storyline to it's culmination, days or weeks of playtime later, it's well worth immersing oneself into the apocalypse and the story that unfolds.
You cannot lose in this game, on many levels it's about learning and having mostly mature fun. In this game you will learn to adapt and overcome in challenging gameplay. You will see some horror that may make you jump or avert your eyes and you will possibly unearth some pop culture references which should make you smile. There's plenty of humor though when interacting with survivors.
If a survivor dies, which is generally the fault of the player making a bad strategic or tactical or 'controller skill-based' decision, you still do not lose.
This game is enriching on so many levels, but primarily it will pose a question to you when you first experience a significant 'loss to the community'.
State of Decay is simply a  brilliant concept that many fans have desired to experience in a game, and thankfully we have a game company that listens to it's fans and gives them what they asked for and more of what they didn't, but are better off for experiencing.
The DLC's are some of the coolest game additions I have seen from any game developer, almost like complete separate games with more of what you didnt know you wanted. You really get your money's worth and replay-ability from Undead Labs.

Tales of Symphonia 2 when?

I will try to review as much as I can do, be objective if I can, and compare with other tales series if necessary.
For starter, I bought the game for only 25% of its original value, so it might affects on how well I am comparing it with those who bought it at original value (such as worth it or not by considering the price value).
Okay, let's get to the point now. There are criteria which I'd like to point out. Gameplay (battle system, controls, enemy encountering, world travelling, and dungeon exploring), storyline, music, and graphic.
GAMEPLAY
As you know, in tales series, the battle system is known as LMBS or Linear Motion Battle System. It is where your characters battle an enemy in a limited circular field with 2D motion (in a later series of tales, there is "free running" which makes it 3D motion but not in this game).
The control is not really that hard, but I'd really like it if the game is more... swift I guess? Basically, I had trouble when I need to turn the character to face off the enemy behind it. It kinda feels like lagging. But well, it could be solve by backstepping though (instead of turning back).
The rate for encountering enemy goes from up to down. When you reach a certain part of the storyline, the enemy encounter rate goes down to in dungeon only. I don't think its bad, you could just get bored sometimes by encountering too many enemy and just wanted to get on with the story. You don't particularly need to grind for level though, just by encountering the enemy in a dungeon naturally, you can beat the game even in hard mode (because I can, why can't you? XD).
If your gamer's calling tells you to play hard mode from the beginning, you might need to put a little effort on managing your item and money in the early phase of the game. I don't mean to brag, but I really made a sweat playing hard mode from the beginning because "game over" would be at any moment I am encountering an enemy. Although, because of this, I had fun (hahaha).
The world travelling in this game is driving you to have this "explorer's soul" in you is what I would like to say but not in my case. As the story progresses, I find it a little too linear, for travelling around of course (not the storyline). There is a possibility that one could get that "explorer's soul", but its based on one's own preference of course. For me, I would like it if I could travel around without progressing the story. Actually, I could, but at the same time, I don't know if I really get something travelling around randomly. Therefore, I would like it if there is a hint or a guide for that. For some people, maybe that's what "explorer's soul" is (lol). Well, in the end, I only travel around to find a new city and other than that is just following the story.
There is no better dungeon crawling that having a little bit puzzle in it. Yes, this game has it. It's not a dungeon where you just fought a monster, battle the boss, and the end of the dungeon. The dungeon exploring is really nice. It really gets me fired up and wondering what kind of puzzle will this next dungeon has.
STORYLINE
The storyline is... wonderful. Honestly, its hard to put a comment with the storyline. There is a certain part of the story that I feel a little bit lacking in expressing emotions but I can't discuss that because it would be a spoiler and I don't want that.
Each of the characters in ToS has its own role and circumstances. They don't make a character just to have a character. As for the main character, the development is pretty nice I would say. In the early part of the story, I got a few questions to ask for why does this character becomes the main character. It got resolved though in the later hours. The climax building is nice too. I don't really feel hanged in the end and pretty satisfied with how the story goes.
I do wanted to compare this with other tales series, but because I only played ToS and not the previous games before ToS, I can't do that. Why compare with the previous one and not the later one? Because the previous one is the things you could called the baseline for measuring how much improvement has been made. ToS was released in 2003, it might have been an achievement in and of itself at that time.
MUSIC
The music is nice. It knows the place well. For me, a nice pace of music is what makes the game flow. Although, it doesn't make me feels good enough to hear it OUTSIDE the game, not to the point where you desperately find a certain soundtrack just to hear it all day long.
GRAPHIC
A graphic is not only define by its quality. HD or not, a graphic is meant to represent what kind of place the game wants it to be, what kind of world the game wants to set. At least that is how I view it. For how well does the graphic does, it is nicely done I would say. Nothing too out of ordinary and well, its not discomforting my eyes.
I guess that's it for my review, I hope this review is useful for those who read it and thanks to those as well. Overall, it is WORTH it. For scaling purpose, I think I will give it 8.4/10. Any comment, suggestion, question, and critics are welcomed. Thank you.

POSTAL is a game developed and published by Running With Scissors (RWS for short). When POSTAL was released, it was deemed a controversial game due to its amount of violence towards the police and towards the innocent. Thankfully, RWS hasn't given up on their POSTAL series (except POSTAL 3, we will pretend that never happened) and has continued to develop and improve their games
So what is the best way to describe POSTAL?
If you heard of the not so recent game, also controversial, called Hatred. Which was a game about a person going rampage and shooting police and many innocent people. POSTAL is like Hatred, only better and more enjoyable
You play a simple guy called The Postal Dude and the main objective of the game is to shoot as many hostiles as possible (after 90%, you are free to go to the next level) which includes shooting police and many, many innocent people and also causing havok which is what made POSTAL fun and enjoyable
Now, I am not the type of person who is easily offended. I've played both POSTAL (and its redux version) and Hatred and wasn't offended, I watch the South Park series and played the South Park games and whenever I see things that other people get offended by, I don't. So I understand why the POSTAL series caused so much controversy but at the same time, I don't care
The game is much more dark than its sequel, and this was a shock to me as I watched so many videos of POSTAL 2 (and now I own the game) where you hit people and urinate on them whereas in POSTAL, it seems like Satan has taken over your soul and you just want to murder people. A huge shift in tone between the two games
The gameplay is that of any type of shooter. Shoot as many people as possible without dying. The controls for me were terrible, on a keyboard and mouse this game played terribly, however with a controller it played moderately well. The camera is that of an isometric perspective, meaning that the camera is of a top down perspective. The graphics are quite ugly in my opinion. The music is sick and twisted which I surprisingly liked and the voice acting by both the Postal dude and the innocent victims is good
To play POSTAL, you will need an open mind or someone like me who isn't easily offended and the game is certainly not playable for people who are easily offended. I would only recommend POSTAL and POSTAL Redux to people who don't mind the subject matter or people who are not easily offended, otherwise, steer clear away from POSTAL, POSTAL Redux or POSTAL 2
If you are interested in POSTAL, I would highly recommend purchasing the Redux version of it and ignore this version completely, however if you are like me and would like to complete the series, POSTAL isn't a bad game for the year it was made

I haven't played many Dungeon Crawlers of this style before: I think I only played Shining in the Darkness, some of the earlier Might & Magic games and Legend of Grimrock, so take my review as a point-of-view from someone relatively unfamiliar with the genre.
So far, I'm really enjoying this one, and I'm seeing a lot of potential for further enjoyment. By far the focus of the game is in the combat, and it's well-placed: the combat system is a turn-based CTB-style (a la Final Fantasy X, Atelier series, and others) that makes excellent use of the time-based mechanics. It also borrows some mechanics from MMORPG-style group content (like Threat and the way many support abilities work). Character progression offers different and interesting paths, it's really interesting to think of all the possible builds and party formations.
There doesn't seem to be an extremely vertical increase in power of gear, most of the loot is somewhat of a sidegrade instead of an upgrade, which means further customization instead of just equipping something that's objectively better.
There's an ingame codex that explain mechanics like shields, weapon stats and so on. Combat interface is pretty informative, allowing you to click on enemies for details and displaying a combat log (though I believe it could be improved, especially regarding summoned units).
All in all, I'm really enjoying all the tactical potential here. Easily recommendable.

Having followed StarCrawlers through Early Access I can now say it has become everything I had hoped for: It's an immersive dungeon crawler with a well made sci-fi setting, an innovative quasi-turn-based battle system and tons of fresh ideas.
The crawling takes place in both pre-designed maps (for story-quests) and randomly generated ones (for side jobs). While the pre-designed maps are more intruiging and have the more impressive settings, all maps shine with a great design of the environment. With widely varying room sizes, well crafted backgrounds and cleverly placed lootable items I'd put these maps on par with my previous favourite, the "Legend of Grimrock"- series.
The combat, however, is completely unlike the one in Grimrock. Instead of realtime combat there is a quasi-turn based combat system. Each attack or ability takes a certain number of time units, based on the ability and the weapon speed. This creates a timeline, depicting the order of action for both allies and enemies. This feature is well implemented into many abilities, (de-)buffs and status ailments.
There are so many more aspects of this game one could talk about: The varied classes with interesting skills, the reputation system, the black market mechanics, weapon upgrades and enhancements.... But that would take us far into TL;DR-territory.
So in short, I can recommend StarCrawlers to anyone who likes dungeon-crawlers (obviously) and/or RPGs. It's like Etrian Odyssey, only less tedious, with story, and you won't be killed by bunnies ;)

It has puzzles, but let's just say it's not trying to be Myst. It's not especially long... although I disagree with the reviews that rage about the walking speed. I felt that the speed was good, and helped me to really take in the atmosphere and feel some tension and danger. There's a story here, and the game ends properly when the story has been told.
I have to admit that, for the time I spent playing, I was fully absorbed in the little world that this game creates. It's not terribly ambitious... but it does a good job at what it tries to be. Overall I would recommend waiting until a sale, but if you enjoy atmospheric exploration, then Whispering Willows will likely be worth your time and money.

So, I JUST finished this game as I'm writing this, and I gotta say, I wasn't disappointed. This game walks a fine line between an adventure game about a young girl exploring a spooky old mansion, and a scary story told around a campfire, and does it quite well.
The story sucks you in. You play as a 13 year old native american girl named Elena looking for her father, who has gone missing some days earlier. The last place he was seen was the old mansion where he is groundskeeper. Investigating with a shamanistic power passed down from her ancestors (astral projection, I think), she finds that the history of the mansion, and the town she lives in, is darker and more sinster than she ever could have imagined. The story is told through conversations with the spirits that haunt the mansion, as well as diary entries Elena writes and notes found on the grounds. Fortunately, you don't have to look hard for the next piece of the story. I found them all in one playthrough.
The art was beautiful, from the cute little spirit form your character has, to the friendly but often times horrorific looking ghosts (Lets just say, it's usually very easy to tell how they died), to the set pieces of the rundown old mansion and its grounds.
Puzzles aren't difficult and usually consist of, go here, get item, take item there, get another item, etc., but this is dispersed between a few environmental puzzles, like using your spirit form to access rooms you couldn't otherwise get to, and a couple that require some thought/observation.
The music and sound effects were wonderful, setting the mood quite well. Creaking floors, thunder and lightining, ghostly whispers, haunting music, all made for an amazing experience that really helped set the mood.
The only gripes I have with the game are the length (But that's my complaint about almost any game I enjoy :p ), and the fact that Elena is apparently so well mannered that she won't run indoors.
All in all, if you want a short, but excellent story, you can't go wrong with Whispering Willows.

This is coming from someone who did not play the first Escapists game.
I purchased the game with pretty low expectations. The youtubers displayed a horribly bugged version many weeks before release, and I was not naive enough to think they would actually fix it in time.
I was right, but the game turned out to have more problems than expected. Instead of expanding THE SANDBOX with more cool stuff to do and cool ways to escape, the devs seem to have focused too much on scripted events.
To summarize what I mean: There are only a few SANDBOX-ways of escaping, called "Perimeter Breakouts". The rest of the escape types are SCRIPTED EVENTS. It means you stand on certain spots while holding certain items in inventory and press "E" and you autowin. This lowers replayability significantly.
• There are no workers who periodically take out trashbags or laundry you could hide in to later get picked up by trucks. Instead there is a scripted event on ONE spot in ONE of the prisons.
• There is no way to hide in boxes being randomly shipped in, around and out of the prisons carrying simulated supplies. Instead just ONE scripted event in ONE of the prisons.
• No way to bribe guards. Maxing their opinion of you does nothing.
• No way to get released for good behavioral achievements.
• No way to hack the security systems to remotely open doors.
Speaking of rooms. On your map you see many different rooms. There are control rooms, maintenance, wardens office and some others. "So exciting! I wonder you can do with those rooms!" I thought. Sadly, the answer is often "nothing". You can't do anything cool in most of those rooms. They contain cool doodads that you usually cannot interact with. Some contain lootable props.
• You cannot build teams or make friends in the social room.
• You cannot hide in the boxes in the maintanence room.
• You cannot shut down surveillance from the control room.
• The desks in the guard rooms seem to have the exact same loot as in the prisoner cells.
• You cannot do anything or loot anything in the wardens office, or even interact with the warden in any way.
But sadly, the disappointments don't stop here.
You literally can't interact with most NPC's other than guards and prisoners. You can't talk to them. You can't punch them. You can't bribe them. You can't do anything with them. They are decorations. Even the warden is just a decoration walking around.
And then there is the crafting. At first sight you seem to have many different crafting recipes and abilities to make lots of cool stuff. To be fair, yes there are some fun SANDBOX stuff in there, but many of the recipes are pretty much useless except for certain jobs and the above mentioned scripted events. Like, why craft a "cup of tea" when you can't even consume it? Give it to a guard or prisoner to get an arbitrary achievement and raise their opinion of you by 10ish points? You could just give them some random raw materials instead for a better result.
To summarize my opinion of this game:
+ Has hardware mouse / raw input.
+ Pretty fun sandbox and good for quite a few hours.
+ Working towards and getting that escape can be exciting and satisfying.
+ Nice graphic style.
+ Fast updates have fixed many of the technical issues by day 3.
- DAY 1 DLC - This is commonly frowned upon for many reasons. Look it up.
- Season Pass - An insult to your playerbase. The Steam store information states "The Escapists 2 Season Pass will feature 3 brand new prisons to be released over the coming months".
It also means you have not paid for the full game (which can be considered fine, but still a negative). But it further implies the devs will spend development time during the coming months on releasing MAPS instead of improving the actual sandbox, which would improve ALL maps simultaneously and increase DEPTH.
- Game somewhat lacks depth and tries to hide this by adding a bunch of scripted events.
- Game was released in an unfinished and heavily bugged state. It would need alot more development time to feel solid.
- Game has some subjectively bad design decisions, such as the stat system, or the non-flexible (non-sandboxy) job-system.
- The "transport prisons" are basically short mini-missions. They somewhat inflate the advertised number of prisons. They can also only be won through scripted events.
-  The game has issues with stuttering.

Where do I start?
The goal here was to improve upon on a good game that many claimed to be a "God of War" clone. Which it had similarities, sure, but to call it a clone is blasphemous. In fact, it possessed many qualities that made it superior even. The story, and acting was much better, for instance.
The original had so many things going for it, and I for one, thought the fixed camera really showed you how beautiful the environments were. Lush forests, large abandoned temples, etc. Those things are replaced by castle, and rainy, dark alleyways. Not much variety there.
The gameplay itself suffers from the new and 'improved' camera system. I feel like the fixed camera was done away with because we're sitting here saying to ourselves "It's 2014, we're past this. Resident Evil was frustrating." The truth is, it functioned very well in LOS, and you didn't have to fight that while also fighting swarms of enemies. That's the real issue with the new camera. You have a very claustrophobic point-of-view, and can't admire the environment even if it was really a sight to behold.  In fights, it backs out a little, but sometimes getting caught in an awkward corner and trying to manuever the camera while unleashing a planned combo at the time is not very fun. It turns making a well-timed block into a "I can't see if the enemy is attacking" kind of fight.
The other issue is the story. The ending of LOS set the bar very high for this game, which is a little unfair, admittedly. I do feel like the game lost some punch in its delivery when it canned the narration from Patrick Stewart. And sometimes during the cutscenes, it doesn't feel like the acting is very into it. Very subdued, and uninspired.
I could say more, but I can barely stomach the amount of time I've put into this game as it is.
In shorter terms; Every area where LOS2 planned to improve upon its predecessor, it instead falls flat on its face.

I have to admit I was a little late to the game when it came to the first game. For those that don't know, the first Lords of Shadow - and by extension this game as well - is a reboot of the franchise as opposed to a continuation of the original canon.
That being said, I have been greatly anticipating this sequel since finally playing and beating LoS and man was it ever worth all that waiting and anticipation! LoS 2 has you playing as the Prince of Darkness, Dracula (Gabriel Belmont in this universe) himself which really needs no explanation in regards to it's freaking cool factor.
Patrick Stuart reprises his role as Zobek (aka Death) and Robert Carlyle is back (and better than ever!) as Gabriel/Dracula, which alone are two good reasons why this game rocks! Also, Richard Madden as Alucard was a pretty splendid choice in my opinion. The sound and music - and the other voice work too - is all quite excellent as well.
I have been absolutely loving the gameplay so far, especially the combat which I feel has recieved a nice overhaul. There is still enough of the old system there that it should feel familiar and comfortable, but they also improved nicely upon some of the smaller snags I felt the first game suffered from. AI is a bit more agressive and (only slightly) less predictable this time, which is a bit refreshing. Also, for all intents and purposes - at least as far as gameplay is concerned - Gabriel and Dracula are two entirely different characters, despite actually being the same person.
Gone is the Combat Cross, Gabriel's signature weapon from LoS; instead Dracula most commonly wields the Shadow Whip which is a manifestation of his own blood that he can summon and control. Instead of Gabriel's Light and Shadow Magic, you now have the life-leeching Void Sword and the armor-piercing Chaos Claws which each offer their own form and style in combat. You can also feed on stunned opponents to recover your health in a pinch. Oh and instead of the consumables Gabriel used to carry around, Dracula wields powerful vampire abilities and other dark magics - Shadow Daggers, Void Projections, Bat Swarms and more; instead of being consumable they all have their own cool-down timers and thus behave more like spells would.
The game is much bigger and better all around for the most part, though there a few minor things that I personally find annoying. For instance exploration is way more 'hand holdy' than it was in LoS... to the point that ledges you can grapple and climb now glow faintly and are surrounded by a small swarm of bats, objects you can bash with your throwing daggers are outlined by a glowing red ring of what appears to be blood, and the addition of an actual function (hold LT) while platforming that outlines possible moves 2-3 steps ahead of where you're currently climbing/hanging. Not really a deal breaker, per say, but definitely takes a lot of the fun out of it. In LoS I actually missed quite a few collectibles due to not being able to find them or simply not being able to reach them once I did locate them - this in turn drove me to explore further and look all the harder for what I may have missed; the possibility for this level of challenge is all but impossible in LoS 2 it would seem.
I won't give away too much of the plot, for two reasons: one I have yet to beat the game and two it would just be a damn shame to spoil something so good. That being said the basic premise is this: a thousand years (and a 3DS game) have passed since the events of LoS, Dracula has been defeated and weakened - by his own blood no less - and thus left vulnerable to an attack from Satan, whom Gabriels seriously♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off the last time they met. Zobek makes a timely arrival to warn his 'old friend' of course and offers him both a way to regain his powers - to defeat Satan - and a way to free him from his curse - death at the hands of Zobek, who has supposedly located the Combat Cross. Thus the battle begins between the Prince of Darkness and the agents of Satan.

My rating for Dreamfall Chapters, Book One - Reborn: 85/100
This title promised us amazing mixture of medieval fantasy world and dark cyberpunk sci-fi reality set in year 2220. Also it was about to show various choices and everywhere-present consequences. Three worlds, two stories, one destiny. Lets see the realisation in detail.
Story is pretty rich, even more due to two main characters - Zoë Maya Castillo and Kian Alvane. Their choices and decisions are shapng the world around them and even himself/herself and also other main character. There is also a possibility to remind you what happened in previous games, so you can be well informed. There are a lot of aspects to solve, with the dark feeling, that something is coming. Joy and happines is well balanced with sadness and despair, even anger and revenge. For every choice, there is a consqeuence, you just have to find out.
Characters are strong and abundant in their personalities. Zoë is changing from scared and happy-go-lucky teenager to a responsible and courageous woman, what brings here one of most positive elements. Strong female protagonist. Also Kian is transformed from zealous religious fighter to the defender of weak and opressed. Episodic chracters are helpful and specific. For me, the strongest one was Teta Queenie (czech word for aunt), who forced us to make very serious statement.
Visuals are nice and realistic, art is catching and graphic is set to support the story and background in the game. Moods  and acts are reflected very accurately. However, there were some funny glitches, but it nothing disrupting the gameplay.
Soundtrack is composed by Simon Poole and truly said, it is a masterpiece. Piano, reasonable amount of remix and other instruments with dramatical choirs are goind right under the skin and makes you feel like you were in another world. Exactly there this game takes you.
Gameplay was heartwarming, it is mostly adventure with puzzles to solve. Quests are not easy, but solvable, you have to earn your success and sometimes try a bit harder. Game provides you a huge number of various interactions, commented with thougts of main characters. By the way, you can even control a baby here! Choices are differed to lesser and main, second one have "balance" symbol next to them, so you can see, how your friends and rest of the world decided. In the end, all your decisions will be sum up with commentary what you can expect in the following episode.
To sum it up, Dreamfall Chapters, Book One - Reborn, is a decent and proud member of the Dreamfall Saga and all, what they promised, they fullfilled, sometimes even overcame. I am glad, this was picked up from the Steam Greenlight, it is an exact sequel, how it should be.

POSTAL is one of those games, even after all these years, you can still pick it up and truly appreciate for what it is and how it affected the view of video games back in 1997. Unlike it's sequel POSTAL 2, this game is extremely dark, (in which HATRED tried to do and then some, but personally found it to try too hard.) Postal is an isometric top-down shooter where your goal is to kill all enemies (or 90% of them) in the map and move onto the next area. Due to what a lot of people believed, you don't actually have to kill innocent people! Though what's the fun in that? ... It's not, it's painful trying to complete the game without killing any innocent people.
The fist thing that really jumps out at you is the menus and the loading screens. These depict some dark images with some seriously dark quotes/entries of Dude exclaiming "The earth is hungry. Its heart throbs and demands cleansing. The earth is also thirsty..." The story behind this is a schizophrenic man (known as Postal Dude,) who has been evicted from his home. He believes that the United States Air Force are releasing a poison gas on his town that only he is unaffected by. He fights his way to the Air Force Base through various areas. During the progress of the game Dude taunts his victims, but actually it's a voice in Dude's head (voiced by Rick Hunter.) The voice was considered as "Demon Voice." Seeing how people liked the voice, they made it Dude's actual voice in the later games.
The second thing that really jumps out is the graphics. Even to this day the hand drawn levels still look amazing and unique! Each level is different, and I found myself just wondering the map just to look at it all. Half the fun is just exploring, then coming across a secret on the edge of the map that gives you a rocket launcher!
The game consists of 3 modes, the main game which has 21 levels, Special Delivery which has 4 extra levels, and the challenging Gauntlet Run which has 23 challenges to complete. In the original version there was a "online coop" mode, but that was removed from this game for reasons (but has made a return in the new "Redux" version of POSTAL,) and you can still see the level order in the game files. One thing that I really enjoyed was the fact you could easily go into the game files and edit the level order. It was super easy to add in the coop maps and play those by myself, or even make my own "campaign" or even add in the 2 exclusive levels that only the Japan version of the game got.
Some people complained about the controls, but from what the controls were in the original game to what it is now, it's really easy. I found it super easy to use only the keyboard. Using WASD to move, and the arrow keys to shoot. Using those controls you could play it more like a twin stick shooter, and be able to move in any directions and still be able to shoot in any direction as well.
Now from a completionist side, this is NOT an easy game to 100%. All of them are pretty easy to get, but there is a few that are a pain in the ars. Having taken me 51 hours, there was only 1 I can not get and that was to play the game on a Linux or Mac, which is something I don't have. There is 2 achievements that just take a long time to achieve, which are hit 100k targets, and shooting 1 MILLION times! Just to get shooting 1 mill took me an extra 27 hours of AFK. But the actual hardest achievement in this game was completing the game having killed only hostiles. Thankfully this was the very first thing I attempted on the easiest difficulty and took my time, having multiple save files. (Only to find out you could actually cheat that achievement. >_<)

They didn't know it then, but back in 1997 the developer Running with Scissors created a game that would become not only a landmark PC title, but one of the most controversial video games of all time. Little did they know the act of violence known as the Columbine Massacre committed two years later would be endlessly tied to both the POSTAL and Doom game series'.
The antagonist of the game is a schizophrenic man, known iconically as The Postal Dude, who has been evicted from his home. Being a conspiracy theorist, he believes that the United States Air Force has been releasing a mind-altering substance within the town of Paradise that has affected everyone but himself. Of course, the only way to solve this problem is to slaughter all of the humanoids and cleanse the earth of their infected presence. This more elaborate plot is not conveyed well within the game itself, despite the short dialogue in the loading screens that appear each time prior to progressing to the next level, rather it relied on the box art and manuals from back in the day to fully understand.
I won't spoil the ending for you, though I will say that it's not just the amount of killing that garnered this game such controversial fame; rather the very morbid subject matter, and dark humor-filled quips from the antagonist himself as he shows no mercy or remorse for his actions. This is a game that, while the plot is kept deliberately vague, taking the story and mental state of the main character into consideration makes it all the more disturbing and gruesome.
There are a total of 21 levels in POSTAL, most of which can be completed in just a few minutes each; the longevity of this title is not its strong point, clocking in at 1-2 hours for a full playthrough at best. Beginning at his home, The Postal Dude works his way through a truck stop, parade, trailer park, all the way to the military air base. This version does include the extra content from the Special Delivery expansion pack, which includes four new levels and the Gauntlet Challenge; the latter being a survival mode. Beware, however, as all of the co-op modes that were featured in the original release of this title are not available in this version; this is a single-player experience only.
The visuals within the game haven't aged incredibly well, but they're nothing to scoff at either. The backgrounds in particular are noteworthy, as they're completely hand-painted. The buildings and environments are wonderfully dark and morose, making way for an incredibly evil experience as The Postal Dude spills gallons of blood onto the ground. The character models are really what have aged terribly, as they're mini-verisons of models that would be found in games such as the original Resident Evil title for Playstation 1, and there aren't many different ones either. As far as a soundtrack goes, there's not one to speak of other than a looping set of guitar chords during the credits, although there are some subtle ambiances to be enjoyed; POSTAL is a game that plays better if you throw on your own "Mix to Kill By".
What will probably feel the most aged for modern gamers are the controls, this title no longer functions like any top-down isometric shooter of the current era. While you can set the game up to utilize your mouse, the mouse control becomes inverted at random intervals and becomes more frustrating than anything. It's best to stick to using the keyboard, where WSAD is used to move and the arrow keys are used to shoot. There's a decent guide in the forums for what's the best control set-up, so fear not if you need help.
With all of that being said, the original POSTAL still stands as a landmark game almost a decade later. For any fans of over-the-top, pointless violence, this is the game for you. The Postal Dude, despite not having a name and only having a small set of sarcastic, witty quotes, has become one of the most iconic characters in cult-classic fandom. Except for a few achievements, the game doesn't have much replayability or longevity, which is its only true downfall. However, at the price of $2.19 CAD, that's not extremely devastating. Still a classic, still dark, still blood-soaked, still fun, still worth buying. Long live The Postal Dude!

An
game, a true and glorious representative of the classic jRPG genre. The setting is, as to be expected, fairy tale-like, with some mature contents which however never reach the level of serious topics. There is everything one should expect from a jRPG: a rich number of characters with individual talents, different locations, an epic plot, challanging sidequests, rare equip and some secrets, everything put together into a very well designed game
PROs
+many characters, non-steretypical, some of them very well design with good background and valid contributions to the plot. Each of them in combat play a different role.
+good plot, non-linear and with quite a lot of twists. It also follows a valid climax, starting from more "local" threats and developing into the usual world(s)-saving theme.
+good technical level: the game, although old, is still graphically enjoiable and polished
+valid sountrack, with a couple of great themes
+large worldmap, with many towns and locations
+a good amount of sidequests and secrets, with challanging optional bosses
+interesting puzzle in the dungeons
+quite challenging even for experienced jRPG player during the whole game
CONs
-while good, the plot maybe exaggerates with the twists, some of them being predictable
-not the best main villain in videogame history, kinda weak in terms of motivations and credibility
-some towns are quite flat in terms of contents
-the final part of the plot insists on a topic which is quite abused in many contexts, and can be annoying at some point
Summarizing: fantastic game, for sure one of the best representatinve of jRPG. As a final note, I didn't encounter technical issues.

Basically Civ Lite - you have only one unit available, but the unit is vastly customisable and upgradable - becoming very powerful.  The unit is used in missions, which give influence with the various planets you visit; and when 4 points of influence are accrued, the planet in question will join your federation, giving you access to all it's resources.
There are several ways to win the game:  domination, population (controlling 51% of the population of the galaxy), science, wonder (building 6 wonders).  You can choose to have them all available, or just one.
There are a good number of leaders available, each with different skills, and with three different versions of each leader to choose from, allowing yet more customisation.
Despite all this the game feels a little unfinished and clunky, and is frankly in need of a decent tutorial level - as it can be a little confusing to start with.  There's also no real warning when the AI's about to win, which would be nice - so something could be done about it, like in Civ 5.
All in all, I'd give this game 7/10 as once you get to grips with things it's a fun game.  I'd like it to be longer, but you can't have everything.  I consider it worth the money.  Took me about 25 hours to complete it on the hardest difficulty, which made it about 50p an hour.
