As someone who just wants to buy a game once, this is a deal breaker.
The really unfortunate part about this game is that you seem to hit a wall if you aren't willing to pay up. A good freemium game should let you play it through for free, with microtransactions providing small incentives to pony up a couple of bucks to save yourself some tedious work. This... This isn't working. I spent nothing and will spend nothing.

Overall, it's a good game.  But I do wonder if this is a pet project under one of Sid Meier's proteges.
Strategy and negotiation are bit limited for space faring races battling for domination.
While it is a good idea to keep the screen readout in a technical/tactical format, the graphics leave a few things to be desired.  They're not bad, but for a Sid Meier's project, I expected more time and effort and definitely smoother eye candy.  I like the idea of controlling planet economies with food, metal, science, energy but I couldn't tell if I had a true effect nor how to make an effect.  The only way to distinguish yourself is choosing Superiority, Harmony or Purity.  But even then, I couldn't see any true benefit other than changing the character's profile or ship designs.
IMHO:  It doesn't engage the player to want to be a part of any side in particular.  Again, I couldn't see any advantages or disadvantages to choosing a particular affinity.  Perhaps what's missing here is more to the Beyond Earth story?

Bottom line:  This is certainly worth a look if you're into the strategy/space/sci-fi/turn based strategy sort of thing.  Consider waiting for a special offer.

He probably shouldn’t have taken that job as a groundskeeper at that spooky, decaying old mansion, but good thing for you he did as it leads you on quite an adventure.  As you attempt to forge your rescue you will explore many macabre locals, uncover fascinating character stories via letters scattered about, and even get to mingle with the dead via your spirit powers.  That’s right, thanks to a very friendly and very long dead Indian shaman you have the power to leave your body as a spirit.  This will be the main tool at your disposal as you navigate through the 2D landscape of catacombs, old mansions, garden mazes and the like.  Your spirit can get to places you can’t, open paths that may be blocked, interact with puzzles and even speak with ghosts of the long deceased who have a story to tell.  The art style is gorgeous and combined with the music and story successfully created a world in which I was eager to explore.  If you enjoy adventure games, good ghost stories, exploration and an occasional puzzle do yourself a favor and give this gem of a game a try.

The closest game I can compare to Whispering Willows is Darkest Dungeons, with which it shares some mechanics (2D maps, changing levels via doors on the back or side walls, can only run from monsters, etc.) but this is a far superior game. Certainly the puzzles aren't anything two write home about, given that the main challenge for the two that I had trouble with was finding it in the first case, and a very specific physical placement in the other.
Rather, where Whispering Willows shines is in the exploration of new areas and, more importantly, the backstory of various characters, communicated via notes found in the mansion and its grounds.  These add a lot to the world, and give context for what's going on in this admittedly creepy environment.
The biggest downsides to the game is the art in the cutscenes which, while not terrible, isn't particularly great either, and the fact that if you're killed by monsters, which at some points is tremendously easy to do, you can find yourself transported quite a ways back, requiring you to start again, including some interminable waits for monsters to finish their paths.
On the whole, I would definitely recommend the game. Its strengths very much outweigh its weaknesses.

I wanted to love this game. I really did. Don't buy it unless you have a morbid curiousity to see what happened after the very entertaining first game. If you haven't played the first, go buy that instead.
The first Lords of Shadow was an unexpected surprise for me, with gorgeous art and a fairly well told story backed up by solid action. Combined with a ridiculous twist and cliffhanger at the end, I was pretty excited to see where MercurySteam took the series next. On paper, it sounds pretty good. Expand the combat systems from the original game, continue the story, and place it in an open, Symphony of the Night style world that favors exploration.
Then they went and cocked it all up. The action is barely distinguishable from the first, despite the huge change in character. You now have subweapons, but they are essentially palette swaps of the default whip with the properties of either the light or dark magic from the first game.
The story is hilariously badly written, and at times borders on nonsensical. Character motivations frequently are completely impenetrable and illogical, and the ending of the game provides very little closure. The first thing that you see when the credits roll is that one man 'wrote and directed' the game. If I were him, I certainly wouldn't take credit for this wet fart of a story for fear of the death of my career.
Classic metroidvania backtracking and openness is a great idea, but the biggest problem is that the map system is absolutely not up to the task. Modern metroidvanias like Shadow Complex frequently combine the classic 'grid' style map with indicators of an item that you have seen but were not able to access. LoS2 has a woefully inadequate 'world map' that is simply the names of different areas with the number of secrets you have yet to access. With all the shortcuts, twists and exits in each area, neither the world map or the local map (that basically confines its view to the loaded in level chunk with no indication of where exits go) is sufficient to make hunting for upgrades anything but a chore.
And then there are the infamous stealth sections. God, the stealth sections. I'm typically against the death penalty, but whoever added those to the design doc needs to be publically executed. I want to watch. There are apologists for them, saying that they're 'more of a puzzle' than a stealth section. That may be true, but they're still a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥, inconsistant puzzle, using mechanics that do not smoothly integrate into the game. If you thought the 'boat stealth' sections from ACIV were the worst in recent memory, boy do I have a surprise for you.
Alright, I've got that out of my system. Don't buy this for 60 bucks. Please don't.

If you enjoyed Dreamfall: The Longest Journey, then like me, you have been waiting for this game for years.  It is finally here!  Well... Book One (of 5) at least.  As I write this, Book Two is in production, and I expect we won't have to wait too long.
Before starting Chapters, my daughter and I played through the Longest Journey and Dreamfall: TLJ .  It was her first time playing the games, and a good refresher for me on everything that has happened.  It really got us pumped for Chapters, so we dove right in.
First of all, the game is gorgeous, at least on Awesome settings (I'm running a Geforce 680 and performance was good).  Maybe this is the first game I've played with "next-gen" graphics, but I am in awe.  Book One starts off strong, then slows down a bit before an interesting ending.  There is an emphasis on choice, borrowing some concepts from The Walking Dead games, and this makes the game stronger and more replayable.  The series has an intentional mundaneness in the beginning to help players connect with the characters.  In the context of one book, it feels a little slow, but as the other books come along, I expect things will pick up.
Definitely recommended.  If you haven't played Dreamfall: TLJ, you would probably want to play it first.  The Longest Journey (the first game) is probably less of a requirement to understand this one, but it is one of the all-time greats, so you should play it anyway. :)
-------------------
Book Two is bigger and better than the introductory episode.  It doesn't necessarily pick up the pace, because it is a longer book and is still building intrigue.  There are plenty of good conversations and puzzles, mixed in with a few slow parts.  You spend more time in Arcadia this time around, but it doesn't neglect time with Zoe in Stark.  By the end, plenty has happened and you will have made many decisions.  The cliffhanger ending will leave you scatching your head a bit, and wondering what is going to happen next.  Can't wait for Book Three.
-------------------
Things kick up a notch in Book Three.  It doesn't take as long to complete as Book Two, but things move along at a faster pace. There is good character development, and you'll start to see the impact of previous decisions.  At the same time, it is decidedly "the middle of the story" and continues to setup for subsequent chapters.
-------------------
Book Four is the best so far and reminded why I fell in love with The Longest Journey series in the first place. On the critical side, this is the first time I felt the game really suffered from being released in episodes rather than all at once.  This was compounded by a long delay between books due to a game engine upgrade that affected all previous books.  My memory sucks, but my daughter also forgot a major character and plot point from previous books.  We had to go back to YouTube to refresh our memories on something that happened in Book 2.  Besides that, things are coming together.  This is the most engrossing so far, while still having a head-scratcher ending.  I'm looking forward to the final book.
-------------------
There were tears in my eyes as my daughter and I finished Book Five. This book wraps up Dreamfall Chapters, Zoe's story, and an entire saga that started 17 years ago.  Indeed, The Longest Journey has finally come to an end. I find myself simultaneously satisfied, nostalgiac, and sad that it's over. It isn't often a game engenders this strong of a response, but Ragnar Tornquist and his team at Red Thread have pulled it off.  Taken as a whole with The Longest Journey and the first Dreamfall, I believe we have a true masterpiece.
Book Five is light on gameplay, but this is the payoff for all the decisions you've made in the first four books.  Sit back, take it all in, and enjoy.  The devs did a fine job dividing the game into five books, but there is no doubt it will be best experienced all played together.  I plan to do just that.  This was my daughter's playthrough, so I want to play again making my own choices.  I'll play through the first two games as well to experience the complete journey one more time.

Ignore my Steam hours played, I've been messing around with Anarchy since late 2013. It is definitely something you should try, especially if you have a large steam/movies/music list. I used it to create FPS or MMO arcades as well as night clubs for my music and movies. The video posted below is an arcade I created with the prototype version a few months back using the PAX map. This gives you the ability to make worlds full of your favorite games and other media. You can also use custom maps from most source games. Models can also be imported, and placed in areas as you see I have done in the video below and those models can actually be set as a shortcut to something. In one of my arcades, just for fun, I spawned a Mario character prop and then linked him to a Mario voice sample I had saved on my computer, so everytime I walked by, I would click real quick and get to hear the sound file play. It's fun things like this that make AA so fun. There are tutorial videos when starting that I Highly recommend watching, as just hoping in and attempting to figure it out might take a while. I have been using Anarchy Arcade on and off since it was an itty bitty beta. It works really well as a 3d desktop app, if you're into that kind of thing. But where it truly shines is on the Oculus Rift. As the Oculus gains acceptance we start to see how the traditional menu > option interaction system become less relevant. Anarchy Arcade is a creative step in the direction of a fully immersive VR-desktop app. As such, it comes with some instructions that you really should read/watch.
One of my main gripes with the concept is that you have to load up one game to play another. But it's more about the time in between games that matters. If you get bored of playing one game and want to play another, you drop back into Anarchy Arcade and get to find your other game through the VR desktop (a.k.a your 'arcade'). If you're using the Oculus this means you don't have to take the headset off, and it's pretty cool too.
This is an interesting concept in human-computer interaction and I recommend people check it out. If you HAVE an Oculus, you cannot miss out on this one.

Wow, I played this game 67 hours?
If you are looking for a quick review: I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the ol' school RPG stylings of Might and Magic or Wizardry. At it's core, this is a turn based combat system focused on strategic use of team skills and skill tree choices. It is based in a Sci-Fi setting where you are essentially a mercenary/scavenger, which I found a refreshing twist considering StarCrawler's obvious RPG influences.
Long Review:
When RPS did an early access review of StarCrawlers, I picked it up on a whim. I was interested in playing a Might and Magic throwback game (turn based, 4 PC dungeon crawl). I found this and more.
Starcrawlers went through several different revamps, looking to polish an identity that started with a strong core. There is a fun, Cyberpunk/Sci-Fi anti-hero vibe in the main story arc that places you as a Space Mercenary who is free to chose... not good an evil really, but the shade of gray you feel most comfortable with.
The art is fun and whimsicle, the classes have interesting builds, and the combat ends up benefitting from the depth of both. There are some classes and builds I found through trial and error that crushed the system, but that is also traditional in ol'school delving games.
Some of the levels are a delight with interesting mazes or puzzles, others not so much, but in the end you will find hours of enjoyment if you like the style of game this represents.
Kudos to the Dev team! I really enjoyed this retro-RPG in a Sci-Fi/Cyberpunk Space Opera.

Starships is a fun game where you play as the admiral of a small fleet. It simplifies the technology and resource managing aspect so that the player may focus on their fleet and the missions that they go on. If you are expecting a 4x game then you will be disappointed because this game was not designed around resources but around space tactical combat and does a good job with it. In the galaxy you do get some resource management but all of those including the techs are strictly focused around building and maintaining the fleet. Then there are the missions the player sends their fleet on, they play out like a good game of chess involving a few varied sets of moves and abilities for each ship. With the longer games taking around 2-3 hours this is far more casual then the Civilization franchise it spawned from which makes it easy to pick up and play on a random day as opposed to a civilization game which takes a little bit of commitment to get through.
Now for the ugly. The game does have some balancing issues at the moment of release but nothing game shattering. The only 2 victories that you ever go for are population and wonder victories as science victory takes forever to get and when you go for a domination victory you will inevitably conquer over half the galaxy (population victory) before you wipe out the last player. There is also a very sad lack of multiplayer which could have done very well especially if Firaxis set up a single mission game (kind of like what they did with X-Com Enemy Unknown). I am hoping they eventually give us a multiplayer because that would drastically increase the value of the game but even without multiplayer this is a fun game and for $15 ($10 if you wait for a sale) it is not a bad buy.

I want to like this game, I really do.
This came from the people who made The Escapists which was a great game. It had its flaws, but it was fun, enjoyable and actually had me thinking about what to do. And The Escapists 2 had everything going for it.
I saved myself from watching all the youtuber hype before the game to keep myself interested. When I heard it was getting released early I was even more hyped.
The problem is that they rushed an unfinished game.
I HATE when companies do this. The youtubers hype up the game because they got it early and dont want to be hard on the devs. They also say "Oh its in early access!" and the devs add them into the game to coax them even more.
But its not all bad.
+The animation is really smooth and much more appealing than Escapists 1
+The core gameplay is still fun and enjoyable
+The menus are much MUCH clearer
+Transport prisons are cool.
However I think the negatives outweigh the positives.
-Items randomly change into other items. For example, my plated inmate armor became a hand fan.
-The devs are lazy. i have seen multiple times on the fourms of people complaining about things such as "My friend crashed, he lost his stats" and the devs said it was intentional. To me, that says that the devs were lazy in fixing a bug.
-Multiplayer is buggy. Clientside sees sniper bullets shooting other players, people crash, its laggy and the multiplayer fighting is very delayed.
-Semi-frequent crashes. Seems to be getting heat or fighting someone at specific times such as role-call.
-Heat is now much harder to realise if you gain it. Escapists one (although very annoying) had a sound that is layed above all others. The new sounds are not, making it very difficult to hear.
This is why early access is a thing. Bugs are made to be squashed. This is a game with great potential! Devs need to listen to the community or the game will die.

I would highly recommend that you play LoS1 before playing this - the premise of the game spoils the 'secret ending' of the first game, but the game does recap the story if you just want to jump in here.
Combat is much tighter than the first game - not only do you control three distinct weapons (a long-range whip, a mid-range healing sword, and close-range guard-breaking gauntlets), but the Mastery system encourages you to play around with and get comfortable with all of the moves in your repertoire instead of just mashing the simplest combo.
Visually the game is intense - this is about as good as it gets from the PS3/360 generation, and the PC version has special HD textures.
As far as the story, I was personally hoping for something a little less safe considering the gut-punch ending of the first game.  I have heard that Konami changed the original ending to the one we have here, so we'll see what the DLC offers.
All in all I think that I may have enjoyed the first game more than this one, but this had moments, especially in the first half of the game, where I felt as if it was exactly what I had wanted out of the sequel.  The latter half also has great segments, such as the Toy Maker, but the last quarter of the game the narrative begins to get a little loose and things just happen because end the game already.  Which is a shame, but it doesn't necessarily ruin it.

Truly an upgrade to the first game, LoS2 brings a nice change of pace. The gameplay itself is solid, responsive and platforming isn't a chore like it was in the first game (fixed camera and 3D should never mix). The enemies are a nice change of pace, forgoing the traditional fodder spam in previous Castlevania games and the removal of the "Grab is the only attack that matters" is nice. Given the track record of 3D Castlevania games, this one is a leap in the right direction. The puzzles are a nice touch, not too difficult and quite creative.
That being said, there are parts in the game that will cause you grief. Wandering around the city looking for an objective is tedious and frustrating, especially when the enemies continously respawn. The stealth mechanics are either stupidly easy or very cheap (I have developped a hatred for the fall season). And certain parts of the game will not give you an indication of what is required until you die (and a tip appears on the game over screen).
All in all, the game is decent and will cater to fans similar games (God of War, Dante's Inferno, Devil May Cry, Bayonetta) and maybe Castlevania fans (if they are open to the 3D element). Unfortuately, the game's frustrating componants may deter players new to the genre. If the gameplay issues could be adressed, this game could truly be considered the stepping stone for 3D Castlevania games.

Emergence was to be the first episode in a series of 9 following up the story of the original SiN. At the time, the decision to pursue episodic gaming in general, and especially episodic FPS gaming through self-funding was innovative and unique - and the return of an FPS brand as classic as SiN was quite something.
To this day, Emergence remains a really great game that plays very well, with terrific level design, solid art direction, good gunplay and an astounding amount of interactivity. The issue is that at times, it hardly feels like SiN. It doesn't help that Emergence essentially only offers up the first 2-3 chapters of what was to be a much larger game, and includes only 3 weapons, 3 enemy types and not a whole lot in the way of secrets, bonus objectives, action-based outcomes, computer systems or anything else.
Much like its predecessor, Emergence shipped with a few serious bugs and, generally, to very little fanfare. It broke even, but did not make enough money to support development of the next episode for an expanded team. Some months later, Ritual was forced to lay off most of its developers and was then acquired by Mumbo Jumbo. The rest is casual gaming history, until someone decided Ritual's corpse was worth resuscitating for a GOG re-release of SiN 1 in 2014. Thanks for nothing, Mumbo Jumbo.
However, Emergence is still very much worth playing today. It's one of the best shooters of the later 2000s and the untimely demise of the Episodes remains one of the great tragedies of FPS gaming. And it also comes bundled with the original SiN, which in my opinion means you get two terrific FPSes for the price of half an FPS. Go for it!

This a brilliant back-to-basics shooter. It provides consistent satisfying action. In many ways it feels more dated than it's release date, but the bread and butter gameplay is spot on. The weapons are satisfying, and marksmanship and quick situational awareness are the key to sucess. This is very refreshing if you are tired of the regen health and cover style of COD clones. There is only the pistol, shotgun. and the smg as the available weapons, but they are very well judged and switching between them in diffferent tactical situations is key. The game features ironsights, alt fire, and granades. All the alt fires are very powerful, as is the blast radius of the granades. You can't carry many of any of these, but once you realise just how generous the supply of these is, you can really cause some serious carnage when you rambo your way through a battle. The 'storyline' elements are so bad and cheesy it's hard to bare but just ignore them and it's ok. Most of the enemies are generic goons, and the enviroments are obvious and forgettable. However it provides a good framework for what is a solid shooter. It feels like an old game remastered in the source engine, but this is no bad thing.

An Overall good game, though it got a bit tedious towards the end. Puzzle mechanics were'nt reused enough, and I wish it had been longer.

The Good:
- Gorgeous in game atmosphere, mostly due to the great music and art style
- Intuitive gameplay, answers to puzzles make sense in the context of the world, and you're rarely left frustrated and unclear what you're trying to accomplish
- Mechanics and controls are smooth and responsive for the most part (stairs are oddly difficult to navigate until you get the hang of it)
The Mediocre (ymmv):
- The story is okay as a framing device, but doesn't really do anything past that
- The puzzles are very easy. If you're looking for a challenge, there isn't one here
The Bad:
- A couple of the puzzles are weirdly finicky. It's immediately obvious what you have to do, but for some reason the way to trigger the solution is actually arbitrarily slightly different. Think of someone telling you to draw a square who actually wants a rectangle.
- While the art in-game is great, in cutscenes it's mysteriously amateurish, like a completely different artist drew the still images. Takes you out of the experience a bit
- Finished it in less than three hours... and I was taking my sweet time. I get that the developers have to make a living, but there isn't enough gameplay here to justify full price (and no replay value that I can see).
So altogether I would recommend it to someone who's a fan of the genre (what would that be, Indie 2D Adventure Puzzler?) and who can pick it up severely discounted. Not otherwise.

I tested out Whispering Willows at an indie gaming showcase and was very impressed with the concept. Now more than a year later I finally got my hands on the game (and soundtrack). The worldset is interesting and while you're lost and confused at first the plot unfolds a little bit at a time. It's very well done. I am not a horror game person.... I hyperventilated while watching someone else force someone else to play a jump scare game...However, this game is perfectly executed it's not just horror for the sake of scaring you to death. The creators have imagined something that is atmospherically creepy with unique gameplay and a satisfying plot and ending. Don't skip this one.

To sum it up, Whispering Willows is a well-made, story-rich adventure featuring interesting game mechanics for an affordable price.
It only took me 4 hours to complete the game (I wasn't going for achievements) but in these 4 hours I couldn't get my eyes nor my thoughts away from it. If you're willing to read through all the notes and diary entries scattered around the game environment you will be rewarded with a deep and interesting story that unwinds as you progress.
A feature that I really liked a lot is the 'spirit mode', which can be used for e.g. to possess and move certain objects, reach certain areas and talk to the ghosts of the deceased.
Despite its dark ambiance and at times gloomy athmosphere I wouldn't slap the 'Horror' label on the game, though.
It's too much about love and 'mistakes made in life' for that.
Nevertheless, I absolutely enjoyed the game and would definitely buy it again :)

I also found the seemingly awkward combination of shamanic rituals and Victorian intrigue not only functional, but unique and refreshing. It was a little too short for my taste (to be fair, I could've played for another week at least and likely wanted more), but ultimately satisfying to finish.
If you're a fan of abandoned mansions, people whose heads are on backwards, tragic love stories, secret codes, hidden doors, homicidal shrubbery and/or picking flowers for adorable little dead girls, I urge you to play this game as soon as possible.

The original POSTAL is a classic. Despite being the most controversial game of the 90's, it still managed to be a very entertaining take on a shooter game. Instead of being first-person, it chose a different route of being isometric. POSTAL opened up a new thing that had never been done, which included relentless killing of innocent people, and those that are hostile to you. This game takes you in the shoes of The Postal Dude, or "Demon", as he goes on a self-deployed mission to destroy the plague brought onto the citizens of his city. This includes ransacking the whole city, killing everyone in his way. Violence never felt so good until you've played POSTAL. But, if you'd like a more grusome take, you should also play Hatred. Furthermore, released in 2016 is the re-make of POSTAL, entitled: POSTAL Redux, an updated version of the game. I would reccommend both, although POSTAL is completely uncut, and is basically the same game as it was in 1997. Unlike the Re-make, this game is not toned down at all. If you want more violence and more grusome energy, play POSTAL. If graphics make or break a game for you, then go and play Redux. Either way, POSTAL is a classic that will never get old, and it's a great game despite its content.
Can be pretty fun, though I'm playing with a mouse and find the controls super hard. Other than that I suggest you to get it for half the dollar.

+ The dark theme makes a good contrast to the over-the-top humour from Postal 2.
+ Reminds me of the Rampage minigame from GTA Vice City.
+ Good art design.
+ Rick Hunter really carried the Dude's sinister personality there. Make for an interesting character.
- Can be difficult with the keyboard.
Recommendation:
This game is best played with a controller. Moving and strafing with the keyboard is tedious at best, but the game is enjoyable nevertheless.
I'd like to give Redux a try, but that'll have to wait 'til the Mac/PS4 ports are out.

I picked this game up a long time ago (maybe a year?) and I delayed playing it. I actually forgot about it, but I was digging through my library recently and there it was. You know what? This is a pretty decent dungeon crawler type game.
First off, the graphics are smoother than I expected. It's grid based, but you can look around freely. The lighting, textures, and animation, it's all top notch.
Each class has three skill trees you can put points into as they level. The weapons remind me a lot of what you might find in a game like Borderlands. The abilities are interesting, with a mix of buffs, taunts, AOE, debuffs, DoT's, all that.
The game has you start out in a hub type area where you pick up missions, buy and sell loot, or hire mercs for your party. You can also upgrade your weapons or trade on a black market.
The game has a faction system, with over a dozen different factions that you gain or lose rep in depending on what missions you take. Sometimes in the middle of a mission you'll be contacted by a rival faction to the one you're doing the job for, where they'll offer you some sort of incentive to do a bonus for them, or betray your current contact.
There's a lot of humor in here, including puns, pop culture references, funny dialog, and clever descriptions for things.
The music is sort of space jazz kind of stuff, with a standup bass, some keyboards, sweep pads, things like that. It's good.
Combat is turn-based, reminds me of Final Fantasy or something, which I don't usually care for, but it flows nicely and doesn't require too much clicking, so it's not bad.
There are secrets to be found on the maps you go on, like locked doors, a few mild puzzles, or maybe a hidden compartment or secret door here and there. If you've ever played any grid-based dungeon crawler, from Eye of the Beholder or Dungeon Hack to Legend of Grimrock, you know what to expect, it's the same here. Look around at the floor, randomly click walls or things that look like they might be clickable, you'll find stuff.
I like this game. I like the randomness, the sense of humor, the upgrade and leveling system, the factions... it's really well done. It's like Freelancer, but a dungeon crawler. The sci-fi setting is refreshing. This one's worth picking up. Thanks to the randomness, there's lots of replayability, so it's something you can keep going back to, jump in, play a few missions, it's good stuff.

As someone who grew up losing more hours than I care to admit playing the likes of Dungeon Hack and Eye of the Beholder, I was pleasantly surprised to come across this game. I see it as a modern day version of those old classics, with obviously a space/cyberspace theme. I enjoy the setting immensely and they have crafted a really engaging dungeon crawl experience.
There are games in my library that I payed triple the cost of this game. They have fallen way short of delivering the fun I have had slogging through derelicts and bases hunting down bosses, doing quests, or just looking for my next gear upgrade in Starcrawlers.
Pros:
Graphics and animations are really crisp, and the coloring is done well.
The different grades of loot quality and upgrade potential give you plenty of reasons for just one more mission.
The music is well done and I enjoyed all the sound effects and ambience in each mission.
Plenty of quests and factions to work on.
Cons:
The factions can feel a little too numerous and bland at times.
Overall I have enjoyed what I have played and look forward to the release soon. I think if you enjoy a good dungeon crawl, this game will not disappoint you. Well worth the price!

Don't let the cutesy, stylized anime art fool you. This game is not a light-hearted dating sim. This game is Game of Thrones, magical princess edition. You'll find out fairly quickly that every decision carries a consequence and one mistep will lead your fair princess to her swift demise. This is not as hardcore as the good 'ol killah DM with a hundred sudden death encounters from tabletop RPGs but this is close enough. There are eleven ways to die in this game and there are even more ways to get an ending worse than death (try life in exile for instance).
The most striking feature of this game is the depth of the mood-class system. The amount of skill gained in every class depends not only on Elodie's mood but also her current skill level. This leads to an interesting dilemma where you might want to level up less essential skills that you can live with 86% so that the core skills can reach 95% in the fewest number of weeks, but you also want to get the core skills up to par before a relevant skill check happens. This min-maxing strategy plays an important role in Elodie's survival once foreknowledge of the events has been obtained.
So far, I have tried heartlesss capitalist warlord build without magic, all-out magician build, and also diplomatic build. All these are viable options that will lead to victory. Judging from the trailer, there are a few more possible builds out there that focus on other skills and trigger other new encounters. This leads to good replayability without the frustration of random dice. The endings are interesting as well. They imply long-term consequences of Elodie's decisions past her coronation.
On the other hand, the chief weakness of the game is the skill checks themselves. Some of them use really arbitrary skills, the silliest of which is definitely
. This "randomness" (at least on the first attempt)  leads to frustration just as bad as any dice rolls. The other problem with this game is Steam overlay, which doesn't work at all for me in Auto mode and which breaks the game completely in OpenGL mode.
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone who can accept the fact that they going to watch their princess die a lot. If you're not a fan of the graphic, I recommend you take a look at "Affairs of the Court: Choice of Romance" title from Choice of Game; it's a purely text-based game of the same vibe.

Long Live the Queen is a poor man's Princess Maker. It has all the right ingredients, however the amounts used and the execution fails. Where Princess Maker expanded your view by making every choice count, leading to a simingly endless variations of endings and possibilities, Long Live the Queen has yet to show me an ending that was not a variation of death or failure. Not very motivating or inspiring to keep playing to see what else is possible. It seems the paths constrict you towards one or two roles if you want to "win". That's the key difference, I believe - this game was only built for a binary outcome, win or lose. (With an emphasis on lose). Furthermore, where Princess Maker would reward you with beautiful art for every ending, give faces to love interests and rivals, Long Live the Queen in contrast feels hollow. For example, despite giving a face to a number of insignificant characters (e.g., a travelling musician) the game fails to give a face to marriage candidates like the MC's childhood friend. I cannot in good conscience recommend this game, even though it feels like it would be in my interest to do so, seeing as I'd love for games of this type to continue being made..

I'm not a huge fan of endless runners but
was so addicting that I unlocked everything in one multi-hour session and lost my good night's sleep in the process.
Keys are as simple as they get: only "jump" is used. Up to four people can easily play on the same computer in split-screen mode.
itself consists of three, recurring stages with randomized sections:
If you're familiar with
, the three stages are rather similar to it. In the regular game mode, the stage changes smoothly but flashily every 20 seconds or so.
While the mode transition looks cool, the resulting mode announcement is distracting and can get in the way of the obstacles and result in a quick death.
If you'd like, you can also choose to play endless runner of a single mode. However, it won't allow unlocking new skins that double as achievements.
Different skins do not have any effect on play. However, they are tastefully created renditions of familiar video game and/or pop culture characters.
Visual style is simplistic but the game rolls smoothly and feels extremely polished. The level design and hit boxes feel almost perfectly fair: you almost always know that it was you, the player, who messed up that run.
Almost: thrice in my 2.5 hours of gameplay I ran into a position in the "block" section that because of the transition and the stage being so close to the bottom of the screen I could not see how the level progressed. This was the only unfair part of the gameplay that I saw.
There's only one tune (that I could notice anyway) that gets faster and faster the farther you survive. It's a splendid, varied tune though.
Playing solo, I got all unlockables in 2.5 hours - a decent lifetime for a $1 game. Fun and addicting, I couldn't put it down before unlocking everything.
But I eventually did. Someone who especially likes endless runners would definitely get more out of it while striving for highscores.

This game is a mixed bag, and by no means outright terrible. There are however many flaws which strike me.
Gameplay in and of itself, with the exception of the glaring annoyance of nonsensical stealth sections is decent enough, and all of the provided mechanics are put to work equally in the combat and in exploring the world itself. This works well enough though it doesn't appear to me to be anything revolutionary or exciting.
Stealth sections very much break the established flow, despite being short and ridiculously easy to get past they are at odds with the rest of the game, disabling your ability to perform any attacks short of stunning opponents and trying to escape. It doesn't make sense when the game plays up the fact you're a character with ridiculous combat ability, and you're regularly destroying enemies twice the size or so of the guards in the stealth section which utterly wreck you in seconds if you get caught. The mechanics the stealth sections use, possesion and transforming into a swarm of rats don't seem to be used to their utmost. Particularly possession, why not allow the player to actually do something with the apparently invincible guard they're controlling aside from use an eye scanner to open a door?
As for turning into a group of rats, when the rat you're controlling dies - you possess the next rat in your entourage.  If all the rats die, you die.  This is used to -some- effect in the first stealth section where you have to navigate tunnels and avoid hazards, keeping your other rats alive. As well as again later on very briefly.  I don't particularly like this kind of gameplay, but the idea was good and for the effort spent in making it functional it seems very underused.
The game world itself is nice looking and well designed in most respects but it's fairly linear, it does allow backtracking throughout though mainly for the purposes of revisiting past areas with new abilities to grab missed collectables, which is more in tow with the series prior, although likely not quite as interesting. If you like collecting lots of crap (increases to various gauges, unlockable challenges, item limit upgrades, artwork) and trying to 100% games, that's a pro and you might enjoy it. The upgrade system for the main set of combat abilities is good, and offers some interesting options.
Enemies are fairly varied, interesting and the bosses are pretty fun. Though the hardest difficulty is locked until you've beaten the game. One flaw is that enemies and bosses (and anyone in combat with you) will quote the same 3-6 lines of dialogue over and over as you fight them to the point of it becoming annoying.  I like about as many of the character and enemy designs as I find unappealing, even then knowing that the ones I do like aren't very memorable and don't actually get that much focus.
Story is a big no sale for me, which is a shame because signifigant portions of it could be considered competent and plenty of time has clearly been spent on it. The main setting is uninteresting and feels generic as a plot point (despite the actual work which went into designing it.) Most of the characters motivations seem either generic, pointless, obvious or some combination of all three. The best segments are generally spent in the castle sequences, but the whole premise behind that is fundamentally pretty simple and renders itself unnecessary on the whole. There's a lot of background information in the journal which updates with entries on your abilities when you get them, and each enemy type/character when you kill/meet them respectively. This is nice if you like these kind of details.
PC controls work well enough, although onscreen prompts still use controller buttons which is lazy. There is a contextual control reference dropdown bound to F1 which shows what action, what button it's mapped too and what key represents that button, which is at least something. Being provided with a HD texture pack and features like being able to disable QTE's is great. Even if I found this game average I feel at least somewhat vindicated in supporting it for providing things like this.
If you're sensible, You'll wait to get this until it's on sale or gets a price drop. It's entertaining, stable and more or less what it presents itself as, but no grand masterpiece unless you're a person who'd particularly enjoy the areas where the game excels and be capable of enjoying it despite its problems.

A definite improvement over the last game.  Better world, story, and gameplay.

Robert Carlyle offered a wonderful dracula and the supporting cast were almost invariably superb.  I'm glad they had the lore portion of the in game menu, because without it I would have felt that they introduced some characters out of the blue without any exposition. Which could be viewed as lazy but I didn't find it too offensive.
The combat is quite fluid and the controls are pretty intuitive.  It only took me about ten minutes to get a really good grasp on the mechanics of the game.The boss fights are pretty good as well.  One complaint about the boss fights is that they seem to be very interesting and tactically stressful to begin with but they gradually push into tedium when you learn what tactics are necessary to defeat them.  This is most prevenlant in the first boss and last two bosses.  Another negative thing about certain sections of the game would be the "stealth" sections.  They were lacluster, slowing the game down unecessarily sometimes, mostly due to the whole system seeming under-developed.
Overall this game has alot to offer in most of its areas with only a few minor misses but doesn't really do anything epicly well or ground breaking.  I definitely enjoyed it.

First lets just put this out there, this game lacks a lot of depth you might expect for this type of game.  It also makes itself perfectly clear in that it was developed for a tablet, be that an ipad or a windows tablet it matters little.  The only reason this is on steam is because there are windows tablets out there.  Making this painfully obvious is the lack of any graphics settings at all other than windowed or windowed full screen.  Clearly this game is aiming at the lowest common denominator and calling that good enough.  Don't get me wrong the graphics in this game look fine over all, but if they were really making this for a regular pc there would be at least a option to change the resolution and play at full screen.
What also stands out is the size of the maps.  Mind you I have just played an 'epic' sized map and cannot comment on any smaller size maps, but if I were to put a label on the size of this 'epic' map I would maybe put it at medium in a range of tiny small medium large epic.
One interesting change from normal 4x games is that all upgrades, ships, wonders, or really anything you have to buy is all made instantly.  No having to wait for several turns for tech to research or a new city to build.  The only nod in that direction is the amount of turns it takes to gain control of a 'system'.  Which even that can be bypassed biased upon the level of difficulty rating of the mission at the planet.
The fights were somewhat interesting in how they were done on the grid like final fantasy tactics.  The only real issue I had here was the computer gives you a rating on what it 'thinks' is your chance of winning.  This possibly is correct on your first few battles, but after that its totally useless.  I had fights that it was telling me I had a 25% chance of winning where I totally steamrolled the enemy, or never even encountered the enemy because of random placement on the map and the mission type.
Overall the game matched up well with what I would think of as a mobile game, but there is a lot left lacking for a game that would be designed for the pc.  Note however, that does not make this a bad game even on the pc, as there have been much worse ones made.
My biggest complaint with the game comes down to its cost.  This is not a game worth 15 bucks, not even on mobile.  I would expect a bit more work, and replay ability for that.  Knock 10 bucks off however, and this game would probably be in a pretty good place cost wise for both pc and mobile.
I would say I'm fairly neutral on the game itself, its neither good nor bad, however it is outside of its price point should be by quite a bit for what it offers.

How much gameplay do you expect from your games? It's a salient question in this post-Greenlight age, with many games offering impressive gimmicks and visuals propped up by only an hour or two of gameplay. Whispering Willows is just such a game, a no-frills adventure game with some charming graphics and a neat mechanic that's over before you know it.
You play Elena, the Native American daughter of a groundskeeper at a super spooky mansion. He disappears, you gear up to find him, and the next thing you know you're in the♥♥♥♥♥end of some pretty dire catacombs. Like I said, it's an extremely straight-forward side-scrolling adventure game with notes to find, keys to collect, and notes to read. The one gimmick is astral projection, which releases your fabulously-coiffed soul to roam, slipping through tiny cracks, moving mundane objects, and talking to dead people. This mechanic develops one or two additional uses over the course of the game, and is pretty fun to dink around with, since there are no living NPCs.
Game flow is clear and steady, for the most part. There's no map but the mansion and its environs are usually simple enough to follow to your next objective. The hand-drawn graphics are delightful and well-animated, though I must admit the horrific condition of the spirits you encounter clashes a bit with the lighter, kids anime art style. The story rides a fine line between dark and silly and I was engaged the whole time, it's just that the whole time was about 90 minutes. It's a short, short game and if you like the simple gameplay, you'll surely be left wanting more. I'm glad I didn't Kickstart it, but if you pick it up on sale it's a charming little adventure and I can't knock it for anything but its length.

As Elena Elkhorn you're tasked with finding your father who has gone missing at the Willows Mansion: your heritage gives you supernatural powers as you can see and speak with the dead or project an astral body that can interact with remote objects.
Whispering Willows is a pretty good adventure game where simple puzzles and gameplay give way to exploration and a quite interesting story.
-great art style, the character model and ghosts are really nice while the backgrounds are pretty detailed
-good sound design with creaking floors, echoing dripping water and distant ghostly moans: the soundtrack is also quite nice
-eerie and creepy atmosphere from start to finish
-the story is pretty interesting and is slowly made clear by interacting with ghosts or finding notes scattered around the levels
-animations are very basic
-art style during cutscenes feels a bit too simple
-gameplay lacks variation or complexity and boils down to finding the right object to appease a ghost or unlock a location
-ghosts could have used some more dialogue and interactions
-puzzles are very easy
-some levels have rooms/areas that look very similar and this, coupled with the lack of a map function, can sometimes make exploration a bit frustrating as you try and get your bearings
-the few aggressive ghosts do not feel too menacing and are just annoying, in fact if you get caught you'll just lose a few seconds of gameplay since there's a checkpoint at every door
-while I appreciate the full controller support the lack of controller prompts feels lazy
-short (2,5 hours)
Whispering Willows lacks a bit of substance due to its very simple gameplay, there's not much challenge as simply wandering around and speaking to ghosts will give you everything you need to pass the few puzzles thrown your way. There's no denying that exploring ther mansion and its grounds is a nice experience though, the sounds make it an appropriately creepy journey and the level design does a good job in representing the abadoned, haunted locales.
The story is pretty good even though it's, for the most part, sadly relegated to the various notes scattered around: the ghosts themselves don't have much to say apart from some details on their death or a few clues concerning puzzles and this is a bit of a shame as I feel that some more depth in dialogues'd have been a welcome addition.
All things considered the game is a decent proposition- especially on sale- if you don't mind its simplicity and are ok with it being more interested in providing you with rooms to explore and a good story rather than an interesting gameplay.

SiN is a 1998 classic FPS based on the good old Quake II Engine. There are many little things that really hit me, both at the time and nowadays. The setting is the Freeport metropolis in a near future where police has been replaced by private security forces, which Blade (the protagonist) is part of. So we see modern/near future-like bank offices, laboratories, slums, sewers, a Dam and more. Besides the nice level design (especially for the times) there are some interesting elements like few drivable vehicles, usable computers with open-close commands and sometimes interesting prompt command menus, civilians and hostages which you need to save, a few stealth situations (optional, but still preferable). Still one of the most interesting and studied news is a well used Ghoul System, so now it actually matters shooting on a head or on legs. And that's not all because both you and enemies can wear bullet-proof protections and they are categorized according to the ghoul system, so you have helmet, jacket and pants which protect those parts. So As you shoot your enemies in different parts they might drop damaged vests. Very clever.
The story isn't much the strong side of the game: in the aforementioned Freeport thre's a criminality escalation. A dangerous drug named U4 is spreading in the streets and the game starts during a Bank heist we must stop. Our "gunned investigations" will bring us to linking U4 to a big corporation that is producing it. Like I said it's not the most original plot, but the gameplay is leading the way As well as some polygonal fan service...

Whispering Willows is a 2D puzzle story game where you control a girl wandering through a mansion and its grounds. The puzzles aren't difficult, pretty easy to beat the game in a few hours. Its not a great game, but its OK.

Whispering Willows is a simple game that blends elements of puzzle, point-and-click, and visual novel games. There is a large focus on storytelling, and very little focus on gameplay.
While the game offers many puzzles, most of them are very simple and will likely not require much careful thought or the assistance of an online walkthrough. However, players who wish to experience the full enjoyment of Whispering Willows are expected to do a bit of reading.
The game features a multitude of brief notes and diary entries which the player collects throughout their playthrough. These notes are well-written and help bring the game to life. While there is nothing forcing the player to read these notes, to neglect them would be to skip the entire point of the game.
This is because simply playing the game will not yield much enjoyment in itself. There is nothing particularly "fun" about the gameplay; the entire two to three hour experience is comprised simply of exploring the game's two-dimensional settings and "examining" your surroundings by pressing the Space bar.
However, in spite of its simple gameplay, Whispering Willows does do a great job of telling a unique story. It does so strongly enough that I found myself interested to follow the game through to the finish while also enjoying the experience.
While I really appreciated this, I understand that a lot of people do not have the patience or curiosity to play a game for its story or message alone. If you are one of those people, Whispering Willows is not for you.
Whispering Willows is a great introduction for players who are interested in but not necessarily familiar with gaming as a medium of storytelling. The price may be a bit steep for a rather short game, but all in all, I really recommend this game to you if you enjoy a good story and contributing to smaller indie titles -- especially if it's on sale! ^_^

Please do not take my negative review as a reason not to buy this game. Obviously by the overwhelmingly positive reviews, it is loved by many. But here are my reasons for not recommending this game. Decide for yourself it is for you.
By the trailer, I thought I was buying a very challenging open ended game. Limitless ways to play, lots of ways to die, but also numerous paths to victory. I thought I was being sold a sandbox. When I bought my sandbox, I shortly realized it was a minefield. A minefield with a very narrow path through it. And with no clue as to where this path was leading, I was left to guess. There is no strategy involved until you do dozens of playthroughs of trial and error. I hope you like clicking through the same dialogue you memorized on your fourth playthrough. Then realizing the strategy you enatacted is now useless once you finally break through to the next bit. Back to guessing, new strategy, finding out it's wrong, back to guessing...
It seems to me, the positive reviewers get off on this pain. I mean no offense, but I just don't get it. Before you buy this game, know that there are a few different paths to victory, but this not really a choose your own path, rule as you see fit sort of game. It's a story being told. And if you can't guess what happens next, you have to start over. And over. And over.
Again, not trying to tell you not to play it. But for me, I cannot recommend. Let me have it and expain what is great about this game. I would actually like to enjoy it.

First thing's first- many mainstream reviewers heavily underrated this game, sometimes to the point where I wonder if they played a different game. It baffles me even more when they say things along the lines of "I loved the first game but this doesn't even come close". That my friends is a lie, it is a lie because Lords of Shadow 2 improves in many areas of the first game and it amounts to it being an overall better game. I'd also like to add that this game performs better on PC than the first one. Let that sink in- this game with a free camera and an hd texture pack performs better than it's fixed point camera, straight up console port predecessor. I'm not entirely sure who was responsible for the port, but whoever it was the port is done well, with all the main options present as well as some gameplay customization thrown in for good measure.
THE BAD
Let's kick it off with the things LoS2 does not do well, because trust me- while it is a great game it is not devoid of flaws and when they pop up, they show. I think we can universally agree that the stealth sections are a pain the the♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's not even that they are boring to some (I personally enjoyed the first two hours of the game where the majority of stealth happens) but that they lack the fidelity to make them truly enjoyable and sometimes that they are kinda going against common sense. The latter comes into play most prominently in one boss pre-fight and one later city stage. Those were the only two places in the game that I was stuck for 15min straight just going "why game, why would you make me do this". Aside from the sections where you are stripped of your powers and must rely on stealth (that being the beginning, around 0.5 to 1.5h into the game) the stealth amounts of about 30 minutes of the entire game at maximum. So while it has some clear issues it's not something you'll be doing a whole lot.
Another negative point I would nitpick is the level layout design (not the design itself), in that this being an open world game it should be easy to navigate it, however I find myself wondering how to get to that one place I've been to previously and my best bet is to just wonder around until I find it. Now let me be clear- this is not a problem when it comes to the main storyline because for that purpose the game gives you a minimap with a quest marker (and it works very well as a matter of fact) it only becomes a problem when you unlock new powers and want to revisit older areas to collect the things that were previously out of reach. This problem I feel is a direct result of the game being as grand as it is- the sheer amount of vistas, sceneries, ruins and wrecked architecture left little in the way of a 100% clear and intuitive way to traverse it. And in contrast to the stealth sections I feel it would be hard if not impossible to make the world easily accessible without sacrificing some of the great art direction and good design choices. That said the quick travel system that you unlock sometime into the game could offer more places to warp to and not just a few general districts.
From a technical aspect the environments, especially in the city sections, could use some higher resolution textures and maybe a bit more detail to boot. Especially on the cars.
THE GOOD
Thankfully the game has more than enough to counterbalance it's faults and come on top. Let's start with the combat system because it is pure bliss here. In the first game, while I enjoyed the combat I always felt that launching enemies into the air is completely unviable and that the dodge move was kinda sluggish. That has thankfully been revised in LoS2 and the combat is smooth, fast and very responsive. The dodge is now a dash that can be chained together to either cover distance (combine with sprinting for best results) or quickly angle around an enemy. It is very responsive and can be triggered from both the ground and air, meaning you no longer have to be afraid of going airborne as you can always dodge out of any enemy attack.   The physics of the world have also been altered slightly so that controlling Dracula feels just right. A change from the original is also the Void/Chaos magic which, when activated replace your default blood whip with either the void sword or the chaos claws. These come with their own abilities and mastery trees. It's a great improvement to the old system where activating either would just apply an effect to your combat cross. Here you actually get a different weapon, with different range and different moves. The Void/Chaos magic extends into subweapons which give you a LOT of variety to your combat style. Overall the combat just feels great and rewarding, rarely (if ever) did I feel like it was the games fault when I died, as there is always a technique or an approach that will result in your victory. That said, it is important to learn some enemies patterns as they can sometimes be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥if you forget that said enemy has a certain pattern of unblockable attacks that you must dodge.
Onto the visuals then, which I feel are absolutely gorgeous. The animations of every character are great, Dracula himself is very fluid in his movements which is quite critical as you'll be staring at him quite a bit. This shows especially in the platforming bits where Drac jumps from ledge to ledge in quite the Spiderman fashion. The texturework is stellar on the characters, great in the castle and great/good in the city. I wish it was more consistent but for what it, it passes in every respect with just a slap on the wrist for the odd texture in the city. Overall I'd say the game screams high fidelity (and don't even get me started on the facial animations/textures, they are finger-licking good). But what are good graphics without good environments to put the into? Thankfully I feel the game delivers that too. The castle has locations that made me just stop for a few seconds (or was it minutes?) to just take in the surroundings, their creative value being just that high. The city, surprisingly, did too. Granted it has some bland locations when compared to the castle, but it also has some stellar gothic architecture melded with a cityscape with some impressive statues to boot. I feel like the first parts of the city that the player sees really do it injustice at it is mostly based around cubes and blocks (sciences district, I'm looking at you). The other districts offer more variety, and in general I really liked going to the city. It also helps that the enemy design in the city is some of the best I could imagine for this game. I half expected to get some generic futuristic solder or something but instead I got Castlevania's version of the Combine from Half-Life. I think it goes without saying I was most impressed with how they handled it. Enemy design in the castle is equally creative, however I'm going to cop out here and say that the castle is the most memorable enemy. I'm not going to spoil anything here, but let's just say if MercurySteam ever got their hands on the Silent Hill franchise, I would actually anticipate the next installment. To wrap this part up, the art assets, the direction and execution are almost stellar in this game. What keeps is from being truly great are the few bland environments in the city, and some environmental texturework that is not up to snuff at times.
CONCLUSION
I'd love to write more but I'm getting close to my word limit, my summary would be that when the end credits rolled I felt like I played a great game and a great final installment to the Castlevania trilogy. It didn't end in a cliffhanger, but it didn't answer everything either (in a subtle manner). If I had to rate the game I'd give it an 8.5/10, the extra 0.5 is for the replay value- after completing the game I only uncovered 30% of secrets and still have challenges to complete. And I can't wait to get back into the fray, completionist style (and trust me, few games do that to me).

disclaimer: I have very little play time but that's only because I'm waiting for full release and just made sure the game was compatible with my hardware. I've watched enough LPs and read enough posts to know what the game is about.
The game is essentially an old-school dungeon crawler which I find really ironic since given that it's also sci fi, you have lots of guns and robots and other hi-tech stuff. I'm not that sure but from my experience this is probably the only SciFi party-based dungeon crawler around, if it's not the only then it is part of a very rare section of games, just for that alone it's worth a look. Add in a very polished product, active development by dedicated devs and some loot based game play and you're in for a good time.
Pros:
-Cheap price! Remember how much Might and Magic X cost when it launched? Well this is like a 3rd of the price and you get an arguably better experience!
-The game is built to support 100s of hours of game play. You have loot-based gaming, the ability to do nigh-infinite dungeon runs and multiple viable classes.
-The polish on the product is excellent. The art is first class and the abilities have the requisite "oomph", sizzle and shine you need to break the monotony of first person dungeon games.
-Very little bugs, this is early access but honestly it's just lacking end game content, almost all bugs are already squashed.
-Speaking of end game content, it's missing but honestly the game supports endless runs similar to what a roguelike would do, if you level up all your men and collect powerful loot you won't even notice the missing content as you do dungeon after dungeon.
-Secrets galore. What dungeon crawler wouldn't be complete without secret rooms you need to discover?
Cons:
-Only 1 hub  and "samey" dungeons. At the end of the day this is still made by an indie coompany and you can't expect multiple terrains so I guess it's not reasonable to expect AAA production values after all the game also costs a fraction of a true AAA title
-Sci-FI theme might not be appealing to some. I urge you to give it a try though, this game will not disappoint if you're looking for a great pc based dungeon crawler
-Puzzles! I hate puzzles with a passion :( But if you like them this game has some and they're not the "click the switch and the door will open" variety
All in all this game is one of the gems in Steam and I hope it gets a lot of success.  A true testament to how a small indie team can create a great product on par with others made by much bigger companies.

I bought this even though it is Early Access because I like Dungeon crawlers but I am more of a sci-fi fan. I am very happy with my purchase. Whether YOU might like it depends on what you are expecting from the game. Let's talk about what Star Crawlers is and is NOT.
Star Crawlers IS:
1) A Grid based movement dungeon crawler.
2) An "RPG-Lite": you chose between sets of backgounds and skills to make your character.
3) Combat is turn based, choose an attack or ability, watch attack hit or miss target
4) Good main story with options to run randomly generated side missions as long as you want to.
5) Sci-fi game in which you operate a party of 4 in a cool universe
What Star Crawlers IS NOT:
1) An Open World go anywhere game.
2) An indepth Role playing game with fully fleshed out characters
3) An action shooter
The game DOES have a difficulty slider that works beautifully.  I really enjoy this game because it gets me my "cyberpunk" fix without  intense tiring action. Keeping in mind what I wrote above, if this is a game you are interested in, it is playable now but the dev has announced the game will be coming out of Early Access  soon , so you might choose to wait. UPDATE: The main story arc invoves puzzles and I am NOT a fan of puzzles. However I am completely happy ignoring the main story and running the random side missions. REALLY enjoying the game now.

Compared to a ton of EA titles I've tried, this was probably the most polished straight out of the box. I had a minimal buggy experience but the devs seem to be quite the perfectionists, they have revamped the classes several times too.
The level of detail is pretty sweet, considering that the "standard" maps are procedurally generated. The algorithm for that seems to try to populate rooms with interesting things instead of ye old "dead end with nothing in it" problem you'd have with some Diablo-ish procedurally generated games.
The freedom to work on your own reputation with any faction is fantastic. You have a main quest to do but you can faff around like an idiot ignoring it to your heart's content, levelling up and probably making the main mission trivial :P
Lots of options with gear, which is generally randomized, but if you've played a procedural game, you're used to that, or something like Diablo or Borderlands. You make do with what you have and that can be part of the experience.
Presentation is good, while most images being static, the odd animation is well done at least. As you can see from the above, the various tiles used to create levels are stylishly done with a pleasing aesthetic.
Combat is fast, fun and furious. You never feel like it's just "click one button over and over" with the various options from classes which are not just useful, but frankly, necessary later.
What can I say but this game has clearly been made with a lot of love and care - which hasn't been touted to replace hard work and knowledge. Don't love it because the devs love it, love it because it's done well.

Starcrawlers is a very good dungeon crawl. It is akin to Legend of Grimrock. Fighting mobs are fun and there are lots of nice itrems to pick up. There is even a story line.
However, this is NOT like other types of dungeon crawls.
First, don't expect a large land mass to explore .  Only one NPC gives quests to go into  dungeons,which are somwhat randomly generated once the quest is given. Secondly, there is also not a lot of conversation with NPCs as you would find in other RPGs.Frankly, I didn't miss either the traveling or the large amount of conversation.
HOWEVER, there is one big failing in the game. The main story lines all have puzzles some of which are very difficult or confusing. Thus, if you can't solve the puzzle, you are stafted and can't move on with the story or the game.
Do I recommend it? Yes, if they got rid of or eliminated the difficult puzzles; otherwise, you will be very frustrated if you are stopped mid way into the game. Moreover, the puzzles have nothing to do with the story line. They are completely unnecessary.
I should also note that the game does not have a lot of replay value. While it is true you can only play with 4 out of a possible eight classes, players tend to level all classes , which can be used for any quest. In addtion the game has four levels of difficulty that some players might want to try it. However,since the same puzzles will get very repetitive and old, and since you can play all the classes in the game, I can't see a lot of replay by players
Bottom line: good game and good dungeon crawl IF they eliminate most puzzles. I will admit that I don't like hard puzzles. Thus, take this review with that in mind.  I think,however, that having a linear story line that can't be continued unless you complete some tough or confusiing puzzles, is a bad game design decision.  I can see a lot of players being very frustrated midway into the game.

I am an old school rpg fan.  I cannot get into games like Legend of Grimrock or games that are pure dungeon crawlers.  I much prefer some story, quests, towns, shops, the full rpg shebang. The stats and character building is on the lite side but that is really my only complaint.  The combat is really good, the missions are good, everything else is good.
This is an easy recommendation for fans of blobbers, or people who like dungeon crawlers but also like traditional full rpg content.

Hello guys!
For all of you (like me) who struggle(d) with the issue of game freezing after Undead Labs logo, dispair not! There is a simple fix : create a .cfg file named "user.cfg" with these simple parameters :
r_Fullscreen=1
r_Width=1920
r_Height=1080
or any of your liking, depending on your monitors native resolution, then place the file in the "Game" folder in the game`s install directory so : Steam/steamapps/common/State of Decay/Game.
Now you`re set to go! Game engine will render scenes and text properly. But remember not to touch the resolution sliders as it will result in a crashdump. You can only alter the details slider (which will be set to min by default).
Now, for setting up AA, this is what you will have to do if you have an Nvidia card :
SGSSAA
Open State of Decay driver profile via NVIDIA Inspector.
Change Antialiasing compatibility to 0x000012C1[4]
Change Antialiasing - Mode to Override any application setting
Change Antialiasing - Setting to 4x [4x Multisampling] or 8xQ [8x Multisampling]
Change Antialiasing - Transparency Supersampling to 4x Sparse Grid Supersampling or 8x Sparse Grid Supersampling
Apply changes.
This method is very performance demanding and may decrease your general performance.
FXAA
If you are a NVIDIA user enable FXAA from NVIDIA Control Panel or NVIDIA Inspector.
Or use FXAA Tool.
SMAA
Use injectSMAA by mrhaandi.
Or use SweetFX by CeeJay.dk.

Luftrausers is an arcade-style game that ultimately fails to give a real challenge.  At higher difficulties and later missions, your success becomes dependent on random change to the point of absurdity.
For example, the last random engine mission requires 25,000 points on the highest difficulty.  In practice, this can only be achieved by killing a particular enemy which only spawns a small percent of given attempts, and hoping that battleships or large numbers of aces do not spawn.  There's little the player can do to learn or improve, just try again.
Luftrausers also manages to have at least one frustrating bug, despite its simplicity.  The last thing you kill on a given life does not count towards your mission score, either for "kill X of Y" type missions or score-based missions.
If you want a difficult game where you can slowly learn its patterns and intricacies without feeling like you're getting punished by RNG and bugs, Luftrausers isn't it.

A coffee break shmup with single stick controls, one stick to bank and rotate, a button to thrust and a button to fire. Health regenerates as long as you aren't firing your guns. The game starts off sdlow but quickly ramps up as you increase your score, adding more, and tougher enemies until you go from little gunboats and fighters to fighting massive battleships, zeppelins, and UFOS, dodging enemy fire, lasers, and skimming water and clouds to avoid everything, until you finally explode and do it all over again. The game's scoring challenge comes from continuing to string together massive combo multipliers, constanly urging you to take higher and higher risks to keep the combo going withouty dropping it, lest you have to build it up all over again.
The player's ship is heavily customizeable in body, engines, and weapon types, allowing for a large variety of playstyles. As a neat touch, the music alters itself based on the type of ship you put together, putting together a new mashup of instruments and beats. The downsde is the game's pocket size, along with quickyly ramping difficulty, means you're going to be hearing the first one to two minutes of the song an awful lot.
Completing achievements and challenges in the game unlocks new parts for your "Rauser", and new color paletes to play the game with.
It's pure arcade action and it's a lot of fun.
A solid arcade game
