If you want it just for SiN, just buy SiN Gold from
instead. It comes with both SiN and Wages of SiN.
Here's reviews for the entire SiN series anyway:
The main game. It did many things that were groundbreaking for its time, but was overshadowed by Half-Life because it launched with tons of bugs that put people off, whom left for Half-Life and never touched SiN again. Even so, SiN's achievements are still unique in the history of FPS because what it did has not been replicated since; not even by Half-Life and its sequels.
Such amazing feats include the much-touted Action-Based Outcomes, where things you do in a level can affect what happens next. Like other old FPS, there's multiple ways to progress through a level, but unlike them, SiN does so in a much more interactive way, such as using computer terminals. You might even find secret sections or levels if you are observant. Other feats include an extremely versatile scripting system that allows things in the game to act in many awesome ways. It ranges from brush manipulation (vehicles, scenery destruction) to enemy tactics. While most games these days are heavily-scripted, none have done the ABO system like SiN did. Also, did I forget to mention this is the first FPS to feature in-engine cutscenes?
Even without these feats, SiN still holds pretty well on its own. SiN features an engaging (if not cheesy) comic book-like character-driven story set in a dystopic city called Freeport where law enforcement is run by private security forces. The most respected one among all; HardCorps; is led by our hardcore and just hero, Colonel John R.(Rusty) Blade; who is assisted by his hacker sidekick, the geeky yet reliable J.C.; and together they must face the menace of evil Elexis Sinclaire, genius biochemist, self-proclaimed Mother Nature, and CEO of the corrupt multinational corporation; SinTek Industries. The story begins in the year 2037, when the highly addictive drug 'U4' (Dyforsanide) is at its peak and it's up to Blade and J.C. to stop Antonio Mancini, who seems to be behind the sudden outbreak of the drug, and find out the source of all the weird happenings around Freeport City lately.
It may not sound like much, but it's certainly more than what Half-Life has to offer (no, having the same plot as Doom but with things that are never explained does not constitute for a deep or good story). Blade is rocking the late 90s FPS hero attitude and his humorous back-and-forth snarks with J.C. keeps the characters interesting.
As for the technical aspects of the game; the graphics is about what you'd expect from a Quake 2 engine game, but it still holds up today and the scripting in the game may surprise you every now and then. The sound design may be a bit shoddy, but the music and voice acting is top-notch and spot-on. The levels are very well-designed; lifelike in the sense that you solve puzzles logically; and allows for endless replayability. The weapons may be standard and the enemies can be difficult at times, but the diverse cast of chatacters and environments will keep you interested until the end.
Overall, I'd give it a 9/10 due to technical shortcomings, but its innovations has certainly secured it a high rank on my list of great games.
Expansion pack of the main game, brought to you by a small team of developers known as 2015, Inc. You may have known them for creating forgettable franchises later on such as Call of Duty, after most of the original team left the company to form Infinity Ward.
Now, onto the actual game itself. Despite being an expansion pack with only 16 levels as opposed to the original's 36, it features a more cohesive experience than the main game. The pacing felt much better, and there was an interesting concept in the game where an action you took in one of the early levels decides the order and gameplay of the next several levels.
Set several weeks after the events of SiN, the expansion pack continues the story with Blade combating the recent increase of mafia-related violence and how it all connects to the rise of the notorious mob boss, Gianni Manero.
The game did not change much from SiN, though it did introduce 7 new weapons and 10 new enemies. The new enemies aren't anything out of the ordinary, but the new weapons are far from the standard FPS-fare like the ones in the main game and are very fun to play with.
Overall, it too gets a 9/10 and shares a seat with the main game.
This 1-hour OVA is a loose retelling of the events of the original game. Thus it features many discrepancies between it and the game.
Its premise is mostly the same, but the plot develops differently. It's set in 2070, Blade is a cyborg, J.C. is replaced by his sister; Jennifer Armack; and they must stop Elexis from kidnapping a little girl or something.
It's your generic cheap ultra-gory 90s anime with forgettable plot. There's really nothing else to say about it.
It gets a 5/10.
The first and only Episode of a planned total of nine. The game is set in 2041. Elexis Sinclaire reemerged from the shadows and with the assistance of the elusive Viktor Radek, her ambitions still hasn't slowed down. After failing to prove the wrongdoings of Elexis and SinTek to the public, Blade returns to combat the threat together with his new sidekick Jessica Cannon, a hot-blooded but skilled rookie officer.
Blade is a silent hero for some reason here. The new sidekick, Jessica, is basically Jennifer from the Movie; bland. As a result of that, we see less of J.C. in Emergence. Elexis is still her same old self. Radek plays the sane man to Elexis' crazy wench, but otherwise he's just an unremarkable lackey. Fun fact: Jessica and Radek are voiced by the actors of Cortana and Sergeant Johnson from Halo, respectively.
Unlike the original SiN, everything it did here is completely outclassed by Half-Life in every single aspect. It's nothing like the original game at all; it instead is a discount Half-Life 2 to be point of running the same engine as HL2 does, and only features 3 weapons and a pitiful cast of enemies. The ABO that was featured in the original SiN is gone. The level design is nothing remarkable and the sound design, apart from the voice acting, is pretty standard and reuses some from HL2 itself.
It does, however, features a Dynamic Difficulty System. The goal of the system is to ensure no player will be stuck in the game or find it too easy. It works by constantly monitoring the player's actions, as well as its own decisions. Instead of altering the enemies health, damage, and speed like other games do, the game changes the difficulty in much more dynamic ways. For example, if the player scores headshots all the time, the next set of enemies you encounter will be equipped with helmets to protect them from headshots. If the player does not take much damage from combat, more enemies will appear and they will start using the weapons' alt-fire. Similarly, if the player is constantly low on health, killed enemies will drop medkits more often. On the other hand, if the player is still low on health all the time after that, the game will try something different to help you. While it sounds good on paper, in the end it doesn't even matter due to how short the game is.
In the end, this game; together with its fellow, 'Half-Life 2: Episodes'; is proof that the episodic format will never work. Sure, you can say it allows the devs to reuse assets in future episodes so they can focus on creating new stuff as well as providing a steady flow of content from beginning till the end, but it's all pointless if they do not have the tenacity, fundings, or workforce to back it up.
Overall, I'd give it a 6/10.

Whispering Willows is a sidescrolling adventure game, driven by its story and atmosphere, about a haunted mansion and the surrounding grounds. It's charming, and can pull you in for a little while, but it's hampered by some cumbersome situations and rudimentary elements. I beat it in five hours, while taking my time, and had a decent amount of fun despite the flaws. There are a few last achievements you can hunt down when you're done, but no real replayability.
The game has very attractive graphics, with nice lighting and glow effects. The ghosts you meet have a cartoony style, but are still depicted with various fatal injuries that add some distinction to each one. I'm not a fan of the cutscene artwork, as it looks a lot more crude and clumsy than the game itself.
The sound is nice as well. Subtle music and eerie ambient noises give each indoor and outdoor location its own feel. Invisible creatures, both helpful and harmful, are signaled by the noise of your character's amulet, or of their own mysterious movements.
The game is played by exploring each area of the mansion. This is a mostly linear experience: talking to ghosts, unlocking doors and collecting necessary items along with documents that gradually tell the game's story. Experiencing new environments and reading the story are really the high points of the game, but toward the end, many of the rooms are bleakly similar to each other, the abritrary size and layout of the mansion leading to some slow backtracking. If you manage to miss something, you'll be plodding around for a few minutes, trying to figure it out, and the feeling of reward when you get it right isn't as satisfying as in some more elegantly built games.
Puzzles are often solved by assuming a spirit form which can pass through openings in walls and ceilings, and manipulate objects like switches or keys. There are a few moments of novelty to this, but compared to some games about changing forms or manipulating your environment, Whispering Willows uses it in a fairly simple and straightforward way. The final scenarios of the game remind me of the game Ghost Trick, but Whispering Willows can't really compare to something like that.
The story is fairly interesting, largely delivered through notes that you pick up. It's fairly easy to find them all, so you probably won't miss out on any details. The story falters a bit near the end, in my opinion, by trying to be a bit more epic than it is, but it reveals some final truths and then wraps itself up without dragging on too long.
In the end, parts of the game shine more than others, but it still all comes together to a decent experience. It can feel slow or annoying in some areas, but I've played worse. If the ghostly atmosphere, solving a few puzzles, and collecting and reading notes and letters to piece the story together sounds fun, you might have a good time with this game; otherwise, I would steer far away from it. Either way, I would wait for a sale. This isn't a game so amazing you just have to play it right now, and $15 is a lot for a short one like this.

This was a very pretty game, with amazing cutscenes and artwork. In fact, if it was my first time playing this game, the best advice I could be given is to set aside 2-3 hours of nighttime and set to it. The game does an excelent job at creating the perfect atmosphere for what it intends. I think the easiest way to describe the atmosphere is with the word 'eerie', with well timed music and the creaking and cracking of old buildings, the whispers that you think you hear at night all provide an excellent setting. The game is fairly straght forward with the only choice I found myself having to make was which room to explore first.
In my opinion there are a few down sides, first for a game that took me 1.5-2 hours to complete the price is rather steep seeing as there isn't much replayability(having completed it on the first playthrough). Secondly for those who watched the trailers, or have played the game, the black ghosts don't have much of a role in the game. Don't get me wrong, when the black ghosts come its fairly heart racing, but I was just expecting them to appear more often and for my character to have to hide from them in some hole or cupboard(though there seem to be plenty of games with that included already, so maybe less of a downside).
All in all it's a really good game, 2-3 hours worth of play time. Again, since there isn't much replayability I would suggest waiting for the game to go on sale, or for the price to drop a tad.

IN A NUTSHELL: I picked up and finished the game tonight, and I'll echo what others are saying: great atmosphere, good-for-the-most-part (but underdeveloped) story, so-so game mechanics, and WAY too short. However, despite my issues with it the game was a fun play. Also, since the last time I've reviewed something Steam has started requiring the recommend/not recommend button (WHY, STEAM? WHY???), so I'm going to give this a thumbs down BUT I do have to say that--while I can't recommend getting it for full price--I still think it's worth picking up if it's on sale or in a bundle.
MORE DETAILED REVIEW:
**WARNING: MILD SPOILERS IN THIS REVIEW**
First, regarding the length of the game: 3 hours (4 at MOST if you want to get all the easter eggs) for a 15 USD game is, in my opinion, unacceptably short. For 10 USD games, I expect at least 8 hours of gameplay. For a $15 one, I'd say that anything under 10 hours is too short. In this case, I would have liked to see additional content that further developed the story and fleshed out the characters beyond the 2 dimensional fetch-quest style dialogue. I would also have liked to see some more challenging puzzles. In general, puzzles should take time to work out intellectually NOT (as was the case with the wine puzzle) in figuring out the basic mechanics of the puzzle or (in the case of the Knight puzzle) in having to adjust it multiple times to get it to be "perfect". As another reviewer mentioned, having some puzzles with multiple solutions would have been nice as well.
Story wise, while I was fairly invested in the dead residents of the Willows estate, I felt like all the characters were fairly stereotyped and thus felt very two-dimensional. I also felt that the pacing was poor; in particular I was disappointed by the lack of any real story development after the first time Elena finds her father. I know that the point of that chapter was to play through a part where you're unpowered, but I would have much prefered more gameplay where Elena slowly powered up by, for instance, helping the rest of the ghosts on the estate.
I also am not sure how I feel about the ending. It's like, dead racist white dude murderer learns the "error" of his ways and gets to wander off into the afterlife with the only real consequences is that he feels bad that he made the wrong life choices? The most flattering thing I can say about that ending is that it was "unsatisfying". Seriously, murderous racist white men don't need redemption arcs that fail to hold them properly accountable for their atrocities. We get enough of that in real life, I'd rather not have it interfering with my fantasy.

Overall, it's a fun game. The story is interesting and you really do feel compassion for the characters but there are some elements of the plot that felt rushed and left a lot of unanswered questions. This is especially true near the end, where a lot of new developments were kind of just thrown out there without getting any proper explanation. Not even a casual "Oh yeah and this is what happened here". Just... nothing. This left the story feeling a bit unfinished, though the depth earlier in the game makes up for this well enough.
The audio in this game is great and definitely helps to give off a creepy vibe that keeps you, at the very least, unnerved. The music, especially, is lovely and fits perfectly with the genre of horror. It's not a terribly scary game when you get down to it, but I'm not really a big fan of super scary games. For me, it had just the right amount of creepy to make me jump and get my heart pounding without actually freaking me out so much that I never open the game again (which has happened a lot in the past).
My only concern with the game is the bugginess of the movement. If you go in one direction for too long the game will get stuck on it and keep you moving even after you've stopped pushing the arrow key. Definitely annoying (and quite terrifying) when you need to turn and run from a monster, but Elena keeps strolling straight for it. The stairs, though not necessarily buggy, could be difficult to ascend when placed right on top of one another, as it was hard to line Elena up in the exact same spot. Neither of these ruin the experience, though, and the game remains an enjoyable one to play. I'd definitely recommend buying it!

I wish I could reccomend this, but I can't bring myself to do so; Symphonia is a lovingly crafted story in a game that hasn't aged particularly well. It was reccomended to me from various sources, and I often enjoy JRPGs from multiple eras, so I was really looking forward to the game. On the surface it has a lot to reccomend it; a charming cast, a thoughtfully-implemented old-school JRPG plot, and an abundance of cute conversations between party members, all wrapped up with a semi-ARPG combat system.
Small problem: actually engaging with the gameplay never felt satisfying to me.
The controls are a touch clunky, the overworld and dungeon exploration are uninspiring, and the visual presentation is caught in that awkward era between charming sprites, and expressive, attractive polygonal models. Exploring the overworld, puzzle-solving in dungeons, and combat all felt like drudgery, and that's pretty much the game.
I've enjoyed similar games in the JRPG genre; later Tales games (a bit of Vesperia, Zestria), Xenogears, as well as the Star Ocean series, and I didn't find the act of actually playing Symphonia enjoyable enough to make it to the next bit of dialog.
It might be different if you're nostalgic for the Gamecube game, but as someone who never played that, I'm just not feeling it. I'm playing Tales of Zestria now, and I find that to deliver everything I hoped I'd get from Symphonia.

I'd first like to clarify that most of the negative reviews for this game were about glitches caused by it being shoddy port. These issues have been resolved.
This game is a real time rpg focused on gameplay with combos, special moves and team composition, and a story with heavy characterisation, strong motives, clear goals, twists and turns, hours of content, side quests and decent writing.
The gameplay is unique. The battles take place in 3d, but each character can only move in a 2d plane, with left and right going back and forward, and up and down jumping and crouching respectively. It seems like a system built of a limited controller however even modern controllers would struggle to undertake this in a better way. The only way to move in the 3rd dimension is to target a different enemy then move forward or back.
Its not as bad as it sounds, most likely because you're always either going forward to attack, staying back to cast spells, or jumping or crouching to avoid attacks.
It also seems necessary for it to be this way. The controls are almost inspired by smash brothers, with inputting a direction altering the attack used, and these attack mappings can be custom made by the player before or even during battle. The point I'm trying to make is since smash brothers works in a 2d plane, players can easily relate their experiences to it.
. If, for example, up would move you forward in the 3rd dimension, it wouldn't be as clean a transition.
.
Anyway, I haven'y really even talked about the gameplay yet. My experience is with the gamecube controller, so I can't say for sure what is like on pc or ps3, but here we go.
A is for normal attacks. Usually you can string multiple normals into each other and change the normal slightly by inputting a direction when pressing A. B is for specials which cost mana (or whatever its called, I forget). There are 3 types of specials; (and I am naming them my own names because I don't know what the official names are or if there are official names)

It all flows very well and changes from character to character. Along with this, there is the unison attack, or what is call the original Z move. You select a special move to be performed for each character in your fighting party. Then when the guage is full, your team unleashes all the special moves at full damage, at no mana cost, and with unique move combinations causing bonus damage.

Having played many FPS Tower Defense Co-Op games - I can definitively say this is the best of the best. There are some areas that could be improved upon, however, overall the game is a great one. This game is still enjoyable in single-player mode and that alone deserves purchase IMHO, yet it is the multiplayer Co-op aspect that truly makes this shine.
The controls and gameplay are both easy to learn, fluid and smooth, and they are fairly intuitive. Most importantly, they are FUN. That is not to say that the game is a simple one, as there are many aspects of trap laying that must be considered depending on the level, and with whom you are playing.
A great thing about this game is that time spent playing never feels wasted. Whether you play for just one session or for 4 hours straight with a friend, your character becomes more powerful through the use of a "Skull Points" system wherein you can radically modify the powers your character has acceess to, how powerful they are, and the types of traps that you have access to when playing. This system is highly modular and never punishes you for poor choice - as you can simply re-distribute the "Skulls" to re-make yourself whenever you wish, as many times as you desire.
Many similar games in this genre suffer from either focusing on the FPS combat too much which makes the traps laying suffer (and become pointless), or entirely reverses the process and FPS becomes such a mitigating factor that trap/tower placement becomes the centerpiece, sometimes to such an extreme that the levels are actually very punishing if you do not place down your defenses in a very exact method. This game suffers from none of these issues, perfectly blending the two and allowing you to make minor mistakes in both FPS and Tower/Trap placement.
However, there are some glaringly annoying things. The most important is the lack of parties larger than 2 in multiplayer. Many levels feel like they were in fact developed with 4 players in mind, and it is very frustrating when you have such a fun game and if there are 3 or more of you who wish to play, you are left odd men out. Who cares that many levels would become vastly easier, the point is having fun and 3 is definitely better than 2, and 4 is much better than 3. More than 4 players would likely have been too much considering the size of the levels (I will concede that much).
A couple of traps or ways in some artifacts combine when your partner is likewise equipped (questions as to whether or not certain abilities or effects stack) is not intuitive.. but altogether not very important in the grans scheme, this was only a very slight annoyance that was applicable in rare circumstances.
The ability to being able to develop your own levels would have been an amazing addition, if not altogether an impossible addition, but this game definitely feels like it would have been perfect for such a companion piece.
Better LAN support would have been appreciated, but also not a deal breaker as long as you and your partner both have decent internet access.
The built-in voice communication never worked for me, nor my friends. Yet with the prevalence of using Mumble or some other TeamSpeak VOIP application, it is a non-issue.
Regardless of these things, I heartily recommend the game, even at full price - it is worth many hours by yourself cut off from the internet to earn more Skulls, and the multiplayer makes this a game that will go down in history as one of the best FPS Tower Defense Coop games ever.
I eagerly look forward to their 3rd installment (hopefully with 3+ multiplayer support!)

I very rarely write reviews.
This game is surprisingly good - much better than I expected.
I feel like I really lost out by being turned off by the "space" aspect.  I know that's what's actually bringing in many people, but I've been looking for a good old-school *fantasy* dungeon crawler for quite awhile.  So I passed over this several times.
I shouldn't have.  This is exactly what I'm looking for, and it's amazingly well-made.  So much more "solid" through and through than any other dungeon crawler on Steam - and I tried the rest before giving in to the cyberpunk.  Ironically (being that it's in EA), it feels much more "complete" than the others...
The one downside is that it takes awhile to "get going."  Classes really have very little tactical depth or breadth - together or alone - until level 7 or so.  On the other hand, the pacing from that point on is possibly the best I've ever seen in any RPG - at least for my tastes.

If you like old-school isometric dungeon crawlers a la Wizardry or the early Bard's Tale or Might and Magic, you're going to immediately fall in love. If you just like the idea of a cyberpunk/sci fi RPG, you've got a good chance of liking it too.
The classes are quirky and fun, the missions and characters you meet are enjoyable to deal with, and the itemization is decent.
As of this writing it's priced at $20, so I really can't think of a reason why you shouldn't give this a go. You're reading the review, so your interest is piqued, and I'm here to tell you to give in to that interest. Pick it up. Run around a ship or three. Get scrubbed clean.

Luftauser is a simply arcade game which re-elaborates the classic Asteroid mechanic of momentum based movement but cranks it up to 11. You fly your airplain on land, which means you will either fall due to gravity or you will use your engine to move where you want. Engines, body and guns can be chosen between a set for a high number of combinaitons of planes, each with his own name, look and soundtrack.
The mechanic of the gameplay is all about balance: you can always fire your engine, but for tight manouvers you will need to turn it off and take it on again, which means that the timing of when you turn off your engine is as important as the time you use it. In this game you will take a lot of damage, but the the plane reparis automatically when you don't shoot your gun, so it is also important to chose when and when not to fire you gun.
The style is minimalistic, but well executed nad the soundtrack is trance inducing, totally fit for the game. Enemy types are rather limited, so you will be fighting the same ones over and over, but their appearence is randomized, making every game play more of the same.
After you unlocked all of the plane parts the only reason to keep you playing will be score improvement and goals, so if you are the kind of player who cares about scoreboard you may get tired of it soon.
In conclusion Luftrauser is a simple arcade game, extremely well executed which is great in short burst of playing, but can only be considered a good purchase if you agree from the beginning to the premise that there is not really anything more than what you see. I wish there was more to it, but what is there...is Great!

LUFTRAUSERS is a game that I love, but will probably never be good at, thanks to it's propelled ship gameplay that is similar to Asteroids, where instead of directly moving the ship like a twin-stick shooter, you pivot the ship and then thrust when needed while it is in constant free fall. Your ship can take some damage before death and will even heal itself if not hit. You will maintain your current damage if you shoot, so you may want to stop your firing if you are damaged.  You must manage your movement to avoid the sea and cloude damage zone, as well as damage from enemy vessels and weapons. The sea and clouds can damage you, but not directly kill you and eventually force your ship out back in to the playfield - allowing for tactics such as hiding from bullets or running into water craft, since your ship can take some damage depending on your ship customization. An enemy kill increases a score multiplier that will go away after a few seconds after no kills and will max out at 20x. You have one life, and once you die, your run is over.
Ship customization is important - it determines how much damage you take, how fast you move, how you shoot, and other interesting abilities such as having an engine that moves by shooting bullets behind you or a Nuke body that destroys multiple enemies when you die on your run. This also changes the music track of your run, as every possible ship combination has it's own unique and/or remixed chiptune-esque track.
The game is run based like a rogue-lite, so expect to die often and try different ship configs for potentially more success. However, each ship configuration has it's own goals such as killing a certain amount of enemies, getting a certain amount of points , or just lasting long enough.  Completing goals will unlock more parts for you to mess around with.

After logging a great many hours in the soldier front universe, and restarting from scratch after a computer failure on this one, I have yet to nail down my official opinion. Now there are a great many pros and cons to SF2. The first pro and one of my personal favorites, is astetic gear that affects your stats. You may buy armor and look like a walking kevlar pillar (almost) but that's going to slow down your movement speed, as will the size of your gun. On the flip side of the coin, you can go without any protection, and in return run like forest gump in his football days. But alas, if you take more than a random bullet at a time, you will not survive to eat ice cream and become a ping pong champion. But I digress. Small gear items increase something called your luck factor, that goes into getting these things called lucky shot kills. It's kind of like a critical in an RPG, but it doesn't really do extra damage so much as it rewards extra xp for that kill (which is actually kind of rewarding oddly).
After that you have your armory selection, new players get a small selection of M4 or AK. Which boils down to "do you prefer capitalism or are you a soviet communist?" in my opinion. However to start you do get your selection of many different avatars from different special operations units from around the world, and I mean THE WORLD... You can be an operative from the U.S., U.K., Russia, France, South Korea (the good ones, not the ones with the ACME rockets), Mexico, and... I believe Germany but don't quote that part fully, because I went with good old delta when I started, and never really looked back (Murica, I know). Anyway, getting back onto the weapons, they really did do their homework on this one, weapons behave like thier real world parents would. However the con side to this is that one must start leveling up violently in order to unlock these weapons for purchase, then you have to pay in game or pay wall points in order to buy them and in game money can get really tight really easy, and the good guns are kind of pricey, so be warned, choose your gun purchases carefully my friends.
Now to break down game play. While some parts of it can be extremely smooth, I find one minor annoyance, you can't go prone, only crouch. So to any developer that reads this, if you guys want to be taken seriously and keep up with all the major COD, BF, MOH labels, you should have all the physical abilities that they offered. The reason they succeed (other than being major sellouts to modern marketing) is that they know part of the excitement of being a support gunner or sniper is dropping down and sawing through, or having max stability when going for headshots on your opponents. It's the little things sometimes that can make or break players opinions on games, the lack of prone position, is one of my pet peeves that seems to plague most FTP shooters. And I pray one day it gets patched in every single one. Anyway, suggestion made, rant over.
The controls are simple, easy, and customizable so brownie points there. The system has really no kill cam to speak of, so fans and haters of the kill cam, think of that what you will. What I do like, is that there is a small respawn delay in death match modes which allows you to stop and think a second when you want to switch your weapon classes (you get up to 3), and you can pay a minor toll of chump change of in game money to skip this wait period if you're feeling impatient. The toll is 30 SP, so like I said chump change if you can discipline yourself to only doing this a few times a match, I find one if you can help it, or just don't waste the money, because if you can keep from the temptation of paying for instant respawn it will save you from potentially having that gamblers moment of clarity where you've dumped all your money in a day, and you realize you have a problem with impulse spending. But again, I digress.
One other con I have personally experienced is bugs and crashes, it's haunted me a few times now and I can't decide if it's actually the game or just my old rig, the dilema being, I can run other games without issue what so ever, but this one and a few others that are and aren't favorites of mine seem to have formed this inner circle of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off by choosing not to work smoothly. Anyway, make sure you're running securely with this game, and it wouldn't hurt to have a reasonably new computer.
Pro, level rewards. When you level you get these random stuff packages that include gear and guns that last from a day up to a couple of weeks depending on the item. And if you put in the time, you can level pretty rapidly. Additionaly they have weekly challenges that reward pretty well, and are fairly easy to achieve. So you don't have to be stuck with only your starter gun, or the one gun you bought for weeks at a time. Which is a very smart and creative move on the developers part, so good job on that one guys.
Over all we have here what I like to call the hidden almost-gem. It's not super out there and popular, but it's got lots of players. It's good, but not the best shooter you've ever played I reckon. However it has features and perks that will have you coming back to it. It makes you feel rewarded for the time you put into it. The more you play, the more it gives back to you. There are going to be people on it that you can get along with, maybe even befriend on a personal level, and there are your social rotten eggs as well, but those guys aren't worth getting that upset over in my opinion. It runs good and is fairly pretty and polished for a free to play. It's got a lot going for it, and it has potential.
My un-official verdict for the time being then is as such, try it out, and if you did because of my review please comment, message, or somehow let me know what you think so I can polish my review.
In the mean time, thanks for reading.

The Longest Journey is back after so many years of waiting, and i couldn't be happier to experience it again, i played both The Longest Journey and Dreamfall when they came out years ago and i got hooked on the fantastical but mature story, the awesome characters and the comedy (oh my god the comedy, despite some dark events TLJ and Dreamfall never ceased being funny and witty and to a great effect.
Now let's see what we have here, the long awaited continuation of the Dreamfall story, Zoe's story, i can't deny i'm a big fan of April and adore her character but Zoe too grew on me, not as much as April but she has her charm too (sadly her sweet accent from Dreamfall is absent her due to VA change but no big deal really as the voice acting overall is still fantastic), the story of Dreamfall Chapters picks up right where Dreamfall:TLJ left us hanging, and it is clear that that the graphics got a major upgrade (which is always welcome, and it was funny when i saw they called the highest graphics option "Awesome" instead of Ultra or something else boring, that was funny XD), Zoe looks a little different after spending some time in the realm of dreams but it's good to see her again and resolve her dilemma early on instead of dragging it on and on.
Now the real highlight is the gameplay, gone are the clunky combat/stealth sequences from Dreamfall:TLJ and now the game actually evolved and adapted new mechanics from the best storytellers in gaming now (hint hint, yeah Telltales), and i love they added their own spin to the mechanics, first you can hear the character's own thoughts before you pick a dialog choice .. not only does it give a chance for the voice actors to further flesh out the characters but also gives us insight into their mindsets, there is also the fact they highlight the important critical choices that will impact the story and let you know what other players chose before you pick your choice ... also .. i was surprised to see The Witcher 2 level of boldness where they block and entire section of the game based on a choice you make early on (now that's some consequence i'd like to see more often, but it's probably why some people might think the episode was short), oh .. and the witty humor that made the TLJ games so much fun is back .. loads of it .. Zoe now is reaching April's level of wittiness with snarky remarks and snappy witty jokes which is great since we don't get much of April in ep1 (won't spoil it more than that), IMO the length of the episode is spot on and the back and forth between Kian and Zoe was nice for sake of variety ... some people are complaining about lack of complex puzzles but i have to disagree, the puzzles here are simple and story relevant in a good way, so while i kinda enjoyed the tough puzzles of The Longest Journey some of them were too hard and ruined the pacing of the game when you spent too much time trying to figure out how to solve them .. i managed to finish them all without any online guides (except one early puzzle that required some pixel hunting), so i'm glad the focus is on the story this time, if i wanted to play a puzzle game i'd go play Portal 2 or The Talos Principle.
Oh, and there is that sweet surprise at the end, although only players of TLJ will know its full significance and recognize the location but either way it's still very intriguing and interesting section that i didn't expect at all .. adds lots of mystery and makes me so eager to play the next episode.
+The return of one of the best adventure games out there, Telltales have a serious competitor now.
+Lovely graphics and attention to details that makes exploring the world a real joyful video/audio experience.
+Fantastic top notch Voice acting and music.
+Evolved dialog/choice story driven gameplay, simple puzzles that don't get in the way of the story.
+Moves the story onward resolving plot points while also leaving Lots of mystery and anticipation for the fans to speculate on.
-Some minor graphical hiccups and frame-rate drops
-It is better if you play the previous games first as some of things might not make sense.
Overall i'm very satisfied with the first episode and didn't regret buying this one bit, specially after waiting for so many years to continue the story, go buy it and do yourself a favor and play the older games as well, despite any problems they have (first game looking outdated, and 2nd game having some cumbersome mechanics) they are still excellent adventure games and a truly an forgettable journey.

**********Original Review***************
As a huge fan of the Dreamfall series I have been really looking forward to playing the newest installment.  The beginning of the game allows you to watch a recap of what happened in the last game, which was a really great refresher. The first hour of this game is great! It’s fascinating and fun, and it made me even more excited about seeing this story unfold….. Unfortunately I was disappointed with the rest of the chapter (about 6 hours worth).
Chapter 1 disappointments:
The lighting/reflections in the town of Propast are driving me insane! My eyes actually hurt while playing because what should be a subtle reflection from a red light is a glaring big red box through parts of the city.  I have a screenshot saved on my profile for an example.
I know it's the standard for a point and click adventure, but I'm really tired of running around the city grabbing my boyfriend’s lunch, buying wine, etc. I've been expecting this rich dramatic story like the earlier games...and it started off great but the last few hours of this chapter were pretty dull.
I LOATH THIS MAP WITH A PASSION.   It’s pretty easy to get lost in the beginning, so you’ll definitely need a map to help you. You don’t get a “use anytime” map, you have to use map stations around this city.  I would have preferred it differently, but that’s okay.  The thing I HATE is the “rootin’ tootin’ cowboy map is extremely annoying. Every single time you use one you have to let it finish its little speech. That’s bad enough, but trying to navigate using the map is even worse! It's just of couple of various colored blocks...looks like it was made in MS paint. It's hard to read and rarely helps you get around.  I suggest you just go online and print out a LABELED map to use. It's still akward to read, but you'll save yourself about an hour of mindlessly running around trying to find your next destination.
I do have hope for this game. I'm not giving up on it...but until I play a chapter that offers more story and less aggravation, I cannot recommend it.

I am a big fan of the series, however after the 1st chapter I am not impressed. I only recommend this game because it is promising so much, but the first chapter is quite short (4 hours) and unconvincing.
I remember how after minutes of the Longest Journey demo (back in 2000) I was totally absorbed by the game, it grabbed me from the beginning - the talking tree, April, everything made you care or curious right from the start.
In Chapter 1 we start where Dreamfall ended, which is good, because I always felt that Dreamfall ended abruptly. However, I found the politics plot of this Chapter quite boring. In April's times, Stark had also funny parts (remember the detective or the rubber ducky), but this time it is just dark, dystopian and dull, it doesn't surprise with anything.
I am sorry to say but after the 1st chapter I don't feel anything for the characters, which is a big letdown, TLJ series made you feel involved. Even the choice/consequence system, which is a great feature, doesn't make me feel more involved. The story so far is thin and the characters sketchy. The only character I liked on Stark in this chapter, worthy of the series, was the lady on the boat.
I also don't like the fact that most characters swear a lot, unnecessary a lot.
The part that I liked was the Arcadia bit. That's the world I want to see more, that's the place that made me love the series, not the dull slums of Stark. So I am hoping to see more of it.
The graphics are quite good, but the drawback is that you need good hardware to play this game which started as a point and click adventure. Also, I don't like the interaction system, it reminds me of action games and it just gets in the way of exploring the details in an area. Which brings me to the quest/goals system.
The action is linear, you get a quest (goal) like in an role playing game and you go from here to there like an errand boy (girl). So much for exploring. You don't need to explore and interact when everything points you towards your goal. The 1st chapter ended much to quickly. I finished the game after four hours, and my reaction was like "come on, that was all"?
I know that more and more games are using episodes to deliver the game, but in Dreamfall's case it is a bad idea. The time between episodes will just disconnect me from the story, it feels like spliting a movie in 5 and watching a bit every month.

Let me start with this: I love Civ Rev.
If that statement alone makes you recoil in disgust, walk away from Starships and this review. I didn't come to this game looking for the depth that VI and V offer--or an experience which would redeem BE (I disliked it in fact). Instead I looking for something that can scratch that X-COMy, Pirates!-y, and straightforward Civ Rev itch which this game handily satisfies.
Bonust points: Really reminds me of the 4x tabletop game, Eclipse--gathering resources, upgrading planets--extending your influence. Also a simiilar 'rubberband'  (escalating cost worker placement) mechanic keeps you from expanding too far too fast in the form of your crew's fatigue level. If you undertake too many missions, or travel too far your combat effectiveness plummets. There are ways to extend your crew's fatigue, but at the cost of resources which could be better spent improving the planets you control.
The game also does a fine job during missions as well. The battles are fast paced and satisfying, even addictive. I often find myself absentmindedly going on another mission when I already decided that the last one was the last one.
Penalties:
They drop the ball in many places. To start, graphically, there's an appreciable difference between stylized and cartoony, and this game veers toward the latter. There's also ample room for imagination in the implemetation of weapon effects, and many missed opportunities to really differentiate the ship classes between affinities. The affinites are basically skin deep, and only add a starting bonus to the civ that chooses it. Another missed opportunity for depth is laying out the actual armament and defenses of your ships, ala Eclipse. There's no 'energy' cost however, for upgrading aside from the resource itself. Hence, with enough resources your could put every upgrade on one ship since there's no energy cap. Even FTL figured out a good balance in this regard.
This game isn't for eveyone but if you found anything I said forgivable or intriguing--for $15 dollars--this game is worth it.

At first this game seemed like a fun and different take on tower defense though in no way groundbreaking. Then the difficulty after the first few levels ramped up so I had to grind on earlier levels to earn money to level my characters and towers. Then I realized the balancing is terrible. You have heroes and towers you can level up, but if you level up a tower it becomes more expensive so if you level it too high then it may even become practically unusable, especially on earlier levels. Not to mention the towers are generally garbage compared to your heroes. In late levels the only real use they have is to slow enemies down - killing any enemy with a tower that has not also been hit by your hero is very unlikely.
The game does a fair amount of the fundamentals of TD right enough that it really makes you realize that the difference between a mediocre game and a great game is often in the small details. Let's explore what else makes MKS medicre instead of even good with a question you never asked:
How do you progress in the game? Grind grind grind. It was not fun. I played the same level over and over again early in the game maybe 50 times so I could upgrade my weapon. I'm not proud of it. By the end of the game I found that the third to last level is the best to grind on as you can usually get blue gems and a red gem each time you play it. Those blue gems can then be spent to get way more gold than any end of level bonus will give you. So then you grind on that level 50 - 80 times because you are now so invested in beating this sucker and getting all the achievements that you just keep going.
You turn on the grind level (with the Bull boss), set up your defenses and Monkey King location then read on your phone while occasionally looking up to see if there are any blue gem treasure chests that need to be destroyed. You learn a lot about the presidential race. Finally all your characters and towers are overpowered (by human standards) and you realize that the last two achievements are impossible to get, not just "I didn't put in an obscene amount of effort or time" impossible but actually impossible. You have to score 15000 on a level and 50000 on a level. On the last level on the hardest difficulty the highest score you could get was around 9000.
Now you're upset (pretending that you weren't also upset before) and don't even really want to write a review for this game. But seeing as you have sunk so many hours into it, you feel like you should warn other tower defense addicts to stay away. It won't make you feel better. Your friends and family are worried about you.

I heard a lot of good things about Tales of Symphonia but I heard a lot of good things about college too and guess how that turned out.  Also, expect spoilers here.  I'm not interested in saving story in a bad review.
In Tales of Symphonia, you play Lloyd who is a good natured slacker during his journey to restore his dying planet.  His friend,
Collette is the one actually in charge of it but every main heroine needs her guardians nearby to protect her. Lloyd sucks at this as Collette gets kidnapped about five times but there are six other people who didn't help either so it’s not totally his fault.
The story starts off reminding me too much of Final Fantasy X (which probably stole its story from somewhere else, to be fair). The woman dressed in white's destiny is to save the world and needs a bunch of people to protect her as she ventures from holy place to holy place and, in the end, dies only for a temporary peace. Also, the religion is total BS and fake and racism is cool. It breaks from FFX when you travel to another world and uncover the mysteries of why the two worlds are connected. There are an abundance of plot twists, some of which are pretty obvious if you’re being cynical because you’re not having fun.  There are so many twists that even the game developers forgot a few of them.  Like the major plot point 10 hours in where the wife of the mayor is a monster who gets free and is never seen again despite the fact she seemed pretty important.  Or the kidnapped store clerk who allows herself to be kidnapped again because she hates you and then spends the next 25 hours in jail despite you being able to free her, pretty much whenever.  And when you do free her, your actions cause her family, to whom you promised the safe return of their daughter, to die and then she disappears from the game.  At least I think they die, it’s not mentioned again even in passing.  A lot of points seem major but end up being meaningless quickly.  Like the sacrifice of that one guy, or the giant world destroying cannon, where’d the Pope go, or why is the legendary hero a 12 year old?  I guess there is the sequel...
Moving on…  As you venture, you meet your assorted cast of characters.  All of whom are terrible.  Besides the downright stupid MC Lloyd and Princess Peach wannabe Collette, you have the white mage who’s abusive to her black mage brother (and the only good character). The stuck up paladin. The ninja summoner who sucks at everything. The suave debonair who might be a child molester.  You also have the emotionless little girl who carries a giant axe and the convict who turns out to be rich.  That's just their personalities. Once you get in battle, everyone sucks.  Lloyd, Genis, and Raine are great. Kratos and Child Groomer are decent since they can do basic heals but Regal, Presea, and Sheena are too slow to be effective fighters on their own. In the case of the first two, they hit hard enough and are tanky enough to warrant taking the fourth slot over the paladin's but Sheena is a waste of a character.  She's slow, has a long windup on her attack and is squishy.  Ninja summoner sounds so cool, too. She shows her bra the entire game so if you’re into that, well, she's legal so good news!
While we're on the topic of battles.  Did you know you can get stuck in a corner of a circular battlefield?  You see, while the game is “3D”, the axis are decided by the enemies and you can’t go up or down (background or foreground) on the y-axis, only the bad guys can.  If they turn then you can change your alignment but otherwise, you’re stuck.  Often, you can jump over the mobs but the taller ones can stun lock you in a corner (of a circle). It is needlessly frustrating and makes a few early bosses take more tries than necessary. Also, for some reason, it's impossible to make your mages get away from the boss with their massive AOE spell thus dooming your entire team because your white mage needed to get her staff hits in today.  The good news is she'll fill in for your actual attackers who run off all the time, anyway.  Again, needlessly frustrating.  The excessive blocking is another needlessly frustrating mechanic.  Pressing square/X allows your characters to block and lake less damage.  Do it for too long and it gets broken and you’re stunned leaving yourself open to crit hits.  Enemies can also block (even those for whom it doesn’t make sense for), for much longer, and don’t get stunned IF you break them. They can also block when you’re in the middle of a combo.  So that iconic four hit/sword rain combo you love?  Much less effective a large chunk of time.
Moving on to the less gameplay focused stuff:
The music is by
of Star Ocean, Golden Sun, and the other Tales of games fame.  As well as some Mario sports games, Dark Souls, and at least one of the Smash Bros Brawl games.  You’ve probably heard his work without realizing it since he doesn’t get the credit he deserves sometimes.  The games OST is four disks and, while there’s nothing super memorable (at least so someone who hates this game), is fairly good.  It’s hard to describe music to most people so here’s an
preview/review.
Graphics seemed to have gotten a slight overhaul (as the steam version is based off the PS3 version) or I underappreciated the GameCube's engine.  Some of the cooler cutscenes are top notched anime and, even 15 years later, look amazing.
Sound quality is..odd.  When it comes to voice overs, it almost sounds like they recorded in different rooms with different mics quality.  While most, usually, sound fine, Collette and some minor characters sound like they were recorded on a budget.
While the story isn't terrible and the puzzles are only mildly annoying, I don’t know if the game just hasn't aged well or if people only liked it because it’s the only RPG the GameCube had but it’s not a good game.  Getting stuck on random edges of paths would suffice to that.  It took me 60 hours to beat, sometimes with a guide, so there’s plenty of bang for your buck But that 60 hours can drag on far too long and is filled with terrible characters and lost plots.  If ToS is the best the GameCube has, then I’m glad I skipped it.  Don’t hate the game because it’s capped at 30 FPS, don’t play the game because, while I can see the charm and nostalgia feel too it, its lacking a lot of substance and meaning.

Jewel of its time - an incredible story with intricate gameplay and a fun combat system.
I thought that 13 years on, after playing the Elder Scrolls series, Witcher 3 and all manner of Final Fantasy games, that I would find it difficult to return to Tales of Symphonia and replay a classic from my childhood. But I found it to be surprisingly immersive and enjoyable, not once did I feel like I was just pressing through trying to get through it for the sake of completion.
The storyline is my favorite thing about this game, I absolutely love sinister yet beautiful narratives with deep character arks and hints of romance, and this game hit that nail on the head. The combat is very fun, you have lots of options to customize it throughout the game, and on top of that you can play as different characters you meet too. The soundtrack is okay, some of the best tracks are towards the end of the game.
Now onto some criticisms. The thing I hate most about this game is its back and forth elements. I have been infuriated countless times with how time consuming the puzzles are in Dungeons. You will find yourself saying "What in the name of Martel were the developers thinking with this?". This isn't some Legend of Zelda style dungeon tediousness, no, this is a whole new level of ebola to which the likes have never been seen... even by Final Fantasy Ten.
In conclusion, you should absolutely buy this game if you have a small amount of money to spare and a love for adventure games like this. With the amount of hours you're likely to put into this game, you're getting more than your moneys worth.

Lords of Shadow 2 is an improvement upon the original in every way. Regardless of how one feels about the architecture of the 'new world' versus the classic macabre, renaissance atmosphere that is a staple of the series, it can't be argued that the game doesn't look absolutely gorgeous.
The combat is improved greatly, as is that horribly static camera angle that gave so many of us unnecessary troubles (that has now been modified to be a completely movable, 360-degree camera). The PC version's upgraded graphics settings are highly appreciated to those of us that have the means to run it. Even then it's not the most demanding game for video cards and being an older engine, it still makes use of every technique in the book to give the game a next-gen look.
The story itself is expanded and the lore is explored heavily; it's recommended that you play at least the first LoS game to get a decent grip on the storyline, but the prologues and 'follow ups' are perfectly acceptable to rely on. If you know the storyline already, then not much needs to be said, it the sequel we've been waiting for an a truly gorgeous take on Dracula's story along with the Belmont clan in general.
The music took me by surprise with this one. The original did a lot of harkening back to older Caslevania staples and did a lot of newer approaches to that old Gothic vibe. LoS2 does a great job at feeling like a standalone title and that shines the most through the music; it still feels like a Castlevania, but touches and nuances to certain tracks (techno-vibes for the future, classic organs for the past) make it feel fresh. There's some really beautiful tracks in this soundtrack.
All in all this isn't the Castlevania I've been fawning for over the years since the series has gone 3D; I still pine for a classic HD/pseudo-3D/2D 'Metroidvania' title. But this has proven that the series can at least work in the 3D realm. Improvements are necessary, and they've done enough to prove to me that 3D Castlevania can not only work, but flourish. It's not a perfect game and there's a few hiccups in both the gameplay and story, but it'd be nitpicking to say that these tiny aspects took away from my mainly thoroughly (and still in-progress) journey through the dilapidated castles and the sprawling wasteland of the futuristic, yet still familiar gothic city.

Castelvania: Lords of Shadow 2 is a wonderful ride from start to finish, with very few road bumps along the way. If you're a fan of action games, exploration games, or loved the first Lords of Shadow, there is plenty here to be happy about. However, if you were NOT a fan of the first game, there is little reinventing of the wheel here to pull you into the franchise.
Gameplay: 8/10
The exploration from the modern areas to the realm of Dracula's Castle is fluid. Dracula moves very intuitively, response time is great, and once the game really starts to open up its areas you really get this sense of a large scale fluid world. The negative here would be the platforming, or lack there of. Platforming in LOS2 is mostly just wall climbing from grapple to grapple. It can feel a little dull at times.
Combat: 9/10
The combat system from the first Lords of Shadow returns, but with a HUGE overhaul. It has been streamlined to perfection in almost every area. The pace at unlocking skills feels perfect, the variety of Dracula's weapons is interesting enough to keep combat feeling fresh, and the combinations of moves Dracula can perform make combat easily the most enjoyable experience of LOS2.
Story: 8/10
Continuing where LOS1's ending left off, the story of LOS2 is a great epic. There are moments in the story that had me jaw drop, the highs are fantastically done. However, there are low points. There are a few twists that you can see happening a mile away that occur, and there are two specific points in the story that really bring down the overall score. Without spoiling for those who haven't played, the two negatives I attribute to story are in the case of a character being VASTLY underused, and the game's ending.
Music: 9/10
It's awesome. Orchestral awesomeness. The somber tones, the high symphonies, everything. It's not classic Castlevania, but it deserves praise all its own.
Graphics (PC): 8/10
Even if there is occasional tearing and the odd lightning hear and there, LOS2 is very pleasing to look at. The game looks great.
Other notes: As many have read, there are *stealth* sections in this game. I am not even going to dignify them to allow a drop in score, because they are NOT broken, NOR are they impossible. They slightly disrupt the flow of the game in some parts, but if you utilize ALL of your abilities (Shadow Daggers, Bats, Mist form, Possession) and use your brain, these sections are laughably easy. The most infamous response to these sections have been from Kotaku, who's reviewer got stuck on one particular section for FOUR hours. I completed the same section in less than two minutes. Use your abilities, and these sections are trivial.
Overall: 8.75/10
LOS2 is a great game that is sadly being underplayed by major media sources. It is NOT game of the year, sure, but this is a solid title that can stand on its own and a wonderful edition to the Castlevania franchise. Mercury Steam should be proud of LOS2, because they made a good game. I enjoyed my 14 hour playthrough, and will continue to play it for 100% and achievements.

You now have a free roaming camera; This makes sense, as whilst the game world is stil split into distinct areas, you have the freedom (of a kind) to move between them as you see fit, and having a free camera lets you search around levels for all of those secret hideaways and stashes. As I just mentioned, the game world this time round is a much more open one. There are a ton of secrets and upgrades to find. Some of the things that made some people dislike LoS return, though they aren't deal breakers (platforming is still ropey and sometimes you think (can) jump to ledges only to "bounce" off them and fall into some lava or a pit and have to restart your platforming. The game starts off slowly but then builds pace nicely. The combat is almost identical to LoS (no bad thing).
There are however some annoying things; "cheap" shots by enemies that are way off screen, unlbockable and sometimes un-dodgeable attacks and the way enemies will keep you in their fight area if you try to run/climb your way out of a fight. Most annoying.
Seeing as this game is around £40-£50 on consoles I would definitely recommend getting on PC. Grab yourself an Xbox controller, ram up the graphics settings, sit back and enjoy another lengthy epic adventure (with minor quibbles (and they ARE minor)) with Gabriel Belmont AKA Dracula.
Considering how EPIC the finale of LoS was, I can't wait to see how this one (as the end of the LoS storyline) pans out.

This game has left me wondering, whether the developer rushed its release.
There are really nice animations, beautifully crafted backdrops and a decent story filled with betrayal.
Even the achievement hunters and item gatherers are provided for by optional achievements and notes that are scattered throughout the game.
Combine those features with some kind of spirit walk, similar to Prey's spirit mechanism, and you can hardly go wrong...
...or so I'd thought.
This game is qute enjoyable up to about 50% to 60%, when there is suddenly no longer any real clue as to what to do.
Up until then, there was always some diary entry or ghost that would give you a rough hint about what the game expected you to do next.
This changes all of a sudden when the game introduces enemies that wll kill you with one "hit" or touch.
And they are invisible most of the time, quite happily killing you again and again while you are devising some kind of plan to avoid them.
The most agonizing example is a sort of spider / headcrab thing that can only be seen when there is some kind of steam or rain touching it - or when you invoke your ghost form and your ghostly self is near the creature.
My favorite part (spot the irony) is when you are ripped of your powers in the game's final part and have to rely on those water sources alone, to make the creature visible.
There is one room, where that mechanism is introduced, where one single spider is crawling along the ceiling.
However, there are only few sources of steam to uncover it - our protagonist spawns perfectly timed and, should she run straight ahead, will die every single time without even seeing the creature.
She just falls to her knees and the level resets...
After enduring several rooms of similar design, I decided that I will not finish this game.
To sum it up, there are some really nice elements but the last half of the game decides to favor strange mechanisms over its story.
PS.: If you would like to get those achievements, then do NOT play in offline mode!
Although most games have been patched to grant you those hard-earned achievements the next time you log in and start the game, this is not one of those games.

What can be said about Dark Souls that hasn't been said a million times already. You know what you've heard about the game, and might be on the edge on whether to buy it. So with that in mind, here are a few things to know about the game:
1. Difficulty - This game is very, very, VERY difficult, especially when you're just getting started. It's in the title, "Prepare to Die", because you will die a lot. But the deaths in this game are a bit different than the deaths in some other game; different in one key factor: they're fair. Any time you die, it's your fault. It might be because you didn't block when you needed to, or you misjudged a dodge-roll, but the game isn't to blame for you dying. There was a guy who played through the whole thing with a guitar hero controller for Pete's sake, you think you're little "the game didn't block when I told it to block" or whatever argument is gonna work? Just keep tanking through everything and learn. Learn to read the enemy.
2. Explanation - This is one shortcoming of the game that I will allow critics: the game does not do any handholding. There is next to no explanation for anything, and after you get out of the tutorial level the game just kind of shrugs and goes "do whatever, I don't care". What's does the stability stat on a shield do? How does bleed damage work? Where do I go now? These are questions just about every new player asks. Don't feel bad about looking up anything you don't understand, we all did.
3. Lore/story - This is another point I will give to critics. Dark Souls gives almost zero exposition past the opening cutscene. In fact, I can probably count the number of cutscenes in the game on 2 hands. Character storylines come and go quickly, and it can be very easy to never finish a character's arc or even never meet them in the first place. There is no do-over button either. If you mess up a character's story, you either have to start over or go all the way through NG+ to try again. And any world-building you might want comes largely from item description text dumps. But that just lets the player get into it so much more, invent their own story. You are a sole undead, one among masses. Your only distinction is your unwillingness to go hollow. Will you be a righteous pillar of hope, smiting foes with spears of lightning? Or perhaps a lowly brigand, content with lying in the shadows and slaughtering any NPC for their supplies. Possibly an evil Darkwraith invading other players for their humanity. Which actually brings me to my last point.
4. PvP - I'll get this out of the way from the start: I don't like PvP. I don't play PvP games, I don't PvP my friends, it's always single player or co-op games for me. With that being said, Dark Souls is probably my favorite form of forced PvP: largely avoidable with trolls galore. Out of 100 invasions, I'd say it boils down to about 50 want to fairly fight, 25-30 want to win by any means necessary regardless of how exploit-y, and the remaining being a combination of helpful people who give you items, themed opponents who are just fun to fight against, win or lose, and trolls being ridiculous. I'll never forget the time I was visited by the fashion police, twas' beautiful and hilarious. Back to my main point, it's also avoidable. If you don't want PvP, remain a hollow. Simple as that. "But I want to do summons": then you're also getting invaded. Humanity is a double-edged sword. And if it really bothers you, go offline. No one wants to fight a crybaby....well some might.
TL:DR Dark Souls is a very good, very well put together game. It has some faults, but they are vastly overshadowed by the games strengths. And never, EVER criticize the game online. You will be bashed with so many "git gud"s it'll be hard to spell "get good" the right way ever again.

Ah, Dark Souls. So often lauded as one of the greatest games ever made, a classic in the eyes of many. To that I must say, they are most certainly blind! Dark Souls is, to put it frankly, a derivative mess. This poorly constructed, unfinished game is a testament to the fact that as long as a game flies in the face of artistic progress in video games it will be received as a masterpiece. Look at any game that is bestowed the moniker of "the Dark Souls of" its genre for further examples.
We humans, we play games to relax. We play games to escape the state of things, which is no more poignant under our new administration. Dark Souls totally fails to provide a relaxing and comforting atmosphere for players, rather it chooses to complicate simple tasks, like combat, and make it the focal point of the game. Rather than engage players, Dark Souls chooses to make us feel uncomfortable and disheartened. This is not what games are about. I am told this game has a great story, but I am yet to see any evidence of this. In my time I have encountered only three cutscenes of any substance. That, in 2017, is simply not good enough. That wasn't good enough even in 2011 when the game was originally released. I was not at all engrossed, I was given no direction, and I was thoroughly frustrated by this mere game. Games are art, but Dark Souls does not help that argument one bit. I am saddened that this game is seen as such a cultural touchstone in gaming, because it isn't. It is a relic of a bygone area that should stay bygone. I would recommend this only to ''Gamers'' who think substance equates to longform drivel about their misunderstanding of contemporary artistic movements in the medium of video games.

SiN Episodes: Emergence is the sequel to the original SiN, unfortuenately this is the first and last episode in a planned seven episode series, so this game is short and is also sadly the last SiN game.
The game is a big departure from the original game, first of all your character John. R Blade, because now he is a silent protagonist, this wouldn't be a problem if it wasn't his speech and acts that made him great, instead your new sidekick (aka: Alex Vance ripoff): Jessica gets all the chararistics, as for me seeing this was like a slap in the face Blade didn't feel like a badass anymore he is now an empty shell. The second big problems is that the levels felt really linear, there is no paths or decisions that alter the game world like in the original game, you also spend more time in crammed corridors than in big areas like in any other game. The last things wrong about this game is the overall feel, right off the get go if you look at any gameplay footage you'll think this is a Half-Life 2 mod, because Emergence looks unappealing from the bad texture work(which steals most textures and lanscapes from HL2) and the bad animations, characters mostly just move their mouth up and down it's nowhere near as good as Half-Life 2. Last thing to mention is that this game can be repetetive to a lot of people as there is only three weapons, four enemy types in the whole game(being two different grunts and two different mutants)and mostly you are just mowing down enemys, unlike its predecessor which had a lot more!
But enough about my rambiling on how bad this game is, surely there is some redeaming quality about it right? Well yes, there is. The pistol and shotgun feel nice and pumpy, the music is great same goes with the voice acting and it all just feels great.

It's all about the starships, so the scope of the same is small and specific. It's fun-size strategy. Like the candy that is either good or bad depending on how much you wanted to begin with.
Despite real space being very empty, the battle maps are full of asteroids, and wormholes, and that gives you cover and shortcuts to work with so there's more to think about than just who to shoot.
The strategic overworld is important though. In several games I've won every battle but lost the game because an AI won more important battles somewhere else.
Equipping ships isn't quite what I'd hoped for. I was hoping for more precision in the choices. Situations where I could determine that one more level of shields would make a world of difference because that would mean a ship would take three hits to defeat instead of two. Doesn't have that. It's more a general: I need more protection-get more protection. It's the strategic layer that more determines how your ships take shape rather than countering something your enemy has.
The wonders that enhance your fleet and the modules local planets specialize in give you reason to choose one design over another. If a planet offers cheaper armour that would be a reason to choose to use it rather than shields or stealth for defense. A wonder making your torpedoes undetectable would make them a key weapon in your fleet.
The resources your planets provide will determine how you enhance your ships. Excess metal leads to wonders, science to research based bonuses, and energy to bigger fleets with bigger ships. Working with what the game gives you rather than a predetermined plan determines how well you do. This adds to replay in that one game may give you lots of science and cheep fighters but the next offers energy and cannons. You could see this as a loss of choice, if your goal is to find one good strategy and stick with it, but if you'd rather be surprised by and adapt to what you have then this will work for you. We should start calling (tagging?) games like this MacGyver games, because you have to win with not what is the bet tool for the job but, with what you can do with what's at hand.
Can't tell yet how balanced the various options are yet, or if having a design theme is necessary or if you can just have all general purpose ships and be fine.
I've had fun. It's only $15. Probably better on tablet.

Sid Meier's Starships is a classic 4x strategy game, that plays very cleanly, and is very well thought out.  The first thing this game reminds me of is the old Master of Orion series.  It's planetary checkers with a touch of management thrown in.  With starships there is also tactical combat, which is where the player spends the majority of time.  That's fine because this phase of the game is also well balanced.
I sometimes shy away from starting up a Civilization game (been a fan of the series since it's inception) just because I don't always have 3 days to spend to play through my own space epic opera.  Starships has just the right amount of story, drama, combat and fluff to keep me hooked, but I can finish a game in a couple of hours.
By fluff I mean this game has components that draw you into the story.  Each planet has a personality, and each empire mirrors what it's planets produce.  Because you are limited to a single fleet, you become very familiar with which ship has which capabilities, and they become a team you care about.  I find that the intro, the voice acting throughout, and the score really add to the immersion.
While this game does remind me of MOO, I think many improvements in gameplay have been included, such that instead of making this the most complex simulation possible, its actually the most balanced and fun to play one that I've seen.  A single fleet at first seemed like a limitation, but it really only limits how long your turn can last, which means the game progresses quickly and smoothly.  Tehcnology tree is very streamlines, but it just makes it very clear that you need to spend your research points wisely.  Planet management includes one wonder option for some planets, and a standard set of upgrades for everyone.  You choose very quickly how to customize each planet, which for me, means you speed up gameplay.
Tactical combat benefits from slick, randomly generated systems, almost always with a plethora of asteroids to hide behind and navigate through.  Along with each combat, you are usually running a mission of sometype for the local planet, which helps give a purpose to the battle.  There is almost a rock paper scissors between beefy slow dreadnaughts, fast fighters, long range lasers, etc. that combined with random terrain and mission objectives works really well to deliver a unique and changing play environment, while still keeping it familiar with your fleet.  You can customze your ships entirely (at a resource cost of course) so you can build out what you need to defeat a particular foe, or try to hold the upper hand with your technology and wonder advantages.
Overall I'd say Sid Meier's Starships is a great, fast paced, space epic that you don't need a whole weekend to get through.
