This review is written after completing book 1, and comes from the perspective of someone who hasn't finished any of the older games. Yes, in my opinion, this game can be played if you haven't played any of the others. It'll take you some time to get into it, but eventually events and things will make sense to you. Obviously it'll be easier if you did play the games though. (I won't discuss any specific spoilers.)
I've heard many good things about the games, and when I found out that this game was coming out, I decided to check it out. I like games with an interesting story and choices that will affect how you as a player will experience it.
The first thing I noticed about the game before I played it, is that two of the three playable characters are poc, persons of color. Now that wouldn't matter so much if they weren't good characters to begin with. Fortunately, Zoë and Kian are interesting characters. I have more to say about Zoë since the focus of the game was more on her in the first book, but from what I've seen during my time with Kian, he'll have to make tough decisions in later books.
The intro chapter of the first book (which I will refer to by its title, Reborn) was amazing. It (re)introduces you to Zoë, what happened to her, where she is, and where she wants to go (which is a decision made by you). In the first chapter, it already becomes clear that she's unsure of her path in life, which makes her a believable protagonist if you ask me. She loves helping people, finding a good cause to work for and she's witty. Additionally, she struggles, just like you and me.
I thought the last chapters of Reborn were a little dull. It involved running around the town and finishing objectives, and when I realized I was about to finish the chapter, I felt a bit relieved. However, that's not to say that the entire chapter is dull. [Zoë Castillo voice] "Nope. Nope, nope, nope." Like I said, the beginning of Reborn was amazing to me, and throughout the chapter, I've found many little things I thoroughly enjoy. I won't address them here, since I was surprised by them and that's the best way to enjoy something.
The voice acting in this game is mostly right. The protagonists have good voice actors, so I don't have anything to complain there. Here and there, there are characters in the game who have questionable VA's, characters who have voices that don't suit their look. But these are small things that won't bother me in the long run.
I don't know what happened with these games, and how Dreamfall Chapters came to be. All I know is that the community wanted it to be a thing and it absolutely deserves the praise it gets. Set in a beautiful world you can (mostly) interact with, believable protagonists, an absolutely enchanting soundtrack... if you like this sort of game, please don't hesitate. I believe in the choices I made so far, and Dreamfall Chapters did a good job of reminding me that they will all have consequences... and that I will have to face them soon.
I can't wait.

Where to begin with this gem. Tales of Symphonia would have to be one of my most favorite games of all time. I dumped well over 1000 hours on the Gamecube version I burrowed from a friend, finished the story multiple times and still love this game to bits. When the game was first released on Steam, I held off on buying it just incase it was a poor port, which sadly it was. But since it's release, the game has been patched multiple times to the point where I felt comfortable that the port wouldn't ruin my memories of this game, and decided to buy it and I'm glad I did as I've had next to no issues with the port.
While the graphics are a bit dated by todays standards, the rest of what the game has to offer more then makes up for it. Apart from the story, which is amazing, the music for this game is astonishing. I go back to listen to many of the tracks from the game. The combat still feels very solid, though sadly you can't take full advantage of the 3D combat plane (Even though NPC's do).
While I could go on about this game for hours, I feel it'll be better to simplify down my views on this classic port.
Pros:
-Great Story
-Amazing Music
-Solid Port
-Tons of Replayability
-Option of ENG and JAP voice's (Unsure of the JAP quality as I've always used ENG)
-Customizable Controls (For both Controller and Keyboard)
Cons:
-No free run in combat
-Dated graphics by todays standards
-The Camera on the world map is horrible
Also, I feel the need to state a small technical issue, even with altered volume levels (in my case, turned down) theres a Fanfare that plays when obtaining an importent item and other events which still plays at default volume. There maybe a fix for it, but it doesnt bother me enough to look for it, nor is it bad enough to be considered a Con.
Overall, I give this port of a classic game a 9/10

Disclaimer: Played close to the end of its Early Access phase.
Do you remember the original Phantasy Star's dungeons? Or maybe Shining In The Darkness? Or that old Windows 98 screensaver of the maze? StarCrawlers is an RPG with optional roguelike elements where the dungeons take on that same first-person perspective through dungeons that only permit travel in cardinal directions. Build up a squad of characters in a futuristic setting and get powers ranging from eldritch tentacles of doom, to covering a screen in explosives and/or explosions, to constantly making enemies trip over the traps you've laid.
Each character has three separate skill trees that you can mix-and-match as you please, and there are 8 characters (of which you can take 4 on any given mission even if you recruit extras) so there's lots of potential for replayability, even before you account for the extra difficulty settings and optional permadeath. The randomized loot is plentiful enough that you generally get good stuff for your characters, and nobody is locked to particular types of equipment so you can't get completely useless equipment.
A fantastic game and a very creative re-imagining of an old genre, updated with modern graphics and the ability to free-look and interact with your environment. Highly recommended, although you may want to wait for the full release - as it stands the Early Access version does not conclude the story, so you just get to the point where you stop getting story missions (but continue to get procedural random ones).
This game has absolutely beautiful artwork, a compelling story, and a haunting soundtrack. Strongly recommended for any fans of puzzles, ghost stories, and gorgeous art styles. 4/5

Whispering Willows is an intriguing horror/adventure puzzle game that takes cues from Native American lore to bring the "haunted mansion" levels so often seen in RPGs to the forefront of the story. The game is about Elena, a girl whose father went missing and who keeps getting nightmares about his disappearance. Determined to find him, she sets off to the mansion, but it turns out that the Ghostbusters hadn't exactly come here yet. (There's actually an achievement referencing this, so I'm allowed to make that joke! :P)
The best part of Whispering Willows has got to be its aesthetic. I absolutely love the art style of this game; everything is so beautifully rendered, from Elena to her spirit to the environment and all of the buildings and effects. Even torches and fireplaces look absolutely magnificent.
Unfortunately, that's pretty much it for the good. The story is extremely bland; there's no voice acting besides some sounds in the cutscenes, and little is actually said by any of the characters that talk to Elena. She herself doesn't seem to have any lines besides the aforementioned cutscenes. Outside of the intro cutscene, there isn't much to what's going on, and it's just "solve this mystery, now solve this mystery, oh hey someone's chasing you".
The gameplay mechanics are there, but even these are under-utilized. What Whispering Willows allows players to do is take control of Elena's spirit separate from her body, using it to get through tight spaces or possess items or switches to help Elena advance. Unfortunately, this isn't used enough times, and it feels like a gimmick more than anything when you do have to use it. Most of the time it's just used to talk to characters that don't really add much.
Probably the worst part of the game is its pacing. It feels like everything is happening so
... Elena walks too slow, or there's too many corridors, or there's too many levers, or you don't know what to do next because almost nothing is explained to you, or usually a combination of all of that. I was getting really bored really fast. Not to mention, every time I tried to press the SHIFT key to start running and speed things up, Elena turned to me and refused. It's like Elena wants to admire the scenery of human bones more than I do.
It's still regarded as a really good game by the few people who have reviewed it, so don't let my experiences completely shroud your potential of playing this game. Especially if you're looking for something based off of Native American lore; there's plenty of that in the journal entries.

A friend of mine bought this game after I expressed interest in it since the puzzle mechanics looked a lot like the ones in Ghost Trick, and while I did have fun playing the game, there were some difficulties to be had with it.
**SPOILERS AHEAD**
First off, while I didn't run into a lot of glitches in my playthrough, getting Elena up and down stairs was ocassionally finicky when it came to placement, which can get sort of annoying. I also don't understand why the choice was made to have her unable to run around indoors, but that's just me. When Elena loses her powers halfway through the game, it really puts a damper on the fun of it all, not to mention it seems unecessary cop out and sort of ruins the purpose of having the powers as a prominent showcase if you're just not going to use them in the second half of the game. Puzzles involving interesting mechanics like this shouldn't be shoved into the corner for the climax of the game only to be brought out to do one or two things at the end.
Secondly, as far as story goes, the game is a little... lacking. It starts out well enough, and a reversal of the Dad Looks For Missing Daughter trope is always welcome. It even continues fairly well with the way that you were able to help a few of the people who's lives Wadsworth ruined in his mad attempts to speak to his wife again. While I liked that you could reconcile Darby and Skyflower, I had a problem with the fact that Elena couldn't explain to Fleur that Wadsworth was kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥ or that you couldn't find out more about the veritable ♥♥♥♥ing menagerie of ghosts milling about the mansion.
It also makes no sense that Wadsworth is showing her the suffering that he's had to go through in his life, but despite it not really being time travel and basically being projections in his own mind, Elena can still somehow alter events and give him knowledge of what could have happened when none of the characters have a reason to know any of this stuff at all. And in addition to that, after seeing that his own greed and desperation to see Martha again lead to a genocide, the murder of two people he'd loved, and the probable neglect of his son, to have him be able to flit off to the afterlife scott-free (especially since Elena's nonsensical foray into what could have been doesn't actually change the fact that he killed two people and slaughtered her ancestors) is unsatisfying and anticlimactic. While it's all well and good for us to consider the nature of good and evil, setting up the Big Bad of your game as an admittedly realistic portrayal of the attitude taken during Western Expansion in the U.S. and then having it turn out to be some mysterious dark lady-shaped force posessing him for no reason is just disappointing.
Finally, merging those two points, I feel like the game could have been stretched out a little more if the random ghosts had been given little miniquests or something that would allow you to accomplish certain tasks for rewards (e.g. tellings about hte history of the mansion, turning the notes or locations of notes into rewards, making it a little harder to get the keys by having a miniquest needing to be done first, etc.). There could have also been more variety in the puzzles and a more satisfying resolution to the story.
Overall, I do reccomend playing the game, because it's actually pretty short, pretty fun, and Elena is a very likeable character. Even with all the flaws it has, it's still worth a run-through at least once.
Honestly though, if you did like this game, I highly reccomend picking up Ghost Trick for the Nintendo DS. It's an older game that has a similar gimick that it does much better, and it's the reason I picked this up in the first place.

This is a cute little adventure game. I was actually a kickstarter supporter of this project, but like many kickstarter projects, they sound better on paper than they are in execution.
This is not to say this is a bad game. The story is charming, the 2D art is incredibly well drawn, and the music is appropriately creepy. This is Night Light studios' first foray into gaming, and they did a decent job.
The overall experience was lacking in a few areas, however. The puzzles are quite simple, your character is rarely in any kind of danger and there's a lot of backtracking involved. This can get tiresome when considering Elena's plodding walking pace (though I hear a subsequent patch has fixed this).
The game is also quite short. You're looking at about five hours of play, so keep that in mind before you decide to spend your money.
If you're a fan of adventure games, you'll probably like Whispering Willows, but I think that the full price tag is perhaps a little high for this game. I'd recommend putting it on your wishlist and waiting for a sale.

A perfect entry in a series now discontinued games, it would have made you wonder what the next episodes would've been like - this game tells the next chapter in the story of SiN, preceeded by the original game entitled simply "SiN"
The game follows the story of the main character, Blade, who (without going in to too much detail) has been injected with the U4 drug, a powerful chemical used to transform humans in to grotesque recombinant creatues, and he must find justice against Elexis Sinclaire, the woman who had the proceedure done to him and who is threatening the lives of potentially everyone in the world.
The game is diverse in it's enemies, one moment, you're fighting jetpack ninjas, the next, giant quadrapedal mutants who throw energized chunks of earth at you; this is part of the game that deserves heavy merit, as the designs of both the mutants and the humans alike are very unique, and much different from those of the original SiN characters.
Furthermore, it's weapon variety, while vastly limited from the original SiN, still manages to keep the game entertaining, with grenades that ignite enemies in it's vicinity of blast, to magnums that fire tracer rounds, and even shotguns that fire ricochetting pellets, you never lose the charm of using the same weapons over and over again to execute the same NPCs, probably the most entertaining thing about these weapons is being able to blow the visor and helmet off a ninja's unsuspecting head.
Finally, the level design is splendid, while the same industrial feeling is kept constant and applied to every single level, giving it a rather unadventurous feeling at some points, it manages to keep it's style consistant; debris covering every area that demands it, stunning views of the industrial regions, cities vehicles, towering buildings and skyscrapers, as well as dark, gloomy sewers and the abandoned interior of a ship, this game certainly keeps on giving, and again, it really does raise the question of what the newer entries in the series could have been like, it can only get better with story advancement, surely, but with the sad truth of the developers, Ritual going defunct, the tale of SiN will never be complete.
For what it is, an episode in what would have been a full series of nine games, it surely does deliver, and provides an excellent amount of gameplay to get you interested in the story, which may have been kept short due to Ritual's demise, but is still effective in encapsulating your experience with the game in the goals that Blade surely strived for himself.
Rating: 4.5 / 5 stars.

I can't even explain how pumped I was for this game. I watched all the trailers over 30 times at least and got kinda obsessed over it, but then release day came. I started playing and it was a great game! Smooth combat which improves a lot over LoS 1. There are many moves for all weapon types and with each mastery level, the weapon's effectiveness improves. The enviroments are stunning (plus with the free camera, you can enjoy them more), and with the HD texture pack only available on PC, the games was absolutely amazing and showed what PC's can do that consoles can not. I enjoyed the game quite a lot infact, but the story did seem dumbed down, especially the ending (won't spoil it for you and besides, it's my opinion on the ending). The modern day city was refereshing, but got a bit boring after going through the same area's multiple times during many missions. The stealth mission's are not exactly as good was Splinter Cell, but they are alright in their own way. Characters in this one seemed a bit bland as well, even Alucard and Gabriel. The only part I enjoyed in terms of characters was the Carmilla part, other than that, the story was pretty dull in most areas. After all, Dave Cox did say that we were going to get an epic, emotional ending as well.
I'll just list pro's and con's on my view:
Pro's:
Great combat system! Way better than that of LoS 1.
Beautiful enviroments (just a bit repetitive).
Great QTE's for boss fights.
Soundtrack is absolutely one of the best I have ever heard in a video game!
The free-camera.
Pretty cool boss fights.
Con's:
The story was pretty bland compared to the first one.
Characters seemed to not be that interesting either (Except Alucard, Gabriel, Zobek, Marie, Carmilla and maybe Victor) Mainly the acolytes and Satan (Dave also stated we'd see how Satan progressed as a character. Didn't really see that at all).
Some enviroments are boring when you keep having to go through them all the time.
Not too many enemy types actually. I came across about 10-15.
Stealth isn't the best either.
The difficulty has been lowered down in this game as well compared to LoS 1.
Final Verdict for me:
Personally, I'd give it a 7 maybe 8/10. The ending wasn't all the good in my opinion, others may disagree. I think the game was pretty over-hyped, but most games are these days to be honest. I would definitely recommend buying this game, but don't expect as much a story as LoS 1. Combat was lovely though as well as the climbing buildings, wires and lamposts etc. I only ever got to use the dragon form once though (found it rare to find fragments of the medallion). Overall, if you loved the first one and MoF, get it! If you found LoS 1 and MoF a bit boring and bland, this game may not be for you then. I personally enjoyed 80% of it, but I feel that it will be another year or 6 months until I replay it.

The pitiable game design choices prevent the enjoyment of the art and scenario from shining through this intriguing tale of Dracula.
Bad design choices? How about displaying the correct keys on the screen for the PC port, instead of still having the XBox controls on screen? Seriously. You can't even turn off the onscreen controller "hints," so I'm fighting a paladin, really into it; he launches an attack. . . I dodge it. . . screen freezes: "whow hey, did you know you can dodge this attack, by pressing the X key on your XBox 360 controller?" I'm already dodging the attack, anyway!! And the game pauses, while I'm in battle, to tell me how to dodge the attack--I've already dodged it anyway--and the instruction isn't even for the right controller!!! In 2014, a majour release title like this, should feature the correct controls when displaying instructions. There's no option to change what controls are displayed, or to just disable when the game displays controller instructions--there is an option you might think would do that: it doesn't. It is an insult to literally the entire gaming community, that a majour video game would not even take the time required to show the keyboard controls onscreen, for their PC release. What does it say about your game, when you do not put forth that level of effort when releasing it?
Recommended, absolutely, if you are very interested in the story of Dracula. I am, and I like the game for it, but at least 60% of my enjoyment of that, is burnt away by the frustrating controls and other bad design choices.
For example, not too far into the game, you fight through a boss encounter of three strong enemies, and then immediately after, you open a portal to the next area. As soon as I got there, I accidentally opened the same portal again going backwards to where I just came from. I figured it out quickly, however the game would not let me just turn around and continue playing in the realm I portalled to: instead I absolutely had to complete portalling back into the first realm that I started from, where, oh the boss is here again, and oh thanks we just autosaved, and also I now only have a little bit of health and no mana left because I literally just faught this boss 15 seconds ago!! This is a design choice for this game. You can't open the portal until the boss is dead, so I almost quit playing at this point, because I could only survive two hits before dying. This is not how you introduce a new part of your game! Just please don't do this in your game. Like, I even understood that I had accidentally opened a portal backwards, and the game would not let me cancel out of it; and then there's a forced boss encounter before I can open the portal again?  It's just really bad game design. It feels like no one actually sat down and played this game.
In another area, you have to get through a high security door. I though "what I'll do is kill that scientist, then the enemy will send another scientist in through that door, and when he enters,  I can rush through the door." No! Because that door is really just an art feature over an invisible wall, and the only way through it is to specifically activate a cutscene. Arhg! You can see through the door when it opens; why would this one door, in the entire game, have an invisible wall behind it? And then you can't really tell: "was I trying to go through that door too early, too late? Did I get stuck on the edge of it maybe. . . ?" You review the hints you have, and it seems like you're doing the right thing. It's frustrating because you're really playing this game against the game designers, and not against any enemies of Dracula. The game encourages you to imagine yourself as Dracula, but if Dracula was really here, then he would just walk through that door.
An enemy has an energy shield, which you have to pound away on to break it. If you cease attack, for literally less than one second, then the energy shield completely recharges. So it's difficult to tell if what you're doing is effective, because it's hard to stay on the enemy as they move around, and other enemies in the room try to attack you. Then, do you want to know what happens when you do break through the energy shield? If you do break through the energy shield, then the energy shield completely recharges, looking just like what happens when you stop attacking it. You actually have to break through the shield three times, but the game offers no signal that you're actually having an impact. If you break through the shield, it looks the same as if you failed to break through the shield. This is a bad design choice which I hope I don't have to explain further, but I will: it encourages the player to cease doing the right thing, maybe even leave the area, and try other things--which incidentally won't work.
The game offers a difficulty setting, but so far as I can tell, the only difference is that you get more health pickups on easy. It doesn't, for example, make that shield recharge after 2 seconds, so you can break through it without being a super expert fighter.
There is an interesting story of Dracula here, but it is wreathed in bad design. Confusion abounds. Fighting is challenging, but difficulty comes from trying to understand what the game expects. A game about Dracula, could be difficult by having strange boss encounters that make you pass unusual trials. You may even think that's what this game is. But I do not think the difficulty present in this game, was intentional. Having a game throw you back against a boss, immediately after you defeat it; without restoring your health, and autosaving at the start of the battle . .  This is not "difficulty" this is "bad design." It is worth playing to experience some of the story of Dracula, but it is not worth playing to see what a good game looks like.

coming from the age of doom, quake, and windows 95: postal 1 has something of an identify crisis brought on from the future of the series.
for starters:
if you looking for any of postal's attempts at risque or snarky humor in rws' first title, you'll find none of it here. this is the descent of one man's grasp on reality. the whole point of the game is to carry out your own personal genocide. there are no daily errands to accomplish. it's just you against the world.
this game is *dark*. the atmosphere is majorly different. something that appeals to me greatly is the ingame music. it sounds like the end result of merzbow collaborating with moozE or lustmord; loops of harsh noise and dark ambient soundscapes define what you hear, and this helps to make the game more distinctive in its presentation.
graphically, postal 1 has aged well.. sorta. the ingame engine works by rendering voxel models of NPCs and items on a drawn 2D background that is surprisingly well detailed, giving you a good reason to explore the maps. i'm not gonna lie - the voxel models look horrendous, but what can you expect from a game that's nearly 20 years old?
postal 1 is also a product of its age, with mixed results. the ingame control scheme feels overly clunky and primitive at worse, or mildly awkward at best. it takes some getting used to. if you guessed that rws tried to translate doom's way of moving about and shooting onto an isometric point of view, you wouldn't be too far off. whether if it works or not is up to your preferences. this is also reflected in the gameplay design: enemies will try to attack you from every angle. you have to master dodging to increase your chances of survival. if you don't, you will die. a lot.
can i advocate this game? yes, but you should know what to expect. postal 1 feels prehistoric in terms of production values today, but if you're into old games like me: you can forgive this. go shoot some people.

Not sure I'd spend the $13 again.  It seems like the start of a good game, but the gameplay mechanics are quite a bit mroe simple than what a couple of friends could come up with after playing Twilight Imperium for a weekend.  Tech trees are incredibly shallow, starships are not visually customizeable, and a few of the wonders are honestly a bit too wonderful. Dual Commands breaks pretty much everything, and the move-while-stealth one turns stealth into a gamebreakingly good mechanic.  I beat the game with untouched starships by just pumping my stealth up to the max and moving around plasma cannon-ing everything without any sort of retribution from the AI.
If you choose not to break the game, by ignoring the wonders, then the gameplay can actually be tactically rewarding.  Even so, while a board game like Twilight Imperium might have a dozen such space battles over the course of the game, literally every mission is a space battle and it gets very repetitive very quickly.  There are a few different types of space battle missions but there could be far more and, honestly, there could be more diplomacy as well.  Diplomacy in the game boils down to the other player giving a simple "take it or leave it" offer... no haggling, no asking for Planet X and I'll leave you alone, nothing.  What if they've got tons of metal that you need, but all they offer you to keep out is energy?  Well, guess you'll just have to go in and take it by force, because you can't even ask for it.
This is the first game I've played that I really felt had a "Sid Meier Markup".  If the game was just called "Starships", it'd be a $3-$5 tablet game.  Unfortunately, it's "Sid Meier's Starships" so it's a $13 game.  I almost felt the same way about Civilization: Beyond Earth, which feels very flat compared to normal Civilization games, but I stopped somewhat short because, honestly, a lot of that is a lack of "history" giving a real feel of advancement as a society rather than advancement as a tech-tree.  But with this game, I definitely feel it.  No strategic depth, no real incentive to pursue most of the technologies, and Wonders that make the rest of the game take a back seat in importance, and quickly push the tactical gameplay toward an undefeatable super fleet.  If you're looking for a good space empire sim, this isn't it.
Disappointed with this purchase, not worth the money.

Bottom-line up front: I'd give this a solid 1.5 out of 10. This is an expensive version of a free Facebook game... read more to find out why.
I REALLY wanted to like this game. From the pre-order description, and the fact that Sid Meier does an amazing job with about 95% of the games that they produce, this had a ton of potential.
Branded as a 4x game that related to Beyond Earth, I was a bit hopeful to see something that played like Master of Orion 2 and had the space-ground gameplay of Star Commander. Alas, I got my hopes up too high.
Also, before you go too much farther with this, just know that I haven't read the other reviews. This is my own take on this game.
Everything from the tech, to the resources, (lack of) diplomacy, (generic) space combat, and AI feels flat.
TECH: The tech "tree" is just a menu of upgrade. There are no new capabilities to introduce and no real choices that force you to examine tradeoffs and benefits. After playing BE, you'll likely be especially let down because NONE of that innovation exists in this game.
RESOURCES: Four resources, and four very narrow things to do with them. Like most campy Facebook games, using your resources requires no more thought than a button click.
DIPLOMACY: My main complaint with most Civ games is that you have options that the AI will not accept... in this case, you don't even have those options. Your two basic negotiating stances are a) war, or b) peace. Given the combat, neither has any particular advantages.
COMBAT: This is probably the only (slightly) redeeming part of this game. For about the first 20 turns, the combat and the missions are challenging. Once you've pumped enough resources into your ships, you can pretty well steamroll the AI with impunity.
Oh yes, the ship customization (and the reason why I was excited about this game)... yawn. Again, like the tech tree, the characteristics of each of your ships can be leveled up to attain greater advantage. There is no researching of new ship hulls, engines, weapons, or shields; just leveling. Facebook flash games have more options than this... such as Battle Pirates.
Final thing that I'll say on combat is this: one fleet? If SM was trying a new twist on 4x games to limit player to one fleet and up the challenge, this was a terrible choice. Any potential challenge is wasted because they let you construct warp gates so that you do not use up movement points while moving between your own worlds.
AI: Now for the AI. Like the rest of the game, the AI is stale and offers no challenge. In three different play throughs of the game (each at increasing difficulty), I have as yet to have an AI player declare war on me or attack me. I can roam the galaxy with my large armada of heavily armed ships and tear through pretty much every other empire with little effort.
What could have been a stellar game (see what I did there?) is really just a black hole for your wallet (even at $13 - as of this writing).
Save your money. Save your time. Don't save this galaxy (or SM's bottom line).

That feeling doesn't subside with the actual gameplay either, you have one fleet of starships that you can upgrade and move around a randomly generated map. You can build more ships but they always go into this one fleet and no matter how much you upgrade them they're always one of a couple of classes and strategy is rather basic.
Like Civilization combat takes place on a hexagonal grid, this time littered with asteroid fields of varying density that you can hide behind and which will lower the power of or block your shots entirely. Unlike Civilization 5 weapons have gigantic ranges of half a dozen tiles or more and more than one unit can occupy the same tile, eliminating what few tactical advantages the hex grid system had.
There's no point building a flimsy cruiser loaded down with torpedoes because the enemy can just shoot its long range lasers past your friendly units and take it down, for example.
Your two main tactics come in the form of asteroids and stealth.
Asteroids as previously mentioned will lower a shots power or block it entirely. It's not always a perfect solution but you can hide weaker ships behind partial asteroid fields and launch fast but flimsy fighters or torpedoes from safety.
Stealth meanwhile is a game breaking ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t button. Hitting the stealth button puts a ring around your ship, enemy ships have to get into this ring to detect your ship and fire upon it. It doesn't take many upgrades to bring this down to a one-hex or even half-hex size, making your ships almost entirely undetectable since the AI seems to forget sensors exist.
Coupled with long range lasers, or even powerful short-range plasma weapons and you have a recipe for domination no matter what the odds. Throw in a wonder that allows you to enter stealth at no cost, activating it for free when you move which allows you to remain invisible and fire at the same time and you've got an instant win that'll allow as little as two or three moderately equipped ships to rampage across the galaxy freeing planets from your enemies influence often with no opposition as the AI attempts to preserve resources by not facing you for fear of being dominated.
Remember that options screen from earlier?
Some flavour is added to the combat via each encounter's random modifier, for example you might not be allowed to move directly right (referred to as "east" in game) or asteroid fields might disappear as the battle goes on, or shields might not work as well. They're minor, sometimes annoying and calling them flavour might have been a bit too generous because after four or five matches you'll stop reading them and just hit next.
Second on the flavour menu is battle cards, again random effects that buff your fleet for varying effects; perhaps adding an extra shield level or allowing you to move two spaces further or even repairing your ships or damaging the enemies. They're useful in the right situation but I've gone whole campaigns without even using one, mainly because my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t stealth fleet was untouchable.

Ooh! Choices! Those are the default selections by the way.
The metagame is likewise light on stategy and content; you have crew morale/fatigue and that limits how many times you can move your fleet each turn. The idea being to jump between planets and secure influence to bring them into your empire in order to gain their resources and benefits.
You do this by taking part in randomly selected missions for rewards. Having them randomly selected is nice but the serious lack of them, I think there's only about 7 or 8 in total, makes for a lot of repetition even in a medium sized galaxy let alone over multiple games. The missions generally come in three flavours; blow something up, run away, or play king of the hill with an AI too stupid to capture more than one of the points.
One mission type I particularly hate, to the point that I let AIs actually take that planet and start a war to get it back later is the maze type. You either get limited sensor range or a limited number of turns and have to navigate a dense asteroid field set up like a maze, sometimes with enemies chasing you too. It's boring and stupid and if I wanted mazes I'd be playing a better game like Rogue, or Shining Force.
Gameplay: Still not that good.
Resources come in four flavours and have a single use each:
Energy allows you to upgrade your ships or add new ones to the fleet.
Metals allow you to buy planetary upgrades and build wonders.
Food allows you to build cities, improving the resource generation of planets.
Research allows you to research things (duh).
Credits, lastly, are for buying the other resources via a Sins Of A Solar Empire style market.
While I can't complain about the simplicity of the resource system, it does turn into a checklist of things to do every turn, since there's not much point holding onto anything because the diplomacy system might as well not exist so you may as well just dump everything into upgrading your own empire as soon as possible.
The only resource you'll really put any thought into is energy, because it's used for repairing damaged ships you'll want to hold a little back each turn in case of a disastrous defeat or, more likely, a ding in the paintwork.
Research is similarly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Wonders make a return too, not every planet has one but many do and they're expensive to build but confer a powerful and ride ranging set of bonuses upon your fleet, and only your fleet.
Bonuses range from the almost useless Torpedo Boosters (extra torpedo move speed) to the must-have Cloaking (free and automatic stealth) or Fleet Tradition (fatigue doesn't lower your crew's performance), making your third battle per turn just as easy to win as the first.
The problem with wonders is that they're also a victory condition, having seven of them is an instant win so if you're late grabbing territory the AI can score an easy victory over you but this also backfires spectacularly as you can just let them build the wonders then go in and start stealing them out from under their noses.
Of course, it wouldn't be Starships if they didn't manage to ♥♥♥♥ up the implementation somehow. Wonders aren't the only victory condition, but you'd be forgiven for thinking they are because it's so easy to accidentally win a wonder victory. For example, if you're going for a domination victory (holding 51% of all the planets) you'll have to grab enemy territory and their wonders along with it which leads to accidentally hoarding seven of the bloody things and winning via the condition you didn't want.

Let me preface: Across three prior platforms (PS2, PS3, and GameCube), I've played through this game in its entirety at least tewnty times. I've bought it four times. Now that I've caved and bought it a fifth, I'm sure I'll play through it twenty more.
Not everything in this game has stood up to the test of time, for sure. The voice acting isn't always stellar; the linear motion battle system was great when this game came out in 2002 when I first played it in Japanese, but now can be frustrating and feels dated; the story is rife with cliches and can be eye-rolling at times, but like all other older tales games, has a deeper theme to it that keeps you interested and compelled to play.
Overall, the PC controls are fine, but I'd still recommend playing with a controller rather than a keyboard. Visuals are dated but pretty: some of the texture tiles can be seen on the overworld map, but towns and dugeons still look nice and hold up well. The 3D cell shaded models are nice to look at and have held up well to time. The soundtrack remains one of my favorites in the series: it has lots of variety, though the overworld and the dungeons use the same theme all the time.
Out of the Tales games available that you can get from Steam, I'd recommend Symphonia head and shoulders above Zesteria or Berseria. The newer titles in the series look better and have updated playstyles, but don't have the same charm, depth, or compelling storylines that keep me coming back to this title. Despite its age, I still wholeheartedly recommend it and hope that anyone who decodes to pick it up gets at least half the hours and playtime out of it that I have.

As a fan of the original escapists, I was absolutely thrilled when I saw they were making a sequel, and I pre ordered it immediately. Needless to say as I'm not recommending it, I didn't enjoy it.
There were a multitude of bugs when I first loaded it up, as music didn't start first time it loaded, not a big prodblem I said to myself I can deal with it, but when I tried to start a multiplayer game for my friends and I, it crashed immediately. I was surprised by this, as I'm playing on a gaming pc, ut I tried again with my friend starting the game this time. He managed to load it I joined him, but when I tried to choose my character, it crashed the second time in 5 minutes. I was getting tired of this and tried opening it a third time, it crashed after startup, but on my fourth attempt I got in with my character. I was not exaggerating with those crashed it crashed that many times in not even ten minutes.
Now that I was in game, I tried to play, and noticed just how distracting the hud was, the mini map took up most of the view on the top right, and I saw no settings that could fix this. The graphics also didn't seem to fit how the game worked, with animations, but thats my opinion, and some poeple like it that way. Items were a joke, as choosing items reuires you to press numbers or tab, but you had to be holding items to do certain things, and if you got spot with a weapon in your hand it was over for you. Personally I didn't like how health and energy were placed and barely noticable, so first time I ran out of energy I got confused, until I noticed it. There were some good things about it, they did decide to add a mini map, which is nice, but it should've been smaller. There was also a much larger inventory space, which I enjoyed, and the crafting system didn't require guessing like in the original, except for a select few recipes.
The gameplay is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t though, for lack of a better word, to interact with something you press either e, q, or tab I believe and it doesn't tell you which one for example you would need to press e to search a desk, but with no tips or anything it was holding e that let you stand on it. Actually that is a bit of a lie, if you take the tutorial, (which I'll get into later,) it says it for like 5 seconds. Snipers can now see you anywhere on the map, so if you did one thing wrong it will hunt you down, granted it doesn't one shot you like it does in the original, but it took out half of my health in the beginning, and didn't stop firing.
The tutorial was too simple and barely went into detail, it showed you what you could do with the mechanics, but didn't go too far into them itself, it starts off by showing you how to craft, this isn't too bad, but it doesn't explain how crafting works, and instead just makes you craft something and go on to the next stage, it then makes you attack someone, which just gets you a key for the next stage the next is basically a poorer version of the original escapists tutorial.
That's all of my problems with the games, and if you down here for the tldr you're in luck
- Crafting system is more in depth, if a little complicated at first
- Graphics if distracting and bad for this type of game, are pretty crisp and nice looking
- It actually managed to stick close to the core values of the original game
- Combat system is in deoth with you being able to block and do special attacks
That's pretty much it

- Hud is distracting
- Hard to notice health and energy in something important
- Graphics don't fit gameplay
- Snipers are BS
- Actions are hard to remember
- Tutorial isn't in depth enough
Personally I bet this game is going to receive more updates as the game goes on, but in it's current stage I cannot recommend it. I will be playing regularly so if the game fixes my problems I'll change my review and edit it.

Very enjoyable multi-player experience.  If you are looking for a single player experience, then this might be less enjoyable overall.  Planning with a partner as you configure traps and run to cover weaknesses in your defense are what make Orcs Must Die! as a franchise shine though.  I am not big on tower defense games usually, but the ability to control your character directly in between staging segments provides the action kick I needed to really have fun.  Add in the ability to determine the traps, weapons, skills, and costumes your character uses in each stage and the antagonistic dialogue in the game, and Robot Entertainment delivers a satisfying product.

Pros:
-Incredibly fun gameplay that combines tower defense with thrid-person-shooting
-A truckload of customization options with different upgrades, traps, weapons and items give this game huge potential for replayability
-Great difficulty curve; The first few levels give you plenty of time to learn the game before the later levels crank up the challenge
-Well designed maps with branching paths and endless possibilities for trap layouts
-The different characters have unique strengths and weaknesses that give them different playstyles
-A distinct cell-shaded style does well to accompany the funny dialogue and equally hilarious gameplay
-Online co-op? COUNT ME THE **** In
Cons:
-The DLC packs are, while plentiful, kinda small- and yet, the game is somewhat short without them
-Not available to Macs or Linux systems
Overall:
This is one of the most fun co-op games I have played- period. Grab a friend and sit down with adjacent laptops and you will have one hell of a time. It holds up equally well in single-player, but seriously- play it with a friend.
8.5/10- Would absolutely recommend.

Bought this game while I was on a dungeon crawler kick. I didn't expect much, at all, from this game. I was wrong...VERY wrong. Has a engaging storyline, filled with rather... odd humor from your crawler crew. The game itself is pretty much simple. You, The player, Assume the role as a leader of a bunch of space mercs. You accept jobs, crawl through random generated "dungeons" as you search for items/kill targets/hack terminals in order to complete your contract. You do, however, also have a main storyline that needs completing, and as you do so, it has major effects on your contract work. Must pay attention to your Factions and enemies. Remember, You might make a friend with one job, but that only means more enemies to put a boomstick in ya.
Graphics: 8/10 The graphics have a cellshaded/hand drawn feel to them. A very science fiction comic book meets cartoon feel. They are rather attractive but have been marred by many glitches and graphical bugs caused by overlapping textures, or camera glitches.
Sound: 8/10 Sound design is rather pleasent, and the ambient sounds of the enviroment  really build to suspense in some areas of the game. even the SE of battle and skills are well done. The only downside I see is the repetition of music. After hearing the same music over and over and over, mission to mission, you kinda put on your own and mute the game.
Controls: 7/10 The controls are ok. They arn't very clunky, but their not intuitive either. at least not at first. After about 1 or 2 hours of playing, it becomes second nature. I do have 2 recommendations though, Use your flashlight and free look always on. The battle controls on the other hand are super easy. A very nice throwback to rpg/dungeon crawlers of old. A simple click and select system, with plenty of ways to defeat your foes. Just make sure you set up your skills and strategies right.
Total score: 7.7/10
Worth your time and money, But will be more worth it once the developers are done with the final polishing. That is about the only way I can break this down to ya.

My biggest criticism of this documentary is that it’s a little long. For each point they interview dozens of people who are all in agreement about roughly the same thoughts. It almost feels like they were trying to use all the repetition as undeniable proof of something, but could have just done 1 or 2 sound bites on each point. The other problem is that there’s only a ‘bad guy’ for about 30 minutes in the middle and the rest is just heaping praise on the machine. After watching the first documentary "From Bedrooms to Billions" and enjoying it I was pleasantly surprised to find this on Steam. I bought it and was not disappointed.
Apparently I'm one of the few people in North America who proceeded to buy an Amiga 1000 as a natural upgrade from my C64. And, then, enjoyed it and my later Amiga 500 through out the rest of the 80s into the early 90s. Especially since most American's went from 8-bit computing over to the NES and later the 16-bit NES and Sega Genesis. The Amiga did a lot better in Europe and England. I am envious of them in that respect.
This video is pure nostalgia as I immensely enjoyed my time with the Amiga. I played everything from "Defender of the Crown" to the Monkey Island games and a lot of games in between.
For somebody like me this documentary scratches all the itches even though the history of Amiga and the rise and fall of Commodore is all over the Internet. It was nice to see the interviews. The documentary as a whole was put together well.
I am really hoping for more from these guys.
I think anybody who enjoys retro computing and retro gaming will find this documetary well worth their time. To think of what the Amiga could have been if it were in the hands of a more competent company.

An easy recommendation for everyone interested in the subject matter, the many (mostly) interesting recent interviews sprinkled with old footage don't provide groundbreaking new information but hearing those stories from the Amiga guys themselves adds a lot, their enthusiasm is still palpatable after all these years. We learn of the beginnings, how Commodore came into the picture, how hardware development was done in the 80s (spoiler: whiteboards), what did and didn't work marketing-wise, why the Amiga was such a big step forward and why it got received differently in Europe vs the USA. Even the demo scene gets a dedicated chapter which is commendable as they often get thrown together with common software pirates, dimishing the scene's longterm importance not only for the Amiga itself but for the gaming industy as a whole.
Only thing I found disappointing was that later Amiga models beyond the 500/2000 didn't get covered at all, neither did Commodore's downfall. At least the A1200 and 4000 would've deserved a few minutes while some of the 'Amiga changed my life' talk towards the end could've been cut and so despite much ground getting covered the docu still feels somewhat incomplete. Only a minor nitpick though, overall there's plenty to love in here and the bonus material I've watched so far is good too.

Whispering Willows is a short adventure game in which you control a girl searching for her father. The story takes place in a mansion and its surrounding locales (garden, catacombs, guest house, ...).
The game world is presented in a 2D perspective and is drawn very beautifully, the only time I disliked the look of the game is during cutscenes which are really quite underwhelming. Couple that with the fact that there is no voice acting in the game, and you have yourself a story hindered by a lack of immersion. I guess it is lucky then that the game is so short (2 hours, maybe less), so that you can manage to retain focus throughout the game.
Besides the movement keys you only have 2 keys, one is for switching to an ethereal version of yourself which can fly, move through tiny openings and talk to other spirits. And the other is for interacting with objects. This probably did not help with making the puzzles challenging, since they are extremely easy. And the only thing which presents any sort of challenge is remembering what you have to do next, because the game does not do a good enough job of tracking that for you.
In the end Whispering Willows is a short, easy game with a likeable protagonist. Thre is nothing particularly special here, but it is most definetly worth playing, if only to experience something slightly different.

In a 9.0 review in EGM from 2014, Luftrausers is described in this way: "Hearkening back to a bygone era of simple-yet-deep arcade games where you played for score, not story, Luftrausers takes basic ideas in concept and execution and turns them into hours of challenging, chaotic fun."
I agree with all the above, so you can stop there if you wish. Indeed, in Luftrausers, you get to make your grandfather proud, who served in an Unspecified War on an Unspecified Side as a decorated kamikaze fighter and managed to fly experimental laser-based *cough cough* Luftwaffe aircraft in the nostalgic era of Unspecified global conflict that spawned such innocent things as Popeye and nuclear fission and resulted in that same grandfather hiding in Rio de Janero for a few decades to conceive your mom and maybe eventually you too. It is a game that depicts acts of aerial valor and ultimate sacrifice on the wings of physically impossible aircraft diving in and out of the water to kill a lot of people for fun and high scores.
I'm not trying to act surprised that this game called Luftrausers is what it is. It's supposedly funny, but I don't really get the jokes. If I throw on a fedora and crack a whip and punch the makers of the game in the face, I'll also go on record saying their game "belongs in a museum!" but specifically in the museum of Things A Lot of White People Thought Were Good Ideas, alongside a collective self-assurance that Resident Evil 5 is not racist or colonialist in any fashion, despite a macho government agent stomping through the Congo to accidentally shoot a whole bunch of dark people in the face for being diseased. I mean, as we all know, Starship Troopers is just an awesome stupid action movie about beautiful people fighting a good fight.
I honestly don't get it and you are free to try to explain to me where all the elusive self awareness or ironies lie in the game. What are we supposed to make of this alternate reality version of Joust from Man-in-the-High-Castle America? What's the point of going after these aesthetics? Is the music that evokes the sound of countless oiled black boots marching only a "gentle nod" to a movement that murdered millions of people? Some idiot thinker coined the phrase "all's fair in love and war" and Luftrausers is low-key cool with donning a crisp SS uniform if there's savage arcade action to be had with an inbound bass drop. How quickly Dieselpunk gives way to Nazi-punk! If you pitched this game to me, I'd say it sounds fun. If you then showed me your private box of concept art next to pop-pop's secret insignias, I'd stop letting you out of my line of sight, expecting you to turn your feckless eyes on me to ask if I actually believe the Holocaust happened as some kind of secret handshake you expect me to accept.

What can be said about Dark Souls that hasn't been said a million times already. You know what you've heard about the game, and might be on the edge on whether to buy it. So with that in mind, here are a few things to know about the game:
1. Difficulty - This game is very, very, VERY difficult, especially when you're just getting started. It's in the title, "Prepare to Die", because you will die a lot. But the deaths in this game are a bit different than the deaths in some other game; different in one key factor: they're fair. Any time you die, it's your fault. It might be because you didn't block when you needed to, or you misjudged a dodge-roll, but the game isn't to blame for you dying. There was a guy who played through the whole thing with a guitar hero controller for Pete's sake, you think you're little "the game didn't block when I told it to block" or whatever argument is gonna work? Just keep tanking through everything and learn. Learn to read the enemy.
2. Explanation - This is one shortcoming of the game that I will allow critics: the game does not do any handholding. There is next to no explanation for anything, and after you get out of the tutorial level the game just kind of shrugs and goes "do whatever, I don't care". What's does the stability stat on a shield do? How does bleed damage work? Where do I go now? These are questions just about every new player asks. Don't feel bad about looking up anything you don't understand, we all did.
3. Lore/story - This is another point I will give to critics. Dark Souls gives almost zero exposition past the opening cutscene. In fact, I can probably count the number of cutscenes in the game on 2 hands. Character storylines come and go quickly, and it can be very easy to never finish a character's arc or even never meet them in the first place. There is no do-over button either. If you mess up a character's story, you either have to start over or go all the way through NG+ to try again. And any world-building you might want comes largely from item description text dumps. But that just lets the player get into it so much more, invent their own story. You are a sole undead, one among masses. Your only distinction is your unwillingness to go hollow. Will you be a righteous pillar of hope, smiting foes with spears of lightning? Or perhaps a lowly brigand, content with lying in the shadows and slaughtering any NPC for their supplies. Possibly an evil Darkwraith invading other players for their humanity. Which actually brings me to my last point.
4. PvP - I'll get this out of the way from the start: I don't like PvP. I don't play PvP games, I don't PvP my friends, it's always single player or co-op games for me. With that being said, Dark Souls is probably my favorite form of forced PvP: largely avoidable with trolls galore. Out of 100 invasions, I'd say it boils down to about 50 want to fairly fight, 25-30 want to win by any means necessary regardless of how exploit-y, and the remaining being a combination of helpful people who give you items, themed opponents who are just fun to fight against, win or lose, and trolls being ridiculous. I'll never forget the time I was visited by the fashion police, twas' beautiful and hilarious. Back to my main point, it's also avoidable. If you don't want PvP, remain a hollow. Simple as that. "But I want to do summons": then you're also getting invaded. Humanity is a double-edged sword. And if it really bothers you, go offline. No one wants to fight a crybaby....well some might.
TL:DR Dark Souls is a very good, very well put together game. It has some faults, but they are vastly overshadowed by the games strengths. And never, EVER criticize the game online. You will be bashed with so many "git gud"s it'll be hard to spell "get good" the right way ever again.

Ah, Dark Souls. So often lauded as one of the greatest games ever made, a classic in the eyes of many. To that I must say, they are most certainly blind! Dark Souls is, to put it frankly, a derivative mess. This poorly constructed, unfinished game is a testament to the fact that as long as a game flies in the face of artistic progress in video games it will be received as a masterpiece. Look at any game that is bestowed the moniker of "the Dark Souls of" its genre for further examples.
We humans, we play games to relax. We play games to escape the state of things, which is no more poignant under our new administration. Dark Souls totally fails to provide a relaxing and comforting atmosphere for players, rather it chooses to complicate simple tasks, like combat, and make it the focal point of the game. Rather than engage players, Dark Souls chooses to make us feel uncomfortable and disheartened. This is not what games are about. I am told this game has a great story, but I am yet to see any evidence of this. In my time I have encountered only three cutscenes of any substance. That, in 2017, is simply not good enough. That wasn't good enough even in 2011 when the game was originally released. I was not at all engrossed, I was given no direction, and I was thoroughly frustrated by this mere game. Games are art, but Dark Souls does not help that argument one bit. I am saddened that this game is seen as such a cultural touchstone in gaming, because it isn't. It is a relic of a bygone area that should stay bygone. I would recommend this only to ''Gamers'' who think substance equates to longform drivel about their misunderstanding of contemporary artistic movements in the medium of video games.

I shall have to lend credence to the game's subtle homage to such books as "A Wrinkle in Time" and "A Wind in the Door". The concept of a hidden dream universe within a Eutopian/Dystopian universe lends an ominous aire of mystery to the first person adventure genre. The atmosphere of these games paints a beautiful, disturbing and haunting picture of the possibilities of alternate universes.
One must stretch their imagination somewhat to fully appreciate this franchise. Especially if one is not particular to the heavily story and dialogue driven adventure genre. If you are a fan of the adventure ga me genre, and are more interested in story than action, then this game will tickle your fancy on a deep and moving level.
I would only recommend this game to someone who accepts story over action. However, if you are willing to accept these gaming parameters, you are in for one hell of a moving story.
Unfortunately, to get the full emotional and psychological effect of this franchise, it is highly recommended you play all 3 games.
My biggest problem with the new entry into this franchise is that the game is being released in overly expensive "chapters", rather than one solid sequel. As solid as this release is, I still feel the chapters are NOT worth nearly 30 dollars per chapter. A few hours of gameplay for 30 dollars economically just does not cut it for me.
This sequel should have been released as one 20 or so hour game...a full game for 60 dollars or so. As it stands we will be paying at least 100 dollars to see this story to it's fruition.
I have to recommend this sequel ONLY to those who have played the previous Dreamfall games. To anyone else? Save your money. These chapter released titles are only worthy of the most die-hard fans of this franchise. If you are a fan of the Dreamfall games and you want to see the story come to a possible fruition, if you are okay with story over action, then I highly recommend you invest in these chapters.
If you love adventure games, and you've yet to play any other Dreamfall games, then forgo spending 30 dollars on each short adventure of the sequels.
Summary, if you aren't a HUGE fan of the Dreamfall series, then wait until the company releases the entire series as a bundle on sale...you've been warned.

This is the kind of game that could astound on a tablet, yet falls a little flat on any desktop.  It's quick to learn, simple to jump into, and the gameplay is simple.  Combat is pretty straight forward with the emphasis on menuevering and flanking other vessels and landing a more powerful shot.  Even though the combat is simple, the developers did a good job at making it still engaging.
This game would be fun on a tablet.  It is not, however, worth the full price.  Wait until it is drastically reduced with a sale, or added as a savings bundle with another Sid Meier's game.  This one has none of the depth that is normally attached to the Sid Meier name.

Anyone who was thinking of buying this game: wait until at least May 2015.  Hopefully by then the major bugs will have been fixed.  And don't buy it for over $10.
It runs for me, but apparently not for many.  One bug I did run into was achievements not unlocking when they should.  (Granted, I fulfilled the requirements for a couple by conquest, when apparently normaly building was the intended way.  But still, these things should be checked for.)
It's generic science fiction that tries to be 4x, but really is all about your single steadily growing fleet rolling over the galaxy.  Upgrading your planets is almost inconsequential compared to upgrading your fleet.  Energy constraints heavily favor optimizing for just one form of attack; in particular, lasers 4+ and 0 cannons, torpedoes, et cetera mean you can destroy most targets from a long distance, often times even through asteroids.  (Just make sure you are strong enough before attacking homeworlds: the defense ships that any homeworld starts with will maul a starting fleet, but they don't upgrade over time.)
As of this writing, the non-military victory conditions are only feasible if you disable the military victory conditions.  (The UI lets you enable all victory conditions, or only one specific condition, with no option to, say, only disable Population.)  Otherwise, someone's probably going to win a Population victory first.  Even the Domination victory is usually preceeded by a Population victory, unless someone (probably you) launches an early attack on the other empires, to score a Domination victory before enough of the galaxy has been claimed that reducing the galaxy to 2 empires (a necessary prelude to reducing it to 1 for Domination) triggers a Population victory.
I do not recommend this game at this time, but if you are reading months or years later - after the bugs have been fixed - and you can get it for under $10, it might be a cheap diversion for a weekend or two.

This game may be of the Civilization heritage however it sorely lacks much of the polish and depth that its predecessors have.
The game is very easy to pick up and get playing and doesn't have much of a learning curve. The visuals of the game are ok but that is not why people play strategy games. Customising your ships is easy and can lend it self to creating different specilisations of your ships.
This game is lacking in depth for a real strategy fan. The battle system is similar to XCOM (turn based) however there now real sense of cover. You can use asteroids to bottleneck your opponent into a sort of kill box but then you might end up being shot through the asteroids anyway. The random environment effects that disable certain features of the ships can be annoying but do not really factor into any kind of strategy.
Lack of information when mousing over various aspects of the game is very annoying. You have no way of knowing what exactly is happening when you are spending energy upgrading your ships. What does upgrading fighters do? Make them stronger? More fighters? There is no way to tell easily unless you commit to it. Upgrading fighters just gives more fighters to that can be deployed by your starship.
The world map portion of the game is another feature lacking any real depth. You can control planets for more resources and wonders but that is all they are good for, you can specialise them for more of a certain resource but that is it.
The map sizes are very tiny and are meant for quick games nothing long and drawn out like the Civ games. I was hoping for a massive epic length battle like in civ but sadly, that is not the case.
Victory condition restrictions only apply to the player. If you wanted a massive conquest style game that allows you to get your starships to the end game you will not see it. The AI can easily win with a wonder victory or science before you have any real chance to see the full glory of your starships. Would really love those victory conditions to be applied to the AI as well.
I cannot recommend this game to any strategy or civ fan.

If it was to have multiple fleets, depending on population and resources available, with different levels of buildings avalable to planets depending on its climate and planet type ie; a volcanic planet for greater metal extraction etc. and a more in depth map it would make this at least a worth while game. It would also be better if there was variation in Starship design and classes so they dont just change from a corvette to a cruiser with a few upgrades but have it so u choose certain ships for differnt roles in combat.

This is my first negative review, and I'm sad that this game has to be it. I had such high hopes for this game - so much in fact that I pre-ordered it. But unfortunately, I refunded it.
I'm a huge fan of the original Escapists game, so when I heard there was a sequel game coming, I was very excited. When I played the original game, there were a few things that didn't make the game perfect, so I was excited because I hoped that the developers would make the second game bigger and better than the first.
The first thing that bugged me was the combat mechanic. In the first game, you pressed a button like tab that would switch between combat mode and normal mode - so you would almost never accidentally enter combat with a guard or inmate. But in this game, I'm pretty sure there wasn't an option like that because in my first runthrough, I accidentally started a fight with an inmate I wanted to talk to just by pressing the left mouse button. I didn't like that.
Following up on that, the controls were confusing and I felt so rushed in the tutorial prison because they weren't giving me enough time to understand the controls and get used to them. I had to pause the game in the first official prison to look up the controls and read about them.
Lastly (because I only played for less than hour so I would stay in the refund range just in case), I didn't like the character customization. Every time I would hit randomize to get new prisoners and guards, I would ALWAYS have at least two YouTube gamer prisoners, which - no offense - but I don't really like in-game. I also was really disappointed at the lack of definition in the difference between male and female characters. I am one of the people who got very excited when they said you could be a guy or girl escapist, as I'm female. But you couldn't tell the difference because the hair wasn't very gender-specific. Actually the only difference you could tell between them was the name you gave them.
Like the other reviewers, I think the game was rushed. It's buggy, the mechanics are off, and the new features they offered didn't live up to their expectations. I think that when the game gets updates - and possibly fixes to some of these things (I don't reasonably expect all of these to change) -, I might purchase and play the game again. But not at this point.

Out of the 30+ hours that I have in this game as of writing this review, about two-thirds of them are from the last two weeks. Yes, it is absolutely the kind of game that will eat up your life.

It does a great job of capturing the sense of wonder that I get from my favorite sci-fi movies and shows. You could devote your time to tracking down the pages upon pages of in-game lore, but the time spend wandering through an imposing fortress or a bustling marketplace will be time just as well spent. You don't have to follow the main plot and save the universe, but said universe is so lovingly crafted that you want to anyway.
The game's learning curve is a bit steep (don't learn the hard way about stocking up on armor and weapons like I did), and the opening section is pretty slow. But once you get your ship fixed and properly get started, you'll be hooked. It's a real treat, and it makes Chucklefish a studio to watch out for in the future.

Working for the man, so that maybe one day he will invite my motley band of Crawlers and myself to one of his wild office parties.
This game showed up in my discovery que one day, so on impulse I bought it to try out, and boy am I glad I did!
It's a dungeon crawler in the same vein as the Might and Magic series, except it's set in a sci-fi space setting with borderlands style humour.
You control a band of mercenaries called 'Crawlers' who perform all sorts of odd jobs outside of the law for shady mega corporations.
One moment you might be escorting a scientist through a rival corporations lab to sabotage their research, and the next, hunting down a rogue trash compactor robot that has slaughtered the crew on a massive space ship.
The humour is witty and the story is interesting and laden with choices, there are undoubtedly multiple endings as every story mission is filled with opportunities to advance the plot in different ways and to chose who or what to assist. Want to play as the good guy? The villain? The Cash chasing morally dead merc? The revolutionary? Choices everywhere, and I doubt I am too far through the story even after 20 hours of playing!
Each of the crawler classes are wildly different from the other, and their 3 skill trees each offer different play styles. Maybe you want an explosion loving soldier who fills the screen with rockets and bombs, to hang out with an insane girl who communicates with and summons Cthulhu inspired creatures from a parallel universe. Said insane Void Summoner also has hilarious dialogue.
Outside of combat, each class offers unique options for exploring the worlds! Some can get access to loot and secret areas that others cannot possibly reach (for example the Cyber Ninja is agile enough to traverse tiny crawl spaces, and the Engineer can send one of his robots into all sorts of places). Various classes even modify found loot. Perhaps, while raiding an office building and, like any good RPG'er, you search EVERYTHING, one finds a stash of drugs hidden in some corporate schmuck's desk. If you have a smuggler with you, he/she (after a good sampling, of course) will put their illicit knowledge to good use and identify the pills rewarding you more valuable loot.
Suffice to say, it's really tough choosing which 4 (out of 8 classes) crawlers to bring with you on a mission, as they all offer really fun and useful abilities and options.
In closing, I highly recommend this game to fans of the dungeon crawling genre, its funny, rewarding, fresh and worth the time!

This review covers both SiN (which doesn't seem to be available from Steam any more) and SiN Episodes: Emergence. I have finished both games, but that was before "the great reset of play time counters" some years ago.
SiN:
An interesting game which had the misfortune of being released round about the same time as Half-Life. It also had the misfortune of being absolutely full of bugs which were only fixed with a huge (30Mb+) downloadable patch, at a time when most people only had dial-up connections. It had an interesting story, and very well designed levels, where actions performed in one map would affect those later on in the game. Many missions had several ways in which they could be solved. Well worth a play if you get the chance.
SiN Episodes: Emergence:
The first game I ever played which used the Source engine that wasn't made by Valve. Excellent graphics and sound, wonderful level design and pretty good AI. Brilliant, but unfortunately the creators sold the company to people who seem only interested in shoveling casual games on people, so we'll probably never see a sequel. Shame. It's not terribly original and you'll finish it in about three hours, but it is a lot of fun.
Solid gameplay and a rewarding experience. Sad to see it end here!

It's a damn shame this series of games was never completed.
SiN was a classic from my childhood, and although it hasn't aged too gracefully (that said, neither has Quake II, Unreal, or Half-Life), it holds a fond spot in my heart. I never played SiN Episodes: Emergence, since I hadn't heard anything about it when it was released, and afterwards, I only heard bad things about it.
Frankly, I don't understand why this series receives so little attention, and so much negativity. SiN Episodes: Emergence has a splendid soundtrack, a very immersive set of environments, arguably better gameplay than most games from its era (Half-Life 2, Call of Duty 2, etc.), competent AI (appropriate use of cover, grenades, flanking, etc.) and a story I'd love to see completed.
Sadly, I cannot say I recommend this series. Not because the games are bad, but because neither of them really have a place in the modern world. SiN has such a steep difficulty curve that it will put off most modern gamers and SiN Episodes: Emergence is merely an introductory chapter to what was supposed to be a game series comprised of nine episodes.
It's a damn shame this series of games was never completed.
