Castlevania: Lords of Shadow 2 is easily in the running for my 2014 game of the year. You've undoubtedly seen the low reviews from people who claimed poor graphics. These claims are groundless, and trampled by some of the screenshots you can uncover in the community hub for this game. The graphics are staggeringly good, and some areas have such incredible photorealism that you have to look twice just to make sure you're looking at a texture.
The free-form camera works great. No longer can whiners throw a fit that they can't see elements of the battle, as you can now rotate 360 degrees in virtually every setting. It not only grants you a breathtaking view of the scenery; it allows you to tactically view your surroundings and analyze your best moves mid-combat.
Platforming and quick-time events have been significantly altered to combat the same list of complainers who hated them in the first game. Platforming now directly shows you where to go, and no longer forces you into long-winded movements where every step is a new jump. You now streamline climb like spider-man over most surfaces, and the ones too far grant you a swift, and simple jump to the new object. Quick-time events have been cut in quarters. No more cinematic sequences where defending yourself during a movie becomes normal. They're limited to combat, and the rare gameplay-to-cinema segue.
Controls are as easy as they were in the first game, with a few minor improvements. Button rotations have made combat noticeably smoother, and grant the player less hectic moments of desperate survival. Moves now have instant-cancellations, (another complaint from the first game) which allow the player the freedom to be as quick and reflexive as they want to be. If you die in combat-- you're just not up to snuff that round. No more blaming the devs.
The music. What can I say? I've never been so excited to tear into a new game just to hear the musical composition behind it. Oscar Araujo does it again with a score so moving and epic that it pulls players back into its immersive world of magic and demons with a slew of trumpet blasts and harmony-driven pieces that are sure to win over even the most jaded action-gamers.
There's never been a better time to jump into the world of Castlevania. I loved this game's predecessor, and I can still hold firmly to my nostalgic love of a classic Castlevania devoid of all the work MercurySteam has pumped into it in recent years.
However, the "Lords of Shadow" series has brought life into a franchise that has desperately needed fresh-blood (forgive the pun).
I strongly urge anyone to pick up this title, even if you're only looking for a new action-game. The battles are challenging; you'll be forced to reconsider how you take on countless enemies that you think you know well enough from the first game.
The story is moving. Piecing together questions and answers from both the first game as well as Mirror of Fate, LoS 2 brings about a conclusion that is sure to yield an uproar from the masses for more of this tale.
You are no longer a pure-hearted man. Gabriel has become a ruthless, violence-embracing monster who is indifferent to suffering and who will stop at nothing to obtain the freedom he desires. Many of his choices in the game will makes fans of the holy-hero cringe as he shows how his transformation into the Prince of Darkness has affected his moral judgment.
This game is worth your money, and it's worth your time. If this game stretches even HALF the length of the first game, then it's going to be a ride you'll never forget.

I recently finished playing Dreamfall Chapters Book One and thought I’d post my thoughts while it’s still fresh in my mind.
I should start by saying that this is definitely NOT a game for everyone. If you’re new to the series, it likely won’t have nearly as big of an impact on you and you’ll be a bit lost at times. For those gamers like myself who have been waiting for a continuation of the series for YEARS, this is a fantastic continuation of a great story.
PROS:
-    Fantastic storytelling. Character dialogue is fresh and engaging.
-    Nice graphics. I wouldn’t go so far as to consider them “amazing” but the in-game graphics definitely hold their own amidst other indie current-gen titles.
-    Great music. The soundtrack stands on its own and provide nice ambient mode.
NEUTRAL:
-    Mediocre gameplay. Very similar to Telltale titles, the gameplay here is very simple and essentially consists of navigating to certain areas and talking to various NPCs. It’s a bit disappointing considering that the original title dating back to 2000 had TONS of puzzles to solve and variety. Oh well.
CONS:
-    Busy work. I hate to say it, but some of the later actiivities in Book 1 seem like busy work. Essentially “here, go talk to XYZ and fetch ABC.” I can forgive that for a bit but after awhile, it gets old and tedious. Especially when certain objectives are on opposite sides of a given city scape.
Final Verdict: Strong B+

# This is version 2 of my review, covering episode 1/5
Starting at the end, when ep. 1 was finally over, our (mine + my SOs) feelings were: "It's a pitty about a legendary series", "Why did I back this [on Kickstarter]?" and "Is this supposed to be finished, it felt more like a tutorial / tech demo than an actual game?". These feelings have not changed.
However, it was brought to my attention that this game would get 5 episodes, not only 2 as I'd originally thought, which means that 5 hours play time is about par for the course. It still doesn't excuse the fact that
a) there's hardly any actual gameplay. AFAIKR the original TLJ Dreamfall was criticised for being more of an interactive movie than a point-and-click, yet I never could see that and anyway, it worked. This time around it's justified and -- so far -- it doesn't.
b) there's no developents to speak of, neither character- nor story-wise, no build-up of mystery, suspense ... anything
Running around doing menial tasks following instructions (a lab assignment, f.i.) is all right for a tutorial and/or to give the player a feeling of normalcy before everything goes wrong, but one whole episode is too much, even if it's just 20% of the game.
c) The controls concept is very nice in theory, but very finicky in practise, at least on PC. And yes, Europolis is beautyful and epic and all that, but the "intelligent" maps got on my nerves in no time and after a while you just want to get there the 2015 way, via some kind of fast-travel system.
If I had to sum up the episode in one word it would be "tedious" and a game shouldn't ever be that. One can only hope that it get better -- the potential is there.

"Just One More Turn" no longer applies.  Sadly, my first game ended with me building enough wonders to get a wonder victory, one move away from an absolutely devastating battle between myself (strongest faction) and the second strongest  CPU.  Unfortunately, I'll never get to play that battle because "Just One More Turn" is now an extinct part of Sid Meier's repertoire.
The game itself is entertaining and enjoyable, if not incredibly dumbed down.  I absolutely love the torpedo mechanic of ship combat, it is something unique and adds a bit of dimension to the otherwise fairly basic combat game play.  However, because of the aforementioned, lack of multiplayer, and other features stripped from the franchise, I cannot whole-heartedly recommend this game.  If it goes on sale for 50% off, it'd be something fun to buy and play for a day or two, but I do not see this game having much long-lasting appeal.  It's more dumbed down that Civ V or Beyond Earth (though the price should be an indicator of that), which I think for some people is a good thing.  However, for people like me, who grew up with Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri, Civ II, the old, "proper" Civ games, this just feels like a massive steps backward from already several previous step backwards (Civ V, and Beyond Earth).
You decide for yourself if this is the type of game you are looking for.  For me, it's a far cry from the kind of game I could recommend to anyone.

Firstly, choosing between Recommending this game, and not recommending this game was kind of a hard choice, but in the end I decided to recommend it for what it is.
The reason: It's a good game.  It's a short game, but it's a good game.
Allow me if you will, to delve into the reasons why I will recommend this; It's a mini-game.  The game itself is made as a companion game but can be played on it's own and is still a bunch of fun.  It's short enough that you can fit in a quick game (an impossibility with other Sid Meier titles), and still leave satisfied.
You choose a different "leader" which gives you a different boost during the game, but overall I didn't find they made too much of a difference.  Then you really just expand, fight off some ships through an asteroid field, and repeat.  There's a few "varieties" of missions, but it's generally just clear out the other fleet, get your ship to a "warp hole", or escort a colony ship.  If you're okay with repeating these missions over and over again (with more or less enemies, and a few modifications like reduced visibility) then the game is a fun little time filler.
If you're not, then don't buy this game.

Tales of Symphonia is one of the biggest disappointments from all of my years as a gamer.
See, Tales of Symphonia suffered from an ailment all Tales of -games suffer from: they are the unfortunate position of being forced to compete with one of my top 2 games of all time, Tales of Eternia, the first Tales game I ever played. Symphonia was also possibly the most hyped Tales game I've played, with many people claiming it to be the best in the series, and possibly one of the best games of all time.
So my expectations were hefty to say the least, and things looked good right off the bat. The fighting felt good, the story sounded interesting, and even the characters seemed... well if not exactly lovable, then at least tolerable.
Unfortunately though, the game ultimately fails to deliver on all fronts. First, there's the writing. It's woeful. It's so absolutely awful that the people responsible should never be allowed near letters again. The protagonists are cliched at best (Lloyd, Genis), and completely uninteresting and flat (Regal, Presea) at worst. Then there's the main female protagonist, who I found even somewhat likeable.. BEFORE SHE GETS KIDNAPPED FOUR ♥♥♥♥ING TIMES. It's ridiculous, who the hell thought it'd be a good idea to have someone get kidnapped FOUR♥♥♥♥♥GURGLING TIMES. What kind of a moron thinks that's good writing? It's absolutely god damned stupid, and because half the game was spent without her in the party, I never bothered to use her in battle beyond the first stages of the game.
The antagonists are better almost without exception,  but not enough by themselves to save the otherwise dull and forgettable cast of characters.
The story is obviously centered around religions and prejudice, two things that could make for an interesting story. Unfortunately, it's handled poorly, and largely boiled down to clichés that are about as subtle as someone throwing a brick through your bedroom window. Granted, it probably was written for a younger crowd who are less interested in the complexities of life, but for ♥♥♥♥s sakes... there's a middle-ground between Dostoyevsky and the ♥♥♥♥ing Smurfs. There are some darker moments, but they ultimately lack weight and meaning because of the horrible, horrible dialogue, which seems like it was written a 10-year old as Bob The Builder fanfic.
FRIENDSHIP, YOU GUYS! LOVE MUST CONQUER THE DARKNESS! etc.
The worst part of the writing is indeed the dialogue, and especially the semi-optional character interactions. There are far too many of them, none of which are of any importance or interest. 20 hours in I was screaming in frustration every time one of them popped up, because I felt like I would rather tear my own head off than listen to one more of these miserable things. Sure, they are ultimately optional, but at the same time they are meant as characterization, which is a vital part of world building, and they fail in every single way. It got so bad that I had to stop playing for about two months because I just couldn't handle the awful writing.
The battle system is fun, but you're forced to go through far too many battles that lack challenge or meaningful rewards, so by the end each battle starts to feel like a chore, rather than the meat of the game. I spent at least the ten last hours dodging fights because it was just such a waste of time. You could try to fight in an optimal and cool ways, but why would you, when there's absolutely no need to? Pulling off a spectacular combo is fine, but when you're forced to do it 100 times in a row, it becomes mundane.
I could go on, but I doubt anyone's ever going to read anything this long in the Steam reviews, so I'll just wrap up by saying this game didn't live up to the expectations. The expectations I had were unfair and unrealistic, sure, but it does not change the fact that I was hugely disappointed in this game. It doesn't really succeed in anything, and it fails HORRIBLY in certain areas (ALL of the writing).
Nothing that jumps out as hugely positive, but a lot of small nags, and a few horrible shortcomings.

What can be said about Dark Souls that hasn't been said a million times already. You know what you've heard about the game, and might be on the edge on whether to buy it. So with that in mind, here are a few things to know about the game:
1. Difficulty - This game is very, very, VERY difficult, especially when you're just getting started. It's in the title, "Prepare to Die", because you will die a lot. But the deaths in this game are a bit different than the deaths in some other game; different in one key factor: they're fair. Any time you die, it's your fault. It might be because you didn't block when you needed to, or you misjudged a dodge-roll, but the game isn't to blame for you dying. There was a guy who played through the whole thing with a guitar hero controller for Pete's sake, you think you're little "the game didn't block when I told it to block" or whatever argument is gonna work? Just keep tanking through everything and learn. Learn to read the enemy.
2. Explanation - This is one shortcoming of the game that I will allow critics: the game does not do any handholding. There is next to no explanation for anything, and after you get out of the tutorial level the game just kind of shrugs and goes "do whatever, I don't care". What's does the stability stat on a shield do? How does bleed damage work? Where do I go now? These are questions just about every new player asks. Don't feel bad about looking up anything you don't understand, we all did.
3. Lore/story - This is another point I will give to critics. Dark Souls gives almost zero exposition past the opening cutscene. In fact, I can probably count the number of cutscenes in the game on 2 hands. Character storylines come and go quickly, and it can be very easy to never finish a character's arc or even never meet them in the first place. There is no do-over button either. If you mess up a character's story, you either have to start over or go all the way through NG+ to try again. And any world-building you might want comes largely from item description text dumps. But that just lets the player get into it so much more, invent their own story. You are a sole undead, one among masses. Your only distinction is your unwillingness to go hollow. Will you be a righteous pillar of hope, smiting foes with spears of lightning? Or perhaps a lowly brigand, content with lying in the shadows and slaughtering any NPC for their supplies. Possibly an evil Darkwraith invading other players for their humanity. Which actually brings me to my last point.
4. PvP - I'll get this out of the way from the start: I don't like PvP. I don't play PvP games, I don't PvP my friends, it's always single player or co-op games for me. With that being said, Dark Souls is probably my favorite form of forced PvP: largely avoidable with trolls galore. Out of 100 invasions, I'd say it boils down to about 50 want to fairly fight, 25-30 want to win by any means necessary regardless of how exploit-y, and the remaining being a combination of helpful people who give you items, themed opponents who are just fun to fight against, win or lose, and trolls being ridiculous. I'll never forget the time I was visited by the fashion police, twas' beautiful and hilarious. Back to my main point, it's also avoidable. If you don't want PvP, remain a hollow. Simple as that. "But I want to do summons": then you're also getting invaded. Humanity is a double-edged sword. And if it really bothers you, go offline. No one wants to fight a crybaby....well some might.
TL:DR Dark Souls is a very good, very well put together game. It has some faults, but they are vastly overshadowed by the games strengths. And never, EVER criticize the game online. You will be bashed with so many "git gud"s it'll be hard to spell "get good" the right way ever again.

Ah, Dark Souls. So often lauded as one of the greatest games ever made, a classic in the eyes of many. To that I must say, they are most certainly blind! Dark Souls is, to put it frankly, a derivative mess. This poorly constructed, unfinished game is a testament to the fact that as long as a game flies in the face of artistic progress in video games it will be received as a masterpiece. Look at any game that is bestowed the moniker of "the Dark Souls of" its genre for further examples.
We humans, we play games to relax. We play games to escape the state of things, which is no more poignant under our new administration. Dark Souls totally fails to provide a relaxing and comforting atmosphere for players, rather it chooses to complicate simple tasks, like combat, and make it the focal point of the game. Rather than engage players, Dark Souls chooses to make us feel uncomfortable and disheartened. This is not what games are about. I am told this game has a great story, but I am yet to see any evidence of this. In my time I have encountered only three cutscenes of any substance. That, in 2017, is simply not good enough. That wasn't good enough even in 2011 when the game was originally released. I was not at all engrossed, I was given no direction, and I was thoroughly frustrated by this mere game. Games are art, but Dark Souls does not help that argument one bit. I am saddened that this game is seen as such a cultural touchstone in gaming, because it isn't. It is a relic of a bygone area that should stay bygone. I would recommend this only to ''Gamers'' who think substance equates to longform drivel about their misunderstanding of contemporary artistic movements in the medium of video games.

If I had known the creators would release a remastered edition of this game I would have simply purchased that one. Make no mistake: I do not mind having played this classic from the end of the '90s I just know that once Postal Redux is released it'll be an immediate purchase for me.

This is the original game with it's simplistic (and by today's standards: ugly) graphics. And while the pixelated characters certainly look aged the game's hand drawn levels still look good. In the roughly 2 dozen levels (in various locales such as farm, factory, shopping center, industrial complex, airport etc.) we control the so-called Postal Dude (do note that this Dude appeared before Lebowsky - they are not the same) who causes mayhem and destruction. We can kill everyone - all bystanders and even ostriches (?), but taking innocent lives is not mandatory in order to complete a level. Getting rid of at least 80-90% of the hostile cops is a must, though.

And this is Postal for you. An isometric shooter with constant action which now has full controller support. Without this I would have definitely given it a thumbs-down. I do not know how its "remake", the so-called "Hatred" fares but I do know this game's content is not that extremely violent by default. Also, the Postal Dude's one-liners certainly create a funny atmosphere. If you remember playing this under Windows 95 / 98 then this is a great purchase for you.

8/10
Postal is an isometric third persons shooter with your objective being to kill a certain percentage of people in a stage. You kill people with a variety of guns and explosives. The game is pretty short and I finished it within an hour but the short length prevents the game from becoming too repetitive. This game, unlike its sequel, takes itself seriously, so if you were hoping for the humor seen in Postal 2 you will be disappointed. The game doesn't have as much difficulty settings as the sequel but this game doesn't really need a large amount of difficulty options, they have the basic difficulty options which is enough for this game.  Other than that I can't think of anything to say about this game. The game is good enough but don't expect it to be as fun as Postal 2.

For this being an early access game and developed by a smaller studio, with a fraction of money that these other AAA studios have, there is more thought, passion and heart put into this title than most. The class selection actually means something in StarCrawlers, no two classes feel like a rip off from another. Each has their own unique trait and fights with a different style, not to mention that as you explore the areas you are sent to on these jobs, they interact with the environment in different ways. Like the Hacker class which allows you to hack into computers and vaults while others do not allow you to do that. The areas always change with what is placed on the map. If you die while on a job and try that job again, the layout will stay the same but enemy, loot, and trap locations will vary. It helps to keep it fresh if you play the same job over and over again or go for a second or third playthrough. The combat is in the style that i love, turn based with visable recover timers. If you pay attention to the timers you can get out more damage if you pick and choose which action you will take. When you look over the ability you want to use, it will tell you how long you will have to wait before you get another action. It really isn't a big deal if you go on jobs that is your level or lower, but on higher and more difficult jobs it matters between life and death. The faction system is in its early stages but with over 20 different factions in it as it is, things could get interesting really fast depending on how they implement the outcomes between you and the fractions at certain reputation levels.
Pros:
-Fun and solid combat
-Unique classes with no cut and paste
-Ever changing assets in maps between multiple plays on same map
-Exploration has few and far between dry spells with secret areas here and there
Cons:

StarCrawlers occupies a niche that is woefully underfilled: that of a sci-fi dungeon crawl. For this alone it deserves attention. It brings a fresh style and aesthetic to the genre of CRPG (computer role-playing games). If you've played Wizardry or Etrian Odyssey you'll be at home here. And definitely if you want the CRPG dungeon crawl experience but are weary of the yet-another-kill-all-orcs game, this will scratch your itch. The music is familiar (FTL) but well-done and appropriate. The humor is just satirical enough not to make the game silly or groan-worthy. In fact, the humor is excellent. It reminds me of the sensibility of Baldur's Gate--that is clever, mature, and in all ways an enhancement of the immersion. The weakest part of the game for me is still the skill tree system. It's not bad, but it's not inspired yet either. On the other hand, the equipment upgrade system more than makes up for this in terms of (for me) originality. As of this review, the story missions are not yet finished, but they are released regularly enough that I feel confident in reviewing the game now. Finally, if you've never played a classic CRPG dungeon crawl game and are curious to enter the genre, I would definitely recommend StarCrawlers as an introduction piece.
For more commentary on the game, please feel free to check out my Let's Play/Let's Look At for the game. These are safe for work.

# This is version 2 of my review, covering episode 1/5
Starting at the end, when ep. 1 was finally over, our (mine + my SOs) feelings were: "It's a pitty about a legendary series", "Why did I back this [on Kickstarter]?" and "Is this supposed to be finished, it felt more like a tutorial / tech demo than an actual game?". These feelings have not changed.
However, it was brought to my attention that this game would get 5 episodes, not only 2 as I'd originally thought, which means that 5 hours play time is about par for the course. It still doesn't excuse the fact that
a) there's hardly any actual gameplay. AFAIKR the original TLJ Dreamfall was criticised for being more of an interactive movie than a point-and-click, yet I never could see that and anyway, it worked. This time around it's justified and -- so far -- it doesn't.
b) there's no developents to speak of, neither character- nor story-wise, no build-up of mystery, suspense ... anything
Running around doing menial tasks following instructions (a lab assignment, f.i.) is all right for a tutorial and/or to give the player a feeling of normalcy before everything goes wrong, but one whole episode is too much, even if it's just 20% of the game.
c) The controls concept is very nice in theory, but very finicky in practise, at least on PC. And yes, Europolis is beautyful and epic and all that, but the "intelligent" maps got on my nerves in no time and after a while you just want to get there the 2015 way, via some kind of fast-travel system.

Whispering Willow is a Very story-rich ( good tag indeed ) 2D Creepy game, Noticed how I said creepy because it is but not sure if it falls under the category of "Horror" for reasons i will discuss in this review
The game sucks you into this deep dark cold atmosphere I actually felt a cold breeze when the character gets cold, The art is done so beautifully it gives the game that feeling of success and the soundtracks are great.
It took me 6 hours to finish the game with 100% achievements probably could'v done it faster , I would say the game goes around 5 hours or so, and it has no replay value pretty much a one-time deal BUT that does not make it a bad game,
Other than the amazing atmosphere it leaves you in , Whispering Willow succeed greatly in the story , all the notes and diaries are well-thought and it seems like it was supervised by a professional author because it is well-put indeed, deep meanings and nice choice of words.
The animations are great I'm not that crazy about the Elena's voice and reactions to objects though.
All those saying this is a Hard puzzling adventure horror , To be honest the puzzles in this game are really easy, it highlights the object you're supposed to move, and uses common sense to know where to put it at next
The reason why i am not calling this a horror game, because they outdone it with the atmosphere BUT forgot the usual jump-scares, Yeah us gamers complain when we see a horror game with constant jump-scares because thats not what horror games are about, But this game really needs some ( in the entire game i had only one ) and thats bad, I kept expecting some but never saw any, and with that set atmosphere it creates unpredictable jump-scares so they should'v used that to make the game much more exciting and alive but its sad that they didn't.
The idea of leaving your body as a soul to do things your body cant is refreshing, though it can be a bit annoying because its not as fast as you'd expect it to be, Same for no-running indoors ... its frustrating but you get used to it, i was hoping for parts where you have to run from monsters or hurry up to get to a place by running but running is restricted only to outdoors, and when you press the sprint button indoors the character breaks 4th wall and says "uh-uh" annoying lol ...
have that said the game does keep its spooky elements, and piecing the stories together with the notes, the character design , the backgrounds the lightning effects, all so wonderful 10/10
So TL;DR
( Its a Spooky 2d game, lasts about 5 hours maybe 6 for full game, beautiful story, great artwork, and great gameplay, but dont expect jump-scares because the game don't do that )
-Pros
1 - Graphics , artwork , style , Atmosphere, Soundtracks, Animations, and effects
2 - Gameplay, Story, Character designs, And levels
Cons
1 - It did not place jump-scares which are a good element in horror games and would'v worked perfectly in this game.
2 - Sometimes i feel that the game is kinda slow because of the ( no indoor running )
3 - The fact that the game went on 2 Bundles  ( groupees and blink bundle ) and both bundles were less than 5$ because i guess they didn't make enough sales ? They could'v just reduced the game's price to 9,99$ and do a 33% sale or something to do it
So basically I would recommend this game on full price but since I did not get it on full price so I wont, its your choice to do it I already did my best explaining what this game is about and the gameplay hours if you're fast enough, Don't get me wrong support devs is something we all love but it kinda bums me out when people buy a game on full price and a few days later it goes on a bundle for 10% of the price that also has a lot of other games.

This was a surprisingly fun and polished adventure game. I wasn't expecting a lot from it when I picked it up in a recent bundle, but I thoroughly enjoyed it all the way through. It has a very polished feel to it with a lot of good going for it from its art style, musical score, sound effects, game mechanics, and even has quite a bit of humor.
It is tagged as a “horror” game, but really it falls more into the supernatural experience than true horror storytelling. While there are elements of creepiness and some scares, it is more of an uneasy feeling of dealing with ghosts and spirits than monsters. There are a couple of instances where you will be shocked, or surprised by events that creep up on you forcing you to run away from danger, but overall the atmosphere is more of a haunted house feel. The music is atmospheric to a spooky story, and fits well with old mansions and graveyards. The music is quite good overall, and mixed with some eerie sound effects you will feel some uneasiness while wandering around the game.
The game is focused on telling a story of a young girl who cannot find her father. She goes looking for him and ends up at an old mansion where it seems an old rich guy who was a mayor and founder of his town used to live and get up to some nefarious practices. Things look abandoned and filled with secrets as all the people that once resided here are long gone. You are introduced to an array of characters through notes you pick up, as well as a neat mechanic that you get almost immediately. You gain an amulet that allows you to switch to your spirit form and this form is the only way you can solve certain puzzles, or interact with other spirits you will come into contact with. You won't likely miss these as the amulet will glow and make a sound when you are near an instance that requires the swap. This is explained in a way that you are part of an Indian ancestry and that you are in a place where spirituality and otherworldly events seem to be more common. I found the story and presentation well done for the majority of the game. While there was almost no voice acting in the game you got a lot of lore for the people in it through messages you find in notes and diary entries, as well as conversations with spirits that appear as a bubble above their heads. These are all short conversations so not having a voice actor for this is no big deal. I didn't find the lack of voice acting to be a negative at all for the presentation. The girl you control does make some noises and sounds when she looks at certain things, or does certain actions at times. Even laughing at weird scenes and the like so there is some of that. The game isn't fully voiced so you will have to read a little bit at times, but never an excessive amount of more than a couple paragraphs at once in a diary entry. The ending may have been a little weak, but the journey to get there was fun and enjoyable so I still was pleased with the story overall.
The art style is well done. It reminds me of the comic book style you see in a game like Mark of the Ninja, except this is darker and more geared towards those old 1800s mansions with the background settings. The gameplay is certainly nothing like Mark of the Ninja, but the graphical style absolutely is similar. It is a 2D side scroller that will have you walking outdoors, or inside mansions and other old time grounds of a mansion like the gardens, catacombs, and guest homes. While indoors you can see a couple of floors at a time, but your room is highlighted and lit up while the other rooms are either completely dark, or just dark enough to where you can see their outlines. This too is very much like how the settings in Mark of the Ninja looked.
As mentioned earlier in the story section, you get the mechanic of turning into a spirit, which is necessary to solve certain puzzles. The way this is used makes the game pretty fun to solve these puzzles even though the puzzles themselves are very easy. You will have to use the spirit to go through walls and small cracks that you couldn’t get through yourself to pull a lever, you may have to use the spirit to possess an object so that you can move it and open a new path for you to continue, you may need it to deal with finding areas you can't find by reading hidden messages with the spirit form. While the puzzles in general were very easy throughout the game, I found the mechanics of getting around and the cleverness of using these mechanics fun. I enjoyed seeing how they would be used and it lead me to strange ways to enter and gain access to ares that seemed to be blocked before.
Although this is considered a horror/supernatural tale, there is good amount of humor in the game. Some is clever, some very corny, and a fair bit of puns are used. The humor was fun and gave me a few chuckles as I played with there begin many instances of a dark humor to lighten the mood at times. Toss in a lttle bit of "cuteness" too and you have a little bit more appeal to the ladies probably than guys besides just the main character being a female.
I would recommend this game to most adventure fans that are interested in a casual and fun experience. Normally I would want a game that is deeper meaning and serious, but I just found this game to be fun to play, cute, and well made. Lovely art style, great music and sound effects, quite a few laughs, fun mechanics in dealing with puzzles, and just a generally polished experience.
The negatives, and things I would like to see in future games from this developer would be more in depth and difficult puzzles and the possible addition of voice-acting. Another negative and something to be aware of is that during cut scenes, the game will SKIP them if you press ANY key on your keyboard. So taking a screenshot with F12 will skip the cut scene and you most likely will not be able to go back to a save before this as this has auto-saves. Also, the automatic save system with no ability to go back, like I mentioned with skipping a cut scene by pressing F12 is a must to change for future releases. Otherwise I was very satisfied with the game, and recommend it.

Now I say in the style of because in reality it’s a near total rip-off. The visual style is almost identical with a silhouette foreground and character with more detailed backgrounds to show off the kind of area you’re in. other than the backgrounds having more colour which actually look a bit out of place they’re basically the same thing.
The platforming is very simplistic, the controls are also very simple but somehow painful to use. Ezra will often drop off ropes or ladders for no reason or even miss grabbing them at all. Ledges never seem to have any indication that it can be grabbed and your jumps will often fall short even though you still manage to grab the ledge. This makes timed puzzles really frustrating because you have no concept of distance.
On the plus side it’s not particularly buggy I did get caught on a dropping wall which stopped me going through even though it shouldn’t but otherwise nothing major.

Honestly, I was skeptical about this game, just watching people play on youtube. My friend kinda coaxed me into getting it, and it's probably the most amazing game I've played in a long time! The game is a bit short, but does provide lots of replay ability through the different modes OMD2 incorporates. This game can get a little monotonous at times, but when playing with a friend it can provide hours of entertainment.
~Pros~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
1.) Enemies are fun and make the game challenging at points; A fair amount of the enemies in this game are unique, and have different weaknesses, attacks and strategies. It makes for interesting gameplay!
2.) Ragdolls are wonderful; When aren't orcs flying through the air into a wall funny?
3.) Replayability is good; The game doesn't make you start over when finished, and gives the ability to reset the skulls you put into your traps and weapons, allowing you to try new things. OMD2 also gives a harder version of the campaign, and a mode called endless; which is basically just play until you lose.
4.) Great customization; I'm mainly talking about the traps here. Each trap has 2 different abilities to it, but you can only choose one. There are lots of different combos you can perform by tweaking at the abilities of your traps.
5.) Differentiation between characters; The sorcerer and war mage are not entirely the same, and have different traps as well as weapons, allowing the player to choose their play style.
~Cons~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
1.) Online seems barren; Ihaven't seen anyone online, so this game can get lonely without a friend.
2.) Traps sell for the same as they were bought; I wouldn't really list this as a con, it's more in the middle of the both. I can't really recommend this game in its current state. Before the most recent update, the game had 5 main resources, each with workers to generate resources; each worker required some of the previous one to buy. Then there were generators for each worker, generators for those generators, etc., kinda like Swarm Simulator. After four tiers of generator, each resource tree had its own prestige, which would wipe all but the highest-tier generator for that tree, cost some of that generator, and in return, generate scientists over time - scientists being a premium resource used for upgrades. One of the trees had generators for the basic workers, which helped with recovering post-prestige. Now, the game was a bit rough around the edges, a bit too easy, and a bit vague in terms of its end goal, but it was fun to load it up, click a bit, and see progress being made. Just before this update, I'd nearly hit a googol.
Then they updated it, and the game pretty much died. Two of the resource trees have been completely vandalised, so that all the generators in the tree now just make the basic resource, rather than the hierarchy there was before. Buying any worker or generator requires a new resource called "comrades", which are generated painfully slowly. The devs tried retooling upgrade costs, but now there are only a couple of upgrades even worth buying, as all others are strictly worse. Even then, comrades put such a huge brick wall up that scientists are now useless. This wouldn't be so bad if it wasn't for the fact that scientists could be bought through microtransactions, and many players did because they enjoyed the game. I appreciate the need to pace idle games, but there's a difference between slowing something down and stopping it dead in its tracks. Some people in the forums actually worked out that some of the generators are now impossible to buy within the Earth's lifetime, let alone a person's. The game doesn't even have multiplicative multipliers - all multipliers combine additively, so exponential growth (i.e. the whole point of idle games) is a thing of the past here.
I hate being sensationalist and melodramatic, but this is the worst early access I've experienced since Starforge; it ranks slightly above, since I didn't actually spend any money on it. Maybe if the devs can work out what they want to do with the game and properly balance it, it might be fun again. As it is, I'm going to shelve this. As for my idle game needs, at least I still have Crush Crush.

There's a Tl;Dr at the bottom for the lazy among us.
This is one of "those" games. It's complex, deep and rewarding but also approximately as welcoming as a brick wall to new players. To give you an idea, the default control scheme needs a video tutorial from the developer in order to make sense. Are you scared by that? Good, 'cause you should be, that's an intimidating intro to a review. However, it's not as bad as it sounds.
While the systems can be a bit impenetrable at first without some help there is plenty of help to go around. There's a big community of people willing to answer questions on the forums, video tutorials covering basically every aspect of the game and, when all else fails, a very informative UI once you get used to it. Communities like that rarely form around games that aren't worth the time. Also, while the systems can be a bit complicated it's for a reason. They're fairly unique and actually kind of elegant in a way, once you're used to them you wouldn't want to change them because they represent the sheer amount of customization possible in the game.
Speaking of systems and community and all that jazz, the dev seems really nice and updates are coming very regularly at time of writing. the last two months have seen two huge updates that not only tweaked and fixed things but also introduced entirely new components and systems into the game that have had big effects on how we design things. I have zero complaints about how this early access campaign is being run, and I've been burned a couple times now so I'm a bit more critical than most.
Now on to the fun bit... you can build pretty much whatever you could possibly imagine (or at least an angular interpretation of it). No, I'm serious, this isn't the typical minecraftian "build anything" shtick, you really can. If you feel like it you can build a working star destroyer in the same game that you build a scale model of the bismark, along with the queen anne, the enterprise (both nautical and otherwise), the avro arrow or some crazy original design that probably shouldn't work but does, all of which can have attached AI's that allow them to pilot themselves. More importantly though, there's a reason to build all that. This game actually has a campaign, with enemies to test your designs against and a goal to direct yourself towards. There's also workshop support for player made campaigns full of player made factions with player made designs that open up virtually infinite possibilities. Personally I think that's what most of these "build 'em ups" are lacking, a point. You have experiences to learn from to make a more efficient design, something to do when you're sick of sticking blocks to other blocks as well as some genuinely good strategy gameplay that let's you take direct control of any unit you bolt a controller to. It's the kind of game that people who enjoy this kind of thing could play for years without getting bored. And I haven't even touched the multiplayer, that's not (entirely) from lack of desire but from just the sheer wealth of things I can do on my own before having to resort to including other people to supplement the fun.
The Tl;Dr
If you're too lazy to read a review to get an informed opinion then you probably should be looking at games that don't focus on menial tasks like building stuff.
Seriously though, this is a fantastic game once you become acquainted with it, containing virtually infinite content for those inclined. There's something for people who like to build unique designs and people who like to watch other peoples unique designs explode into confetti. It provides a structured challenge to lend a point to the creative aspect of the game with systems that promote experimentation. It's one of the more well managed forays into early access with consistent content updates that have significant impacts as well as being a game that's good enough to play already. Basically, buy it is what I'm getting at.

In recent months, I've become obsessed with the Soulsborne series created by FromSoftware. Ever since, I haven't been able to stop playing these games and my enthusiasm continues to grow with each passing day.
Having played all three Dark Souls titles several times over, and in myriad ways (i.e. as a filthy casul, a glass cannon, SL1, fists only, et al), I can honestly recognize why this first game in the series is so highly regarded.
The level design is unparalled. Not quite an open world game, Dark Souls still gives players enough leeway to carve out their own adventure as it suits their fancy. Don't want to fight Taurus Demon? Go through Valley of Drakes and go straight to the Gargoyles. Want to skip Capra Demon and Gaping Dragon? Pick the Master Key as a starting gift, and go straight into Frame-Rate Drop City (a.k.a. Blighttown) from the other side. Received the Lordvessel but you don't want to fight Seath immediately? Go cheese the Hell out of Bed of Chaos (seriously, bring firebombs to that fight; it's better than trying to take on it head-on).
The level of freedom in the game is staggering and Dark Souls doesn't hold your hand through it all either. The game wants you to get lost and explore its treacherous landscapes. Otherwise, you can go through entire playthroughs and completely miss out on the Painted World and Oolacile. Lots has been said about this game's design and its structure, but it's still not enough. By depriving you of so much as a compass to get your bearings, the game pushes you to play smarter.
The gameplay mechanics hold up incredibly well for a game that is 6 years old. Combat is fast, punishing, but never unfair. If you take the time to learn its inner workings, Dark Souls features some of the most intuitive and fluid combat in any game you will get to play.
The online component is a bit faulty after so many years and two and a half sequels, but, fortunately, DSCM is a thing and it makes jolly cooperation and invasions run smoothly. Sure, there are griefers who will play most of the game at SL1, get to Kaathe and then invade new players in the quote/unquote first area of the game, but most online experiences I've had have been very enjoyable.
Oh! And the bosses! Some of the most challenging bosses I've ever encountered in all my years playing games are in Dark Souls. Ornstein and Smough! Artorias! Gwyn! Even Pinwheel deserves a shout-out!
I could pontificate on end as to why people should give this game a try, but I suppose I can summarize my feelings best with the following statement:
Dark Souls will make you hate it until you love it more than anything else you'll play. If you're güd enough for it, that is.
Praise the Sun and get rekt, scrubs!
Enjoy the ride!

Is Starbound a good game? Depends on what you do with it. I've spent a long time testing the different portions of the game, from servers, to steam multiplayer, to the singleplayer campaign to modding it to high hell.
The game has a bustling Roleplay community, despite how toxic it can be. It's got some real good people wanderign around in it, and plenty of bad people. If you're just starting out, people can and will help you with starting out, and offer mods and tools to help you.
Steam multiplayer has gotten somewhat better recently and far mroe stable. It still dies pretty easily when you have more than 3 people, but works well enough for a pair of people wanting to play together.
The actual game itself, with the story is a little lackluster, and I find that, without mods, it's not all to good to get into. The story is mediocre and lore seems to be built up quite quickly. The wiki for the game has enoug hinformation on the game to help you get into the world, but not enough to keep you engaged. (Most RP servers have their own personal lores)
In terms of modding, this game is ridiculously easy. Modding comes in two forms: Multiplayer modding and singleplayer modding. Multiplayer moddign relies on exploits and such in the code, and this is all done using existing in-game assets. Singleplayer mods, like Frackin' Universe are those that add things to the game. For note, DO NOT GO ON SERVERS WITH SINGLEPLAYER MODS. You will quite quickly get booted and banned. To mod, the only real languages you need to know are JSON or Lua, and Lua only if you want more advanced modding.
Overall, this is a pretty okay thing to use if you like roleplaying, or even if you want to learn some basic coding. It's where I started with both, really.

Postal is a Single Player shooter, it's also one of them games that even though it was made in 1997 it is still a fun game to play. It was the start of the Postal series, some may argue that this is the best one, while the others don't really like the old school graphics and the way the game is played. I myself personally love retro games, it really shows us how much we have developed through gaming history.
Postal hasn't really got that much too it via the gameplay. There isn't really any story line to the game, it's pretty self-explanatory when you first enter the game. What's your objective? Kill everyone. Yep that's right, your soul purpose in this game is to literally a certain pecentage of the population on that map in order to proceed. You'll find a variety of guns as you progress through each level, as they get more and more challenging as the game goes on. The controls are pretty basic, WSAD to move and the arrow keys to shoot in the direction you want to shoot. This kind of control scheme is so much better then using the mouse to point and shoot (in my opinion). You'll obviously have to dodge other police guards and other random people that will try to kill you at any cost, using rocket launchers, shotguns, machine guns ect. A small complaint I do have with this game is that if you get hit by a rocket launcher, then you fall on the ground. If the AI is smart he will continue to shoot rocket launchers at you before you can stand up, therefor killing you in a cheap sort of way. I'm not gonna say that this is a big complaint to make, as this game was made in 1997, but it's just something to keep in mind. Keep your distance. The variety of levels is rather nice as well, you may find yourself in a wide range of different locations, but with a not a lot of variety of enemies. I like the way that the game also has a quick reset, so that if you do die, or you feel like you have messed up then you can quickly and easily reset the game using space (by defult). This a nice feature to the game rather than waiting everytime for a laoding screen, losing the pacing of the game all together. That being said, this game is by no means easy, okay the first few levels are just a warm up to what you are going to encounter later of, with a large number of enemies attacking you from different sides, you can't simply just run into a area and kill them all. But this game is also by no means very strategic. I guess you could be, planning out what enemies you're going to kill that you see in the screen then going forth with that plan, but other than that it's not strategic at all, and that's perfectally fine for this type of game, a fast paced single player shooter.
The graphics of this game is obviously gonna be judged from the time that this game was made. 1997. Well I wasn't even born then so I don't really have a standard of what games should've looked like back then. Some of the graphics seem to stand out more than others, some of them are really well detailed and done. While some others look a bit out of place, what I mean by that is that some are nicely polished off, and then some just seem to be hand drawn and not bothered polishing off. I guess that must just be because of the time of when this game was made, but like I said I don't really have much to work on since I don't really have any 'standards' for what games where meant to look like in 1997. The characters look well done, and the animations are smooth.
The game itself diesn't base around the music very much, sometimes you will find some levels don't have any music at all. There has obviously been a lot of time and effeort for the sound effects of this game, each gun having a different sound effect when you shoot and reload the weapon. There is obviously a lot of screaming and grunting as you are literally killing every living person you see. It works very well with the whole murder spree situation of the game just because you can.
The game itself evolves around you killing every living person you come across. While collecting a variety of different weapons that you can use to kill other people. The graphics are fairly good for the time I guess...? I don't really have a standard for what graphics where suppose to look like in 1997. You will soon realise there isn't much music to the game, but I'm sure you will be too busy murdering people for no apparent reason to care much about that. Smooth and well done animtations.

I’m pretty sure “teen princess management visual novel” is enough to get serious side-eye from most folks, but what if I told you this one takes royal intrigue seriously? Despite the anime characters and outfit selections, keeping track of court politics and avoiding death by poisoning are going to be your primary concerns in this one. There’s a surprising amount of depth in the decisions you need to survive to coronation, and plenty of ways to get sidetracked into an early grave. In fact, this one is so technical that it might even put off fans of intrigue from the other end, with the impressive volume of numbers and skill checks to keep up with.
Elodie is the fourteen-year-old princess of Nova, and with her mother gone is on the fast-track to the throne. With the guidance of the outgoing king she has a little less than a year until coronation, leaving plenty of time to learn, train, and die. The numerous dukes and regents of the land will not miss this opportunity for a power play, forcing Elodie into situations where she must choose suitors, settle disputes, wield military might, and root out spies. As if that weren’t enough there are the mysterious circumstances of her mother’s passing to look into, and equally mysterious powers at work surrounding those events.
Put any fantasies of some kind of anime Crusader Kings out of your head, because this is still a visual novel and that means lots of reading and not much action. For each of the 40 weeks until Elodie’s coronation, your main concern will be selecting her two subjects to study. Once her classes are complete, you’ll read through the week’s key event which can branch or offer choices based on the skills she’s studied up on. The week ends with your choice of activities that change her mood, which in turn provides bonuses and penalties to studying certain subjects. The actual gameplay, then, is figuring out which skills to train when, and how to get Elodie’s mood to support what she needs to study.
This is no mean feat, because there are over 40 skills to train all on scales from zero to a hundred. Their applications won’t be obvious until you’ve attempted a few runs either, unless you’re somehow clairvoyant enough to know what value flower arranging, naval strategy, or falconry will have on the road to coronation. Skill checks can also be shockingly steep, as I failed one I had at 70 not even halfway into the game. With the added layer of the mood system which can essentially lock you out of training certain skills, you really need a plan for character progression and you’re very much not going to have one on your first few runs.
You’ll come across quite a few ways to die here, whether it be on the point of a sword, wracked with poison, or mystically suffocated. Each time you perish, you’ll hopefully make note of what skill checks you failed when and take steps to overcome them the next time. Events are not random in Long Live The Queen, the same things happen on the same days (though the story can branch significantly based on choices). That means you can identify ideal paths and how to reach them via skill training, which forms a gentle if potentially tedious learning curve. Some of this tedium is eliminated by the promise of finding new scenes and new ways to die, but ultimately it’s still very technical, number-driven trial-and-error gameplay.
Assuming you get into the surprisingly detailed story though, this shouldn’t be much of an issue. There’s a lot to learn about the world and the nobles here, complete with elaborate titles and dense webs of intrigue. As light and fluffy as the anime art style makes it look, there’s some real Game of Thrones gravitas in the narrative especially when you’re passing judgment on murderers or navigating a ballroom of suitors. You’ll also get a load of backstory when studying up on subjects like history and foreign relations, actual fleshed-out facts about the subjects within the game world.
You can run through a single game of Long Live The Queen in thirty or forty minutes, but it’s going to take you hours upon hours to suss out what you need to see everything the game offers. Mathing out skill checks isn’t going to be compelling gameplay for everyone but the detailed story and narrative branches do a lot to make it appealing. I’ll admit not being very invested on my first few runs but once I found hints at some of the more obscure branches, I was compelled to see them through. I haven’t actually managed to make my queen live very long yet but even failing to keep her alive has been fun, and only gets more interesting the deeper you dig into the many plots hidden here.

I would run to my best friend’s house every day to play and we would sit there, side by side, for hours in front of his brother’s tiny CRT TV until his mom would tell us to turn the game off and go outside for a change. We would to run to a nearby forest and pretend to be characters from the game on a quest and slay imaginary enemies with wooden sticks for swords, each with a different role and a different mission.
when this game came out so most of the brilliant dialogue and worldbuilding would go way over my head but certain bits and pieces like spell names –
– would struck and we would keep yelling these out loud in our plays. Small details like the victory theme after a successful battle had such a lasting effect on me that I still sometimes find myself humming to them if I’m lost in thought. You don’t really need to understand the dialogue to feel the atmosphere of a colorful and buzzing small-town, or to feel the heat of an intense battle when you’re running low on health and your team has to pull it together or you’re dead. These are the things that completely absorbed me into the game as a kid and which are still there in the remake, a decade later. In a way every game I’ve played since has been a search for the same kind of high I felt back then playing Symphonia for the first time in my friend’s bedroom.  For people like me this release is the punch in the gut nostalgia trip back to our childhood’s we’ve yearned for.
This is a game that receives almost universal acclaim whenever it’s brought up but without the nostalgia to back it up that’s a bold claim to grasp just by looking at it. By today’s standards it looks hopelessly outdated. I mean, for crying out loud, what the store page calls a
is nothing but old tech that hasn’t aged well and an awful framerate caused by a bad port of an older port. The mechanics and the battlesystem are kind of wonky on PC and if these are things you care about – and honestly, maybe you should care – you are probably not going to get as much mileage out of this game as you would hope to.
Sylvarant, the world the game takes place on, and the story of the game are both incredibly interesting and your quest to save the world from a looming doom actually gets you racing. Sylvarant is full of different small locations you can wander off to for side-quests, which all work to slowly unravel new details about the story for you. But the best thing about Tales of Symphonia are the characters. The odd gang of heroes led by a young hothead, Lloyd Irving, on a common quest to save their own world. Each of the main characters has such an interesting backstory and own personality, which you get to know better and better throughout the game by completing hidden tasks or by reaching specific locations that hold importance to the characters. The lengths the developers have gone to build meaningful relationships between the characters through hours and hours of casual dialogue still amaze me, I can’t think of any other game series that would go that far.
– that work so well together to build that amazing world and the incredible characters that made me fall in love with Symphonia in the first place and which I still hold so dear to me.

Orcs Must Die 2 is the sequel to the game of a same name, but without the 2. The best way to describe this game is a mixture of MOBA's like Smite and LoL combined with tower defense games like Kingdom Rush. So, does it succeed in killing 10/10 orcs, or does it fail to defend it's original? Well, that's obviously why you're reading this review.
Gameplay: While at first glance this game is just a trap spammer, that's quite untrue, each level (24 to be exact) has many waves of monsters coming at you, orcs, kobolds, ogres and more! You need to carefully plan your strategy in order to stop them from bypassing your defenses and getting to the rift by placing traps, and boy are there a lot. There are 3 kinds of traps: Weapons, Trinkets, and Traps. Within the trap category there are various kinds as well, but I won't go into detail. By combining traps with your own battle prowess you must fend off waves of orcs and othe creatures until you eventually win, and by completing certain tasks in a level you can earn skulls, which are used to upgrade your traps and get new ones, though the majority of traps are earned by playing through the game. You can also play in co-op with another player to help you out, and co-operation is very important. If I had an issue with it, it's that it seems like you have to replay levels to earn skulls so you can upgrade your traps in order to beat some harder levels, but chances are you'll be replaying the levels to try and earn a perfect 5 skulls anyways, so it isn't a big deal. It's strategic, hectic, and most of all, fun.        9/10
Presentation: Orcs must die 2 sports a cartoony, yet somewhat epic style with loads of effects and both silly and threatening enemies. At the start of each level you'll get some dialogue between the 2 playable characters, the warmage and the sorceress, they both show some character development, though it's slight, and the dialogue is hilarious, you'll also get occasional lines when you kill monsters and place traps, a personal favorite of mine is when you place tar, the war mage will sometimes say: "That'll slow 'em up." The orcs also have some dialogue too, and boy is it hilarious to hear them yelling in pain as they get hit by a swinging mace to then be thrown into acid, or complain about not taking battle school before they went and invaded the fortress. Unfortunately the graphics are a bit rough around the edges, looking somewhat pixelated and making the framerate abysmal if effects fill up most of the screen, but it doesn't happen too often and is a minor inconvienience. The game looks good, and is funny while still retaining a level of epicness. 7/10
Sound: Orcs Must Die 2 re uses a lot of songs from the original, but has some great new tracks as well, but that doesn't really matter because this game has one of the best soundtracks in recent gaming history, I'm talking Donkey Kong Country Tropical Freeze levels of quality, while all of the battle tracks are orchestral rock they still sound unique to one another, and between waves there is some ambient music that makes you shake in your seat, not knowing what the nesxt wave will hold. There isn't a whole lot of variety, but it makes up for it with quality. The soundtrack suits the game perfectly, and I highly reccomend you buy the sountrack even if you don't want to play the game, especially if you like rock. 9/10
Length: 24 levels may not sound like much, but when you factor in the 2 different playable characters, upgrades, and that drive to get 5 skulls on each level you'll find this game has a lot to offer, it may get a bit repetitive playing the same level over and over trying to get 5 skulls, but by swithing up your strategy you'll have to play differently and have a better chance of beating the level. There are also 3 DLC packs with extra traps and another 3 levels each, increasing the total to 33 fortresses. The game will last you a long time so long as you don't get frustrated and adapt your strategy to suit the level.  8/10
Orcs must die 2 is a great game and will make you come back repeatedly, even if you ragequit frequently. The game has a great sense of humor and an amazing sound track to go along with it, I highly recomend this game to anybody who happens to find it, it's one of my favorite games ever, and for good reason.       Final Score: 8.5/10

Whispering Willows is a nice, short game with an intereasting story about a little girl trying to find her missing father in a haunted mansion.  It leeans more on the story side of things than a game.  You do have puzzle elements to figure out, but you can solve everything just by exploring everywhere and picking up the items you come across.  It really is unravelling the mystery of the house through talking to ghosts and reading the notes and letters you find that is the fun part.  And the artwork for the game really is quite nice looking.  Takes about 2 to 2 1/2 hours to play through from start to finish.

Whispering Willows is a puzzle adventure game with some horror-esque elements (nothing to make it the next Amnesia though). You play as a young girl who decides to run off and hunt for her missing father at a supposed haunted mansion. Using a necklace that you were given by that very father that had been passed down for generations, you can separate your body and soul to solve puzzles and talk to wandering ghosts.
The puzzles are somewhat simplistic from the ones I did and thankfully they did not spike in difficulty early on. The art style, while cartoonish, I feel makes it feel a bit unique. As a flagship game, I'd give it a strong 86/100, not the 65/100 metacritic score.
I've done a video impression on my YouTube channel, known as Neo Tanner. I'll link the video below.
I've played more than 20 minutes, just to get more feel of the game. It's very impressive for a company's first game and makes me believe they know what they're doing, definitely. If you're a fan of puzzles, horror-esque elements, and adventuring, then I recommend this highly to you.

Whispering Willows is an adventure and puzzle game with horror elements.  The
main story of the game comes from notes and diary entries, and it is a bit
heavy in reading.
Graphically, the game looks charming, slightly cartoon-ish, and it creates a
theme and atmosphere that draws you in.  The ghost animations are very well done,
but there is a disconnect on the motivations and back story of the main
character; the game assumes you know things that would be helpful to know, and
add another element to that character.
Unfortunately, the excess of save points take away from any sense of meaning when
battling monsters, and gives you a feeling that if you die, oh well, you can just
move along to the next thing.  The levels are mazelike, and designed to drag out
the experience, instead of complementing the atmosphere. Only made worse with the slow walking inside buildings.  While the main mechanic of this game, being able to become spectral, is a good one, it is overused to the point of becoming tedious.
The puzzles are oversimplified, and while the story and level design complement
each other, they also make you feel as if you are doing mindless repetitive
busywork before you are permitted to continue.
Unfortunately, the combination of all these thing takes away from immersion into
the game.  I felt that it didn't respect my time, and sadly I am unable to
recommend this game.
For more details, see the linked video review, as this is a basic
summary of what I cover in my video.
Thanks for your viewership and support for more videos check click here.

As stated in other reviews, Whispering Willows is  a solid enough game but it is ultimately too unambitious for its own good and doesn't fulfill its potential, especially when you compare it to the Blackwell Series and Ghost Trick, both fantastic ghost adventure games. The atmsophere is quite good, but the writing when it comes to dialogue is serviceable which for a more narrative driven adventure game like this  ends up being a detriment. The lore is good though. Puzzles are also quite easy and its pretty disappointing that the Metroidvania elements are rather barebones, because I really would love some more narrative driven Metroidvanias like Waking Mars. Looking more into it though this seemed to be the devs first big game and one on a Kickstarter budget and it really feels like that.  On the bright side, hopefully Night Lite can really improve on their next game because for a rookie outing, Whispering Willows is a solid start.

Whispering Willows is a charming 2D adventure in the spirit of Another World and Finding Teddy, featuring smooth hand-drawn animations, immersive sound design, and a clever spirit-mode mechanic reminiscent of the Blackwell series. The gameplay feels a little disjointed from the story at times, but the whole package is well worth a three-to-five-hour playthrough.

Whispering Willows is a shallow game both in terms of story and gameplay. The shallowness is eerily reminiscent of Atari's Haunted House. The game makes a fizzling attempt at being scary/creepy. The few puzzles the game offers require zero cranial activity. The main character may have been improved by utilizing a stronger personality, but with the limited story elements it probably wouldn't have mattered.
The character movement is unnecessarily slow. As I progressed further in the game, this slowness eventually started  giving me a feeling of "God, hurry up and end." Being able to run outside was nice, but the slow pace inside seems to be the result of a developer looking to extend an already short game. You know a game has issues when it tries its hardest to make you not want to finish it. And yet sometimes I amaze myself at my persistence, or maybe I'm mistaking that for stubbornness.

A neat short little game. Whispering Willows is an atmospherically well done adventure game. It is not so much a horror game as a horror themed game with some scary bits strewn about.
Gameplay is a bit slow which discourages the player a bit from exploring the beautifully drawn levels which are even further enhanced by a fittingly atmospheric soundtrack.
Despite the slow gameplay, the pacing is is done well, especially near the beginning and end of the game which benefits such a short game that can be completed on a first run in under 4 hours.
A negative point would be the lack of actual universe building. The player meets a lot of ghosts and finds various notes, letters and journals during the game yet a lot of your supernatural new friends seem either boring or like developer cameos if they do not play a central role in the story. That's is definitely a missed opportunity where this game could have shined. Give the ghosts a little backstory. For example there is a piano player who lost his sheet music which you'd have to bring back to him but then there is an ex-person just outside a building who serves no other function as to give you a hint to an otherwise already obvious puzzle which solves itself as you progress through the story.
Another point would be the difficulty. Now I don't want to say that it's bad for the game to be easy but players should not look for difficult puzzles in this game. Nevertheless the lack of frustrating puzzles makes the story more enjoyable and the pacing work better.
I'd recommend this game to all people who prefer a more light hearted, romantic approach to ghosts and horror than the r-rated kind. It's reminds me strongly of Luigi's Mansion for the Gamecube in both setting and atmosphere.
Beautifully drawn artwork and quite enjoyable with a dark story.

Whispering Willows is a Horror(ish)/Adventure puzzle game by Night Light Interactive. In it you play as Elena, who is looking for her father. Elena has powers that allow her to spirit-walk (or astral-project, as you may want to call it), which will help her solve puzzles, talk to ghosts, and help them move on. The game has some basis of Native American folklore, which might make it of particular interest to some.
Although the game is fairly simple and short, it has a lot going for it.
The story is interesting enough, though to get the full impact of it you really need to read all the notes you find, and not just skip them. The 2D graphics quite beautiful in their simplicity, yet still detailed enough in the backgrounds that you find yourself noticing all those little special things. The soundtrack and sounds are quite fitting the mood of the game throughout.
In Whispering Willows you're searching for your missing father at the Willows Mansion, which is full of secrets and ghosts and passageways. You will spend most of your time moving around the maps trying to find items, secrets and such, sometimes on your body, sometime by spirit walking.
The puzzles aren't too easy, but they're also not incredibly hard, making them just about the right spot where you won't necessarily feel compelled to quit or look up the answer, but will also not find it immediately for most of them. Some do require quite a bit of backtracking though, and when I played the game you could only walk and not run. I hear this has been fixed now, as the developer is very present on the forums.
It can be a bit easy to get lost as it has several locations, and at the time of playing it the game had no map system (I don't think it's been added, but I'm not sure) which had me backtracking and getting lost in a few parts.
The game might also seem a bit slow to some, though if you're used to Adventure games, the pacing shouldn't be a problem.
The replay value of this game is decent - you will probably want to play it again at some point, but likely not soon after finishing it.
All in all, I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a short, more paranormal than horror story with a good story.

Whispering Willows is a side-scrolling adventure.  It does have its horror elements (and a few "EEK!" moments) but overall this is a game of exploration and story-discovery.
Options include choice of Controls (I used the default), separate sliders for Sound Effects and Music, a slider for brightness (so  we can choose how environmentally dark we want it!), Language, Fullscreen/Windowed, Screen Resolution, and Graphics Quality.
All of the controls are given to you as you play but I'll list them here for you, anyway. ;)  The default controls are as follows:  Arrow keys or W-A-S-D for movement, E for Inventory, Q to switch to your astral form, Esc. for Menu or Cancel, and Space or Enter to interact with things.
Since the gameplay is exploration-based, the devs chose not to add a running ability... but they changed their minds after getting feedback from the fans.  You can run when you are OUTSIDE ONLY by holding down the Shift key.
You CAN miss things if you don't take the time to explore everywhere -- don't make assumptions that what looks like a dead-end is *actually* a dead-end!  For the most part, you won't be able to miss things, however.  Any time your character touches something important, you'll get a pop-up at the top of the screen telling you to hit the Space key to pick it up, possess it, move it, or whatever interaction is necessary at the time.  You can look at your inventory at any time, but you don't actually need to -- all inventory items are automatically used when you need them.
The story is told via notes and letters that you find as you explore.  I recommend reading them immediately, and you can do so by hitting the Esc key when you find them (the game will tell you that every time you find one of them :p )  If you're not sure which character wrote the letter, just hit the Esc key -- you'll see the newest note's name highlighted.  ie. William Wortham 3/15.
As you explore you will discover and -- in your spectral form -- be able to talk to the many ghosts that populate the grounds, as well as "possess" items for a short time and squeeze through small openings.  Although these openings have little sparkles around them, I *still* managed to miss a couple.  Another way to notice those small areas is to switch to your spirit form.  When you get near one, you'll switch from your full-form to a little bluish flame.
So how do you know when to switch forms?  You are wearing an amulet, and when it starts to glow, you know that you are getting near a ghost.  Otherwise, you just need to keep an eye out for small spaces, and things that don't quite look right.
You might think that being a side-scroller, there would not be much depth to your environment, and you'd be wrong. ;)  There are multiple layers to every area you visit, not just "front" and "behind".  My preferred method of play is to fully explore an area before going through any doors or going up/down stairs, but that's not necessarily what works best in this case.  'Nuff said.
You CAN die in a few spots, but luckily you won't have to re-do much, as the automatic saves are well-spaced.  Survival is not dependent on reflexes, it's all about patience and/or moving your character to the right place.
Overall, I enjoyed the game, and think it was definitely worth playing.
