This is a game, or rather two games, by the creators of the Escape Goat series, which while in a different genre are a pair of games I'd recommend wholeheartedly. Soulcaster actually came out before Escape Goat, and like it was available on the Xbox Live Arcade, but unlike it had quite a long wait through greenlight. It's finally here, and pretty worth the wait, I think.
You play as a nameless wizard on a journey to...do something. It's not explained right away, but on the way he bumbles across an area protected by monsters guarding the statue of an ancient warrior, Shaedu the Archer. She lends him her aid to help him survive. Not long after you find Ajax the Warrior and Bloodfire the Bomber; you'll need the help of all three to survive your journey.
Soulcaster is sort of a mix between an old-school dungeon crawler and a tower defense. You're presented with levels either one screen long or big enough to be miniature dungeons, each with a set amount of waves that spawn in when you pass a certain threshold, step on marked tiles, or just kill enough of the previous enemies. Shaedu can shoot enemies in her line of sight, but can't fire through allies or cover. Ajax can only hit what's next to him, but has a higher amount of health and can hold down choke-points extremely well, but can't take much punishment from the back. Finally, Bloodfire can throw bombs past allies for area damage, but is quite fragile and explodes when killed, which has friendly fire.
At the start you can put down three of them total, which can include multiples of the same hero; to unlock more you'll need to visit the merchant, where you can also buy upgrades for all your heroes. Unlocking a fourth and fifth slot is expensive, but a good investment, as the game wastes no time getting difficult. You can move around as the wizard while fighting is going on, and recalling your heroes before they die heals them completely, so you'll often need to make some snap decisions and reposition yourself. Collecting potions gives you a full heal if the wizard's life hits zero, and finding scrolls gives you a bomb that hits every enemy on the screen, but if you're surrounded without one you may as well restart the level and save yourself some time. It feels like a puzzle game at times, and it is fair about its challenge.
Like Escape Goat, it seems like both games might be short and sweet, with some other reviews noting both chapters can be finished in about two hours each. There is a hard mode and some challenge rooms available for each game to increase that a bit, but they're still not huge games and aren't intended to be. It seems like the developers, Magical Time Bean, are working on Soulcaster III at the moment, and I don't doubt they'll keep up their track record.

A first look, especially just from the screenshot, this game might look like an old school dungeon crawler with some 8bit flair  but Soulcaster presents and interesting gameplay in combat and progression through each level progression making it a quite modern and innovative game that deserves some attention to any fans of dungeon crawling games and tower defense games.
With its RPG and tower defense background, Soulcaster could look like a copy of Defender's Quest.  However, Soulcaster suprisingly innovates in the way the tower defense system is implemented.  Unlike Defender's Quest that uses a basic ressource management to handle defenses, Soulcaster system is based on selecting the right defense (from the 3 Soulstone you collected) and moving them along with you as you progress in a level. Each defenses have its pros and cons, so you need work out the best strategy from level to level.  This make the game much easier to play than usual tower defense games where you need to worry constantly about your ressources for placing the right defense at the right time.  But although it is easier to play, it does not make it un-interesting at all...

I highly recommend Soulcaster I & II as they are wonderful experiences and I found them quite fun!
I first played both games back in 2012 and finished them both. I was part of the beta test for the Steam release and additionally finished the first game three more times and second twice. I greatly enjoyed the games for their simplicity and also depth. I'm not sure I could put the games into a specific genre, however they remind me of a mix of tower defense, real-time strategy, and puzzle games. The simplicity of the games comes from only having three unique warrior types that can be summoned, only being able to have 3 - 5 warriors active at a time, and only one special attack.
While this may not sound like much, the depth of the game comes from the amount of combinations for placing the warriors and also what upgrades to purchase at the store. Unlike a typical tower defense game, you can recall your summoned warriors and place them elsewhere, which also restores their health, and both of these strategies are important to master on later levels.
The puzzle element comes from the levels themselves, where walls will crumble and new enemy portals will open unexpectedly. You will also have to decide the optimal order to trigger switches as they open portals sending waves of enemies at you. The extra challenge levels are also much more puzzle like as they often have limited resources, which requires figuring out specific strategies to complete them.
A play through of either game will be about two to three hours, with my fastest time just under 1.5 hours in Soulcaster 1. Finishing the game unlocks hard mode and the challenge rooms. I don't consider the game length to be a detriment to the experience and instead it means I am more likely to go back to playing them again given the low time commitment.
The music is also great and fits the game nicely.
I think the list of cons for these games will vary pretty widely by player, so I am not going to go into what I consider weaknesses. Instead I would encourage trying the games to see for yourself if you like them, which is a pretty low risk given the Steam refund policy and with the games being so short.

I played and completed Long Live the Queen in one setting. It was not my intention to spend four straight hours of the late evening (and early morning... up until 1:45 AM) playing this game. Nevertheless, once I began, I felt a tenacious urge to figure out how to beat it.
I came into this game knowing that there would be some frustration - there would be many different ways to die, no matter what strategy you chose. While this is true, and there were several times I had to completely start over because I played myself in a hole from which there was no way to survive, it only took me five main tries/restarts before I reached a successful ending. Given all the screaming reviews on Steam talking about the challenge, I thought it would take a little longer to win than four hours... I'm no supreme strategist... so while I would say that the game isn't easy to breeze through, I also wouldn't call it a BEAST of a challenge. It can give you moderate frustrations, nothing to the point of making you angry, but simply amused at dying yet again, and more determined to best the game.
I will say that, even though it took me only four hours to finish the game my first time, I feel as though it was worth the experience. I had fun!
From a gameplay standpoint, Long Live the Queen doesn't sound interesting. The gameplay aspect certainly didn't sound interesting to me when I first heard about this game. You basically click a few buttons and then read what happens. That's the full interactive element of it. Yes. All you do with this game is click choices. You click which classes you want to take (aka, what skills you want to invest in), you click which political/dialogue choices you want to take, and you click which activites you want to do over the weekend (to change what bonuses you get for learning different skills).
But again, there's this gripping quality of taking on the challenge. The game does have a way of making you not want to quit until you've made it to the end. You WANT to figure out how to survive. You WANT to beat this game when it tricks you into dying yet another way. You WANT to see if your gut choices will lead you to a good ending, or if you'll be surprised by something turning sour. That's the reason I played this game straight through with no break... I wanted, stubbornly, to reach the end.
Long Live the Queen is, in some ways, a game about the story. I wouldn't say that I found the story particularly gripping or the characters all that interesting. No character seemed to have much personality, for instance. It was also hard to keep track of the countries and characters in Long Live the Queen. The plotline does have a rise in action to a decent climax point, but it's not that deeply satisfying narrative you get with a story well-structured. But where Long Live the Queen has an interesting story is in how your choices affect yourself, the people around you, and your kingdom. It's interesting in how you will or won't survive, and in what state your kingdom will be if you finally do get crowned queen. That is what is primarily engaging about this game: the multitude of options, and the player's choices to tackle any one of those options. So it's the strategy, and how the strategy that affects the story, that makes this a worthwhile experience to have.
It really does have a multitude of options, by the way. I'm sure I've only experienced a fraction of what's possible to occur in the story. This will probably make the game have some good replay value... I can explore other choices, strategies, and avenues... and see if I can survive those treacherous routes, too!
One other small thing that's cool is that you can save your file - with the full text of the version you played - for a keepsake. It's a small thing, but I like that a lot. I can automatically store the choices I made and see what the story was start to end for my personal playthrough.
Altogether, I would say that this is an enjoyable game. I would recommend it to people who want to get mildly frustrated for a few hours, people who like the puzzle of beating semi-challenging odds, and people who like to explore many possible routes and possibilities.

This is my first foray into the visual novel genre, so I might have a skewed opinion. Long Live The Queen is wickedly engrossing, with interesting dialogue and subtle lore.
At first you feel exactly like little Elodie, dropped in this world of unknown danger and far too many choices to choose from. Which path will lead you to victory? How can you possibly save your kingdom and survive the dangers of dark royalty?
Eventually, you start to get the hang of things and recognize which skills will benefit you, and which alliances to make or break. You learn how to make the right choices, becoming a powerful queen -- good and evil.
This game caught my attention with the education system, promising not just dialogue with characters, but forming Elodie into any kind of queen-- a military force, an awe-inspiring magical girl, an economic savant, a sly spymaster, or even a cruel and sadistic empress. And that's just scratching the surface, all the ways you can shape your reign.
One thing I was not expecting was the depth of this world. You can't get a full picture of things in one playthrough. There's things to be discovered in every path, from uncovering the secret of your mother's death, to going on an adventure in the dark forest, exploring the depths of your magic, romancing a commoner, to finding out family secrets... and so on. Seemingly small choices can come back later or change the course of the story.
My only critique might be the music being a little repetitive. Found myself turning it off to listen to other things instead. Also, the opening music is an old patriotic america song which seems like an odd choice for a game about monarchy.
Nevertheless, love the game. I found myself exploring every nook and cranny, and can only imagine what a bigger version of this would be. I will absolutely drop cash on any DLCs or sequels in the future, if it happens.

Developer quickly addressed issues with performance in the game and overall I am impressed by the speed in which this was done.

Graphics and user-interface are mostly the same as in Dreamfall, just with a few improvements here and there. The fight system seems to be gone. Sneaking is still present, but toned down and only used in a single situation. One new addition in Chapters is the choice&consequence system, similar to what Tell Tale is doing. Hard to tell how that will pan out, as so far there hasn't been much consequence for the choices you make.
On the negative site, the performance is at the moment pretty bad, but patches for that are incoming. The choice&consequence system is also a little obnoxious, as it gives large on-screen indicators whenever there is a choice, this really should be toned down and be pretty much invisible. Animation are also a bit lacking, as it's still the old hand-animation stuff, not the fancy motion-capture that is used in most other bigger titles.
As for story, not that much happens in the first book, a few new characters are introduced, you revisit a few old places, but nothing big is so far driving the plot. I personally like that, as it gives you time to familiarize yourself with the world and the world itself looks amazing. Chapters has easily one of the best representations of near-future sci-fi you'll find in gaming.
Puzzles are, as in Dreamfall, still rather streamlined.
Overall, this is the Dreamfall sequel I have been waiting for, it doesn't radically change the formula and continues right where it left of. If you liked Dreamfall, get this game. If you haven't played Dreamfall, play it before you dive into Chapters, as Chapters doesn't bother much with retelling what happened in Dreamfall. Playing The Longest Journey couldn't hurt either.
So after having played through all five books the above review still mostly stands. Dreamfall Chapters manages to be a solid Dreamfall sequels, that fails to live up to the original The Longest Journey, just like Dreamfall before it. But it does make a good conclusion to Dreamfall itself.
The puzzles in Dreamfall Chapters do actually get a little worse in succeeding books. A lot of the puzzles in the mid of the game are based on running around on a really large map and finding that single item that you can interact with or the place to go to. The game often fails to indicate what that item might be or where to find it. So you spend a lot of time just running around and there is nobody around you could talk to to get further hints. Overlapping puzzle sequences (i.e. Monkey Island style) that you can solve in parallel on that large map are pretty much non-existent, everything plays pretty linearly, just with a lot of walking in between. By book 5 the game ditches puzzles pretty much completely and just goes interactive-movie.
The story also takes a long while to get going and you spend an frustratingly large amount of time backtracking through the same locations over and over again. It takes until book 4 for there to be something that feels like actual adventuring, before you get to see new locations and before the story starts kicking in, but once it gets going it's quite a tour de force until the end.
The game also happens to be quite a nostalgia trip, as you end up revising many places from previous games or otherwise reference events that happened earlier.
The choice and consequence system didn't end up bothering me all that much, as the consequences tend to be mostly minor.
Overall I am quite happy with the game, it fails to correct the mistakes of the original Dreamfall and introduces a few faults of its own, but it answers a lot of questions that Dreamfall left open. The biggest problem with the game is how uneven the different plotlines are. You spend a lot of time with the rebellion against the Azadi and other side stuff, that ultimately feels almost irrelevant compared to the bigger picture. The game doesn't manage to have real driving force for most of the time, just stuff to do. Since the game wanders and revisits many places previously seen, it is also missing the adventuring and exploration aspects that TLJ had, since everything feels a little to familiar. But as said, as a Dreamfall sequel it gets the job done pretty well and it's quite a lengthy game as well, but it doesn't manage to reach the quality that TLJ had and the developers don't quite seem to have learned from the criticism that Dreamfall received.

I was really hyped for this game. I watched so many hours of other YouTubers playing it together and was just eager to get my hands on it when it came out. Even after how bad they handled the first one.
However, upon buying it there were a few issues I saw right off the bat.
Just overall, multiplayer is awful. Since I bought the game for multiplayer, I'm very dissapointed because they had time to fix it since so many YouTubers played multiplayer.
The first problem with multiplayer is how it handles you as an individual.
The devs changed multiplayer so you keep your stats, but if you leave and someone else fills your spot, they get your stats. Not exactly where it should be, it should be more like Minecraft's multiplayer where you have your own inventory, and a different inventory for each server.
The second problem is the desync issues, this one is more game breaking than the last. Lag I can deal with, but desync is a huge no. When me and my friends were trying to break out of a prison, we had gotten out of the wall and were trying to make our way to the fence. To do this we had to avoid spotlights, no problem. However, the spotlights were in a different place on each one of our screens, and if we touched any of them the prison would go into lockdown and we would be knocked out. Unplayable.
The third problem is some of the actions not working such as exercise equipment and jobs. My friend had this issue more than us, and he just could not rise his stats up because it wouldn't let him interact with any of the equipment. Also, the jobs are broken. Overview:
A decent turn-based strategy game that doesn't require days to play through. However, after about 4 hours, the fun is starting to wear off for me. There's more cons than pros for this game. I'm really on the fence about recommending this or simply saying skip it. On the one hand, it's fun for a few hours, on the other it gets repetative and isnt very immersive. I'll only recommend it if you want a change of pace and have the $15 to blow.
Pros:
Strategy-based gameplay is fun at first. You have to plan your moves around asteroids, debris fields, etc. You have to pay attention to which way your ship is facing, manage your weapons systems and keep track of enemy movements. Once you get past the initial learning curve (there's really no tutorial aside from some "advice" boxes) it's easy to play through. Upgrading your fleet and managing your systems is easy (perhaps too easy).
Early on the game is challenging. Go into the wrong system and you might run into a fleet of carriers while you only have three cruisers. However, there is no shortage of "easier" battles to build up your fleet.
Cons:
It's repetative. After you expand your fleet and upgrade your ships, every battle becomes repetative and very one-sided (in the player's favor). I was pretty much destroying every fleet I encountered with little resistance (this was on the medium difficulty setting). I have a feeling regardless of the difficulty, once you reach a certain level of upgrades and fleet size, every battle turns into move ship, destroy enemy, repeat.
System management. You can upgrade each planetary system by building cities, and resource generators (food, energy, etc) but again, as the game progresses it becomes unbalanced. Every time I won a battle, I had enough resources to pretty much build out each system with every module (food, energy, metal production). At that point there's no challenge to resource management.
Enemy AI is not aggresive. I dont think I ever saw an enemy attack one of my systems. Again, this makes the whole game too easy and too one-sided. Since the AI never takes over my systems, I just continue to expand and build my fleet.
Ship upgrades are confusing at first and too simplified. You basically increase the number of lasers, cannons, torpedoes and fighters. This isn't clear at first and I was left wondering if upgrading my weapons increased damage output or range or some other spec. Lasers or cannons are automatically chosen based on range - which I guess is ok but not very immservie. Increasing fighters gives you more fighter groups to launch. As you upgrade your ships, they also automatically change class (frigate, cruiser, battleship, etc.)
Torpedoes are way overpowered. Put a torpedo in the right place and you can destroy any number of ships within the blast radius in one shot.
Very little in the way of a tutorial. Some basic advice like "upgrade your fleet" or "research this technology". Aside from that, there are no real details on how weapons systems work, etc. Even the in game info section is lacking.

The game is interesting, but shallow.
Like most reviews says, it's more and IOs game than a PC One and even if the gameplay is interesting at  first, I feel it will become very repetive soon. So, I guess the replay value is rather weak.
Yes, there's more than 40 differents missions( fighting, escort, prevent escaping, labyrinth, etc), but they all have the same core mechanic. so they are not that différent.
For a 5$ to 10$ game, it would be fine and I would recommand.
BUT, the real problem  is the incredible amount of bugs. I believe no beta testing were done at all.
After reading some reviews and comment, I felt luck I can launch the game unlike so many other. But I can't save, and I've had some graphics issues.
So, the game is good: no more, no less.
Probably too repetitive, so it'll lack replay value.
And have way too many bugs  so I can't recommand.

The most effective praise that I can give for 'LUFTRAUSERS' is that it is simply crafted, yet because of its simplicity it is wildly addictive.
It has been a good long time since I've had a game hook me so quickly with its combination of a fantastic soundtrack, pleasant visuals, and easy to pick up & go gameplay.
Every single aspect of the game is finely honed and effective.
Before I'd even realized it, an hour plus had passed and I was just itching to launch my newest version of my plane and do battle in the skies once more.
Let me be clear about something however -- I am not a young gamer.
I am firmly from the generation that favored gameplay over graphics, and I still hold that aspect close to my heart.
And that is why I believe 'LUFTRAUSERS' resonates so deeply with me.
It reminds me of days gone past of NES games like 'Air Fortress' (in the Air Base phase, at least), 'Raiden', and even as early as ATARI's 'Tempest', except in this new age of games 'LUFTRAUSERS' brings all of that nostalgia to the table & adds a pulse-pounding soundtrack as well as other current gaming tropes.
Another thing to note is the difficulty of the game -- it's elevated enough that I can imagine it turning off gamers from a younger generation, but it's a welcome inclusion for me -- as (in my opinion) too many games today trade in difficulty for excessive content.
All said & done, I would HIGHLY recommend 'LUFTRAUSERS' to anyone who can appreciate a game that is able to bring many classic 'flight' & 'shoot 'em up' ideas all together into one cohesive package.
EDIT 11/26/2016: Nominated for the Steam(y) Awards under the category 'Best Indie Bullethell with an Amazing Soundtrack'.

Yus I would recommend Orcs Must Dies 2. It is a fast paced third person tower defence game. The gist of the game (if you couldn’t figure it out already) is to kill orcs and defend your rift.  Omd2 has an amazing multi-player, a completely new spellbook and great replayability. The replayability comes in endless mode. If the name was not self-explanatory… it is a game mode where you just hold the rift for as long as you can against endless waves of orcs. Omd2 is very satisfying; there is clear objectives and progress. I would like to touch on the multi-player aspect of omd2. The multi-player really makes the game. To play through the lvls alone can get really hard and boring because most of the lvls have dual spawns and rifts made for multi-player. It’s really fun to get is a Skype call and just play with a friend for an hour or so. There is never a shortage of people to play with, there is a forum were people post if they wanna play co-op. I’ll briefly touch on the spellbook…….. It has been completely re-designed. You have a potential to attain unlimited skulls (currency) provided you want to farm them on endless mode. You use the skulls to upgrade every weapon and trap in your arsenal. The game starts out fairly easy, you could probably win with your melee and crossbow alone. But omd2 quickly turns into a tactician’s game. You have to set traps and use your spells wisely. I will blatantly say I am no tactician in omd2. I just set up a kill box and spam lightning. However, the game can be as complicated or as simple as you want it to be. I don’t mean to bore you, so I’ll wrap this up. All and all, omd2 is a great game with a great concept. The developers have worked very hard to make a game they can be proud of. Don’t bother reading any farther, just buy the game.

I'm going to be talking about the immersion/atmosphere/mystique in Dreamfall Chapters as it appears in Part 1 and appears to be the trend for the currently unreleased parts, i.e. the quality of the writing and the mechanics of how the game conveys you that writing. See other reviews for stuff like graphics and whatever. I played TLJ and Dreamfall in like 2012 or something and loved them so those don't really matter to me too much.
The expansion from point-and-click 2.5D static background in TLJ to the simple 3D corridor in Dreamfall survived decently well, but Dreamfall Chapters just drops the ball on the atmosphere as far as I'm concerned.
With TLJ the technology limitations and game type worked fairly well together. Fixed background allows easily for design to really make it feel more like an art piece and really define what it is that the player sees. The nature of clickable things being part of the fixed background though kept it on the game side via interactive exploration. April growing and shrinking also gave a more effective sense of distance than I think game developers these days are willing to admit.
Dreamfall managed to keep the transition to 3D decently since 3D world capabilities were probably fairly limited back then. Our world's cities were fairly narrow without too much "open world", but there were enough things to interact with to not feel like it was simply a walking simulator. Marcuria's city was the same way.
What happened in TLJ when you clicked on things and they had no purpose in the story or its progression, it simply gave you no response. There were things here and there you could look into, but there weren't that many and they gave you a feel of the situation, things that felt like they were there to speak for the music, the art style, and the premise of the story.
Dreamfall somewhat removed this with its eye/highlight system, but it was a reasonable system. The system had a very narrow range of view when selecting things to highlight, and although scanning was a lot easier than running a tiny cursor over the whole screen, it retained enough of the TLJ spirit to it to feel like I was still exploring and finding things out. The world shown was fairly small, but the way things were talked about made it feel fairly big and alive. Sort of like Remember Me, if you played that. The small corridors with glimpses of a huge world behind it are pretty good design choices. Creating a desire and hinting at it is often stronger than fulfilling a desire that one is unaware of; see skimpy clothing on women and basically any PR/hype for any product before it's out.
The population of the world in Dreamfall Chapters completely reversed this. I can remember the look of some people and some of the things of TLJ and Dreamfall. The autotaxi I thought was super neat, and the space station scene and the type of people in it have been strongly imprinted in my mind.
Whereas the technological limitations were implicitly acknowledged in TLJ and Dreamfall by its design, Dreamfall Chapters makes it way too obvious to the player. Now instead of a few things that you really pay attention, there's a torrent of repetition. In Europolis no matter what I higlighted in the market I heard the same things over and over again. Why are there 20 or so market tables but only 2 or 3 messages I hear about all of them? What is the purpose of 10 selectable trash cans? The adbots of Dreamfall Chapters nowhere near compare to the Screens of Dreamfall. There's a bunch of people now walking around that I really don't care about, and a lot of things strewn about that I don't know if I should really care about.
And I know where every single one of them are because with almost no effort on my part any time I look in a general direction, I'm told exactly what is and what isn't selectable.
There's something else that causes this complete lack of atmosphere or mystique.
In the opening of TLJ and Dreamfall we're introduced to a bit of the mystery and the scale of the story we're about to uncover within the first several minutes of the game. TLJ opens with a girl in underwear clearly from a time and place we can relate to and in a world which is clearly not. Dreamfall opens largely the same way with some vaguely modern guy with a bunch of kooky priests doing kooky stuff.
There is none of this in the opening of Dreamfall Chapters. We're told everything matter-of-factly, Zoe Castillo seems to perfectly know what she's doing except when she doesn't, and whatshisface opens his mouth too much in too many stupid ways and there's nothing amazing about any of it at all. Storytime used to be this really unknowable timeless place, now it's, oh, it's basically just where dreams happen. And we have this guy who has a poor command of the english language who appears sometimes. And we have superpowers somehow. We're told that we need to go back and stop the undreaming or something, which could be great even if the intro was poor, but we don't do any of that. We go back into the real world and all we talk about is Zoe's feelings and politics. There's nothing tying this to anything at all.
Not knowing the whole story is integral for a story to move forward, but thinking you know the next step is necessary for a story to even happen. April knew what her next step was going to be at all times, even if it was wrong. Zoe Castillo in Dreamfall knew at all times what her next step would be, even if it was wrong.
What was the 20% point for the average playthrough of TLJ or Dreamfall? Surely it's different from this. Looking over various Steam reviews it appears the average time to completion of Book 1 was somewhere between 4-8 hours (mine was 6 at time of writing). I took 13-14 hours to get through Dreamfall and about 15-17 to get through TLJ. I've seen a lot of defenses about how gameplay time isn't representative or whatever and this is true but the flow of the story is undoubtedly different and whether by percentage or by absolute playtime (which cannot be completely ignored) and in basically any story you see by the 20% point or in any game/movie/TV series/book by 4-8 hours in (unless the story is several hundred hours long) you have a fair idea of what is going on. At any time the audience can feel disengaged and you always have to have something around the corner to keep them turning the page or whatever it might be in that medium.
I don't think it is reasonable to say that Dreamfall Chapters is good. I have no real reason to come back to it except for the fact that I backed the game and want to see how things turn out. I cannot recommend this game to anyone who has not already played TLJ and Dreamfall, and even to those who do I cannot really say it is a worth spending money on.

TLJ was one of the first adventures I played and I liked it a lot. The sequel  - Dreamfall, was attempt to cater to new audience with 3rd person view and some arcade elements, but puzzles were still here followed by rich story,  descent game overall. The new game changing it format again, now they decided to ride on Telltale success. If you like "The Wolf among Us" and other Telltale games you would probably like Chapters as well. No more puzzles (unless usage of key on lock is puzzling for you),
barely any objects to click on (2-3 hotspots per scene, whole city has like 10 POI) but a lot of dialogs and "choices".
The choice system is a classical approach with "moral" dilemmas which will affect development of your storyline. On good side - they put some efforts to help you understand your possible options better as each choice is provided with inner monolog with a detailed explanation. On other hand it still not enough and unless you share mindset with dev-team you can't predict reaction and outcomes, common flaw of such games.  Unfortunately there are no saves in game (only auto-save on checkpoint) so you can't play around with different options and need to start new game to see different outcomes.
First chapter has around 3.5 hours of gameplay 2.5 of which is dialogs and cutscenes and other hour is you running around city between people you obliged to talk to. Main area of action is very small, even claustrophobic with a lot of reused props.
On bright side of the game - dialogs and NPC are good, music is pretty good too but it is hard to judge a story yet. Visual style is far from being impressive and also struggle to perform properly in open area of the city. Animation is on bare minimum as well.
Can't recommend unless you are Telltale fan, Also chapter is pretty short so it worth to wait for full pack on sale if you just interested in story continuation of old games.

After so many years of believing that I'd never see a true sequel to The Longest Journey/Dreamfall, I was very excited to see this long-awaited new chapter emerge! I 've always felt that the conclusion to Dreamfall left so many unanswered questions so when Chapters came along, I had to jump right back in and see where the story would take me.
Thumbs Up:
- A well written continuation of the events in the previous game. Zoe feels very authentic regardless of the decisions she's faced with making. I can only assume that Kian will be given the same kind of development as the additional Chapters are released.
- A fully realized environment. The layout of Propast feels filled in and lively.
- Interaction with almost everything in the enviroment. Even if Zoe or Kian can't touch or use something directly, they will have thoughts and feelings to share with the player.
- Continuity and nostalgia. So many story elements from the previous games are faithfully touched on and added to. There are a number of little tributes to Dreamfall and The Longest Journey if you know where to look!
- Every decision counts. I particularly like this feature. It makes doing multiple playthroughs worthwhile.
- An AMAZING soundtrack. So much of the score is just brilliantly done and it does a great job of conveying the story without being overbearing.
- Driven by narrative. Chapters definitely covers a lot of ground in a short amount of time. It feels like a really good book or TV show. However, as it does not feature combat (so far), this may not be everyone's cup of tea.
Thumbs Down:
- Some of the voice acting is a little hard to listen to. Additionally, the amount vulgar language just seems to be overkill. A little bit can add spice and depth to a character. Too much just makes them uninteresting.
- Some of the puzzles and goals could stand to have a bit more explanation to them. I'm not talking outright hand-holding, but a gentle nudge or exposition could go a long way. Especially if you're negotiating between two people...
- Many of the NPC are too identical. Repitions in hairstyle and clothing tend to break up the immersion, unfortunately.
- Optmization issues. Even with settings at the lowest, this game could suffer from framerate issues on some machines. The is VERY noticeable in Propast.
Overall:
This is a worthy sequel. It feels finished and fully fleshed out. I'm enjoying it immensely and I cannot wait to see what happens next.

This is a game that has the complete package, a well paced well crafted survival experience, great base building and interior design options that can keep you engaged for hours, bosses and missions that advance the story as well as ground each race, the missions are all very interesting as well, 12 quadrillion planets to visit and explore, a really deep mesh system that streamlines mining and also allows you to trade between space stations, visit friendly and hostile ships, and explore anomalies that can be something as simple as a crashed ship to a space vaccine lab, some of them even give out bits of lore, a very in depth colony system that allows you to attract colonists and get rewards from them as well as getting them to join your ships crew, you can also build space stations to act as an orbital colony, there is even an in depth collections menu that gets you, if you like, capture pets, try to collect action figures, catch exotic planetary insects, uncover fossils, cook food, and catch fish(which is no pushover) and that collections menu alone can rack up your hours, there is also a lot of really fun really satisfying weaponry, you can get the random ones with a unique combo of perks if get an amazing legendary weapon, these weapons are handcrafted and are always unique as well as powerful, you can get items such as the electro whip, the boomerang,  the alien worm gun, the tesla's wrath, the firestorms fury, or the doom cannon, these can enhance the combat experience,  there are also cosmetics... Lots of cosmetics, which is good because it allows you to make your character have whatever outfits or looks that you want making your character feel like your own, there are microbiomes that motivate you to travel onto the planets and find new furniture to attract rare merchants to your colony, as well as gain new cosmetic items and foods, there is even stuff after you have beaten the main game,  there are these challenging zones where you fight a procedurally generated boss, after you have beaten the boss you can upgrade legendary weapons and get terraformers that allow you to change a planets type, there are also all of these planetary structures and towns that add a lot more depth to each planet, there are 7 races you can play as all of which have their own ship and armour sets, these races all stand out from one another, some hate each other some have alliances with one another, the races add a whole New layer to the game, this game does not tend to get super gfinch compared to other survival games. overall I recommend this game.

I've spent over 300 hours in the first month after the purchase, so it's avery good investment for the given entertainment.
I'll begin with the cons:
- Beware for your social life...
- This game is in no way finished, and considering that it's a one man work, it will continue to evolve for years.
But, there are rumours of modding support that's coming in, and with the actual community I'm sure that will accelerate the development drastically.
- The game is laggy with huge creations or when there are too many missiles, and I honestly don't think that will improve a lot, it's a simple matter of "people always want more", so if the game is optimized, people will make bigger creations and launch more missiles.
- The game is complex and without the help of the forums and youtube tutorials it is not even possible to know where or how to begin.
- I mean, the game is really complex, you've been warned...
So, why did I spent over 300 hours in a month on this game?
- After the first 15-20 hours, things begin to fall in and you understand the most important mechanisms.
- I'm a builder, and this game is about building.
- I like to have the possibility to create complex things, and this game is just that, you want to add a cannon? You have to build the cannon piece by piece, trying to find the balance you need for this specific cannon and this specific ship and I love it!
- You can automate some actions/reactions (not enough for now, but the game is expanding month after month...).
- I love ships.
- I love submarines even more (and I did not even began to build one!!! I want it to be perfect so I continue to learn how to make better ships...).
- The creator is dedicated to his work and he is very present on the forum (10.55 posts per day from him on the forum, and all that while working hard on the game).
- The potential of this game is HUGE. So many things can be added that I know I will be disapointed because everything that is in my mind will not be included in the game (but with mod support... who knows...). Anyway you can only be disapointed by something you like, else you don't even care, and I definitly like this game.
The point is, if you like legos, building war machine, destroying war machines or watching huge explosions and bits of vehicules falling appart, then why are you still reading this?? Buy the game, and play.
Thanks to Nick Smart, the author of this game, you're wonderful!!

TL;DR : Genius.
The game works, as a game, and it runs incredibly smoothly considering the astounding complexity on display.
The base vehicle AI (i.e. not counting the LUA scripts one can implement) is surprisingly flexible and isn't much of an obstacle in the way of your imagination.
As complex as the game may be, it's very approachable and easy to learn.
Do use the default "keyboard" controls vs. the "mouse" ones. The game implies they are long/hard to learn that is a lie.
Do use the symetry feature for symetric vessels ;) .
Do familiarize yourself with the basics in the vehicle designer before attempting a campaign. Why not?
In all my hours of gameplay I haven't yet touched the campaign (though I feel that I could, at any time... it's just that there's so many designs to build and test, and so little time! Oh the misery.)
Start small.
Keep an eye on your craft's center of mass. A lot revoles around that (pardon the pun).
Thus place your means of propulsion appropriately; for small adjustments to the center of mass I recommend lead blocks.
Learn only a few systems at a time in order to not get overwhelmed.
(So don't be discouraged if you fail to build a working airship armed with every type of weapon as a first build.)
You'll get there sooner rather than later, and nothing can compare to the satisfaction you'll feel when one of your cherished design performs better than intended and obliterates similarly priced stock vessels.
I'm still in awe such a game actually exists.
It's still in early access, sure, but each major update introduces new systems or improves upon a previous one, and it just works so well. Walking around on a very fast-moving and unstable vessel can feel a little jerky at times, but only because you've become habituated to how smooth it feels in every other situation. Anyhow, navigating a "sinking" airship feels appropriately cataclysmic, and I know of no other game that can deliver a similar experience with such fidelity.
As I said earlier, it just -works-, and the amazing (yet very approachable) complexity of the systems on display is an incredible stimulus for your imagination.
The game, even at this (early?) stage, truly lives up to its premise. If you have any doubts, there are a few youtube Let's Plays floating around; Lathland and Rosefall come to mind, but there are others of equal quality which I shall not name here because I am lazy. I've learned quite a few tricks watching their videos!

Summary:
Luftrausers is an arcade shooter, where you control a fighter and shoot enemies in a beautiful sepia-toned setting. The game is difficult, but with tight controls and good enemy designs, Luftrausers may offer one of the most satisfying  experience ever. The gameplay is simple, but it's hard to master. Destroying enemies in the game would give you combos to rack up scores, but to maintain the combos, you need to destroy enemies continuously. However, your fighter's health will only recover if you are not mindlessly holding down your firing button. This leads to a pretty hectic gameplay, where you need to constantly make life or death decisions during combat. Also, completing missions would reward you with many different weapons and body parts for you to customize your fighter, which then unlocks a whole new experience!
Overall, Luftrausers is a must buy for anyone who is looking for a difficult but fun shooter!

Spoiler Alert: Elodie dies. Like, a lot.

This game is best described as "Princess Simulator: How Will You Die This Week? Edition". The artwork sets you up with the expectation that is's a happy and cheerful game about . . . a princess whose mother just died and is about to inherit the throne. OK, well, tragic backstory, right? Then you go on a happy fun adventure . . . and die of blood loss because you don't have the medical knowledge to stop the bleeding from when you were ambushed and shot in the shoulder with a broadhead arrow. Or when you fall off a wall. Or when your ship sinks. Or when the peasants rise up and stab you with pitchforks. Or when your country is invaded because you insulted someone. Or when you try to channel too much magic and self-immolate.
It's interesting to me how there is so much choice in the game and yet, a lot of the decisions you make are based simply on what you've managed to teach your poor hapless Princess Elodie. You kind of end up setting a trajectory for Elodie and sitting back to watch the fireworks that, hopefully, set people other than you on fire. And not your father either. Or your dukes. Or your castle...
Although each game is pretty short (30-60 minutes?) and all the events are completely deterministic, there's actually a pretty large amount of replayability in the game. I still haven't found all the different paths through to winning (or "winning") the game, and there's lots of events that seem like really good ideas to pass, that actually aren't important. And vice versa! Never judge an event by how trivial it seems. Otherwise, you will die.
Repeatedly.
Actually, that's going to happen anyway. Poor Elodie.
(Just as a quick note: I've played this game significantly more than the 0.2 hours Steam claims I have. Just so happens that I like to play this game off-line...)

Orcs Must Die 2 is a game I'm too old for. I love it but I know I'm too old. Too old, too rich, too soilt. Don't get me wrong, I can still enjoy it but I can't help but look at the hundreds of enjoyable hours that could be had unlocking absolutely everything in the game and wish I'd had it when I was a time rich, money poor 13 year old.
It has a great ebb and flow to it. That is the best thing about it. You'll spend a lot of time fighting desperately to finish off orcs that have evaded your traps or rushing to set out traps before the next wave starts. There'll come moments of almost blind panic when you hear the battle mage cry "sappers!" or see a gnoll jump a barricade and start ruthlessly tearing through your archers but then they'll come moments of calm when you realise your traps have totally got this and you can sit back and just watch the carnage. And what carnage. There is just something that never quite gets old about watching the havok physics engine toss orcs about.
The game's main weakness is that eventually relies too much on spamming the large ultra-tough enemies that won't be stopped by your traps and are in turn best defeated by spamming your attack button. That ain't so fun. It feels a bit cheap. Still this only becomes a major irritation in 'endless' mode which is a sideshow to the main set of story missions. Although at the game will all too frequently remind you: 'endless' mode is great for grinding for the skulls needed to upgrade your arsenal of traps and weapons. Mind you since skulls are refundable and you get a fair few in the normal run of the campaign completing the game without playing 'endless' mode at all is quite doable. Unlocking everything though, that is a task best left to time rich 13 year olds.
Recommended for everyone, especially time rich 13 year olds.

If there were a "meh" button I would use it here.
I'll start with the good:
The combat system is great, albeit too easy a lot of the time. It reminds me a lot of the Batman games in the way that you can sort of dance around between enemies and perform various attacks. It's a lot of fun.
The Uruk Captain system is unique and very well drawn-out as well. There are so many various features for each and every one of these Captains, and in spite of most of them being randomly generated I haven't found anything about them to be repetitve. The looks, dialogue, and motives of these guys are so unique to themselves and it makes it feel like you've actually made a personal enemy when you're fighting these dudes. It's easily the best aspect of the game in my opinion.
The bad:
The story is extremely lacking. The character designs are generic, the dialogue is dull, and it feels like there's an extreme lack of substance. Everyone is so one-dimensional and lacks any sort of personality (excluding ratbag. That little guy is great). I just can't get myself to care about any of the events in the plot, and I'm usually really into story mode stuff. Whenever I'm doing a required story mission or watching a cutscene, I'm just wishing I could go back to fighting things.
And the world design is plain boring. I've done a heavy amount of exploring and I've found the scenery and environment to be pretty disappointing. Despite all my exploring, I always have to check the map to see where I am because everything just looks the same. Stone ruins, some grass, a few ledges, and a couple locations with some wooden shacks. Brown and grey everywhere, with an occasional touch of green. This is Middle Earth for god's sake, they could've thought up something better than that.
And finally, the handholding and lack of challenge. It's borderline patronizing how often these control hints come up. You can clearly see that I've put a decent chunk of time into the game, and I still get frequent notifications telling me the basic controls for the game. And not only that, but in missions the main character (Talrion? Talon? I can't even remember his name because I don't care) talks to himself in order to tell the player what to do. "Shooting that firepit will help me clear the camp", "Stealth would be of advantage to me here", shut the ♥♥♥♥ up Talor I know how to play the game.
Oh man and the controller hints..."Press RB to heal", "Press RT+X to perform a stealth attack", "Press Y+B to perform an execution". It acts like gamers are incompetent brickheads who can't remember anything for more than 10 minutes. The worst part was how it *always* popped up the control for countering an attack. Every. Single. Time. I was playing the freaking game with a giant "Y" in the middle of my screen. Thank god there was an option to disable that at least.
In the end it's a decent game if you can get past the flaws and boring substance. Ruthlessly killing swaths of Uruks and stealth murdering Captains is pretty freaking fun, but remember :
"Hold RT to sneak"

After some thought I decided to recommend this game, but with some caveats.
The best way I could describe this game is as a simplified version of Master of Orion I, with more emphasis to strategic battles (that cannot be skipped). We have battles, simple planet management, a very simple tech tree. You control only one fleet. You can add ships to it, or upgrade them by increasing the number of weapons, shields, etc...
There is no limit on the number of components on the ship, but the cost of additional components increases exponentially.
Another difference from MOO I is that you cannot colonize, and every planet is already populated, and by visiting them you can take battle missions, By winning them you gain influence and eventually the planet will become part of the federation. And yes, everything is turn-based.
The main focus of the game are the missions. Indeed, you're going to spend very little time managing the planets and more fighting. Battles themself are generally short (about 5 minutes), and you can perform several battles per turn, as you can move your fleet multiple times per turn.
Don't try to have long gaming sessions: you'll get bored very soon, because even if there are several types of missions the game mechanism repeats itself over and over again. This is not Civilization, Or Galactic Civilizato, Or Masters of Orion.
You are an admiral. You lead your ships, run missions, earn influence of the worlds you visit.
The emphasis is tactical. Expect to spend a lot of time on a battlemap.
Lasers are long range but planets block them and asteroids can block them or reduce damage. (There are a LOT of asteroids on a map!)
Plasma weapons do more damge but are shorter range.
Torpedoes are area affect and can pass through asteroids. Great for flushing quarry from a spot thats too good.
You also have fighters, stealth systems, shields...
You will build wonders, improvements and the like, but as I said, the emphasis is tactical or these elements are lighter fare.
The game can be small and played quickly. The hardest victory conditions on the biggest map is about a six hour affair on easy level.
A lot of people complain about the small window but playing full screen is trivial. There is a fullscreen button you can click in the menues...you can also simply maximize the window.
A lot of people want a longer game...I recommend if you feel that way you play a "Population" victory, or "Domination" if you want an even longer game.
In the end there is not as much here as there is in Civ or Beyond Earth. Then again, look at the price tag...
On a 1 to 10 I give it an 8.2
It's entertaining.

Tales of Symphonia was probably the best JRPG available on the Gamecube (though, there weren't many). By today's standards, the game is actually still quite good due to the fact that the combat system is unique and more action-filled than your typical menu-selection-driven combat games of traditional games in the genre.
The game is set up in such a way where if you are just interested in the story, you can get through the game without too much effort or grinding, but there are plenty of optional things you can do if you are a completionist.
Typical JRPG tropes are abundant in this, and the story is really not unique to the genre. In fact, it's actually incredibly similar to Final Fantasy X. Regardless, if you like this sort of game, it's certainly worth a playthrough, even today.

I always considered The Longest Journey and Dreamfall the work of art more than a game. Judging by the short 1st chapter that is available now, Ragnar and his team still have this narrative and artistic power over the game that most other developers lack.
As with the previous game, most of the game you're looking for a way to find/hear/watch the next piece of the story. No you won't be shooting bad guys, you won't build tanks, but you'll experience a very beautiful story staged in a very exciting world.

So far, this is a wonderful experience. The graphics aren't exactly up to par with current PC and console games, but for me it's the story, seemingly forever unfinished and constantly unfolding, that keeps me coming back to the bridged worlds of Arcadia and Stark. After eight years of waiting for a cliffhanger to be resolved, it really feels like things are finally coming together. Even though only Chapter 1 has been released at the time of this review (and I admittedly seemed to whisk right through it, but I just couldn't stop playing) I cannot WAIT for the rest of the story. I'm so happy this was made, and I remain a fan of this series who finds themself immersed in the story, environments, and characters and I just want more and more.
Bring it on~

I bought this game for two reasons: it was ridiculously cheap, and I recognised the type of game it was and thought "I haven't played one of those in a while".
Why the thumbs down? There are plenty of flash games on the internet that do this better, and of course for free. It's a very simple formula, and yet this game manages to mess it up.
1.) First time running the game, I was treated to a splash screen advertising a different game by the same developer, complete with embedded youtube video. (I understand they were giving it away for an email address, but still guys, this is bad).
2.) This was followed by a config window for resolution that can't be accessed from within the game.
3.) Navigating the menus with the mouse was frustrating as the pointer displayed as higher on the screen than it really was. This meant having to guess where the volume bar was to lower it, and in some cases clicking the button above the one I wanted to click to get the desired effect.
4.) The 'tutorial' level gives you controls, but doesn't really say what they do. I was plonked on a planet that I couldn't leave using thrust alone, instead having to toggle gravdrive first. I'm still not really sure what this actually did.
5.) Those purple lines. Oh god those purple lines. These are horrific for three massive game-ruining reasons:
a.) They constantly move back and forward in a swaying motion, standing a really good chance of giving you a horrible headache after about 5 minutes.
b.) As the lines are all parallel and always in the same direction, it makes it really difficult to accurately judge the boundaries of the area they surround. Just from the screenshots you can see this. Look at the stage in the shape of a 'W'. Where do the edges parallel with the lines even start? It's not where they're purple, because the space between them also kills you, and the lines are constantly shifting....
c.) This is the worst part in my opinion - the purple-lined 'death zone' only kills you if you go a certain way into it, which isn't marked in any way whatsoever. From part of the trailer I thought that maybe just the purple lines themselves would kill you and you could maneouver between them, but this isn't the case. There is an arbitrary distance which you're allowed to travel over the lines. Worse still the game actually depends on this and gives you levels early on that require you to skip those gaps, with no way of knowing how far is too far.
It frustrates me that a game like this can make any money at all. Bugs can be forgiven, but this is just an absolute masterclass in terrible design.
tl;dr - I spent more time writing this review than playing the game, and I also had more fun.

Luftrausers is a game where you fly around in a plane that can do crazy maneuvers and shoot enemies until you die. Pretty simple, pretty hectic gameplay, pretty insane, and on that note, insanely fun to play.
The gameplay is controled with 4 buttons; left, right, boost and fire. These buttons can be configured to your liking in the options menu, and you can even play with a gamepad. The goal of the game is to eliminate as many enemies as you can before you get shot down. Fortunately, you don't die in one hit; instead, the game makes a shaded circle around your plane indicating your health. The closer said circle is to your plane, the lower your health. You can recover health by simply not firing, but this means you'd potentially lose any scoring combos you had going, encouraging high-risk, high-reward gameplay while not penalizing you for playing it safe.
The missions (i.e. subquests that unlock parts for your Luftrauser) start out simple, but quickly get tedious, annoying and often luck-based; as such, I would not recommend this game for hardcore completionists. However, it's fairly easy to unlock all ship parts relatively quickly (except for the final ultimate Luftrauser obtained from 100% mission completion), allowing for flexible gameplay that can suit your playing style.
In conclusion, Luftrausers is a fast-paced aerial shootout that only loses its fun value if you focus more on completing the missions for achievements rather than obliterating every enemy you see.

It started off simple - got this as a gift from a friend, was bored didn't have anything else to play. Okay why not - she got me the game may as well try it. I am extremely glad I did because this simple tower defense idea became Orcs Must Die.
The gameplay is simple which follows a tower defense sort of idea. Instead of bland towers and a bird's eye view of watching the action, the game puts you as a player in 3rd person view capable of unleashing an array of weapons. Some weapons included are a bazooka and a spear. All weapons have secondary attacks such as turning orcs into stone or unleashing a proximal blast. On top of having a variety of weapons to choose from, the player is also able to deploy a variety of different traps or towers. Deploying defense mechanisms is very simple; it is easy to remove and add defenses almost anywhere on the map. Some of these defenses include arrow walls, tar pits, blocks, giant swinging gates with sharp cone pointing things, floor spikes etc... Basically there isn't a shortage of what to choose from when it comes to beating up the orcs. Defenses and even weapons can be upgraded with the amount of skulls you collect per level. The amount of skulls is dependent on how well you do throughout the level.

Kyu's Review for this game, Sid Meier's Starships:
Me:  I play way too many games, almost all the time.  I grew up on RPGs and turn based strategies, but I would play everything given the time and money.  That being said, I mostly stick to strategy, rpgs, fps, arcade, rhythm, ccgs, lcgs, board games, fighting games, etc
I am going to tell you how I boiled the game down, and win relatively easily.  I don't have a sample size of 100 games, but I am 3 for 3 on easy, moderate, and hard, with max players, small and epic sizes, all 3 affinities, etc.  Impossible is the only mode i have yet to touch.
#1 strat:  Fighters.  The names may not be exact, but here is what you need:
Dual Command Wonder -- allows ships to perform 2 actions per turn (but cannot Fire twice)
Hyperlauncher Wonder -- allows your fighters full movement when launched
Upgrade as you normally would, engines, armor, shields, primary weapon.  Get more ships, 5 or 6 is a good strong fleet.  Then, get 2 or more fighters on every ship.
Here is why 1 starfight is not good --> If you turn is to move ships up, and launch a fighter from each, opponent can move up, and destroy them easily.  So nothing is gained, your fighters are dead, effectively a waste of your energy on that upgrade, right?
However, with the Dual Command Wonder, you can launch two fighters.  So even if half of them are destroyed, you are now up the other half on the enemy. If you have 4 fighters per ship, you can do that again next turn.  The Swarm is an achievement, and its a very real thing.  Make sure to science upgrade fighters 2 or 3 times for the random modules on them.  Even on hard, I had Fighters that could take 2 or 3 hits from enemy ships.  You can also use the Hyperlaunch to get a full move out of the fighters, and hit them, before they are destroyed, even if you dont have the dual command wonder.  Dual Command Wonder also applies to your Fighters, though all they can do is double impulse, or fire+impulse.
The rest of "how to win" is upgrade sensibly from the bottom up, find the cheapest thing, upgrade it first.  Get the most for your money.  BE SURE to get every planet a WARP NEXUS.  This will allow you to be able to protect all of your planets from any of your other planets.  You will be able to move between them without crew exhaustion.
A note on torpedoes, use them to Zone the enemy fleet.  You can see where they will be in 2 turns, so aim for places you dont want the AI to move into.  If they do, boom they die, if they dont, fine they are in worse position and you get to move in.  Just watch out for their torpedoes, especially if they have stealth torpedo wonder.
So what will happen is, you do your turn, the AI does theirs, and if you have a strong fleet of Fighters and Warp Nexus upgardes everywhere, you can defend everything successfully, taking little to no fleet damage, meaning you dont need to repair or worry about attrition from battle to battle.  New turn, go dominate someone.  Survive the counterattack, and this continues until you finally win.
I will say that on Hard, the AI fleets were better upgraded significantly.  They are more dangerous early on, so be a little wary.
All in all, a 1 thing beats all strategy means its not good gameplay balance.  But... its just comp stomp i guess.  So nobody can be too mad.  For $15 you will get your value out of it, but it doesn't offer any super great planning or depth of thought.  I was hoping there would be more to it, I thought you would be making separate fleets, possibly an actual tech tree, so on.  I don't hate what is there, I just think it could have been a little better.

First let me just say that Starships is a decent and fun game to play for the low price it costs. The game has really good graphics which is what I have come to expect from Sid Meier's games.  The loading time into the game is a lot quicker than the standard civilization games which I also liked.   To me it was like a board game based in space using the basics from the civilization games. Their is some micro managing you can do in Starships but its not overwhelming like it is in other civ games.  I also like that the planetary jump gates allow you to keep moving your fleet without adding fatigue.  I played a game on the easy  level and had the largest map. I still finished it in under 6 hours, which is kind of cool considering their is no multiplayer option for starfighter.
I do feel their is a few drawbacks that I feel could have been improved upon.  The game seems to randomly shut itself down, which isnt that huge of deal considering it has the continue option when loading back into the game. The saves could use some work. I dont know where it saves it, I am assuming it is in some kind of cloud. I was unable to locate the save file directory on my computer for starships. I prefere to be able to manually delete my own save files without having to fire the game up first to do it. So if Starships is updated I would like to see a save file directory on my pc.  The in game maps do not seem to be that big in my opinion. The tool tips could use improving, it kept wanting me to develop my ion  engines even after i increased the tech and took ship engines to 5.  Finally their is no multiplayer option with starships. I think starships would be a lot more funner if i could have the option to play with my friends against the Ai's or each other.
The one thing I dont understand is why only 1 fleet? Im guessing that is because the fleet is used for visiting the planets and attacking while the planetary defence's are for when you get attacked.
So over all the game is fun to play if you dont mind playing it by yourself against the computer.  For the price of $15 I paid for it, I feel it was worth it and recomend it to play.

Having played Sid Meier's Civilization since its first incarnation, I was interested to see how a $15 combat focused spinoff would play out. Starships possesses minimal depth and is far cry from what fans of the series are acustomed to. This is not Civilization, but it also doesn't pretend to be. It is a fun $15 game that focuses almost entirely on fairly rudementry combat mechanics. I have been enjoying the game and I highly encourage people to purchase it. Take a look at some Youtube videos and make your determination from there. What you see is what you get. There are no surprises.
On a hours played to money spent ratio, Sid Meier's Starships is absolutely worth a buy.

A leap forward ? Or a step backwards ?
When I think of Sid Meier Games, I think of complexity, good balancing,  time investment. If I think about the first day I saw Starships announced, I was very enthusiastic about a space game made by the creators of Civilization. I couldn't wait until the day it comes out on Steam, checking every day the time left.
And then the time came, and I made the leap of faith to buy it and play it. What happened next not only puzzled me, it saddened me quite a bit.
The first time I launch a new game I always check the options menu to set up my audio and video settings. This time I couldn't find ANY graphic options and I started thinking of Starships like I would an unfinished/unpolished game. It felt like an Alpha version of a future game.
Nevertheless, I still wanted to see the game mechanics and what was in this game content wise.
A couple of clicks and choices later I was in a brand new universe managing a planet and 2 starships.
5 hours later and a few restarts I already finished the game on domination and I slapped my face because of the lack of a challenge behind the game. I'm not even inclined to open it another time for another game. :(
If you are looking for a quick, skirmish like, march of war style, starship game, this is the game for you, if not, don't bother.

Get a glimpse at what could've been!
The failed attempt to continue the SiN franchise lives on in some kind of zombie limbo on Steam. Before the advent of digital distribution, this would've been the kind of game that would've showed up as a few screenshots in a magazine before quietly slipping beneath the waters only to resurface a decade later on eBay when some former employee of the company finds some old build burned on a DVD in a shoebox in storage somewhere and decides to try to cash in on the collector's market.
Instead, we can play the first playable chunk (which is a reasonably polished and fun little bit of shooter) and get the entirety of the old first game all nice and legal-like. Worth the price if only because it's the kind of thing that normally nobody outside the company making it would ever get to see. All you nerds who go digging through torrent sites or eBay trying to find old builds of unreleased games so you can check 'em out, you should be all over this.

So we can expect at least 25 hours of TLJ goodness for a fair price of just under $20.
For those of you wondering - please don't expect Red Thread Games to charge you more for each episode. You buy the game now, pay once and get the episodes as they're ready to roll.

Postal is the first in the Postal series and it definetly stands out for being different from the rest in tone only. In my opinion this is one of my favorites in the series, infact it's one of my favorite top down shooter.
The story isn't that incredible and is just there because there needs to be one, basically life in paradise is♥♥♥♥♥♥ and you are being evacted from your own house, you (The Postal Dude) believe a disease is going around, and you are the cure. You go on rampage with your shades and memorable one-liners to ♥♥♥♥ up Paradise. That is basically the plot, although there's a diary entry in the manual, showing the character's thoughts and feelings through his madness.
The aim of the game is simple kill all the hostiles, and kill all bystandards (if desired and if you want to get 100%). You are told to kill a certain amount of people, however it's best to kill everyone for the 100%, after you kill everyone you press F1 to proceed, this is what confused a lot of people who didn't read the instructions, but funnily enough you get a achievment!
The game can become difficult as you progress, so it's good to take you time, however not only does the difficulty increase, so does your roster which become very useful in certain situations. You have a stock standard weapon roster, but you'll be using the SMG the most since it has unlimited ammo. Although some weapons are utterly useless like the mines, grenades are made frustrating however by the co-ordination of each grenade throw.
As I said this game can be very difficult at times, which is why the gameplay becomes very strategical making you want to plan your moves, the game isn't as frustrating as for example: Hotline Miami, the game is the sort of difficulty you would expect from Quake, a game that influences POSTAL quite a bit and was definetly the type of game RWS were aiming for.
If you were a fan of the sequels, then you may be disappointed with the game, and I wouldn't see any reason to play the first, if you're expecting the game to be like the second, which is a overall better game in every way. But if you're curious, or want a fun top-down shooter get Postal.

The first time I played State of Decay, it didn't quite grab me. Years later, I gave it another go, as I had a craving for some kind of single player survival/crafting game.
I very much enjoyed it. State of Decay has a good mixture of exploration, town/base management, quests, and story.
The story line was a little bit weak, and a few times I would get stuck with no quests to do. This left me frustrated with nothing to do but roam around and kill zombies.
I felt that the game handled deaths very well. Generally in todays games, you die and there is no real down side, you just restart at your base with a slight penalty. In this game, deaths are permanent and that character is gone for good. This left me swearing a few times as a feral zombie was all over me. This game is great for a few reasons.
One: it handles microtransactions well. In this game, real money usually only gets you cosmetic upgrades like weapon skins and apparel. Even then, much of that stuff can be bought using the normal in-game currency. This game doesn't force microtransactions onto you, and you can't get much of an advantage over people by spending tons of money here. I haven't spent a penny, and I'm placing in the top few in the scoreboard after a match.
Two: the controls. This game handles very well. The guns feel tight and the movement is responsive. It's been fine-tuned very well.
Three: the visuals. The HUD is clean and the environment looks great. My only complaint with this is that there's no way to lower graphics settings to smooth the sometimes shaky performance, but that's easily redeemed by how great the rest of this game is.
Four: it's fun. Games are supposed to be fun, and this game is some of the best fun I've had in a while.
You can really tell when a developer puts time and effort into their game, and Soldier Front 2 is one of the best examples of that in a while.

Ghost Recon Desert Siege is the first expansion pack for Ghost Recon, developed by same Red Storm and released in 2002,  one year after original. Yep, still same tactical shooter. It added new single-player campaign, new weapons and expanded multiplayer.
Well, since multiplayer is kinda dead, you probably not going to care about those two new modes. However, you can play 5 multiplayer maps in custom mission if you choose Firefight or Recon mods.
Also I didn't notice new weapons personally. I mean, how different they can be from whatever realistical weapons Ghost Recon already had.
But it does add a new single-player campaign made up of 8 missions. And this time things are going south, from cold Russia into whatever hot African country, where you will be annoying everybody off by the border. Yep, it's still same Ghost Recon gameplay in different enviroment. Still with frustating AI, with enemies now even more happy to throw grenades that teammates AI doesn't bother to avoid, feeling sometimes unfair. Still quickscamming.
It doesn't add new gameplay elements, the only new thing are enemy jeeps, which have driver and machine gunner. They can screw you up and are nice addition. But it's puzzling that Demolition's anti-armor weapon is useless against jeeps. I mean, direct hit may not even harm anybody in the jeep. It should blow up!
But the levels themselves felt much better designed around Ghost Recon gameplay. They are now much more wide open, consisting of huge spaces. And I feel it makes it more pleasent to deal with teammate AI, as they are much better at providing support and cover over such distances. While you place them around to cover each other and move on slowly, taking baddies out from a far. Unless you once again have to enter building with only one path where you get one-shot instantly. Missions also didn't try to be gimmicky, the only armor escort mission has a very slow-moving convoy.
And well, this expansion is good. At least if you liked the original. Overall I think I had more positive experience with Desert Siege's 8 missions than with original's 15 levels.

Ghost Recon: Desert Siege expands the world of Ghost Recon from Eastern Europe to the deserts of Africa. Small tweaks to the game make this a worthy addition to the original Ghost Recon. In comparison to the original game, the maps are also larger fitting into the desert theme. The long distance engagements can actually be quite interesting because more often than not, you are spotted in the wide open and there is little or no cover in some areas so approaching the situation is quite important.
This is definitely a worthy addition to the original Ghost Recon game. Anybody who is interested in highly tactical games and already has the core game would adore this expansion. And if you don’t have the original, get on that because you’re definitely missing out.

Desert Siege has an uninteresting plot behind a short campaign on boringly similar wide open and desolate maps. There is only one convoy escort mission, and there aren't many engagements with armored units to be had. There are fewer specialists and weapons available.  Even as someone who prefers an infantry focus and long distance engagements, I didn't like it much. The package isn't complete without it, though.

I bought this because I was desperate for more Ghost Recon missions. The maps are not that good. The desert gets dull easily, and if you have a good sniper on your squad, the long sight lines of the map make this a cakewalk. Only buy this if you really want more Ghost Recon.

The expansion mod of the original "Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon," "Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon: Desert Siege" replays the experience, sweat, suspense, and 'awesomeness' of the first Ghost Recon in a desert enviroment.
It stages in a war against Etheopia, and gives you the feeling of being in the heat of the sun while you play! Though there aren't as many missions as with the first Ghost Recon, the missions are harder, and take a bit longer to complete.
