This is a pretty dang fun game to screw around in when you've got nothing else going on.  It controls well and is extremely fast-paced and engaging.  I love the little flavorful elements they injected into the game, like the music changing depending on which parts you're using.  The selection of said parts is cool, and they each change the feel of the game drastically.  I really dislike the homing missiles because even with the bomb or melee body it's just too hard to kill anything large, and their accuracy is surprisingly finicky given that their weak damage and low rate of fire suggests that their one trade-off should be an inability to miss.  I still have two challenges to complete (not counting SFMT challenges), so I don't know what the [CLASSIFIED] is like, but my favorite Rausers are "Holy Diver" and "Staff Pick."
However, I feel fairly emasculated by the number of digits in the score display.  Do people actually score hundreds of thousands of points at this?  My high score is like 30,000, and that's because most games I play spawn three battleships in on me at the same time and I honestly don't understand how you're supposed to deal with three battleships given their range and rate of fire.  I mean, seriously, even though I'm pretty good at killing battleships now, how the hell am I supposed to kill three of them when a new one willl just spawn in its place?  In other words, I think this game would be better if it chilled out a bit when it comes to what it spawns in and how quickly it spawns it.  To be fair, each game certainly gets interesting quickly.
That aside, highly recommend it.  It's stylish, extremely well produced and just plane fun.  PLANE FUN GET IT

is an action shoot-em-up with a rogue-like system of customization. The basic gameplay involves you shooting down enemies while avoiding fire, racking up as many points as you possibly can before your inevitable demise. The premise is simple and the execution is superb.
The combat is also simple, yet very hard to master. It combines some of the aforemented rogue-lite elements along with bullet hell shooters (Think of the Tohou Project). Gameplay is fast paced and intense, as you rack up points and gracefully weave in and out of gunfire. It's fast paced and sometimes even mesmerizing at some points, with bullets all over the screen. The amount of customizable options makes the game even more in depth, and allows players to create a plane that accommodates their playing style.
Of course, this being a Vlambeer game after all ensures that the presentation is top-notch. The graphics are silky smooth at 60 frames per second, and the music perfectly sums up the onscreen action at any moment.
In short, Luftrausers is a great game to spend a couple of minutes on.
Be careful though, because those couple of minutes will soon become several hours.

Great game and I am really looking forward to the next chapters, I think our long wait have been worth it!! Dreamfall chapters seems structurally similar to "the walking dead" game, where choices with consequences seems to be one of the main features, as well as the episodic content. However, unlike the walking dead - this game actually seems like the choices matter more and have real impact compared to "the walking dead". The setting is fantastic, the characters are very good as well - especially Zoe.
Pros:
- The music is immersive, and really really good.
- Story is very interesting, very unique.
- Zoe is a great character! And there are few games with female protagonists, which is something this industry definitely needs more of.

If you have never played The Longest Journey or Dreamfall, be warned that this game is dialog heavy. Like its predecessors, Dreamfall Chapters is an interactive story.
The Good:
- After eight years we are FINALLY moving forward toward a resolution.
- Beautiful graphics. The city of Europolis is huge and feels like a real city. You can eavesdrop on conversations! I loved just poking around the city looking at everything (remember to look up at the sky).
- Protagonists are interesting and relatable. Zoe's journal is a nice addition.
- New, fantastic characters introduced. I can't wait to learn more about them.
- Some new, imaginative ways to interact with the environment.
- I love the costuming - even the NPCs. Really well designed and I can tell a lot of thought went into every outfit.
The Bad:
- The controls were almost unbearable for me. I really couldn't get used to them and I got very frustrated at times trying to click on elements to interact with them. Some puzzles took me a long time to solve purely because had no idea an item could be interacted with, despite moving it into the centre of the camera field. Moving around felt very slow and clunky, even after several hours of playing.
- My computer has above the recommended specs and I got some brutal fps drops.
- Some ham fisted dialog and story elements. I get that Ragnar is trying to make a statement about the political situation in the West at the moment, but really. Lea Uminska's campaign posters are exactly the same style and colour as Obama's "HOPE" posters. Konstantin Wolf's posters have a Futurist/Constructivist lean to them like old Soviet propaganda posters.
- I noticed quite a few small errors - maybe some were intentional? They were distracting. A jellyfish is *not* a cephalopod!

I wish this ran a little smoother on my system, but I have been waiting for so long for this game that I can ignore a little jitter caused by a slightly old laptop. The story so far speaks only of even more depth and intrigue to come. I cannot wait for the rest of the Chapters to be released!

The Escapists 2 is a sequel to the Escapists in the way the Binding of Isaac: Rebirth was a sequel to Binding of Isaac. The game takes the original and amps it up on every level. The graphics are gorgeous, combat is great, and they added more cool items.
On top of that, none of these prisons are boring. They all have different and unique themes, such as the Wild West or Area 17. There are many different options to escape them too. It makes the prisons repayable.
One of my favorite features is customizing your characters. Instead of the old game in which you selected from around 6 pre-made characters, this time you can create 10 of your own with many customizables, including headphones and beanies with bear faces. As you play the game, you unlock more customizables.
And alas, the multiplayer feature! Something that was for sure missing in the original. You can play with up to 4 friends over the internet or locally, and it works great! The online has very few latency problems in my experience
The one thing that bums me out is the bugs. I know this game just came out, but the amount of bugs from an everyday prison run is just irritating. Sometimes you will not be able to attack (this was a one pointed out by YouTubers before the release, yet the bug still exists). Other times you will not be able to push buttons required to open doors. Often I get a glitch in which a sniper shoots a character over and over again but the character isn't being affected by the shot.
Most of these bugs are fixed with a simple reload of the game, but when it comes to playing online multiplayer, the reloading can become quite a hassle. This is something I know will be fixed, but it's good to keep in mind if you are planning on purchasing it early.
Overall, I'd definitely recommend The Escapists 2. It has more than enough content to be its own game apart from the original. It also feels way more polished.
Whether you've bought the original or not, you should give this a try. You probably won't regret it.

First let me say that I came into this game knowing nothing about it but being a huge Civ's and Ace Patrol fan.
This game is similar to Ace Patrol in its combat, though you dont have pitching and height mechanics, it feels the same.  Its out of combat screen however is a simplified 4x map.
You get one fleet, it travels between planets and does missions to gain trade routes (similar to Spore) if the planet is owned by someone else you go to combat with their fleet, simple enough.  The planets can have their facilities upgraded and more cities added, each choice gives you more resources per turn.
Your fleet can be upgraded, better weapons, shields, armor or change to new tactics like cloaking, torpedos, and launced fighters.  You will be able to do all of these eventually, you wont lock yourself out of any design, though you do have to balance your ships components with speed.
The tech tree is tiny unfortunatly, the prices scale quickly so you will be sitting there a while if you're trying for a tech victory, its small but not short.
The victories are done poorly, instead of a civ style advanced setup option you get to pick between all the victories (Population, Science, Domination, and Wonders) and any single one of them.  In practice the All games tend to end in domination or population quickly, wonder victories can come out of no where and science takes too long.
The starting options are a bit generic as well, each civilization has a unique bonus and each captain has a bonus, the captains are the same reguardless of race however their portrait gets a slight change.  Some say that its lazy I think its cute.
It has a pretty cool integration with Beyond Earth, you can earn starting choices for Starships and Beyond Earth by playing the other game.  For example because of some Starships gameplay I get a new starting option in Beyond Earth as well as a map for an achievement and for playing Beyond Earth I can choose hybrid civs with double the bonus abilities in Starships.
Over all I hope it gets polished because it does have short falls.  Its not a bad game, its pretty fun in fact, and the cross integration with BE is something I can't support enough I love it.

I don't write reviews very often, but after reading the negative posts (currently about 50/50 love it/hate it) -- I feel like SID's Starships is becoming a victim of negative "sheepism".
(There are a ton of well written "Recommend" reviews and "DNR" reviews out there that cover the mechanics/features of the game.  Go read the top positive and negative reviews if that's what you are looking for, I won't rewrite the same info here.)
I will clear up some of the "top rated" negative review posts by players who spent ~2 hours in game and therefore believe they have it figured out based on the depth of their experience, and then share negative posts with the rest of the strategy gaming community:
- "All you have to do is capture the enemy homeworld and you instantly have all of their starsystems and resource production.  Rinse/Repeat to an easy victory."
--  Congratulations, you beat the game on Easy Mode (about 10-20 minute gameplay once you figure out a few winning strategies).  However, play the game on Hard/Impossible and you'll find that feature is disabled.  The player must now conquer each system to wipe out an opponent.  Additionally, once you start crushing your current enemy and it looks like you're about to waltz through their empire, the AI is smart enough for that oppenent to *surrender* to another NPC party ts friendly with, thereby converting all of its resources to them rather than allowing you to have them.  Smart.  And a great way to rebalance the game so that the entire game is challenging, not just the first 50 moves.
-  "This this a cheap iOS game port.  Not worth $15"
--  Opinions will very on this one.  I agree that the UI and standard PC control (display settings etc) are lacking, but I feel the game works very well on PC in spite of being simulataneously developled for Phablets/Tablets.  I PC game across a triple monitor display, and unlike most recently released titles, the game is solid across any resolution I choose and any window size, while also having multiple other windows/programs open and running.  And its solid.  Not one crash, no glitches, no weird anomolies (granted its not a resource hog).  That's rare.  How many new games out lately suck until version
Besides, dev's are going to follow where the money is.  Think about that when complain about paying $15, the equiv of a fast food meal or a movie on something that you'll arguably get many more hours of enjoyment from.
-  "There is no depth like other SID titles."
--  I'll agree that this game isn't as deep as the CIV series, but it has its place (15 minute to 3 hour long games).  If you are looking for a space based Civ, write the devs, wait a few years, and be prepared to pay $50/60-ish.  But play the game on Large or Epic, and on Hard/Impossible (only after you've played it through a few times on Small/Med -- or you may get crushed), and you'll see some depth.  You'll see how the opening moves are critically important not only in how you design your ships, but where you do the upgrading.  Same for Planet/Star Systems.  BL:  Judge the game for what it is..not because you wanted to Pay $15 for a huge game like Civ
-  "The AI cheats."
--  ...      ....      .............         .................... really? in a strategy computer game? <every AI cheats, harder the level, the more the cheating.>  honestly, I get the frustration at not being able to set victory conditions for both sides (users can only determine/limit their own vic conditions, AI will choose whatever strategy it thinks will help it win).  It'd be a nice feature that might be added by the player comm or devs down the road, but thats more a problem with players not handling their own expectations.  Think outside the box and the feature is just another way of adding difficulty.
Final thoughts/Overview:  The game is mostly about it sequential-tactical combat sequences.  This is a direct contrast to the SID Civ titles where global strat/management is the majority and combat isn't developed. There is still a strategic element that if mismanaged will result in a loss, regardless of how good you Tactical execution is.  For the tactical fights, there is something altogether gleeful in a stealthed torpedo exploding in the middle of an enemies battleship formation. Take that you "17% chance of winning" estimation!

For those of you who have never played Orcs Must Die!, it is a tower defense game that allows the player to freely roam the environment.  You’ll be allowed to pre-pick what traps and weapons you’d like to use before the waves of enemies start coming, place said traps, and then take an active role in stopping them yourself.
Orcs Must Die! 2 keeps with the general theme.  The player will be allowed to pick between two characters (a male war mage or a female sorceress) and will immediately begin their trek from level to level, unlocking new traps and earning skulls to purchase upgrades.  The spellbook is a lot more impressive, providing the player with more traps and upgrade options.  There’s also a page for trinkets that give both passive and active effects…a welcome addition in my opinion.
All in all, Orcs Must Die! 2 is a great game that I’ve had a lot of fun with so far.  I look forward to unlocking more of its content, all the while listening to the game’s soundtrack.  If you liked Orcs Must Die! or just enjoy a good tower defense game, then give this game your attention.

This, was quite an interesting, unique and fun game!
So, you control the princess, send her to classes to learn skills and get better at things, and do your best to avoid getting taken over or killed.  This is actually QUITE difficult, as there are many different ways for you to die, and you will experience quite a lot of them (but that's good, there's 3 achievements related to this).  So don't feel bad, or a failure, or anything: it's to be expected!
The game shows you the 'checks' that it does to trigger certain events, so you can figure out something to try to do differently the next time around.  And this is certainly not a 'single playthrough' type game by any means: there are so many events that can trigger, and so many ways to try to do things, that you really can't help but try again and again to do something different!  (I put in nearly 30 hours just trying different things out!)
The story is interesting, the characters have their own interesting personalities (and own different stories and actions that you figure out through multiple playthroughs), and the game is definitely worth it, even not on sale!  My only regret was that I got this game, promptly put it on my backlog of games to play, and only got to it now!

So... honestly, it's not so good as I was expecting. The base gameplay is simple: play the game until you die or fail, then try remember what skills you were tested on, and play again while learning those skills. It's not like you can predict what's coming up, as the other reviews point out (you can die from the most arbitrary of conditions, many events don't test the skills you'd expect them to, and some skills that sound useful do very-almost nothing). So the gameplay really isn't the reason to play this, but it's really supposed to be centered around the writing.
Which is why it's unfortunate that the writing is incredibly generic. There's seriously nothing unique or witty about it. It's like the writers went "Let's think about an ordinary thing that might happen. And then write it exactly how you'd expect it to go."
In fact, really, the only reason I can see why people play this so much is because it's addictive. Which is a pretty poor reason to like a game. So no, I don't recommend it.

Iv'e been waiting for Dreamfall Chapters to come out since the last game ended on a cliff hanger. and so far it does not dissapoint!. (there thats for fans of the series)
For newcommers, Dreamfall Chapters is a 3D adventure game in the manner of Walking Dead and many of the old point and click games from the early years of video games on PC.
Now Ill say this now. you should play The Longest Journey: Dreamfall before you play this game (you do not have to play The Longest Journey but its got some usefull backstory and can help expand your appreciation of the world) now you do not have to in order to enjoy the game but it will have that much more meaning and you will really understand the characters and events at the start of the game if you have finished the earlier game.
on with the rest of the review:
What sets this game apart from its forebears is that it has a tree based structure to its storyline. so for each choice you make there is a real consequence. Now thats the claim from Red Thread the studio responsible for the game.
As there is only the first part of the game available, it remains to be seen how extensive this system of choices is, but after some time playing the first book and trying every choice I could make. I am fairly confident that the game will deliver in its promises with upcomming episodes.
The game uses two choice systems, one is the Balance system a set of events that have a coinflip answer, where the resulting choice greatly effects future outcomes for the character. the other is a walking dead esque system where characters remember your reactions to various events and these are taken into account with future conversations and events.
while many of the choices and events presented provided numerous choices and possibilities, there were very few choices available that had immediate results. I am greatly looking forward to the second book to see how these choices pan out.
Now, it would be remiss of me to not mention some current issues with the game:
It has some known graphical bugs and issues with resource usage they are working on fixes for.( they fixed the large framerate drop happening in Europolis and other areas)
Some people are having crashes and freezes (not me but some people are)
The save game system needs work because it just makes a ton of autosave files without any sensible naming system or organisation.(only an issue if you want to try a different response or load a non current game)
The game is mainly about making choices and solving puzzles, this in future will include things like stealth and probably some light combat. but it will be unlikely that combat will be particularly reflex intensive or action oriented.
Characters in the dream world seem to have various powers so a kind of magic is also featured in the game in certain areas.
Will you enjoy this game?
If you liked games like myst, the stanley parable, any older point and click adventure  you will love this game.
if your into combat and violence, you may still enjoy it but it will feel slow and boring due to long heavy dialogue sequences and alot of travelling.
I love what they have done with dreamfall chapters and am looking forward to the next chapter to see how far they will go.

I'll say this right now. If you haven't played the previous two games
or
please go out and play them, even if you only play
. This game references them heavily, requiring the player to have some prerequisite knowledge in order to put events in the game into context. Thankfully it doesn't sacrifice the pace of the story in lieu of accessibility.
It's a recurring theme actually. In a choice between story and something else, this game chooses the former. Every single time. You'll need to set your own expectations, if you come into this expecting something akin to a fantastic interactive story with some extremely well realised characters, you will not be disappointed. If you're the type of person that gets bored with dialogue and skips cutscenes to carry on playing then refrain from purchasing it.
Like Myst, Gone Home, and The Walking Dead, this is an experience that requires you to take a back seat, and just enjoy the narrative presented. After seeing a presentation from Red Thread a year or two back, I was worried that the new choice system would be a cliched binary "save the puppy" or "eat the puppy alive" moral dichotomy, and that it would compromise the main characters' intended personalities. Thankfully that isn't the case. Choices never fall outside their conceivable paths of action, but there are clear distinctions between them. Neither do a lot of them centre on a moral choice, instead them being a personal one.
Art direction is as fantastic as ever, and they really manage to drive home the wider state of the world, particularly in Europolis. Last time around it was Arcadia that blew me away so it's a nice change. There are some flaws in execution, such as weirdly skinned characers, art assets that can be a little rough, and some minor shader issues. But if you a consider it a tradeoff to prevent a situation as in Dragon Age 2 where areas and assets were just constantly re-used I'd happily take it.
I do have issues with framerate in some parts, but since I haven't updated my drivers in ever I'll refrain from making a judgement on it just yet.
tl;dr: If you played and like the previous two, it offers everything they did and more. You won't be disappointed with it. If you're new to the franchise purchase and play the previous one first, if not both. If you like them buy this one. If you hate games with cutscenes and dialogue, only wanting to get to the next level, then stay away like the plague.
Always the major draw of Longest Journey and it's sequels are the world building. Love love love this game already, can't wait for more :)

- Bad language. Too much of it - 'DC' has more bad language per square millimeter of gameplay I have ever seen in a computer game. I have no idea what the developers wanted to say. Well, I've played this game a lot in the last year, I've played the DLCs too, got 100% achievements, but I still don't know what kind of rating I can give to this game.
There are a lot of things that I've loved in this game, but there are also things that I hate.
First of all, this game is not that kind where you "shoot everything that moves like a psychopath" like L4D2, but is about surviving the zombie apocalypse by scavenging, finding resources and being silent while you do it.
The main story is actually boring and unoriginal. You start as a survivor called Marcus with his useless friend called Ed, and after discovering that there's a zombie apocalypse, they decide to searching for more survivors. They found a community made by other survivors, they join them, and with their help they try to escape the county.
Even if the story is not so great, what I've liked about the game is the gameplay and more of its mechanics and details.
- The game is open world. You can visit every part of the map, where and when you want.
- You can build your base with Infirmary, Kitchen, Sleeping area, Storage etc., but you need materials for building them. For getting materials, you have to scavenge all the abandoned houses, shops, farms and other buildings all over the map.
- Every character in your community is playable, and have different skills that need to be increased by normally playing (Stamina, Fighting, Shooting etc.). Once you increase a specific skill to a certain level, you can unlock special abilities that are helpful while fighting, like dodge zombie attacks, being more accurate with rifles by slowing the game time, grab a zombie and smash them to the ground, and other more...
- During the night, the zombies became more aggressive and are harder to spot them. Their eyes glow red, but sometimes are hard to notice.
- The zombies are attracted by noises. If you shot with a gun, or do a lot of noise while scavenging, all the nearby zombies will run where the noise has started. Sometimes they come in horde and you can't handle them, and force you to escape or you will die.
- You can't use only one character. If you use a character for too long, his stamina starts to decrease, and if his stamina decrease he can't defend himself from the zombies if he gets attacked. So, is advisable to let him go back to the base for let him sleep, and switch character.
- If your character dies, it doesn't respawn. It dies forever in the game, and you can't load a previous save, since this game saves automatically.
- The attack animations are great
- Fantastic atmosphere, especially during the night. It gives a lot of tension and I'm worried about being seen by someone and attract a horde
- A really nice soundtrack
- Mods
If those are the positive things, there are also a lot of things that I hate.
- Boring story
- If you don't play the game for a while, you lose part of the resources.
- Side missions are repetitive.
1) Apparently, the other survivors in my community, can't do♥♥♥♥♥♥on their own and they're always in trouble in the most annoying parts of the map... and obviously I have to save them, or they probably die.
2) A member of the community is always♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥for something, and I have to "talk" with him (going in a random place and killing 5/6 zombies)
- Lot of bugs that aren't fixed. If you want those bugs to be fixed, you have to REBUY the remastered version of the game!!!
- NO MULTIPLAYER! A huge map like that, with those game mechanics without multiplayer, is only a WASTE!!!
For concluding, this game is... great, and deservers to be played at least once. Just buy it, but ONLY during sales!

First of all: this is not Civilization. If you go into it expecting a full scale space 4X-game, you will probably be disappointed. I see there are a lot of negative reviews complaining about this fact, but honestly, I don't think it is fair to blame Firaxis if you neglected to do your research before buying. Firaxis actually did a pretty good job of showing the game in advance through livestreams which were also posted to Youtube.
For what it is, Starships is a pretty good turn based game, with a nice mix of strategy and tactics. It is quite lightweight and simple, but I don't think there's anything wrong with that. The game seems quite polished, and runs really well, as you would expect, as an identical version is available for iPad.
And that brings me to my biggest criticism of the game: the PC version seems to actually be *identical* to the iPad version in almost every respect. This means hardly any options menus, and some really annoying interface issues. For example, moving the cursor to the edge of the screen doesn't scroll the map like it would in just about every other modern strategy game. Instead, you have to click the left mouse button and drag the map, just like you would on a touch screen. That's just lazy, in my opinion.
Still, I have enjoyed my time with this game so far, and don't really have any problems recommending it. Just be aware that it is a considerably lighter offering than a full 4X. If you are unsure, I recommend that you check out the gameplay videos on Youtube, in which Sid and others at Firaxis also talk about the design of the game.

Bias warning: I love strategy games, and so I am more inclined to view them positively.
Starships is a good game for the price. Its based on an extremely simple mechanic with a few randomly shifting variables that try to introduce some variety (things like: environmental effects, mission types, etc) that can alter the gameplay on a per-mission basis. Its based on the Beyond Earth universe, and will actually read characters out of your Beyond Earth savegames. The whole game is squarely focused around Starships (hence the name), and everything else is built around giving starships modifiers and abilities to make them more effective. Its a turn based game, with the only reflect mecahnic being the "push button detonation" ability on the torpedos.
Good game, but a very small game without much variety. There's a lot that could be done better. But considering the price-tag, its about what I would expect for that price. No this is not another Civ or Civ-sized game. Plays differently, looks differently, feels different, price is different.

It is a fun game set in Beyond Earth universe.
I enjoyed it and would recommend to anyone who liked the setting (or enjoys flying around in a star fleet of stealth bombers :D).
---
+Easy to learn!
+Awesome ship/fleet builder. Do you create a hulking flagship, or a swarm of smaller ships? Speed vs armor? Drones? Torpedoes? Stealth? Fun choices.
+Engaging tactical battles. Always nice choice whether to create an ambush, flank the enemy or charge head-on. Different missions have varied objectives and modifiers that can affect the randomly-generated battlefield.
+Wonders. They can be the cornerstone on which you build your entire battle tactic.
---
-Lack of depth. It's a lite game and is nowhere near Beyond Earth - let alone Civs - in terms of depth of its mechanics.
-As result of above, the replayability will be lower than in BE/Civ.
-UI could use some improvement.

Just finished my first game (on normal), so these are all initial impressions:
Much like the Civilization ports for iOS, Starships is linear and short. I actually stumbled into a Wonder Victory while stomping through the galaxy to little resistance -- a domination victory probably wasn't that far off. I'll definitely have to increase the difficulty level in my next try.
I didn't find much use for researching tech other than the ambiguous notion that it's helping me somehow. There's little context to tech developments like Artificial Intelligence (what does it mean for fighters to have a 'random module'?). It seems, though, like once I got fighters, the only thing I really needed to focus on was making sure that my starships had too much HP to be taken down.
And there's absolutely no use to diplomacy other than to use it as a war on/off switch. You won't find the modifiers that you're used to in the Civ franchise, no helptext around why someone is angry/happy with you other than the general assumption that the closer you are to their border the less likely they are to want to be your friend, and maybe I'm an idiot but I didn't see anywhere where you could trade goods. Also, I found the fact that the other leaders were willing to give up all sorts of information about their empire (like how many ships they have, what their upgrades are, etc.), even in a peace treaty setting, a little weird, especially since war can be ignited as easy as clicking a button (there's no penalty for breaking a peace treaty, near as I've found).
Though, I have to say that it's not like I had a bad time. The game seems fun enough for $15. I guess I haven't had a chance to experience the AI at a higher level, so maybe I'll feel like there's more strategic depth to the game once I do that.
I mean, it's $15. Obviously not a fully fledged game. It's a time waster, so look at it through that lens before you pull the trigger.

Puppet Kings is criminally overlooked.
On the surface, it's a breakout style block-breaking game.
But it goes deeper than that.
The game is made up of entirely bosses and mastery of the paddle and ball is absolutely necessary in order to see everything this game has to offer.
Many bosses feature a hidden way of defeating them - one example being an alien space ship can either be easily defeated by killing it's captain, or you can start by breaking each energy orb of the spacecraft. If you break all the orbs, it summons a chuthulu-esk creature and subsequently leads you down an alternate progression path filled with new bosses and hidden ways of defeating those too.
The music and art of the game are also fantastic. There are no reused/reskinned bosses in the 15-20 I've fought so far and many of them have unique themes tied to them. There's some fantastic animations associated with them too.=
The fact that this game isn't doing well is an absolute travesty.

The artwork for this game is amazing. It features pretty art for every of the protagonist's expressions and costumes, some unique special artworks and animations for certain events and different adorable drawings displaying the demise of our heroine Elodie.
A negative point would be the look & feel of some of the menus - imho they could need some improvement here and there.
The soundtrack is fitting/good. I think overall it features 17 minutes of unique music, and even though some are repeated really often I didn't get tired of any of them.
The story is quite linear, but imho only in this way a strategic VN like LLTQ is possible. All in all it was a rather simple, yet enjoyable story with a lot of twists, depending on your own choices. Certain plot points and situations are always going to happen, while others can only be seen or experienced in a different way depending on which skills you learn.
Most characters in the game, besides the heroine, are nobility and nameless commoners. Some have names and portraits while others are barely mentioned or don't even have a proper name.
While you have to try to please or subdue all of them in one way or another, Elodie herself is a lot more complex than that.
Depending on your decisions and skills, she might become a timid and quiet ruler, while in other situations she can be an upright and confident leader or even a cruel tyrant who is feared by her commoners.
After a quick basic tutorial, the game throws you right into the main action. You are told to learn skills and balance your mood to improve your studies each week, and every learned skill influences the events that you will face.
You might find multiple ways to get through situations - some more and some less forgiving.
You have a set amount of time until the end of the game and most of the game events happen at the same point on each playthrough, so it allows you to find different ways/strategies to deal with them.
The game is challenging (I read people calling it the "Dark Souls of VNs", and I'm inclined to agree to some degree) and I think most players will meet a certain death during their first playthrough. When you grasp the general concepts and know which events you have to expect at which point of the game and how to get through them, it becomes alot easier.
Due to all the different methods to win (or lose) the game, it has a high replay value until you have found most/all of the secrets.
I really enjoyed LLTQ, and to me it was money well spent. I will definitely spend some more time on that game to unlock all endings and achievements.

Dark Souls is a test. Dark Souls is a challenge. Dark Souls is a commitment to who you are, to your values in life, to the person you want to be. Many see a game as a childish venture to be easily dismissed, easily forgetting that the way we play games exposes who we are as a person. Dark Souls will lay you bare. And if you reach into yourself and find the fortitude to experience a moment of the game over and over and over again, until you overcome--you will find supreme joy.
You play as a character of your design (it’s an RPG), who is thrust into the situation of being dead--yet never dying. You are cursed, the Undead. You must fight your way out of your prison for the Undead to find yourself part of a plan to free the world from the curse, and earn yourself a deserved rest. The world you must face is full of Hollows, undead who have lived too long, who have experienced too much, who have lost their minds; and of gods, who stand in your way at the twilight of their lives.
The entire game is a fight, a struggle. All the enemies are placed and before you encounter them they don’t move around very much. So each fight begins the same. That sounds boring, right? But then you engage the enemy. That’s where the game comes alive. It’s as if the game itself is a god who watches you, and alters reality in order to test you. You’ve fought this weak trash a hundred times before. You know the movesets. You are aware of your surroundings. But then you get too complacent, too familiar, too secure, and, OH♥♥♥♥♥♥ you forgot that other guy was there, and now they’re both wailing on you. YOU DIED. You made a tiny mistake and the game punished you. This is what you’ll face, over and over and over again.
Sounds boring, but if you have the courage you’ll discover that it becomes rather thrilling to win against the odds. You face large and powerful bosses and you think there’s no way you can defeat this thing, it’s huge and the game cheats and ♥♥♥♥ all this♥♥♥♥♥♥ you’re not going to play again. But you do. And with each death you find yourself getting a little better, learning something new about the boss--and yourself. And finally, after who knows how many tries, you win. YOU DON’T DIE. You will feel this euphoria wash over you, and you will push on. This, this is what Dark Souls is about. And this is why you’ll love this game.
Don’t be fooled, however: it’s not a fight simulator. It IS an RPG, but it’s very minimal. You design your character and you interact with characters in the world. But nothing is handed to you. I meant what I said about the game being an entire fight. Much like the fighting, you have to put in an effort to world-build. Much of the story is told through the descriptions of the items you find. You just fought an AWESOME BOSS who looks SO ♥♥♥♥ING COOL, but who the hell is he? He dropped a reward, read it, it’ll give you a hint. Oh, you found a weapon somewhere else that makes you think of that boss? Read the description and you’ll find more to the boss’ story. An NPC makes a remark that’s a clue, although the NPC doesn’t know you know about the boss or ever fought him. The world is waiting to be discovered, as well as conquered. The levels are all connected, with hidden paths, alternate paths, and all have a hand in telling you the story that you found yourself in.
And if you’re wondering about replayability, this game has it. You can play this game single-player as many times as you want and it won’t get boring--I promise you. But there’s also a multiplayer aspect to it, where you can help other players with their boss--or you can fight other players. Much like the game itself, it can be frustrating to experience. But once you “git gud” you’ll end up enjoying the chance encounters.

I’m so horribly disappointed by how this game doesn’t even come close to the excellence and the magical otherworldly atmosphere of The Longest Journey. This is something that Dreamfall:TLJ, the second game, suffered from, but not to such an extent; and at least, it didn’t suffer from such weird pacing and writing issues.
The Longest Journey sometimes frustrated me by how arbitrary the solutions to puzzles were. Dreamfall Chapters takes this annoyance and dials it up to 11. There is also no explanation for your powers in the Dreamtime world; they’re just there, they’re not explained, and the game has to point to you through dialogue in a really hamfisted way that you have to use this “slow time” power on characters before doing another action in order to progress.
"Show, don’t tell": the golden rule of narrative, and it was thrown away here.
As a result, the game feels like it’s forcing you through itself, it just doesn’t have the Longest Journey spirit and atmosphere at all. Remember how outlandish and “out-there” the universe of the first game was? You got thrown by accident into this parallel universe with its huge city, full of unknown and not relying on any conventions. Dreamfall:TLJ slightly dialed that down (but it wasn’t that bad), and in Chapters, you’re pretty much ending up with a generic mashup of cultures.
A good comparison for this is going from Morrowind to Oblivion; you go from something very original and unique to something you’ve seen in 50 other games already.
Two technical things also bug me here; character animation is almost non-existent. They very rarely move while talking! And sometimes the game just fades to black for a second when a character performs an action instead of showing it through animation.
There are also really big performance problems, even on a high-end GPU.
As a long-time TLJ fan, and as someone who backed the Kickstarted for this game, I just can’t recommend it… I’m just really hoping the other 4 books will raise the quality but this isn’t looking good so far :(

Shadow Of Mordor is an action game where you have to slain enemies in Sauron's army. You acquire perks, talents to boost your character by defeating generals and commanders which are stronger than regular soldiers with their own weaknesses/fear and strengths.
I was going to write a lengthy  review but I'm too lazy so I'll just list pros and cons.
PROS :
- musics are great
- graphics are good, game is well optimized
- the game has a good replay value if you don't mind its biggest flaw
- the middle earth is well reproduced
- gameplay is responsive
CONS :
- THE GAME IS WAY TOO REPETITIVE. I understand it's supposed to be a game that you play a couple hour here and there, quit and get back to it another day but your missions just consists of killing orcs while they are surrounded by dozens of soldiers. You can interact with he world but I  never found a way to effectively draw my target away. Arrows aren't strong enough to kill them, fireflies just scares them, mouting a cougar (forgot the name) is pretty rare etc.
So you just end up doing a stealth attack then killing 20+ enemies.
- SoM is ludicrously easy. Spam normal attack until you have a QTE then parry or evade, rinse and repeat. You can cancel everything with your parry or roll so the game feels responsive but there is no afterthought about attacking, just keep spamming Square/X until you have a QTE.
- The map is boring. It's an open world with cliffs, mud and wooden constructs. There's no caves, no forest, no volcano etc. It doesn't help in the long run.
Shadow of Mordor is not a bad game overall, it's just that it's not for me and I didn't really get into it, or maybe I didn't play the way it was intended to be. I felt that the game was way too repetitive for me and that's why I didn't push myself to continue, so maybe I missed some good content but that's my opinion from what I played.
Got it for 4€ during a steam sale so it's definitely a good value.

Transport Giant was a game originally released in 2004 by Jowood. Initially I played it as a demo and got very curious( when i was younger I used to play Transport Tycoon Deluxe followed by Industry Giant 2). These kind of games are quite rare(complex ones like TG,TTD,IG2 even rarer). The game puts you in the position of a owner having plenty of cash to start a Transport bussiness with the ultimate goal being to become a Transport Giant. You can extend on many fields of transport (at first horses,trains,trucks,ships,blimps,etc) and carry all kinds of goods (from people to steel). The game is mostly based on a classic system of supply and demand. You can play in 3 different places (USA,EUROPE,AUSTRALIA). The interface and setting up can be a burden at first but once you get used to it you won't have any problem. The biggest 2 minuses so far to the game(mentioned in cons) are : Inactive AI and the new interface.
Appealing, but in the end utterly frustrating. The interface is user unfriendly, games a decade older were often better in that regard.

I've been looking for this game for years. I played it about 10 years ago when JoWood first released it.  It also came with an editor in which you could build a multitude of different 'unique' buildings requiring different materials.  However this isn't included with the Steam Version.
The Campaign missions for the US and Europe are the same as the original game. I haven't played the Australian missions before this release, so that's all new to me, however i know they were also released as an add-on a couple of years after the original game came out (I bought the add-ons but my crappy computer at the time wouldn't even recognise the discs).
Pros for the game is it's diversity of starting points. If you start in 1850, it's with horse and cart, simple ships, and a 'horse train' options. As you start in later years, more updated modes of transportation become available. Road quality is just a gravel road in the 1850's, but can improve to Autobahn standard later in the game. An endless number of maps can be created depending on what type of game you want to play, from a mountainous continent to a small island archipeligo and everything in between.
I love the view of the game. There are plenty of in-game options eg if trees confuse the view, or the names listed are in the way, then you can simply remove from your view by clicking on the appropriate button on the bottom of the screen. Discrete but effective.  I always remove the trees, they dont really serve a purpose in the game except to clutter the screen. The mini-map is movable or can be removed from view is you require. I personally leave it in the upper right corner as it becomes a quick guide to locations.
The only part of the game that bugs me is the train connection system.  If you start a line, then future additional railway lines additions MUST come from the lines already placed.  There is no other way to create a new railway line. If you want to create a line on an separate part of the map, then it must join with an existing line before it can be built. Many a time I have wanted to create a railway line far away form my original line, but have had to use other forms of transport, or spend a lot of money on getting a virually useless line to my new setup.
I haven't had any screen issues as what may potentially happen as per the game page. The game seems to run as it did many years ago.

I HIGHLY recommend this game, though the graphics are dated (but not aweful mind you) it is gameplay that really counts.  At a glance the routing and schedule making system may seem broken, or overly complicated, but with just a little patience you can figure it out.  Another way to help with that is to watch the one-off lets play of this game by PewPewChewChew on Youtube.  Though there are a few performance problems with later OS, they dont seem incrediably game-breaking.  Occassionally the game will freeze for a few seconds (literally 1 or 2 sec) whilst routing vehicles and such, you cant go clicking things quickly because the delay between the click of the mouse and the implimentation of the click in game WILL lead to buildings being placed incorrectly, but PATIENCE is a virtue.  The only major thing I have incountered is that occasionally, usually after scrolling in to fast (which the game processes REALLY slowly compared to scrolling out and other things) AND clicking things a tad quickly the game will have a permenant (from my experiance) brain-fart that prevents you froming interacting with the UI (you can still move the mouse and check on map info, and the vehicles still move and make money so the game is not frozen) which prevents your from really continuing the game (escape key does not even do anything) so you will have to Ctrl-Alt-Del out of the program and restart the game, which will make the UI fully functional again.  With that in mind I can not stress enough SAVE EARLY AND SAVE OFTEN.  We all know it is not fun when we make lots of progress and suddenly a game crashes and we lose all that beautiful unsaved progress.  Otherwise the gameplay is just the right combination of Complex and Simple that we saw so often in older titles, but sadly lacks in more modern games.  The game is highly reminiscent of Chris Sawyer's Locomotion, but in a more (I would say) completed and flushed-out state, with things like company takeovers (Note it says you can do it and I have seen it mentioned in game, I have never attempted this myself)
IN SUMMERY
Do buy if.....
-you like indepth transport/tycoon games
-enjoy creating/developing complex systems of roads, tracks, airlines, and shipping lanes
-have patience
-can cope with a few minor issues of functionallity
-enjoy a wide frame of history
-If you like Industrial Giant 2 and Chris Sawyer's Locomotion (my personal fav)
Don't buy if.....
-You NEED the best of cutting edge graphics
-Have ZERO tolerance for lag/momentary freezing/and semi-"Crash"-type thingys
-Don't enjoy slower gameplay
-Have little to no Patience
-Don't enjoy games with a moderate degree of complexity

Do not let that disuade you from picking up this VN, as that familiarity is definitely not necessary to enjoy this VN.  I would definitely recommend this one if you were ever curious about the BB franchise but just aren't into fighters, but it is a fine story that can stand on its own as well.
To go even further, I completely played through the story of the first three core Blazblue games (CT, CS, and CP) and this story actually cleared up a lot of what I always thought was not clearly explained in those games.  I love the BB series but its lore can be a little overwhelming to understand completely (if even possible) and this VN can double as a good primer for those games instead of just as a prequel.  Also, one of the characters in XBlaze will be playable and a have a pretty significant role in Centralfiction's plot, so there's that.
This VN is not a linear story, and there are multiple endings.  You arrive at these different endings by whether you read particular articles in Toi, an in-game phone app.  The game does tell you from the very beginning that your choice of reading will change the story's outcome, but how is somewhat ambiguous until you play through the story at least once.
The game's text is available in both English and Japanese, but the speech is limited to Japanese.  The translation to English for the most part is pretty good and certainly much better than a lot of translated anime and video games (including the main Blazblue games). There were a few discrepancies here and there, but I only recall one that I felt was significant (in terms of how it characterized that character).
I would recommend picking it up if the store's description of the game piques your interest,  On a personal note, I am normally not very interested in visual novel games, but this one held my attention throughout and admittedly produced some major pudding-related feels at certain moments.  Give it a try.

The Good:  Interesting story (kind of required for a visual novel) and multiple paths give lots of replay.
The Bad:  It is very easy to miss reading an article on the TOi, which can ruin your current run.  Make sure to have multiple saves!
The SaHD:  Admittedly not much of the plot was a surprise to me, since I reviewed the sequel to this before playing this game.  I also found I prefer visual novels on a portable device to the PC.

XBlaze Code: Embryo is a game set 150 years before the events of Blazblue Calamity Trigger, serving to explain some of the lore behind the game, Don't worry if you have not played the main series, this game does a good enough job of explaining most of the things. I think one of the great things about how they went about doing it is that lore is first introduced then explained (such as
). This gives some satisfaction to those who are fans of the series as well as not alienating the new comers.
I have been a great fan of the game, ever since I saw a preview of the first game, Blazblue: Calamity Trigger, in a magazine. This game was great in helping me answer some questions (
) as well as providing me with more questions for this already confusing lore.
The art is not that amazing. It looks abit pixlated and stretched on my monitor. However, the music featured was nice, some of the tracks even paying hommage to the blazblue tracks. Starships is a Fast-paced, Turn-based, tactical and strategical game aimed at modern players, who prefer a short campaign with a strategical depth that they can grasp while playing it casual.
Something that a Fan of Sid Meier, Civ, Firaxis and PC-Strategy just isn't used to. And therein might be the reason for most negative reviews: every feature is reduced to its bare essentials to provide a dense and fast strategy experience. It doesn't want to fill your evenings! It want's your small chunks of spare-time, entertaining for 30 to 90mins at a time. Your trip to work, your break, or that 40mins that you can steal away while your kids watch their favored show.
(Things you should get accustomed to, to enjoy it)
I love strategy games, no longer hardcore, but "normal" ones like Civ. And yes, this game isn't for me, at least not for that part of me. It can't fuel a strategy addiction with dozens of hours, but Starships never wanted to! It tries to offer tactics&strategy to casual and short-time players; Or old ones, who can only relive the old days for one hour or two at a time.
It deserves a place on the gaming market, but right now it is drowned in negative reviews of players, who expected something else.
Please understand, that Starships weaknesses are a strength to a lot of gamers out there. Give them a chance to find it!

Sid Meier's Starships......an out of the blue title that generated a lot of anticipation and more than a little wonder at what the package would bring. Now it's here and while it's not socks from Grandma at Christmas, it's not quite the game you were hoping for either. Good but not great, worth the price but perhaps unworthy of the legend that is Sid Meier.
This is not a 4x game nor was it ever advertised as such. It's more Ace Patrol than Civ, something fun that won't require huge chunks of your life to complete but something you can come back and jump right in to. While lacking in chrome, this game retains Sid's famous "one more turn" quality. The game is fun to play and the deeper you get into it the more strategies become apparent. I started it, played a few turns and stopped to do something else several times, then fired it up again after dinner and played it straight thru to midnight, surprised at how much time had passed.
The lack of chrome, i.e. the ability to rename your starships and planets, the lack of any leaders, not nearly enough starship models, etc..... is disappointing but not a show stopper. Hopefully, given the track record of Meier products, this will be addressed in future updates. I hope to see steam workshop support added as well to let Sid's passionate fanbase come up with their own ideas. This is the kind of game that cries out for a Star Trek/Star Wars/BSG mod from some basement genius and I can't wait to see that happen.
Over the years I've bought and played every single game Sid has ever made. This game won't add to the legend that is Sid Meier, but it won't detract from it either. You'll get more than enough gameplay from Starships to justify the cost, you just won't be sitting around 15 years from now saying "remember Sid Meier's Starships?!?! Now that was a game"!

It's senseless, it's a nice tower defense, it has options (flavour!) for killing orcs, has a co-op (worth it), AND it's cheap?! Oh sign me up. Good derpy-graphics and animations, a decent amount of shock and violence, an in-game, reset-able upgrade system for weapons, traps and trinkets (so you're not locked in to any mistakes, and are able to refund your skill points to better suit the map upon which you're killing) and staggered difficulty for a range of players. This game is wonderful. Then why such a low rating? Well, it's a bit buggy, as gridless TDs are want to be. Occasionally a monster will cut a corner and "glitch" over a barricade and some of the guardian (living and mobile) towers clutter around each other and don't keep a precise line of fire. Yes this makes for a more realistic experience, but in the heat of a wave of orcs when you're trying to go for a take-no-damage and use-no-mana run, it can be one of the most maddening experiences of your life - particularly when the harder maps tape between 15 & 25 minutes to complete. My little brother decided to buy me this game. Twenty-five cents was all it costed, and he bought it because he has no impulse control.
I decided "what the hell" and decided to take a look at the game. My very first words were "what do i do" followed by "PURPLE SPACE STRIPES WHAT THE HELL". And thus began my descent into madness. It began simple; fly to the portal and avoid the majestic purple space stripes. It was a simpler time. But things began to pick up, as I realized three things.
1. You can shoot purple space asterisks out of your face.
2. You shoot white space asterisks out of your butt for propulsion.
I failed to achieve thought number three, as I was dumbfounded by exactly what the hell my ship was supposed to be; an enigmatic green mountain with snow against the fluorescent stripes directly from the depths of hell. Eventually, the endlessly looping music gave me a new question; why do I have no hitbox? The purple space stripes are fickle mistresses; sometimes, you could fly deep into their embrace; other times, they'd simply tear my tiny little space mountain into tiny space mountain shreds.
I then proceeded to punch my little brother in the face, and continued my adventure. All I could see now was planes of darkness, travelling across the purple space stripes. Travellers against the legions of hell. And as I flew, my little brother called the "space portal" a purple space hexagon, causing my final drop. I fell so far, that I pierced straight through hell, and found myself in the abyss.
The abyss of purple space stripes. That's about the time when, for the safety of my sanity and the entire universe at large, pulled the plug on my computer and lobbed it out a window.

A bait-and-switch of regal proportions, Long Live The Queen wears the facade of an anime visual novel about a young princess becoming a queen (and indeed still is that), but is at heart a complex stat allocation and time management game.  Every in-game week the princess can choose to study a wide range of seemingly mundane skills, but in the dramatic life of royalty any skill might suddenly become relevant, from World History to Interior Decorating to Archery, and the princess’s untimely death might lurk behind any unassuming door!  This leads to complex strategic trial-and-error gameplay in determining which skills are needed when, what actions cause which ripple effects, and how much slack is permitted while avoiding a point of no return.  The game itself is incredibly open-ended and allows for hundreds of winning skill combinations, all while still following a coherent and interconnected story, so as long as the player can keep the princess alive they can turn her into any kind of princess they want, even a heartless dictator, and watch as events unfold.  While the marriage of two rather polarizing game styles will likely alienate many prospective players, it is that same absurd combination which makes the game so unique and enchanting.

The game is "OK", for those who truly like transport games (Transport Tycoon / Locomotion), but with a lot of micro-management that takes work in the UI.  There is a learning curve and some clunky controls at first, but then the game works once you understand the mechanics.  There is no tutorial, and it is rather confusing at first to figure out how to setup 2 depots, setup routes, and have things run efficiently enough to finish in the scenario expected timeline.  In my first play of 80 minutes, I frequently ALT+TABed between the user manual linked from steam, and watched a video walkthrough of the frist level.  It gave me a headache, and I about gave up.  But once I understood the mechanics, I started over on the scenario on the second day, and now I could control it well and won the first scenario.  If you aren't a fan of transport games, this is probably not the first such game to try.  But if you like the concept, and watch someone else play a walkthrough, then you get how it works and can have some fun.
Works great on my Alienware Alpha (i7) with Windows 10, full screen on my 1080p TV (smaller window until you adjust the settings to 1080), has not crashed during my initial sessions.  What I like about the game is it starts in 1850, and really makes you use Ox / horse carts to achieve the mission.  Then in the 2nd scenario it gets into trains.  They are picky too, because you might forget to tell it to stop at a station in reverse order on the way back, run out of water and crawl, or forget to specify which items to pick up and lose money.  Laying track isn't "fun" either, and is a bit of work, but is serviceable.
A few tips for things I didn't understand at first:
1. You must build truck depots, you can only schedule things between your depots.  Put them in an area that overlaps (and turns buildings green) that you want to handle goods.  You can have multiple depots servicing the same building from the shared stock, and may be more efficient with less traffic.
2. Pay attention to the right & left arrows at the top of menus.  They are the key things that purchase (move to the right side of menu), or add a vehicle to a schedule (move to the left).
3. Still in scheduler, click each depot to add it to the route list, BUT you are not done.  Also beware of scrolling by dragging with the mouse righ-click and pull as it exits the scheduler menu, but arrow keys work, zoom out, and pan by mouse to the edge works.
4. Still in scheduler, select the depot that services the goods to pick up, and you *MUST* select the good to pick up, click the left arrow to add it, *BUT* only for the station to pick up from.  You can also select the up arrow (wait-for-full-load) on the first stations and select the down arrow (wait-for-unload) on the second station.  You might think you select the good to unload, but if you keep it selected on the second station it will not unload.
5. You can easily duplicate routes by clicking the duplicate button instead of the checkmark.  It took me forever until I realized this.  Also, once a route is created, you can duplicate existing routes by a single click if you select a vehicle on the route, as long as you have enough vehicles left unused.  Once I got this, it got a lot easier.
"OK" for the transport enthusiest, when on sale.  But is hard to recommend.  A mild thumbs-down.

If you ever thought to find your normal everyday life wasn't normal, then you've come to the right place, we start out our story of the Azure/Blue/etc. with Touya Kagari, a normal High School student with his pals Hinata and Akira, but when Touya comes to a place of remembrance, he meets a mysterious girl by the name of Es, and the two start their journeys together.
As it is, XBlaze is the prequel story to the popular fighting game series "BlazBlue", the lore you'll seek from BlazBlue will also be mentioned here as well, including some characters within similar familiar names and other viable info. Originally available on the PS3/PSV, the Steam release is more or less the same as it is, with a few PC options to tweak to your style, along with the option to have the subtitles either in full English or Japanese. The game is pure Visual Novel, so the game relies on its own system called the "Toi" (which also has Character Bios), using it wisely will decide your fate, from getting the good, bad, or even the gag endings. Using "Tips" will let you know on info of the XBlaze world, though some of it will differ depending on which character route you're planning to clear.
Either way, the port is great, and it loads scenes and such faster than the console version (also, bonus extras if you happen to clear all routes in the game), but yes, as usual with majority PC players, there will be problems with people trying to run it, it happens to some, but not all, but it happens. This game is actually pretty great. I, for one, was someone who thought that the original escapists was a brilliant game that was merely just flawed in some areas. I pre-ordered this game thinking that it was going to be "meh" due to the new art style and such, but I was pleasantly surprised. The multiplayer is undoubtedly the best addition to the series- I have played through every prison with my friend, and it was an absolute joy to play through. The game retains most of the elements of the original, but offers some new welcome gameplay elements, tweaks, and a new art style. If you were one who thought the original was too hard, I think you will be satisfied with this. There are many things to make your escape more convenient, such as a hidden compartment in your desk that can only be seen by you (meaning that even the guards cannot check it during cell shakedowns. When damage to the prison is found, the guards call in a repairman to repair it, rather than immediately sending you to solitary. There are some things to balance out this difficulty, though, such as being forced to spend a few minutes in real-time to get out of solitary. As previously mentioned, this game is meant to be played in multiplayer, as it adds a lot of fun to the game, but is still 100% playable in singleplayer. Another thing that this game improves on is the means of escaping- there is a perimeter breakout on every normal prison, along with one special singleplayer and one multiplayer escape, that are achieved by interacting with certain things on the map. Speaking of the maps, all of them are fun and involve a good bit of thought. I thought all of them were great and a joy to play through, with the exception of the HMP Offshore. Three of the base game prisons are "transport" prisons, in which you have a frame of time to escape and the guards are constantly on the lookout for you. These sound like a chore to play, but they were actually some of my favorite in the game.
TL;DR The Escapists 2 is a large improvement to the first game (that I already found great) due to the dozens of quality-of-life improvements, fun and enjoyable maps, good art style, and most importantly, a multiplayer that makes the game as a whole much more enjoyable than it already was.
Strongly recommended.

It is great to know what a player expects prior to buying him because in the previous GSM one would sometimes need to spend unnecessary amount of 'turns' to figure it out. If you want to have the CM feeling you should buy this game. However, that doesnt mean it is CM or should become it. If you're looking for a football management game that is easy to learn and play but filled with stats and data, you can't go wrong with Global Soccer Manager 2017.

One thing that it does have over Football Manager though and that's the number of countries, leagues and teams simulated. If you've dreamed of managing the champions of Angola, your dream can be lived with GSM!
Plus, you can grab it for just over a fiver.
Too simple to be worthwhile.

If you can look past the misspelling of names (not like an indie can use real names, it costs a fortune), you've got a pretty decent football management sim here. It's literally just team picking, training and transfers, none of that backroom morale, team talk and press conference tripe you have in Football Manager now, and it doesn't bog you down in the economics of it all like Club Manager 2017 does.
21 countries have real-ish names similarly misspelled due to licensing issues, but if you go for Fantasy mode, it's like a whole fresh football world. Hell, you could even imagine it's an alternate universe where vowels are different if that's your thing. XD
The dev is very active, and I know this from the previous game (yep, this is a sequel. It was just called Global Soccer Manager) which even though I didn't buy, I lurked on the discussions for a whole. After a quick chat about stadium expansion, the dev's going to put it in for the first update.
Not to mention I haven't even touched on how you can play in literally any country yet, have I? Database of clubs is great, and the tournaments are realistic as well, though due to the gamne starting in 2016/17, half the international World Cup qualifiers are done, so you won't see that in full effect for a while.
The match engine is very CM99/00 esque, and that's a good thing. 3D is just fancy pants tripe that doesn't work, SI nor EA can do it, why should anyone else bother. 2D match engine would be nice, as it's proven those can work, but I like the presentation of it.
The auto team picker needs a bit of work, it seems to work quite oddly, but it's still a nice thing to have. Training needs a set week or set month button, IMO and transfers could use a suggested offer that isn't just the wage they already earn, but it's pretty good for what it is right now. And the price? Just right in my opinion. Club Manager is way overpriced for an indie and FM is AAA, so it'd be apples and oranges here.
Anyway, do I recommend it? HELL YES! I think the dev has struck gold here and honestly, if he keeps the updates flowing, he could make a lot of people happy, as I know a lot of people are upset with the Sports Interactive monopoly.

To be honest, I love this game but can't in good conscience recommend it right now.  Yes, it's early access.  Yes, I know the game will change.  Yes, I know that make tutorials hard.  None of that softens my stance that this isn't worth the time it takes to find out how to play.  Not learn how to play because there's nothing in the game that is useful in *telling* you what to do.  Throwing together a hull and propellers isn't hard, but once you get into building engines or weapons the built-in guides are so scanty that they are very little use.  Especially since some parts only connect in certain ways and there is no easy way to see what is connected without tracing the entire path.  And you need those long paths since the guide examples with one (or a few) of each part are useless in the real game.    Don't get me wrong, the guides are good.  It's the game that doesn't give me the info I want in a useful way.  There's no way to know the number of parts I need without building them.  I *think* it's the ratio between parts that's important, but there's no way to verify that.
There are ways to find out what to do, but "Look for people playing the game on YouTube" is not a substitute for in game info.  Let's say you want your base to have a horizontally-rotating turret with a single gun in it to shoot aircraft; that sounds pretty cool!  *Open build menu* Hmm no turret listed.  Let's try custom cannons.  Nope.  Advanced cannons?  Also nope.  Misc tab? Nope^3.  As a noob you didn't go to  'New Object'->'Two axis turret'->'One Axis Turret'.  But let's say we found that and started construction.  We slap down the main piece and hook up the ammo boxes and other blocks to give us the explodey, armor piercing goodness that we want.  How much of each does your gun need?  Beats me.  Just slap things on&off and figure it out.  Finally, we need our gun to elevate to attack flyers.  Oh look, a block called Elevation Barrel!  How many do I need to hit 60-70 degrees?  Beats me.  You have to slap them on and then either scroll your way back to the firing piece block or just try out the gun to see if you put in enough.
Figuring out how to play the game should be a choice of tradeoffs.  I should be asking myself "Is it worth the resources to have guns that elevates to 80 degrees or is 60 enough?", and not asking "How in the gently caress do I get a rapid firing gun that elevates to 60 degrees with alternating explosive and armor piercing shots!?"  The entirety of my issues with the game could be solved with a 'design wizard' that would let me see how the number of parts affects the final stats.  I'm fine with something that let's me see that I need x gauge increasers, y cooldown decreasers, and z recoil dampers.  I'll take it from there and work on fitting them in.  Without something like this, I find that I need to regularly stop playing the campaign mode and go into the designer to get a weapon I want.  I would much rather prefer trying to fit in the parts I know I need under the time pressure of an approaching enemy.
Full disclosure:  I have still haven't gotten belt-fed autoloaders to connect properly(They work now!  Details below).
Gun stats provided in game: -Max shell diameter: 0.020 -Gun has 1m ammo clip and loader
Ammo stats: -Shell diameter: 0.018 -Clip size required: 1m
Error message that gun cannot be loaded.
Can you guess what the problem is?  If you guessed that the shell was too big to fit in the gun, you're right! (although it beats me how I should have known that)  I reduced the number of shell parts and now it all both fits and tears up the Onyx Watch flyers.
If this was helpful, please stay tuned.  I'll happily update the review if things improve.

Imagine Civilization Beyond Earth as a tablet game about spaceships, and you have this.

The leaders are not animated in any way, there are very very few voice files, so expect to hear the same things on repeat.
The combat is an extension of Civ V's system aplied to spaceships, and not much else, some battlefield obstacles mixed in perhaps.
I'm glad they only charged £11 for it, because this isn't worth £15, let alone a full game.
If you take it as a concept mini-game, it's great. As a standalone, you'll be done in a couple hours, easy.

This is NOT an epic strategy game with the level of detail of a Civ 1-5 or a MOO (if you want to think of space strategy games). If you don't have those expectations upfront, then the game can be interesting in it's own way. At it's most basic level, Starships is actually "Ace Patrol" set in space with themes from Beyond Earth thrown in. The battle hex board layout is exactly the same as Ace Patrol, but the mechanics of how weapons play out is now space themed. There is definiely more detail here than in Ace Patrol when you look at all aspects of the game. There is a simplified research system, planets that are "upgradeable" to harvest more resources for upgrading your ships. All of this is simplified to a point where each aspect of the game could be thought of as an upgrade system, less discovery, and faster. The mission system is also simple and can get a little repetitive, but by mid-game it becomes only battles against other empires. This is a mobile game for the most part, but I don't mind playing a quick game on the PC when I have a moment. Some might say it's not worth $15, but that's actually cheap compared to the $50 epic game. For a fast playing strategy game with more depth than an "Ace Patrol", Starships is definitely worth it. The expectations around this game were poorly set up, so watch a gameplay video to decide if it's right for you.

As a fan of The Longest Journey and Dreamfall, Chapters has been on my radar pretty much since it became public knowledge (I cursed The Secret World for delaying it).  With such a lead-time, games generally will either fail to live up to the hype (possibly being objectively terrible [sorry Duke]) or be truly amazing.  I am happy to report that Dreamfall Chapters falls closer to that selective second category (a bit too early to tell if it'll stay there).  The music, voice acting and sound engineering are excellent, the graphics are beautiful (the landscape/background design particularly), the environmental details greatly amplify the realism of the unabashedly-surreal world and the writing, well, it's Ragnar Tornquist & company (need I say more?).  While the episodic format is a significant shift in pace from the earlier games, it makes sense on many levels (not the least of which being developer budget) and allows the content to remain fresh enough for multiple different playthroughs, which is more important in Chapters as the choice aspect is central to the way the story plays out.  The start is a bit abrupt if you haven't played the other games in the series, so I recommend playing through The Longest Journey and Dreamfall first (and in general), though Chapters does stand on its own.
Right now it's short and sweet; highly recommended.
TL; DR:
Pros: Story (writing), dialogue (writing), graphics, music, voice acting, sound editing, environmental interaction, world design.
Cons: Short (episode), heavily focused on previous story content (with brief synopsis), some minor clipping/finishing detail issues
