I have followed (and enjoyed immensely) Sid Meier games from the very first one in the early 1980s and I must say that StarShips is my first major let down.
At a glance, this game looks like a hybrid between Civilization Lite and Ace Patrol. After playing a few games, Starships fails to live up to either one of those titles; it is an unbalanced mess with very little replayability. The only reason to replay it is to unlock perks in Civ : BE. (Scroll to the end of the the review for info on this feature).
An iPad app at best, Starships is devoid of personality, customization and meaningful choices for the player.
Ship upgrades could have been this title's saving grace but after a certain point, all your ships will have impenetrable shields, lethal lasers and cannons and enough fighter squadrons to avoid combat almost entirely. For a game which is supposedly centered on tactical gameplay, this seems like a pretty major flaw.
Sadly, after a few rounds, brute force seems to be the only way to win the game. Once you have built a few key wonders and expanded your empire beyond 3-4 systems, the game becomes one of patience as the player waits to see his galaxy coverage slowly reach 51%.
Pros :
- Great Art for mission summarys. Might not be your cup of tea but I really like it.
- A full game session from start to finish can take from an hour to an hour and a half.
- Playing Starships unlocks new perks/loadouts and maps in Civ : Beyond Earth.
Cons :
- No option to play fullscreen. The settings menu makes it painfully clear that this is a port of a tablet game. For a company like 2k/Firaxis, this is inexcusable.
- Most of the textual descriptions and "story elements" are nothing but flavor text.
- Diplomacy only serves to artificially lenghten the game.
- No customization; you cannot rename starships, planets or change the colors of your spaceships. Funny as this is one of the bullet points on the game's store page.
- The end game often occurs without player input. More than once I've won the game because the AI did something which triggered something else which gave me victory. No way of knowing what exactly happened.
- Sound guy annoyance : A capital ship explodes and the sound it emits is that of a single person screaming in agony. Rookie mistake.
To sum it up, the game feels unfinished, untested, unbalanced and unpolished. I have nothing against shorter games or games with more limited scopes (Ace Patrol was a great example of this) but this just feels rushed. There are many ways to better spend 15$.
The connectivity between  StarShips and Beyond Earth is one of the redeeming (I use the term verrrrry loosely) values of this game. Achieving certain things in either game will unlock content in the other. The downside is that there doesn't seem to be a way to know what the requirements are for unlocking content, forcing you to play blindly and hope that you eventually unlock something.
Note that if you are currently playing a game of Civ : BE, a new option in the menu will allow you to <Continue Playing in Starships>. This saves the current factions, their affinities and alliances and allow you to start a new game of Starships with these parameters. Cool idea but it makes absolutely no sense in either game's narrative.

With the right expectations, it's a satisfying experience. Easy to pick up and play, without the massive time commitment of most 4X games. Yes, it's a fairly casual game, but if that's what you're looking for, it's hard to go wrong for the price point.

After 8 years without knowing Zoë and April's fate, it's finally here! And it has everything you can expect from a TLJ/Dreamfall game: Zoë's witty and funny comments about pretty much everything, her inner conflicts about her life, carefully woven storyline and even the Crow! (somehow)
Kian's parts were shorter than I expected, but I am sure he'll get enough spotlight on the future chapters. Changing the course of the story with meaningful choices is a great addition to the series and it really makes me wonder what'll be the consequences of my actions. Also that opening scene was like a punch in the gut, but I'll leave it at that so you can see it for yourself.
Overall, Dreamfall is back with it's full glory! There are some minor technical problems, but I haven't experienced anything game-breaking. If you are a fan of the adventure genre or a dreamer, you should definitely play Dreamfall Chapters.

Book One
=======
The long awaited 3rd chapter of The Longest Journey series has arrived albeit in the somewhat unfortunate episodic format.
The majority of the first 'book' (Episode) in Dreamfall: Chapters is played as Zoe Castillo, Dreamfall: The Longest Journey's protagonist and the game does a reasonably good job of recalling some of the finer moments from the previous game, however during the 8 years since, you'd be easily forgiven for being confused after the games opening cutscene and it's not till about an hour in that the game starts to fill in some of the blanks. This could have been avoided by the promised Journey: Graphic Novel which was due to be released beforehand to recap the previous games stories - sadly this was nowhere in sight for those who backed the game on kickstarter in the $75 and above tiers which has left a somewhat bitter taste in my mouth and ruined some of the experience for me as I was not able to go back and play the first two games before playing chapters.
Moving on from this - chapters has started a whole new story in the TLJ universe and one that I'm ready to get involved in, the first episode is clearly aimed at laying the ground work and some will be dissapointed by the fact that half of this episode is spent running around the same environment completing quests that will clearly become big story beats in the future. After a few quests in the main area the game began to feel a little stale and almost like the developer needed to provide filler by making you run around a lot to lengthen the episode. I'm hoping that this doesn't become a common sight as the games remaining episodes are released.
One feature that is new to the TLJ series is The Walking Dead style choices where RedThreadGames promise that choices made throughout the game will have consequnces in future endeavors, it's not yet clear if they'll pull this off as well as TellTale(The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us) but it's certainly something I'm excited to see as the episodes get released.
In terms of puzzles, Dreamfall: Chapters contains everything you'd expect from an adventure game of this type, from inventory based puzzles (Combine everything!) to puzzles based purely on a piece of dialogue you had with someone an hour ago. I didn't find myself ever getting frustrated with any of them and they all made logical sense unlike some of the series early work(Fans will remember a certain rubber duck puzzle) however some may rightly criticise them for being a bit too easy, which is slightly alarming considering this was the main complaint fans had with Dreamfall: The Longest Journey
Overall if I had to be honest with myself as a massive fan of the previous games, it's really difficult to recommend Dreamfall Chapters as an episodic game and personally I'd wait for the full series to be released, however if you can't wait to continue the story then by all means Book One is still a solid game with solid mechanics that you'd expect from this kind of adventure game and I've come away with a definite interest in seeing how the story develops going forward.

This has been a long wait, but it was definitely worth it.  I had some startup issues which I see a lot of people has experienced and I was a bit worried that it would ruin the game. But after getting past the initial issues it was smooth.
Really looking forward to the next chapter.

If you're a big fan of the story in this universe, even playing the first 5 minutes of this game will cause emotional turmoil for sure.
People were craving for a more omnipresent "tlj vibe" than we could get in Dreamfall and this new installment offers a bit of both, as it is - ofcourse - a continuation of Dreamfall: The Longest Journey.
The visual dreamy modern cyberpunk vision of Europolis (a new area in the game) has enough "infusion" of that new layer of story introduced back in 2006 to peak your interest as a fan, and to finally traverse the cliff we've been hanging on for 8 years.
Zoë and Kian continue their adventure across dreams and realities, in detailed and story rich worlds like the storytime, Europolis and Arcadia. This first episode - with immersive story telling and descriptions of the world around you - sets the pace for what's to come in the next 4 books.
And if you think that one added layer of story to the universe is enough for RTG ? Well it's not. Not to spoil things but even in book one it's appearent there's a new depth to be found in this already rich story which makes it very "meta".
The story builds up and becomes very "ominous" in many ways. There's that layer which is in front of your face. Zoë wakes up from her coma, has to follow therapy to find her place in the world again, finds a hobby in rallying for a political party as volunteer, and goes back to work in what she has been schooled for.
So its obvious that we continue the obvious bits from Dreamfall, we resume our relationship with Reza, we remember bits and pieces from our ordeal with Waticorp but not everything. But something is ominous, not everything is like it seems. And I'm not only talking about how you can make regarding your relationship with reza, the political party and your Psychiatrist. Nothing is like it seems, and the pedestrians you encounter as Zoë sometimes send you weird messages.
As Kian, you get a new chance to redeem his character and he'll have to help the resistance to the Azadi, and he does so because we find out that he feels he owes a debt to the "northlanders" after killing their scorpion. So he came to his senses and is now helping the rebellion against his own people. In that quest you'll be making some hard choises and this is what makes the game interesting.
Story wise it's all okey. It hands you interesting choises and bits to ponder about and it's fun to replay the game so you can see all aspects of the story unfolding and see un expected outcomes.
Running around in marcuria and europolis is also very cool. The city is big but not super huge. After a few runs, I start to remember and orient myself and that creates a bonding with these areas. The game offers no compas, just an inworld map. As you learn to localize the different sectors in both world, I have the feeling that I'm drawn more into that fantasy because it makes me think about the location names and pinpoint their location as I walk. The old town market in marcura, the souk in Europolis, I start feeling like Zoë and Kian and start associating locations just like I would with my real life city.
The only few negative things I have to say about the game is some puzzle stuff and the technology side of t hings, but there's positivity in there even:
I feel that unity 4.6 (the engine they are using) seems to be unable to render the game at fluid fps even if you have a geforce 970, but having the misfortune to have an i5 from several generations back doesn't help the case ofcourse. Because the engine is very cpu bound and runs on one thread.
I have to be intellectually honest as well and say that these guys did a massive job of creating such a rich and detailed world in that engine. Even some professionals are in awe to see such a densely populated world can be created with that engine. So they really push it to its limit.
Kinda like what we did with our left 4 dead expansion, we were constantly flirting with the source edicts limitation. But this as a side note.
The great thing is that, to release the game (I am talking again about Dreamfall Chapters) on playstation 4, they need to port everything over to unity 5 and optimize. When they completed that task which they said almost wrecked their company, The game ran almost at double the FPS for the same settings on several computer configurations including mine. Unity 5.2 offers lots more cpu optimization as well as improvement in the rendering engine. So as the road is evened for the game to be released on PS4 as well. So that's the positive about this negative point I'm describing.
Another little "meh", is that you only seem to be able to activate a multi task puzzle from one option, which will activate all others. For example: in Marcuria, when Kian has to blow up the Azadi weapon stack, you HAVE to start outside the south gate and pick upo the black powder, then all other options for that puzzle inside the south gate (such as the nails) will become available for pickup or interaction. To me, this was confusing at first, as I just knew from visual inspection that there were a few opportunities for that puzzle.
There are other "jittery" puzzle activations like that such as the azadi runner. You can manipulate it in such a way that you can shortcut his loop. I know this is done for convenience so that you don't have to wait for him to run the entire loop, but as you learn that you can just wait for him at the junction where he has to go left and right, you ofcourse adopt this procedure of working.
Book 4 is such a wonderful journey that takes me back and makes my heart jump because you revisit several crucial locations and new wonderous places that are really really having the TLJ stamp on them.
It's so nice that I kinda wish the game wasn't such an interactive walking simulator at that point. I wish that when Zoë arrived in the 2 magical new locations, there would be some kind of puzzle for you to solve, so you bond more with the place other than to live the story, which is very superb, but a puzzle where you had to work a bit to get to see these story bits, would have been nice.
The game is such a nice modern crosssection of what TLJ stands for, but with slightly less tedious puzzles. That's it for now. I'm adding to this review as consequent books come out.

Short said (and not completely true) the game is the same as the first one. You also have to defend your fortress against a big army of Orcs, with traps, guards and magic, but the game, still looking the same, changed a lot of things:
Coop: The whole game can (and should) be solved in 2 player Coop mode. Both players choose their weapons of choice and defend the tunnels and floors together. The big contra is, that money and inventory is not shared, but seperated.
Since every player has at least one weapon, and mostly have one spell and one artifact, you have to ask, which slot you should use for traps.
If one player use 3 slots for said things, he still has 8 slots for traps and other things, but two players with each a weapon, spell and artifact only can choose 2 traps each, so coop means less varity in trap placement.
Still, two players can be at 2 places at once and can do better crowd control. A lot of maps from the first game (some of them are playable in the second one, if you have both games) are way easier if played in coop.
No Skilltrees but big unlocking system: You no longer have a skilltree (which is bad) but have way over hundred different traps and items you can unlock and upgrade, so even after playing the campaign, you still wont have unlocked everything.
The simple trap system from the first game is gone. Now you have a ton of new traps, you can upgrade and customize (a bit), big weapons like the magic rocket launcher, all spell rings from the first game and new artifacts, that give you boosts and special abilitys.
With a good campaign, a lot of challenge maps (some of them are quite hard again), some DLCs, the game has a lot of content you can play for hours.
It is recommended to play this game in coop, because some maps are way to hard alone.
All in all the second game feels way more easy than the first. The big variety of weapons and abilitys and the use of two players at once spamming their weapons, the orcs feeling weaker and the traps are able to be upgraded, it is more casual than the sometimes nearly impossible nightmare mode of the first game.
Grab a friend and destroy all orcs, its worth every intense level

Well I've completed this a few times to deem a review I believe. Now origonally when I heard about Dark Souls I initially ignored it because ALL I heard about it was that it was difficult and that was it which degrades the truly beautiful game that it is with a wonderful story of a dying world that is filled with undead, monsters and people on the edge of sanity.
The difficulty of the game comes from that you need to take your time to understand when an enemy telegraphs an attack and how to dodge or parry a weapon. Certain classes are easier than others, such as the easiest being the Pyromancer as the power of spells isn't based on your stats, but on how much you beef up your pyromancer flame, meaning you can also become a decent and powerful mellee character that throws fire at creatures.
Another edge, which brings the game down in my mind, is that certain elements are not entirely explained to you and you may need to watch a few introductory vids on youtube to understand poise, uses for humanity and other small things that you may not know and could hinder you, however the game rewards you for exploring, finding things hidden behind fake walls or odd scenes that make you wonder what happened before you got there.
The PvP I find somewhat annoying as I've seen many cases of people far too powerful invading my world and being able to kill my 12th level character whilst they use dark magic and other items that you can't get anywhere near that level. It's also a bit of a pain as the only way you can summon an ally to take on a boss in certain areas, is if you're human and not hollowed.
I highly recommend it due to the awesome story behind it, but also recommend that you have patience and understand that the game doesn't cheat, you just need to focus on the situation and the enemy's abilities along with how to avoid their attacks.
Again, I highly recommend this and wish any who play it, good luck :)

This is a bit of a cautious recommendation. I will say that the game is pretty fun on its own, with an interesting theme going on. It's basically a bullet-hell game (with, I'd argue, some rogue-like elements). Point of the game is to las as long as you can over dangerous waters, fighting bots, planes and Zeppelins. I will say that the gameplay is really solid and interesting; you'll be flying all over the place while shooting, and can even cut off your engines to pull off maneuvers to get the edge on your enemies. It's a good arcade experience that you should have some fun with, and that's added with the unlocks that you get from completing challenges. The unlocks include new bodies of the plane, as well as weapons, wings, and engines. These pieces have their own stats, but also have a few interesting quirks, an example being an engine that shoots bullets. With the customization, it's a good bit of fun.
So why is it cautious, you ask? Well, what cuts this game off from being great is its price at ten dollars which, in my opinion, is very overpriced. While the action is hectic, you'll be fighting in the same area and with the same enemies over and over and over again. On top of that, while the unlocks are great fun, there are too few to unlock (I got all of them at the 1.5 mark). It really isn't that hard to get all of the items in this game. Once you unlock all of your parts and essentially the hard mode, the only thing to strive for afterwards is completing challenges (which kind of loses its luster once everything is unlocked). Don't get me wrong, it's a fun game, but I'd highly recommend you buy it one it's on sale. Got my copy on Chronogg for a dollar fifty, which I think is a much more fair price.
All in all, a fun game, but doesn't offer enough for its asking price.

Postal is the kind of game that only certain people can appreciate, but those who do appreciate it will have the time of their lives.
The game's plot is intentionally vague, so the player can formulate whatever backstory they want. The most common interpretation is that the Postal Dude (yes, that's his name) has been evicted from his home and, fed up with his luck in the world, decides to kill everyone in it (although civilian kills are optional). Strangely enough, the Dude has what appears to be an M16, implying that he's probably not evicted, only leaving his home to slaughter the masses.
The tools of disposal range from shotguns to heat-seeking missile launchers, with a variety of explosives and flammable weapons in between. Each weapon, despite the age and apparent budget of the game, works incredibly well. Although the machine gun has unlimited ammo, players may find the crimson splashes produced by the shotgun more satisfying. The flame thrower torches everything in sight with ease, but the missile launcher allows equal damage from a much further distance. The grenades and molotovs require a bit of practice if an earlier version is played, but a recent update adds a targeting system that greatly increases the accuracy of throws.
The game is most often portrayed from an isometric view, although there is a level (or two, I can't recall) that is played from a completely top-down angle. Each level is surprisingly detailed and hand-drawn, with blood decals and corpses becoming part of the environment as the killing proceeds. NPCs will often crawl on the ground before death, sometimes begging the player to put them out of their misery, which can be done with the machine gun or ground-contact explosives.
There have been imitators as of late, but updated graphics and blood levels are not enough to usurp Postal's throne. The recent announcement of Postal: Redux, an HD remake, solidifies its legacy.
If you're a misanthrope with a penchant for older games and black humor, this is an experience you don't want to pass up.

Transport Giant is yet another "tycoon" game that was made back in 2004 and attempted to bring back the excitement of playing transportation games. Unfortunately, as far as I am concerned, the game fails to bring that excitement. A decent amount of work was put into making this game, but that is all - just decent. Although for a 2004 game the graphics are up to par, there are notable interface and menu design problems that make it difficult for players to play as smoothly as they did with Transport Tycoon and the Railroad Tycoon series. To be specific, the menus and features of the game-play are not  not intuitively designed (hard to navigate). Another issue is the limited amount of information the game provides about vehicles, stations, industries and cities.
I will not say that I am disappointed at this game, but I will say that I hope whoever continues the legacy of making transportation games, uses way more care and attention in desigining such games by learning from the mistakes of their predecessors.
All in all, Tranport Giant is a FAIR attempt at reviving the dead era of transportation games, but in falls short of being exciting and addictive. JoWood Entertainment, the make of the game, is no longer with us! Hopefully someone will come around and end our wait by making the next awesome "transport tycoon" game.

Score: 10/10
Controls:
The controls worked great on an xbox 360 controller. I personally had zero issues. I've heard mouse and keyboard works great as well.
Visuals:
I mean some of the guys look a bit to cartoonish, but beyond that minor gripe this game is current gen. The lighting is truly  where it shines. The atmosphere it creates feels correct.
Sound:
I bought a copy of the first two games on GOG even though I had them on steam just to get the soundtracks after I had beaten both games. This game is no exception and it may actually greatly surpass them by the time all five books release. The voice acting is spot.
Gameplay:
No odd fight sequences so far thank god. The gameplay feels very natural as you explore the world considering it is an adventure game and adventure games have yet to truly find solid ground on what it means to be an adventure game in todays gaming scene. Though because Dreamfall Chapters is not your standard point and click adventure game of days gone by so some old schoolers may have gripes on the amount of puzzles and difficulty of them. You will not be relentlessly bombarded with inventory puzzle after inventory puzzle involving a duck, but they do exist and they play out quite elegantly in the world.
Story:
It's basically what the game is about so if you want explosions and gun fights similar to a 90s action flick go buy Marlow Briggs. The story is very incomplete beings it is only book one, but if this sets the tone for future releases you can expect the most atmospheric story game in history so far. I've heard if you read the journal entries the game makes more sense if you haven't played the past two titles, but I would imagine you'd be confused unless you play them honestly.

Be advised o ye potential newcomers, there are four issues with this game as of October 2014. First, be advised that there is only one 'book' available in chapters, i.e. one episode, so you're only getting roughly 4 hours of gameplay out of this. Second, you're going to want to have played both The Longest Journey and Dreamfall completely before picking this up or you're going to feel like this game is an acid trip. (Frankly if you haven't, they're incredible games worth the money.) Third is that the graphics are a little unoptimized so it will make even some rigs capable of running Glorious Star Citizen cry in pain. Unfortunately, this is not helped by the fourth concern, that the character models animations are a little sub par and that does cheapen an otherwise brilliant and immersive experience.
That said, there are a ton of positives. The setting is fantastically designed and believable. The writing, dialogue and choice system are on par with anything put out by Telltale. Zoe's internal monologues are plastered all over the game and are reflective of the choices she (ahem, YOU) will make, Effects on the storyline are VERY noticable and yet seamlessly woven into the game. It appears that quite a lot of effort was put into making the consequences of actions matter, at least in the short term with Zoe's attitude.
TL;DR - I like where Tørnquist and RTG is going with this. This is what TLJ/Dreamfall fans -- as well as fans of the adventure games genre -- have been waiting for. I recommend a buy after more chapters have been put out there. (And FFS, if you haven't played TLJ and Dreamfall, drop everything and do that right now.)

It's hard to properly express how I feel about this... I have waited over 8 years for the continuation of this story that has meant more to me than any other story ever told. The wait is finally over, and it seems it has been worth it! Seeing these amazingly well written characters again is like being reunited with old friends. I would recommend this game to anyone who is a lover of good stories, even non-gamers.
Disclaimer: This review only covers impressions from book 1.
So... About the game. If you are looking for a fast paced game with a good combat system, this game is not for you. There is no combat. If you are easily offended this game is probably not for you either. It is a mature game, and characters in it reflect the wide variety of people you find in the real world. There are offensive characters. There is profanity. It is relatable. On the topic of characters, that's one area where this game truly shines! The characters you meet feel genuine, they feel complex. Real. This is a reflection of the overall fantastic writing which is revealing a thought provoking, deep and mature yet magical story. The dialogue alone had me laugh out loud on several occasions, while other moments pulled at my heartstrings. Of course this is only book one, but it is clear that great things are set in motion already.
About choices. Choices make up a key aspect of the actual game-play. They are difficult! Generally there are no obvious good vs. evil choices. Most are morally grey. But they do impact your story in important ways. To help you make the choice you will hear the PC's inner though process as you mouse over each choice. This very effectively serves the dual purpose of letting you get to know the characters better while helping you guess at what the PC will say.
This game is visually stunning. Sure, if you compare it to the flashiest of the AAA next-gen titles you might find the graphics a bit lacking. But the artstyle is fantastic and it is clear that the world has been crafted with a careful eye for detail. The two worlds of Stark and Arcadia feature very distinct styles, yet there is a cohesiveness that tie them together.
The Soundtrack is simply amazing amazing. There is one spot in Europolis where you will find a crowd of NPCs around a musician, and I found myself standing around for a few minutes just listening. But even the music coming out of radios, night clubs and the "atmospheric" music is all highly effective and does a great job of underlining the impact of the story. The voice acting is also absolutely superb. Better even than most AAA titles I have played. I must admit it took some getting used to the new voice for Zoe, but she does such a good job I quickly got over it.
TL:DR - If you love a good story and great characters, buy it. The interactions with Shitbot alone are worth it.

Full disclosure: Possible backer syndrome.
That said, this is the way to make a modern adventure game.
Funny, touching, beautiful, expansive. As others have said, if you're familiar with the previous games you'll be on board with this from the first seconds. Otherwise, if you've any interest in adventure games at all you owe it to yourself to check this out. It's only the first few chapters of the story so far, and it starts off slowly, but once it gets going you'll find yourself in the largest, most free form open world environment I've ever seen in an adventure game. This isn't the tiny rooms of the Walking Dead, we're talking huge cityscapes.
You have the choice and consequence of modern adventure games, and the best of dialog and inventory puzzles from the classics. You won't be hauling masses of stuff around with you, but you will be combining items. And, while we've not seen the outcomes of many decisions as yet, there's at least one major character who you can entirely miss depending on your choices.
And, most importantly, it absolutely lives up to the writing of the classics. There's more dialog then you'll ever hear in one play through, often with escalating jokes hidden away behind examining items multiple times, incidental background events and internal monologue. Zoe has matured into a witty and engaging heroine, and you will relate to her problems and struggles as you wander her world. It's a game that genuinely deserves to call itself mature, because of the themes it fearlessly explores, not the amount of blood it splashes around.
Pleased to have backed it, and hope it sells a ton.

Such an amazing game. Its anything you could ever want in a survial game. Thats not to say its without its faults, but lets start with the positives.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Positives
This game has amazing pixel art. Each element of it was so carfully and wonderfully crafted, I have yet to see a mishapen, weird, or unclear sprite in the game. The backrounds are astonashing for each planet, I can only imagine how much time went into the art of this game.
Now lets talk about gameplay. I love the fighting mechanic, it requires more skill that most pixel games such as terraria as its not just constant swinging of a sword that only does one thing, and this is credited to all the power moves that EACH individual weapon comes with. With each different power move for a weapon in the game it adds a whole new way of fighting and strategizing.
It has a decent amount of flow, your character isnt to slow and you can upgrade your suit power module to help you along in the game, and recieving these upgrades is always rewarding.
The Mechs are a wonderful new adition to the game aswell, they opened up a whole new world of exporation and a whole new way to play the game. I just wish you could explore space more easily without it, like maybe a propulsion pack/jet pack type thing?
I always feel like collecting and eating food is overdone in video games, but in this game its so easy to go out and kill a monster for some steak and just eat that, its hardly even a problem. Which is why I enjoy the hunger mechanic in this game more than any other game with the mechanic, your not ALWAYS searching for food spending 80% of your time on scavenging like most hunger mechanic games.
Now lets get on to the bosses, im not gonna spoil the story (which is amazing btw) but these bosses are amazing, excluding the final boss which I will talk about when I get to the negatives of this game. Each boss is so creative and I just love fighting them. I wish there was more bosses, if theres one thing I love in a game its an abundance of bosses. Maybe make randomly generated bosses? This game has been described in the past using such fine adjectives as "Amazing", "Groundbreaking", "Engaging", "Enthralling" among others and I'm pleased to report that a cool twelve (12) years later, these sentiments still hold true. It's no wonder Tales of Symphonia (TOS) has made the rounds from the Nintendo GameCube circa 2004, to the PlayStation2, PlayStation3 (bundled with Dawn of the New World sequel) and now PC. The latter's launch day state was actually quite atrocious with the nasty DRM that impacted performance negatively regardless of system builds which has since been killed off and blurry visuals that can now be fixed and spruced up using Kaldaien's TSFix Mod (links to which are available on the Steam forums).
This is just as well since TOS' story isn't one to be missed. In a nutshell, you play the unassuming Lloyd Irving, a boy of uncertain parentage who finds himself embroiled in an adventure involving the fate of worlds. Trying really hard here to keep story discussion to a minimum since going any further than that sentence will really mess up certain twists that you really need to experience first-hand. Let's just say that these twists are executed masterfully, the pacing is excellent and by the time you get to the end, the story is given a sense of closure that you do not see often.
If you are familiar with the old-school game-play mechanics from previous Tales games then you should be comfortable with this entry. Combat on a 2D plane that is real-time with special attacks and passive skills thrown in for good measure. In the beginning, these passive skills (referred to as "Compound EX" skills in-game) can be somewhat obtuse in their setup, but when you link them up right to feed into your characters' strengths, their stat boosts can end up being incredibly awesome.... and a lifesaver.
Speaking of characters. TOS has a pretty diverse cast that in some ways epitomizes typical JRPG tropes, but these are offset by the great story. In my play-through, I did manage to unlock every party member possible, but there IS the possibility on missing out on a certain magic user so paying attention to story beats is critical.
Now, audio. Sound effects are run of the mill (might be the age of the game), but the music stands the test of time and is quite frankly appropriate in most scenes.
In conclusion some quick points. First; yes, there is a NewGame+ available using your game completion data, certain side quests that may have been missed can then be completed. Second; a music player will be unlocked at the end of the first play through. Third; due to the combat's fast paced nature and the volume of info shown on the screen, players who are visually impaired may find it difficult to really appreciate this aspect. So, for them, finding a comfortable resolution to play at including enlarging game text would be a big help. The mod comes to its own in this regard opening up more resolution options and cleaning up visuals.
And with that. Go. Get. This. Game. NOW!
PS: If still in doubt at least consider it on the next sale.

As the very first visual novel I've ever played, my bar of expectations for VN's has been set extremely high. Long Live the Queen goes beyond the literal name of "visual novel", where you click furiously through pages and pages of text. It is a fully interactive experience where your choices actullay affect the outcome of the game! I know, seems pretty mindblowing after Telltale made a formula on how to fake your way through that and still makes piles of money everytime, but you will encounter no smoke or mirrors in this gem. In Long Live the Queen, you guide a young princess on her path to queenhood before she comes of age on her 15th birthday. You must manage and raise her skills so she can handle the various problems that come her way. If you don't get the right skills to a high enough level, the princess will die. (little hint: Reflexes is an absolute must for the very beginning of the game) And there are so many skills to level up! This VN is perfectly designed to make you feel like a young teenager in over their head with daunting responsiblities, sometimes forcing you to make what some may consider "Evil" paths just to survive. Thats not including the hidden values that may or may not affect the chances of assassination attempts on your princess; commoner approval and noble approval. Certain dialogue options and choices will change how your commoners and nobles think of you, and if one side or the other thinks too negatively of you, expect a lot more unpleasent surprises in the weeks to come.
And if you manage to keep the princess alive, you will discover multiple branching paths that will drastically change your experience. I never got the right skills to unlock it, but I heard the scenes in the Enchanted Forest are really intriguing.
The other characters are very interesting too. I was just as invested in keeping my allies safe as my princess, and intrigued in learning what made my enemies tick.
Overall, this is an outstanding experience that proves that "illusion of choice" is not a necessary evil in every case. Even if you don't like anime art styles or stragety, I encourage you to pick this up at some point. Everyone can get something out of Long Live The Queen.

Sid Meier's Starships is a very light 4X game. You control star systems and move a fleet of upgradable ships around while competing with the AI doing the same. There are four victory conditions (wonders, population, domination, science). Once two fleets meet or you attack an enemy planet the game switches to 2D hex-based, turn-based tactical combat.  You can attack enemy ships with lasers, torpedoes, plasma guns and fighters. There is a simple stealth option and there are obstacles on each map that can be used as a cover for ships.
On the strategy map you can also upgrade your ships, buy new ships (but you can only have one fleet at a time) upgrade your planets, build cities and wonders and improve your tech level (there are different resources for each task).
Now before I start on listing my personal pros and cons I'd like to get this out of the way first: The game is in no way comparable to great 4X games like Master of Orion, Endless Legends and so on. It's a simply game, designed for tablets much like Sid Meier's Ace Patrol. If you want a large, complex 4X-game then don't buy Sid Meier's Starships. Starships is much more of a "let's play something for 20 minutes" game than anything else.
That said, here are my pros and cons:
Pros:
- Good Interface
- Fast paced combat and strategy map
- Fames don't take long to complete (I finished an epic game on normal in 2 hours)
- Enjoyable if simple turn based combat
- I really, really like the artwork in the game.
Cons:
- Diplomacy is useless.
- The options are a joke (for example: Fullscreen mode only works on my system if I hide the task bar. If the task bar is   not hidden it's always visible and the game doesn't go fullscreen)
- The different factions really don't play all that different. And choosing an affinity is mostly about what color you like
- The turn based combat is simple. It's really easy to find a strategy that works for you (I enjoy mass torpedo spam for example) and stick with it. Once you have upgraded the first two ships to the max level there is almost nothing that can stop you)
Conclusion:
I recommend buying the game if you look for something to just play for a couple of minutes and if you enjoy simple turn based combat.
I do not recommend buying the game if you look for something complex or challenging.

This is a good game if you know what you are expecting. First, you need to put two things in mind: one, it's only $15, so don't expect some huge game like Civilization V or Beyond Earth; two it's not a Civilization game.
Now with that out of the way, Starships to me, is a unique game that takes the gameplay from many other types of strategy and space faring games. I stated before it isn't a Civilization game, but it still borrows some of the game mechanics from Beyond Earth. It's still mainly just a turn based clicking game, with many different options to start your new game with to spice it up a little bit and to offer some diversity, such as the affinity system from Beyond Earth and the same leaders from it, too. I also like the new feature where you can interact between the two games.
Now, to the pros. I've played a lot of Beyond Earth, and this game was still quite confusing when I started. It seems like it's very complex, but once you play the game for about fifteen minutes, you get the hang of it quite easily. Planets are like cities, and you can apply upgrades to your planets to increase science, metal (production), energy (money), and food. You also use the food to increase the population of your planet, which increases the production of all materials slightly, the only thing that's different in this aspect from Beyond Earth is it doesn't take time. The game is turn based, yes, but it mainly only applies to the battles. This game goes by much faster than a traditional Civilization game, which is good if you just want to kill a couple hours. The customization/upgrade system is pretty alright, too. You can use your materials to apply certain upgrades to certain ships which all have their own effect, you can upgrade the planet as said before, and you can instantly upgrade technology with your science points. There are also four ways to win: population, wonders, science, and domination. Also, another thing I liked is the map, I love the variety of planets and all the planets have their own special aspects to them that alter what they exactly do for you when you control them. And the missions you do for the uncontrolled planets are also pretty unique and fun. The game has no lag or glitches in it at all as long as you have a good enough computer to play.
Cons, I'll make this short. I don't like that you can't trade with the other factions, you can't go through their territory at all unless you are at war which is hard if you don't like having war all the time, and the interactions with leaders are just pretty limited in general, all you can do is wage war, be at peace, see their progress, and very rarely do they offer you a technology if you fight someone for them. Unless you consider the uncontrolled planets as secondary factions, there are no secondary factions to interact with. You can't name the planets or ships if you're into that, either. Most of the wonders are very limited in their use, and you can only build one per planet and it depends on the planet you control.
Conclusion, Starships is a pretty good game to play if you got a few hours to kill or are up at night and can't sleep and it's relatively easy to pick up and learn as well. While it has it's good things, it also has it's flaws, but in Starships, the good outweighs the bad for this one. For $15, you can't really expect a perfect game especially when Firaxis only put a few months into it, but they put good work into this game. While it serves somewhat as an expansion to Beyond Earth, it is it's own game entirely, and it's very fun and time consuming. Remember though before you buy, just because it has Sid Meier's name on the game does not mean it is a Civilization game, it is it's own game with it's own likeness. For $15, it completely worth it to me, and if you can catch this game on sale, I would definately get it.

I think most of the negative reviews around this came come mostly as a result of overly high expectations. A lot of the criticism is that it's not as in depth as civ, or other great 4x titles for that matter. But the fact is, this game isn't trying to be complex. Let's not forget that "Sid Meier's" games are not confined to complex strategy games. I've had just as much in my time playing Sid Meier's Pirates as I have playing Civ, and the difficulty gap between those games is enourmous. Just because this game is light on strategy doesn't mean it should be a let down. Also, this game was barely mentioned at all until a few months before its release; clearly this game isn't supposed to be a big deal.
What's more, it really shouldn't matter if it's a mobile game, because it's still a good game. The only reason mobile games are a bad thing is that they are frequenty riddled with poor design and are little more than money-making schemes for their developers. I think it's good that Starships is a mobile game. You know why? It sets a good example. More mobile games should be like this. It's relatively simple, has a low learning curve, and yet still manages to be engaging and entertaining.
It's easy to enjoy this game as long as you don't go into it expecting to play a 12 hour long game. I finish games in 30 minutes to 1 hour, and that's fine, because for what it is, this game is great.

Full disclosure: Possible backer syndrome.
That said, this is the way to make a modern adventure game.
Funny, touching, beautiful, expansive. As others have said, if you're familiar with the previous games you'll be on board with this from the first seconds. Otherwise, if you've any interest in adventure games at all you owe it to yourself to check this out. It's only the first few chapters of the story so far, and it starts off slowly, but once it gets going you'll find yourself in the largest, most free form open world environment I've ever seen in an adventure game. This isn't the tiny rooms of the Walking Dead, we're talking huge cityscapes.
You have the choice and consequence of modern adventure games, and the best of dialog and inventory puzzles from the classics. You won't be hauling masses of stuff around with you, but you will be combining items. And, while we've not seen the outcomes of many decisions as yet, there's at least one major character who you can entirely miss depending on your choices.
And, most importantly, it absolutely lives up to the writing of the classics. There's more dialog then you'll ever hear in one play through, often with escalating jokes hidden away behind examining items multiple times, incidental background events and internal monologue. Zoe has matured into a witty and engaging heroine, and you will relate to her problems and struggles as you wander her world. It's a game that genuinely deserves to call itself mature, because of the themes it fearlessly explores, not the amount of blood it splashes around.
Pleased to have backed it, and hope it sells a ton.

I shied away from this game a bit when I read that it was "complicated." Then, it went on sale and I thought "It can't be more complicated than setting up a military in dwarf fortress," and it isn't. From the Depths is a complex game, but it is not that complicated. At the time of this review, I've spent only two hours playing it, and feel that I have a basic understanding of the mechanics available. I havn't touched any of the guns yet though, so we will see.
In my two hours;
I watched a tutorial on mouse controls, it was all very straight foreward, and by the end of the 6 minute video I felt I was ready for some basic gameplay.
I played with the sandbox "spawn a ship and test it's effectiveness" thing, which was fun time for about 15 minutes and served to get me acquainted and interested with what the fights would be like, but didn't really tell me much about how it would all work, so...
I went to select the campaign, but was met with a popup stating, basically, "are you sure you want to just jump in? The games kind of complex, maybe you want to start with the build a ship sandbox? just until you feel you are ready?" I liked that, so I went to build something in the safety of the sandbox.
I spent about an hour and a half in the sandbox, generally getting used to how it controlled, playing around with blocks an then decided I wanted my raft to move. I went into the build menu, clicked the button that said "engines" and noticed two red flashing boxes. I clicked one, and it was a guide on how to build a simple engine. "well thats nice" I thought, and using the guide I built a small single cylinder engine. after checking the guide again to see what I did wrong (becuase it didn't work) I realized that I had installed everything on the wrong end of the engine block and so corrected the problem. before moving my ship, I wanted to stabalize it. as a simple wooden raft, it rocked about horribly on the oceans swell and with the new engine making it a bit top heavy, it only got worse. I endeavored then to build a pair of outriggers and expand the main body of the ship a bit to make it more stable and bouyant. To my immense pleasure, it worked and I drove my small boat, no longer a pathetic raft, around in circles for a bit before deciding that "From the Depths" is not nearly as difficult as playing dwarf fortress, no where close to as complicated as people say it is, and that I would rather like to play more of this very nice ship building game.

This game is ridiculously excellent.  Like, the kind of excellent that's bizarre and unfair to other games and just generally wonderful.
In a lot of ways this might be the most purely "fun" game I've ever played.  It's an amazing mix of shallow and deep -- where you can have a very satisfying 20- or 30-minute game just beating a single level, or lose yourself for hours working through its campaigns or its extremely fun "endless" mode.  The game also rewards all of this time with in-game currency ("skulls") that you can spend to progress your character and your arsenal of weapons and traps in absolutely any way you like, which makes all of the time you put in feel very worthwhile.
The gameplay itself is the most amazing thing about it.  I've compared playstyles with a good few other players and everyone seems to approach things completely differently, and all of them end up being completely successful, given enough practice and strategy refinement.  This game happily plays out like an action game if you want it to, and just as happily plays like a strategy game if you choose.  (There's always at least a bit of a mix of both, but still.)  And in any play style, there's enough active involvement from moment to moment on the player's part that it's never allowed to be boring (and often just the opposite -- a very satisfying and madcap kind of chaotic).
The game is also hugely polished artistically -- in terms of both its art and its setting, and moreover its general "tone."  It's funny in a "but like, actually funny" sort of way, both for its dialogue and its combat (orcs flying everywhere, often while on fire, often while shouting amusing death quotes, often while being wittily gloated to by the main characters).  Between that and the general maniacal laughter of watching a strategy play out the way you hoped, the whole effect just feels amazingly satisfying to play.  (And it's almost as fun when the plans go wrong.)
I've found an absurd amount of replayability in this (especially for its insanely low pricetag), and all of the DLC more than delivered its fair share of the hours and fun.  (Any kind of bundle that combines these is an effortless, instant "must.")
The co-op needs at least a quick mention -- this is some of the most fun I've ever had in multiplayer, and it is every bit as fun or moreso with a partner.  It works well, it's built well (integrated directly into Steam), and it's deeply satisfying whether you're dividing and conquering or working together to weave your respective halves of one cohesive plan.
Seriously, just buy it.  It's just completely and ridiculously fun.  (And insanely well-built, and rock solid, and well-balanced, and clever, and replayable, and deceptively strategic, and satisfyingly deep, etc., etc.)  But mostly fun.
Easily and enthusiastically nominated for my "5 More Minutes" award, given how excited I always am to load the next level, or survive just that one more wave...

Stories of Bethem: Full Moon is a game a action RPG game where you go through several dungeons to save the world. The game style looks like a zelda game combined with shooter games. (Actually, I want to say bullet hell but it doesn't as extreme as those)
The music are great and sounds relaxing. I really love them, especially the one in The Meadow because i can feel the adventure vibe in it.
The graphics in this game are using 2D pixelated graphics. The mappings are great and each map looks beautiful. However, there are times where an item will be hidden behind a tree which can't be seen from our perspective. I'm sure it's intended from the developers, but inspecting every trees that you find to make sure that you miss nothing isn't cool.
I enjoy the character dialogues, especially the conversation between the red witch and the main character, Khoma. The main character, although is kind hearted, he can be mean at times which makes it quite funny. All in all, i'm enjoying the story and the ending is quite good
.
As i said, the game looks like zelda games combined with shooter games. You'll explore a map and kill enemies (if you want to). There are bushes which can drop some gold or heart or even grasses. Unlike zelda games, the "heart" in this game is converted to numerical values so you'll have a lot of hearts (read: HP) in the game.
Because you'll play as a "wizard", you'll need to cast a spell in order to attack. Each spell will cost a specific amount of MP and although the MP can recover by itself, it takes a significant amount of time to get it to max MP. Luckily, there are "MP orbs", save point, and those "healing fountain" which can restore a significant amount of your MP (and HP on the latter two).
There are also some potions that you can take to fight your battles. You'll have a cap of 3 HP and MP potions although you can increase it to 7. There is also a yellow potion which can fully restores your HP and MP although you can only carry one at a time.
There will be a lot of spell that you can learn (up to 10). Some enemies are also weak to certain element so you might need to switch your strategy for different enemies. However, the few "end game" normal enemies tend to be very strong that it takes several hits (around 5, i think) to beat. Not to mention its nasty attacks which can kill you if there are a lot of them in the area.
This game also provides a lot of dungeons. These dungeons are zelda like; meaning that you'll explore the room and find keys until you reach the boss room. Each boss needs a different strategy to defeat although there are some bosses (not main bosses) that uses the same strategy. Since there are a lot of bosses in the game, i thought that the final boss will be difficult. However, the final boss is much weaker
rather than one of the mini boss in the area
.
Some areas have puzzles that you need to solve before you can advance. These puzzles are usually the same kind, although some puzzles might be a bit hard to solve. These puzzle areas are usually marked with a purple piece on the bottom left in normal mode. Some of the areas also have enemies that's quite tricky to beat.
There is a map in the game. However, the map doesn't really helpful since there is only a bigger map of the continent outside the dungeon and squares (which determines the area room) inside the dungeon. You can't navigate between floors and there's no detailed treasure tracker (will be explained later).
There are also a lot of collectibles in the game which helps you to 100% the game. Most of these collectibles can be found in the treasure chests in the area. Some might be hidden and some might need a specific skill that you'll learn later to open. The problem is, there are too many chests on the latter case which forces you to backtrack the area several times just to get it. I ended up forgetting most of it after i get the required skills and i ended up having to re-explore all areas again and again.
There is also a treasure tracker to help you treasure hunting. However, you need to learn a specific skill in order to use it and it only tells you the unopened chests. Not very helpful in case you stuck. Luckily, there are some people that can help you to find all of certain collectibles.
This game also have costumes which will change your clothes once you equipped. Most of them also provides some interesting bonus when you wear it.
Pros:
- Tons of dungeons
- Puzzles
- Costumes (with some bonus)
- 10 learnable spells
- Elemental weakness
- Some unique bosses
- Potions
Cons:
- Unhelpful mini map
- Slow MP regen
- Some enemies take a lot of hit to beat
- Too many backtracking
- No replay value except for achievement

To put it quite simply, if you are a fan of 2D zelda you will like this game. Any complaints I've seen about it in reviews are from people who clearly don't like Zelda style games.
It's a very charming well desgined top down action RPG similar to zelda, where you collect items, do dungeons full of puzzles, and explore a giant overworld map. The thing that makes this game unique is that you only use spells, so it's very interesting to see all the different types of spells you get to cast. There is a lot of content including lots of hidden collectables, and lots to explore, items to collect and upgrade. There is backtracking just like you would expect from any zelda style game; You backtrack and try to find areas you haven't been to before as you get newer items. My one complaint is that unlike Zelda, the map isn't very good, so you won't be able to rely on as much to find where you are; the game even jokes about this itself. (There is a great map that someone created in the guides though).
Overall it's quite good, and if you are at all a fan of legend of zelda, you will be a fan of this game.

By mixing and maching 6 diffrent parts in 3 catagories (weapon,body,engine) you can design a rausers to meet your specifi needs and goal. What are those needs and goals? To blow up everything in the sea and sky!
The focus of the game to complete various missions assigned to each part and to gain new highscores. These missions range from "destroy your fist X" to "score X amount" or "get X number of kills in a single combo" and can become significantly difficult to accomplish.
Your score is
dependant of building, maintaining, and killing powerfull enimies in combos. after killing an enemy, your multiplier will apear, starting at x1 and increasing by 1 every kill, to a max of x20. While you can kill wimpy enimies to gain huge combos, the challenge and reward lies in killing the toughest enimies while keeping your combo up and not dieing.
How about a list of pros and cons?
+ Huge diversity of possible combinations
+ Unique parts to your rauser, each with it's own benifit and weakness
+ No two parts are polar opposites: one body gives health at the cost of speed, while another lacks health
+ Soundtrack that changes to mach your current build
+ The unique movement of your rauser allows you to stall and float through the air, allowing you to deal with all those pesky fighters on your tail without changing direction
+ TONS or replayability, because you may survive between 5 seconds and 5 minuets
+ you can ram boats and planes to blow them up and dive your plane underwater! How cool is that?
+ Challenging missions
- Challenging missions relying on the random number genorator to spawn key enemies, especialy when you need to kill that [Classified No.1]
- Random nuber genorator will
you over and over with ridiculous enemy spawns
- The diffuculty of some missions will likley be what make you leave the game behind, with some of the last missions being nigh impossible, especialy the unofficsl the last 1 mission
- The big, high health enemies will kill enemy spawns, making it highly difficult to keep your combos
- Almost too much importance placed on combos: enemies give small numbers of points, and the combos are needed to make any progress
- Some bugs and exploits
All in all, I recomend it, but prepare to be frusterated more and more the longer you play the game until it gets close to being an unenjoyable chore.

Let me first say: most of the legends in the gaming community about this game are completely true.  Yes, it's crushingly difficult at first, especially if you're not used to playing with a controller (which I wasn't).  Yes, there are times when the game will make you want to ragequit, and all the boss fights that are widely known as hard really are pretty much just as hard as you've been told.  Yes, the base game needs mods to the netcode and the graphics to really unlock full potential on the PC.  But the positive legends are also true; beating the bosses, and then the game itself, are supremely rewarding.  The world design really is as great as you've heard.  The immersion and emotion you feel as you play really might amaze you.
All games are works of art, but this one really is a masterpiece of the form.  It showcases why games are art, and it does so spectacularly.  It's intimidating, no question.  But you're doing yourself a disservice not to play it.
Best game ever.

The game may at first present itself to you as being overly difficult and mysterious. You will probably go the wrong way more than a few times, run when you should stop, button-smash the attack commands when you should defend, and not really get what the hype's about.
Then you'll pass some threshold - you'll know when you do - and discover that this game presents layers upon layers of mystery, each bringing both more clarity to the story and lore. You'll eventually grok how to fight, and move past "Dark Souls is hard" to "Dark Souls is increadible". It's very much a Hero's Journey, where you and your will to continue is the archetypical Hero.
From a technical perspective, it does have its frame rate drops (install DS fix to solve this), the UI and controls are unconventional (but you'll adapt, and may grow to like it), and it's fairly low-res (which there are mods to solve, as well).

This game is absolutely amazing not just to me but for others in my family too. My father used to be a gamer himself back in the days of the atari followed by nintendo days as well. He was also my gaming buddy during those days. After the nes/snes days however, he kind of gave up on gaming as a hobby because he said he did not feel the magic in the kind of games that were being made on the pc/ps2/xbox etc.
Fast forward to 2014 or thereabouts which is when I discovers dark souls and introduce him to it as well and this is one action game that did love.
He said he felt the same kind of magic in this game (and Portal/Portal2) which he had felt in his early days of gaming on the atari/nes and I having experienced those games myself I have to agree. While being a modern game, dark souls does do a lot of things in the style of older games and this is one of the things which makes it endearing to so many people I guess.
I have also introduced non gamers to these games and even they could immediately see that this game is something artistic and different (in a good way) from most AAA trash that floats around in the world of gaming these days. The sense of being in a once magnificient but dying world is so beuatifully communicated to you by everything from the visuals, music and even the excellent combat that its easy to get lost in this world.
I have had so much fun playing this game the last few years both alone and with friends and family and its something that I recommend every gamer at least try to do. I know that this its not a great PC port but using a controller and simple ini file mod like dsfix solves most of the issues it has. Then there is another mod DSCM which makes the multiplayer come alive.
The final hurdle you might have before you can dive in and enjoy this gem of a world is that this game has slower more deliberate combat compared to any hack-n-slash game you might have played. On top of that, a lot of the ingame stats and systems are never explained to you for which I recommend you read one of the many brilliant starter guides for this game. Oh and after you finish the game (or even before that) be sure to go on youtube and watch some of the lore videos for dark souls 1 especially from a creator called vatividya. I guarantee that you will find yourself shedding a tear or two on several of those videos...

As the very first visual novel I've ever played, my bar of expectations for VN's has been set extremely high. Long Live the Queen goes beyond the literal name of "visual novel", where you click furiously through pages and pages of text. It is a fully interactive experience where your choices actullay affect the outcome of the game! I know, seems pretty mindblowing after Telltale made a formula on how to fake your way through that and still makes piles of money everytime, but you will encounter no smoke or mirrors in this gem. In Long Live the Queen, you guide a young princess on her path to queenhood before she comes of age on her 15th birthday. You must manage and raise her skills so she can handle the various problems that come her way. If you don't get the right skills to a high enough level, the princess will die. (little hint: Reflexes is an absolute must for the very beginning of the game) And there are so many skills to level up! This VN is perfectly designed to make you feel like a young teenager in over their head with daunting responsiblities, sometimes forcing you to make what some may consider "Evil" paths just to survive. Thats not including the hidden values that may or may not affect the chances of assassination attempts on your princess; commoner approval and noble approval. Certain dialogue options and choices will change how your commoners and nobles think of you, and if one side or the other thinks too negatively of you, expect a lot more unpleasent surprises in the weeks to come.
And if you manage to keep the princess alive, you will discover multiple branching paths that will drastically change your experience. I never got the right skills to unlock it, but I heard the scenes in the Enchanted Forest are really intriguing.
The other characters are very interesting too. I was just as invested in keeping my allies safe as my princess, and intrigued in learning what made my enemies tick.
Overall, this is an outstanding experience that proves that "illusion of choice" is not a necessary evil in every case. Even if you don't like anime art styles or stragety, I encourage you to pick this up at some point. Everyone can get something out of Long Live The Queen.

So I'm going to be honest about this review. +Useful building tools
+Whilst only haveing a few types of basic block, there is a very wide variety of types of said base materials
+Nothing is indestructable
Now, some of the negatives:
-People may not like the learning curve
-The game recently became much more complex with the advanced cannons
-Non-rebindable controls (will remove when added)

Minecraft and Carrier Command had a baby, and this is it.
Yes, there is a learning curve, but it's a painless experience; building boats and vehicles in the designer, and practicing against whichever AI you choose to spawn is complex, but fun.  It will probably take you a while to figure out to make a ship, and make it move, but the satisfaction once you do is enormous.  You'll soon be churning out design after design in minutes once you've got the hang of it; and once you've got the hang of it, you can try your hand at the entertaining campaign, which an almost RTS-like / x-com management experience, punctuated by nail-biting, real time battles.
Make no mistake, this is a PC gamers' game, old-school and simmy, with a steep learning curve, fiddly controls (at first), but the rewards are deeper than anything you'll find in the majority of games.  Weather you're expressing your creativity, or min-maxxing your builds, watching your creations come to life and SMASH THE **** out of other ships and craft is deeply, deeply satisfying.  It's not a quick-blast, but the kind of game you settle into for months on end.  We're talking Ultima Online and Eve levels of depth here, and that's not a comparison I make lightly.
Oh, and in terms of content and stability?  I wouldn't have known it was early access if it didn't say so on the steam page.       Seriously, it's that good.  Patches are frequent, and there is already enough here to keep you busy for months on end.
I heartily recommend this game.

Review as a standalone game:
Let's be honest here, it's probably not worth the $15 (or about $20 AUS, as the exchange rate goes). The combat is kinda fun, and the simplistic universal overview is easy to pick up. That's about as far as it goes.
It is reminscent of other tactical space-combat games like Star Wars: Empire at War. Despite space being 3D, your ships can only move in 2D. The objectives are always some variation of "destroy target, get ship from A to B, or survive for x turns". Ship combat is sometimes satisfying, but otherwise plain and unoriginal.
Empire expansion has no real downside. You have a number of different resources which are used for different things. Energy customises your fleet, food lets you expand the population of a planet, etc. You gain resources at the start of every turn. You only have 1 fleet, and it's actions are limited by "morale". Morale is one of the only limiting factors in the game; once you're out of morale, your fleet cannot take any more actions this turn. Morale is consumed by moving or by instigating combat, and is fully replenished each turn. Lower morale makes your crew less effective in combat. Empire expansion is done planet by planet, and there is no downside to expanding your empire.
The key interesting feature of Starships is the fleet customisation. Ship classes are solely dependent on what customisations they are given, and every ship is 100% customisable witht the same base stats. You can experiment with what works and what doesn't, and come up with some interesting combinations. Ship size is dependent on it's maximum HP. For all intents and purposes, there is no cosmetic customisation options. What your ship looks like is determined by what your starting affinity is, and the stats you give your ship. I've enjoyed making different roles for my ships, from slower and tankier carrriers to fast, hard-hitting stealth assassins.
All in all, there are some interesting elements, but nothing that hasn't been done better in other games. If you're looking for a tactical space game, buy it when it's at least 50% off.

The other review:
Sid Meier's Starships is, for all intents and purposes, an overpriced standalone DLC for Beyond Earth. It's main purpose is to unlock content in BE, and likewise BE can unlock extra content for Starships.
It's an interesting take on an expanded BE game, and people who enjoy roleplay and immersion might enjoy continuing games of BE in Starships (yes, you can do this). The unlockable content for BE might even be worth it.
If you're looking for a breath of fresh air for BE, you might want to look into this game (treating it as a DLC). However, I would recommend getting it at a discount.

Greeting all, Lets get this train moving shall we? :-/ sorry, I could not help it.
I snapped this up from steam quickly without reading anything about the game as this is the type of game I love.
I wish I did, But let me get to that in a minute, Firstly on loading this game I was greeted by the main menu, It was fast loading as the specifications for this game is not high at all, Where do I start, I guess a tutorial would be a good place........Wait...What......No Tutorial? Strange, but it's OK, I have played railroad tycoon, Can't be much different.
Before I go much further, I must say that I did not expect this game to be visually pleasing, I was expecting something low spec. And I was not disappointed, with old 16bit block graphics style game play smoothed off a bit.
But that aside, I started playing, I choose an open play "sandbox" style of UK, and I started from the beginning, 1850.
Wow was I wrong about it not being too hard to pick up, I have a total of less than ten hours on this game, The first two was setting up a transport link and trying to set up a route.
After all that, I was suddenly drawn to how much it had cost me, How much it was costing me to maintain buildings, And how much I was loosing on each run!
After a few more hours setting up different trade routes It struck me as how hard it was to make any money, I was just keeping afloat mostly,
Starting from the 1850's I only had access to horse and cattle, a few years on I got a train and some ships, One of which was 6.5MILLION!!! to buy, you start the game with 15M and I was fast down to less than one million, So I fast forwarded time to gain some funds, and for some reason, The white house appeared in Cornwall? Quirky.
I also noticed at this point the lack of transport options, I was still in "horse and cart" mode, Starting on my railway, I did a long link between two factories, That was great fun and was a money earner, I was back up to a few mill in no time, So I went to do another rail link.....And For some reason, I cannot place another station anywhere on the map? I looked this up on the internet and apparently it is a bug, And to my surprise, one of MANY! No, Seriously!
Many of the bugs I have not come across yet, But this along with no hover over tool tips, The inability to do roads/rail in 8 directions (can only be done 4 directions) and the awkwardness of setting up routes (route manager disappears when you move the map with the mouse, you have to use the arrow keys!) just makes the game look underdeveloped.
I have reluctantly decided to call it a day for this game, And it cost me a GBP £10.99, Steam will not give back money for you buying rubbish that they offer, You have been warned, Please research what you can about a game before you give it to steam.
It might sound a little harsh, If you decide to put up with all the flaws, your a better person than me, I just can't play this game.
Thank you for your time.

During a battle in which I had to kill one of the reigning warchiefs I quickly found myself vastly outnumbered inside of his stronghold, now I was strong, but every man has a limit. Quickly my health bar vanished in thanks to the multitudes of Uruks surrounding and attacking me, the final blow struck by a seemingly no name grunt. The warchief was happy that he had managed to fend off my attack and the Uruk that killed me, one name Bubol was promoted from a lowly Grunt to a captain. Quickly Bubol rose through the ranks, at first I ignored him but by the time our paths crossed he was a bodyguard of one of the war chiefs and i now had to fight and kill Bubol the War Chain (or something like that) who was now considerably more powerful and was an Elite Captain. A little shocked from me being alive, Bubol acknowledged that he would have to put me down once more, however the number of Uruk around him was only about 10-15 which i dispatched quickly and put an end to Bubol. Eventually during my travels in completing the main story I was clearing a camp full of Uruks and a familiar face greeted me, Bubol had survived, however now weakened and just a captain. His armor was broken, only half of his helmet remained, scars covered his face and there were stitches  in his chest where my sword had impaled him, it seemed he had survived my attack and was waiting for his revenge. Bubol fought as hard as he could but he was killed eventually, this time, for good. That is the story of Bubols rise and fall, created by one of the most innovative systems in gaming history. If I hadn't killed Bubol I could've branded him and made him work under me to become a warchief. To my suprise, at the end of the game in one of the final missions, the first thing you have to do is face your nemesis in battle, and none other thean Bubol was that nemesis, he had survived once more and in another epic battle I finally dominated Bubol, this time his head was gone ensuring his defeat.
Aside from the amazing and innovative nemesis system, the gameplay is pretty good. Combat is seamless and fun, similar to the Batman Arkham series except in Tolkiens middle earth. You dont really face too much challenge unless up against a lot of people or a captain or warchief with inconvenient strengths like the invulnerable to attacks thing. Some features can get pretty repetitive but there are certain abilities and quests that tend to spice it up a little at least.
The world is amazing, this is singlehandedly the best game set in Tolkiens Middle Earthm the two maps are relatively small but I dont think it serves to its detriment, It makes it easy to get around without easily accessible vehicles, there are the monsters; caragors and graugs but its   a little inconvenient to get ahold of them. Running everywhere doesnt take too long. By the world I do just mean the environment and lore. For an open world game it does feel quite empty and somehwat crowded, you wont find much except the same Uruks overlooking slaves who are preforming some sort of menial task.
RPG elements such as upgrades are balanced, there arent too much but not too little either. They certainly add interesting elements to gameplay.
Though some tasks are reptitive, there is a lot of stuff to do and the nemesis system is neverending until you own everyone in Saurons army.
Story is okay.. its good at some points and dissapointing at others. Overall a pretty good and solid game that can at least provide a few hours of fun with the nemesis system.
