After watching the short anime based on this game, I "fell in love" with the "Tales Of" Series and always wanted to get into the games of that series. Thus, after playing Tales of Zestiria (which I also liked overall), I was SO HAPPY to see this game make it to PC (as I never played the original game due to not owning a GameCube at that time). Thus, after finishing the story mode yesterday, in short:
Pros:
1. Beautiful Soundtracks (definitely the first thing that comes to mind when thinking about this game).
2. Loveable characters, each with his/her own personality and backstory.
3. The fact that you can play as multiple characters (not just stuck with Lloyd).
4. Cool game mechanics (much more simplified than Tales of Zestiria's seemingly "complex" stats/items system).
5. Multiple areas with different landscapes/music to mix things up (so you never get tired of the same place/music).
6. The story itself is very "charming" and the backstories of all other playable characters are very interesting as well.
Cons:
1. 30 FPS. Now, as someone who never played the original game (which played at 60 FPS), I wasn't really "bothered" by playing this game at 30 FPS, but if you are a returning player who played the original games (or someone who really values high settings and playing games at 60 FPS), I can see why being "locked" to 30 FPS can be bothering to some people. But honestly, it wasn't game-breaking and the game still felt "fluid" overall nonetheless.
2. The "illusion" of a choice when answering a question. You see, whether on the world map or during certain parts of the story, you will be asked a question and will have to decide between 2 answers. The sad thing is that, no matter which answer you go for, the RESULT IS SAME with only a slight change to the "dialogue" on the basis of your choice (but nothing affecting the story really). I find that slightly disappointing as, imagine if each choice mattered and that each choice could lead to a different scenario/ending, not only that would let the player feel more responsible and involved in the story, but it would also increase the "replayability" of the game as well. Oh well not a big deal honestly though...
3. As someone who watched the "anime" version of this game, comparing both stories and the different "events" in each story, I feel the anime did a better job in "most" of the areas in which it differed from the game (not all but most parts IMO). That's NOT to say that the story of the game is "bad or inferior", absolutely NOT! I'm just saying that I felt more "engrossed/attached" to the anime's story (which did a better job in making you feel more attached to each character, especially their backstories) as compared to the game's method of handling those backstories and certain events, but still, even then, the game's story was GREAT in the big picture nonetheless.
Final Rating: Despite those 3 Cons, I can confidently say that those cons were "immaterial" to my enjoyment of this game in the big picture and so, my final score for this game is definitely a 10/10! AMAZING GAME! LOVED IT! :D

My favourite game of all time. I first played the GameCube version back when it was still an exclusive, and was soon captivated by the game's imaginative story and character-relationship-development - but what really got me was the fast-paced and action-packed battle style fused with RPG grinding, level and equipment system and overpowered bosses found throughout the entirety of the storyline, only beatable through sheer persistance, trial and error and strategy. In fact, for such a fast battle system it shows incredible tactical depth an planning both in and outside of battle. For instance, every character can equip up to four "power stones" called "EX-Gems" that bestow upon them additional abilities and/or powers. These very stones, however, are also marked with a T (for tactical) or an S (for strike) that indicate the character's growth "direction", which in turn dictate which Artes (special attacks and spells) said team member will learn.
Taking the main character Lloyd as an example, after using the Lvl. 1 Arte "Sword Rain" 50 times and reaching Character Level 21 he may learn either Sonic Sword Rain in the Strike route (a standard Sword Rain ending in a powerful thrust that pushes the enemy away) or Sword Rain: Alpha in the Technical route (an extended Sword Rain ending in an upward strike). Though there is a very clear distinction in each character's selection of artes for each route, they are varied enough to justify trying each one out, seeing as you can "forget" Artes previously learned in order to learn the opposite path, and this may be done as many times as one wishes.
Looking a bit complex? Well, new players needn't worry about complicated optimisation strategies, for all paths are viable and fun to play and more in-depth knowledge comes very naturally as the game progresses, but it does serve to illustrate how this game is both very accessible to new players and full of neat optimisation options for the power-hungry min-maxers such as myself. :p
On my original playthrough, way back in the Gamecube version, what really took me by surprise was not the absurd number of sidequests and collectibles, nor the 40-hour main story and character development, but how much work has been put in this games' replayability: upon completing the story for the first time, a "GRADE Shop" is unlocked. Turns out the GRADE earned at the end of every battle (sort of like a rating system: the faster and cleaner each fight is, more grade is earned) is used not only to buy materials for a (now-outdated) crafting system and new ex-gems, but also to begin a new playthrough with data inherited from your completed game. Among the inheritable parametres are your Titles, money, itens and equipment, cooking ability and recipes and many more.
There are also new parametres that may be input to the new file, such as 2x EXP, 10x EXP, more GRADE earned (and lost) and, more importantly, the Monster List data and the Collector Book's data. These are books that keep track of the monster analised through the Magic Lens item or Inspect Magic spell and items collected throughout the game, respectivelly.
If that seems too large a task to overcome, I can only assure you that it is not: by remembering to Magic Lens every new enemy, I ended my first playthrough on PC with 88% Collector Book completion and over 90% Monster List completion. There are, however, some items that can only be found in subsequent playthroughs (such as Character affection items or items that are mutually exclusive), which means one WILL need to complete the game multiple times in order to TRULY complete it.
All in all, this version of the game presented no technical problems for me, although I am aware that it has been patched since launch. I can safely say that it has never acted up. It doesn't have loads of new content when compared to the release version, the the graphics and interface have surely been further developed. With this in mind, it a game that's WELL WORTH the price it's being sold for; although it shows its age in its graphics and animations, its gameplay and story have triumphed over the test of time.

Have to say I first played "AdVenture Capitalist" which I found to be quite addictive. This one is similar but different, if that makes any sense.
Not as addictive but fun.
With Adventure Capitalist it is buy buy buy, build up angels, reset and buy buy buy.
With AdVenture Communist it's more trading to progress.
For example to get a farmer you need 12 potatoes and 7 land. But to get 1 worker you have to "trade" 5 farmers (plus other commodities). Then you need 5 workers to get 1 miner++. So to get 1 miner you need a stock of 25 farmers. But if you trade all your farmers how do you get potatoes?
And there in lies the beauty of this game. It's a trade off between manufacture and upskill.
You need to be strategic in your purchases and not expand too quickly, whilst always making sure you have enough of the good old "common folk" to build your workers, miners, soldiers, etc.
Fun game if you have time on you hands, you don't have to think to hard and there are daily "activity" rewards. So you get out what you put in, so to speak.
Recommend.

I would describe this Stories of Bethem: Full Moon as a game which wants to be a Zelda game, but fails at every conceivable point to understand what makes Zelda games appealing to play.
Let's start with the basic game mechanics. In Bethem, you have a mana gauge. You can only attack with spells, so every action you can do costs mana. This mana refills slowly, at a speed depending on your currently equipped bracelet -- more powerful bracelets give faster regen. Except, once you've regenned about 10% of your MP, the speed drops dramatically anyway, and seems to drop off almost entirely once you reach 50% MP.
See those bushes? The ones everywhere? You have to waste MP to get past them. The little logs and whatnot? Waste MP. The holes? Waste MP. Exploring actively makes you more vulnerable in combat by wasting magic you could be using to defend yourself. Irritatingly, the spells which don't have combat uses (for example, the one that fills in holes) cost even MORE than your attacking spells, which serves no purpose other than to try to make you waste time or magic potions, which you can carry in limited supply.
As a result? When I find a new exploration tool, my knee-jerk reaction is not "Oh cool! I know a bunch of places I could use this!". It's more along the lines of "Oh, it costs even more mana? Great. Just great." I cannot describe how bad that is in the context of a Zelda-like.
The dungeons also leave a lot to be desired. Here's a rundown of the first four. 1) Block Puzzles, the dungeon. Agonizingly slow block puzzles. There's literally a point where the game wants you to push a block down a long hallway with no obstacles for a treasure chest -- in other words, they went out of their way to waste your time. 2) Warp Mazes. Because we all enjoyed Sabrina's Gym in Pokemon Red, right? Trying random exits in entirely identical rooms to eventually trial and error your way to the goal with no other gameplay challenge? 3) Dark Dungeon. And by dark, I mean you can see literally your own character and the tile in front of him. You walk in without the fire magic you need to see, do half the dungeon (fighting against ranged monsters, in the dark) to get it, and then things are a little better... if you spam the fire magic every five seconds, which will make you run out of mana. There are candles to light, but hey! You can't see the candles. Hope you enjoy firing randomly into the darkness. 4) Statue land, where lighting candles will move statues that only exist in this dungeon. Oh, except for one particular statue near the end of the dungeon, which is activated by a kill room you get to at the beginning. Y'know, because consistency in game mechanics is too much to ask.
Oh, but don't think you've seen the last of slow block puzzles or warp mazes or can't see more than one tile in front of my face gimmick once you've gotten past their theme dungeons. They just sprinkle them in everywhere, and they remain the same horrible, unfun gimmicks as they were in the first place.
Let's see, what else? The combat! The combat in this game is trash. Because you're a mage, the game has the smart idea of introducing elemental resistances and weakness. Mostly, this consists of giving all the enemies in a new area resistance to the things you've got and weaknesses to things you won't get for literal hours. Powering up your bracelet helps increase your attack power, but it's done through limited collectibles. About that third dungeon, where you can't see anything -- it's also full of fire spiders, which take eight hits to put down at the time, are hard to dodge, and do a very healthy amount of damage to you for that point in the game. And you can't see them, because it's dark. Don't forget that you're probably somewhere between 10~50% mana because you had to waste it all getting rid of bushes, and therefore will run out of mana and have to kite until you recover enough to attack.Oh, and almost every enemy is faster than you and/or can attack diagonally, which you can't.
Even basic, silly things contribute to making this game a chore. You'll sometimes -- often -- find pit traps under bushes, which need a mid-game spell to fill in. In the early game, the fact that they're hidden by bushes is a form of cheap damage. But it also shows up in other ways. There are no holes not covered by bushes. Which means that you can go all the way through a maze, get to the last little row of bushes, and discover a single hidden hole blocking your way... so you have to walk back. Why was the hole not at the beginning of your path, if it's meant to gate progress? Why was it not visible? On that note, your basic spell penetrates up to two bushes at a time, so obviously they're usually placed in threes, or fives -- anything to make you waste an extra point of mana.
That's what this game is. Every single little thing is just lacking that element of consideration that would make the game fun to play, and it all adds up to an insulting, unenjoyable experience. On every screen, you'll find something and ask yourself, "Why are they making me waste my time and mana on this? Why does this need to be here?" The music is good, and the graphics are good, but don't let that and the nostalgia for a real Zelda game fool you. This game is a waste of time and a wasted opportunity, and my advice is to leave it well alone.

A slick Zelda clone. There's a high chance you might like it. And I really wanted to like it but I'm requesting a refund out of specific reasons. Hate to be that guy, but here's why.
I'm a parent and don't have much time. And this game tries too much to waste my time.
The attack animation stops movement. Pushing boulders takes such a long time. And the first dungeon is filled with sokoban involving pushing boulders.
What led me to quitting the game: I made it past a certain gate, past the first sokoban puzzle behind, and failed at the next puzzle (balloon). Then I realized that if I wanted to reset the balloon, I had to backtrack and do the sokoban again. Slowly pushing boulders. I don't ragequit in competitive games, but here I did. <<-- Edit: apparently there was a shortcut that I overlooked!
Now I appreciate the older Zelda games even more. They were limited to (mostly) one-screen-at-a-time, which led to slick and elegant design. Sadly, this is not what I can say about this game. I guess there is fun to be had for people with more patience and time, but it's not for me.
Best of luck with your next project.
One last thing: the game does establish the sense of discovery, but apparently I'm to collect eight... objects? Just about any other word would invoke more sense of w onder: amulets, shards, essence... but objects?

When reviewing Dark Souls on PC one has to talk about two different thing, the game and PC version/port of the game. And if you want to understands the problems of the game, you also have to see through the meme crap and the fanboyism you inevitable will encounter whenever people talk about DS.
PC port:
The game, as it is, is extremely badly optimized for PC. You can find tons of negative reviewes that confirm this.
The devs made it run on PC, but that's it. While you can choose keyboard and mouse, it is basically unplayable with it. The only way to play the original game is a controller. But if you want more than 30 fps or higher resolutions, the game doesn't support this by default.
Multiplayer is not working.
Result: Not recommend
BUT, thanks to a dedicated fanbase, there are fixes for all of these issues. You can get better graphics, you can make the multiplayer work again and, finally, you can play with mouse and keyboard. The only thing that's still annoying are the key and button prompts, that don't correspond to your input method, but you get used to it quickly.
The game:
I can totally see the appeal this game has to some people. The art design is great and it still looks good today. The difficulty is very high, the combat rewarding if you win. The exploration is fun.
BUT... the combat, or the game in general, is only hard IF you are a new player. Once you understand how to beat a boss or traverse an area, honestly it is pretty easy. I'm watching a playthrough of a decent player and he basically needs only 1/10th of the time to get through the same part, I managed to beat. Some of the boss fights are ridicously easy if you "solved" them. Don't get me wrong, it still requires quite a lot of skill and some parts will still easily kill you if you are unlucky. But a player who knows how to beat a section/boss, will be able to do this over and over with a reasonable success rate. The problem is how the game teaches you how to master game, or better, how it not teaches you at all. The game barely gives you any help and the info you get is also quite often simply wrong.
What helps to beat some bosses is the multiplayer system. You can get random strangers to help you, and I used this for the Taurus Demon after several tries to beat him alone. The issue here is that it didn't feel like an accomplishment, but more like a cheat. I was mostly dodging, healing and doing the occasional hit. I felt like the most damage was done by the other guy, who doesn't seemed to be greatly affected by the boss. It just felt wrong and not satifying.
Another help I used was the Internet where you can find tons of info about the game, because fans dissected the game almost completely. The issue? If you use guides and wikis, you also don't feel like you accomplished anything. You still have to execute the tips and often they are not that detailed enough, but it still lessens the gameplay experience. And if you really want it easy, watch videos how to beat sections.
So, the only solution is to play for yourself and figure out how to beat the game yourself. And this is where the fun turns into grinding, into tedium, into work. And this is where, at least for me, the fun is gone. E.g. if you have to get over and over from a bonfire to a boss to just TRY to kill him or even how to approach him for a little progress, this gets old quickly. Even if it's just a dozen of small enemies that you can one-shot, the few minutes to get to the boss will add up quickly. If you have no clue, what a boss does, you'll probably die within moments. Then you have to get back to him. This time trying running, next time blocking, then you slowly learn the attacks of the boss, then you might try different weapons, different move sets, magic, magical items... the combinations of how to (mostly unsuccessful) approach a boss are almost endless. And the game doesn't really help you in determining the best strategy. You do this over and over, each and in the end you will probably beat him. But at the same time, you've spent hours killing the same bunch of weak enemies over and over, which IMO is a waste of my time and not worth beating a hard boss. I simply hate doing the same stuff over and over, which makes me not like or recommend this game.
Another way to classify DS is to say that it is a trial-and-error puzzle, because that is how you build your "skill", i.e. solve the game. As I said, the "trial" part requires you to transverse easier sections just to be able to try out a new technique and the "error" part is where you die. Death in DS isn't comparable to other games. Death in DS is a gameplay element. You actually never die and load an earlier save, but the game resets the monster and takes away your "currency" souls. Basically the game takes away your progress (although you can get some back) and makes you start over and hopefully you learned a piece of the puzzle to kill the next boss, but that's it.
Overall: Not recommended ... (unless you like tedium and constant repetitiveness)

I finally did it. I finally completed Dark Souls, and now I see what the hubbub was all about. Dark Souls, while not perfect, will be considered a classic two decades from now the same way Ocarina of Time is considered a classic today. One of the most satisfying gaming experiences I have experienced in my entire life.
I purchased Dark Souls in September 25th, 2013, and I only recently beat it for the first time, more than 4 years later. I estimated this is my fifth attempt to beat the game, since every other time except the most recent attempt I stopped due to frustration. Throughout these 4 years I’ve  moved between three residences, had multiple jobs, got engaged and married, as well as acquired all of the other Souls games (in my ADHD habit, I have failed to complete these games as well). It has taken a long time to finish this game, but by golly am I happy I finally did.
Dark Souls is a game spoken about in hushed whispers, and fearful reverence. It is known for its vague story, “clunky” combat, but most of all, its difficulty. After completing the game, I can say that while the game is challenging, it’s certainly not impossible. You're not some kind of 1337 gamer or super badass for beating Dark Souls, you are likely just somebody who didn't give up in spite of failure, which is an important life lesson in it of itself. As long as you can press the buttons on your xbox controller without looking down at them, I can safely say you are capable of beating the game, as long as you are patient and willing to learn.
I’ve read the opinion stating that while Dark Souls is hard, it’s also fair. This is true, but only maybe 98% of the time. I don’t know why the developers put in some clearly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t moments in the game that will likely kill you without any chance of you avoiding the death, but thankfully these are pretty few and far between. The combat system in this game is fantastic, I can’t think of another game with as great of a combat system as this game, which is why we have seen so many imitators, such as The Surge, Necropolis, Salt and Sanctuary, Lords of the Fallen, etc. Other games like most modern FPS shooters have only one choice in terms of combat mechanics; you point at a guy and click. Congrats, you win. Reminds me of Yahtzee’s assertion that modern military shooter fans are people who enjoy adventure games, except the only puzzle is “Use Gun on Man.” In Dark Souls, the ridiculous abundance of weapons, magic, and armor means that there will certainly be a loadout you find personally enjoyable. This is one of the reasons I take issue with the patently false statement that Witcher 3’s challenge is comparable to that of Dark Souls. The difficulty of Witcher 3 is very different since in that game you are ALWAYS playing as Geralt, and as a result you only have the Longsword as a primary weapon and some basic spells to mess around with, no matter your level. Nevertheless, from now on, if I read anybody comparing these two excellent but very, very different games, I will be sure to chastise them for their near sightedness and stupidity. Don’t go into Witcher 3 expecting a Dark Souls-like experience, and do NOT go into Dark Souls thinking it’ll give you a Witcher 3-like experience, or else you will just be disappointed.
The way Dark Souls scales in damage numbers means even the starting equipment you can continuously upgrade all the way into the endgame, which is fantastic, since the player’s relationship with the weapon they have is something the game takes very seriously. The “clunky” combat system will eventually feel smooth and natural as long as you’re willing to invest some time into it. The “Hard but Fair” axiom is the reason why the attacks queued up by your character felt slow and clunky. The enemies in this game attack slowly but hit very hard, so in order to be fair, the player’s character attacks slowly as well. This means there is a tendency for the average new player to over extend, to get greedy and spam attacks regardless of how much stamina is left, and then get killed because they don’t have enough stamina left to roll/ parry/ block incoming attacks. Patience is the best advice I can give to those trying to get into the game's flow of combat.
As for story, I liked what was there, and if anything, am happy about how vague it is. I’m pretty sure the entire game is some kind of allegory for your character’s experience in Purgatory, but that is far from a unique perspective. Many have criticized this game’s vague story, but I don’t think we would have such a beautiful wealth of fan created content if every story beat was exhaustively spelled out, or if there was a thousand page long codex endlessly explaining every bit of lore the game has to offer. Feel free to delve deeply into the fan theories, or peruse the item descriptions yourself, but regardless of how much you invest in the background information of Dark Souls, the story telling in this game is one of its strongest, most memorable aspects, regardless of how much you want to get into it.
Like I initially mentioned, Dark Souls is a modern classic in video gaming. However, it is not perfect. First of all, it is a ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥ PC port, be prepared to download a simple Dsfix file to get it running at a desired resolution and at 60 fps. Seeing how small this file is makes me wonder why the developers couldn’t just fix it themselves. Another thing is that I think the magic and ranged in this game leaves a lot to be desired. The melee combat is brutal and satisfying, often feeling like a deadly dance between opponents in PvE and PvP, but the ranged/ magic feels like an afterthought. It is extremely useful in the game, if not almost essential to have some kind of ranged ability, I picked up Great Chaos Fireball in my first playthrough, but there isn’t nearly as much thought required to just spam magic spells compared to the tense split second decision making of melee combat. Many enemies don’t have any ranged abilities, therefore can’t react appropriately to you hitting them from outside of arm’s reach. Not really a big deal, but definitely something to mention. Thankfully, the limited spell slots means that even hardcore magic users will have to rely on melee combat every once in a while. The final and biggest major issue with Dark Souls is that I honestly believe it is unfinished. There are several areas of the game that I don’t want to spoil, but after you fight your way through and defeat the boss, you will think to yourself, “That was it?” It’s not like the game is too short, it’s a long, content filled game, but I don’t see many reviews criticizing some of the less complete/ polished areas of the game. This doesn’t ultimately detract too much from the overall experience, but it’s just a painful tease of what COULD have been created if only the developers had the resources necessary. To be honest, from Demon Soul’s release to Dark Souls, From Software only had about two years of development time, and it’s mind boggling what they managed to put out in such a relatively short timeframe.
If you are a fan of Action games with deep combat, you most likely have already played Dark Souls. If you were scared off by its difficulty, or got frustrated and quit, I suggest you do what I did and get your head out of your butt and complete this wonderful, satisfying experience.
I understand it now. The fanaticism and intense love and camaraderie that fans of this game share with each other is one of the most beautiful, hilarious things I've ever seen come out of the gaming community. And for good reason as well, I can't think of something better to unite gamers in mutual love than sharing the weird, dark, and brutal experience of overcoming insurmountable adversity in the land of Lordran.
Praise the Sun, indeed.

At a glance, the simple graphic design would lead many people to pass this game.

The main mechanic is gravity, or rather the lack of.
Your goal is simply to get your ship from point A to point B using only your thrusters. Simple... except there is no assistance. There is no gyroscope or breaking thrusters. Once you gain momentum you keep that momentum.
One thing I found odd is the only unlockable in the game was the final level. All other stages and levels, as well as 6 ship designs are available as soon as you start playing. This isn't really a bad thing, as it allowed me to skip more challenging stages and return to them later, as well as try out the different ships.
So if you enjoy a nice 2D space puzzle game with gravity challenges, this is a nice fit for you. But be warned, it's not as casual as it appears, as the levels start to get tricky real fast.

Before even playing this game, please note:
The first Postal game is definitely the black sheep of the Postal series. Released in 1997, this game spiked immense controversy with its dark and gruesome style. Its a 3/4s isometric view style of game with prerendered backgrounds. One of my problems with the game is that the controls take some time to get used to. The graphics are pretty standard and use 3-d characters on top of prerendered backgrounds. It works quite well for a game like this. The game is about averagely long for a five dollar game, which is another thing I'd like to bring up; the price tag. While others may disagree with me, and you're free to, I believe a five-dollar price tag for this game is a bit much. It goes on sale often however, so I'd buy it when it's around one dollar, maybe slightly more.

Strategy thick starship tactics with adrenaline stimulating tense action. Sid Meier's Starships has a incredible unique mix of elements which come together to create exciting suspenseful battles where fast skillful maneuvering to get in just the right sweet strategic position to fire hull shattering hits upon enemy ships then take off engines blasting behind a planetoid or some asteroids before the enemy can counter attack with devastating effect.
Sid Meier's Starships is the first turn based strategy game i may have ever played which felt fast and furious giving a fps shooter adrenaline rush in of all things a turn based strategy game. It was like playing a table top game with friends but against the ai instead.
Graphics have an old school style to them with a great hex map setup with many environmental variables which can mean the difference between life and death depending on how the player utilizes them to their advantage. Weapons have varying ranges and levels of damage with lasers delivering heavy damage from long range while missile weapons like torpedoes are usually slower with a chance of being avoided if one keeps their attacks fluid and mobile. Stay still and you are probably dead like a sitting duck.
You can buy and upgrade ships to become lethal space faring dreadnoughts of unstoppable destruction. In my first game as i was learning my way around i built two heavily armored ships which were able to take on a group of five enemy ships and fighters for awhile letting loosing terrifying barrages of laser fire into their midst before eventually being defeated with blood curdling audio and visuals during their horrific demise. Talk about getting lost in fun abandonment as if watching a starship battle in a episode of STAR TREK.
Planets you rule are used to get resources and do research to improve your battle prowess and keep your empire going. You will come across other leaders which you form alliances with or who will form alliances against you as everyone does their best to thrive and survive in the infinite vastness of the universe.
Audio and music is excellent bringing home those peaceful space traveling moments only to be shattered by battle inspiring man your weapons music. Voice acting is quite good and am glad to say the female robotic voice of the computer is quite informative and comforting :)
Cons-
Ouch that user interface is not intuitive to put it mildly. During my first game session i couldnt even figure out how to move my ships until i watched a Youtube video by AngryJoe who was doing a first impressions playthrough. Also i have to hover my mouse pointer above my selection when giving a command otherwise i will choose the command below it or none at all.
If your into fast paced turn based combat with plenty of thrilling tension while not expecting a CIVILIZATION BEYOND EARTH experiance then Sid Meier's STARSHIPS is the game for you. Just enjoy it for what it is and you will find its more then worth the few credits you have paid to enter the star ship bridge for.

Amazing game with great music, fun battles, and easy to get used to controls.  There are so many factors into choosing how you play.  You can unlock a large set of skills for each char and choose what they will / will not use.  The only real issue with the game is there are subtitles that don't display what's being said at all times.  I have not encountered any bugs that were present at release.
I will try and explain what is fantastic about this game.
You get a very deep and rich story-line that if you really wanted to learn its full history would give you plenty to read / experience.  The complexity of the story still has me finding new pieces to this day that I overlooked.  After 12 years of being out, it stands the test of time with me.  This is one of those rare games that really melds everything together to create a fantastic player experience.
As you play through the game from start to finish, there are new features added to keep you learning new things constantly.  There are many puzzles to give you a break from fighting, and some puzzles with fights in them to keep things interesting.  They really tried to reach a good balance with exploration and fighting.  The battles on the world map are not random encounters so you have some say as to the power of enemy you will have to deal with.
When you play the game depending on what you do / how you play you may unlock titles for your characters.  With these you can adjust the stats how you see fit.  You can also unlock hidden abilities throughout the game for each character. Even after all this, there is so much to see in this game.  If you enjoy story-rich games with fantastic controls, variety in playstyle, and an experience that you want to remember for years to come, I strongly recommend this game.  If not I don't know why you are still reading this when you missed the charmander that was outside your house on pokemon go just now.  Oh well your loss and he's mine now bwahahaha!

Let's start this by saying Orcs Must Die! 2 is far better played as a duo. Being able to communicate is rather important as well. With 2 people you get a little more freedom in what 'towers' you can place. Plus two people beating the Orcs back with clubs is better than one! Grab your best bud and go to town smashing Orcs' faces in!
Orcs Must Die! 2 is a Tower Defense with 3rd person combat and equipment. The Orcs come in waves and there are different types just like any TD. The towers are the more innovative part of this game. Some can be placed on the walls, such as arrow shooters. Others go on the ceiling like a big mace that swings back and forth, pushing Orcs down and off edges. Useful ground spikes and slowing tar will keep the Orcs' movement a few steps behind. Hire bomb wielding Dwarfs & Elven archers and place them wherever you see fit.
You can make pretty wacky scenes by using logic with knowledge of the physics and death triggers such as endless pits, lava or void portals. Maybe toss them in the Orc grinder! You manually control your chosen character (one of two - male or female, who have many different tower and weapon choices) while the wave is in progress and can use melee or ranged combat, along with magic to help
off their advance. Trinket choice and passive effects are a big game changer as well, once you unlock them.
They have different challenges, time trials and survival tests as well to keep occupied with. All you really need to know is there are Orcs... and Orcs Must Die! (2!!!)

This game has potential, but it is still very much unfinished. It doesn't take long to finish all the achievements/medals/etc., and then there's nothing to do but spam more and more workers and buildings. The game could really use a reset/prestige mode feature like angel investors in Adventure Capitalist (and most other games in the idle/clicker genre). It has a limited reset feature - the last building in each category resets your worker count and most of the low tier buildings in the same category - but once you get past the early game, it barely disrupts your economy to do it, and you'll recover what you had in a minute or two. The game could also really use more interesting upgrades to spend science on, since science generation is basically the 'endgame' progression mechanic but all it gives you is simple multiplier bonuses.
All that being said, AdVenture Communist has a really solid core gameplay/mechanics loop. In AdVenture Capitalist, there really isn't any interaction between building types, aside from msot of the Newspaper unlocks giving bonuses to other buildings - you can't really "screw up" aside from claiming angel investors too early, since everything just costs cash and generates more cash for you in return. In AdCom, there is no universal currency - there are 5 resources, and each one has its own type of worker and several buildings. At first, you'll be clicking the food button and spending food to make farmers (who produce food for you passively)... But as you progress to the later resources and building types, they start to cost other workers and buildings in addition to resources. This makes it much more complicated to figure out how to progress efficiently while avoiding bottlenecks in production. In addition to being more complex and interesting as a game mechanic, this is nicely thematic - AdVenture Capitalist is about investing Capital to produce everything, while AdVenture Communist is about trying to balance the production needs of a planned economy.
TL;DR: there's not a ton of content before you're just making numbers go up with no more unlocks, badges, or other goals to aim for... But what's there so far is great, and I'm really excited to see what they do with the game as they flesh it out during Early Access.

This game seems to take some of the best parts of classic Zelda and only make them better.  Similar to Zelda, you have to travel to 8 dungeons to collect 8 artifacts.  Along the way, rather than tools, you will collect spells with different effects.  These spells can be used for attack, but also for clearing obsticles, such as the fire spell that lights torches and burns wood obsticles.
I am also impressed with the way they have handled the dungeons.  It takes effort not just to find the dungeons, but sometimes subquests to gain access.  For example, the fourth dungeon first requries you to find and light three candles hidden elsewhere in the world.  While I do like taht they added some extra challenge that encourages you to take new powers and explore areas you could not reach before, there is one minor negative.  It can lead to some frustration trying to find an obscure location without any decent clues.
There are some good side-quests as well.  A trading game where you start with one item and trade with various NPCs throughout the game.  there are collectables in the form of red opals and candy for various quests as well.  Overall, the game is a fun experience with many things to keep someone entertained for a few dozen hours.

Long Live the Queen
About The Game: At a glance this game might look like a dress-up princess game, but that would be pretty far from the truth. Long Live the Queen is a decision, RNG (Random Number Generator) game that takes you through the life of a princess who is to be crowned queen in 1 year. Your mother has died and your father holds little power. So it is up to you to gain the skills and knowledge to run your kingdom and stay alive. Your mood affects what skills you can learn. If you are too depressed you wont learn anything from your Courtly Manners class. The game time runs on weeks. You spend your weekdays with tutors learning, and your weekends as free time around the castle which will effect your mood in some ways. Between your classes and the weekend there is usually a story part where something will happen, your mood might change, or sometimes you are forced to make choices. Such as putting a lady to death for trying to poison a lord, or calling that lord a liar, or even sentencing said woman to prison. Once you reach at least 25 points in all 3 skill types in a class you get a costume that supports that class, hopefully giving you the edge you need to pass a test. I died many times. I was shot by bandits over 8 times before I finally got to go to my cousins birthday party. So death is a huge part of learning.
Pantsu's Rating (out of 5)
Graphics: 3 Clean anime artwork but it is mostly still pictures.
Playability: 3 Simple controls mostly dealing with the mouse.
Fun: 3 The story is mostly the same each time, so as you play through you know what is comming up next. Whether or not you have the skills, or the luck, to pass the test.
Sound: 3 Happy music changes in an instant when the story gets all serious. Sometimes your mood will affect the music as well. There is not much for sound affects at all.
Replay Value: 4 With so many choices to make, you can play over and over again with different styles, and different outcomes.
Final Score: 3.25
Final Thought: At $9.99 it is definetly worth waiting for a sale, but if you like stategy games with challenge add Long Live the Queen to your wishlist.

Sadly, I'm disappointed. I had envisioned a well polished 'modern' vision of the classic Transport Tycoon, instead what was presented was a somewhat watered down half-cooked revamp.
On the plus side it supports 'modern' wide-screen resolutions (to a point), however even those didn't seem fully supported as there was screen flickering and artifacts around menu text. The game feels very slow and awkward when navigating around the 'huge' maps (which aren't as HUGE as I'd have liked). I appreciate this game isn't about animations or breath taking graphics and lightning, yet it doesn't capture the charm that the Transport Tycoon had with it's design and spites. Something just feels... lacking.
"Ingenious signalling and guidance system for trains" isn't really that ingenious considering it's been used elsewhere before and after this game was made, released and re-relesaed.
Further more there's no tutorial for this 'ingenious' system, which is all fine and well for veterans of the series who can sort of understand and work it out for themself, but will leave newcomers totally bewildered.
In fact there's no real on-screen help or prompts at all - not even pop-up tool tips, so if you are a newcomer to the genre I wouldn't recommend this at all, simply as it's not going to help you get used to the game/genre mechanics.
At this point in time, I regret buying this game. I might have had a little more hope and belief for improvement it was an Early-Access game.
Tempted to request refund and spend the little extra on a similar game currently in Early-Access, as I have more hope it'll be supported and developed beyond this game's current state.
Overall at the current price of just under £10 (discounted) seems way too much for a poorly optimised retro game that somehow feels like an Early-Access game. I would have been way more forgiven if this had been £5 on GOG, or a clearly labeled Early-Access release (at least then I'd have hopes for improvements over time).

Despite the actual gameplay being solid, it needs a lot of work from the developers to be somewhat playable.
To start with, the performance is absolutely terrible. It felt like the game was running at 10-20 fps (20 fps with game on normal speed, on max speed (8x) it felt closer to 10 fps).
Then there are some problems with the interface. Even though it is an older game, it is no excuse to release it in this state. Several interactions are very unlogical. You have to start a campaign using the enter button (you cannot double-click it), but there are no hints about what you had to do after selecting the US compaign. The screen that follows requires you to press an OK button and enter doesn't work anymore.
Another problem I'm having is moving over the map, you can use the arrow keys but this is very choppy and slow. You can also use the right mouse button that is smooth and fast, but when you are working on something (road/schedule) and you right click the mouse the current action gets cancelled and you can start over. As a result, when you are creating a schedule you might want to zoom out first, otherwise moving around the map is very tedious.
There are many of these inconsistencies in the interface and with the lack of a tutorial it might be hard to find out what you actually need to get starting. That said, once you figure everything out it does not become such a problem anymore. The performance, however, needs to be fixed. I also noticed some other bugs, one in particular is that you can build modern airfields and chopper platforms around the 1850's, but you cannot build the planes and choppers yet (for obvious reasons).
I do recommend this game if they fix the performance. In the current state, wait until they do.

I have played from the Depths for quite some time now, and the one thing i will say is that the learning curve is quite steep. The sub menes and construction UI may dazzle your eyes at first, but after a few hours (took me about 4)  you will be well on your way to making AI controled ships planes and even space craft.
The main fun in this game for most people (and i guess the main draw) is that the game has very few limits on what you can actually do with your creations. Want to make a submarine that can surfance and then fly ? well its entierly possible in this game as long as you know how to do it, and there in lies a problem. As the games in game manuals really dont go into enough detail on exactly how they work. After time though you will just learn these things with experimenting. Its the same with missiles - you can make so many different types - torpedos, flak, anti missile missiles flares mines  you name it you can probably make it, but the manuals dont really tell you how - only how to construct the actual functioning weapon system. The games does use LUA programing how ever and these blocks can be placed to run custom scripts and AI  on your ships, which is nice.
The other main draw of this will be ofcourse - the Co-Op Campaign which is just alot of fun from the get go as all players can work on the smae construction - making some truely massive flasg ships and world destroying craft. In the campaign the AI will attack you quite regulary so its essential to protect your resourse gathering areas, how you ask ? well he is another cool feture of the game - your not just able to build ships - but you can also build structures and floating fortresses  that while are not mobile - will be able to carry the biggest and heavyist weapons you can dream of with out you haveing to worry about the physics affect that such things would have on ships.
All in all - for the price - you really can not go wrong !

Gun Rocket is a very cool game, but VERY hard. If you wish to try your patience, you can hardly do better than this.
The premise is to move a rocket through space to a target. The challenge being that space, having no gravity, has no means by which to slow or stop your ship, other than its own rockets. So, you fire your ship's rockets to move, to slow, and to change direction. Generally pretty much all at the same time. Thus the challenge is great.
You do all these things in a contrived, shaped space. As such, not only must you do all the above pretty much concurrently, but you must stay within areas of unusual shapes and proportions. Only one level at the time is available for play (so far, at an early level), but 100 levels are available over the life of the game. You are attempting to succeed in reaching the target, but also with the best time and least fuel consumed. Thus, it's possibe to play with great caution, or "hell bent for leather", while consuming fuel rapidly. The feeling of success is substantial!
There is also a multiplayer aspect, which I haven't explored. For this price ($1.99US), you can hardly go wrong.
High recommendation.

If you're looking for an epic 4x space strategy game like Endless Space, Galactic Civilizations 1-3, or something else, this is not that game. If you are looking for a game with spreadsheets and lists, this is not that game. If you're looking for a game where you command hundreds of ships divided into multiple fleets, this is not that game. If however you're looking for a lite 4x space strategy game that includes tactical combat and can be played start to finish in a few hours, then this might be worth consideration.
The unique element of this game is how it's focused around your single fleet of ships. In the beginning of the game, the fleet is not very strong. However given enough resources it can grow in size (up to 8 ships) and strength to become a formidable force in the galaxy. You'll be faced with the decision of choosing between engines, shields, armor, and different weapons. Do you continue to upgrade your existing ships or buy more ships to add to the fleet? Do you choose speed over armor? Do you build out your ships for specific roles? What tech do you research to compliment your upgrade strategy? Then there are wonders which further enhance your fleet and can provide huge advantages. You'll also find battle cards which provide bonuses during missions.
Another fun element of the game are the missions. When you visit other planets you'll be faced with missions that range from escorting transport ships while protecting them from pirates, escaping with sympathizers aboard your flagship, defeating waves of attacking ships, and so on. Successfully completing missions will provide influence or other rewards.
As for the complaints about this being a tablet or mobile game, it is true that the options screen is missing some common options available on PC games, the game isn't a true full screen in that the taskbar isn't hidden, and the screen doesn't scroll automagically when the mouse hits the edge. However none of these things have prevented me from playing the game. The map can be moved with either the arrow keys or the left mouse button. The taskbar can be set to auto-hide if it's that distracting (or just deal with it). In regards to price, I do think that PC gamers unfortunately do end up paying a premium over the mobile platforms. This isn't the first game and it won't be the last.
Finally, in regards to expectations, I think people saw Sid Meier's name along with this being set in space and left their expectations unchecked. First, the low price point should have been a major indicator that this wasn't going to be anywhere near the scale of a Civilization game. Second, a Sid Meier games doesn't automatically infer an epic game. The past few years 2K/Firaxis have had smaller Sid Meier titles such as Ace Patrol, Ace Patrol: Pacific Skies, and Civilization Revolutions which were on the mobile platform.

Tales of Symphonia is considered the definitive entry of Tales Series/Tales of Series for Western fans. That alone should explain a lot for this games popular reception. Do note this game was first released in Game Cube.
Also, point to note that the negative/mixed reviews are mostly from the older version of the steam release due to bugs. Currently I haven't face any game breaking bugs so I would say it's OK to grab this if you're worried about bugs.
Some good points about this game, with some of them being the selling characteristics of Tales Series in General:
- This is a great game for JRPG fans featuring compelling storytelling with the touch of classic RPG. The characters are well design in terms of their personality and backstory, can be considered one of the better cast among the Tales games. Some might nitpick that the plot is generic, but we all know that's part of the features of classical JRPG works
- Tales Series is the first to introduce realtime action combat in comparison with other JRPG franchise. The current combat system is linear (aka 2.5D) and revamped based on the earlier combat systems of the franchise. I've seen some people complaining about this combat system but this is mainly because this is a re-release of a classical game. Don't expect extraordinary revolution of gameplay.
- Anime style arts and character models which are really appealing
- Offers replay value with some unlockable bonuses for New Game +
Overall, my recommendation 8/10 for general players, 9-10/10 for JRPG lovers.

(This review is coming from someone who hasn't finished the game[Literally gave up playing it])
A great game. Definitely recommended for RPG lovers + Grind lovers.
Visual-wise, its not bad, but it's not great either(When I see it in 2017). The landscape has pretty much nothing other than Uruks - your enemies, similar looking structures, similar looking plants with different colors, and... That's about it. Although you can find different things such as caves, creatures and etc in hidden locations. However, these things make a harmony and makes it easier for you to see where something is without much difficulty.
Sound-wise, it's awesome. The sound effects when you enter the Wraith-world - it really feels as if you're seeing the world with the eyes and ears of a ghost. The clashing of metals, the sounds of your enemies, voice acting, and various wraith-effects such as the one you hear when you run using the speed of a Wraith are all well-made.
Battle-wise, I always hear that it's very similar to the one you see in the Batman game series. Although there isn't much customization in the early stages of the game. For example, you get to do one of two things in the early game. Fight with your sword, or stealthily kill enemies. I tried both - and I died and died again with one or two hits when I went for the sword. You can't do anything but click your mouse - and watch out for the *Evade Signal* to click your other mouse button. You have to grind and grind to gain runes and powers - and this was just a bit too much for me as I went through similar missions and similar enemies with little variety.
Enemy-design was spectacular. Each and every single boss- AKA captains, warchiefs and etc had different skill sets that seemed very random at all times. This made every approach to these bosses different from each other. One, I had to kill using stealth, and another, I had to kill him using stealth... Again because I almost died when I tried using the sword. And again and again. But if you're skilled, this will not be a problem for you.
Mission-design wise, it was meh. Especially the side missions. They felt the same all the time. Kill the boss, kill all enemies, kill a boss, kill a boss, kill all enemies - with little variation. But some side missions were cool - you could invade a party, make enemies kill each other, and etc.
The reason why I quit this game is: When I compare it to some other games that I played, it was very.... Restrictive. For example, there's only ONE OR TWO SPECIFIC WAYS to kill a certain boss. There's no other way. For example, there's a boss and you want to kill him. You can either kill him using.... Your sword and archery with the maximum of FIVE arrows. There's no other way. That's it. You can try using your abilities of your sword! That could make a difference - but NO. You have to grind in order to unlock those skills. A bummer. So what you do in the early game is simple - click your mouse. That's it. No skills, no nothing. Less-restrictive games like Tomb raider allows you to gain multiple set of skills and weapons as you pace through the game - with less grinding. Skyrim, there's multiple ways to approach a boss - you can either summon your allies, hit it with magic, weaponry, and etc. In Mordor, there is no *DIFFERENT APPROACH* to bosses.
Although according to my friends, you gain sword abilities as you grind more and more -> giving you more various choices to fighting bosses.
In conclusion, its a great game - but its' just not my style as it restricts player choice when it comes to combat - especially in early game(And this early game continues for a LONG time).

I remember way back in 1994 when I was just a wee lad and me da had been cooking a nice stew for the family just before Saint Paddy's. As an Irish family, we often spent many a day toiling around the bars and brewrooms and whiskey was often the closest smell. I can remember the soft singing of me nan as she toiled away on her latest brew. I suppose it was around that time or near abouts that I became infatuated with a man name Desmond McKinney. See the thing about Des was he never knew when to stop. Whether it be jokes about your mum or your nan or even your bird he would never cease his constant buggery. We use to call him Beagán buachaill, which in Irish roughly translates to funny boy. Of course, Desmond wasn't always funny and when he did take it too far we had to scold him.
One of those rare auld times was back in the cold winter of 21 January 1995. As I recall it was one of the coldest most blustery winters I ere saw. The whiskey chambers fell silent and the soft dew which often filled the air around Upper Baggot Street fell faint. Replaced now with a biting cold like the teeth of a shark across a school blackboard. Annoying and persistent yet jagged and hurtful. As I recall it were early in the morn' when I walked upon Desmond out in a field in nothing but his knickers. Covered in snow the young lad had yet noticed me so I let out a loud holler.
"DESMOND!" I yelled,
I don't reckon he heard me, now that I'm looking back on it. Especially now considering the howling winds prevailing like starved wolves in the night. Yet he turned and looked. Not in a way that bespoke a heralded mate but instead the one given as if in deep anguish longing for assistance. I suppose to him it must have just sounded like murmurs falling through an avalanche of thick snow. Yet he called out, "Aye you wee nobby spacka' am in a sherp ned of sumthin' fierce!"
Desmond was a wiley fellow but I ner took him for the one to yell for help. So I had supposed he had gone on in his usual way, disregarding myself and those around him and instead, continuing on in his trivial pursuits. I, therefore, took a sharp turn and just waved goodbye to the lad as I made my rounds before the next blanket of snow came through, How I long now for a return to this day. If perhaps, I had only just been able to run to him, to yell out to him, maybe things could have gone differently. That's not what happened, however, and instead, I carried on down the road to the turn leading to Wellington. Then I thought I heard the sound of some distressed being muffled by a myriad of attackers.  I whipped around only for a second as the snow began to blind what was left of my vision and the sound disappeared with the wind.
I didn't see Desmond after that, I don't know what became of him but I remember the days we used to spend in the pubs along St. Mary's. I wondered that, in the wild circumstance of this infinite universe, one day he might appear, just as he had back in those lustful summers all those years ago. Maybe, like an apparition haunting the lost isles, reveal himself just like he was rarely changed from days past. I frequented these pubs until they, much like him gave way to the new Ireland, filled with many a concrete covered slab. The memory of him much faded along with the beauty of Dublin and the trades that gave me father and his father their wealth. Likewise, I was forced into a differing lifestyle than the one foreseen in my destiny foretold by my ancestors dating to the time of the celts. And as the years went by so did I, leaving the areas I once so cherished in search of better tidings amongst a more guilded society.
I found myself in the town of Birmingham in 2004. That year toil had long befallen me and yet somehow I felt that with each passing day a momentous occasion may yet still come to pass. I wished away each day like the last ever hoping for that whisper to materialize and sweep me away in its soft bosom as a loving doe would coddle her fawn. However, the days passed into weeks and the weeks to months and before I had realized it the year had long past me by. It was then on the anniversary of Des's disappearance on a day not unlike that one that a happenstance did occour.
I found meself alongside a young bird with a black velvet band tied tight round her neck. 'Fore I could steal a glance at her she took me in her arms and kissed me lightly upon the lips.
"
" she said as I fell back with wide eyes. "You mustn't fret for I have come with great tidings." My heart began to race and I could feel my pulse vibrating such a chorus I found myself wondering if she too could feel it.
"But... But why have you done that and what is it that you want with me, lassie?" I said softly and with great curiosity. My skull filled with a question and my mind buzzed with thought. "Unless yer' tryin' to start a family I suggest you open yer' gabber." Her white skin flickered in the light and her bright red hair scorched like the sun during a midsummer's day.
"Nye ay I spose yer' wonderin ere I hail and t'nature of me callin', but ye' must hold fast and follow me lead for there as nowt much time." She then took my hand and hustled us up the cobbled road toward the grand manor which sat steadfastly upon seemingly Birmingham's lone majestic hill. I felt there were many questions to ask yet I held back for I had supposed that if I were to break my code of shrouded silence she would end the escapade just as it had begun. Once we reached the gates of the manor, she took me in her arms tight against her breast and whispered warmly in my ear, "Martin McKonnely, you have longed for somethin' so extensive if ay' were t'walk yer' ambitions I'd find meself amongst t'brightly lit and ruckus surroundings the yanks call New York City. Can you find int' your dearest heart of hearts that one thing you hold with such ire?"
I spoke then to her only to be cut off by the sound of what I presumed to be the angels calling down to me much as they would have Jesus on Easter day. The lady of wistful mystery was singing a tune which found its home in my heart as well in the souls of my fellow countrymen. I listened closely as she hummed, whistled, and musingly recited that auld number.
"But a lonely prison wall,
I heard a young girl calling
Michael, they have taken you away,
For you stole Trevelyann's corn
So the young might see the morn,
Now a prison ship lies waiting in the bay"
Low did lie those fields of Athenry and the tune began to sing within me building wrathfully through every cockle of mine own being out into the world like an arrow from the bow of a hardened marksman. The song we carried within our hearts and about our airs began to set out into the world around us and though the Britons of this country knew naught the plight of the song they surrounded us one and all just the same. As we carried on in harmony the lady turned to me and said, "Martin, the one ye seek lies in and amongst t'banks o' t'Roses. With all due haste make yer' way t'Pimlicoe and find it."
It was in that moment when I sat back in anticipation of the reunion with my dearest long lost friend, I remembered that back in 1998 The Undertaker threw Mankind off Hell in A Cell, and plummeted 16 ft through an announcer's table.

First off, the game looks absolutely incredible. It is a huge leap from Dreamfall: The Longest Journey, some of the characters I had trouble recognizing. Visuals aside, the story finally continues the story of Dreamfall, and it is doing it well so far. It definately is on par with Telltale's The Walking Dead in terms of the storytelling department, as there is plenty of "feels." Controls are completely changed and makes interacting with objects and walking around a lot more easy, you can even play the game with just the mouse so that you may pick your nose while you play! The voice acting is supurb and believable, some of the dialogue is comedy gold. The music really sets the tone and plays a big part depending on the situation, really well done. The animations are vastly improved from the last Dreamfall, naturally. There's many choices to make to alter the outcome, they will all have concequences. I wished I supported the kickstarter back in 2013. If you even remotely liked The Longest Journey, or even Dreamfall: The Longest Journey, pick this up. It certainly was worth the wait, unlike Duke Nukem Forever.

Part 1 of Dreamfall Chapters is a great successor to the Longest Journey/Dreamfall legacy.
The voice acting is top-notch, the visuals impressive, and the music is lovely. There are so many things to click on, each with several different lines of dialogue, and there are plenty of people to talk to and loads of ambient conversations to eavesdrop on.
Although you will explore other places, the bulk of the game takes place in Europlis, a fully realized segment of a cyberpunk megalopolis. It is teeming with people and details: protests, weird fashion, confusing slang, neon signs, hovering ad-bots, vending machines, market stalls, and fascist police shaking people down. There is so much detail packed into this world, and I found it really enjoyable to wander around and soak it all in.
Traversing it can be confusing, though there are map kiosks that help to a degree... I wish there had been a map/compass that was easily accesible at all times, but I may just be directionally challenged.
The story itself feels a bit mundane at times, introducing characters and setting details by essentially showing us a day in Zoe's life... but the characterization is great, and the dialogue is interesting, clever and at times, quite funny. There is a lot of setup with little conclusion, but hey! This is only part 1.
It took me just short of 5 hours to reach the end of this "chapter" and I can't wait to see more. I loved both The Longest Journey and Dreamfall, and I'm so glad I backed this!

I've waited a very long time to be able to write this review, and I was not let down. If you're reading this review and you haven't played The Longest Journey and Dreamfall stop right now and buy them. There are both here on Steam as well as on GOG. If you have played those two already then I’m sure you’re curious if Chapters lives up to being the long awaited third game in The Longest Journey series for almost a decade. The answer is a resounding yes, heck yes. Chapters is already pretty great one episode in and I’m really glad I backed it.
Chapters is just as well written as its predecessors but one thing that really stands out is how freaking beautiful and immersive it is. After the first two parts that show what Zoe and Kian have been up to since the end of Dreamfall, Chapters puts you into Europolis, the huge megalopolis that’s Zoe moved to, and for an adventure game it’s a lot bigger than I expected. It’s also really dense without a lot to see and conversations to overhear. It’s really great and something that TLJ and Dreamfall didn’t achieve as well.
The gameplay takes a lot of inspiration from Walking Dead and it honestly suits it well. A key difference is that instead of timed dialogue segments that force you make decisions on the fly, Chapters is a lot more contemplative, you're not timed and the characters will actually think about the dialogue options to themselves when you mouse over them. The gameplay is also your standard adventure game point and click fare but the interface is now extremely streamlined and minimalist in all the right ways, especially compared to Dreamfall’s clunky♥♥♥♥♥interface.
It's still early to really tell if your choices really make some changes (Though as the game hints, your choices are going to affect the journey, not the destination) but there is a nice substantial deviation from one decision that you can make early on that can lead you to meet different characters unique to the path you choose. So if they keep that up it will be really neat.
The end of the first episode also has the best run animation for a video game character I've ever seen.
The only negative is that looking at other reviews it seems it's not only me and that the game isn't totally well optimized, the game can suffer slowdown in Europolis and there are graphical glitches. But that's something that can be fixed with a patch so its far from a dealbreaker.
Chapters is shaping up to be truly great and potentially the best game in the series. It has all the heart and wonder that the previous games had and then some. Backers have no need to fear and those who didn’t back it definitely need to check it out.

New patch rolled out and its definitely improved performance. Now this game really doesn't have any real flaws!

EDIT: Book Three out.
As soon as a new episode comes out or something gets fixed, I will update.
The bad:
-God-awful optimization. Constant fps drop in busy areas in both books, even on a high-end gaming PC. Multiple people have these issues, which I repeatedly checked on. In the two biggest areas in both episodes, the frame rate can drop to around 15fps. Unacceptable, especially since those are the areas you are stuck in for the longest time. Some people however can run and play the game fine, even on lower hardware, so it's a really weird issue, but it's still unacceptable to have these frame-rate issues on stronger machines.
-What used to be occasional bugs has gone berserk with the release of episode two. A big chunk of bugs, starting from even the menu that sometimes spades out and will just do what it wants. There is a surprising lack of bug-testing and polish.
-Very noticeable difference in quality and polish between models. Some textures look really good, some look pretty damn dreadful. Some character models are really good, some just fail to impress in comparison.
-Animation, although sometimes relatively solid, at other times just seems very weird and especially walk cycles of some characters as well as how they rotate and/or talk seems very out of place.
-Barely any explanation of the games that came before. Newer players will most likely feel lost.
The good:
-The game looks really nice. The art style is really good, it has a really nice range of colors, and some areas like the main city you explore in the first episode are insanely detailed and look alive and believable.
-Really interesting characters, both from older games in the series as well as new ones. Mostly good voice actors, although some sound a bit amateurish compared to others.
-Relatively lengthy episodes, which can easily take around 3 to 4 hours per episode to finish.
-The story continues right off of the last game and brings a slow but interesting new start to the series.
-Good choices that actually change whole parts of the books (episodes) themselves and do offer an incentive to replay the game again.
Dreamfall Chapters is almost a game that should be recommended to every fan of modern adventure games. It is very slow paced, and it completely consists of walking around and talking with people, with little variation and very simple puzzles in between. Taking all of that into consideration however, it does manage to (so far) tell a really interesting tale with fun and colorful characters, and has a beautiful art style as well as decent length and structure to it. The only thing holding it back are the poor optimization and the bugs found every now and then (More so since book two). Even though players new to the series should have no big problems getting into the game, they might be left a bit confused at the start, and it does seem to target older fans more than anything. Everyone who loved the last Dreamfall game should also be in for a treat with this one, anyone else who is new to the series should still risk a look if they are primarily interested in good story telling and a slow atmosphere-focused game with little action, but a lot of wonder to breathe in. The lack of polish is the only thing keeping this game away from being as good as its predecessors.
EDIT: Game still has huge performance issues and some bugs, but apparently the transition to the updated engine has helped for some people. Stay tuned for how it turns out once that engine update is out of beta and/or we get episode 4.

Short Review: Stunning setting (visually and thematically), great voice acting, story is top notch, but gameplay is a little lacking. If you're someone that plays games principally for story and setting, then this is for you. If not, and it breaks my heart to say this, then I would avoid this as it is narrative heavy. If you've played previous Dreamfall/TLJ games then this is definitely a worthy successor. If you haven't, then this review might not be helpful for you but give it a shot anyway.
Long Review: This is a difficult game to review. The first in the series, The Longest Journey, was released around fifteen years ago. The second, Dreamfall, was released eight years ago, and was riddled with cliffhangers that are only now being resolved. I honestly couldn't tell you whether someone who hasn't played the earlier ones would enjoy this, so I won't bother. This is a review for the original fans of the game.
The game is visually stunning. It's not next-gen graphics or what have you, but it's modern and the love and care the team at Red Thread Games put into making Europolis feel like a 23rd century proto-dystopian city which still manages to look fantastic and somehow make me wistfully want to live in such a place. The darkened, rain filled, sky with neon all over the place and an odd mix of 19th century, 21st century, and 23rd century architecture is fantastic, with neat little details. You'll walk past a big modern skyscraper and see parts at the base which are crumbling and showing brick walls or the original iron supports.
The voice acting and story is great. The voice acting is phenomenal, and in all characters you can feel the genuine emotion and thoughts running through their dialogue. Better than most AAA games. The dialogue system they've set up should be the gold standard in games, where you can mouse over each of the answers and hear the protagonists thoughts on why that would be their answer. We only see a small snippet of the story in the first episode (called a 'book'), but already you can see how the threads are beginning to weave together into a coherent whole. And when I say a small snippet, I don't mean that it's short. My playthrough lasted four hours (it flew by so fast, I could've sworn I wasn't playing more than an hour), so in total this is looking to be a 20 hour game of pure content, and not achievement hunting, or pointless side missions, or collectibles. It's certainly got me itching for more. There appears to be genuine choice and consequences as well, though again - it's still too early to tell before the other books are released. That said, this is where one of my main concerns lies. The game has the option to track your decisions, and the majority of decisions I made, so too did 80%+ of other players. Hopefully they address this in future so there's more genuine choice, instead of obvious ones.
The gameplay, sadly, is a bit lacking as well. Which is understandable, this is essentially one of the old 1990s adventure games, transplanted and moderately reworked to fit a 3d setting and is a bit lost as a result, but there haven't been any sections that have been unenjoyable as a result, and it hasn't detracted from the games main strengths. Fortunately, they haven't included combat (thus far) as they were forced to do for Dreamfall, but so far there have been none of the 'impossible puzzles' that were common in so many such games if only because there have been few puzzles full stop.
I was in my early 20s when Dreamfall first came out, and it's probably the game that's moved me (emotionally? spiritually?) more than any other game. I say this with considerable relief, Dreamfall Chapters evokes the same kinds of feelings now that I had when first playing Dreamfall back in '06. If you're a fan of the series, or of top-of-the-line storytelling, this is a must-buy.
