So first off i dunno what people are expecting with this game.
This is an IPAD game that they released on pc. So go into it thinking that it's an ipad game.
So yea it's missing some key things for a pc title, namely resolution settings and a borderless full screen mode.  It also currently doesn't have multiplayer, it's biggest flaw i feel and one i hope they patch asap.
So gameplay:
You control a fleet and click on planets completeing neutral missions to try and convince the planet to join your empire, the harder the mission the more influence you get.  2 influence and they start trading with you, 4 influence and they join your empire.   The reason you want these planets is they produce 4 resources and you can upgrade these planets, build wondes, and increase their population as you see fit to get more resources to buy more things.   In addition you can completely customize your fleet.  Do you want 10 capital ships or 4 super beefy ones, long range guns or short, speed or stealth.  All can be customized indivdually.  And it's really nice.
Like civ there are other players doing the same thing, and you can be peaceful with them or you can fight them. The neutral planets are actually kinda cool in this aspect because you might have went did a quest and got 2 influence but the other players are going to get another quest to go there and might take it from you or knock down your influence.
Again like civ you all repeat this process with better and better things until a victory condition is met either by population, galactic domination, or science.  First person to one of those wins.
All in all it's fast paced you only get 1 fleet so at most you can only do a couple things on your turn and planets can change hands quite quickly if you don't build up defenses.  The ai isn't amazing but it does ok i haven't tried the harder difficulties yet so perhaps they get a lot better there.
This game would be amazing if it had multiplayer.  This game is made for pass and play on an ipad or online multiplayer for pc.  Why they didn't include this in the game is anyones guess.  If a firaxis person is reading this please please give us multiplayer!
If you're looking for a quick paced game that you can pick up and put down after 10-30 min and a full campaign takes about 3 hours then this game is a lot of fun.  Could it be better? I am a fan of Sid Meier and FTL: Faster Than Light.
I thought this game is a mixture of Beyond Earth and FTL and preordered it with this dream (actually I dreamt it would be a mixture of FTL and Master of Orion but I'm sure most of you don't know/remember the best 2 MoO games).
Actually, well it is. But it's a lesson called "How you can ruin the mixture of these games".
Honestly BE has many flaws but it's a fun game overall. The fun facts are; 3 tendencies have a meaning, the story is cool,  science means a lot, logistics mean a lot, and it's a challenging game.
FTL on the other hand is a small budget, short game with bad graphics. The adventure concept and clever micro control (over crew, weapons and economy) are what make it shine.
Now first off take FTL - substract choices. Substract micro control. Substract clever battles. Substract any interesting encounters you may follow. Add stupid, meaningless battles. You move from system to system as in FTL but all you do is to click yes and blow stuff up. Add huge amount of resources that breaks ship development.
Secondly take BE. Substract any meaning of factions (bonus wise and storywise). Substract meaning of leaders. Substract challenge. Substract story. Substract science (there is science in this game but it's the same thing with ship development, nothing new comes out of science except "your shields work 25% better). Substract logistics - cities are only additional source of income, they don't mean anything at all.
Imagine a Sid Meier game that anything, including tech, wonders and  buildings are done instantly with a single click - no planning is needed.
Even worse, imagine a Sid Meier game that looks ugly. A Sid Meier game that wonders (or anything) you build has no visual, at all.
But worst of all, imagine a Sid Meier game that shows no sign of intelligence (pun intended).
I am sorry to say this but I have played better 1$ iOS games... There is absolutely nothing attractive about this game except the fact that you can literally rip your opponents apart in 3 hours in Normal mode (Not that it's a hard game but undetectable torpedos wonder break the game too bad).
So, if you MUST try this out, wait until it gets 90% discount. It's not worth more.
I kept the worst thing to the last: There are no aliens in this game.

ENGLISH
"Sid Meier's Starships" is like these three parents become a baby: "Civilization - Beyond Earth", "Star Wars - Empire at War" and "Strange Adventures in Infinite Space" (which had a sequel: "Weird Worlds")!
Civ-BE contributes a background story and the Optics.
SW-EaW adds the idea, that everything takes place in an entire galaxy. You just see the planets, but you can only see the appropriate suns are only visible in the ultra-cool space combat mode.
And SAiIS delivers the general feeling! You are put into the role of a Fleet Commander, assigned to a spacefaring civilization. Your civilization is always called "United Federation". It's purpose is to spread its light over all other planets in the galaxy. Unlike SAiS you have up to six opponents, who try to do the same things like you.
In "Starships" you always control exactly one fleet, consisting of a handfull of ships. You're heading from one quest to the next with these ships, until - after a while - it hopefully turns out, that you've been better than your opponents.
I can raise my thumb for "Starships", for I like the immersion (that means: "atmosphere") of the game and because - being a 35-year old Gamer - I worship Sid Meier as a God! The game is cheaper than Sid Meier's unforgotten milestones, so don't expect a pretentious masterpiece, that makes history.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DEUTSCH
"Sid Meier's Starships" ist so, als ob diese drei Eltern ein Baby bekommen hätten: "Civilization - Beyond Earth", "Star Wars - Empire at War" und "Strange Adventures in Infinite Space" (dem späteren "Weird Worlds")!
Civ-BE liefert die Hintergrund-Story und die Optik.
SW-EaW liefert die Idee, dass alles in einer kompletten Galaxie geschieht. Man sieht die Planeten, aber die dazugehörigen Sonnen sieht man bestenfalls im überaus coolen Raumkampfmodus.
Und SAiIS liefert das Spielgefühl! Du schlüpfst in die Rolle des Flottenbefehlshabers einer raumfahrenden Zivilisation, die beschlossen hat, ihr Licht auf allen anderen Planeten zu verbreiten. Du erkennst Deine Fraktion immer an dem unveränderlichen Namen "Vereinte Föderation", aber im Unterschied zu SAiS hast Du bis zu sechs Gegenspieler, die das Gleiche wollen, wie Du!
In "Starships" kontrollierst Du immer genau eine Flotte, bestehend aus einer Handvoll Raumschiffen. Mit denen kämpfst Du Dich von Quest zu Quest, bis sich irgendwann hoffentlich herausstellt, dass Du besser warst, als Deine Kontrahenten.
Da ich Wert lege auf Immersion (sprich: Atmosphäre) und als 35-jähriger Gamer den guten alten Sid Meier als Gott verehre, kann ich meinen Daumen nur heben! Das Spiel kostet weniger als Sid Meier's unvergessliche Meilensteine, also erwarte kein pompöses Meisterwerk, das in die Geschichte eingehen wird.

First impression after getting 3 chapters perfect (there are 8 in all), while it's still on sale on the IndieGala Friday bundle: I like this game.
It's a stealth game, but it's different: you don't get a knife, you don't get to kill anyone (but you
get shot), there are some surveillance cameras (but you can't disable them), the guards will not stop looking for you just because they lost sight of you for a minute (but you can see where they think you are), there is no easy way to sneak in to the loot and then out again (but you
distract the guards), the levels are fairly easy to beat (but some of them are hard to beat perfectly).
You also get a film noir vibe (except it's black and white
red), complete with gumshoe investigator, long-legged femme fatale, and jazzy music - the perfect athmosphere to bash your heads against some of the challenges, because of course I want to do those levels perfectly (but I'm not ashamed to sneak onward when I'm out of ideas for the moment). Those challenges, well, looking at the global stats it is suprising that more people got the first 3 chapters perfect than got chapter 4 at all -- it seems after level 3 mostly those players stick with the game who are able to put off perfection until later. The game can sometimes be frustrating because on some levels, perfection means trial and error, learning to translate the red indicators on the map into paths the AI is going to send these guards, and finally understanding and getting it right. You also need to learn how to use the distraction devices properly. But like I said, if you allow yourself to put off perfection until later, and get on with the story when frustration looms, it won't spoil your enjoyment of this game. A good game needs to be diffcult, or beating it won't mean anything.
Mobile port -- of course it is one; you drag with mouse a lot, and sometimes  I miss not being able to WASD my way around, but by and large, this works well: the dragging is the right interface mechanic for the semi-animated graphic novel cutscenes (static screenshots don't really do justice to those), and dragging your path lets you take the shortest path around corners without having to develop prime keyboard twitch skills, and it also is the natural way to operate the decoy you get in chapter 4. There are keyboard shortcuts for the devices, which means your mouse does paths, your keyboard hand activates devices, and your brain outwits the guards -- if I failed a level, the latter was usually at fault.
Outwitting the guards is indeed mandatory: while it is perfectly ok on your first runthrough to reach the exit with all of the guards in tow behind you, perfection often requires reaching the exit unseen or unhurt, which means losing the guards around a few quick corners, and then staying lost: especially important as the fat out-of-breath rent-a-cops get reinforced by better-trained collegues who are able to outpace you -- maybe your alter ego should've cut down on the whiskey and cigarettes (not shown in the game) and gotten some exercise.
If you've always wanted a stealth game where the guards keep looking, look no further: you should be eyeing (and playing) Third Eye Crime.

Pixel Boy and the Ever Expanding Dungeon has the potential to be a very solid game. Despite the simple voxelized graphics, the devs clearly put in effort to make the game ascetically pleasing. Their choice in color scheme was clearly well thought out, and enemy design is attractive. From an auditory standpoint, the game is honestly lacking. The music isn't awful, but it's not anything special either. The narrator is really annoying from an adult point of view - however, I'm pretty sure a kid would be highly amused by both the narration and the narrator.
The powerup system is honestly pretty cool, as you get both semi-permanent and one time use powerups that you may equip. These are dropped by both enemies and treasure chests, as well as available to craft in town. You also gain experience and level up as you go, which does offer significant performance boosts.
The gameplay itself is where the game is lacking. Although bug-free and smooth, the gameplay is simply boring. There is little challenge, and there aren't enough styles of gameplay for my tastes. Yet, a gaming newcomer or child would probably find this game pretty enjoyable.
If you're looking for a well-made cheap game with roguelike, dungeon-grinding elements this game is for you. I'd say it's worth the $0.99, and really does offer value for how much you're paying.

Pixel Boy is a top down dungeon crawler which brings a wide variety of enemies and tries to emulate a ‘bullet hell’ experience. Some what of low polygon graphics, interactive gameplay, beautiful music and the price of one dollar – sounds like a sick mix to get busy for a few evenings.
I’ve spent quite some time playing this game. I enjoyed it for a bit but then I was triggered. I can’t believe that it’s not in an early access since there are a few bugs and glitches that I’ve encountered. I’ll start with a few things that I liked and I think are awesome.
First of all, the best part of the game, in my opinion, is the variety of enemies. There are a lot of them and all of them are different. It feels great when your dungeon has melee and ranged enemies at the same time. Moreover, killing lots of them in a limited space is challenging. Also every time you start a new round mobs are randomly generated via MobMaker 9000 which is great also because if you want to replay a level, the game or whatever it’s not going to be the same experience.
As for the powerUPs in this game, they are cool too! There are a lot of them and you can combine all of them in one mix and enjoy your play through :J. However, what I didn’t like that they are limited. It makes no sense, frankly, it only creates frustration. There’s no way someone is going to go for the fire rate max build. Also there are a lot of crates and objects on each level which can be destroyed. So, devs, do you expect us to use our really expensive powerUPs to do so?? For me that makes no sense. Thus, after act 2 I stopped buying anything and finished the game without them. Honestly, I came here for the ‘bullet hell’ kind of experience and I didn’t get it. But still you got a credit for creative powerUPs.
Now I’d like to address some issues that I didn’t like and they actually triggered me.
The shooting mechanics. OMG, my bullets didn’t go through powerUPs, coins WTF? Excuse me, but this is INSANE. You can be really good at shooting and etc but if your enemy dies all the coins/drops from it they start to follow you that’s why you can’t kill the next enemy because it’s hiding behind the coins. Moreover, if you encounter a large pack of mobs and you start shooting in every direction the closest mobs die and they create some kind of cover for the next enemies. This is a joke seriously! You can be in your tier 5 GREEN RANGE armor and still get hit because of that.
Sometimes mobs behave weird. They jump out of the rooms, some of them freeze, and some of them don’t attack.
Okay, let’s also talk about the doorways… Why aren’t they transparent? I lost a lot of armor because I couldn’t tell if someone’s hiding there. You just can’t tell. That’s bad.
All of the points above are controversial and you can ask me what did you expect from a one USD$ game? I agree with you but here’s the real reason why I give this game a negative review.
I would still recommend this game if it was an early release, but it’s a ‘finished’ game! So, it’s not even about the price it’s about the quality. And don’t even talk about the price. It is not an excuse. It’s like comparing allegro coffee to a double double from TimHortons! Double double is also tasty.

So I've played the game for a bit so far (all but one achievement which isn't available yet) and I have to say that it's a pretty good game. There is decent depth with a variation in towers and enemies together with a skilltree which lets you choose three different routes. In the beginning you will stick with mostly one route but later on you will combine two (Atleast I recommend you do).
The game is quite balanced, some things are still being tweaked but overal it's in good shape. There are some things that could be better such as me not personally liking the coop, therefore I would rather have an option to not do this. But even with that negative it's a good game, obviously there are still bugs present BUT the big difference with this game compared to other games is that the developers are extremely active! When you report a bug they will reply within a day (my experience so far) and fix it in the next patch. The patches come often with about one each week and you can really notice that they take into consideration the points that the community makes.
Just the developers themselves make the game worth it, it's a solid game in itself but they make it even better. I have high hopes that they will continue improving the game as they've done so far. I do hope though that they add a larger variaty of units or upgrade possibilities (more and higher than currently, but they're still in early access so it's to be expected). It's worth the money espcially taking in consideration that it will get improved upon, if the second chapter of the game will be included in this price is still the question (I recommend they do so as that will make the game a worthy competitor for TD games like Kingdom Rush)

In Orcs must die they take the annoyance out of placing turrets by making them refundable and also allowing for breaks after every few waves. Even more engaging and interesting is the emphasis on personal interaction while waves are coming. It combines first person shooter elements with RPG style combat and truly makes this a fantastic game.
Tonnes of fun to mess around with. It's a nice little mix of tower defense, hack and slash and rpg elements.

Orcs Must Die! 2 is a great game where your are playing it solo or multiplayer.  It is a third-person viewpoint and now, unlike the last game you have your choice of two characters.  You can choose from the main chacter from the last game who is a warrior type or the main villian from the last game who is more of a magic character now together on the same side for a greater purpose.  The graphics are a similar style as the last, cartooney looking but easy on the eyes.  The sound is one of the things that sets this game much higher than others.  The actors who did all of the voices in the game did an amazing job!  There is plenty of humor in the game too as the two characters will often banter with eachother and the orcs and creatures they are fighting.  The music is well suited, even though it is a bit repetitive suits well to the battle style.  The controls are very solid and seem to respond very well whether using a mouse and keyboard setup or a xbox style gamepad.  In addition to fighting off the orcs, you also place towers and sentry guards throughout the map in strategic locations in order to deter the incoming hordes of enemies.  Some traps are trigged automatically when an enemy gets too close to your trap, other are trigged when you shoot them with many enemies around (such as an exploding barrel).  The game really shines when you can play with a friend and take out the hordes together.  This is one of my top games of all time, just on the tremendous amout of fun everyone and I have had playing it together.  I would highly recommend it if you like a bit of humor in your games, enjoy third-person action, tower defense or want something to play with a close friend and have a great time.

tl;tr: It's not Civilization in space! It is a small and fast game, perfect to play after work for an hour or two and have fun. Not very deep but funny! Don't expect too much, if you want to play deep and long games go to Civilization. If you want to relax after work for an hour or two this game could be for you.
What is Sid Meier's Starships? You have an intergalactic empire and the goal is nothing less than to rule the galaxy. You can build some basic industry on planets which produce resources like food, metal and so on. With those resources you build your fleet and travel to other planets where you can do missions to gather influence. If you have enough influence the sytem joins your empire. Very simple.
There are several mission types like "kill all enemies", "protect a convoy" or "escape from a asteroid field". You can customize your ships, which means you can add long range lasers, short range plasma weapons, torpedos, shields, hull, fighters etc. The fights are the fun part, with the different weapon types one can develop different tactics which makes really fun. The torpedos e.g. are good for a crowd of slow ships. Once fired they can't change direction but you decide when they explode. If the timing is perfect one explosion hits several ships and can even destroy them. Asteroids give you cover and the back of your ships are the most sensitiv part. I managed to destroy a big ship with two or three hits from my fighters in the back of the enemy.
The research is very basic, 9 (if I'm not wrong) different techs which can be upgraded some levels. The results are weapons with more damage, faster engines and so on. No new weapons or other ships.
You can build wonders, like in Civilization or Beyond Earth, but they do not cust so much. As far as I could see those wonders are powerful, one e.g. gives you clocked torpedos so the enemies don't see them anymore, which makes them even more powerful.
Sooner or later you meet the AI players, they want to rule the galaxy too. The diplomacy is very basic (not that its counterparts in Civilization or Beyond Earth are better in my opinion, but...) and is like "hey, how are you, what have you done in the past, lets compare our genitals (fleet strengths, plantes, etc), do you want peace or war?". Sooner or later one AI will declare war on you and you must try to conquer their planets. Or go straight to their home world and end their suffering.
The integration with Beyond Earth was promoted as a special feature. You need an extra 2K account for this (not sure if this hasn't been possible with Steam, but anyway). Then you are able to "continue" a save game from Beyond Earth in Starships. Not sure what this means in detail. I managed to unlock some kind of bonus in Beyond Earth, but haven't played this again. I'm sure they extend this feature over time and it might add some replay bonus to both games. We'll see.
As I said at the top, don't expect too much. It costs only 15 bucks, I got it for 11 on GMG which is ok for the game. If you are unsure wait for a sale.

Note: Summary at the bottom of the review.
First of all, you should know that Sid Meier's Starships is a game more reminiscent of the Ace Patrol series than the Civ series. Do not expect deep or complex gameplay here. What you CAN expect is a turn-based strategy game that delivers a "pick-up-and-play" experience, tied into the "Beyond Earth" story.
The game is simple to get into, easy to learn and master, and perhaps not that challenging. This does however not stop it from being fun, but sadly there are some sides to the game that is, well, not shoddy. But perhaps not entirely well-thought out. There is little difference between the plasma cannons and the lasers (the two main types of weapons) in terms of visuals and mechanics, and you have no control over what your ships use. Close up? Plasma. Long range? Lasers. More depth would have been welcome. The maps do offer some nice mechanics (asteroids that block shots, "corridors" that open and close, wormholes that will teleport you and so on), but I still think they could have included gas clouds to hide in, rather than the (somewhat pointless) stealth system.
One area where I've always felt that the Firaxis games has excelled, is in the "feel" of different factions. I may have missed something here, but it seems that your opponents are generic in the extreme in "Starships". You can fight them, or not fight them, but you probably won't care much about them whichever way you decide to go. And they won't really care about you and what you do, unless you fight someone they don't like (they'll give you something or other as an incentive) or you pass through one of their starsystems (which results in an immediate declaration of war).
Pro:
-"Pick-up-and-play" turn-based strategy.
-Simple and fun in its own way.
-Some pretty good ideas.
Con:
-Not very polished.
-No real depth.
-Abrupt ending.
-Oversimplified game mechanics.
-Not really great graphics.
-Ship explosions are extremely lackluster.
Summary:
Sid Meier's Starships is a turn-based strategy that offers quick "pick-up-and-play", wrapped in a plain package and with mechanics that falls short of what they could have been. This is not deep strategy, but rather "Ace Patrol in space". Keep that in mind, and be ready to forgive the game its simplified graphics and gameplay, and you will likely find a fun little game underneath it all. You may want to wait for a sale before picking it up though, as it seems to me that it is a bit overpriced relative to what you get.
5/10 -Recommended, if on sale.

First off, a lot of the negative reviews focus on the scope of the game and comparing it to other "bigger" Sid games.
You have to understand - this isn't that.
So, if this isn't Civ - in any shape, what is it?
Honestly, its a board game.
That's the thing that stuck me. This plays like a board game you'd pull out with friends over beer and pizza. It is quick, fun, and has just a touch of strategy to make it interesting.
So is it worth the $15? I think so. When you compare it to the price of other board game on the market. $15 is fair.
A quick breakdown of my pros and cons (granted I have only 1/2 dozen hours playing).
PROS:
- Tactical combat is simple but a LOT of fun
- Research and ship upgrades are also simple, but the right touch if you view this as a board game
- Fast pace
- Not bogged down in complex mechanics
- You only get one fleet (annoying at first, but made for some interesting challenges)
CONS:
- Is not apparent what benefit some of the research or upgrades have (so why should I invest in X)
- Influence system is INTESRESTING but feels like an alpha version of the concept, more work could be done to refine it
- Wonders are simple BUT could be used more in a strategic way (maybe make them more scare)
- Terrain and facing in combat adds a nice touch but also feels like an alpha (or maybe a beta) version
Overall,
Despite that this feels like a beta release - this is a small, fast game that is a ton of fun IF YOU VIEW IT AS A BOARD GAME. If Firaxis continues to work on balance and strategic elements, this could be a great game.

Stranded Deep is a early access survival game that have been on the market a couple of years now. The first period I used to play this game, I really enjoyed it and found it very interesting and exciting. The reason is because the game gives you the opportunity to let you go wherever you want to go, as long as you are surviving the days. The game is filled with a lot of islands that you can travel to in your raft, explore, look for food, animals, and other resources that is life essential for survival. Another thing I like about this game nowadays, is that the developers have added some new animals, crafting opportunities, and tools. The landscape forms have also changed a bit (stone hedges, cliffs, new plant types ect.) I have always loved diving in the ocean after ship wrecks and loot boxes, and hunting down sharks. The only negatives I find with this game, is that they have changed the graphics and environments too much. I appreciated the earlier alpha version in the older days much more, because the mechanics were much more easier. I must say that the FPS has improved a bit though.

“We don't want to work on Stranded Deep forever. If all goes well, we're hoping to have it completed by the end of 2015."
Coming back after a year since I played, I'm a little disappointed to see it is still EA, as this game has a huge potential.
There is a lot to improve, and the devs are certainly taking their time, or simply have given up on the game.
What the game could improve on:
- Bigger, more interesting islands. For instance it would be cool with a beach cove or small caves (with clay deposits). Volcano islands or underwater volcanoes.
- More wildlife. Could be simple thing as poisonous spiders, scorpions, chameleons, mosquito swarms - or bigger ones like iguanas. Including underwater life like whale sharks, groups of dolphins spotted in the distance etc.
- Less coconuts - More varied sources of food. Bananas. Berries (including poisonous ones), papayas, other exotic fruits etc. In its current state it is too easy going from island to island and replenish on food and water from coconuts.
- Different sound effects. Example: Hacking trees or paddling in the life raft should have 3 or 4 sound effects each. Yeah, it does actually make a difference when you do it a whole day.
- Cutting out the cheesy voice lines saying "Eww, gross" when skinning a crab and trying to survive. Add more random dialogue that could occur from time to time, like how he's hoping he will be rescued soon, how he's curious about the new island he's arriving on, how he hopes there are no sharks around when he goes for that shipwreck etc.
- Random drops; Traces of previous ancestors, history relics, ancient ruins, message in a bottle etc. Maybe some personal belongings from the people on the plane.
- Less frequent shark encounters. So that you actually have the guts to take a swim but will get more freaked out when you meet a shark. Not having them swimming around your island constantly.
- More objectives/ quests: Would be awesome finding a treasure map / key belonging to another island (in the same island group) that you have to seek out. Maybe a bigger island, having to fight a panther boss or something.
They have indeed made a few new improvements, like adding storms with huge waves. But all in all the process is too slow. I'm sure if they pick up the pace and make some new features and more varied content, this will be a 50+ hour game (add multiplayer on top and it's 150+), rather than its current state where you get more or less bored after 10 hours.
Don't get me wrong, it's not a bad game, and with gorgeous graphics. I'm just disappointed seeing the progress with just a couple new features since I last played, over a year ago. For me personally, there was no replay value, which I usually have with most games. If it was a FULL release when buying, it would be something different. But I bought it in EA, thinking a lot more content would come.
I'm not at all expecting them to make all the ideas above, but it's just some suggestions to make the game less repetitive. I hope they continue in the right direction and will be more than happy to change this review later on. Like mentioned this game has potential, and could possibly be among the best games in 2018 if done right!

Third Eye Crime - Raymond KT
It might not fully live up to its promise, but Third Eye Crime is good enough that you'll find something to enjoy. Stubborn adherence to the modes of the past only goes so far. Third Eye Crime would be a better game for recognizing this. If you are willing to deal with some problematic controls in the more complicated levels, Third Eye Crime offers up a slick collection of levels for a modest price.

Some people come at this game expecting Metal Gear Solid.  It may feel like a let down if you're expecting MGS.  Instead, expect a puzzle game, and you'll find it to be a mind-bending, challenging, rewarding experience.  As you progress, additional game mechanics are introduced, and as you play you'll find additional ways of working around each mechanic.
You get a "rumbler" (noise maker) to place.  Do you put it down and run across the map so that the enemies are drawn to it?  Doing so will allow you to break the laser, and even though the alarms will trigger, nobody will be around to catch you.  Or perhaps you'll place the rumbler so that it goes off after you've triggered the laser, so the enemies will think you ran somewhere else after triggering the laser.  Or maybe you want to run past all the guards, through the laser and around the corner, where you'll drop rumbler.  Then you'll proceed to the exit, and as you turn the corner, the rumbler goes off so everyone figures they missed you and they turn around.  Unseen, you walk to the exit.
Let's be honest.  Every good puzzle game has those levels that make your brain melt and you're super glad to be done with them.  You can expect a bunch of those as you make your way through this game, sneaking, picking-locks, wearing disguises, and distracting the guards with all manner of tactics.

A fun idea, and I love the cutscenes, but it tears like nobody's business.  The storytelling could also be a little bit more integrated with the game - it feels like an iPhone game, which I think may be how it started.

The only thing I don't like about this game is that it is more of a puzzle than stealth. I wish that it is more stealth-focus, because graphics, awesome soundtrack and noir atmosphere blend perfect, like an old movie, where you would expect to see a guy who operates from shadows instead using trick-skills to make guards chase you everywhere.

Third Eye Crime is a game developed by Moonshot Games. In this game you will be taking on the role of Rothko a thief with a special advantage. He has the third eye, he can see where people are looking and he can also see the most likely places that people are going to look for him as he tries to stealthfully make it through 120 levels.
This game definitely has that Noire vibe, all though there's a bit more color that the normal Noire theme, you can definitely feel the sexy number who is all kinds of dangerous, but you feel the need to help her, and of course you quickly find yourself in a heap of trouble. The level designs vary to a degree that you are going to have to constantly be thinking of new ways to distract, mislead, and get away from the obstacles in the level.There's also something about the slide comics between levels that speak to me. It just further pullls you into the world, the environment, the pulse of the game.
The music, I know this is not going to be a big surprise, but it is the type of music you would have heard in one of those old detective movies, where you see the PI's door, and a tendril of smoke curling from the PI's desk.
The controls definitely show off the fact that this game can land on several different platforms. It is all about path planning. You will click on your character, Rothko, and then draw the line of movement that you will be taking to try to get through the level. There are also power-ups, or helpful distractions (that's what I like to call them) that you can place or use throughout a specific level to help you achieve your goal of finding the door.
What I will say about this game is that it doesn't completely swallow you in story, but it definitely has enough that you know what is going on, and what the twists and turns are in the game. The interesting thing about this game is that the difficulty of the levels, I believe, depends on the type of gamer that is trying to conquer the level. In my experience with the game there was definitely not a constant building difficulty to the game. There were some levels that I breezed through, but the very next one stumped me to no end. I do have to say that I enjoyed the fact that you could skip a level after failing a couple of times, but I will warn you, there is a very good chance that you are going to have to come back and beat that level anyways. You see there's a certain amount of levels in each chapter, and the only way to advance is to complete enough of the levels in that chapter.
To me probably the most difficult twist that they throw into the game, and don't worry its not going to give anything away, is the fact that you are going to get to a part of the game where you are going to have to help more than just Rothko to escape the level. That is where it really gets tricky for me. I apparently was always able to get one or the other out of the level, but never both. Oh speaking of ramping difficulty you will see a progression in the enemies that you are trying to avoid you will start with slow moving guards, but don't be surprised if and when the enemies that you are facing off against can gun you down, which of course makes the chances of outrunning the enemy damn near impossible.
There is one more thing that was added to this game that will of course have the perfectionists going wild. In each level there is a set of three badges. It of course is possible to complete the level without achieving any of the badges, but there are those out there, I know, who will want to get the perfect completion of the level. Some of the badges range from getting through the level in a specific amount of time, never being seen by an enemy, using one continuous path through a level, not taking a bullet, and so much more. Now I will be the first to admit that I have probably completed about 20ish% of the levels to perfection, so I don't know if there's anything special other than feeling accomplished, but you never know.
Alright so lets get down to the nitty gritty. This is a puzzle game that will have you tested in your skills of stealth. I will admit it is not for everyone, but if this seems even slightly in your wheelhouse you need to at least check it out, hell just go ahead and get the game, it is that good, and that challenging that when you come out the other end you will feel like a rockstar. So with that I have to give the game a 9.0 out of 10.

When I first discovered that game, I had no intention of buying it. Luckily, there was a sale a few days later so I gave it a try.
And oh boy, I was not disappointed.
The first few hours were nothing but trial and error, however, after a few deaths I managed to survive until my coronation. From then on, it was nothing but exploration.
And this is exactly what makes this a strong game. It allows you to train various skills which may unlock new paths. The pace at which you learn these skills is influenced by the mood of our heroine, said mood can be achieved by your actions and your weekend activities.
Moreover, you can change Elodie's clothes and this is NOT only for fanservice, as those costumes yield benefits for your chosen skills.
Combine this with the freedom of choice (in some cases you need specific skills to actually HAVE a choice) and a world full of plot twists, intrigues, alliances, sea monsters, civil wars, poisoned chocolates and several pink, fluffy, chubby deaths await you.
PROS
+ Lots of choices
+ Dozens of more or less usefull skills for your crown princess
+ Mood system allows for specific "archetypes"
+ Different ways to beat the game, thus different endings
+ Some kind of morale system, allowing you to either be a merciful queen or a tyrannical overlord
+ Quite cute, if you like the manga style
+ Release the kraken
CONS
- Heavily based on trial and error, especially at the beginning
- Some achievements are really hard to get (although saving on a regular basis and taking notes will help)
- Relatively short (I managed to get all endings and achievements after ~ 20 h)
Still, I defenitely recommend this game due to its many paths and secrets, the artwork and the fun I had watching my princess getting killed over and over again.

TLDR: A neat little game with some cool ideas, but mobile-game production values and a lack of long-term depth don't justify the $15 asking price. Worth picking up on sale or if you're desperate for some bite-sized light strategy, though.
Store page description aside, Sid Meier's Starships is a turn-based strategy game wherein you try to conquer the galaxy. There are multiple ways to do this, but they all essentially boil down to building an unstoppable battle fleet and destroying your enemies.
The game is divided into two layers. On the greater strategic layer, you see the galaxy itself, taking your fleet from planet to planet and performing missions to convince the inhabitants to join your empire. The tactical layer puts you on a hex-based battlescape and maneuvering your individual ships to do whatever needs to be done (and almost always involves the destruction of enemy ships). Complete a mission to gain influence with the planet's population. Gather enough influence and the planet will join your empire wholesale. Of course, your rivals will be doing the same thing in their section of space.
The first half of Starships is basically a race for territory and resources, like in any classic 4X. Players will try to expand their empires, pulling in neutral planets and building infrastructure to fuel further conquest. Eventually, borders will start pressing up against each other, the galaxy will run out of neutral planets, and from there, it's a matter of the major players fighting it out to settle who will become space overlord of humanity. This is where things start to fall apart, as massive power swings can come out of nowhere and end a game without warning.
There are four victory conditions. Capturing all other players' homeworlds obviously wins you the game, as does maxing out three fields of technology, controlling seven wonders, or governing over half of the galaxy's total population. The big swings come out of the way homeworld battles work. When a player captures another player's homeworld, the losing player's empire is immediately turned over to the conqueror in its entirety. A player with 15% of the galaxy's population can shoot up to 40% or more in a single battle, or zoom past the seven-wonder victory threshold before anyone knows what's going on.
The actual starship combat is simple and easy to learn. Lasers have long effective ranges, while plasma cannons boast superior firepower once you can bring them to bear. Firing one means not being able to fire the other that turn. Torpedoes have a delay before they can be detonated, but are effective at area denial. Cloaking technology can make ships untargetable if there's no sensor-equipped enemy nearby to reveal them. Strike craft are weak, but they're fast and they can be replaced and repaired for free. Attacking a ship from the sides or rear generally provides hefty increases in damage done, and doing more damage increases the chance of scoring a critical hit and damaging the effectiveness of a ship's systems. Controlling various wonders, as usual, allows a player to break some of these rules.
The economy side of the game exists purely to support the combat side of the game. You will not be building fantastic monuments and converting heathens to your banner using the power of your culture. You will not unlock the mysteries of the universe that bring your people to a new stage of enlightenment. You will research bigger guns, heavier armor, and more efficient engines for the ships. You will build ships, or you will build factories that build ships, or you will build factories that build factories that build ships. All roads lead to ship. The ship is love, the ship is life.
Speaking of the ships, customization here is kind of weak. Rather than picking and choosing modules that change the way the ships function, you simply pick a category, choose a rating from 0-8, spend the requisite amount of ship-specific currency, and move on to the next. There's a certain amount of technique involved in weighing tradeoffs between speed and armor, or pure firepower versus stealth capabilities, or fighters versus torpedoes, but if you're looking for omnidirectional shields, stealth torpedoes, point defense cannons or any kind of customization that's any more complex than making one number larger than the others, you'll have to hope that there's a wonder that'll serve your purposes.
Sid Meier's Starships was released simultaneously on PC and iOS, and it really shows. The UI is clearly designed for a mobile crowd, and it values clean visuals and uncluttered space above all else (including, at times, functionality). The ingame options menu is a joke, consisting of volume sliders and the options to turn tutorials and fullscreen mode on or off. There are no resolution or detail settings, which might be for the best because there's not a whole lot of detail to be had in the first place.
Installing modules on a ship changes the model itself, but those changes don't exactly carry into the battles themselves. A battleship bristling with weaponry won't show off all of its guns firing with separate particle and lighting effects, just a slightly-larger salvo of lasers inexplicably curving in space as they approach their target. The backdrops and leader portraits have a painted look that washes them clean of finer details. All leader audio has been lifted from Civilization: Beyond Earth, and the only other voicework ingame consists of short combat barks along the lines of "critical damage" or "nice shot." Completing the game, regardless of method, affinity, or faction, yields the same unskippable victory cutscene (yes, a PC-centric developer released a game with unskippable cutscenes). If another player wins, their victory is announced with a quiet pop-up before the game unceremoniously dumps you back to the title screen--a title screen that lacks a proper exit button.
Sid Meier's Starships boasts connectivity with Civilization: Beyond Earth, but you have to sign up for a My2K account to take advantage of that connectivity, and I'm not interested in juggling yet another set of login data. I doubt that it's a game-changer for either game, but I could be wrong. Either way, it's the cherry on top of the Bad Mobile Port sundae. As a proof-of-concept, Starships is great, boasting several ideas that I hope can be refined and make their way into future games (flanking-based damage, one randomly-determined wonder per city-equivalent, mission-based diplomacy), but it's all buried under a huge pile of the stereotypical money grab (content gated behind company-specific login, subpar production values, halfhearted PC port, gameplay that bottoms out within three hours). It really feels like an iOS game that got ported to the PC as an afterthought, and for $15, you might as well catch a good movie instead. Starships is a decent guilty pleasure, but I'd only recommend it if you can catch it on sale.

It's the classic issue where all the surface content-- the theming, the design, the "hilarious" narrator --was developed without a compelling game to put it on.
I'd advise the crew to check out "Radiant Inferno" for an idea of how a game like this could work better. It has the *opposite* problem. A fun, involving shooter that's just boring to look at.

This is a very simple roguelite.  It plays to be more action oriented but the enemy variety doesn't play to that strength.  There just aren't enough of them in the game and a few overlap what they do.  Even the room variety is very low.  You'll see most if not all the rooms in the very first floor with 16 total.  The game is even designed to get you permenantly stuck if you die too much since you'll be stuck in a later floor with only your basic attack.  Fortunately for that point (unfortunately for the game), this game is very easy.
Early on you have to be careful.  Avoiding enemies and their attacks and conserving your ammo.  Not helped by the fact the doors to each room can easily obscure enemies and their bullets.  However, by the time I hit the second zone, I was already a death machine and things only snowballed for me from there.  Bonus health, lifesteal, and  bullets in all directions made me nearly invincible.  The only way I was dying at that point was if I decided to stop shooting and hug everything instead.  Bosses included.  There is a reason why the rarest achievement in the game is getting 100 deaths.  Personally, I won with only one death.  That may be the most damning sentence for a roguelite.

I’ve played for an hour and I made it to the prison. I like this game I think it’s pretty well done. There were a few issues I had with it though.
If you don’t already know you have to sneak through locations, stealing valuables and getting past the goons without getting caught. For the most part it’s easy to play, I don’t mean difficulty-wise. As you can probably see, you just drag lines to create a path for the player character and tap special items and powers to activate them. The controls are simple and intuitive, so how to play the game is really easy to pick up straight away. I felt that that the difficulty was challenging but not unfair at all. It’s fun sneak past the goons (that’s what I call them lol) especially if you are able to slip past right behind when they go the wrong way.
The game look’s really cool. The music obviously is great. However it was a bit loud and there is no in game volume control only on or off. I had to turn down the volume in windows. I hope that people can still hear me over it in my videos! I didn’t pay 100% attention to the dialogue in cutscenes and during stages. But I think the fact that the game actually has a story is really cool for a puzzle game. From what I absorbed of the narrative it’s cliche, you are private investigator and a beautiful woman walks into your office one day, she ends up getting you into trouble and so on. But still it’s seems interesting and competent.
There are couple of little troubles I had with moving around which you will probably just get used to. To cancel a path you need to click near your character otherwise you will add to it and if you need to change course quickly to avoid enemies that will get you caught. Also there’s not really automatic pathfinding for your character. So if you click on the other side of a wall a path seems to be made straight into the way rather than a way that takes you around to where you want to go. The other sort of more serious issue I had with game was crashes. It crashed twice the transitions from cutscenes to parts 2 and 3 of the game. However it didn’t happen after completing the third part of the game before the prison which I thought it would because it seemed to be a pattern. But anyway even it crashes it only takes a moment to restart the game and it didn’t set me back much time. If it happened more often and/or during actual levels i think it would have been a more serious problem then, but it didn’t matter too much.
Okay, so yes I recommend this game. Honestly I can’t say a lot about the length of the game because as you probably gathered I haven’t completed it yet. But I think I think it is fun, overall good quality (aside from the occasional crashes) and it’s only $5.

You know one of these games in which you ask  yourself, "What were the developers thinking"?
This is one of this, and this game has a really basic concept, but, after all, it's a really fun an entertaining game.
All you need is a friend to play with, and clicking few buttons.
The game's concept goes like this;
You and your partner are meant to set up an ambush, and traps, to keep an X amount of Orcs getting through the Rift. The rift is shown up as a door with a dim yellow light coming from it, like something god-like. It's a defense game with waves; you can upgrade traps, outfits, gear, trinkets, and many more. Depending on what level you're on, the amount of waves and the enemy types may vary alot, and you'll have to figure out which is the best way to keep them from going through your 'fortress' in time.
The game revolves around the basic and generic-kill everything theme, warriors and orcs. I don't have many hours in it, but even if you're a fan of extremely realistic, indie, or 2d games, no matter what, this game is pretty decent. At first you'll think it's plain simple and boring, but after you played it for a bit you'll get used to it, and the fun will start showing up. Play it with a friend, make up a plan, tactics, strategy, and then prove who's the king, the orcs, or your "devilishly handsome" protagonist, ha-ha.
Good luck!

############# FULL REVIEW #############
I'll start with the positive things about the game.
- It's easy and fast to learn and pick up at any time.
- Infinite replay value
- Great gun play. All guns require some degree of practice to be able to use properly and they all a very different from each other. Some guns will require a lot more skill to master than others.
- The graphics are decent and run really well on most computers. They're aren't amazing however.   Definitely not blockbuster or AAA.
- The weekly event system is awesome as it encourages the player to try new things and get rewards for them. They even give away things such as SP (in game currency) just for logging in!
- Monthly updates and maintenance which brings new content.
- The variety of guns is great. There is a gun for everybodies play style.
- The new weapon camo system is pretty neat as it allows for some degree of weapon customisation.
- The maps are designed quite well, the maps are from small to medium sized which allows for intense fighting in close quarters. Pretty much every map has parts in which people who like to fight at range can take advantage of also.
- If you buy a weapon from the game shop it is permanent. Unless you sell it of course.
- I love the different game modes this has to offer, such as slaughter which involves one team playing as aliens and the other as humans, Smash with involves two teams of players fighting on three layers of easily broken glass. If a player falls through all three layers they go plummeting down to a spike floor with a small chance of landing on a moving bouncy pad and getting back into the fight. There are the regular Team Deathmatch, Deathmatch, Sabotage (planting and defusing a bomb) and seizure (capturing an item) game modes too.

Some things I'm not too impressed by
- The menu system is a bit off, It doesn't properly run in full screen mode and can be hard to navigate around at first, but overall quite bearable.
- The rental system is a bit annoying. You can't buy permanently owned character items - you have to rent them for a certain amount of days.
- No weapon upgrade system
- If you want special skinned weapons with EO tech and ACOG sights you have to win them by gambling which means spending AP (Aeria Points) which costs actual money. I could buy 100 capsules/tokens and never receive a single permanent item, just some rental gun. They do give away free capsules every now and then which is good.
- The odd glitch such as disappearing HUD and camera not functioning properly is a bit of a pain. Good thing it doesn't happen often.
- The mamba character. This is some blonde chick in some tight clothing in high heels. It's a sexist portrayal of women in combat. The male characters in this game are all wearing combat gear.
The gameplay is this: Kill or be killed. It's easy to kill and easy to be killed. There is no aim assist. So if you can't aim for headshots you're dead. Thats about it.
If you're new to this kind of game don't worry, there are servers dedicated for you to get to grips with the game. Once you're good enough you'll graduate and move onto the open servers.
Some people think this game is "Pay to Win". I think not because you don't actually need some fancy AUG Mk4 weapon to win. Many of the best pro players use the basic AK 103 and M4a1 given to player from the start. The special paid guns do make it easier but you don't actually need them to be good at the game.  The special weapons, character items and VIP subscription may help you to a extent but you can still be very bad at the game and lose to a player who pays nothing.
About hackers, there are a few out there but not too many. Most people kick them from the game and are dealt with quickly. So you don't have to really worry about them.
Hope that wasn't too long.

text:
Best described as the FF7 of its series, ToS is the one that helped the franchise really breakout in the west. I owned a GameCube, but ultimately decided the console wasn't worth constantly plugging and unplugging and let it gather dust because PS2, so I passed up on this title. Over ten years later, I ended up preordering Zestiria to get the bonus Symphonia and see what the fuss was about.
ToS launched in a deplorable state. Bamco launched the highly anticipated port of one of their most beloved titles as an unstable, buggy mess, which I'm pretty sure violates several Dwarven Vows. Months later, they finally updated it into a workable, playable game that doesn't require a fan-made mod to not be awful (but still helps).
The story initially revolves around a trio of friends: a swordsman named Lloyd, a tolerable child mage named Genis, and Colette, the "Chosen of Mana". The mercenary Kratos and their teacher, Raine, soon join up. Colette is foretold to regenerate the world and save humanity from the Desians, half-elves who keep humans in work camps and see themselves as a superier race. The story quickly complicates as more characters appear and the story unfolds.
The battles are real-time. You target an enemy, move away or close the distance. One button allows you to use standard attacks while another uses one of four assigned special attacks depending on whether or not you use it with a directional button. The result is a fast and fun system that allows and rewards combos. The characters you don't control can have their AI customized and specific attacks disabled. Stat growth can also be influenced by assigning "titles", which are awarded by story events or in-game achievements.
The game starts out sticking closely to its tropes before throwing them out the window. How it bends and twists things were more novel at its launch, but many of them aren't as special now that other games have done the same. The game also doesn't do the best job of hiding some of its twists, or simply foreshadows far too hard. The writing and voice acting is still solid, and certain parts WILL leave you feeling emotional.
The game is stable and plays very well, and TSFix (check the forums) enhances it further. The 30 FPS cap is still annoying, but tolerable. The game has aged well, and I found myself wanting to hurry home so I could resume playing it. I've come to kick myself for not buying it back when it was new. Depsite its initial issues, the current product is enough to make a Tales fan out of me.

I love this game. Definitely in my top *mumblemumble* of all time games.
For those who played it on GC, you need no explanation. I think the port is great. Previous reviews indicate there were snafus when it first came out, but it seems golden now. The only bug I've encountered is how Sheena got stuck in muddy clothes (from her fall through the mines the first time you meet her) and they have never updated back to "normal".
For those unfamiliar with the game: it's a JRPG, and a rather amazing one at that. The story is immense and compelling, and the gameplay is just fun. There are so many elements to it, but none feel clunky or tacked on. The combat is real time (not turn-based) and you can choose your party and which character to control. Unlocking skills is one of the funner aspects of the game, along with figuring out synergies and combos, etc. It would take too long to explain everything but basically the combat is solid and hardly gets stale as you can just swap to another character for a while if you get bored of Lloyd (blasphemy!).
The game also has immense replay value as you get to buy perks for your next go around, which just makes it all the more awesome. It really makes you want to get that 100% complete every time, but not in a grindy forced way like a lot of JRPG.
If there is anything to be called a "con" it's that I would love to see this game with updated graphics on the levels of recent FF games. It's already a beautiful game but I would pay solid money to have it more "realistic" (and I'm not usually picky about that sort of thing, I just think this game would be absolutely gorgeous if it were updated).
Anyway, for $20 I highly recommend it.

Since every negative review I have read is regarding the port, I thought I'd address that first. My game crashed once during a cutscene in my 118 hours of play. Other than that, I haven't experienced any technical issues. If you haven't played the game before and are looking for an overview, here are some highlights.
PROS:
• Catchy soundtrack that inspires emotion and really highlights the particular scene.
• Graphics look good over a decade later. The cel-shaded style is timeless.
• Meaningful decisions which affect your relationship with other characters (affection system).
• Deceptively complex story that is told well and has some nice surprises.
• Characters are genuine and likeable.
• Variety of outfits which aren't expensive DLC.
• Creative and diverse dungeons with fun puzzles.
• Control and play as any character in your party. Local co-op for up to 4 players.
• Worth playing for several NG+ for fun upgrades, optional content, and 100% completion.
• Multiple character endings and opportunities to explore their personalities in-depth.
• Combat is essentially hack and slash on a fixed plane; breaks away from turn-based combat.
• Earn "grade" depending on your performance in battle. Grade is mainly used for the NG + shop.
• Three difficulty settings to choose from.
• English or Japanese voices.
CONS:
• Old school sound effects can be annoying, like when navigating through the menu.
• A few grammatical errors such as missing spaces or minor misspellings. At one point the text states that one character is talking, but it is actually another one. In addition, the text does not match what the voice is saying at all during this quote.
• World/field map camera behaves poorly so just look at the mini map. A non-issue later in the game.
I highly recommend this, especially as your first Tales game. Symphonia really shows what the series does well in terms of story, characters, and additional content. This is a favourite of many for a reason and deserves more attention on Steam. I hope you give this classic a try!

Not the best port, but Durante's fix helps solve the most crippling issues with resolution, character outlines and stuttering. The 30FPS lock seems to be an unfixable issue, but considering this is a straight port from the PS3 (which in turn is a port from the PS2), it kinda sucks that they couldn't take that cap off. This is PC gaming, Namco. You don't have to cheap out by making a straight console port and changing almost nothing. The GameCube ran this game better 13 years ago, but it's still playable at 30FPS, albeit nowhere near as crisp as the GCN release. At the end of the day, this is still Tales of Symphonia, and it's a fantastic game in a beloved and underrated series that everyone should play. But if you can, try to get this game at a reduced price- the GameCube original is still somewhat reasonably priced these days, and $20 for this port just seems too steep for such a cheap port.

Postal is a grimdark isometric shooter by Running with Sisscors, with their balls to the rotting walls grim installment about committing mass murder/genocide for fun. A game of pure edginess that it makes Manhunt weep, cower and kiss it's pillow every night (well...sort of).
Isometric shoot 'em up with a focus on a variety of weapons used to painfully dispatch your opponents. Using the arrow keys or the mouse to move and shoot, X when you have committed the act of violence and they beg for your mercy, you can kill them with that X key. You must cull a certain percentage of the filth that roams in front of Earth and then hit F1 to continue to a next area requiring your cleansing.
Creepy atmosphere and visual style, blends with the 'video nasty' era really well.
The sound design for the game is a bit hammy (occasional humorous quips from Postal Dude) but works brilliantly in portraying a grimdark world in which you look through the eyes of a psychopathic serial killer. Alone that makes the game unique for it and recognizable.
Postal itself is a dark self-parody of itself and of gaming in general. It is mocking the absurdities of the gaming industry's reaction to ultra-violence and decadence in video-gaming. Dark humour is present and making fun of your victims deaths in many ways proves this.
Diverse weapon selection to use on victims from machine guns to rocket/napalm aunchers.
Simple control system makes it easy to play but hard to master with a sandbox-like environment to plan out attacks.
Ignore the critics (IGN, Gamespot), this game is above average. It's "low ratings" are because of Postal's overall nature. That of advocating violence and murder is what gave it those low ratings. Beyond that, it's a competent title with challenge, style and is fun to play.
Extremely difficult in later stages due to the way the rockets track, this can be rectified via holding CTRL but leaves you open to attacks from other NPCs. Being immolated (set on fire) is realistic but can grate you if you're trying to avoid the large hurtbox which causes your character to spaz out uncontrollably.
In terms of camerawork, the camera angles are horrible and heavily distract you while shooting.
Graphically antiquated and looks awful if upscaled.
Graphics obscure the player model making it hard to identify where you are in-game.
The games length is questionable at best...at least the original version I'm reviewing here.
Use the number keys 1-9;0 to change weapons that you collect during the episodes. Burn them alive and watch them turn into crispy human bits or blow 'em up and hear their screams!
Grim industrial music booms as you slaughter dozens of bystanders and aggressors.
A mixture of 3D models superimposed onto a 2D isometric view of your character, giving the game a very grimdark, urban and hand-drawn feel.
Shoot a sizable amount of citizens then press f1 to go to new levels, there is health, weapon and armour pickups scattered around all of Paradise, different weaons such as Molotov Cocktails produce large AoE of flame causing DoT effect on the place it is thrown and the person that is on fire.
The Postal Dude sees a disease take over Paradise, making the deizens looks deranged and violent...it is time to cleanse the Earth of all that remain who are infected by this disease. Kill them all.
Passable recommendation, due to it's difficulty and short length.

This game is the best early-access I've ever played, If you're into survival, exploration, and crafting : GET THIS GAME!
It's a very good bargain. The fact that this small Indie a team has a faster, better and friendlier response to its players than other Early-Access games *cough* dayz *cough* should be enough to convince you to buy this, because it means your money did not go to waste, as these devs will fix and solve the bugs you actually post.
But enough about the devs, lets talk about the game!
The intro to the game is pretty generic to survival games (crashing off a plane) but at least you get to make your own martini before descending into your doom. It is also very well made, the intro looks realistic and its not just some stupid black screen at the end of it.
Afterwards you wake up on the raft you climbed on before being blown to ♥♥♥♥ with your trusty paddle and you will find a tiny island : your new home.
There you can gather resources and craft new items and tools necessary for your survival. The crafting in this game is very original, and you will not be disappointed. Instead of depending on a generic crafting screen, this game actually handles that in the physical game world, meaning you have to lay down some sticks, rope and rock before you before you can start crafting your spear.
You have the ability to hunt crabs (easiest) or fish from the ocean, even bigger fish near the reefs and deeper into the water. Hell, if you're brave enough you can actually chase that stupid shark thats been circling your beloved raft for so long, and kill it, and COOK IT! As of now you cant eat shark fin soup, but you can still eat the fin, and other parts.
The cooking is quite realistic, you will have to wait a while before your crabs become crispy and tasty, instead of insta-cooking.
You will have to manage your resources as they are quite finite, which after a while will force you to navigate to other islands in search for more wood and rocks. Especially if you want to build a nice big hut.
This game has a few bugs, but none of them are game-breaking which is something very worth your money these days.
The main reason why I think you should get this game is because it has so damn much potential. And when all the amazing new features start coming in you will start to realize how you should have bought this game early on, you can wait, sure. But you'll miss out on alot of fun. It is always nice to support such a promising game. Even more when you've got community friendly devs, and amazing gameplay.
Was fun, now NOT fun. Thumbs down.

To start off this review, as a warning, it is still in early access and still full of bugs. But the developers seem to be frequently adding features, even two years later after it started!
TL;DR: Its a fun game, to be sure, but it still needs a lot of issues fixed.
To begin, I saw this game start awhile back and my computer was old, so i wasnt able to grab it. When I did start playing today, I was surprised with how far it had come when i kept track of it. Enjoyable exploration, large map, survival elements mixed in with essentially a water world. So far, I have not experienced any really glaring issues. Maybe a few buggy instances of physics deciding to toss objects around, but thats more of an engine problem which may eventually be ironed out. My main problem, however, is the building system.
To proceed this, recently the devlopers added in a UV system that made you get sunburned. Presumably, to encourage you to build a shelter.  Seems logical. Except Im having a major issue where im trying to simply build a flat roof, and It wont let me place more than three floors in my 2x3 square house. included in this review is a small screenshot album of what i mean(
) , but it is very frustrating in where a building system is bugged but the building is encouraged and sometimes required when a heatwave hits to prevent yourself from getting burned by our pesky sun.
The ocean exploration is tense and the ship exploration is downright terrifying, if only because the shark AI is very aggressive. In my first run of this game, in almost no time at all in diving into a wreck to gather supplies, I had a shark swimming around the mangled steel. This would make the deeper wrecks difficult if almost downright impossible to gather materials from, as they seem to latch onto you like you are constantly bleeding profusely into the water.
Overall, I would give this game a so-so if possible, but it seems Steam wont allow me to do that. Its a fun game, to be sure, but it still needs a lot of issues fixed.

Overall: A pretty solid game. Decent amount of content, very easy to pickup as well. I love having the option to make a custom map and design it myself, that's very cool. I'm hoping for more crafting and sea creatures in the future!
Playtime: Take this with a grain of salt: I've pretty much went through all the game's content withing 11 hours, except for the 'boss' missions where you have to hunt down giant sharks / eels / and a squid. I'd expect those tasks to take a few hours each!
Surviving: If you want the expereince of "Castaway", this game is for you. Very atmosphereic and a nice break from 'grindy crafting' games. The crafting progression is pretty good, and the fact that you don't run out of food/water after 5 minutes (like you do in many other similar-themed survival games) is a welcome mechanic. I'd say the food/water/energy meters are really excellent and pretty realistic, you won't need to worry about them very much once you get yourself sorted out.
Cons: I'd appreciate more backpack room & the ability to tow rafts together.

I must admit that I came into this game not expecting much.  But what I got is a game that is quite enjoyable.  Whilst the game borrows from the lore of Civilization Beyond Earth the game itself doesn't hold much in common.
The game works by having you perform missions at each planet you stop at.  Complete the mission and your influence on that planet rises till you control it.  When you control it you can improve it, gain resources and wonders, and generally have access to more "stuff".
The strategy comes in utilising your fleet (you only have one) to your benefit.  You only have a certain number of actions per turn so make sure you choose well.  Do you do a mission on a nearby planet?  Make a run for an emey's home world?  Or spend a turn to repair and make new ships in your fleet?
Overall a really good game that ties "tried and true" Sid Meier concepts into the one game.

The good

The graphics are functional and colorful, but i cant say the game is especially pretty.

Sid Merier´s Starship is a lightweight mobile game that aimd in providing a on the fly fast CiV experience. I think the game achives it goals. Its the Sid Meier´s game you choose to play on  the train, before you go to school, a late friday night before a date or a party, If you dont like that idea and want something more substantial, i would not buy this game. LUFTRAUSERS: Mein gehirn schmerzt
LUFTRAUSERS, yes the name is in all caps, is a really fun indie game by Vlambeer; the people who brought us Nuclear Throne. And as you might expect this game is hart wie Scheiße.
Luftrasuers is a fast paced arcade shooter that consists of you avoiding literally hundreds of thousands of bullets flying at you in all directions while enemies swarm you from all sides. Except instead of being a little mutant out in the nuclear wasteland, this time you’re a little Nazi lookin dude flying around killing… non descript enemy forces. And boy are there a lot of non descript enemy forces.
Luftrausers is a score attack game at it’s heart. Each run is short, fast paced, and freakin’ hard. Like Teleglitch, Luftrausers is a jerk. Except it doesn’t toy with you while you die. It kills you so fast that sometimes you have to take a second to process what hit you. There is so much going on at all times in Luftrausers that it can be hard to even parse what’s happening. But this also adds to the challenge. In the four hours that I have played I’ve managed to unlock almost everything, except the super secret final unlock. And have completed all but two achievements.
And now I’m just trying to get better… And that is an uphill battle. A game is hard when a ‘good run’ is long enough to hear the music kick in…
Luftrausers isn’t a deep game. But it is a fun one. There isn’t a lot of content here, but what is there is a frantic game that requires you to think quickly, make decisions, and act as fast as possible. Don’t mess up.
What’s nice is that there are a decent amount of ‘parts’ for you to customize your rauser. Machine guns, shotguns, missiles, lasers… They had those in WWII right?
As well as a ton of different body parts and engines to change your play-style to suit your particular skillset. How does a flying hover laser-tank sound?
Luftrausers is an interesting game in that despite being incredibly hard, and not making much progress, it’s fun to just dive in for a few runs here and there and see how I do. The individual ‘runs’ are fast enough to not be irritating, and long enough to have a sense of achievement.
Currently Luftrausers is $9.99 on Steam. If a beinhart arcade-y bullet-hell shoot’em up is in your wheelhouse then give this game a shot. Personally I think Luftrausers is a bit light on content for $10. Personally I wouldn’t purchase this game for the price. But that’s me, I also got my copy in a large bundle... So unless you’re really into hard games maybe wait. However, I want to support Vlambeer. Because, those guys really, really deserve the support. So go give it a try if you’re interested.

This is a pleasing twist on your typical zombie game. Here are a few things I liked and disliked.
Things I liked:
+The combat is atypical, but fun. -- Mostly, you melee the zombies. The combat is fluid and there's a good bit of mechanics that make the combat satisfying. NPC's are also incredibly useful fighters, so you really think twice about not going out with someone.
+The zombies are less of a monster and more of an obstacle. -- There is zero benefit to killing a zombie in this game, aside from the fact that now you won't die from zombies. This was a more enjoyable approach because it allowed you to focus on other elements of the game, rather than about mindlessly mashing zombies.
+The management of your home-base and crew members is pleasing simulation element. --  The game gives you a home base full of people in which you have to manage and "take care" of. It's really actually quite fun although the occasional "Marko is depressed" moments can get a little annoying.
+The story is reasonably short and fun -- I'm always glad when developers don't stress having a long story to make a fun game. It's a good length and almost all of it is quite fun.
What I didn't like
-You can send people on raids, but they often get stuck -- At first this was an issue as I thought I was forced to rescue them, but you don't even have to. If you ignore someone in trouble they make it back just fine. It was frustrating not knowing this when It happens so frequently. Overall it's an annoying mechanic that caused more stress than fun.
I played this game for 12 hours straight after purchasing, so I have to recommend it if you like zombie games or simulation games.
