I never learn.
I told myself after Civ: Beyond Earth that I wasn't going to pre-order any more of Sid Meier's games, that I was going to wait and see how they were recieved first and then make an informed decision. But the lure of Firaxis is not so easily resisted.
Sadly, in this case it should've been. The sirens have once again lured us all onto the rocks.
Now, full disclosure, I am writing this review with less than an hour of play time on this game under my belt. It honestly doesn't take all that long to get a feel for the game, I'm afraid. The entire thing was obviously designed for the mobile platform release first, and then reverse-engineered for the PC relese as an afterthought. It was bad enough when this was being done with console games...
The interface is a joke. The game starts off windowed, has no graphical settings to change other than setting it to "full-windowed" (And when IN "full-windowed" mode has no way to exit the game other than reverting to windowed mode or alt-f4... seriously, there is no "exit game" option on the menu.), and everything inside of the game was designed with a touchscreen in mind. And then there's the gameplay...
If you ever wanted a "simplified" version of a civ game, this is it. Tech tree? Nope. There's a set list of technologies, and you just level them up from one to six. If you get three of them to six, then you win a Science victory. Because you're smart. But what about unlocking buildings? Nope, there are set buildings ("Improvements") that you can make on planets. You build them, you upgrade them, they make more of resources as they're upgraded. You can build Wonders, if you stockpile a ton of Metal over a lot of turns, and then if you have enough of those you can win. You can win by standard Domination, but if you're playing against the AI be prepared for it to be its standard cheating self-- don't bother using cloaking devices. It will go straight for your position every single time even though it supposedly can't see you. (...why no, I'm not bitter.)
Planets have cities, cities produce metal, food, energy, science. You spend science to research tech. You spend metal to build improvements. You spend food to build new cities. You spend energy to build and upgrade ships. And... that's it. Everything else is going from planet to planet and fulfilling "missions" with your ships.
Oh, and they even managed to put one more annoying mobile thing in-- a limited amount of stamina! Yes, your fleet has a "morale" limit. It goes down each time you do missions, or travel. When it goes down, your crew becomes less effective. This keeps you from taking your potentially awesome ships of awesomeness from mission to mission, getting every planet to join your federation, all in the same turn.
Oh, wait, it's not really a turn. You don't hit "end turn", you hit "shore leave" in order to end your turn. It refills your morale. That's not made entirely clear, but that's what it does.
There's more I could bring up, but really I think you get the gist of it by this point. This is not a game worth spending $14.99 on. This is a mobile device time-waster that should be on an app store for $5 or so.
I suppose we can at least be glad that they didn't put the name "Civilization" anywhere near it.

I knew before it was released that this game would be ranted and raged about on release. Why? Because a number of people had expectations which were completely out of line with the game that Firaxis promoted repeatedly on their YouTube channel.
Sid Meier's Starships was announced as a tablet game with a PC version from the get-go, but a certain segment of gamers saw the name Sid Meier and convinced themselves that this game was going to be Civilization In Space (a.k.a. Sid Meier's Master Of Orion) despite all evidence to the contrary.
Here's what it is: a simplified tactical space game with colorful graphics and impressive music. It has some depth -- it might be worth reading the in-game rules section to understand the game's strategic layer -- but it's basically a tactical starship battle game.
Does the game have problems? Yup. The lack of a true fullscreen on PC, for example, really annoys me (you have to manually set your taskbar to auto-hide) but there's nothing wrong here on day one that a few, inevitable post-launch patches won't fix.
So, if you're undecided, wait for the patching. Some people report not being able to start the game at all, but I've seen none of that here. (If it won't start, I've heard that skipping the opening cutscene may be a work-around)
Day One Verdict? The things I like about Sid Meier's Starships outweigh the things I don't, by a fairly wide margin. I expect a number of issues to be corrected with patches, going forward. This isn't the next great strategy game -- it's a "play it for fast, fun starship battles" tablet game.
You won't devote days and weeks of your life to this game, but I think Sid Meier's Starships does what it set out to do very well.

I will not write an extensive review of this game for a few reasons, one being that the problems with this game are already being vocally expressed, and secondly because I believe the game in it's current state is very incomplete and has the potential for change over the coming months if the developers are open to feedback and implementing it.
I will probably just focus on the one thing that bothers me most about this game and that is
.
Civilization 5 is already universally accepted as being a great success in the Civ franchise, while lacking in some of the hardcore elements of the previous titles, it still makes for an enjoyable and immersive experience from start to finish, with engaging mechanics and DLC.
Civ:BE - A game I wanted so much to fall in love with, being a huge fan of SMAC, lacked in new and engaging mechanics, and felt slightly hollow, despite it's somewhat empty nature I still found my experience with Beyond Earth to be fairly immersive, and this immersion is what drives me to commit a few hours to enjoying the games content.
Now onto SM: Starships, unfortunately the immersion for this game ends not long after you've chosen your leader and faction, and gained your first territory, after that you begin to realise the game offers very little after that in terms of a feeling of progression, success or any kind of immersion in the world.
I like the mechanics of how the missions are fought, I like turn based strategy games played on grids so I enjoyed these aspects somewhat, but found they were not very challenging or interesting enough to remain immersed in the action and cause of the game.
The AI at this points seems fairly dead, they will make their presence known and then afterwards there isn't much diplomatic use for them. You will find at some point you're either going to have to betray your allies or make peace agreements with them which completely block you from travelling into or through their territory to reach new unclaimed planets, this can lead to you getting completely isolated and unable to progress.
The game needs a lot of work, it has the workings of a great game, but it feels as if it hasn't been worked on enough yet, the UI needs to be more engaging and helpful, think back to Civ 4 and 5, while Civ 5 did not offer as much as Civ 4 did in terms of the advanced customization of how you can play the game, both titles gave you enough to build yourself an engaging and immersive experience. It seems the developers have been limiting that customizable freedom which has been such a defining feature of the Sid Meiers Franchise, starting with Civ: Beyond Earth and now with Starships, I hope the devs are able to look back to the past and remember what made their games so successful and work on keeping their reputation alive.
One of the main criticisms of this game right now is that it feels more like a mobile app which is what it has also been released for, and right now it seems as if it has been limited more for the mobile app platform, rather than developed as a fully functioning game that can stand the test of time on both platforms. While smart to break into the booming market of mobile applications and mobile gaming, I feel they should of perhaps decided on either releasing a standalone mobile app, a desktop exclusive release, or simply put more effort into developing the game mechanics and elements further.
At the moment I cannot recommend it, for the very simple reasons that I don't believe you will get much enjoyment out of it for too long in it's current state, and is certainly not worth it's current price in what it offers.
I look forward to following where this game goes next, and what the supposed cross-game functionality with Beyond Earth will offer (it seems to me that whatever that feature is has not yet been released), but for now I'll be letting this one sit in my library.

I am on the fence with this one, because it probably would never have "mainstream" appeal.  However, I like it.  It is relaxing and no pressure.  You basically are given unlimited time to roam about the corridors of the ship.  You have to solve some minor puzzles and collect items to continue to the next section.  For what it is, I enjoyed myself.  Unless you are OK with what I described above being THE ONLY gameplay type and with a minimalist story, you should probably stay away.
As for what could be improved: I think that increasing the variety and pacing of the puzzles would be a good start.  Also perhaps cut down on the size of the corridors.  People are less likely to get bored if they are spending less time simply walking to a location they already know about.  It may also be a good idea to vary the theme more.  That is, have different sections of the game have a distinct visual theme, instead of all of them being identical.
The only reason I am giving it a positive mark is that I got it on sale.  I am not sure I would do the same if I bought it full price.

However, the last save checkpoint before you finish the game has the 2 most tedious puzzles in the entire game, and it doesn't feel worth trying them out for a different ending. In any case, according to the discussion forums a few people tried at least one different method but got the same ending.
In short, if the game had not padded out a couple of the puzzles and made a even decent ending (wasn't even expecting great or amazing plot twist) then it the game might be worth it. The space station exploration is simple but still enjoyable for a chill sci-fi mood, sadly a few of the puzzles and ending ruin the entire experience. In other words the negatives ruin any positives this game has, so I recommend not getting the game.

So, if you are reading this, then please understand that this is a game you should try at least. The reason why is because I both love and hate this game. For almost every positive aspect, there is a negative one. The reason why is cause of the devs poor quality for customer service and polish of the game. Lets go over the pro's and con's.
Pros:
1. Characters are unique. There are various characters in the game, each with their own traits. Some may be better than others but each has their ups and downs. This changes the game flow for each character you play. One may be a soldier with amazing shooting skills but is an absolute jerk and a coward who is very good at cooking. The vary in character traits makes each playthrough a little different.
2. Breakdown DLC. This DLC is crazy fun. Its a DLC to test how long you can last before you meet your end. You also have to choose which character to bring with you to the next level because the goal in it is to find and fix and RV to move up the level. Each level you progress increases the difficult. The higher the level, the more zeds you will find and trust me, fighting them is hard. This game is unforgiving since characters can die permenantly. You can retrieve the dead characters gear but it will be a huge impact on your survivability. You also start out with a randomly generated character and by completing challenges, you unlock Hero survivors that have crazy bonuses. Once you unlock those Heroes, they become playable themselves in your next playthough, giving you an advantage on each playthrough, though some Heroes are painfully better than others. This DLC itself has issues but we will get on that in the cons.
3. The mechanics. In this game, you need to make sure your group of survivors can live on by gathering food, medicine, weapons, ammo, etc. As you continue to fortify your base, more survivors will want to join you. Of course, you are given the option to take them in or not but it is a hard choice. More survivors mean better defenses against hordes but also a cost of more resources. You also need to build special buildings in your base. Although some are far more important than another, the essential buildings are medical tents and a workshop. This game makes you think as well has play carefully. This isnt like L4D where you can clear 100's of zeds in 10 seconds with a auto shotgun and pills, this is harsh. Fighting 1 zed is easy but when there are 3 or more, the difficulty in fighting increases drastically, making you the prey and them the hunters. There are also special infected like the feral who is agile and can take your survivor down if you are alone. So always be prepared even when scavenging.
4. Lifeline DLC. Now this one may be the most challenging of them all. This DLC puts you as the military during a zed outbreak as you try to control the situation. Almost everything is bleak with hordes everywhere, many soldiers lost to the zeds, and survivors in need of help. This paired with the fact that the number of playable characters you get is very small makes every soldier count. Losing one soldier is much more impactful in Lifeline than in Breakdown since there are barely any other surviving soldiers out there. In exchange, you get a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of ammo and guns to defend your outpost along with support from the military that you have to capture yourself. This puts people at the edge of their seats wondering if they should go scavenge for supplies or save another citizen in need. The choices are yours to make.
Cons:
1. Bugs. Bugs everywhere. I am not joking. This game is so buggy that it even puts Assassins Creed: Unity to shame. There are questionable bugs like cars thrown into the air for no reason, small taps of the car on an object can explode or throw the car 30 ft away, survivor AI is mostly buggy and braindead, floating survivors, falling through the map, etc. The devs have not fixed many since its release and it really sucks. This game is fun but you gotta go through a lot of bugs.
2. Breakdown DLC. Why is this in the cons when I put it in the pros? Cause this DLC also has issues. The map never changes when you advance in level, making it repetitive and dull after going through 2 levels of it. Certain Heroes can make the game far too easy like the church guy who can give you max stamina when tired along with the radio operator who can do the same thing, making you go on with 1 guy for the rest of the playthrough. Another is a soldier Hero who can call in artillery, has leadership skill, amazing gun skill, and has good stats overall. Not only that, once you play the map enough times, you know where to go to get supplies, where to get weapons, what bases are the best. It gets very repetitive fairly quickly. Oh and did I mention this is on a real time mechanic? That's right. After you quit the game, the day can continue on, making you lose resources depending on how long you left it alone and items can reset. For example, I had 400 rifle ammo with 300 shotgun ammo, 10 of each med, 500 snacks, and 3 cars outside. After leaving it for 2 hours and hoping back in, I am down to 100 rifle ammo, 50 shotgun ammo, 5 meds, 30 snacks, and all the cars outside are now different than what I once had. This game gives you items when you leave based on the resources you have. So if you have 500 ammo for a pistol but a resource of 10 ammo, you will get ammo equivelant to the 10 ammo of resources instead of the 500 ammo you got, making things frustrating as hell to get it all back.
3. Story. This story sucks. The story is very boring and most of the characters I shrugged at or didnt care. I only cared for characters that had good stats die and even then, the character are never fleshed out well. Oh and did you know the ending of this game is a cliffhanger? That's right. The devs were planning on making a sequel without even making us understand most of what the ♥♥♥♥ is even happening. Since then, the devs have been silent on the sequel since. I dont know if they are even working on it or not but this is absurd for the devs to give us this♥♥♥♥♥♥of a story. The Lifeline DLC is a little better but I would have much rather play a COD or BF story than that.
4. Maps. There are literally only 2 maps, the original and Lifelines. That is all they give us and these maps arent even huge. The original is okay but its not very far. Lifeline is small and closed off more than the original. This can make playthroughs dull.
Overall, if I was to rate this game, it would be a 6/10 or a 6.5/10. This game is average with some interesting mechanics. It is worth a shot but dont get it for full price. I got mines with all DLC half off and that felt just about right for me. The devs really need to polish this game and if they are making a sequel, they better have more maps and better quality cause I dont like it when I am playing a game then the frames suddenly chug from 30 to 10 just from 10 zeds on screen.

It's Dark Souls. Everyone knows about it. So I'll just do a quick review trying to highlight the main points with some comparisons to other games in the series.
Merely calling this game difficult is inaccurate. It is, but the otherside to it is that it's extremely rewarding. Clearing areas and bosses truly feels like you're achieving something which makes the game so much more enjoyable.
This game's environment is just beautiful, even when comparing it to its sequels. It's not only refershing when entering different areas, it's also very atmospheric and immersive. Also, the way this world is mapped is just amazing. They always know how to surprise you and subvert your expectations in the most wonderful ways. This is one aspect where you have to see it and play it to believe it, but you'll know what I mean once you finish the game.
There are many choices to make when building your character, and this is one of the beauties of it. Want to focus on huge swords and great hammers? How about being skilled with a large number of swords, axes, bows and also weilding shields? Maybe you want to be a mage? Or a paladin that uses utility spells? How about Katanas? This game has it all. Replaying the game with a different build makes the game feel so new.
The backstory and lore of this game is just beautiful. It's great hunting for the information hidden in different items and piecing it together, and there are many details of the story hidden in the environment of the game. Also, in comparison to the sequels, this game was the most neatly packed-up story and lore-wise. They couldn't replicate what they did with the original.
Character interactions are cool, too. Voice-acting is up and down, but each NPC you meet has a story arc which meshes well with the NPC's personality.
Secrets. So many things hidden in this game. Even when it's just a simple item you can't help but appreciate how they manage to hide it even though it's right in front of your eyes.
All in all, a lot of games are claimed to be the "Dark Souls" of their genre.  And a lot of games try to imitate some elements (with varying success). But in reality, seeing how these games are so far, there is at the moment only one true Dark Souls, and that is Dark Souls 1 (btw the DLC included with this verison is just incredible). As a gamer, you owe it to yourself to play this game.
Final note: the modding community has done wonderful stuff with this game.

Luftrausers is an entertaining if short lived arcade dogfighting game. The core concepts presented in Luftrausers are a strong backbone for what I would hope the next entry would hopefully embellish. I say this becuase Luftrausers has a delightfully simple control scheme, neat retro visuals, hints at a curious larger universe, and has many fun enemies to combat. However, Luftrausers is lacking in some areas. Namely that the store page bills this game as having over 100 missions, but these are not quests or levels or specific scenarios which change base gameplay in any real way. The missions they refer to are more like challenges. The "story" is extremely limited.  Luftrausers only has a survival/score attack gamemode which doubles as the campaign for the couple hours it takes to play through. While playing through the first "missions" and "story" things were hugely entertaining to discover and every new unlock, every new enemy fought, and every slideshow of "story" was good. But, this is a game which does not have a lot of content past about 3 hours of gameplay. After that, you'll pretty much have seen everything and just be trying out plane combos you didn't try yet, or trying to beat your own highscore.
Now I DO recommend Luftrausers, but it is a game I wouldn't recommend too highly because I feel it lacks some features I feel would really round out the package and make it basically perfect. First, as you may have guessed, I am bothered by the lack of a story for the single player. The story isn't a large concern of mine, but an expanded universe would be welcome. Second, the score attack/survival mode in this game is basically perfect except for stopping when the boss is destroyed, but I think Luftrausers could actually benefit from different modes, maybe an objective based mode with specific targets, twists on normal gameplay, and possibly even special plane powers not typically used. Third is leaderboards. This game tracks your score locally for each plane, but you have no comparison to anything but your best run. For competetive people, this may not be enough. I think online leaderboards or even traditional arcade local leaderboards with initials are A MUST! Fourth, local multiplayer with friends with frickin' jets with frickin' missles man. Make it happen in a sequel please! Competetive or cooperative, this is a game I really would love to share with people when they come over!
All said and done though, Luftrausers is still a unique game which is undeniably fun for a few hours. Playing as a super fast jet with a nuke inside the body and firing homing missles at crowds of smaller enemy planes to the harmonious and legendary Welcome To The Dangerzone by Kenny Loggins is a memory I will cherish forever, and I have Luftrausers to thank for that. I can also thank Luftrausers for allowing me to finally pilot a Bond movie type vehicle which functions as a jet, a battering ram, and a submarine all at once, sinking destroyers by dropping into the ocean, and surfacing like a majestic humpback whale by crashing straight through the prow of the destroyer and thereby blowing it up. 7/10 overall.

BYTE SIZE REVIEW:
I don't post a lot of reviews, but I have long been a fan of Sid Meier's games.  That being said, despite not playing this game for very long (and I will updated this review at that point in time), I don't have much time to play games anyway so thought I would share my thoughts thus far.
This game is amazing.  It so far reminds me of a space version of Pirates! which is fun in and of itself.  The object of the game is to control over half of the galaxy.  This can be accomplished, by spreading your influence, completing missions, etc.  You get to choose both your faction (for lack of a better word since I don't recall what each group is called) as well as your hero (much like nations and skills in Pirates!).  I'm really looking forward to playing more of this, but I am definitely recommending this for now.  :)

Ace Patrol in Space!
No real Strategy game like the Civilization games, but a nice little tactical game.
If you like Ace Patrol, you will surely like Starships.

If you can handle knowing there is a Sid Meiers game that isn't very complex then you might enjoy this spin off title.  I was pretty skeptic when I started playing, but it grew on me a bit.  Imagine an odd combination of Beyond Earth, Risk, and any of the better mobile games out there and thats what Starships is. You are mainly going from planet to planet completeing one of the 4-5 combat missions (elimination, escort, escape... etc) and then slowly taking over the galaxy. You upgrade your starships and planets via resources you gather from the planets and move on. It will be much more straight forward than any other Sid Meiers game. But if you go into knowing its pretty much a glorified mobile game, then you might just enjoy and keep playing.

This game is obviously designed to be a tablet game that would have run alongside Beyond Earth. This is most obvious by the apparent lack of a simple exit button on the main screen, something very common on tablet games.
With that out of the way, this game is a decent PC game and the strategy is very well done. The war game events seem at first glance boring and strightforward, but they are quite complex if you plan it out right and adapt in game.
I have tried it on a Surface Pro 3 and it works fine. Once you start it on a device with touchscreen then the options gice the choice for the controls to be touchscreen.
Overall it is a good game. I would recommend waiting for a BE/Starships combo sale as it is worth about $15 in my opinion.

Ever since Civilization 5, the Firaxis team has been focused on a casual, arcade-like feel for their games. Civ V never had the intensity that Civ IV and before had, yet it was very agreeable to the eyes and had decent replayability. Moving onwards, we got Civilization: Beyond Earth. A pale comparison to Alpha Centauri, but still a fun game if you were in that arcade mentality. Firaxis continues the trend with Starships, a very simple and pretty game that is practically a tablet app game.
Pros:
- The visuals are stunning as usual, and seamless graphics for the most part
- Very interesting use of tactics, looks like they took a page from their X-Com game
- Once you get rolling, the game is straightforward and can bring that "one more turn... one more turn..." feeling that every Civ player has come to love and hate.
- the variety of planet missions are great and makes every encounter different.
- the save-link between Beyond Earth and Starships is a nice touch
Cons:
- If you hoped for a intense space domination game, this might not be the best bet for you
- It is really casual oriented, and that does give the feeling of emptiness and being unfulfilled after playing a game (which could last up to 3 hours)
- space combat  does get monotonous, and once you fire torpedoes enjoy watching the AI scarmble right into your lasers.
- Controlling only one massive fleet takes a lot of tactical potential away, especially on the large/epic maps if your fleet is on the other side of your federation and your planets get attacked.
verdict:
In the end, I did enjoy this game more then I hated it, and I hope with some modest mods the game can really shine, just like how the mods for Civ V have made it a new game entirely. If you go in with a asual, arcadey attitude, you will not be disappointed and will find this game enticing and refreshing. Just don't expect any long epic campaigns.

In my first episode we find ourselves in the station walking down corridors that look almost identical from one hallway to the next and every so often you may find a room with a monitor that explains a bit of what happened, and it up to you to solve the mystery.

This game is not an amazing title. But it gave me a couple of hours to kill. I do recommend it for those that enjoy puzzles and a lil bit of exploring. My review is below:
TL:DR
Video trailer pretty much sums up the game in a whole.
Pros:
- Some puzzles (slide puzzles, switch piece, match grid, etc)
- A story without too much depth. Believable for a futuristic real world setting.
- Music and environment that keeps you a bit on the edge of your seat.
- Story is on text screens. (If you like reading this is a pro)
Cons:
- Repetitive rooms, items, walls, boxes.... lots of boxes... (Story explains why there's so many though...)
- Puzzles aren't for einstein and can be solved relatively easy.
- Most Puzzles are "Explore area, find a part, put the part in, flip the switch."
- Story is on text screens. (If you hate reading, there aren't any voice overs, it's all reading)
The full Review:
I can understand why many have a negative review. This game isn't really one to appeal to all audiences, but it does have a niche that some may like. I personally enjoyed it because it's set in a theme that seems real to what our own real world possibilities in the future could be.
The corridors can seem somewhat repetative, but seriously think to yourself, the worlds governments create spaceships and space stations that are not asthetically pretty or unique. The game is in a setting of such a world. Therefore, the corridors, boxes, rooms, etc all being similar makes perfect sense.
Also, the very story of why you and the planet station are there is described in the story. I won't go into details because I don't want to spoil anything for anyone. But it's obvious that the reason you're there and the way the base is designed/set up are in unison with a realistic future.
Conclusion:
In the end, it took about 3 hours to complete (literally my play time).
- If you want a quick enjoyable read in the form of a video game, I'd recommend this to you.
- If you don't enjoy reading or expect some awesome amazing horror/gore game with tons of action, look elsewhere.

I don't think this game was incredible, but it wasn't as bad as some of the other reviews make it sound. Sure, it has issues. Early on you get to look out a window and see a large satellite dish beyond a wind-blown dusty landscape, which was enticing, but it's just decoration - you never do leave the corridors. There's also not really that much adventure except for getting killed by the randomly-timed lightning). The locations are also a little bare - a few signs would have been nice, for instance, even if just for decoration.
But the story, while fairly light, was interesting, and the resolution isn't as silly as some of the other reviews claim (I don't know how to do spoilers here but I'm pretty sure it only has one ending which is just vague enough to misinterpret). I enjoyed the logic puzzles, and wouldn't have minded a few more. There's not much backtracking - you might have to hunt around a little but you're never going to discover you forgot to pick up something three autosaves earlier. The graphics were pleasant, and the physics system was surprisingly functional for a game that didn't even need one. And most importantly, it kept me entertained while I listened to audio from another program.
So if you want a game that doesn't rely much on sound and doesn't need your full attention (hint - the maze 'left/right-hand-rule' will get you through most of the segments), and don't mind a few gaming cliches... this isn't too bad. Plus it's short - I had the game alt-tabbed a lot; my real completion time was a little over three hours.
I did pick up a memory disk early in the game and never found anywhere to use it, though. I wonder what that was about. (Edit: Mystery solved.)

This is the epitome of the stat-driven visual novel!  There are 42 different skills you can raise from 0 to 100, and every 10 points in a skill, you get a great blurb on how that skill increase has translated into some tangible lesson that Elodie has learned.  And those blurbs really determine whether or not you succeed or fail royally (pun intended) when you're making choices as the main story progresses.  The flow of the game is that you spend time training skills (and you can use mood bonuses to help when focusing on certain skills), then something in the story happens where you have to make your choices.  The default mode shows you the skill checks as they happen, so when you die by failing a poison skill check, for example, you know what you have to do in order to not fail at that part on your next playthrough.  There are a couple of macro-level decisions that alter the course of the game as time progresses, such as political relations and amount of money in your treasury, and there are quite a few different endings.  Getting each ending requires a very specific skill profile- for example, one ending might require Elodie to have become a skilled military general to get, whereas another might require more of a magic-centric Elodie to get.  The key is to make decisions that compliment the type of Elodie you are building.  Oh, and the game is also set up to make sure you die a couple of times before you get any of the endings!  Yes, it can be frustrating to have to start over, but there's another aspect of the game where you can set out to try to unlock all the possible deaths so it isn't always a failure if you die, just another ending that you'll collected.

It's an interactive story where every choice you make is key to survival, but instead of yes and no choices like most VA's of today, all of your decisions are made primarily through the skills you choose to work on via classes. There are dozens of classes to choose from, each teaching a new skill along with tidbits of real world knowledge that I found amusing. Lots of characters you interact with can come back to help or harm you in plenty of ways, and depending on your skills, you can learn surprising facts about each of them.
There's a lot to this game that I don't want to spoil, but if you have plenty of time and you're interested in one day becoming pretty princess, maybe you should look into this game too.

Would love to post a cliche "git gud" review or joke around on this review in general, but this is too much of a masterpiece and I just cannot..picked this up on steam recently to give 60fps dark souls a shot and also see a bit of an upgrade in the visuals.
However, I've logged, lord knows, probably at least 3k hours minimum on this game between the PS3 and X360 and have seen everything the game has to offer.
Granted, if you play it for the first time these days, you may not be able to appreciate the game as much as others could when it originally released. One of the best parts of this game is the online functionality, and there is just not a high volume of people who play it anymore. So you shouldn't expect to find many PvP encounters or co-op partners. There is however, a solid number of dks faithfuls who still play the game, so who knows, perhaps you may find a few others throughout your journey.
Although, with that being said, do not under estimate the story of this game as my first time through I may have never been so lost in a fictional world. The enviornments, bosses, and enemies are all fierce and the game seems so overwhelming in scope when you first start. There is wonderful scale to the enemies, and many times you feel like a 5'6" woman going against a 6'11" MMA fighter. I remember feeling this way the whole game but truly realizing it once I matched up against the Silver Knights in Anor Londo. Mostly because they are knights just like me, yet they still tower me and I feel like a dwarf in comparison to them.
The whole world is interconnected, and set up in more of a vertical fashion, with many layers in between. You can even see places that you will visit in the future far off in the distance, and once you get there, you will realize how you journeyed there from start to finish. There is a great feeling of accomplishment in advancing and overcoming obstacles in this game, as well as upgrading your character and finding new gear. There is a lot to upgrade (stats/build diversity) and many items (weapons/armor/spells) to find.
There is also a whole crazy lore universe to this game. The NPCs in this game are extremely memorable..need I mention Solaire, Patches, Big Hat Logan etc. There's no doubt that I thoroughly enjoyed all of the character's side quests. Even if I wasn't building my character around the stats/items that the particular NPC could help me with, I still found myself completing their questline, all because their stories were so immersive. Much of the game is told through the dialogue of these characters, however, there is also a large number of the games stories just told through item descriptions, and creating your own story out of them. The enviornments in this game are breathtaking, and there is some vistas that just make you forget that you live in the real world. I think the fact that the area's are interesting and have their own stories as well makes a big impact on the lore. You can spend hundreds of hours immersing yourself in this games lore, and there is a large number of YouTube channels that are solely focused on the lore of DkS. I consider myself to be very knowlegable about the lore but there is a whole other level to it for those kind of people. The overall atmosphere of this game is just a 10/10 and the characters, enemies/bosses, and levels are incredible + unforgettable.
Many people talk about how hard the game is, but once you learn it, it is not hard at all. As a matter of a fact, it's anything but hard, it's completely fair, and if you're a good player you will rarely die or be bested by "challenging" situations in the game. The difficulty of this game does not need to be balanced or changed around in any way.
The majority of my time spent in this game was after I finished the story and competing in PvP. Random fight clubs, invasions, and just dueling friends became my favorite part about this game. Even more so than the story, which to this day is up there, if not, my favorite in any game. The original DkS has some of the most skill based and addictive gameplay I've ever experienced, and it could shine and thrive the most while fighting other players. In the big picture though, DkS PvP fell so far short in terms of what it could been if there was just a little more care involved. And to be honest, none of the future Souls titles really improved upon the PvP in any way, at all. The only things they improved in my opinion were the backstabs in DkS 3 and the connectivity to other worlds. (to a certain extent)
Back to the subject I was touching on, the game, especially PvP, isn't without its flaws. While it is my favorite game of all time, there were some imbalances with the weapons as well as some overly powerful rings (in my opinion). There is also your typical OP Havel Mom players who in my opinion ruin the game. Then there is your extreme backstab fishers who are hands down the most annoying to fight, this wouldn't even be possible if they would have refined and thought out the backstabs a bit more. Everyone knows that hitting backstabs in the original DkS was like taking candy from a baby. When fishing for backstabs, I understand the mindset that you want to kill your opponent any way you can as quickly as possible, but there is so much more variety to the combat in this game when you're not just mindlessly circling eachother for backstabs... that's not enjoyable to me. The game could have benefitted a lot even if it would have just had a DkS 3 backstab system. Poise system could have been much better as well, you should never be able to get hit by a Zweihander without having to hit the Toggle Escape to get out of the stunlock. The final few things that I definitely want to say that I disliked, even though I already touched on OP rings, is that the Hornet ring was just ridiculously powerful and so many people abused criticals (backstabs + parries) because of it. The Darkwood Grain ring (flip ring) is also incredibly annoying and the masks (mother, father, etc.) are OP as well.
As I just mentioned a moment ago though, I am most definitely in favor of the toggle escape for those who know what it was. To me, the button glitches such as toggle escape, move swapping, etc. added a much higher skillgap to the game, as well as just more stickwork in general. I liked these button glitches regardless of if they were intended by the developer or not. Every time I played DkS, there was a certain flow to the gameplay.
Pretty much, if Poise (basically armor/equip load/edurance), rings (specifically Hornet/Wolf/Havel/Darkwoodgrain), and backstabs would have been more balanced, this game would have had a huge skillgap and while it was competitive, it could have been ridiculously competitive.
I truly believe DkS could have been a top online game and even an eSports game if it would have had a matchmaking system with ranks (level 120 or 125 max, one or the other not both), as well as a more streamlined search system (easier to find a fight, option for 2v2s, 3v3s, etc.) <-- I know 2v2s + 3v3s were in the arena, but no one really played the arena and the settings and rules could have been much better. Honestly, I even think you could pull off 4v4's in dks. There was such great build diversity and I couldn't imagine a 4v4 with two knights and two mages on both teams.. would just be so awesome.
With all this being said, you may think I listed a lot of negatives about the game. BUT trust me, the positives overwhelmingly outnumber the negatives and this game, and even though I wouldn't give it a 10/10, the original DkS is still a MASTERPIECE, and my favorite game of ALL TIME.

short version:
Like a bad golf swing. Starts out strong but the follow through was rough.
Bad: Not nearly as good as the lord of the rings games for the gamecube era consoles.

Long Version:
I enjoyed the game but the overwhelmingly positive reviews are more a result of a thumbs up or thumbs down rating system. Not a reflection of how great the game is itself- Most of my gripes are with the story itself, some gameplay issues. Here they are. **spolier alert**
Story issues:
-you spend a number of story missions helping an orc named ratbag get promoted to warchief. The idea being you have a war chief that you can influence. But it was a total waste because ratbag is quickly defeated and you end up just mind controlling all of the war chiefs anyways
-There are a few story missions involving a dwarf. These writing for these missions is a total failure. even though you are half elf there is no animosity between the elf and the dwarf which seems like a big miss. At one point the dwarf tells a really long story about how the Caragor creature HATES water to the point of becoming uncrollable. moments later you and the dwarf ride caragors through water with no problems.... The basic arc of the dwarf story is that you are learning how to kill a giant creature. However, all of the techniques he teaches you are pointless because in the final mission with him, things dont go as planned and you never use a single technique you learned in the last 3 missions.
-you collect 32 items to finish the image of a secret elf door (like the one gandlaf has to remember the password for) but nothing happens. all you did was complete the image. Its not actually a door and it does nothing.
-one cut scene shows your elf half having the ring of power in his possesion at the start of the war that is depicted in the prolouge of the fellowship of the ring movie....idk where that came from.
-the entire morrdor map is full of slaves to the orcs- called outcasts, they are men throw out of gondor. They serve absolutely no purpose in the game.
GAMEPLAY issues
- nemis system is interesting but never amounts to anything. Every enemy can be pretty easily defeated no matter what rank or stengths and weaknesses. Meeting a character more than once through the nemisis system has no real impact on gameplay beyond a new phrase being said during a cutscene.
-as you work you way up from low level orcs all the way to the black hand of sauron the difficulty stays the same. Defeating the black hand of sauron really only took a few button taps during a mostly controlled cinematic fight scene.
- it is not an open world map, it is basically like mario 64. There is a large map but that just means you have to walk across empty terrain to be able to start your next mission.
There are more issues but thats the idea,
Strengths: it is always great to be back in middle earth and in this cae that makes up for any of the games short comings. Get it on sale if you are going to get it.

Best early access I have ever encountered. Ever. I write this as my first decent attempt at a campaign fortress is slowly being ripped appart by the AI after disabling my weapons systems. I'm not even angry - just impressed that there is so much depth in this sandbox/strategy/vehicle builder game. Block by block construction is both simple and leads to intricate detail possibilities for construction. I agree with other reviews - research & planning is essential for this game if you want to enjoy it - and ends up being part of the fun.
There are numerous strategies that can be employed for the fleet & ship based fights - naval & air vehicles need to be allow for in this game. It lends itself toward letting the AI do everything in controlling ships/weapons however it is possible for the player to use both. I haven't tested out the fleet systems properly yet but going by the AI it looks to work fantastic - seriously the AI kicked my where it hurts with a pincer movement - then from above- seriously who attacks you from directly above????
Any lack of documentation is made up for by an incredibly supportive and involved community - the developer has obviously gone to much lengths to ensure that all learning styles are accounted for.
Replayability:
*If you are like me and love tweaking those designs just that *little bit more* and getting satisfaction from a good system, I can see it proving hours and hours of additional time.
*The current campaign is great for getting a feel for construction techniques and tactics to use in your own creations
*Not really a story based game - but why would you think that is what you are playing for
Pros
*Lasers
*Really, really big guns
*Customisable missile systems
*Smart/programable systems - seriously takes hours just to scratch the surface.
*Amazing tactical/strategic possibilities - I have not seen a game I would rate higher in this regard (I would love to see some tutorials on the map systems & maybe some more depth on campaign for this reason)
*Very customisable interface
Cons:
*Steep learning curve
*Requires a level of sophisication & engineering mindset to truly appreciate it. (Think minecraft bashing creeps with a sword to using automated traps to farm them) Not truly a con but may be a consideration for gifting.
*Some of the interfaces such as battle seem buggy (the intent is well documented but can be confusing when starting up)
**Very customisable interface - makes it difficult to remember what key map to press for certain situations (take this as an advisement if considering how much time you want to invest rather than a con.
Well recommended and cannot see what comes next as it develops. I only hope that the community gets behind it and allows it to continue to develop to its amazing potential.

A small and short strategy/sim type game that should have been a fun and quick game but ended up being overall annoying with how the game progressed.
You start off on a small island after a plane crash and start with a small group of workers to collect resources, to upgrades your structures, complete missions and build new structures that unlock as you level up.  This isn't a negative up until you realize there are 4 islands and that every time you move to a new island you don't get to take anything with you and start the whole process over again.  So as you progress through the story you do the same steps over again three times from the starting island, it stopped being fun after the second island.
Another problem was resource gathering.  Some resources that could be gathered would be collected automatically after the plant/tree/stone was harvested, however some of the resources that generate from your buildings had to be collected by clicking on the building.  So this just led into an infinite loop of sending workers out to gather the various resources, then clicking your buildings than back to the workers again and repeat x 100.  Would have been nice to auto set workers to collect some of the basic resources so you could do some of the minigames or other things, instead of repetitively telling them to collect one thing over and over.
Also most of the islands seem to be gated by a single resource or two, so you have to work around that resource that stops you from progressing as quickly as you could.  I get why it's done in these types of games, but its silly that in the last 15 minutes of the game I acquired as much money as the entirety of the rest of my play time.
I think the overall game could have been a bit more enjoyable with some quality of life improvements, however what is here isn't something I can recommend.  If you like these types of games I'd recommend something like The Promised Land (from the same developer/publisher) instead, has more depth to it and its more than just mindlessly clicking.

LUFTRAUSERS is a delightful little game. The mechanics are remarkably simple, as well as the art style; but the overall package is incredibly fun. The best thing about the game to me is that it doesn't require much of the player. It is easy to jump in and out, but still make progress. The player is presented with attainable goals that are based on the modifications that are available and each modification is actually unique, which adds a great deal of variety to the game.
All in all, LUFTRAUSERS is a ridiculously fun game. It is definitely worth a purchase.

LUFTRAUSERS is an arcade-esque dogfighting game that has its gameplay refined to perfection. The entertainment and satisfaction other games need hours to provide, LUFTRAUSERS can give you in a matter of five minutes. This game simply never gets boring and can remain engaging years. Its definitley worth the price.

Finders is a resource collection game with excellent fishing and Match-3 mini-games.  Though very goal-driven, many of the details of how to gather the resources to meet the current set of goals is left to you.  This leaves room for some strategy in optimizing the fastest way to achieve these goals.
Although most of the time in-game is spent harvesting plants, chiseling rocks, chopping down trees, processing ore, and cooking, there are two mini-games that stand out:
The first mini-game is fishing.  This is mostly a timing game - throw out the line, wait for the fish to bite, then carefully reel in the fish.
The second mini-game is mining for ore, which is done by an excellent timed Match-3 game.  I like Match-3 games by themselves, and the time you see I have spent in this game is in large part due to replaying this specific mini-game - I'd buy it even if it was stand-alone.
Though Finders may not be for everyone, the game balance was a very good match for my tastes, and I heartily recommend it for lovers of this genre.  You don't need to work your brain too hard, and mining using timed Match-3 (with fantastic power-ups that include a buzz saw) makes it tremendous fun.

Luftrausers reminds me of my days in highschool where, like most highschool students, I used our generously donated school computers to log hours on mofunzone and teagames playing flash games.
At first glance, Luftrausers seems like a poorly named copy of a game you've seen done 100 times before.... that being said, it's not neccessarily a bad thing to bring back something we've seen before provided you make it better than we've seen before.
Luftrausers does this to a T! Everything about this game looks and feels as fine tuned as this genre could possibly be! The feel of your aircraft, the pull of gravity, the speed at which enemies come at you (SMFT barring of course)
Each match is short as you're lucky to live to the soundtrack chorus (which is usually my goal as the soundtrack is awesome!) making this a great game to play if you only have a few minutes to kill. That being said the point of the game is not so much about survival as it is on chaining kills together as your score grows ridiculously fast at Max bonus. Also, whether you beat your high score or not, you're pretty much guaranteed to make some progress towards unlocking new pieces.
Plane customization in this game is zany and brilliant, and while some upgrades seem less handy than others (gun engine is by far the slowest engine I've seen in my life!) each upgrade brings something unique and never feels forced in there. Each combination of aircraft not only have their own unique name, and unique remix of the main theme, but also have a completely different feel of game play.
All in all, if you have any love of this genre at all, then I highly recommend Luftrausers to you! If not.... Well give it a try when it's on sale! (It is currently $2.19 at 80% off at time of this writing) You may find a love you never knew you had!

WARNING: PASSIONATE AND SLIGHTY MEAN REVIEW UPCOMING
This game isn't bad. Like the reviewers before me I say that this game could use some work, and it seems that all it's really good for is getting that 5 minute feeling of awesomeness from creating the ultimate pixel spammer. However, this game has more than just that.
Effects
Honestly, I HAVE to say that the music is very fitting for the world of Pixel Boy. It makes you feel like you really are in a pixelated world adventuring in dungeons. The narrator is also very funny, throwing great jokes and being quite silly with his netural tone. The world is also quite colorful and many details are put in that you normally wouldn't expect for a $10 game. 9/10
Story
There hardly IS a story in Pixel Boy, as the entire town and dungeon appears as just another punchline. This CAN work out if you do it right, and I really think they did a good job making sure they didn't need one. 8/10
Gameplay
Now here I have an issue. The game itself just feels... empty. As if the developers didn't put it something or got a little lazy. Sure, the dungeon is always randomly generated by randomly arranging rooms, but no matter how you arrange it or whatever value your math textbook says it will add (I know this for myself how tempting it is), you CANNOT cahnge the fact THAT THEY ARE STILL THE SAME ROOMS. The same goes for the enemies. Sure, each level has diffrent mobs, but there are only about 10 or 12 of them. This makes the levels get repetitive after a short time. When Sprial Knights did this, they created HORDES of enemies, easter eggs, and special events. DO IT RIGHT, PEOPLE.  I know the game wanted to focus on the creation of the bullet spammer, the ULTIMATE WEAPON, but the lack of weapon mods limits your creativity more than you'd think. If you're not grinding for your ULTIMATE WEAPON to complete it, you are using it while worrying about AMMO COSTS. Don't listen to those trailers, those people having been playing that game for HOURS AND HOURS on end. It's true that damage is still a little OP. By that I mean it's the MAIN STAT you go for. Armor is completely broken because it's just not worth buying for the lack of creativity it has. All it really does is improve your stats, doing something on HIT (bad ideas are bad) and SAPPING YOUR MONEY THROUGH REPAIR COSTS. Still not worth the coins.  Overall, it feels boring and unnecessary to have such a medicore system.   5/10
Overall, if you've played some bullet hell games like Touhou, and you've always wanted to have that kind of ultimate power, get this game. It probably won't be consuming my time like World of Warcraft and Terraira, but it's worth my $10 and definitely has the pontential to become more.

Starships is simply brilliant.  The game is tightly focused on the tactical missions, which is the whole point. The strategic layer is intentionally light to keep most of the playtime in the battles, where it belongs.
The missions and ship configurations are varied enough to keep the game interesting through many iterations.
Starships is short.  A standard map game can be finished in a few hours, even a huge map game will take a tiny fraction of the time needed to play Civilization. Short is good. I love Civilization, but I can count one hand the number of games of Civ5 I've actually been able to finish in the last two years. And more often than not  Civilization ends with a grinding game of attrition or acumulation of culture points that is simply not that much fun. The strategic game in Starships does a good job of avoiding this kind of slog. The action in Starships builds steadily throughout the game until a satisfying climax in a decisive big fleet battle (at least in my games so far.)
There is no multiplayer. This is also a good thing. If you really want a multiplayer online TBS game with both a strategic/political level and a tactical battleboard, then IMHO you really, really have way to much time on your hands and need to get a life.
I strongly recommend Starships.
I do have two minor quibbles.
First, players cannot rename their ships (or I haven't yet figured out how.)
Second, the game could use an empire management screen/table to make it easier to find and develop your planets on the larger maps.

update:
The actual game is fun. It's basically a board game where you have your little band of ships and you go around between planets doing missions to get influence. The missions are tactical turn-based battles. It's not as deep as a proper 4X game but it is fun.

Games last anywhere from about 30 minutes to a few hours depending on difficulty and galaxy size. If you remember the ship combat from Master of Orion 2, this game is similar to that. The wonders in this game taking the place of some of the more exotic ship components from the earlier game. No one aspect of the game would be enough to win an award by itself, but everything is competent, pretty and the level of polish is excellent as you would expect from Firaxis. All in all, a really good value for just $15.

In Fate/Extella, you have a main story, which has 4 "routes", each rout is telling the same story, but from a different character's perspective, and 13 side-stories for each servant available.
I will give props to the fourth route, it is much better than the other 3 on every possible aspect.

Combat is fun, but just like every musou game, it can get really boring after a while. If you are not a fan of this "musou" style game, I suggest skipping this one.
Moving on to Extella, the Camera is indeed a horrible disaster. It slowed me down quite a lot while I was trying to figure out where I'm going exactly, or when trying to properly execute a full combo on an Aggressor. It was also a pain in the *** when navigating through a complex area.
The level design wasn't really that good either. It was kind of impressive while playing the first route, but after seeing the same levels again and again, while fighting the same enemies again and again, it became boring and I grew tired of it.
Characters are interesting and fun to interact with, the Bond system also adds and it's
satisfying once you get the right choices which increase the bond level.
Overall - If you enjoy the style of musou games, beating up thousands of enemies, and you are a Fate fan, this game is perfect for you.

Fate/Extella is set in the Fate franchise an anime doujin game series that has sat mostly in the visual novel field over the last decade and a bit. Coming into the game with no prior knowledge of the story didn’t seem to matter too much and I quickly felt up to speed and what followed was one of the coolest story-driven games I have played all year.
Originally released on the PS4 & Vita the game has now hit the Switch and PC.
EXTELLA’s story follows the events of Fate/EXTRA on the PSP in which a massive conflict known as the Holy Grail War was fought inside the digital-only realm of SE.RA.PH. The War saw different groups of ‘Servants’ who are incarnations of historical and mythological figures with human ‘Masters’ controlling them trying to gain control of the Moon Cell, a digital lunar lifeform that can grant its bearer any wish of their choosing.
You really need to stick with this bit of the game as getting your head around it to start with is hard but trust me it is well worth it. The game kicks off with the player character (a human who controls servants) alongside Nero Claudius (The Roman emperor digitally reborn in female form) being under attack and threatened to lose control of their kingdom by an incoming force. Where the genius of the game really comes in though is the way the story is told. Without giving too much away let’s say that the game is fairly short clocking in at around 4 to 5 hours but must be played a number of times with a different player character each time with the events changing and being told from a different character’s perspective. The game plays with the idea of dimensions and realities as well as time travel but tells the story in such a fantastic way I was totally gripped from start to finish even though I had no previous knowledge of the fate series.
Gameplay wise the game is essentially a Dynasty Warriors type game with hordes of enemies on a maze-like grid with a number of objectives to complete and stronger characters to kill. The game is fun and the characters are different enough to keep you going but the story is something that is essential to the game.
There are a number of different special attacks that are gained in a variety of ways. Some attacks you charge by killing enemies and other you gain by collecting items around the map. Equally, as you progress through the game and unlock levels you gain access to new moves as well as unlocking points on a very customisable skill tree.
Gameplay is quick and fast and while not perfect great fun and well worth playing if you have any interest in similar titles like dynasty warriors or Hyrule Warriors.
Visually the game is simplistic but works never once giving slow down as the crap tonne of enemies fly around on the screen. Obviously, the PC version is the most impressive but the Nintendo Switch version really holds its own and the game is a joy to play on the small screen.
There are a few issues, however. The game doesn’t tell you a lot as you go through and a lot of things need to be worked out for yourself. Equally the range of enemies in the game is almost nonexistent with the same basic grunts from the first level of the first campaign being the same as the last level of the last campaign.
There is no multiplayer here but Fate/Extella the Umbral star has so much extra content even after you finish the main story that it is likely not a problem for most.
This review was largely based on the Switch version that I played in its entirity. I have played a few hours of the PC version to ensure it runs well.

Imagine yourself waking up in an abandoned space station on a planet that's beginning to fall apart. Through terraforming, mankind wanted to make the planet habitable but while doing so something went wrong and now you try to find your way through the space station and its dangers while simultaneously looking for answers as to what might have happened there.
I personally see the game in an ambiguous way. On the one hand, it is interesting because neither the protagonist nor the player knows what has happened which again motivates you to search the space station and look for answers that you occasionally find on various computer screens. The numerous riddles blocking your way keep you from getting bored (although I sometimes happened to be annoyed by those sliding puzzles especially). On the other hand, though, the game is a bit dull, first and foremost because it has absolutely no music! A nice soundtrack would have done the game much good. Also, those cool space station doors didn't make any sound when opening. I mean, every space door I know usually makes some hissing sound when opening, like the doors in Dead Space for instance...
Aaaaaand then there is the ending... The problem with the "ending" is that it's not a real ending! In fact, when I played the game I didn't even notice it was the ending until I suddenly saw the title screen! What I find a real shame is that the game doesn't really answer any of the questions that accumulate over the course of the game...
Well, long story short, I am having trouble recommending the game. In my opinion, only half of it is worth the money, so I´ll give it a 5/10.

A pretty good game.
But not a good Ace combat game.
Would recommend to non-ace combat vets.
Details:
Alright, so, let's start on top with the story. It's rather lackluster, not much twists. Just some dudes defecting to the other side, there's no interesting thing going on here, there's the lack of the "oomph" you get from the older ace combat games.
While in Assault Horizon, you're a sgt. mcBadass out here ripping through hordes of enemies because you're the hero, and a nightmare tells you who your arch enemy is. There's no interesting message being delivered here. It's all kick♥♥♥♥♥and take names type of game.
Now we get to the mission, some missions are just boring. The helicopter sections are quite interesting, you get to pilot an AH-64 really dropping the heat and supporting the ground troops and whatnot. The door gunner? C'mon now, that ain't fun at all. We've had enough of turret sequences. AC-130U sections... are quite frustrating, other than sometimes we might miss the opportunity to kill off the enemies before they kill us, and we die. It poses a fun challenge, but, it kinda detracts that "Ace Combat" feel. But then again, some people likes it. The plane missions? Rather interesting, but can get very boring. One of the most interesting missions to play is the one where you fly a bomber and chase down an ICBM with a jet, and the part where you fly an A-10 to really deal damage to some ships. The idea of flying a bomber around in an Ace Combat game is just quite intriguing. We're used to fly highly maneuverable jet fighters, but not a slow, bulky bomber. Especially at low altitudes, and then doing carpet bombings. That was just simply awesome. The chase with the ICBM in an F-15 was just freaggin hysteric. Way over the top. The Naval warfare mission is just top notch, that's how you do a mission over the top correctly. Explosions everywhere, the BGM suits it very well. But the rest? Well, they're okay, but, rather lackluster. Some missions wants to be over the top, but not there yet, not as face melting as the 2 I've mentioned. They don't make up for what they lack in being over the top with intrigue at all. Ace combat 5's mission to find the shot down Captain Nagase was rather great. You feel the pressure, yet enemy resistance is light. But it's still there.
And one of the most deal-breaking things about this game is the DFM. I know I know, you're tired of people b*tching and crying about DFM, but heck, I kinda liked it, if I forget that this was supposed to be an ace combat game. Get up close and start making metal bleed with machineguns and missiles, just my stuff. But, it gets you stuck following the guy in rails, you lose control of your plane. But in terms of the aesthetics of DFM, I really enjoyed it. But on a gameplay level, no, it doesn't give me the thrill I get when I followed one of my friends by the tail and start spraying missiles and machineguns when we're playing splitscreen back then.
Overall: it's like a Call-of-dutified Ace Combat. Which makes it a bit more interesting and dull at the same time, but just a tad bit more interesting. A *bit*.

The lore is good, especially to those who love to explore every nook and cranny of Tolkien's Middle-Earth.
Nemesis system is a nice addition to a game which feels like we've played elsewhere, many times, but it doesn't hold the title up by itself because, again, it ends up feeling repetitive. Again, the game isn't bad, but in my humble opinion, it's extremely overrated, and it's something you might enjoy if you get it for sale, like I did.
The verdict is a 6/10, barely above average, though if you ARE a hardcore fan of The Lord of the Rings, the value of the game might be increased exponentially, if you're willing to read every bit of lore the game gives you. Sadly, I'm not that much of a fan of it, and I'm reviewing it as a videogame solely.

State Of Decay is a commonly overlooked gem. It excels at nothing and does a vast variety of mechanics quite well. The game has bugs,glitchy AI,save issues,base building issues,broken missions, and wonky visuals at best.
And it's one of the most entertaining games I have ever played.
An open world where you scavenge for supplies. Food, Medicine, Building Materials and even Fuel. Where you have 5 different locations to build your fortress and survive with your chosen community of misfits. Where survivors get get sick, injured, sometimes even pass away leaving critical security issues with your bases defense and operation.
The base building aspect is where this game crushes all other zombie games to date in my opinion. It is extremely satisfying to upgrade your initially sparse home to something of a fortress. There's also RPG style leveling per survivor so you can build them up across many paths of specializations.
If you can overlook small nagging issues, you will love this game.

Finders is a game of resource gathering, camp building, making and selling products, and a few mini-games, all wrapped up in a multi-stage search and rescue quest. Finders has no time pressure or "levels": you get to choose whether and how you challenge yourself. (Me, I always try for "most efficient," but everyone's different.)
The gathering, building, and production have just enough depth to keep me playing 10 (or 20, or 30) minutes longer than I intended, but they're simple enough that you can fit in short sessions between other tasks. The game isn't too short, either: following the entire story line took me more than a few hours.
In fact, Finders is one of the most enjoyable casual resource management games I've played in quite a while. If the art, sounds, and writing were polished, I think this could easily be a top seller. As it is, some of the art is fine and some is weak, much of the text is awkwardly translated, and the fishing mini-game needs work to be more than just a chore. If those kind of things bother you, don't get the game. But if you like clicking to gather and craft, especially with no time pressure, you're likely to enjoy this.

+Not using your thrusters is just as important as using it. You get significantly more turn control when your engine is stalled, allowing precision aiming and redirecting your movement in ways that defy realistic physics in favor of exciting gameplay.
+The health system is interwoven into the weapons system. Pausing your onslaught lets you recover your health pool. The game plays alerts and puts an iris-in on the player when health is at dangerous levels.
+Working together, there's an interesting and frantic dynamic of healing, attacking, moving, and steering that I've not seen any other game pull off.
+Your planes, the 'Rausers', are customizable with the parts available. Mix and match for 126 different combinations that suit your style. Each of them even has their own name.
+Soundtrack is dynamic. Each different Rauser part introduces a different melody, percussion, or bass-line to the song that is constructed for your session.
+Camera is pretty solid at keeping itself oriented around what the player wants to be looking at based on where their Rauser is pointed and their current velocity.
*Artstyle is minimalist, but minimalist is perfect for this type of game as it keeps visual noise on the down low so it can bombard your eyeballs with waves of bullets and enemy planes.
-Scoring and combo system is heavily conflicting with the random enemy spawns. High-scores are incredibly dependent on a particularly rare enemy unit to spawn and then subsequently dispatched with a x20 multiplier.
Overall, it's an incredibly well-tuned and fast-paced experience that is immensely satisfying to pick up and play for a few rounds, just don't go in expecting to be plugging hours away doing score attack as the numbers are ultimately meaningless beyond a certain point.

I give this game two thumbs up!
This Tower-defense game looks similar to games such as Kingdom Rush. That is where the comparison ends, however. You do not have personal heroes to fight on your behalf. Rather, you invest into three school of skills as you level up.
The skills are divided in magic, warlord and treasurer. The magic skills improve your mana pool, your prowess with casting spells on the battlefield like an angry god. The treasurer skills improve your ability to earn and to spend gold on towers/warriors more efficiently. Finally, the warlord mostly improve your warriors' strengths. (The knights hit harder, the archers shoot further, for instance.)
The campaign is lengthy, ranging over 33 missions, (mostly solo play, with a healthy mix of PvP and Coop missions throw in for a measure.) PvP is exactly that- you play against another player by beefing up your warriors to send against the other players while also beefing up your own defense. The trick is to find the correct balance between allocating your resources between the two. While Coop is two players (you and another random player) setting up defense against an onslaught of AI-controlled waves.
Even then, each mission has three stars you can earn, by achieving certain goals (Example- complete a mission without casting spells). Finally, each star can be achieved in terms of difficulty- bronze for easy, silver for normal and gold for hard difficulty.
This allows for many replays, both for resources and for experience as you level up your own personal avatar. I've been playing for a while, and even then there's still many more stars and achievements for me to earn yet.
I've not even touched up the ability to upgrade your army with resources, the ability to earn resources by building things such as a gold mine, or the ability to upgrade your spells by investing into them at the mage tower, the rewards you can earn by completing the quests given to you, and so much more.
On the surface, it seems like another gimmicky tower-defense game, but it is surprisingly and delightfully deep, more comparable to  games such as Gemcraft than anything else.
TLDR; This game rocks. If you're a fan of tower-defense games, get this! It's a must-have for your collection.

For now I'm just going to write about my experiences with the game and why I recommend playing this product
As you can see I spent 20 bucks on a game and played it for over 50 hours and honestly I didn't find myself disliking most of the game.
This is a pure tower defense game that uses mana to keep the player active and attentive to what is happening during the game.
You have 3 classes to play as and get more distinct as you level. The warrior is a raw power class that focuses on buffing units and sending them to the battle quickly and amassing a numbers advantage. The Sorceror uses spells to his advantage to actively deal with the enemy at hand with much larger mana pools to use than the other 2 classes. The Treasurer is a gold based class that brings some serious firepower to the table and actively plays by removing and creating new units quickly.
You can refund your skill tree for free and craft it however you like. You can also freely mix skill trees and take the stats that you value the most. For example I value archers morethen mercinaries so I focused more on buffing them using the warrior path while grapping the 15 starting gold from the treasurer path.
The gameplay is interesting enough to keep it from getting stale. There are different objects, difficulty levels, and also 2 different game types one being TD mode and another being a mix of an assault/TD defense mode
Each unit has several upgrades and special abilities that you will need to take on harder difficulties. I will say that this game does have a grind to keep you busy but the developers plan on lowering that eventually and making it easier for everyone which is something else I want to talk about.
The devs are active in the community and will respond to you. I seriously haven't seen this in a very long time so thumbs up to the devs for staying active with their community.
As for my final statement quite a bit of the game is still being developed and the game is changing for the better as its still in early access but for 50+ hours worth of gameplay this sure was worth it for only 20 dollars.

Servants used to be a really big deal, Noble Phantasms and especially Command Seals were trump cards you only used as a last resort. There was an interesting story going on in Fuyuki, with properly fleshed-out characters behind the scenes of the Holy Grail War. When conversations happened, they had real weight behind them most of the time, questioning the reader on how far should you take your objectives before you start to hurt yourself and others around you.
Now those elements have lost their meaning entirely. Servants are merely pawns, meant to execute the same repetitive actions over and over again, while being dressed up in Barbie-esque DLC costumes. Command Seals and Noble Phantasms are things you spam mindlessly in order to get to your objectives faster. The story makes Fate/Grand Order's plot look really promising, and that's a feat in and of itself. Your character may as well not even have a 3D model, complete blank slate that he is. Conversations bog down to downright nauseating flirting between you and your Servant. And just to rub salt on the wound, the game runs like a snow plow in windowed mode, even though it looks as simple as an upscaled PSVita novel.
The Fate series is dead, it arguably peaked at Fate/Zero, and died not a minute after Fate/Kaleid Liner came out. There have been some interesting experiments like Fate/Extra for the PSP and what could have been the Fate/Apocrypha MMO, but not even Nasu himself seems to know what to do with the franchise, introducing magical girls, time travelling, and numerous novelized spin-offs that all lead into their own parallel universes. It has become analogous to the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise.
Fate needs to be dragged to the back of the shed and put out of its misery. It has had enough to drink, and this game, in my opinion, is empirical proof of that. I feel the worst for fans of this series, not because I want to take away their enjoyment of this game, but because they deserve much better than this.
