As others wisely said (sadly, after it was too late for me) Avoid this pitfall of a game. This has got to be by far the dumbest-downed Sid Meier's game in history. Let me just list some things this game lacks that are just inexcusable in this age of gaming, no matter the price:
1. Any form of Diplomacy or for that matter, interaction with other factions and AI players.
2. The tutorial is hilariously lacking, even as a Civ 5/BE player with well over 1000 hours I struggled to understand what all I had to do and how to control the game both in battle and out of battle.
3. Customization of your units by picking Harmony, Supremacy, or Purity at the beginning of the game ends there
4. Basic information in tool tips is non existent
5. Graphic Settings. Yes, that's right, there are absolutely no graphic settings. No resolution, no v-sync, heck you can't even change the brightness of the game. The only setting is full screen or not.
6. Auto-Saves. Yep, there is no autosaves in the game, and no options to turn it on
Loading from an In-Progress game. Made a mistake and want to reload? Sorry, exit to main menu and reload.
7. Balancing is non-existent. On hard mode, factions will declare war with you within 5 turns of the game starting and will have ships that do ten times the damage yours are capable of. They will also take all of the planets possible, leaving you no resources to upgrade after your first turn.
8. Settings in general are missing entirely. No key bindings, no controls explanation, no sound adjustments beyond volume level, no game customization beyond Race, Bonus, and opponents.
Honestly, Beyond Earth stripped away dozens of features and I thought that this game was thier answer, that this would plug the gaping holes in thier most recent 4x Game. Unfortunately, they stripped it down even further to it's barest of bones, literally leaving you with a game so very simple that you can play with one hand on your mouse as you beat your head with a hammer held by the other hand for buying this game.
Do not buy this game unless it's in the $2-$4 range, I'm not kidding, it's that terrible.

On asmosphere? This game feels empty. Like, there's no immersion. It's cold. Soulless. I don't recall any sort of ambient music. Just hums and rumbles from various sources. I get that I'm supposed to feel alone, but the world doesn't feel alive at all.
Speaking of being alive, a few cheap deaths happened. I might be at fault on a couple, but when you die just because you turn a corner just to be shot with a laser you couldn't see before? Oh, and don't expect any real ending for your hard work.

Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor is a game where you murder lots of orcs. Sure, it's got a plot, and characters, and a setting, and some other window dressing, but it's fundamentally about murdering tons of orcs and nothing else. Fortunately, it's great at that, so the game is great generally.
It's also the first Lord of the Rings game I've played since I spent a year of my life in LotRO a while back, and played a bunch of the Lego tie-ins with my brother. That's not relevant to this review; I just thought it was interesting.
In terms of basic gameplay mechanics, Shadow of Mordor is a third-person action game that has a lot in common with the Arkham games: it's got a broody white guy protagonist, stealth, parkour-ing, an alternate vision mode that highlights important things, and most importantly the same kind of combat.
You play as Talion, a Gondorian Ranger who gets himself and his whole family killed in the first 15 minutes by orcs who're retaking Mordor for Sauron (in between The Hobbit and the main trilogy). Luckily for him, he gets reanimated and used as a corporeal suit by a High Elf ghost, giving him powers including archery, magic vision, mind manipulation, and immunity to permadeath. They then decide to basically tear through Mordor an indefinite number of times until there's no more Mordor to tear through, which given the fact that they're basically immortal seems like a solid plan.
The stealth basically works, and does a good job of conveying that thrill of not being discovered that makes stealth worthwhile. The only somewhat weird thing is that, because of the orc population density in Mordor, the orcs' vision radius is unintuitively low, which can take some getting used to.
The parkour-ing, and movement in general, is a little jankier. The basic movement is kinda sluggish, and sometimes Talion gets confused about what you obviously want him to do, and starts just walking into walls and jumping off cliffs instead of climbing or getting out of the way of enemies' throwing axes. It can certainly be frustrating, but most of the time it's functional enough.
The alternate vision mode is fine. Not much to say about it.
Then, of course, there's the combat. Like Arkham, it's pretty basic and shallow at a mechanical level, but like Arkham, it remembers that the fun is in adding lots of increasingly powerful things to do over time. Additionally, Shadow of Mordor is delightfully over-the top brutal, and seems to genuinely ♥♥♥♥in' hate orcs; the amount of♥♥♥♥♥♥you can do to them, and the murderous gusto with which you can do it, is honestly quite impressive.
You can stab, slash, and decapitate them with your sword; stab and slash them with a broken sword you use as a knife; snap their necks with your bare hands; knock them down; toss them into their friends and off ledges; jump on them from above; drop swarms of flies on them; stun them with ghost punches; set them on fire; drain them of life; shoot them with ghost arrows, or teleport to them with those same arrows; subject them to ghostly AoE attacks; poison their alcohol; intimidate them by killing the ♥♥♥♥ out of their friends; throw ghost daggers at them; explode their heads with ghost powers; invade their minds for information; trample and maul them with giant armored dog things; smash and eat them with giant troll things; and brainwash them to be your lifetime mind-slaves, then make them fight each other. Truly, this is a marvel of game design.
Adding context to this violent mayhem is the Nemesis system. Basically, distinguished orcs (including those that manage to kill you) get names and titles, and become Captains. Captains have specific strengths, weaknesses, and personalities, and constantly squabble amongst each other in order to move up the ranks. The top Captains become Warchiefs, who get to have lesser Captains act as bodyguards. You can kill Captains like other orcs (except they have more health), but if you fail they rank up and taunt you for being such a crapout. The game's great at making you really hate these ♥♥♥♥ers, and most of the game's emotional investment comes from getting revenge on troublesome Captains. To make these stories even more interesting, they can occasionally come back and require being killed repeatedly; unless you actually decapitate them, there's always a chance they can return. It gets even better when brainwashing becomes a thing, as you can make Captains yours, then help move them up the ranks to Warchief. I still remember my first Nemesis and brainwashed Captain. Dûsh the Bloated recently made Warchief—an accomplishment of which I am inordinately proud—and Dharg Runny-Bowels had his vacant spot taken by, like, three different Captains in a row.
The sandboxes (there are two) are pretty nice. They're small—you can run from one end to the other in about five minutes—but they're the right size for the game, and full of interesting stuff to do. There's not too much busywork, and there's an orc you can do something horrible to every 20 feet or so.
There are three different upgrade systems, which seems like a bit much. They all work alright, but I feel like it could be reasonably condensed to two.
I think I got overleveled pretty early on in the story, but it didn't affect the difficulty curve much because the game can expertly scale up any combat situation by just throwing more orcs at you. Made half the tutorials kinda weird, though.
There's a little indicator in the corner that shows how much battery you have left, which is a wonderful feature that all games should have.
I got a bunch of really good runes right off the bat, and I'm not sure why.
As I said at the beginning, the game has a lot of things to do, but it never loses sight of its core concept: killing tons and tons of orcs. It's good at organically encouraging you to do so, too; you'll be going to an objective, stumble across a group of orcs, and think, "Well, might as well kill those guys. It'll be fun and I'll get some XP." From there, it's off to the races, as you stealth kill as many as possible before being spotted and then their friends show up and then a Captain and his whole entourage appear out of nowhere and it just keeps escalating until either you die or you kill every single orc within a mile radius. Like all the best sandboxes, it's a story generator, one that accidentally and intentionally works with you to create experiences worth telling other people about. I really like Shadow of Mordor, and I think all of you should play it.

With one part time management, one part risk assessment, and one part visual novel, "Long Live the Queen" is like none other. You have forty weeks to prove you are worthy of the throne, but your friends, your family, your political enemies, and the world at large want you dead, and trust me: They'll get what they want.
Each week you pick two classes. Examples include world history, accounting, archery, horses, flattery, divination, and more. Lots more. What's that? You're depressed? Then you get bonuses in some areas (animal handling and expression) and a penalty in others (royal demeanor, conversation, and athletics). You have to manage your mood to learn the skills to keep yourself alive and guide your country to a bright new future.
You can: get killed by arrows, drown, get poisoned, get run through with a sword, choked by magical chains, pulverized by a sorcerer's magic, get strangled by tentacles, and much more! Send a friend to die in a magic forest! Execute your dad and become an evil minion! Build a hospital, put down a civil war!
Easy to learn and difficult to master, "Long Live the Queen" is a fantastic experience and great fun. It's slow and relaxing, though you may find yourself outraged at your own inevitable failure.

Eternity's Child is an indie platformer made by unknown studio Silver Sphere. The story revolves around... I don't know. The game starts with an intro in form of wall of text that is scrolling, and it's scrolling pretty fast, you won't get enough time to read it.
So, let's speak about the story as how I felt it through the gameplay. You're something between bunny and elf, with emo bat-elf friend who is shooting laser balls. You are jumping through unique grotesque world full of weird mechanical enemies that are evil. To save the world, to get a heart of your lovely bat-elf and... whatever, you just collect gems with your girlfriend and shoot at mechs.
Let's talk about gameplay. It's praiseworthy the developers put their time into their own engine but it's not much praiseworthy that it plays terrible. You control movement with keyboard, shooting with mouse, nothing surprising, but the whole movement and jumping feels bad - you are now sure of platform edges and objects react with a lag.
Though the game is not even finished (and don't expect it'll ever be), it offers several levels that will make you ask your conscience for not doing anything else. It also has a level editor (beta), but I must admit, I didn't dare to try it.
If Eternity's Child was supposed to be an art project (with removed gameplay), it could end up being pretty nice and interesting "experience". The environment feels weird but that's definitely something positive I can tell about the game. Sadly, there is also some confusing visual design on places - there'll be too many things on the screen and you won't be sure what's supposed to be platform (to jump on) and what's just on the background.
Overall, this is one of the worst platformers I've played lately, it has terrible gameplay and unfinished content. Unique visual style can't save it when everything else is bad. Don't even think about buying it.

It's a really casual and fun game to play. You're stranded and need to take action to find missing coworkers and ofcourse the hero of the game. You need to manage your resources and sort out which actions to perform first in order to keep your operation running smoothly. I would've loved the game being double or triple the size it is now, I finished the game in about 13 hours now (with doing lots of side-quests).

I should preface this by saying that I usually do not play casual games. They usually do not appeal to me. Yet the premise of this game "Superhero goes missing and now you and your team must solve the mystery to find him!" peaked my interest.
The game is quite short, and there is no way ( that I could discern ) to objectively "lose". Your team goes from island to island solving puzzles and playing small mini games to complete quests. Nothing is ever taken away from you, so the game is very low-pressure. (I suspect that its made for children. But its fun for adults too, especially if you just got out of a really competitve game and want something laid back to help you wind down.)
There is a strategic element to it too, but more about build order and building placement to optimize your economy, rather than commanding armies.
The story is a little cheesy , but moves right along (especially if you don't follow all the side quests, which I initially did until I realzied they are procedurally generated and infinite). The integration of archeology and comicbook style superheroes was genius. It worked amazingly well, and its something I've never seen before.
If I have any one major criticism about the game, its that its so short. Even going off and doing a lot of sidequests, I completed it in something like 10 hours. Which isn't bad, it just left me wanting more. A few of the puzzles, for example, were only done once. I'd really like to see some DLC or expansions with more islands and more puzzles.
Anyway: thoroughly enjoyed it. I bought it during the Steam summer sale when it was under $5. Its definitely worth more than that. Probably $10-$15.

There's some strategy involved in setting up your camp, and doing your best to fine-tune it.
But here's the game's biggest flaw, in my opinion.  After fine-tuning your camp, you have to move to a new area and complete a very tedious process in order to bring some of your progress with you.   This happens several times over the course of the game.
Additionally, the fishing minigame needs to be shot out of a cannon into the sun.  Overall, this is a very annoying game.

Gameplay
Warstone is tower defense strategy game with a big amount of new features, fancy graphics and really cool story! The main feature of the game is absence of the usual towers! Instead, there are warstones. You can put them anywhere you want and summon a unit upon them. There are 7 basic units: peasant, archer, gunman, healer, eagle, wolf, elemental. Each basic unit can be upgraded into another 7 units. For example, peasant becomes a mercenary, who can be upgraded into a knight, a fearless warrior with high damage and slow attack, or a witcher, a demon hunter with rapid sword attacks, or into a monk, an unarmed figther with strong abilities. Each tower has a unique damage type, gold cost and special abilities. So the main feature of the game is pure strategy. You must think hard to find the best solution for every level.
Class system
Commander has skills which improves the power of your units and has unique abilities. He can transform usual warstones into powerstones which gives extra bonuses. He can destroy the stone for dealing a lot of damage to nearby units.
The weapon of the Treasurer is gold! He does everything to get more gold: bounty is increased, units are cheaper, drop coins give more gold, unique gold spells like transmutation into golden statue. All these will make army of the treasurer three times bigger than others. Also he can carry twice as many items and artifacts.
The power of Sorcerer is spells. He can have three times more spells at once than other classes. He regenerates mana faster than he spends it. He knows powerful spells like Elemental summon or Meteors rain. He can transform units into mana. He can pass level using only spells.
Diversity of towers plus different game classes open unlimited number of game tactics in PvP battles!

Its a bird? its a plane??? NO ITS... a bunch of space hippies in green ships planing on stealing my planets... darn...
at first glance this game is something to be admired. It takes Civ BE, and expands the story into space and allows you to unite planets colonized by humanity during our exodus into the stars into your federation. So i thought "WOW COOL ITS LIKE CIV... BUT IN SPACE!!!" i was quickly given the idea of galactic Civ games, with a touch of that good old Sid meier's magic. and who wouldnt want some of that magic!?! Those damn space hippies thats who!
Then i was hit with a game i can only describe as a briliant and stunning idea... that was hastily designed with the sole intent of making a quick buck based off the name brand...  this game would be perfect... if it were for Iphone IOS or the like. The only justice it does to the sid meiers name... is that it has the name "sid meiers" in the title. while visually decent, the animations for combat (I.E. explosions, weapon firing, movement, missiles and ship destruction and what not) are just... no... to call them bad is giving them too much credit. The voice acting for the combat senarios are just as bad. Every civ leader from BE who has been "expanded" in this game all share the same dialog with their predecessor. and the game just tosses you into the map with a horrible "tutorial" if it can even be called that, with an equally bad user interface... the tech tree is very strange at first, the way you gather resources and spend them was confusing, and from my very small amount of play time all i have seen are the same ships with different extentions on them, nothing different or new, just different shiny objects on your already similar body ship.
it makes me sad writing this review... i want to give it a thumbs up... because i have never thought bad of any sid meiers game... I want to like this game... i really do... I am a huge fan of the sid meier's brand and absolutely loved Civ V and even BE, to an extent (personally i feel like they need to add more DLC's for BE creating religion and a united nations like body like the expansions for Civ V did), but this... this just made me a little sad. maybe in time with some patches and tender love and care, this game can truly blossom into something beautiful like it should have been. but it seems sid meiers has fallen into the "lets dish out as many "games" as we can and profit from them because our fans will pay anything for our "products"" pit just like ubisoft with Assassins creed, and the publishers for Call of duty. I hope this was just a test run for an idea, and that they will expand this game... or at least expand BE... because ive been waiting for that for a long time and it doesnt seem to be going anywhere.
All i can say is that if you want to put forth the money for this, go ahead. Maybe you will enjoy it? and i hope you do because that is what i wanted for myself. however, as of now i have to say im truly dissapointed in this game in its current state. maybe in a month or two il come back and see a picture of what it should have been, and i will change it to a thumbs up... but for now i just see something that could have been the greatest thing ever, and fell so far short of its potential.

I spent a few hours playing this today. I have not played Beyond Earth. I've enjoyed the game so far.
What it is:
A $15.00 space title, with tactical combat, decent graphics, and some compelling aspects.
Ship customization (modular)
Tech Tree
Lightweight turn based system
Low maintenance.
This is a great game to play on your ipad or machine when you have a couple of hours to burn and want to unwind after work. It is not a Civ game and will not have that level of cmplexity. I think it has potential to be very moddable if they make that an option.
Now with that said there are some things people need to know:
The tech tree is very imited and has no appreciable effect outside of combat
The game centers around space combat and gathering territory
You can only have 8 ships and they always travel as a group
It can feel a little rinse and repeat in the late game on Epic stick to shorter games
None of those things surprise me this is not a $50.00 game. What it does not have is any bugs I have found, it performs perfectly, and I have had fun playing it. I like space games, I like to unwind, I do not like to feel like I am managing an empire when I get off work during the week. This is exactly what I expected when I bought it, I watched a lot of game play videos from the creators before buying.
I suggest if you like science fiction and want something to play thats simple and fun. Give it a try, watch a few videos first if you are unsure.
If however, you are expecting the next Orions, Civ in Space, Galactic Civ or what have you then you will be dissapointed. It plays like a lightweight X-Com in space. This would not be a game for you.
Hope this helps!

Game is super boring and repetitive. You go into a dungeon and go through 4 levels before a boss level. You do this four times, and every time is the EXACT same. Each level has the exact same layout of similar looking square rooms with barrels and boxes in them. No level felt different in the slightest. Each level has a shop/exit room, a secret locked chest room, and 3 hidden colored keys (thought we moved on from that after "Doom" and "Duke Nukem"?). There are about 6-7 total different enemies and each level there is a fake computer slot machine to decide which 3 of the 7, but after you've played a few levels you will have seen them all enough to be super sick of them. For some reason the whole system and mechanics are flawed. Lets start with money. You made money INCREDIBLY slowly. Each level you might make 200 or so, and thats the cost of 1 special weapon shot, or the cost of combining a few types of shots. Each barrel only gives you 1-2 gold, so they are worthless, and even the secret chest that seems like a lot gives you like 100. Oh but lets not forget how there are 5 tiers of armor, and the 2nd one costs 500. Yes it costs about 2-3 levels to afford it. Oh and guess what, it gives you stats and another health bar basically, but its just like health, which goes down super quickly, and once its gone, its completely gone, and you're out 500 bucks and 2-3 levels of gold farming, and it usually is gone by the first or second level you use it. You can repair it while its low, but oh wait, thats 150-200, about equal to what you get per level, meaning you can't repair it until you beat the level, but if you lose it during the level its too late. Horrible system and made me not want to use it. Why cant you sell things you pick up to make extra money you ask, as you will get multiple extra shots and will have like tons of materials each level when you only need 5, and can't use more for some reason, to make armor. But oh wait, those semi-rare shots you picked up, they sell anywhere from 1-2 gold to 10 gold, meaning they don't do sh!t for your gold. Oh and those materials that have tons of that you don't need, those sell for 2 gold or so, meaning you can make a whopping 50 gold from selling everything, which won't pay for anything. If it sounds dumb to you that's because it is.
And if you die on a level you lose your entire equipped shots, meaning something you spent 300-500 gold to make is gone. The best part is, now that you have no money, and you've used all your good shots, and it costs money just to put shots together, you are super weak and do no damage at the next level, which just makes things worse for no reason. The funny part is, combining shots doesn't even make it stronger, it just adds effects. I had 6 things combined and it still took about 6-7 shots to kill 1 single guy, and there are like 4 per room, and 50 per level. Oh but you can level up, at about once every 2-3 levels. And you super boringly can put 4 total points in 5 categories such as damage, speed, fire rate, etc. There are no cool abilities or any excitement in leveling up. And seeing as you gain 1 point in a few stats, it makes almost no different from level to level. Then there's this moronic ammo. So lets say you spent 3 levels worth of dough, actually got good types of shots, spent good money combining them, and haven't died so you don't drop them all, that's all it takes right? Wrong. You actually have set ammo, which drains 2 ammo per shoot, and about 50 guys per level, and 10 shots per guy or so, you got it right, that means even for playing well you run out of all that money you spent on shots in ONE LEVEL or so. Yes there are a few ammo pickups but they add 10 ammo and you spent about 100 before you find each one. The system makes no sense and basically means you run out of the money that takes you foreever to make, no matter what you do. There are only a few shots, and you use the same ones every level. Super boring. Oh and don't let me forget the genious idea of mushrooms, which you spend money or keys on chest to get, and they either give OR take your stats away. And as everyone on the forums can agree on, its about 4-1 ratio in favor of those taking away your stats, so just a dumb idea, a waste of money, and almost no value to them as a mechanic as they are illogical. There just isn't really any fun reason to play the game. Super repetitive and boring, no spells, boring leveling, never make money, don't do any damage, everything is too expensive. So save yourself the trouble. 4.5/10.

After a long session of Call of Duty I can honestly say I couldn't be happier my friend suggested 'Orcs Must Die! 2' when I asked for a good tower defense game. OMD!2 will honestly be considered one of my favourite games of all time despite only having it for 1 month... it's incredibly fun, addictive and rewarding all at the same time.
The story mode was entertaining due to the variety of strategies you could employ to complete them and the fact that each level can be completed at a different success rate. Beyond this there is an unlockable 'nightmare' mode which adds another layer of strategy to the game as well as making the game more addictive. However the story mode lacked any real in-depth storyline, there were only 2 cut-scenes that I can remember and each were short.
Beyond story mode you could play endless which was interesting due to the more advanced enemies, it could however be deemed a touch repetitive or tedious. I didn't see it this way as it was always rewarded. There are many acheivements to obtain and none of them felt grindy, completing the story mode got you most of them and the others introduced you to other dimensions of the game such as combo'ing (however you will have to pay for DLC to get 100% completion).
Overall I would say the game is definitely worth a purchase at it's cheap price due to it including Steam trading cards / achievements and being thoroughly enjoyable.

The thing I'd like to do in this review is to try and dispel the myth that Dark Souls is some uber-hard, ultra-difficult game where only the most pro players can even complete the tutorial. As I've said before, this is a myth. While Dark Souls is challenging and you will make mistakes, you will learn from these mistakes and you will surmount these obstacles. Dark Souls isn't going to kill you over and over, giving you no benefit. It's going to beat you down, showing you exactly why you died (enemy animations, status effects, et cetera), and let you learn from your mistakes, eventually turning you into something better than you were before. Dark Souls doesn't try to break you down, it tries to build you up, giving you all the tools to get better.

Enemy AI makes no sense: sometimes swarms of enemies will gleefully dive-bomb you from off screen, and other times the same enemy types will sit perfectly still, ignoring you as you shoot them. You have health, but levels are mostly made up of insta-death pits. The story mocks itself and the game's arbitrary mechanics right from the first level. Even more embarrassingly, the first thing you see in the game is the fact that two-thirds of the game's content (the second and third acts) are listed as "Coming soon!", despite the game having been released seven years ago (as I write this). It doesn't matter what price point this game is offered at, there is no enjoyment to be had here.

Short version:
If you like tower defense games, this one is a must have!
Besides the classic isometric TD playstyle, the game offers a "town" screen were you expand and build your town to unlock new "towers", collect resources, research upgrades and level up in a RPG-like manner.
Long version:
During the TD missions:
Like in most classic TD games you heavily rely on upgradable "towers" (cost gold) to defend against the hordes of enemies. The towers have an OK balancing and certain strengths/weaknesses against the enemies - thereby you usually require a healthy mixture of towers to beat the level.
You can/need cast a set of spells (cost mana), which can make quite a difference.
Tower placement is usually restricted to the area flanking the path towards the mission exit, but in some missions you can choose the placement of the towers freely and thereby control the pathing of the enemies.
Throughout the campaign you accomplish quests and unlock more upgrades for your towers/spells and playstyles (four difficulties for campaign, challenges, survival and there is also  pvp)
Town screen:
By advancing in the game (= doing quests/missions) you unlock new buildings, which in turn unlock new upgrades and new quests. So the town screen is sort of a clickfest, were you also select your next mission, level up (3 skill trees) and choose from a large variety of upgrades. This game is an interesting one. I was thinking of not reccomending it, but I still play the game to this day (read on for why), and have 180 hours on record at the time of writing, at least 80 of which weren't because of the reason you'll soon discover. So, I reckon it's worth trying.
Also, this is a long review. Buckle up.
Starbound is, or was, at its core, an exploration and survival game. However, with the full release of the game, it started to lean heavily on the story, compromising other areas of the game to do this. Don't get me wrong - the story missions are all quite fun, and while I'm not a fan of the clue-hunting padding the game throws in, it doesn't take too long if you've explored and bookmarked enough planets.
The problem with the story, however, is that it has resulted in severe diminishing of other aspects of the game. Before full release, there were loads of unique technologies you could unlock, including techs that would let you fly and such.
But, presumably to stop players moving out of bounds during missions, these techs were mostly removed in favour of a less characterful system. And it doesn't stop there - progression gating is a big problem in Starbound. Sure, after the starting mission you can go and explore to your heart's content, but alot of content - mainly the stuff centred around the outpost (where all of the main shops are) - stays locked away until you've tackled the story. The story is presumably why the dynamic temperature system was removed by an early update, and why the new EPP (Environmental Protection Pack) system is so bland.
In essence, Chucklefish killed off a chunk of their game for the sake of balance - something I implore budding game developers to not do. This limited the playtime of the average player from what could have been 500 hours to a figure more like 50 hours. Still a lot, but nowhere near as much.
The game is fun enough to play in the moment. The combat system, while not groundbreaking, is fully functional and enjoyable. And the building and farming systems, from my point of view, are exceptionally effective, to the point that they're something other games could learn from. Plus, the musical intrument system is ridiculously fun to play around with, especially in multiplayer. On top of that, one thing I can't complain about is the variety of planets - they all have unique landscapes and are all characterful, although some setpieces re-occur frequently. Seeing a pleasant village in a volcanic wasteland is a bit off-putting, to say the least. And some things in the game, like the liquid physics system, are simply worth seeing. Plus, the soundtrack was composed by a genius (plural?).
Unfortunately, the buiding system is almost completely obselete from a gameplay point of view - you don't need a house when you can just put all of your crafting stations on your ship, do you? Plus, unless you're on survival difficulty - which means you drop EVERYTHING on death - you won't need a farm for food, either.
Also, it seems that they removed - or at least reduced to the point of non-existence - the unique abilities for each of the races. The only one I've found is that one race gives off more light than usual. All the other races give off light in the darkness anyway (for some reason), making this difference very subtle.
Some of the weapons in the game are highly unique and fun to use. However, their strength is based on planet you found them on. So, unless you're at a very late game planet, you'll be replacing that ultra-exciting weapon with a boring broadsword soon enough. Plus, the different armours don't seem to do anything differently - all of the different races armours are just reskins of each other from what I can tell. They branch out a bit towards the end of the game, but it's far too little, far too late.
The procedurally generated monsters don't feel procedurally generated. They all look broadly the same, and mostly favour the 'RAM IT UNTIL IT DIES' tactic. There are some unique monsters, but when you see them on almost every planet, the novelty wears off quickly.
On top of that, the performance is abysmal for a game of this genre. When a 2D game lags more than Skyrim, you're doing something VERY wrong. If you have a decent PC, you should be able to run it, but if you're lower end (like me) you may have to make some sacrifices in the quality department.
You would think that, from reading this review, after your initial playthrough, you'd never touch it again. However, there is one key point I have yet to touch upon - mods. If you don't plan on modding the game, then expect a boringly average playtime (unless you truly love building, that is).
There are mods out there that fix the tech system, mods that fix the story gating, mods that fix the temperature system, mods that fix the racial abilities, mods that add exciting new weapons and armour, mods that fix the difficulty settings, mods that add new missions and characters, mods that add new planet types, mods that add new setpieces, and even mods that improve the performance.
With mods, the game becomes so much more than what it is alone. Mods are why I still play the game to this day, whether creating them or playing with them. A draw of this game (and perhaps why the performance is so poor?), is that it is incredibly easy to mod. Think something's missing and can't find a mod for it? Make it yourself!
Starbound is still being updated, however. Whilst this is a good thing, changes to code mean that many important mods become incompatible with new updates. And it's anyones guess as to whether the mod creator will update the mod to compensate. If you use bigger universe-changing mods, saves can become corrupted very easily, and if your mods aren't updated, you'll never be able to play them again.
In conclusion, I would say that, without mods, this game is still worth the price tag due to the playtime you're likely to get. Just don't expect anything revolutionary, UNLESS you truly love building. If you love building, and are willing to do it despite the relative pointlessness, you'll be able to siphon off a good few more hours. Some of my favourite memories from the game involve trying to build a base at the bottom of a poisonous ocean on a radioactive planet.
If you use mods, however, you'll have a whale of a time. Keep your mod list fairly minimalistic, and your saves should survive indefinitely. Use bigger mods, and you might have more fun, but your saves might not last past an update.
And that, dear reader, is the true dilemma of playing Starbound.

Eventually I became more invested than anticipated.  Soon, I WAS Elodie and she was me and we were a terrifying force to reckon with.  I am a benevolent princess who will show mercy to misguided subjects, but I am no fool.  If you do not take kindly to my mercy, you shall fear the hellfire I control at my magical-girl fingertips.  If you will not bow in respect, then you shall quake in fear.
Sadly my magic was not strong enough to defeat an entire navy....this time.
Bonus suggestion:
Try getting a group of friends together and playing in "democracy mode."  Everyone has to debate and vote on all decisions in Elodie's upbringing.  Then, when no one listens to you, blame them for the princesses death!  Family fun for all!

If you played Fate/Extra (And if you havn't, I highly recommend it) then this game is for you. If you havn't played Fate/Extra, you might well enjoy this, but do yourself a big favour and pick up Fate/Extra first.
Brief: The game to my mind acts as a sort of epilogue for Fate/Extra, telling a very happy story of events after the  MC Holy Grail War - This alone is brilliant, as one normally never gets to experience the "happy ever after" part of a story, but here it is!
As a result, the story is bubbly, upbeat, with appropriate ups and downs and a lot, and I mean a lot of romantic content.
One downside is that the story can get repetitive, since it tells mostly the same story from multiple perspectives. That's par for the course with Nasu, but Extella's routes are pretty short, so the sense of repetition is real.
The gameplay is, well..I thought it was a lot of fun. It's a very chaotic musou game with relatively simple controls and the ability to swap heroes around added a new layer of fun to it. While I can't say there was anything particularly special about obliterating Plants (Robots) and capturing zones, it felt very satisfying to carve a swath of destruction along a map and watch it turn blue. Pretty fun, all in all, but dont expect anything complicated here! Graphics are not exactly a masterpiece, and I get the feeling it wasn't supposed to be.
The servant fights are also quite simple but still very fun. Nothing more to add there.
Conclusion: This game is made for the fans, really, people who enjoy the Fate Series and -especially- those who played Fate/Extra and it's related games - It's about seeing what happens after the War, and the gameplay mostly plays a supportive role, with most effort seemingly having gone into the story, My Room Events, and cutscenes.
It's a lot of fun if that is your thing.

One of the best games of the decade. A tight, fun, challenging experience with an interesting world, loads of options for gameplay progression, and a bunch of secrets that are fun to find. It is made even better with Artorias of the Abyss, which adds 3 of the best bosses FromSoft have ever had.
Very little needs to be said about its good elements, as this is the game that built a franchise on challenge and mystery in the era of handholding and objective markers, but suffice to say it feels a lot more like an adventure in a fantasy world than many other games with that premise in your early playthroughs, and it remains stimulating even after you become very familiar with its content.
The main issues you will encounter are related to online and a select few enemies. Connections are typically shakey and lead to invasions and co-op that are very unreliable, and the fact that backstabs are so powerful makes PVP matches usually just devolve into circle strafing. The power of backstabs also trivialize some enemies, most notably the Silver and Black Knights who lose almost all of their menace once you begin circling them. A few of the unique enemies are seemingly not designed to actually be fought, such as the Hellkite Drake and giant tick in Blighttown.
The game initially feels like you're trying to break-down a wall with your face, but unlike many other games proud of their "difficulty", you routinely discover the sledgehammer you didn't see once you take a step back and look around the room. Unfortunately for you, though, there's a famous midgame boss who grabs your hammer and will probably beat you to death with it dozens of times your first time through, but once you snatch it back there are few examples of video game catharsis better than riding that elevator up to the most amazing chest in the game.

A very simple game, but fairly priced for the amount of content. The demo-video on steam shows it locked to 4:3, however the game DOES scale to fill your monitor (looked fine at 1080p widescreen for me.)
My wife absolutely loved the game, and actually beat its campaign today, the same day we bought the game.
Mechanics are very, very, simple. It's a "casual" game. You can play the entire game with only a mouse. Scrolling with a keyboard feels kinda slow, so using just your mouse is very preferrable.
You control a limited number of workers and order them to complete basic tasks, gather food, wood, stone, water, and so on. Your workers cannot die, from starvation, animal attacks, or anything else, so theres really no "mistakes" you can make, other than just being innefficient. It's completely safe to leave the game unattended for hours, however you won't gain anything beneficial from doing so.
There are no microtransations or time sinks. Some actions/activities take longer to complete, but it's only to scale with the importance of the task you're doing (ie, scouting an important cave for a main-questline might take a few minutes) and to give each of the maps some longevity. There is no "speed up" options or anything like that in the entire game, although on particularily longer tasks you can "accelerate" the process by using extra workers and food.
Gameplay feels a lot like a mobile game with all the microtransactions and time sinks removed.
For the price I paid, around 5-bucks, I feel I received sufficient game depth. If you're a fan of "Casual" titles, where the challenge isn't about avoiding failure, but instead, maximizing efficiency and enjoying the experience along the way, you're more likely to enjoy it.

Hello All,
First for the price you get a much more involved game than you would think.  So far I haven't seen any bugs that I can tell, and its got good game play.
This game has one major drawback that I didn't see others mention, the constant clicking.  You have to micro manage everything, constantly.  Now most of us are used to that in some fashion in these type of games, but this is where the short cuts where taken, no matter what about every 20 seconds you have to click on everything that produces food, water, or cash, as well as all the resources that respawn for your workers to go harvest/collect.  This gets old fast.  clicklety click click click.  Thats all you do in this game.  keep clicking on the same tree, bush, same everything every 15 to 20 seconds as it respawns.
Even using the resources you gather, every few seconds click on the kitchen, to make more stuff, no auto queing.  After 10 hours I was clicked out.  Just way to much clicking.   That said, if you can suffer through that, the rest of it is as others said a fun little game.
if the workers would be auto gather on where you send them once, and the wells, tents, and grills would auto collect after the first upgrade, that would make the game much more tolerable.
Edit the next day ... ok so once you get to level 19 ... you get a reprieve from most of the clicking.  They finally give you a perk where you only have to click on one tent, or one water well, or one brazier, and you collect everything from them all.  Also by that time, you aren't so desparate for collecting the respawning wood stone and food as much so the game play is much more enjoyable.
I finished the game today ...  nice game, well wortth the price, but i don't see any real replay ability.   I also got the feeling like I had played this game before or one very very similiar.
I would highly suggest they patch this and put that once click resource perk so you get it before you leave the first island, that would really make the game play much more enjoyable.
Also for you planners who like to max resources before you jump to the next new place ... um as far as food, water and cash go ... don't bother , you basically start over each time.  When you get to the third place .... thats when its worth really going for it, and purchasing most of the big stuff.
Enjoy, looking forward to a second one.

A very nice, very casual, but highly involving resource gathering/management game.
It's not a time management game, as you can do any given task at any time, in any order, totally at your leisure.
It's hard to pigeon-hole this game to any specific genre. It's not a Virtual Villager clone as there is no set roles for your people, no skills or anything. You just have whomever is available do the job you need done.
It's a pretty long game IMO, as I've put in eight hours already and am only in the second area. It has a main storyline quest, lots of side quests, and quite a few items to buy and upgrade.
It has some mini-puzzle events, but in keeping with its casual theme, no brain cells will be harmed in doing them and they do fit in with the game, such as match-three for tunneling into mines to find ore.
All in all it is exactly as described in the description. It's a fun, addictive casual game that just wants to entertain and involve the player, and it does so very well. Highly, highly recommended.

Finders is a casual resource management game where you and your team of workers set out for a journey to rescue the guardian of the world, Altair. It is a lot more casual compared to other titles in the genre, for better, or worse, personally I appreciate Alawar for trying to bring a different experience to the table.
Despite being a resource management game, the levels in Finders do not have a time constraint, or even a failure state, this can be a huge turn off for some people as the game in turn offers less of a challenge. However, the game does offers you a surprising amount of freedom when it comes to building and expanding the camp and allows you advance through the level at your own pace.
The core gameplay is solid to say the least, you are given the task to complete a variety of different objectives in the game in your own time, in order to progress through the level. At first it mainly consist of setting up your camp and satisfy the basic needs of your workers, but the game opens up considerably afterwards and introduces you to a plethora of new mechanics and features, including a well made match 3 mini game, completed with power ups and abilities.
In short, Finders is a great game if you’re looking for a stress free, casual experience that is chock full of quality contents that’ll keep you entertained for a fair amount of time.

Finders:
~~~~~~~
Altair is missing!! Since his disappearance phenomenon, the likes of earthquake have become more frequent, even animals react strangely. We need to find Altair, this hero who is well known for his good deeds. Our only hope is to retrieve an artefact that may guide us to his whereabouts. Your mission is to find him.
Finders, is a casual management / strategy game where you have to achieve tasks to be able to move further into the story. In some instances, you will play a match 3 types puzzle game to collect specifics resources.
There is plenty things to do in this game, your workers will have to build tents, braziers, barbecues, kitchens, wells, storages etc. Also, you will have to gather plenty of resources like foods, wood, stone and herbs to make a revitalizing cup of tea! You can take your jeep to town to sell or buy articles that you may need to achieve a task in progress.   However, keep in mind that every action will cost you food and you must keep this resource well stocked.
You will be able to get some interesting item at the shop. For example, you might need a helicopter, a plane or a truck. All articles in the shop cost money but you must achieve a specific level to be able to purchase some of them.
Finders is very easy to master and will appeal to players who enjoy a good casual game.
The graphics are nice and the game runs well.
Positives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Nice graphics
-	Plenty of things to do
-	Easy to master
-	Nice combination of management /strategy and match 3 type a gameplay
-	Achievements
-	Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	A bit repetitive
In a nutshell, a good casual game.
8/10

This game is just plain awful.
I really don't recommend this game. It's basically unfished it even has levels in the games code that were never used.
The problem with this game is that they sold this with the promise of more content in the future. Then completely backed out and left this game unfished. There are actually menu options for these chapters and they're just blank.
Essentially Luc Bernard sold us a game in beta and never finished it. Imagine buying a game in early access to then have the developer announce they weren't going to finish the game and just left you all with a buggy beta mess.
Of course you ask: "But what of the content that is in the game?"
It's... average at best. The level design is not interesting at all and all levels are just "find 3 gems and get to the exit." If that sounds boring it's because it is. There is no story in this game save for some scrolling of text and then some poorly written, and unfunny banter between the two main characters in the game. I spoke to Luc Bernard about this before in the past, when his game had just been release and he claimed that the game was going to have a deeper story but his collegue thought it was "too cheesy" and so they dropped it. Oh wonderful.
The combat is mostly just shooting some rather bland enemies with boring designs and poorly coded AI. Hell there is a robot bird enemy in this game that will stop chasing you or attacking you if you move past his "activation point."
I hear what you're saying: "But this game is just so gosh damn beautiful."
Absolutely. Excluding the poor monster design Luc Bernard has done some rather pretty artwork. But it's all ruined by the awful sprites. The beautiful mind that is Luc Bernard chose to stick with ragdoll physics instead of actual animation.
Oh speaking of physics! Do you like falling damage in your 2D side scrolling platform games? Because Eternity's Child has it.
So to sum up.
-Painfully average level designs
-Below average gameplay
-Mixed presentation
-Unfinished game
Is it worth it for the price? No. Absolutely not. Don't even give this man money because he doesn't deserve it.
Use your money to buy a better game on Steam. Because there are loads more better indie platformers and other games.

I never thought I'd play a modern video game that reminded me of Action 52, but here it is.
I don't even know where to start with this terribly unfinished game. First: Who are these characters? What is going on with the story? IS there a story?? I found there is supposed to be a plain text crawl explaining the story & characters of this game (a lazy move on part of the designers there, one of many), but when the game starts, there is no such thing. Everything you do has no context as to why you're doing it. The bubbles that slowly describe the game's few controls on the first stage are so slow that you're trying to read these things as you're endlessly shooting stuff that wants to fly right into your face and at weird angles, even for a platformer.
The controls are a total mess, you slide off platforms if you don't angle your blurry jumps just so, if you can see where you're jumping that is. The camera likes to stick on your character's position in such a way that you are often jumping blindly into who knows what, more likely than not, it's something that will kill you. Jumping is iffy at best with having to learn the trick to getting a decent jump without slipping off edges or even getting to a higher up platform. This would be fine if there was a way to grab platform edges, there isn't.
I don't understand the point of having two characters to worry about if the one you actually move doesn't do anything else but that, the flying girl shoots at enemies & nothing else. This is really unnecessary & could have been done better with just one character doing these things.
Many, many sections of the game, both while playing & in the menus, appears to be either really buggy, unfinished, or both. I'm betting on both. Even for an episodic game (which I can see why the sub-sequent chapters never saw daylight), there should have better effort on cleaning this game up, at least so someone knows wtf is going on when they start playing. Again, an intro would have been nice here. Another odd happening is that I got a totally different level 3 on later playthroughs, sometimes happening before I was done in the last area. No warning, just a new level out of nowhere. I even fell through solid walls a few times.
I can say good things about the art style of this game, it's vibrant, pretty to look at & a gothic sort of cute. It's pretty much ruined by the camera motions & animation style they used in this game; very bland, lifeless & marionette-like. Plenty of other games pull off a 2-D world with life & emotion, why didn't this game?
Seriously, save your money. Maybe buy this as a gag gift for a friend if it's on sale for $1. Try the buggy demo, but do -not- pay money for this disappointing and unfinished fragment of a game.

I'll cut to the core (of the bad stuff). The game is HEAVILY relying on server communications for absolutely everything. No connection and the game doesn't start. Bad connection gives you poorly synced animations, skills that miss or skills that don't even trigger. Not only in multiplayer maps, but every campaign map as well. Monster takes an arrow to the chest and loses health a second later. It's jarring to watch.
So before you invest in this be aware of two things:
1) If you are on a poor connection the game plays like♥♥♥♥♥ Like really bad. Perhaps it's enough to be far from the servers. (I'm in japan)
2) The $10 price is a rental fee since if the popularity doesn't go up then the servers will go down (as seen again and again with other games).
So buying this is a gamble. Steamcharts says there are about 30 people online at any given time, and maybe double that since the last sale (could be a local variation).
There are also a bunch of bugs in the game, but the team actually seems to be on top of those.
Other than that the game is good. Graphics style is cool. Gameplay is not terribly deep, but the progression is fun.
Recommend?  Not right now. I wouldn't have bought it (even at sale price) if I had known what I know now. Wait a few months, maybe more. If the player base is not shrinking, and the updates keeps coming then yeah, probably safe to get then.

I remember spending hundreds of hours playing this game on the Gamecube, and was excited to see a PC port of it. I waited to get it, though, after seeing the flood of feedback on poor framerates and other issues, but when I finally caved in to my desire to relive my memories, I was thrilled to see that the game ran smoothly AND had the option for Japanese voice-overs, something that was sorely absent from the GC version.
However, I've barely made any progress at all, due to opting to start off on Hard Mode, and thus needed to grind a bit to both gain much needed strength and to regain my skills with Lloyd. That said, I've just managed to get Kratos in my party, and now have the Sorcerer's Ring... but I've discovered one MAJOR FLAW that will make this game almost unplayable for me once I make further progress...
WHERE THE ♥♥♥♥ IS MY FREE-RUN?!? THAT IS A CRUCIAL PART OF THE BATTLES!!
Seriously! Without the free-run (I discovered the lack of it while fighting the Golems during the puzzle to get the Ring), there is only one way to fight any large monster or boss... running face-first into them - which, as we all know, is a Total Wipe waiting to happen at worst, and suicidally recovery-item-dependent at best. No free-run means having to COMPLETELY change how I play!!
That said, I'm still gonna play the game, but this NEEDS TO BE FIXED!! And the fix is ♥♥♥♥in' simple! Change the default input on the gamepad (I use a usb-wired 360 controller) to the D-pad and put the free-run on the left bumper!
Despite this painfully suicidal issue, I still love it, and that love will never be diminished... or extinguished. And I would still recommend it, as it's one of the three games I'd ever consider doing a 100% Completion run of... the others being its sequel, Dawn of the New World, and Skies of Arcadia: Legends (which needs to be ported properly to Steam as well).

Alright, so, I finished one playthrough and tried to start few new games with different settings, here is the impression so far:
Gameplay:
+Simple to understand resource management
+-Some super basic diplomacy that creates a light feeling of space empire game, although, you can break peace and attack your opponent the very same turn which kind of completely defeats the point of a diplomacy
+Few different ways to build up your ecocnomy\strength
+Fleet upgrades are very flexible and allows for some interesting ship specialites
+Fights are decently strategic
although:
-(huge minus, I ragequit the game few minutes ago because of that) Asteroid moving system(unless it is a bug). So, let me make an example: I hid my fleet behind a formation of really big asteroids, launched a few fighters, checked my LOS and every ship on the enemy team was untargetable. Clicked Next Turn. First thing I see is that an asteroid that was right in front of my fleet dissapeared and now 5 enemy ships are shooting me with 100% damage modifier. Now. If it is a system, there has to be some form of an indicator of which ones are moving(not necessary the location, but just an idea of which cover cannot be reliably used). If it was made for preventing people from defensive camping - good, but in this case you might remove all the asteroids as there is no way to predict your enemy's next turn(it is a strategy game , afterall). If it is a bug - GOD, this has to be fixed as soon as possible. I am EXTREMELY interested in the point of view of any developer\community manager on that topic.
UI:
+planetary management is simple enough and UI does it's job
-No HP/Weapons/Modules indicators (that I've seen) on enemy ships aside from the info on a pre-mission briefing. How can I tell if the ship is going down soon? How can I tell if that ship is stronger at close combat? Which ship should I target?
-Line of sight is really hard to manage, there is no visible indicator if the ship is in range of attack OR if the ship will be able to attack after the move (again, it is a strategy game not an aracde shooter). Defeats the idea of tactical movement, you just HOPE that your lasers will reach
-No Indicator of which weapon will be used at the certain distance, Would be great to see a tri-colour targetting arrow that shows which weapon will you fire at what range. I think it is a simple to implement and yet very important feature(again, we are trying to make tactical decisions in a STRATEGY game)
-Diplomacy screen is super-simple(also, very small for some reason) and a bit hard to understand from the first glance, and I am used to the complex screens of CIV and other 4x games
+Global view gives just enough information to the player, very functional and not cluttered.
Graphics:
+- Functional, nothing to praise, nothing to complain about
-No options. I want to skip\speed-up animation on a global view, same in the battle screen. Every CIV game has it...
Overall:
I REALLY want to like this game, I was excited from the moment I heard about it. I have done the pre-order and... I think it was a mistake. The game has potential, but it is buried behind tons of questionable decisions. In ideal world it is a fun, fast, strategy game, that can be finished within an hour. As it stands, I have very little desire to start a new playthough after I learned some of the flaws. I helped design\QA some UI for Network Software and I am genuinely surpised how most of the things I mentioned as a negative were missed\not mentioned during the development process.
You might have a different experience than I did, maybe it is just a matter of personality.

Sid Meir's Starship may not at first seem to be the be all end all for a PC game.  You are playing a Sid Meir game, you are not here for the textures or graphics but rather the gameplay, and oh boy the gameplay does deliver. In a short quick game session you can finish a type of victory (I use type because if you go all dominiton and alliance the game can be won in about 3hrs). However, replayability is high.
Where it fails to livy what Beyond Earth failed to do, it does however stay  true to it's true purpose. Being Admiral Adama and fighting the Cylon in a race for time to stay alive...Well it's not about BSG but you get the feel of it. Every time you are in a battle, you get the tense feeling. Constantly studying the battle field and thinking 4 moves ahead. Should you place your fighters there in hopes they get the brunt force and not your destroyer, or maybe yet use the torpedo you launch 3 moves ago to wipe out a hub of enemy. When not in battle, you get to grow your Planets with cities, buildings, improvments, money/science making improvment, buying influence in order to gain control of the galaxy vastness of population.

I have owened every Sid Meier game made.  I am a fan.  I am a Civilization Fan as well.   I am also a turn based fan in general.  That said I haven't been near the fan of Civ: BE as prior Civ games, and was a disappointed with it.  That said when I heard about Starships I was interested though I didn't jump on it like I would normally have done.  That said when GMG offered a great sale on the game for just over $10 prior to release I went ahead and figured what the heck and picked the game up.
First off I do believe that Starships was going to be an expansion or even part of Beyond Earth.  Does it feel like a AAA game?  No, but then again it is not selling at AAA prices.   Does the fact that it is tablet friendly make it less of a fun game? No I don't think so.   Is the game complex?  No, but it is fun for when you want to kick back and just have a relaxed turn based game.
I know that the game is getting mixed reviews, however I haven't seen any bugs in the game, and have enjoyed it for the small amount of time I have been playing it so far.  Is it ground breaking?  Not  in the least.  But for even the asking price I have hundreds of games that I paid double the price for and found far less entertaining.

To me it is going to be one of those games that I turn to when I am watching TV and have other distractions yet want something to do when I don't feel like forwarding through commericals.  That said if you like space games, and like Turn Based games, I personally feel the game is worth the money as is.

I thought I'd be playing a classic because of the positivity of the reviews.
The game started out awesome, lots of good features, but I was quickly and brutally disappointed very soon.
SFX and graphics are pretty good I think, especially because it's a console port. Very fast loading which is great for this genre.
Atmosphere is decent enough, but walking through Mordor freely is a bit weird... although I don't know too much about LOTR.
Which is why I don't discuss story in the LOTR universe. The story as a standalone is pretty cliché at every turn, but I wouldn't give minus points for it.
The characters feel real enough. They're nothing special, but they aren't forced on you either, which I can appreciate.
The nemesis system is quite creative, I'm happy to see new features like that especially in supposed AAA games.
Killing orcs is satisfying and never feels too much.
Even after a few hours it's painfully obvious how terrible the controls are.
Your character will often stop near walls instead of climbing them or running next to them.
This is partly because climbing and running are assigned to the same key, and partly because the way the game determines your movement direction is extremely inconsistent.
In this game you'll never need true sneaking: you can run into an uruk from the front and can still perform a stealth kill, therefore sneaking alongside walls is ultimately useless.
Directional climbing and directional jumping are severely limited, not allowing you otherwise trivial movement.
The game has a really hard time distinguishing between "dodging" and "vault over enemy", which is bad during most fights, but a torture while fighitng a boss that can't be vaulted over.
During quick time events inputs are often disregarded.
It gets even worse when you're fighting big groups - you know, when QTEs are a matter of life and death - where 25-30% of the QTEs are forfeit because the game just refuses to register the keystrokes.
There's also a last stand QTE which doesn't trigger half the time and you just get auto-killed for whatever reason.
It seems like the game takes your last input much before the QTE animation event starts.
When there are lots of small, descending steps following eachother your character will jump-stop-jump-stop-jump-stop.
It's not a serious problem by itself of course, just an example of how little thought went into the game engine/map design, even though it should've been made for parkour.
Combat and exploration are the heart of the gameplay.
They're outdated and/or broken. I've had smoother gameplay in the first Assassin's Creed.
But I'll continue since the problems don't end there.
Can't lock onto enemies, meaning your attacks and abilities just go every which way, even if you have an important target.
Your camera is often force-turned into another direction even during fights.
You can't restart missions. Not main quests, not sidequests.
You can replay them if you failed of course, but if you want to restart because you missed the bonues objective, well... you just have to start a new campaign.
If you abandon a sidequest you'll be magically teleported to the closest forge tower which can be a 1000 ft away from the mission you want to replay.
Running through Mordor will stop being fun pretty fast.
You can't fast travel to sidequests and quests, even if you're repeating them.
Unskippable cutscenes waste your time on almost every captain encounter. Possibly stopping your executions and abilites to go off, sometimes resetting your hit streaks.
This is unnecessary and annoying by itself, but especially a problem when you find a challenging captain that you can't kill on first try.
And torture while you're trying to do the trials (these are highly repetitive challenges that can require from a few /many tries to do, depending on player).
If you're already in pursuit of a captain and run into another then the cutscene can allow the chased one to escape.
Captains can randomly disappear, nullifying all your progress on them during that encounter.
The most extreme case was when a captain ran behind a wall, about 10 feet/5 meters away from me, I was looking at his direction when the despawn happened.
After killing captains in strongholds the alarm have likely been raised, so you're surrounded by enemies, making it impossible to pick up the rune they drop, forcing an unnessecary trip away and back so the uruks despawn.
There's no reason whatsoever that runes are not picked up automatically.
After the captain cutscene the game will resume a bit before you gain control of your character, or even see anything, forcing you to take a hit if you're in close combat. During this time some captains/warchiefs will kill you in 1 hit, allowing captains to escape possibly resetting your mission.
Neither one of these would be a problem by itself.
The game is quite casual, trivial and easily exploited so my problem with these issue is not that they made the game difficult, but the fact that they completely go against common sense and/or break immersion/gameplay.
Of course these might not bother you, and obiously there are lots of problems that I anticipated and worked around, since it's not my first console port.
The overall effect of the awesomeness and buginess of the game was that I mostly felt a relief after completing a mission and very rarely felt genuine achievement or acoomplishment.
Kill, mock, rinse, repeat.

So, my first review after 12 years on Steam. Warstone is easy to learn and horribly hard to master, it is designed to keep you entertained for a long time, in my opinion absolutely worth the price if you like TDs in general.

I really enjoyed the campaign, there are more than enough units with 1-4 ingame-upgrades, each of the towers is needed and makes sense. 3 scenarios with 4 difficulties each. You'll get new possibilities to constantly upgrade units after nearly each mission. After some time you'll get daily farm, I wasn't expecting that this keeps me coming back nearly every day to play a bit, but it did. Expect to upgrade for (at least?) half a year if you would want each update or replay a ton of games. I am miles away from getting all upgrades and I will never get them all, for the first playthrough you don't need a lot of them, you'll get enough during the campaign. It will take at least 15h just the clear the campaign on normal difficulty.
The campaign starts that easily, that I desided the play it on the highest available difficulty setting without leaks from the start... I ended up playing some of the missions on "easy" just to barely survive. In order get the a gold star you'll have to fulfill a condition (like not to build a certain tower) and have no leaks, i still fail to get some gold stars on the easiest scenario. In some missions on harder settings I still don't have a clue how to even survive, but i feel it's possible. So i retry from time to time with a new idea on my mind and sometimes it works.
You'll have a nice time and use some of you brains to get to the end.

Coop: In order the get all stars and upgrades, you'll "have to" play Coop for some time, at first i didn't like the idea to be "forced" to mp, but it's really fun, especially since a friend of mine got the game. If you dont have someone to play with, it can take some time to find a game, sometimes really strong players help you to get a star in an early mp-lvl, i really liked that. In order to just finish the campaign it is not needed to play any MP.
PvP: First of all, yes I repeat myself, you don't need to PvP. I didn't PvP a single time, i somehow dislike that all the upgrades count in PvP, so I guess the 10 most farmed players are constanly winning. I would be reconsidering if there is a setting that both are on the exact same tech-lvl somehow or have the same lvl. But generally I don't care about PvP in a TD.
All in all I consider Warstone TD absolutely worth the price and time playing it, really a good TD with some smart dev's, they still really try to improve the game and are responding quickly in the forum. Give it a try, you won't regret it. :)

From time-management to resource-gathering, then on to crafting and mini-games including match-3 and logic puzzles, Finders has a little from each of the casual classics. The game frames this all in an adventure story, which plays out as you accomplish goals and build up your camp and add little bits of interesting tech as you go.
Finders is an easy and relaxing game, with no time pressure or tricky strategic maneuvering to ramp up the difficulty. The game saves whenever you exit, so you can easily play in tiny increments without having to redo anything.
If you're looking for a challenge, you will probably want to look elsewhere. If you just want a relaxing experience that rewards the achievement of simple goals with a cute and colorful adventure story, then check this one out.
The trading cards are nice, but I do wish that the in-game trophies were available as Steam achievements.

Finders is an addictive casual Time/Resource Management game that both feels familiar and manages to put its own unique spin on the genre.
In Finders you direct an expedition that crash lands while in search an artifact in order to help locate a lost hero.  You're left to send survivors out to gather resources and build up the camp in order to continue the mission, which has 4 separate chapters.
Where Finders diverges from many other casual time management games is that it's area based rather than level based and you get to stay in one area for a long time. I found I liked this style of gameplay a bit better than hurrying through multiple levels as I felt more invested in gradually improving my camp and gathering resources since I would be there for some time.
You get a constant stream of mini goals that usually involve building or gathering resources and in some cases may even include short puzzles. Some of these will further the campaign along while others or merely optional goals to allow an opportunity to gain experience and levels.
The pace of the game is relaxed (with one exception; more on that later) and seeing the camp grow over time made the game fun and addictive for me. In addition to the building, upgrading and resource gathering there are a couple of mini-games.
Most notably is the mining mini-game which is done as a match 3 game. These segments are timed which and I found much more hectic than the pace of the rest of the game. It's worth noting though that they are mostly optional as there are few places in the game where you're required to do it to progress and there's no real penalty for not getting very far down in the game other than using some of your water resource, which is replaceable. You can also retry as many times as you like.
The other main mini game is fishing. It's a bit of a timing mouse click sort of mini-game that's pretty quick and fairly simple once you get the hang of it, but again this is optional and later in the game you get access to a boat you can use to gather fish without doing the mini-game.
One area I thought could have been handled a little better were the transitions between areas. You don't take money you've earned over. You can take your resources but you have to transport each resource separately by helicopter which is a bit slow and tedious as well as carries a per item fee, but you do get the option at least to bring some items over. It's all optional however as you can just as well play from scratch in the new area and there's some things you can do to maximize effeciency in transporting previous accumulations like buying up lots of the most expensive items and then selling them at the new camp.
Overall I really enjoyed Finders and found myself wanted to go back, build up my camp and progress through the campaign and its quirky story right up until the end.

Finders is the latest of Alawar Entertainment's simulation games to
its way onto Steam.  Although a bit more casual than I usually enjoy, after getting used to the gameplay I found it to be quite a relaxing and pleasant experience.
First, let me note that if you're looking for any type of challenge, even if it's an arbitrary goal that you can impose on your own gameplay to perfect your play, this really isn't the game for you.  Finders is a true casual title in that there's no time crunch, no goal that must be met to earn yourself any type of trophy (other than some easy to reach in-game achievements), nothing at all that places stress on the player.   This lack of challenge may prove too bland for some, but those who are looking for true casualness in gameplay may find it just the thing for them.
Gameplay consists of completing various quests by directing your "finders" about an area of the map, completing tasks, solving puzzles and leveling up which unlocks more actions, quests and options for the player.  As you build up your camp, gather resources, complete quests  and cut a path towards your overall objective, a simple story unfolds giving a bit of meaning to everything you're doing.  There is an element of freedom present in that you don't necessarily have to complete any task in order, but to progress you will need to work through those quests. Still, without a ticking clock hounding you, you can take your time planning out moves.  Even the resource management aspect of the game is quite forgiving as you can always spend time gathering foods or other materials if you find yourself short, then get back to questing without issue.
My main complaint is that the tutorial isn't quite as intuitive as it could be.  I spent quite a bit of time in the beginning trying to figure out just what I was supposed to do and what exactly the game itself entailed.  Once you have a grasp of how everything works it gets better, but this may be frustrating for those looking for something easy to jump right into.
For the price, Finders is worth a look if you're in the mood for casual gaming without the rush and stress that most titles in the genre employ.  Perfect for whiling away an hour here and there on lazy afternoons, if only there were Steam Achievement integration of the in-game Awards, but I'll just have to be content with trading cards for now.
Bottom Line: Recommended for players looking for a truly casual experience without the usual time crunch madness of other "casual" sim games.
