I would play this game so much I'd pass out from exhaustion and not realize it, surrounded by whatever junk food and blunt roaches i had survived on the day prior, my on-screen character at the feet of a Blacksmith pounding away at his anvil for hours upon hours until a buddy who lived in the basement working 3rd shift would angrily wake me up and tell me to shut the game off because the blacksmith hammering was making him want to actually stab me to death.  Stumble off to class (not praising the real life sun nearly as much after being in a basement for so long).  Blah blah something about economics, something about statistics or foreign languages.  There were people there I guess, opportunities and stuff, potential friends or girlfriends.  Relationships with professors I could have built to get into grad school.  Several tenths of added GPA that slipped away.  Then back to whatever dark allure this game had over me.
It wasn't enough to beat the game.....no I had to do it with the most radically differing character builds I could think of, choosing the most odd or broken paths through the game I could find or read about.  I once spent 2 whole days trying this trick where you can sequence break the game and skip a mandatory boss encounter that is designed to kill you and force you to end up in jail.  It requires an extremely difficult bit of not entirely intended platforming where failure usually means death each time.  Each time you do it you probably get 3-6 thousand souls from the enemies in the way.  I finally succeeded and had a pile of 1.6 million souls from trying it SO MANY TIMES.........and I lost them all.  Utter devastation.
Fantastic game though.  Not even as hard as everyone says once you get the hang of it.  Best designed gameworld of any game I've ever played.  Visceral, weighty, skill-based combat.  Good variety of character build possibilities (not quite as many as Dark Souls 2 but still a lot).  Fascinating lore and story, some amazing secrets and just crazy things you would never expect or ever find without some serious digging or wiki reading (this level of obtuseness may not be the proverbial cup of tea for some).  Beautiful music, responsive controls.  Not necessarily the best graphics from a texture, resolution, or dynamic lighting standpoint.  But the art style and mood totally qualify it to be a beautiful looking game in my opinion.  Camera isn't perfect but is generally good.  PvP is a bit uh.....well lets just say at this point anyone still playing it is probably gonna destroy you but there are some highly recommended mods out there and instructions here on steam to make that experience much better and less likely to run into cheaters.

This won't read like a Thumbs up review, but there is no maybe button.
First, a disclaimer. I have been looking for a Twin stick shooter rpg for ages. This almost fills the void.
Pros:
The controls are solid. The character responds well to commands.
The music is pretty fantastic.
The graphics, while simple, are pretty well done. I love dem square trees.
You can feel pretty powerful.
_______
Cons:
The bullets (pixels) are incredibly glowy. After a few levels, it's just about all you can see. But it doesn't matter much because;
The game is waaaay too easy. Once you implement resource management and get a few upgraded equips, you neve run out of ammo. Which isn't even a complaint really, I hate ammo hunting, but when I can one shot an entire room and kill the final boss before I get a good look at him, things are a tad too easy.
The game is waaaaay too short. I put like 3 hours into it and it's done. Which is unfortunate, because I was a lot of fun,
The interface. It's not pretty, and doesn't offer a lot of information about what you're looking at. For example, if you're crafting and you want to know how much ammo one of your equips have, you have to leave the crafting table, open up your inventory, and equip the item. There are no tooltips, except to tell you what each item does (also not available while crafting). Some simple quality of life enhancements would make this game a TON better.
Small gripe, the monsters don't die as soon as they take a killing blow, and that can be frustrating. It's like, ok, he's dead, but he still got a hit on you after taking all that damage and oh look, now he explodes.
_____
The Breakdown:
I like this game. I really do. I'm also glad I got it on sale, because at it's current state, I would have felt a tad dissapointed. I DID have fun with it, and I think a lot of people will, but it just doesnt feel complete.
The BrightSide:
The developer is being very active. There have already been a few updates that introduce new features, with more on the way. So if you can bare with it through some of it's growing pains, then I would say it's an absolute buy. Now get out there and shoot some pixels!

Luftrausers is a superficially simple, but perfectly tuned dogfighting game. Before your inevitable death, you dodge, weave and stall around the enemy hordes in your custom superplane, trying to take out as many of them as you can before the end comes.
Every death brings the promise of higher rankings, and more unlocked options for your craft, each with their own challenges.
Something like an even more arcadey version of the old Amiga game Jetstrike!.
As with all Vlambeer titles, it's also terribly hard, especially in the later stages of challenges (I'll probably never unlock everything), but the design is perfect, down to the music (which remixes for every possible custom craft!).

Hm... I really tried to like this game, but to me the controls are too "floaty" for a bullet hell. The physics just feel weird and you take damage randomly because the gravity sends you flying across the screen. I think LUFTRAUSERS is probably a good game, it's definitely well made. It looks good, it sounds good, it runs well, but it just isn't.. fun. I'm sure some people will like the controls but I personally prefer more tight controls, less "get thrown off into the distance" gravity, in a game that relies entirely on being precise. It would be so much more fun and a testament to actual skill by feeling like you're learning enemy patterns and dodging accordingly but instead I just feel like it's random whether a run goes well or not. I never felt like I was learning anything about the enemy patterns and I couldn't even focus on my objective because I was struggling just to feel in control of my plane. I get that it's an arcade-style game but lack of content and "loose" controls just make LUFTRAUSERS so hard to enjoy for me. Your mileage may vary and if you're looking for a neat score attack game and don't mind having imprecise controls, you'll probably like this game. Maybe I'm just bad at adjusting to the physics and trying too hard to play it like 95% of twin stick shooters/bullet hells, but controls like this just don't feel right in a game about precision and accuracy. It feels like I'm adjusting more to myself moving than what any of the enemies are doing. The menus are also really too simple for their own good. I wanted to look at controls to see if there was anything I should know because I skimmed past the tutorial. It then made me remap every single control and I tried pressing b to exit because I had no intention of changing controls, just viewing the defaults, and it changed my controls for good. I then had to delete the inputs config file to reset it, still confused as to whether there were deeper mechanics.
In conclusion, LUFTRAUSERS is not the twin stick bullethell shooter I wanted it to be but rather a weird, floaty physics shooter. If you can get used to the gravity of your plane, I'm sure you can have a good time with this, but I think some people will just find the control scheme too esoteric or obtuse.

This is where I wish Steam had some sort of "middle ground" for reviews, as it really does pain me to give this the ol' thumbs down.  However, I can't say I'd recommend the game as an overall experience at $10, despite all that it does oh-so-right.
As many others have said, the game controls great, and it really is a lot of fun zipping around and shooting stuff.  The problem is that aside from the various part-specific objectives to complete, there isn't any progression when it comes to the actual game.  You pick your parts, head into combat, fight the same random assortment of the same seven or so enemies, eventually die, then repeat.  There aren't any other levels or anything, so the game ends up feeling more like a proof of concept for a much grander concept.  I saw all the enemy types in the game within about half an hour, unlocked all the plane parts before the two hour mark, and got tired of attempting the remaining objectives soon after.
Still, it was really fun and unique before I hit the "this game's really not going to throw anything else new at me, is it?" point.  While "leave them wanting more" might work to some degree, I shouldn't be wanting as much more as I am out of Luftrausers.

I absolutely love this game. I bought it back when it was new on GameCube and loved the blend of smooth action combat, surprisingly detailed environment, engaging and sometime dark storyline, and that wonderful soundtrack. It's showing its age, but it's still very playable and a lot more approachable than Tales of Zestiria.
Sadly, this port is based on the sub-par PS3 port, which unlike the 60fps GameCube original, is locked at 30fps and missing many subtle graphical effects such as heat shimmer. That said, they have done a lot of work since release to make this game very playable on PC. It runs perfectly now, even on very basic hardware, and supports high resolutions, MSAA and anisotropic filtering. I still miss the 60fps from the original release, but the development since this port was release was enough to get me to rewrite my review.
In conclusion, this is probably the best way to play Tales of Symphonia now.

That being said, I really enjoyed Long Live the Queen and played it quite a few times even after winning. There are multiple paths to victory and several different endings that you might all consider to be victories.

Fortunately the playthroughs are relatively quick, which is good as it may take a play or two to get the hang of what exactly you are trying to do and come up with a plan. It also good that playthoughs are quick because you will die. A lot. And then you can jump right in to the next storyline that will likely end in your death once more.
The mechanics are simple without being dumb and they have importance to the gameplay. Choices very much matter in Long Live the Queen and a certain amount of learning is done through failure and then changing strategy on the retry.

This game has shown me that indie games can be absolutely awesome.
Maybe I'm just a fast learner, but after a bit of messing about I'm already making great things. And I'm still just messing about in the designer, building stuff without constraints and such. Which is beyond fun by the way.
And you see all those ridiculously fancy pants thingos in the screenshots? I just want you to know that while all these things are huge complex things which probably took whoever made em days on end painstakingly working everything out to the very last block, they're things you and I can make too. I get the odd sensation when I'm playing From the Depths that, yes, anything is possible.
Unlike Minecraft, you've got way, way, waaaay more block shapes to choose from. There COULD be a few more shapes, but I'd say that'd just be going overboard, as it is I'm perfectly happy with it. I can make good looking boats, planes, helicopters, anything with what I've been given. In addition, you've got blocks that MOVE. As in, you point your mouse, a tiny spin block points to where your mouse is pointing.
Unlike Garry's Mod, you have far more freedom with your weapons and materials. You don't have to hunt through the prop list to find exactly what you need, no, it's always right there in front of you, ready to be grabbed. And it's actually fun killing stuff. Obviously less physics based than Gmod, but, well, you're never really going to want to pull out a catapult to fight a boat when you could fire a cannon instead. Or a laser. Or a missile. It's fun killing stuff.
And unlike Robocraft, this game is not actually♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's satisfying to kill things. When things lose blocks, they get blown off and float around for a while before disappearing. When you hit something with a really really big cannon, and it does a lot of damage, it really feels like it. There's no stupid block limits or anything. Unless you build something outside of the designer, which I have not done, since the designer gives me all I need: materials, and infinite space.
Seriously, I know this looks like just another block-based building game, but it's the one that I've been waiting for (metaphorically). I wasn't expecting this even to be good. But it is. Just testing out my designs against enemy ships and planes is beyond exhilarating.
If you've got $20 to spend, pick this game up. It's eyebrow-raisingly expensive for an indie game, but I'm saying it's well worth it at present.

WARNING: this game has a quite steep learning curve!
Also one could call it a trial and error simulator.
Now with that out of the way, once one actually gets to grips with the mechanics the game is awesome. I'd describe it as a combination of Space Engineers, Supreme Commander and probably some Kerbal Space Program for the physics.
This allows you to wage an rts war on the scale of Supreme Commander with custom built units. These units are build like in Space Engineers, from many blocks. However, it is more complicated as something as simple as an engine already consists out of several different blocks placed together. The way these blocks are placed together also has an effect on the efficiency and power output of the engine, a similar system is in play with the weapon systems.
Then there is the physics system, which reminds of KSP as it takes placement of thrusters and weapon recoil into account. This in turn allows for some amazing builds and systems.
Example of things I have build so far:
-frigate
-submarine
-battleship
-propellor plane
-jetfighter
-balloon airship
-wooden satelite
-wooden rocket to get to space to build said satelite
-artillery cannon that can shoot beyond the borders of the battle map
-floating castle
-spectre gunship
Currently wheels are not yet fully implemented, so i haven't build any ground vehicles yet.
Pros:
-ability to build massive battleships AND use them against enemy forces
-semi RTS style gameplay with 100% custom build units
-very expansive list of possibilities, leaving new things to learn even after many hours of play
-devs listen to the community
Cons:
-steep learning curve (not really a con for me, but i'll list it as a con anyway as it can well be considered as such)
-massive battles on any pc will lag

I'd been eyeing up this game since I first saw it. I wasn't necessarily following it, but when I saw it on the Steam wishlist I instantly added it to my watchlist, so when the money was right I could get it. Couple years down the road, and the money still wasn't right, but some kind soul bought it as a Christmas present for me. And now, having sunk a good couple hundred hours into it, I feel I can properly comment on it.
Story
There's a story here, but it's mostly just fodder to get you exploring and to provide bosses for the hell of it. I personally tend to ignore it, though it can be a bit annoying when starting a new playthrough, skipping the intro section and then still having ridiculously long cutscenes towards the start of the game. A 'skip cutscene' button would be nice.
Anyways, all this time complaining about the story being mandatory. Why? Because having a story feels abrasive to the very concept of the game. I'll get more into that on the gameplay section. Aanyway, the story. It's pretty barebones: world-killing threat on the horizon, you're the only one who can stop it, so you need to grab the doohickeys from each race to open a thing and kill the world-killing threat. It's simple, to the point where you have to wonder why it's there at all. The characters are barely fleshed out at all, because you only meet them for their little mission to grab an arbitrary thing before the people who want to help the world-killing threat can, so character development is miniscule. But then again, I can't expect much from this type of game, can I? As previously stated, the story feels more to add to gameplay than anything. Anyways, onto the gameplay.
Gameplay
The game is a 2d, exploration-and-combat based roguelike adventure game. The similarities to Terraria are not lost on me, though I'd consider this more-so taking the idea in a different route to copying.
In Starbound, you'll find yourself zipping around between planets, gathering resources, talking to the locals, raiding little dungeons for loot and slaughtering the fauna before it can kill you. You won't often spend long on each planet, unless you plan on recruiting people to your ship for those sweet, sweet upgrades. The planets are all procedurally generated, with a couple of big dungeons or towns, alongside smaller encounters within each of the many biomes.
If there's something I can commend Starbound's exploration mechanics for, it's the pure variety of crap you'll find on your adventures. There's so many different biomes, planet types and dungeons that, for the first playthrough, it'll feel like every planet is different. Note, however, that I said "for the first playthrough" because, while Starbound hosts a lot of planets to explore, the emphasis it places on exploration makes it feel same-y on repeat playthroughs. There's no real reason to 'settle' anywhere outside of "just because"; you don't gain anything outside of more money (which you'll be rolling in in the endgame) and consumable items which are oftentimes obsolete. Your ship will oftentimes hold plenty enough space for not only all of your crafting stuff and storage, but decorational amenities for the crew you'll inevitably gather.
That's enough harping on the exploration, though. The combat is where I feel the game really shines. The game focuses on finding weapons more than crafting them, and each weapon (outside of a few legendary weapons) has different stats. Think Borderlands but there's other types of weapons outside of guns. Each weapon, alongside with having its own attack method (depending on the weapon type), has a special attack which can be anything from guided rockets to a long-ranged dash attack to an exploding teleportation. The weapon variety is great, and very commendable (though I do feel like common encounters are just broken by guided rockets), and makes each playthrough feel different in terms of combat for the early-game at least (until you get one of the few legendary weapons).
I mentioned in the Story section that it was just an excuse for bosses. These are some brilliant bosses. Each one feels really unique in its execution, and first time through will feel really difficult until you get the hang of the patterns (an inevitability in any boss fight situation) or got lucky with loot. These are where combat feels really good, and the final boss of the story in particular is an incredible boss fight (I won't spoil).
The building and such mechanics of this game are quite a prominent part. Each of the races in the game has a different style, and there are plenty of block and furniture varieties to really allow you to make the most of this. Any random thing you can find will be grabbable and usable in your own buildings.
That's not even bringing up the relatively new mech space-flight dealio. Your mech is basically a ticket to breezing through a huge portion of a planet with ease, or flying through space at designated spots (which are basically the towns/dungeons on planets but in space) or go to space stations to talk with the occupants. You can raid these places for new stuff for your mech, though it would be nice if duplicates weren't so common. You can also establish a space station of your own, though it's basically settling on a planet but in space and roughly 500x more expensive.
My main issue, however, comes in the length of the progression tree. This game feels like the progression should go on for even longer than Terraria, but it feels more akin to Minecraft, boasting only 6 different tiers which you'll find yourself working up quickly and reaching end-game within a couple hours at most. It feels hollow and anti-climactic on repeat playthroughs.
Graphics and sound
Graphics are pixel art. Nothing special there, though it does work well for this sort of game. The game goes for a more minimal approach to the art when compared to Terraria's (admittedly messy at times) detailed spritework. And - to be fair - it looks amazing. Everything about the game is pleasing to the eye. Not a masterwork of pixel art, but just good to look at. Perspective is worked well and it all just leads to a game with a very distinct but simple look.
The characters models in the game are also very emotive, with actual emotes and stuff which just help this universe you're going through feel much more alive. Heck, you can play around with emoting in the game yourself, which is a neat little touch.
Now, to talk about sound. The music in this game is great, and fits the game well. However, I can't comment on it too much because I don't tend to listen to in-game music too much (just a personal thing). There are also instruments to play with a selection of songs (which you can add to as MIDIs), which is fun with a few friends.
Other notes
-The game has an extremely large variety of mods to grab. Most mods for this tend to be little quality-of-life things or small content packages. They can just be grabbed off the Steam Workshop too for maximum ease.
-Multiplayer is fun, though can be a pain to set up with mod conflicts and such, which is just a pain.
Summary
A great looking, really fun game with an extreme emphasis on exploration. If you enjoy flying from planet to planet, gathering resources, like No Man's Sky but with more to do, this is the game for you. While I feel the planets get a bit samey after a while (head to a few ice planets and tell me you don't get tired of endless sewers), which in the end hinders the replay value, and the building felt lackluster which gave me little to do at the quick-to-reach endgame. There are many things I enjoy about this, but some issues are too glaring for me to feel myself revisiting this too often.
The game for a galactic adventurer, indeed the best game for a person who would like to save the galaxy.

Personally, I enjoy this game a lot. I've been hyped to get it for around 2 years since I saw it, but was put off by all the negativity it has received since that time. If you have $15 to spend, I'd recommend giving it a try because you just might like it. If you're looking for an oceanic survival game, I'd refer you to this one. In my group of friends, Subnautica is seen as the better option; however, I can't see myself thinking the same. One thing I love about this game is the lack of futuristic and alien aspects that Subnautica offers. Stranded Deep is the gritty experience of someone miraculously surviving a plane crash in the Pacific Ocean, and having to use whatever they can scavenge to survive.
Addressing the complaints of some:
While it doesn't seem right for the developers to add "Boss battles" to a survival game, I can't really blame them. The complaints this game (a SURVIVAL game) receives for not having a definite objective or endgame is ridiculous. With this in mind, I choose to support the developers' decision. This game has evolved tremendously over the past years, and it can be traced through videos on the internet if you don't believe me.
Personally, I'm excited to see what the future holds for this game, and I hope it doesn't die out like some of the other titles on this platform.

This game is a mixed bag.
The combat is pretty much the best part of the game and is fairly good for a warriors-style game and kept me entertained for many housr (hence my play time). The attack sets for characters is distinct enough to provide a nice diversity, but suffers from all "super moves" (extella/noble phantasm) being identical.

Character progression is basic with your stats increasing upon level-up (xp gained by killing enemies). Character customization is limited to a set of passive slots, that can increase damage/speed/defense/xp or add elemental bonuses to your attacks, essentially what you upgrade your weapons with in recent warriors titles. Furthermore you can bring along up to 4 spells (each with a differet number of charges) that grant temporary buffs; the combinations of which is tied to non-cosmetic items that can be crafted with a very bare-bones crafting system.
If you like warriors-style games and either can put up with the parts outside the misions, or are actually interested in them, I recommend it for you. Otherwise, stay away.

When this game was released it received a lot of critical acclaim with people citing that this was the license game that didn't suck. What a load of rubbish.
This games basic mechanics are lifted straight from assassins creed. There’s the basic attack, counter stun combat from the Batman Arkham games and of course assassins creed. There’s also the simplistic stealth from both too. The combat is just boring as there is no challenge (I even turned off the counter indicator and the game was still easy) and because there is no variety. There are four types of orcs you fight and of those 80% of the time it will just be the normal type. This means that combat is very repetitive. The stealth is stupidly easy. Enemy orcs can’t spot you beyond 8 metres eliminating any challenge whatsoever. I also wonder why stealth is in this game at all. In Batman Arkham games stealth makes sense as you die fast from armed enemies. In AC you’re an assassin so being stealthy makes sense. But why should Talion go stealth? The enemies are weak and it’s not like his character is supposed to be sneaky within the story. It makes no sense. The one innovation in the gameplay is nemesis system. The idea is great, you kill the orcs in Saurons army to prevent them from becoming more powerful. The orc officers all have their own personalities and strengths and weaknesses, making them interesting to deal with. If you are killed by an orc he will gain power and so forth. Initially it’s fun to hunt out the orcs in the randomly generated missions. But eventually you realise that no matter how many you kill more will inevitably get promoted and trying to take them all out is aimless as when you eventually die your progress killing through them all is lost.
So the gameplay isn’t very good. That leaves the slack it leaves to be picked up by the story. The AC and Arkham games have ok stories which make their simplistic gameplay bearable. The story in this game is terrible. Five minutes into the game Talion’s, the player’s character, wife and son die. There is an immediate disconnect between the player and the character. I don’t care less about Talion’s wife and son so their death has no impact. This is already a pretty cliché plot device but what’s even worse is that in the game Talion doesn’t seem to care either. He never really talks about their deaths or if he feels sad or not. The story just continues, forgetting this. The rest of the story is an absolute snorefest. No one in the game has a shard of personality. Is it too ironic that randomly generated orcs have more personality than the characters of the main story? The wraith comes across as a♥♥♥♥♥♥ he just says things about the impending doom and how humans suck and whatnot. The only mildly interesting character is Torvin, the dwarf hunter. He’s the only character with any real arc and his making fun of Talion is the only interesting thing in the entire plot. But after 4 missions he’s gone. The story is non canon for LOTR as well, so forget about learning some new interesting side to the lore or anything. Oh and I can’t forget Gollum’s horribly shoehorned cameo either. The story in this game is just abysmal.
The games presentation is pretty good. The visual design captures the look of the LOTR movies well. The graphics are good, characters are modelled well and textures are pretty good. The game sound effects are ok. They do their job well enough, not really worthy of praise though. The voice actors may be voicing boring characters but they perform fine. The only real complaint I have about the games presentation is the pre rendered cut scenes. Pre rendered cut scenes always have and always will look crap. The game also has fast loading times which is nice and surprising considering how new it is. The animations look great. The combat may be bad but it looks cool with nice visceral attacks. It’s funny to see the orcs heads rolling around after they have been lobbed off.
This games presentation can’t save it though. A boring story and mediocre gameplay make this game painfully average. The nemesis system was the selling point of this game but one good idea in a sea of terrible and rehashed ones isn’t a compelling game. Even if the game is heavily discounted there are much better ways to spend your money and time than this game.

I know, I know, I should have rewritten the review in October 2015. But hey, I only decided to retry Postal now that the devs changed the controls, so that it's easier for people to play it. And indeed, it's better.
And as to be clear, I'm not doing it because my negative review seemed to be not helpful (6 people on 9 downvoted it) at all when it was clearly constructive. I'm doing it because the change the devs made allowed finally to appreciate Postal like I should have if it wasn't for the controls.
Another thing: I don't mind old games. I didn't write first a negative review because of that. Like I've said in my old review, having played on PC, NES and Game Boy in more or less 1989-1990, at age of 6-7, I've seen a good part of the video game history. And I don't mind games like Postal. I could play them (or an old GTA) without problems. I don't mind Postal at all. Now that I've played enough, I can finally say more.
You have to understand that when you can't play a game because of a control layout, you can't fully explain it. Postal, it's a game where you kill everyone, hostile or not hostile. Well, you can choose to spare innocent lives. Anyway, the hostiles are mainly cops. The view is an isometric one, that's probably why the original layout for the controls didn't match my own pattern in these games.
True, pressing "right" for me is equal to going right and not anything else. Back then, it wasn't doing what I wanted. The mouse wasn't easy to use. Now, there are several layouts. I don't remember if there were so many options, but now, when I press "right", I go to the right! I don't even use the mouse anymore. I've still yet to adapt some stuff, as I fire in the same time when pressing the arrows, but it's a matter of keys. Two actions are binded with the same key, I've just to change it, because I'm currently killing everyone and if I want to spare innocents, I need to stop firing.
The result was immediate. Now that I could move more freely, I've reached the fourth level, I've unlocked more achievements and I'm finally appreciating Postal. I'm finally appreciating the run in the levels, ducking under the rockets, when I remember that I can duck, executing people still alive, though it's just not my style to do it, I prefer to run and to spread bullets everywhere.
True, I die a lot because I've no strategy apart running wildly around. And I don't even use the other weapons, don't ask me why I'm willing to use the infinite ammo one, though I suppose it will be hard to keep that strategy in the next levels. But hey, I'm willing to try.
The only downside of this is that I still need to find the best layout for me and that I read about an achievement with Mac and Linux and that I'm sad to see that the 100% completion can't be done for many of us. Well, yeah, I'm too lazy to install a virtual machine. Anyway, apart that, because the devs made the effort for the controls and that this was a saving update for the game for the players, I can't keep the negative review. That's how a game can go from a negative to a positive review: by listening your players and by improving the game to make sure that the majority can get fun.
Sorry for the lateness though. This update is around since October 2015. I wouldn't have tried the game again and rewritten this review if this update wasn't in my head somewhere. Good job!

Ace Combat in name only, and a master's course in anti-fun design.
Ace Combat is a series known for it's excellent gameplay, epic plots, beautiful vistas, and freedom of movement;  this game throws all of that out the window in a failed attempt to court the Call of Duty audience.  The well established world and nations of Strangereal are replaced with a generic Russia vs. America plot that feels lifted right from Call of Duty, the beautful visuals and art direction have been replaced by sand, run through a brown-filter, and are now subject to constant shakey cam.
The most aggregious change to the formula is the highly scripted missions.  In previous games you were free to move around the map and prioritize targets as you saw fit.  In Assault Horizon, you are given brief tastes of this freedom, only to have it constantly taken away as the game forces you into mandatory quicktime events called "dogfight mode".   The only way to engage the majority of targets, or to escape from enemy persuit, is to complete these quicktime events; and in doing so it strips away everything that made Ace Combat so special.
Shame they decided to port this turd to PC rather than 4, 5, Zero or 6; hell, even the PSP and 3DS games would have been better titles to bring to Steam.

I never thought I'd find a PC flight sim that made me miss HAWX, but there you go. Proven wrong.
I'd been thinking of making a comparison to the proper flight sims that I grew up with, such as US Navy Fighters or Jane's USAF. But that's unfair, because those are flight sims, and this is an arcade game. Then I thought about comparing it to Crimson Skies, but that's wrong too, because that's a
game. But maybe I should break it down a bit.
Ace Combat Assault Horizon is the first Ace Combat game to come out on PC. The aforementioned HAWX was Ubisoft's attempt to capitalize on that lack (so far as the demo mission, and one of the mid-point missions feel like they've been ripped right out of Ace Combat 6), but it was very milquetoast. I haven't played the console Ace Combat games, but I did look up LPs of the golden trilogy (Ace Combat 4, 5 and Zero) to see what it was like.
I'd liked HAWX for what it was, which was a very easy, very pretty game about flying around and shooting things. The story was stupid and the combat was simplistic, but at least it didn't force you to use its gimmicks (though I did like the OFF mode, especially the way you could actually stall the plane). The A-10 breaking the sound barrier bugged me no end, but you can't have everything.
ACAH is very pretty to look at, all that it does have the grungey, unwashed, "I'm-so-gritty" colour palette. The jets are beautiful, the backdrops are nicely detailed, even the people are animated nicely in the door-gunner section (which is a great way to do the credits I will admit). Sound design is similarly decent, though I was barely paying any attention to the radio chatter while struggling to control the aircraft.
That, then, is the first strike against ACAH; the controls. I don't have a controller, nor do I intend to get one, so I tried it with a keyboard, where it was passable. I tried it with a mouse and keyboard, which was horrible. I dug out my old Saitek joystick, and that was playable up to a point... but it's very unpleasant.
See, because that's the second strike against ACAH; the gimmicks. They have this mandatory Dog Fight Mode (DFM). You see a lot of people complaining about it. And they're right to complain about it. You can't beat enemy aces without it. And lest you think that's an occasional thing, it isn't. Aces aren't a special thing, there are three or four of the buggers with every single flight, taunting you with "TGT Lead" on your HUD, turning sharper than you can, and shrugging off each and every missile you throw at them. The only way to defeat an Ace is through DFM. And that's not because they're that good, it's an actual mechanic. I think they have a switch which doesn't allow them to be shot down without DFM.
And that leads to the third strike; dogfighting. The jets don't feel like jets. When you turn, you're not rolling, you're turning along the x-axis. You can't just bank and pull back on the stick to turn sharper, you have to pull back on the throttle so that the game knows that you're trying to do a Sharp Turn(tm). It's so awkward, and I know (from looking at videos on Youtube) that it's something that came out in Ace Combat 6, but it's still so terrible.
I paid USD 3.99 for ACAH from Humble Bundle. And I still think I paid too much.

Warstone is a tower defense game with some extra depth that makes it really stand out versus other games in the genre. I think Kingdom Rush will always remain my favourite in this category, but Warstone has really raised the bar and exceeded all my expectations - especially given the low price.
At the core of the game you build and upgrade towers (units) of varying strengths and weaknesses that automatically attack moving targets to gain resources. It's what makes a tower defense game, and this game plays out very similarly in those respects. You additionally have some spells/abilities, and you can also equip and find items to help you.
It also has a "town" screen where you accept quests, learn about new things, construct buildings and upgrade them, purchase items, manage your skills and so on. It has resources that carry over and you then use to improve your base. These resources are infinite technically as you can repeat maps, but in reality that's grindy - so you have to make a strategic choice about what you're doing. This adds an extra layer in addition to the standard defense map.
It also has the addition of multiplayer in two different modes, either co-op or vs. where you can work with (or against) another player. It has leaderboards and multiplayer is a lot of fun - although the playerbase is quite small so sometimes you do have to wait a while to find a partner.
This game is early access, but at the time of reviewing, even if this was the full game, I would be happy with my purchase. It has an absolute ton of content, and seems very well polished. Yes, there are some bugs and some things that need to be tweaked/balanced - but there have been regular and consistent updates both bug fixing, stat balancing and content additions. Several suggestions made by players have been implemented, and the devs clearly listen to and interact with their players. I'm very happy with how this has progressed, and think it's worth picking up early. I bought this on day one and have no regrets.

I wanted to like Pixel Boy, I enjoy roguelikes and this game has all the right ingredients to make for a compelling game, unfortunately it fails to deliver in a lot of ways.
The graphics are basic, they have tried to make something of the lo-fi RGB theme but in reality it just looks like exactly what it is: low poly everything masked with too much bloom and an unimaginative colour pallette. The gameplay is basic top down action fare, the controls are fairly well implemented but the moment to moment gameplay of moving and shooting is simply not that satisfying. Bullets waft out of your character and slowly float towards their target, enemies wander around in basic patterns often getting stuck in doorways and getting obscured by the scenery.
The roguelike elements also fall short. Levels are randomly generated but in the most simplistic manner possible, essentially a grid of identical square rooms with the occasional corridor or removed walls. The enemies are picked from a pool at the start of the round, and while they are fairly varied there are never any great surprises. The customisation systems feel unecessarily micromanagey and don't afford any real variety. In short you aren't going to feel like you're getting much of a different experience when replaying the game, arguably the most important feature of roguelike games.
Good points: the music is excellent, the narration is humorous and well voiced.

I had this game for about 30 minutes. I was promised sharks, danger, base building, and BEAUTIFUL graphics. None were delivered after I realized my game looked bad, I cranked up the settings and generated a new map, and nothing. Shortly after this I refunded this game.

So let me begin by saying, I have only played this game for a few hours. I really like this game, and with a few tweaks this game could be great. That said, some things keep the game from being genuinely fun.
The cons:
For starters, players need gratuitous basic supplies like rocks, sticks, and fiber. Rocks are IMPOSSIBLE to get enough of, which is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ considering the island is littered with gigantic rocks-but even with a pick you can only mine certain, rare rocks(devs please make ALL rocks mineable). Secondly, there should be a way to raise animals in order to increase the population somehow. Leather is so scarce because there are litterally two animals per island. It should also be said that it takes 4 spears to kill a pig(holy♥♥♥♥♥♥how would a pig still be able to run after being impaled 4 times?). Players should also be able to turn palm fronds into fiber. Everything on the island should be deconstructable, but its not for some reason. Small pine trees can be cut down, but large ones cannot. This is a real problem, because the trees take up space and can impede roof placement. Also, the flu is absolutely ridiculous, draining food and water SO FAST that all you can do is run back and forth eating coconuts for a solid 12 hours in game. That is stupid. The days should pass MUCH slower. I would like it closer to real time, because construction, and harvesting of items is all happening in real time even when the time is flying by. Players should be able to place walls and roofs on rafts, along with all crafting centers, lights and bedrolls. Sharks are everywhere underwater, and keep the player from enjoying the underwater exploration. Can we also get a fishing pole? Anyways, these are my gripes. Now for the good things about the game.
The pros:
I love the graphics. Everything is absolutely beautiful in this game, and it runs surprisingly well on underpowered systems. The current animations look very nice. While alot has yet to be done with the survival aspect, the game is surprisingly playable and developed, and ideas like the coconut(drinking, then eating) go a long way in determining this games potential. The sea life is wonderful, and i love seeing different fish whenever i go for a swim(although my vision is lined with a blood red border for some reason everytime i swim, which is ugly and makes no sense). I really like how the trees are harvested, how the player first deconstructs the tree, then cuts it into sticks and palm fronds. I think the storms are awesome, and wish they caused more havoc on the island, forcing the player indoors to wait out the storm. The premise of being stranded after a plane crash is very cool too, in a despairing sort of way.
Verdict:
If you are a player who likes a challenge, likes survival games, and is willing to overlook a select few shortcomings (at the time being) then you should buy this game hands down. If you are more casual and less apt to put some time into a game, or are just getting into survival games, then maybe wait or do some more research on this game before purchasing. All of this said, I am sure the devs are going to put more work into this game, and iron out the rough patches here and there. When all of that is complete, this game will be on of the best survival games ever made, and will be a hands down must have for every steam owners library. Keep up the good work Beam Team!

You think you know, but you don't.
You've heard the reviews: "Dark Souls is the hardest game to exist. Dark Souls is so soul crushingly difficult I can't play normal games anymore. Dark Souls seperates the casual gamers from the elite."
Ridiculous. Dark Souls is a game for everyone. You will play Dark Souls. You will like Dark Souls. You will "Git Gud". But Dark Souls isn't a litmus test. It's not a bar that seperates the wheat from the chaff. It is a transformational experience for the benefit of all of those who enjoy video games. Dark Souls believes in you. It challenges you because it knows you can do better. And you will. Everyone is capable of success in this game. All you need is a willingness to keep trying- a willingness to lose all that you have. Once you realize that everything that you have to lose in this game is all obtainable again; once you realize that there is no penalty to trying your best and failing- that is when Dark Souls truly challenges you to transcend the current limits of your play and evolve into something more. Many RPGs have a sense of progression. There is a satisfaction, a catharsis to growing stronger as your character gains attributes and statistics and you have the opportunity to fight some enemy that provided challenge much earlier in your playthough, and now dispatching them is mere child's play- but this catharsis transcends merely gaining numbers on a character sheet in Dark Souls. In Dark Souls, your character doesn't level up: you do. And as you get better, as you grapple the controls and the inventory system; as you familiarize yourself with the weapon animations and the combat mechanics, you can feel yourself eclipsing the terrors the game faces you with. You begin to feel safe, to feel certain in yourself. There is no danger the game can throw at you and leave you running scared- you have won, by virtue of your persistence. You know the map now. You know where the enemies spawn. You know precisely where to obtain the weapon you love and the resources you need to level it into grandoise preportions. You can roll, parry, and backstab your way out of any combat encounter. You have achieved mastery. This is what makes Dark Souls brilliant. The appreciation you acquire on subsequent playthroughs. Dark Souls affords you the power to play the game however you may like if you will only try. Try and you will prevail. Try and you will be rewarded with the purest sense of accomplishement to grace modern gaming. Link the fire, Chosen Undead. Lordran awaits you.

Pros:
- Good combat.  When the game is working it does a good job of making you feel like you are becoming stronger until you can take on hordes of enemies and come out alive.
- Challenging quests that don't feel too repetitive, making the leveling system feel at least a little more organic than your typical action RPG.
- Interesting lore.  I think it was very smart to pick important but less familiar characters like Celebrimbor to include.
- Gorgeous landscapes and weather.
- Excellent use of sound.
- Excellent controller support.
Cons:
- This game crashes on the  regular.  I'm running an 8700k and a 1080ti.  I probably spent three or four hours trying to get to run in a more stable fashion - vsync on/off, underclock GPU (yes really, this was suggested by WB Games), tessellation on/off, newer/older drivers, fullscreen/borderless/windowed, etc etc.  Eventually I found a combination of settings that lets me play more than 10 mins, but I can still count on it to crash every two hours or so.  You can imagine this doesn't pair well with the "challenging quests" point above.  Can't count how many times I was nearing the end of a quest only to have the game crash again.  And based on what I've seen on the support forums, everyone needs to find their own combination of settings based on their hardware to get it running *somewhat* well.  I can verify this personally as my secondary desktop uses a Haswell i5 and an R9 390.  Requires different settings to get it stable, and still crashes fairly often.
-  Bungled controls.  At first I loved the huge moveset this game has.  Unfortunately this eventually makes it nearly impossible to execute the intended action unless you are aligned juuuust right with the object you are trying to interact with.  Try climbing a wall only to watch your character roll away or drop down instead.  This problem impacts the midgame moveset the most, particularly mounting beasts until late game when you get a new skill that circumvents the whole thing.
-  Bugs.  One of the bigger ones I encountered was how the game would hitch fairly severely after cutscenes.  This is a bit of a problem since you are often thrown into the middle of the action while your FPS tanks for 5 or 6 seconds at the start of nearly every mission.  Died a few times thanks to that.  Another is that it seems you can't shoot arrows between gaps in fences, walls, etc even though enemies can spot you through them.  It seems that even the (large) gaps are all one part of the asset and your arrow just appears to stop mid-air.
- FPS capped to 100 max, no workaround to go higher.
Conclusion:  I definitely can see why this game got decent reviews from other people.  It's one of the better action RPGs I've played recently, and the 'super human fights hordes of enemies' theme works particularly well with the Uruks of Mordor, giving the game decent immersion.  Unfortunately, I've spent about as much time troubleshooting issues as I have just enjoying the gameplay/dealing with botched controls.  I don't think I've seen a game this unstable since Fallout 3 or the original Witcher.  As a result I can't recommend this game at full price.  It does go on sale regularly though, so maybe consider picking it up if you have the patience to fine tune it.

A good oportunity lost, maybe by time exigencies and budget problems of an indie study based on crowdfunding. Let's be upfront about something: This is not a Civilization game, nor does it pretend to be. If you're looking for Alpha Centauri 2 or a rehabilitation of Beyond Earth that isn't a weak Civ5 mod, you're in the wrong place.
If you want a board game to play on your computer, then this is exactly what you're looking for.
Starships is a compact game probably designed primarily for mobile devices. And you know what? There's nothing wrong with that. Where Starships excels is in its vision and execution of making a game that recreates the board game experience.
What's so elegant about Starships is that it takes common board game mechanics and takes advantage of the fact that since the game is being run on a computer, it can develop those mechanics to new heights. Developing planets as your resource generators very much mirrors how a board game might have a chart where you move tokens around to determine how much you get per turn. Special abilities function like cards drawn out of a deck, and the map looks like a game board. Even the victory condition, "Control 51% of the map" sounds like something out of a board game.
The combat is simple but deep. You get full customization of your units, and you move around on a hex grid shooting at each other with stuff like line of sight, distance, and cover to calculate. It would be unmanageable as a tabletop game (unless everyone playing is a total Warhammer junkie), but as a video game it's very easy to let the computer do all the calculations for you.
Like any game worth its weight, the rules are very simple to understand after a turn or two, but there's enough nuance to them that you'll be spending quite a few hours understanding how to optimize everything and adjust on the fly.
Major strikes against the game: Missing a lot of basic computer game functions (come on, let me up the resolution!) and no multiplayer. The latter is pretty bad, but then again, it takes a very special group of people to have the patience to sit through a multiplayer 4X game.
In short: It's a board game. Don't fool yourself into thinking otherwise. But it is a great board game that takes advantage of not forcing the players to calculate anything on the fly, and blossoms because of that. If you even enjoy the occassional game of Settlers of Catan, this is probably a game you'll enjoy.

So I'm going to give a tentative thumb to Sid Meyers enthusists, board game enthusists, Gotta have every starship people, and "I buy every game collectors."
If you're wishywashy on it, wait and see how patching goes - Sid does a good job of steering into user issues and games often come out with low scores and end up masterpieces via udpates/freeLC (or sometimes DLC that later becomes free.)
I'd like to see the team add more content, more story, fix some bugs and generally improve the title however - but the bones of a fun game for people who play these sorts of games exists here and the price of entry is fairly low.
(as of now) For enthusists and boardgame freaks only.

Adakah game RPG yang di-port sampai 3 kali ke platform baru? Pasti sangat sedikit, & salah satu dari sedikit game itu adalah Tales of Symphonia. Game original yang dibuat untuk Nintendo GameCube (2003), tak lama kemudian dihadirkan untuk Sony PS2 (2004), yang beberapa tahun kemudian dirilis versi HD untuk PS3 (2013). Masih belum selesai, PC Windows pun mendapatkan port pada tahun 2016 ini lewat Steam.
Grafis/Port (3/10)
Cuma satu kata untuk kualitas port ToS, "kacau".
Mapping button yang asal ambil dari PS, masalah save windows 7 yang lama, lock 720p, lock 30fps, crash, dll. Cukup memberi respon negatif untuk ToS. Untungnya masih ada  GeDoSaTo & Kalaiden yang memperbaikinya dengan Fix hingga ToS dapat dimainkan dengan lancar.
Cerita (10/10)
Tak ada yang perlu diragukan soal cerita ToS. Meski dimulai dari cerita yang cukup klise, ToS berkembang begitu kompleks. penuh intrik & plot twist & menyedihkan namun tetap menyuguhkan kelucuan & terkadang begitu konyol. Konsep cerita fantasi pada game terkadang membuat kita kesulitan memahami ceritanya namun ToS menjelaskannya pelan2 hingga setidaknya kita mengerti apa yang sedang terjadi.
Gameplay (9/10)
Sistem pertarungan & eksplorasi dunia ToS sangat klasik namun keunggulan utama ToS ada pada saat dalam dungeon. Berbeda dengan game2 baru yang cuma meminta kita berjalan maju & mengalahkan monster untuk menyelesaikan dungeon, dalam setiap dungeon ToS hampir selalu ada puzzle yang memaksa kita untuk berpikir bagaimana membuka pintu, jalan atau mengakses tempat tertentu. Sorcerer ring selalu berubah fungsi sesuai puzzle dalam dungeon. Cukup membuat kita untuk membuka google atau walkthrough.

Lloyd and his friends suddendly leave the safety of their village to help Collette- the "Chosen"- in her journey to regenerate the world: what starts as a difficult yet straightforward proposition soon turns into an epic adventure to find out the truth behind chosens and the world's salvation.
Tales of Symphonia is a traditional JRPG that still serves as one of the finest examples of the genre despite some aging mechanics and design choices.
-great story and narrative featuring a good amount of twists
-nice soundtrack
-great combat system and tight controls make fights really enjoyable, even against trash mobs
-an huge world to explore featuring a good amount of different locations
-a good cast of characters that manage to be interesting despite adhering to the genre's tropes
-the few FMVs used in the game still look gorgeous
-while the overall story is serious there's lots of humourous dialogue and scenes to be found to lighten the mood
-great length, expect at least 40/50 hours
-the game looks its age, don't expect sharp textures or alot of detail
-certain scenes can be a bit too verbose or drawn-out
-while most dungeon puzzles are fairly interesting some can be a bit annoying due to vague directions and/ or having to do the whole process again if you screw up somewhere
-AI can be a bit too stupid sometimes, like when it doesnt steer clear of enemy casting zones or tries getting near melee enemies as a caster (even when setting strategies that say the opposite)
-tutorials are quite lacking, expect to have to read up a few guides to really get a feel for how certain game mechanics work
-the world map is pretty inadequate, there's also no zone map when you are in cities or dungeons
-patches improved stability and solved bugs, still the game can hang if you alt tab and can glitch slightly at times: nothing gamebreaking on my end though
Tales of Symphonia does follow most of the tropes of the genre and is truly conservative in its adherence to JRPG standards but thankfully does so in a very competent way: you can expect a good story that slowly expands in scope, characters that are quite well developed despite not being too original, an huge world to explore and hours of content to dig through.
There's some things that make it feel like a "diamond in the rough" at times, the tutorials don't really do a good job at explaining the intricacies of certain game mechanics and believe me, some of them can be hard to get without a guide. You can set strategies for AI controlled party members but they can act pretty stupidly at times and this can be problematic around bosses or particularly hard enemies. Still I realize most of the problems are simply due to the age of the game rather than downright bad design, I'm simply playing something from 13 years ago and games have evolved alot since then.
If you can look past its shortcomings and don't mind its age Tales of Symphonia is a really great game that any JRPG fan'd at least once, it also serves as what is probably the strongets entry in the Tales series as far as story and characters go.

Played it twice, in the second run I didn't bother with Armor at all, as it isn't really efficent or needed.
Right now, I just wait for Daily Dungeon (the Game Menu states "coming soon") and hoping I will find a more challenging experience there.
Everyone who is frustrated with other Dungeon Crawlers should check this one out, as it is quite forgiving.
For those, who appearently find this game hard:
Every time you collected the RGB-Key, you can use the elevator (before opening the "Danger"-Doors) to go to the Town.
Going to Town heals you.
Combining Weapons also replenish their Ammunition. So if you have a lvl.6 Weapon with 1 shot left, you can combine it with something and get a lvl.7 Weapon with full ammo.
Don't waste your Attribute-Points. The only needed ones are Health, Damage and Range. (@Devs: Do something against that :P)
If you tend to die: In a Dungeon, run to the "End"-Room first (its always displayed on the map) there you can buy a health potion for 30 Gold. Always have a secure way to this room and run back to it, when your low on HP.
As soon as possible, I run around with 4 identical Weapons and use only 2 of them. If for some reason I am low on ammo (never happened) I can switch to the other ones. (Later in the Game I have 6 and use 3 of them)
NEVER use the last shot in a weapon! It vanishes into thin air. Stop using it and replenish the Ammo once you're in the city.
The Best Weapons seem to be: Life Steal, Fire, Spread shot and Heat Seeking. At some Point, you can eliminate a Room with 1 shot.
Really fun with friends, of course it gets a bit boring after a while but it'll keep you entertained for hours.

I bought this game because the video looked cool and most of the reviews were positive. I was expecting a game with customization, progression, and creativity. It failed to meet my expectations in any of these categories.
Right off the bat it says that it's an "action RPG". I thought this meant all these cool powerups were things I could invest in with things like skill points. No. You just find/buy the powerups and they only last 250 shots. Not much of a point using them except for the 'bosses' which will be discussed later.
You do level up and get stat points which is cool... but then again it isn't. All you do with your stat points is put them into damage as you do very little. Attack speed? So my powerups can run out even faster? Very lame options here. Just get damage. Zzz...
The armor system is yet another under delivered concept. Cool you get customizable armor? That sounds great. Oh it breaks after 5 or so hits? Well I guess that's fine... Oh it isn't really customizable? You just pick 5 of the same boring stats (damage x 5)? Hmmm but they have unique effects! Could be some cool combinations! No. It only has 5 types, depending on what type of 'orb' you use the most of. They all are just an effect on when you get HIT, something you should never do. And the effects hardly do anything other than cause lag. Miss.
Bosses I mentioned before. I've been to 2 before I stopped playing. The FIRST boss. Even if you put ALL of your points into damage and save all of the powerups for this fight it will take a very long time. It is pointless to use the 'mechanics' of the lightning trap as it seems to do nothing. All you do is run around in a circle at the bottom of the map shooting it... and shooting it... and shooting it. It has a ridiculous amount of health and isn't interesting at all. I finally figured out that the only way to hurt it is the fire powerup. Dumb.
The 2nd boss isn't much better. Once again it has near infinite health. Boring. Once again it is just a reskinned mob. Boring.
The mob types are very repetive as are the environment"s". "Act 1 and 2" were the exact same. The same boring environment and mob types, just more hp and probably damage. Horrible.
There were only 2 things that weren't terrible about the game and even then they were just fine and ripoffs of other games.
The graphics looked fine. A copy of Geometry wars and Minecraft, but not as well done as either.
The narrator was okay. Very similar to Bastion to have an involved narrator but nowhere as good.
I regret buying this game. It feels like an alpha or an early access game. Not finished at all and the updates they are planning on adding don't address any of the short comings. Not worth $10, maybe $4. Save your money and get Binding of Isaac if you want a game like this, much better. The large amount of positive reviews I suspect were written by the Devs or their friends/family. I could find no reviews of the game online.
Sorry if I was harsh Devs, I do not mean to hurt your feelings but this is a bad game and I feel swindled.

I have played this game for awhile, and im here to give an honest review. This game is very fun, and addictive, but has some issues, more on that later. Firstly, the game is fun, the "pixel powers" are a unique and fresh feature for a rouge-like game. You get powers like bigger bullets, more spread from your shots, and you can even get flaming bullets, and tons more. You can combine the powers to make them even more deadly!! The enemies you encounter are kinda random, you face against ants, frogs, skulls, snakes, slimes, etc. But each have unique attacks. I have gotten to Act 3 now, and the levels never look the same, which is a cool feature. As you would expect in a rouge-like game, once you die you basically lose everything, except the levels, coins, and attributes you gave your character, but i feel like once you die, you should just restart the game, since you lose all the powers you got, and probably dont have enough coins to resupply yourself, but thats to be expected in a game like this. And finally, the bad things/glitches that might happen. The first bad thing, for me, is that the game is short, only 4 acts, and has little replayability, for me of course, but the devs said they are gonna add daily dungeons, so look up on that. The next thing is that the game kinda feels repetitive, other than the Mob Maker 9000 which randomly generates the enemies, you just look for the same three keys, or the RGB, and then you beat the level, and of course, at the end of each act there is a boss, each one i faced was fun and fast paced, really good fights. Those are the bad things, for me, now onto the glitches that you may get, and the ones i experienced. Some enemies or coins will fly off the level, and end up in the blackness, which makes it impossible to get or kill, and the other one is that the enemies will get stuck in the doors, and just wait for you to kill them. Other than that, no more glitches, that i experienced. Overall, this game was very good, i still havent beaten it, but i will. I recommened this game to anyone who like rouge-like games. 8.5/10

I want to love this game, I really do, but it left me with a hollow disappointed feeling and by no means lived up to the hype. There are some great ideas for game mechanics, it fairly easy to pick up, the storyline is pretty good and it does a good job at making you feel like a bada$$. My suggestion? Only get it if it is on sale.
Movement:
The movement feels a little clunky and you will find yourself getting caught on a lot of things or jumping places when you dont want to. There are several mounts you can ride but they get stuck on things more than you do.
Combat:
You get three weapons to use (sword for close quarters, dagger for stealth and bow for ranged)and you will absolutely have to use all of them.
The combat feels great and flows well while running around and getting into little skirmishes throughout the first 2/3 of the game.
However you will get completely swarmed if you walk into one of the main camps and will spend most of your time countering.
Unfortunately in the later stages your bow and dagger are almost useless because 9/10 capitans and warchiefs will be invincible to both stealth and ranged, oh and combat finishers... and they will probably be in a camp with 60 followers and infinite reinforcements.
At that point it sucks the fun out of choosing how you want to deal with the orc and forces you to do it one way (usually spamming stun and getting 1 hit on them before you have to block his followers and re-stun him)
Dont get me wrong it is a decent game but I was sick and tired of it by the time I finished and I am dreading the thought of going back to get the last two achievements.

If there were a "meh" button I would use it here.
I'll start with the good:
The combat system is great, albeit too easy a lot of the time. It reminds me a lot of the Batman games in the way that you can sort of dance around between enemies and perform various attacks. It's a lot of fun.
The Uruk Captain system is unique and very well drawn-out as well. There are so many various features for each and every one of these Captains, and in spite of most of them being randomly generated I haven't found anything about them to be repetitve. The looks, dialogue, and motives of these guys are so unique to themselves and it makes it feel like you've actually made a personal enemy when you're fighting these dudes. It's easily the best aspect of the game in my opinion.
The bad:
The story is extremely lacking. The character designs are generic, the dialogue is dull, and it feels like there's an extreme lack of substance. Everyone is so one-dimensional and lacks any sort of personality (excluding ratbag. That little guy is great). I just can't get myself to care about any of the events in the plot, and I'm usually really into story mode stuff. Whenever I'm doing a required story mission or watching a cutscene, I'm just wishing I could go back to fighting things.
And the world design is plain boring. I've done a heavy amount of exploring and I've found the scenery and environment to be pretty disappointing. Despite all my exploring, I always have to check the map to see where I am because everything just looks the same. Stone ruins, some grass, a few ledges, and a couple locations with some wooden shacks. Brown and grey everywhere, with an occasional touch of green. This is Middle Earth for god's sake, they could've thought up something better than that.
And finally, the handholding and lack of challenge. It's borderline patronizing how often these control hints come up. You can clearly see that I've put a decent chunk of time into the game, and I still get frequent notifications telling me the basic controls for the game. And not only that, but in missions the main character (Talrion? Talon? I can't even remember his name because I don't care) talks to himself in order to tell the player what to do. "Shooting that firepit will help me clear the camp", "Stealth would be of advantage to me here", shut the ♥♥♥♥ up Talor I know how to play the game.
Oh man and the controller hints..."Press RB to heal", "Press RT+X to perform a stealth attack", "Press Y+B to perform an execution". It acts like gamers are incompetent brickheads who can't remember anything for more than 10 minutes. The worst part was how it *always* popped up the control for countering an attack. Every. Single. Time. I was playing the freaking game with a giant "Y" in the middle of my screen. Thank god there was an option to disable that at least.
In the end it's a decent game if you can get past the flaws and boring substance. Ruthlessly killing swaths of Uruks and stealth murdering Captains is pretty freaking fun, but remember :
"Hold RT to sneak"

This TD game has a lot of depth. Unfortunately, it is one of those games where you will invariably make irreparable mistakes that make it pretty much impossible or at least tedious to finish the game if you just start playing without reading up on it before. And, there is no reset button either.
The issue is basically that there is [note: was - see edit2 below] no way to farm resources, at least not in single player mode, while multiplayer mode is tedious since it takes forever to get a game going.
Resource income is finite, but it's easily possible to waste resources. For example, if you choose to complete a mission on "easy" the first time you do it, you will never be able to get the resources that are awarded by doing the mission on hard. They are just lost, which will mean you will not be able to afford the upgrades necessary to continue the game.
This mechanic isn't explained in the game, either. I found out after having done most missions on easy and as a result I am now unable to continue the game. You should not be able to irreparably kill your progess just because you decide not to try the hardest difficulty first. Also, every time you refresh the shop, the gold necessary is just lost with no real way to regain it.
For these reasons, the game is unplayable for me in its current state. I decided not to give a negative review because the game is still in early-access and this issue will hopefully be corrected, but in its current state it is a very frustrating game I cannot really recommend.
Edit: If you're fine with playing multiplayer the balancing is fine and the game can be recommended.
Edit2: The latest patch finally introduced grindable solo rewards. So, it's now possible to progress even in single-player.

In early European gothics--Ann Radcliffe, Mary Shelley, Bram Stoker, Mathew Lewis--monsters and ghouls were a way to vent or exploit social, economic, political and cultural phobias. This was mostly due to the fact that in early Europe, science and medical knowledge was not so present as they are today.
When the United States was founded, it was at a time of Enlightment. Science and medical advancements and discoveries gave psychological and biological explainations to those ficticious vampires and ghosts, casting them away into the shadows. This paved way to something unique to American phobias, and ultimately what came to define American horror--human monsters. The American boogeyman is not a vampire, a stitched together corpse, or any other monster of the sort. It's Michael Myers, Leatherface, the hillbillies from Deliverence. Most of all, it's the crazy guy with the gun, and that's what makes Postal unique and brilliant. It takes that concept, and also takes another part of American culture--the second amendment--and perverses it into our wildest nightmares.
Postal 1 is a brilliant horror game, and I'd rank it up there with the likes of Silent Hill or Amnesia. It's discomforting, disturbing, exploitive and most importantly, real. I'd highly recommend it, but only if you can handle it.

It's a great game for a number of reasons, but it has a lot of flaws.  Obviously the port is bad.  This has been talked by plenty of people and you can install DSFix to make it much better, but be aware that if you buy this game on Steam, you shouldn't be expecting a good port.   But even while being a lazy port it's still the best version of the game you can get.
The gameplay is for the most part pretty solid.  The melee combat is great, but magic is boring and makes the game too easy, at least at lower levels.  I would not recommend starting with a caster-type character.  I mean, there are loads of ways to exploit every playstyle if you know how, but magic is broken from the very start and easily exploitable for a new player.  I'm saying this because I wasted probably 30 hours playing a pure sorcerer and actually quit the game out of boredom.  Thank god I came back and made a new build because I really would have missed out.
The netcode is awful.  I can't see how anyone could like it.  You will fight against people who will one moment be in front of you and in the next killing you with a backstab.  That kind of teleporting is prevalent online, and even using mods that are supposed to improve the matchmaking don't help enough, so take that for what you will.
The world is great.  It's very open, meaning after you get out of the starting area you have options.  It's also interconnected, which makes it feel more real.  I definitely miss this in Dark Souls 3.  The level design is for the most part pretty good.  Some areas felt rushed though.  Everyone says that the first half of the game is a masterpiece and the second half is a mess, and I agree that the second half is nowhere near as good as the first.  The pacing gets messed up because you have to backtrack all over and a few of the later levels are very underwhelming in both level and boss design.
The upgrade system is a pain.  The game doesn't really tell you much about how it works, and they split the upgrade types up and gave them to different blacksmiths around the world.  While it is pretty cool to venture out to find a specific blacksmith for a specific task, it's a system that will have you looking at a wiki page A LOT.
My last gripe is with the platforming.  Some people love this part of the game, but I personally do not.  Simply put, the game uses a lot of tight platforming and the engine and the camera suck for it.  Death in the game is supposed to feel fair, but I don't get that feeling when I die while platforming.  This is something I got very sick of by the end of it, and I'm glad that they cut back on it a lot in DS3.
It's a great game.  I wouldn't call it a masterpiece, or even a "flawed masterpiece" like I've heard others say, but definitely unique and worth trying for anyone who wants a challenging RPG with a somber atmosphere.  I always see people asking which Dark Souls game they should start with.  Start with this one.  It's worth playing and the references in Dark Souls 3 will make more sense if you do.  And the game's flaws will be more apparent if you start with DS3 and then go backards to DS1, potentially hurting the experience.

Long Live the Queen is an interesting game about learning to navigate politics in a fantasy setting. The writing is excellent and makes for amazing replayability. I had myself doing intentionally faulty builds, not just to experience the many interesting ways to die, but to see the flavor text on classes and choices that may not otherwise have been open to me.
The game was updated ages after release with even more content, much to my surprise, and had me coming back to play it again for even more new stuff. Every choice you have bears some kind of consequence on the narrative, be it on the influence on your mood, your popularity with your people and/or court or changing the narrative entirely. You can cause civil wars. You can be overthrown by your own court. You can have assassins come for your life for reasons you won't understand until you've played through several kinds of routes. The setting is dynamic and it will take many, many playthroughs to learn how everything pieces together, without destroying the narrative experience for your first, single playthrough.
It seems like there's always something new to find. Would absolutely recommend to anyone.

I waited over a month for this game after hearing that it would be released.  I was eager for it. As a fan of BSG and Mass Effect, I felt the idea of a nomadic fleet finding purchase on cooperative starsystems would be a unique experience.  After just an half-hour playing the game I can say it is a feeble attempt.  I expected more from Sid Meier.  This game is a shallow, flimsy attempt to expand on the Beyond Earth franchise.  The resource management is rudimentary. The story is nonexistent. The language is belittling (I feel it's condescending and dumbed down). There is ultimately no difference between choosing any of the affinities as the leaders all give the same rewards no matter which affinity one selects. This is a sad, sad iOS port to PC.  It's a vapid shell.   The starbattles are tactically childish.  I might have some challenge with the game if I were 10 years old and suffering from some kind of brain trauma.  Starships is a poor title as a few minutes of playing the game is sufficient to eliminate any exclamation the player might have expected.  Meier must have lent his name and his name only to this hunk of junk, but frankly, a man that I have idolized for years as a trend-setter and revolutionary designer has seriously let me down.  I would never have attached my name to such a trivial, casual game, not that casual games themselves are bad.  Just this one.

I was very excited to play it, and now I'm completely turned off.  This all happened in about 10 minutes of gameplay.  I don't even want to give it another chance, because it's not even the right type of game.  It looks like a 4x, but wow does it fail.
Also I want to add that the user interface blows.  I expected to be able to interact with and rotate planets when I was zoomed into them, but no.  However, you can slide the top of one of the lists up and down in a klunky, unnecessary and superfluous way.
Sid Meier made one of the most brilliant games ever in Civilization.  He's cloned that model so many times now, that it seems he has forgotten what a fun game is.  He got money from me this time purely because of his name, but he won't again.  I'm bitterly disappointed.
