**UPDATE** - This review was written with the game running on "Hard"
This is the worst game I've played that bears Sid Meier's name.
"Surely it's not that bad" You say.
I'm afraid it is.
In the build up to the release of the game there was little doubt that it was going to be a less involved game to play then the typical Sid Meier fare, more Ace Patrol then Civilization 5. When developers were discussing the game, that was pretty clear and I have no qualms with that.
In fact I was quite happy with the idea of a strategy game designed so I could play over an evening after work.
The 3 hour play time of this review was playing a game to completion on a "large" map.
Initial impressions are poor. The game launching in a tiny window and into a bare, personality-less main menu that could have been ripped from any sci-fi title (it reminded me of the Sword of the Stars 2 menu). I sought out the settings menu and within that I found volume controls and "Windowed Full Screen mode".
I'm sorry what?
I know the game was being made for tablet as well, but this is Firaxis. I asked another friend playing it "Am I missing a settings menu somewhere?" bemusedly. "Nope" He replied "It really is that sparse"
Oh well. Not a great first impression, but not necessarily the end of the world. I setup a game.
Setup lets you pick a faction and a leader. Each faction gets the same leaders, with slightly rejigged artwork. Which comes across as a bit lazy. The factions have a unique bonus with the leaders adding an additional bonus of their own. I was a little bemused at what the various bonuses meant as I only knew about one aspect of the game (crew morale) from previews nothing else made a lot of sense and there was nothing to explain the benefits of a choice, no tooltips, nothing.
The lack of tooltips persists throughout, with a general lack of accessible information.
I setup my game, stabbing blindly in the dark at things that sounded useful
The galactic playing field looks alright and I wait for the useful tutorial to kick in and explain things to me over my first few turns. I get nothing. I understand there's an info button to click but I don't understand why there's a lack of tutorial and I fumble around the first few turns getting to grips with the games systems.
As the game is all about moving a fleet around space bringing disparate planets into a federation you'd expect load out/designing of the ships to be one of the most involved aspects of the game. Instead, you're presented with a list of things to click away at to upgrade or downgrade (removing components nets you some resources back to spend elsewhere) different aspects of each ship.
My fleet consisted of three ships throughout the course of the game, starting as corvette's, ending as battleships through upgrades and the games automatic ship classification. All 3 focused on speed, one was paticularly tough and loaded with close range weaponry. One was less tough, also had close range weaponry and could cloak. One had longer range weapons. The limitation to what you can actually do with ships meant all of them had max speed, and were stupidly tough by about mid way through. But this simple setup felt game breaking. I could defeat any mission or enemy fleet, outside of the missions where you have to defend an outpost that can only survive two hits with fast enemies that just head straight for it.
The empire building aspect of the game is no more involved. "Click this to make numbers go up, because numbers" about sums up this aspect of the game. There's no interesting trade off between balancing metal, food or energy. Get lots of whatever you can, click stuff to have more stuff.
I actually beat my game accidentally. I was working my way from planet to planet, building one ludcriously over powered wonder after another because why not, then a conquered a planet which also had a wonder and triggered the wonder victory.
Well victory nets you a much more rewarding end then it does in Beyond Earth at least. You get 10 seconds of video which is better then a text box. But does it really matter when the rest of the game is so unengaging?
Overall, it's an ok game to have on a tablet, nothing stand out, even where there isn't much competition. But on the PC there's tons. Weird Worlds in Infinite space did something similar but better years ago and it's Early Access sequel likely will to. There is no reason to buy this game for the PC, and very little for a tablet.

This game is something I can not recommend enough to everyone to play through at least once. However - at the same time, I must take a moment to give words of caution. If 1080p and 60 FPS are huge selling points for you, this game might not be for you. And, unfortunately, due to a poor system in the port, the game is unplayable with certain OS's. Do research first and make sure you can play the game before buying - buyer beware on this.
However, I do think that this is a great game for those it works for. I happen to be one of the ones who had no issue running this, so my experience was only positive. I loved getting to revisit the lands of Sylvarant and Tethe'alla. The game is exactly how I remembered it, for all the good and bad.
The fight system is its strongest point. The LMB (Linear Motion Battle System) is just as great as ever, and the lack of free run, while confiding, is something you become accustomed to very quickly. I've missed this system, compared to more recent tales systems.
The story is still as corney, cringe-worthy cheese as it ever was. At the end of the game, you feel yourself rolling your eyes a little at just how cheesy the story is.
But that's part of the charm of the game, isn't it?
The graphics are still enjoyable, though - I will say, it feels like a slight downgrade from the original. There are some jagged issues around characters that I get on my system, and I am not sure if it's a port of personal setting issue.
Soundwise, the MUSIC of tales of symphonia is as amazing as it ever was. Fatalize still gives me that pumped up feeling it always gave me when I was a kid. The angelic themes for some fights still make me feel as though I'm fighting an insurmountable foe - whcih makes it all the more sweet when I beat them.
So. Overall. I can recommend the game - but do your homework. Ask yourself. Do you care about 1080p/60fps, or do you care if the game is good? And, can your system run it? Do not be afraid to refund if it cannot. Ignore the naysayers and decide for yourself.

Ace Combat: Assault Horizon is a turbulent attempt to combine intense cinematic style with a modern day aerial combat game.
The story of Assault Horizon is one of revenge, rebellion, and a really bad plot.  It is poorly written, poorly conveyed, and painfully obnoxious.
You are Lieutenant Colonel William Bishop; a U.S. pilot working with NATO's 108th Task Force in East Africa.  The Task Force is currently combating the rise of a group of "rebels".  Who these rebels are, who they are rebelling against, and why is never even considered worth talking about by the game.  The Rebs need to be put down and that's that.  A few missions into the game, the rebels are traded out entirely for a new faction of other rebels whose motives are once again completely left in the jet stream.  These rebels at least have a name, but suffice to say by the end of the game, you'll really start to question why so many of them even follow the primary antagonist on his suicidal crusade.  Some missions will be given a modicum of context before you leap in.  Others will just dive right in and by the end you won't even know who you were shooting at and why.  Major plot events transpire that are not even conveyed to the player, making for plenty of confusion when what HAS been conveyed would imply that the situation you're in should be entirely the opposite of what it is.  Character writing is flat and devoid of depth.  Dialogue is 50% radio chatter and 50% unfunny banter.  It all wraps up with what is written to be some sort of inspirational statement about overcoming perceived obstacles in life that rings incredibly hollow in light of the plot that preceded it.
Half arcade combat and half flight sim, Assault Horizon is a game about launching missiles at distant targets or chasing them down yourself.  Player aircraft can take a fair beating before going down and regenerating health will keep you in the fight on every difficulty except Ace.  Everything will be flown from fighters and bombers to attack helicopters and AC-130's.  Each war machine comes loaded with anywhere from 30 to 100+ missiles and munitions as well as their own flight parameters and loadouts.  You can really feel a difference between the older models and the modern 5th gen's.  Flight controls feel very good.  The camera isn't so much locked to your plane as it is an entity that follows it.  Turns feel tighter and G-forces rattle the screen.  Although the standard three-axis flight model is available as a control option, the Optimum setting keeps your controls tied to the relation of the camera.  It works very well in all situations except an invert, and since you can't roll, inverts are only automatically corrected if you relinquish control of the craft for a few seconds.  Helicopters controls are a little more awkward.  You can strafe back and forth; left and right, but you can only rotate left or right.  Looking up or down keeps the chopper completely level but aims the chin cannon's elevation.
The majority of the game's 16 missions will put you snug in the seat of a jet.  These are broken up by two attack helicopter chapters and a few on rails turret sorties.  Assault Horizon's biggest attempt to stand out lies in it's Dog Fight Mode.  While most targets can be downed by a couple missiles; many will require you to enter DFM.  Working your way to the rear of an enemy plane while in close proximity will allow you to initiate DFM.  At this point the game turns into a sort of gamified on rails system in which the opponent you're pursuing lays down the track.  DFM gives a certain level of magnetism to keep you direclty behind the enemy at break neck speeds, but failing to steer yourself long their same path will see you drop out of the chase entirely.  You will automatically keep up with their velocity, but can modulate your speed.  Slowing down widens your ability to stay on their tail, but makes aiming your gun or lining up a missile lock incredibly difficult.  Punching the throttle will bring the nose of your plane mere yards from your target.  Attacking them at this distance is easy, but one tight turn will knock you straight out of DFM.  Missile lock-on's gain extra damage if you also manage to line up perfectly with the enemy craft before letting it fly.  Victims of DFM can pop flares to ward of missile lock-ons, and can also decelerate.  Slowing down will make them risk your wrath, but allows them to then engage a counter DFM, looping around to come in behind your craft instead and reversing the roles.  These same options are available to the player.  On the whole, the system works and it is incredibly gratifying.  Although repititious, every chase is a small little combat challenge about keeping up and taking aim while you hurtle across the sky at a thousand knots.  Successfully staying on the tail of a particularly dodgy fighter is a blast and the ability to chain DFM's if other planes are within range can erase entire flights in seconds if your aim is true.  The kill cam that end caps many of your kills is a real treat too.
Sadly, this fun new system is often used in all the wrong ways.  Far too many of the the DFM's you'll engage in are cutscenes that attempt to show you a cool chase where you fly under a falling crane or strafe over exploding bridges.  These enemies are completely immune to the dozen or so missiles you'll ram up their exhaust and rather than build excitement, only make you wish the chase would end so you can actually shoot them down.  The final boss fight in particular is absolutely egregious.  It breaks all of the combat rules you'll have learned up to that point and you'll be forced to chase the same jet multiple times while nothing you do to it has any effect whatsoever, but you still have to avoid his game breaking attacks.  It drags the entire last chapter down and has given me a new appreciation for quick time events in video games.  At least when I push a button during a QTE, something happens.  Blasting an invincible jet to oblivion is incredibly demoralizing and completely sucks way all tension or fun.  The game is at its best when it lets you DFM freely and rule the skies, but these patches of genuine fun or broken up consistently by frustrating scripted chases.  It's a real let down.
Free Missions let you replay the campaign chapters in whatever craft you please while tring to earn the highest score you can.  This mode cuts out most of the cutscene fat, but sadly the scripted chases remain.
The Player Archive contains a pretty bad hangar viewer for any aircraft you've flown, player stats, a page of 150+ unlockables to chase after, and an incredibly limited replay feature of moments you may have saved while playing.
Players can also customize craft with a myriad of color options.  Even their missile exhaust trails.
This is where Assault Horizon manages to fire on all cylinders.  The game presents an impressive level of detail on a macro, mid, and micro scale as you soar through the sky, run low altitude helicopter missions, and listen in on first person cutscenes presented in real time.  The crown jewel of the game is aircraft destruction.  Each kill results in a glorious explosion of showering sparks, gouts of oil, and the slow motion rending of metal from metal.  Hapless pilots are ripped from their cockpits, thousands of feet in the sky.  Steel Carnage indeed.  Highly aggressive camera work frames the entire game and adds a lot of energy to it.  Music is often subpar but drowned out by lock-on tones.  The opening mission is an exception.

is a game about “superweapon dogfighting in a world with World War II-era Thunderbirds”. It takes place somewhere between the Second World War and the Cold War, or in an alternative reality in the ten to fifteen years after the Second World War. We’re talking the age of fear for mind control, floating sky fortresses, orbital rays, weaponised dolphins, cryptography and submerging warplanes. The player is part of an undefined enemy force that was not on ‘our’ side during the six or seven decades in which military intelligence was effectively telling us to prepare for a laser-equipped hoverboat assault. It's pretty awesome.
As a Vlambeer game,
has a lot going for it. The game is all about big bullets, lots of screen-shaking explosions, fun mechanics, and ridiculous controls. Like with all Vlambeer games, it features a high skill ceiling and difficulty while maintaining easy accessibility and addictive gameplay. Aesthetically, it has simple but great pixel art and vibrant color palettes. KOZILEK's soundtrack is amazing; it subtly changes as you customize your Rauser with different guns, hulls, and engines. Everything about it just
amazing.
There are a few flaws, however. The user interface is a little clunky; I've had trouble remapping the controls and the menus are a little hard to navigate. Players might get turned off by the simplicity and lack of content as well as the difficult missions. Still, I definitely think it's worth the $10. It's one of the best air-combat/dogfighting games I've ever played.

GAMEPLAY.

I'm not a huge fan of shooters or tower defense games, but this game is an exceptional exception. It is essentially a third-person shooter that takes place within a tower defense game. You must stop the horde of orcs by placing traps in strategic locations to kill and slow down the orcs. While attacking them with your character. All action is in third-person perspective.
What I love about this game is how simple it starts off and how complex it can become. It can be played just to clear each level, and gain skulls to power up your abilities. Or it can be played to try and get a high score, and that is where this game becomes very fun and challenging. tl;dr - Yeh, it's worth the price! Well-balanced, varied with a good progress system.
With numerous duds plaguing the Steam Store nowadays any TD game that uses the standard "classic" formula, of laying down towers alongside a path of creeps to mow down, needs to have an extra angle or two to keep players coming back. Thankfully,
has the bells and whistles you're after. Bearing a graphical resemblance to
you'll be kept busy using the usual tactics and strategies that you've come to expect from this genre: lay down the right tower type on the build square; use the right special ability at the right time; time your upgrades correctly; use trial and error to get the elusive gold star etc. All pretty standard - but all balanced and pitched admirably to create that on-the-edge tension required in TD games.
So with all the standard stuff ticking the box, what else does
bring to the table? Well apart from those varied and interesting special abilities (one of which allows you to place your own build squares) you also get quirky levels that step outside of the norm. In one, for example, you'll need to build your own army and send them down a path yourself; while in another you'll have only one hero unit which you must teleport from build square to build square in an effort to stop the march of the creeps. On top of this, there is an involved Main-Screen Area where you'll use collected rewards to purchase buildings and extra upgrades - all of which greatly helps with that feeling of progression.
It's still EA so, yeh, some tweaking is definitely required but it's a positive recommendation from me.

I feel that the pacing is way off on this game. There is too much emphasis put on doing repeat runs of the same levels. When I finally made it to the first boss, and wasn't successful on my first try (I died), I ended up having to do two more runs of the level before the boss before I was able to save up enough money to get the power-ups and armor that I would need to even beat the boss. I understand that you get to keep money when you die, but when I drop 75 coins on getting some nice abilities that I want to save for the boss battle, and then I end up dying on the level before the boss battle, I end up wasting all those coins. This means I have to do at least one full run through before I have enough money to repurchase everything. I also always seemed to be one damage point behind the amount of armor I could afford to repair. If it cost 80 to repair, I only had 67 coins, but then when I had 80 coins saved up, it then cost 100 to repair the armor. It would be nice if you could improve lesser increments of the armor for smaller amounts of gold. I'd rather put 20-40 gold into repairing the armor temporarily than lose the whole armor and have to use 100-250+ gold to craft a new set.
While this game may be similar to The Binding of Isaac, it is not on the same par. There's no sense of dread, no sense of being alone in a world set against you. The atmosphere of this game is lost when the pleasant town is just an elevator ride away. One of the most annoying things though, is having a really nice group of abilities, and you're doing well in a level, and then they all run out of shots, and you're left with the default shot, which is pretty terrible. You can only hope you have found enough gold in the level already (or have some left over from before the level, haha) to purchase a key and hope it's a good ability.
I hope that there are some great updates in the future of this game that help bring it up to a level where I would favorably compare it with The Binding of Isaac. The people involved with this game are really nice, and I hope to see them improve the balance and pacing of the game.

Ok, there are many reasons to write a positive review for this little indie relaxing game, the first of all is that the very first achievement, named "support an indie", has a completion ratio of 8% as I am writing. And this is completely crazy, since it unlocks only by opening the game, without even pushing the start button.. so that means that no one played this basically!
And being a very pleasant and relaxing game, I think it deserves not only a positive review but also some visibility and many players :)
The graphics in my opinion are awesome (unfortunately the menu doesn't allow you to change quality or anything but the sound, so you can choose only between full screen and a windowed mode in a fixed resolution), super relaxing and in line with this kind of game, set in a starry night.
Your main objective will be to collect the falling stars with a bucket, which will eventually fill up and you'll be able to unload it by going on the left or right side of the screen - you can do this even if it's not full.
The WASD controls are smooth and nice and that contributes to the soothing nature of the game, paired with the very pleasant music and graphics, as I said. Very cartoonish and dreamy :)
Plus, you'll earn in-game money that will let you buy new buckets (they're called baskets in-game, but thank God it's only available in English so no crappy unplayable Italian translations by default even in the game hub page XD), and of course the game will be filled with other contents!
The money you'll earn by catching stars has lots of in-game uses: you'll be able to buy a bucket capable of holding many more stars, and the enter key will allow you to use the bonus you'll have obtained, so that you will be able to slow down the falling stars, to be faster with your own collecting basket, to eliminate the wind (which can of course change a little bit the mechanics of the game) and, lastly, to have less falling ice.
As I said, from the sky you'll have other things falling and the ice shards have to be avoided at all costs!
Plus, I enjoyed a lot the addition of a wind system - you'll see on the upper right side of the screen where and how the wind will blow, thus affecting speed and everything on the screen. And you'll also have to collect power ups falling from time to time from the sky too! And avoid the bad ones, since if you collect them you'll have to deal for some seconds of "more ice" or "slow bucket" downgrades ;)
For 1€ as a full price, it's a must have if you're into casual relaxing games and well, it's perfect to play with your keyboard only so it's not a crappy mobile port as we often see here.
I saw already many beautiful, lengthier and way better written than mine reviews so I won't go into other aspects, although I covered the most of them.
The basics of the game are all here and it can be a little bit boring just if you really want to play it for every single achievement and buyable object, but this isn't a thing worth to consider in my view here.
Just keep in mind that it's not a "5-minutes" game (on Kongregate we have that hashtag xD), every session can take Idk, maybe twenty minutes, and it's increasingly difficult so you'll have to buy upgrades and well, I think this goes on to the replayability value of this game - it's best played in multiple sessions (everything's of course auto-saved) so that you don't get bored playing it for an entire day.
Oh, by the way it can also be played with a controller, it fully supports the XBOX one for instance but to me it's perfect on WASD keys, you'll need only the movement ones and enter (or A with the controller) in order to activate the bonuses, and if you're a right-handed who plays with the left hand like me trust me, it's perfect and not damaging at all :)
Considered its price and the value of this indie-developed Unity game, it's super relaxing but also gets challenging if you go on with the levels, it also has trading cards so if you've already got it into your library or if you don't have it in your wishlist well, buy it or simply play it and it's really worth the time :)

A quick addition for people who think this game could never have been done as DLC:
It wouldn't have been hard to get this to work as a DLC.
The game may look different, but it uses the same basic engine (albeit greatly slimmed down). All they've really done is replace the flat terrain maps of Civ with a star field and planets and replaced the normal ground and water based units with space ships. It's basically CIv trying to give the impression of space when it's actually just a 2D hex based RTS like all the other games in the series. Basically the ships aren't flying through space, they're moving along an invisible ground plane, or the equivalent of, with a star background replacing the terrain we normally see. With all that in mind, it wouldn't have been all that difficult to add the maps, units and other features to the main game. There's nothing in Starships that couldn't have been accomplished in the base game.
It could have been an add-on for the base game, and added new gameplay features, in the same way that The Sims add-ons often add in new features that weren't built into the base game, but expand upon the original game mechnics.

Not a normal Sid Meier game where you can sink 100s of hours into, takes 1-2 hours to win and worth multiple replays. Not bad for 15 dollars. 8/10
===More In Depth Review===
Simple Space 4x where you have to get enough of the galaxy fighting for Team Player Character to win the galaxy super election.
You start off with one planet, and venture out to other planets to win their allegiance (either through doing quests, buying influence, destroying their factions fleet or simply ending your turn there). On each planet you can make upgrades that will either increase their resource output or add a warp gate (giving you free movement to the planet) or constructing a defensive fleet. Each planet rolls 1-2 random strategic attributes that give it an advantage (such as +50% energy output or 1/2 cost on resource buildings). Each planet also rolls a random tactical attribute such as torpedos being undetectable or more powerful cover from asteroids. A planet also has a chance of having the ability to have a wonder being built on it. All of this is somewhat simple, but there is a real swing factor in gaining or losing a planet with a great combination of attribute that adds a lot of fun to it.
Combat is great and where most of the enjoyment is. It's hex based TBS that has a heavy emphasis on cover and positioning.  Ships have three weapons at their disposal- Lasers (long range light damage), Plasma (short range medium damage) and Torpedos (Long Range Massive damage, but very predictable). Ships can also activate stealth (can't be hit with targeted weapons, enemy has to use sensor to find you) activate sensors (for finding stealthed units) or activate impulse drive (trade an action for a single movement in any direction without turning). Effectively, how combat goes is you use asteroids for cover while denying cover to enemies with your torpedoes.
Unlike plasma or lasers, torpedoes don't lose damage when fired through an asteroid field. They can't explode the first turn they are fired and continue moving in a straight line for up to three turns. As they automove on the second and third turn you are allowed to make them explode remotely as they move in "real time". Being near the center of a torpedo explosion is usually a one shot kill. The explosions also clear asteroids. Torpedos almost never directly get kills against you so long as you move out of their path. The AI doesn't seem to respect them enough though - in the last battle of the game I played I got a triple kill with a torpedo as three ships maneuvered close together to take pot shots at one of my fighters.
Your army is a persistent fleet of ships that you purchase upgrades for. Upgrades are pretty predictable (engines give you more moves per turn, lasers do more damage) and there's no real incentive to specialize other then you can't afford all the upgrades at once. There's also a fairly mild experienced mechanic tied to a ship's performance in battle. Science ties into all of this as well, but it's just more simple upgrades to laser damage paid for with a separate currency that effects your whole fleet at once.
Wonder balance seems a bit wonky, there are some extremely cheesy wonders like the one that gives you an extra action in combat. It is somewhat limited in that you can't use it on firing lasers or plasma twice in a single turn... but you can fire two torpedos, or release twice as many fighter fleets or attack and then immediately cloak to avoid reprisals.
===Overall===
+Interesting, Fun Combat
+Understandable UI
+Powerful feeling planets attributes
-Somewhat Questionable AI
-Economy and Diplomacy seem simple even by the low standards of economy and diplomacy in Space 4X
-A lot of uninteresting upgrades
I'd love if it were multiplayer because the combat seems like it'd be more fun if there were living human beings on the other end but for $15 I won't pitch a fit over it. It's an entirely fun single player 4X that doesn't overstay it's welcome and is simple enough for people who don't normally play 4Xs.
Sidenote: There's also a lot of mutual unlocks with Civ: Beyond Earth but I haven't explored any of that yet so I'm ignoring it.

Straight from the Science Officer:
---------------------------
Sid Meier's Starships is the continuation to Beyond Earth. While BE was more focused on 4x empire management, Starships shifts gear to commanding a fleet of interstellar vessels as you run around completing missions in turn-based strategy fashion. In-depth customization of your ships' systems is the center of the game as lasers tear through your hull because you thought having maximum sensors was the smartest idea.
While the tactical map is where you'll be battling, the galactic map is ultimately where you win the war. Here, you'll be competing for influence on various systems against your rivals from BE as you seek to rid the universe of their annoying one-liners. Victory is achieved by eliminating all of your rivals, controlling over half of the galaxy, researching enough technologies to the maximum tier, or spending enough industry to own seven wonders.
"Yes Commander"
---------------------------
(+) Well thought out tactical gameplay - Do I stealth this turn? Fire my weapons? Launch torpedoes?  "Oooh let's hide behind this planet and when the enemy comes, charge guns blazing"
(+) Great ship customization - With your fleet of ships, you'll be able to craft each ship to fit your battle plans. You could make a fleet of ships with many engines and long range weapons and kite the enemy or brawlers that hide behind a planet and charge out when the enemy nears. Maybe you'd like to have a stealth carrier that pops out, launches some fighters, and goes back into the void or a sensor ship to detect an enemy fleet that relies on stealth fighters. The options are vast. A bonus kudo goes to the fact the game auto-classes your ship based on its setup. A ship teethed with guns and armor will be labelled as a battleship while a fast ship with high damage would be an assault corvette. It just provides an additional, nice immersion feature.
(+) Simplicity - While it can be argued that this is a negative as some people perhaps expected a complex 4x game reminisicent of MOO or Galciv, Starships is a game focused on ...Starships. The focus isn't on managing a large empire but instead on controlling your fleet and completing missions with that said fleet in order to build your empire.
(+) Missions - There's a decent variety of missions so you won't get too bored until a few playthroughs. While the mission types get similar, the map and the ships in each mission can change.
(+) Price - $15 (in the US) is a great price for a game like this. You'll definitely get hours of gameplay and like most Sid Meier's games, once you figure out the controls, it's hard to pay attention to real-life.
(+) Bridge Visuals - Each bridge depending on which faction (harmony, purity, supremacy) you picked gets it's own unique bridge. It's a really small thing but it's something that definitely stands out.
"We'll get them next time..."
---------------------------
(-) No Multiplayer - One of the things I was hoping to do was get a nice game going with some friends. The game definitely has unexploited MP potential. A decent size map can be finished with some friends in a day. It's not going to be like playing a MP match of Crusader Kings or EUIV which can last weekends on ends. The AIs only going to be able to be so unique on designing fleets.
(-) One Fleet - Having only one fleet really limits strategic gameplay on the galactic map. There's not going to be any strategy where I can defend one location and fight in another on AI turns. I won't be able to create a fleet for defense and another for attack or specialize one fleet for certain types of missions.
(-) Squishiness of Ships - Hopefully this gets sorted out but ships seem like they are glass cannons no matter how you build them at the moment. Unless you're literally building all armor / shields (which makes that ship pretty useless since it has no weapons), most ships die in a few hits. Fighters die in one shot from basically anything short of a maximum range pea shooter. This makes the tactical gameplay more arcadey and will hopefully be improved upon in later patches.

(-) Lack of 'One More Turn' - A fundamental Sid Meier's feature. Sometimes you just want to continue but you win, victory, that's it. This was an easy feature that was just simply and unfortunately overlooked.
(-) Modding Tools - There's a lot of potential for modding a game like this. It's not a stretch to imagine someone trying to recreate a Starfleet or Star Wars based mod if the tools are provided. Some of the best additions that enhance the value of old Civ games were fan-made maps and mods.
"Close Victory"
---------------------------
Overall I'd give this game a 6.5/10. The gameplay is addictive and the tactical battles are in-depth. Ship customization and fleet design is well-developed and serves as the main anchor for this game. Nontheless some pitfalls exists, mainly in the fact that there's no multiplayer in a game that would obviously benefit from having the ability to play a match against your friends. If you're expecting a big 4x game then you might want to stay away but if you want a quick game and you have a love of starships and fleet command then you should definitely pick it up. Sid Meier’s Starships is simple and to the point. It's a hex based strategy game focused around fleets of starships. Don't expect the moon, but what's here is pure and well developed. The mechanics are clear and intuitive, as with any Sid Meier creation. You use your fleet to garner influence with planets by either performing missions or taking shore leave there. The planets provide resources and can be upgraded in a few ways. Combat is turn based. Your ship's shields are weak in the back and strong in the front. Asteroid fields either block sight completely or reduce it. Weapons vary with long range lasers, short range cannons and torpedoes that cover a finite amount of space per turn. Researchable technologies are tied to specific ship systems and planetary wonders affect a given gameplay mechanic. It's streamlined down to a fault, but it's a fault they're not trying to hide from you. This is a $15 game made with tablets in mind as much as a PC. The games are quick in comparison to the ‘oh it’s dawn now’ syndrom that’s inherent to the Civilization franchise which is refreshing.

There’s no deception by Firaxis trying to build it up into something more than it is. But it’s inevitable that the game’s disinterest with being bigger than it is will bother a number of people. Thankfully it’s interested in what it is beyond the backlash.

Alright, first of all let me tell you that if you like Fate series, Simple yet good combat, Complex Fate Story Line and moe waifus, then you'll like this.
Fate/EXTELLA is a combination of visual novel-ish with Dynasty Warrior based combat with Moe Waifus and handsome men in tight suits. The visual novel-ish portion of the game is done justice, really well written with emotions clearly existed. Laughter and tears, you got it all. Now the Dynasty Warrior part is surprisingly well done, with visual and music done right (Fate style, of course), with fast pace action and a LOT of killing (And I mean a LOT of killing). It might take you awhile to get to the portion where your character (servants) have their epic combo moves since there ARE grinding here in this game.
However, what I don't really like about the Dynasty Warrior aspect of it is their zone based system. It's a bit too restricting, and the way you're going to reach to the next zone are set and thus it gets annoying manuvering around sometime. Also the allied AI in this game is really annoying to the point of becoming almost useless. They only move to other zone based on scripted events, and once they captured the zone they'll stay there until the game is over or they get killed by random mooks (Yes, they're THAT useless). At least make them move from zone to zone because this make them look like a glorified Mooks.
But other than that the game is spot on. The event animation could sometime be 'Eh', but overall its great. From 0-10 (Unplayable to  Epic) I'll give it an '8/10', worth the price. But if you DON'T like an Anime based, visual novel-esque game you probably won't like it, and if you never watch, heard or even play a Fate Series then you might get confused at the plot so be warned!

Overview:
An arcade style flight simulation game with bomber, helicopter, and airplane missions.  An extremist Russian group with a new type of bomb threatens the region.  It's up to the American military to neutralize the threat.
Pros:
Controls: Easy to pick up and fast paced.  There are some interesting airplane gameplay mechanics that adds some variety to the combat.
Polish: The game is very playable.  I never ran into glitches or control issues.  It is a complete game with a story and fully voice acted cutscenes.
Cons:
Story: Very generic.  You will not feel connected the characters or care what is going on in the game.
Gameplay: Very simplistic.  If you're a hardcore flight sim buff looking for a challenge this will not be it.  The combat can feel a little repetitive after playing for awhile.
Content: Some variety in airplanes you can choose but ultimately there isn't much content in this game.  Only about 10-12 hours of single player gameplay.
Conclusion:
I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone.  Hardcore flight sim buffs will find this way to arcadey and unrealistic.  Anyone looking for arcade style high intense action will find this lacking and get bored quickly.  There just isn't much good about this game nor is it particularly fun to play.
Score: 7.0 / 10

A surprisingly decent Ace Combat game.  I had heard tell that this was something of the dark horse in the Ace Combat series, so I was pleasantly surprised when it ended up being pretty alright.  For reference, I've played Ace Combat 1-6, plus Zero, so I feel that I have a decent base to judge this game on in relation to the rest of the series.  The air combat stuff itself is pretty similar other than the new dogfight duel mode thing, where you lock in behind an enemy you're trailing in basically a mini-cutscene.  There's also some counters where you can flip around people behind you in the same vein.  It's honestly not that bad of a system, though it does get a bit less cinematic and more repetitive the more you do it (which is a lot).  Another major change is the introduction of bombing routes, where you line up to a predefined route and the it locks your plane over a path cutting across ground forces, slows you down, and increases your weapon damage to do a full bombing run.  I didn't really like it that much, I've always had more fun doing low flybys and hugging the ground at high speeds when I do bombing runs, picking my approaches and whatnot, and this feature sort of sterilized it.
There are a couple of new mission types, too, namely two different helicopter mission types and a mission type as an AC-130 gunner.  One of the helicopter mission types is just as a door gunner and it's basically an on-rails shooter with not much variety going on.  Probably the weakest parts of the game, to be honest.  And they drag on for far too long.  The other helicopter type is taking control of an attack helicopter and flying around providing ground support.  This was by far my favorite new addition to the game/series and I wouldn't mind seeing it pop up in future Ace Combat games.  You get the full agency on the battlefield like you do with normal flying, as you move around to different hot zones that need your attention.  The air-vs-air combat kinda sucks, though.  Every time you have to fight an enemy Hind is kind of disappointing, because I'd always rather be shooting up the ground forces.
There was also the story change for this game, which was kind of weird.  They moved the setting out of the Strangereal setting of the previous Ace Combat games and into the real world for some reason.  It definitely feels weird and out of place, but not to the point where it ruins the game.
Overall, if you liked previous Ace Combat games, I think you'd probably enjoy this game, even if it's not quite as good as the rest of the series.  There's still that core kernal of Ace Combat here.

Short, short review for long-time players of the Ace Combat series: this is not an Ace Combat game. It has the right name, yes, and some of the original arcade-ish feel. However, missiles are no longer all-aspect; you will almost never get a head-on shot, no matter how lousy a plane the opposition picked, and no matter how good yours is. Doesn't matter what type of missile you're packing.
Winning is mostly a matter of using the new "dogfight mode" (what else have we been doing all this time!?) and trying to use "special weapons" (that is, anything but the stock missiles--MSL) whenever they're ready to fire. Regular missiles rarely hit, even though you're probably going to get hit BY them on a regular basis. Enemy aircraft have full access to "infinite ammo" and "no reload" cheat codes, same as usual.
I've actually gone back and fired up my old PS2 to compare to the AC titles that were available. It's not a matter of a difference in controllers (PSX2 vs. X360 on PC) or my forgetting how bad I was at Ace Combat (I wasn't). Not only have the core mechanics changed, but the game is overall much harder.
Even on "rookie" difficulty, enemy missiles will hit more often than not, and as soon as you run out of flares (almost immediately), there's very little you can do to stop a missile from hitting you. In some missions, you'll have multiple enemy aces on your tail at a time, and your supposed wingmen are more interested in comms chatter than scratching your back.
Even the introductory mission had a large number of enemies constantly spawning, and now that I've sort-of mastered controlling the other, terrible mechanics (AC-130 overwatch, H-60 door gunner, Longbow really-bad-flight-sim), I'm another couple of actual JET COMBAT missions in, and the odds feel impossible.
I thought the whole point of having adjustable difficulty was that I could turn it down until I didn't feel like there was enough of a challenge, then back up until I'm having fun. Instead, I haven't had any actual fun at all.
PS: Hi, Namco? Your introductory disclaimer won't hold up in a court of law. It's all well and good to disclaim that no actual persons, countries, companies, etc. are intended to be portrayed in the game... but when the main characters are mostly wearing US flag patches and USAF patches or grunting "Yes, but WE'RE RUSSIAN! We don't follow standard procedures!" then everyone knows exactly what countries you're portraying. Same with "Mogadiyu, Africa." Maybe also don't say "from the Air Force base in Texas" or "US Carrier, Persian Gulf." You probably should have stuck to licensing real warplanes and making up the names of countries and locations. I think everyone was fine with that.
PPS: Possibly you can get away with claiming that no real events are portrayed, 'cause, yeah, I don't remember any massive air battles over Miami Beach.

I'm saying this because I wasted probably 30 hours playing a pure sorcerer and actually quit the game out of boredom.  Thank god I came back and made a new build because I really would have missed out.
The netcode is awful.  I can't see how anyone could like it.  You will fight against people who will one moment be in front of you and in the next killing you with a backstab.  That kind of teleporting is prevalent online, and even using mods that are supposed to improve the matchmaking don't help enough, so take that for what you will.
The world is great.  It's very open, meaning after you get out of the starting area you have options.  It's also interconnected, which makes it feel more real.  I definitely miss this in Dark Souls 3.  The level design is for the most part pretty good.  Some areas felt rushed though.  Everyone says that the first half of the game is a masterpiece and the second half is a mess, and I agree that the second half is nowhere near as good as the first.  The pacing gets messed up because you have to backtrack all over and a few of the later levels are very underwhelming in both level and boss design.
The upgrade system is a pain.  The game doesn't really tell you much about how it works, and they split the upgrade types up and gave them to different blacksmiths around the world.  While it is pretty cool to venture out to find a specific blacksmith for a specific task, it's a system that will have you looking at a wiki page A LOT.
My last gripe is with the platforming.  Some people love this part of the game, but I personally do not.  Simply put, the game uses a lot of tight platforming and the engine and the camera suck for it.  Death in the game is supposed to feel fair, but I don't get that feeling when I die while platforming.  This is something I got very sick of by the end of it, and I'm glad that they cut back on it a lot in DS3.
It's a great game.  I wouldn't call it a masterpiece, or even a "flawed masterpiece" like I've heard others say, but definitely unique and worth trying for anyone who wants a challenging RPG with a somber atmosphere.  I always see people asking which Dark Souls game they should start with.  Start with this one.  It's worth playing and the references in Dark Souls 3 will make more sense if you do.  And the game's flaws will be more apparent if you start with DS3 and then go backards to DS1, potentially hurting the experience.

POSTAL, one of the most violent, yet Interesting games around 1997. POSTAL Is one Interesting title, and caused much controversy back In the day. After reading some of the other recent posts about this game I have edited my review:
This game is for casual gamers not for veterans of Galactic Civs or Sword of the Stars are anything remotely on that level. I am a little disappointed that some gamers compare epic games (that cost 60 USD) to this 15 dollar offshoot of Beyound Earth. If you are looking for a an hour to kill this could be for you. If you are looking for 3 hours to get lost in go Mod a copy of Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion.
One hour in and counting:
Pros:
15 USD excellent value
Starship customization
Graphics are solid
Munition animations
Good Voice Acting
Intelligent Diplomacy with aggressive AI
Planetary missions have a sense of urgency (if you wont help them a rival will and soon)
Lots of detail without being overwhelming
Very Fluid Gameplay (not nearly as micromanaging as some 5x space strategy)
Cons:
Surprising hardware requirements (Less stable than Endless Space)
Cannot Rename Planets or starships (There is a reason for this, planetary names are spoken aloud adding to voice acting quality)
Limited scope compared to space strategy genre
Overall: Excellent buy for 15 USD. Simple to enjoyable to those outside the genre. Detailed enough for regular strategy players. In summary: More than the sum of its parts

This will contain "spoilers" for the end boss, so if you have not played the game I would reccommend not to read the rest of this. Before I do start on the end boss however, I would like to talk about starting out in Stabound.
Starting out in Starbound can be a real pain if you have no knowledge of the game. When I first started out, I almost quit because of how evertime I walked somewhere, I got killed by a random enemy. After a little while however, I got better gear and I was able to slaughter enemies at ease.
Now that we got the beginning out of the way, lets go into the "spoiler" part of this review. I felt like the final boss was kind of a let down and the ending as a whole was rushed. Lets start with the boss. This is the thing that destroyed Earth, so it must be pretty tough right? Not really, as a matter of fact I had more of a problem fighting Asra Nox then the final boss. I also felt like the boss fight itself was to short, like wouldn't it be awesome if when you first defeated the boss and "The Ruin" exploded, the big chunks of "The Ruin" would fight you while your on another chunk of the ruin avoiding obstacles? Finally lets get to the part where your "dead" after the bossfight. The scene where everybody is gathered around the portal felt rushed aswell. I felt like that scene could have been more touching if it was slower, and more of the characters talked instead of just one.
Besides all of this, I found this game very fun and addicting, and I do reccommend it to people. I would like to say however, that all of this is my opinion of the game.

As a disclaimer, I am a fate series veteran, played/watched most of all translated available material. Finished most of the game by now, am waiting until the end to summarize properly what I think regarding the story. All other points are still the same.
The plot is a direct continuation from Fate/Extra CCC, the Japan-only highschool holy battle royale and waifu/bro simulator for the PSP.
Being a direct continuation, you are quite literally thrown into the thick of things right from the start. Following in the footsteps of the Fate/Stay Night visual novel, you cannot choose a route from the get-go, as they are meant to be experienced in a specific order. Whereas in a game it might be seen as archaic for newcomers, I feel like it does help to tell a more cohesive story at the end.
Written by Nasu with help of Hikaru Sakurai, the plot in the first part is, without mincing words, very predictable. As I have not finished the game yet, I can't tell if the first part serves the same purpose as the Fate route in F/SN (or, in a broader sense, the entirety of Fate/Extra) to better ease the reader into the world and by the third part it is more interesting and wild. Regardless, it was still very much a product you'd come to expect from Nasu, immensely poetic and descriptive as it is.
More to the point, it is almost fanservice-y in parts, from character interactions to the roster. Many if not all quips might fly above the head of even someone that is used to the fate series but hasn't played the Extra duology; newcomers even more so.
Gameplay is standard Musou/Dynasty Warrior fare. Murder mooks until the big guy comes out, murder big guys, use your big finisher move on the boss, yay. For me, as a fan? It's very cool. For those who don't even know what happens when Archer uses his UBW? Less so.
It works and fits the theme of the game. If you've played Fate/Extra, you know what to expect.
Graphics are on the cheaper side of the spectrum. Sometimes it does look good, but some of the moves and special cutscenes that zoom in the characters look stiff and very low definition. Elizabeth Bathory's scenes are one of the biggest offenders. Just looks hastily put together. With the roster as frankly small as it is, when considering the franchise as a whole, this kind of thing is hard to defend.
My opinion is that you should play this game mostly because of it's story. Even then, that story is a continuation of a game that was never localized, that was a sequel and proper closing of a game for the PSP when it was already on it's way out.
For someone like me, this game is entertaining, funny, and honestly what I'd expect from all parties involved.
For someone who never touched the fate series or universe, I can't see them overlooking the repetitive gameplay, frankly boring first chapter, hard to understand story and apparently random selection of historical/mythical figures that may or may not be genderbent for whatever reason.

>> Gameplay
There are 4 main towers: Peasant, Archer, Rifleman and Novice. You can upgrade each unit and unlock further abilities or strenghten them.
You can earn gold, wood, stone, elexir, mithril. With this you can purchase upgrades, town buildings and items. There are many upgrades available for each of the 4 main units and some more. The town buildings produce some ressources, or you can play coop or pvp to gain them. On a market you can purchase items to use during a battle - i prefer to not use them if possible :)

Incredibly deep build-things-to-blow-things-up sandbox game.  Unique from other titles in this genre (but there are more and more solid, similar games, with different elements), boasting not only competetive play and casual sandbox play but also a number of preset scenarios to challenge your design, and a great big delicious campaign mode, which I've barely scratched (at >300* hours).
You can tell I just enjoy blowin'♥♥♥♥♥♥up trying to get that perfectly balanced, ordinance-spewing, sleek, sexy war machine.  SO MUCH LOVE.
* Update after many more hours of enjoyment: still fun as hell just figuring out more effective ways of blowin'♥♥♥♥♥♥up.  Still an amazing game with frequent updates, a lively community, and an absolutely incredible diversity of creative content.
The updates are not to be understated.  Recent additions range from railguns and advanced cannons (which are custom built) with customizable ammo (in addition to missiles that have long been customizable) to a complete engine revamp to detection systems (more on that later) to a UI tweak that *finally* laid out block varieties logically (THANK YOU! YES) and this list will grow too lengthy, you get it.  They've also progressively added some pre-built components to help folks get started or simply save time - like several types of engines, which are now fairly involved in their creation from the prior 'more of these and these and these = best', as well as weapons and other components.  Oh, and particle cannons.  One of my favorite ways to say hello - with shiny blue lights of DOOOOM!
Here's some more if you're not convinced.  How about different styles of play?  What's the most difficult playstyle to include in a game where destruction is the focus, besides diplomacy (which is also implemented, but I'm not experienced with)?
Stealth.
Well, guess what?  There are now robust detection mechanics in-game, including detection via optical camera, IR camera, laser, retroflection (seeing the glare of optical and laser detection systems), radar, sonar, and more - and counters to each.  Want to hide from radar - i.e. the simplest, most straightforward way of missles and craft finding targets?  Each type of block has a certain radar profile - everything functioning with precise physics - and by using both a slim profile design (think of a B-2 bomber) and passive detection systems, like passive radar (for above water targets), by staying below water and detecting via active or passive sonar (since radar can't detect subsurface targets), or even using a "wireless snooper" (which detects transmission between a vehicle's AI computer and components connected wirelessly, as opposed to physically block by block), you can effectively minimize your opponents' ability to detect your craft.  You might also do these, AND deploy radar bouoys to 'ping' your opponent remotely.  Of course, your opponent might pepper an area with sonar or radar buoys of their own to search you out; they may be able to detect your engines' heat signature via infrared or flat-out see you with a camera...
...you can see where this is going - this game has endless depth (har har) and is growing constantly.  It's absolutely worth every penny, and I'm saying this as someone who STILL hasn't gotten into the campaign, because I'm a bit crazy and have this problem where I say "ok, I'm going to design a nice cheap ship to get my fleet started in the campaign."  A few hours later - or ten, or fifteen - I have something 3x more expensive to build that can annihilate a weak enemy fleet in minutes that's about as stable as a cannister of compressed hydrogen over an open flame and handles like dung.  So you could say I'm still pretty new.  That said, I've just completed a reasonable little destroyer that just might work and looks pretty slick (and it doubles as a sub! not that I've managed to get the whole diving/submerging when needed automatically finished), so the next time I revisit this review, I may have some campaign experience under my belt!
I have nothing bad to say about it, and I'm critical.  It doesn't feel at all incomplete.  Things are always reworked and added - part of a living development cycle - but nothing feels missing.  I do have a wishlist, though... automated control blocks (which already exist serving SO many roles, like deploying/releasing hot air balloons or controlling air pump bouyancy) would be even more awesome if they could enable/disable detectors.  I'd like to be able to switch off active detection and be able to "go silent" using passive systems only (think disabling active sonar when surfacing a sub, or disabling active radar at low altitude flight).  I'd also love to have AI connector 'wires' - effectively extended blocks of connectors ala beams.  Maybe have a version that's a little sturdier with only connectors on either end (an armored/insulated conduit, basically).

Dark Souls is a game of two extremes. In limbo, if you will.
On one hand its a game filled with death, misery and dispair. Its carefully crafted world of Lordran is a rotting kingdom where everything is out to get you. Everything, from its many inhabitants, to its environments to the random encounters with other players are solely there to ruin your day. Its environments are macabre and often grotesque, which is match by some of its enemies. And, of course, the game is hard. Brutally hard at times. All of your achievements can be wiped away in a second. The game can and will pin you to the ground and leave you there if you let it.
But, on the other hand, it is a game filled with life, joy and hope. The many messages left by other players are there to cheer you on, to lean you onto a secret or just to make you laugh. The bloodstains are there to show you that other players are having just as bad a time as you are. Its environments are starkly beautiful, and show that there is still a shimmer of light in Lordran. And, finally, it is fair game. No matter how many times you die, the game encourages you to push on and to
give up. The game encourages you to change or upgrade your equipment and encourages you to change your playstyle. Other players are there to help you during boss fights. Ultimately, the game
you to become a better player and it

Yet another trading card money farming game that the devs put basically no effort at all. Looks and plays like your average 10+ year old flash player game except that... it manages to be a much weaker game than those somehow. It has incredibly dull and badly thought out mechanics, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mobile-looking interface, unity engine, only one level (which is an infinite/survival level), power ups that more disrupt your gameplay than help, only allowed to use ONE bought power up per run (as if they being almost useless wasn't already enough), which in turn makes money completely useless after you buy the extra star slots (you can buy backgrounds and skins for your star-catching platform, but that is just cosmetic)
The gameplay is pretty basic. You have a Breakout-style moveable platform (no balls tho) that you use to catch the falling stars and additional items that spawn at random positions at the top of the screen and fall gradually in a direction determined by the current wind value. The stars are the only essential items that you need to always collect, failing to do so resulting in the loss of one of the the 3 lives you start with (you can store up to 5 lives at once by getting the 1+ life power-ups). The other items that spawn are ice droplets (which are negative and slow you down if you grab any), 6 power-ups that can be either positive or negative gameplay modifiers, and coins that provide extra score.
You have an upgradable limited "inventory" in which you store the stars and ice. Whenever the inventory reaches its full capacity you won't be able to get any ice/stars and will need to deposit your items by moving your platform in one of the extremes of the screen (this is when your points are finally accounted for). Every time that you reach the max capacity of the inventory the game slows down for a few seconds to allow you to have time to empty your inventory. The extreme of the screen that you were farther away from when you captured the item that reached the max capacity of your inventory will be the side that provides the 2x multiplier to your points when you make your deposit. Funnily enough, despite the game telling you in one of the tips that "Going for the 2x multiplier is not always the best choice!", it IS always the best choice because there is always time to travel to the other side and still have enough time to catch the next star wherever it spawns from. In the end of each run you get to see your score and given the option to submit it to the global scoreboard, + you get an amount of money based on your score, which you can use to buy one time use per run power-ups (the same♥♥♥♥♥♥ones that drop throughout the game), increase your max inventory size, and buy cosmetic items (backgrounds + skins for your platform).
There are 6 types of pick-up items that modify the game, each (besides one) having 2 variations: one intented to negatively affect your game and one intended to positively affect your game. Sadly, they are not very well thought out.
The 6 power-ups:
- Bubble power-up cooldown decreaser: this lowers the amount of time you need to wait to re-use the bubble special ability that you buy from the store.
- Ice amount modifier (more than default/less than default): hardly matters at all because it is still extremely easy to dodge the ice even at the max amount
- Wind modifier (no wind at all/max wind): higher wind barely affects your ability to predict where the stars will fall, in fact the stronger the wind the better, because that way there is less risk of missing the stars that spawn near the corners as they will be thrown by the wind to the star capturing wall, which automatically captures the stars and does not make you lose any lives.
-Star fall speed modifier (slower/faster): this is the worst of all. You would assume that slower falling stars would make everything much easier, right??? it is actually almost a straight-up negative because they didn't implement it properly. Yes, the stars do fall slower, but the spawn time of the stars remains unchanged (or not changed adequately), so you often end up with 2 stars falling at once (which normally never happens). Then when your power-up expires, both stars that are on screen will start falling at the normal speed again and basically 100% make you lose a life, especially in the later stages of the run. There is no reason at all to use this power-up, the normal falling speed is completely fine and it reaches a cap by 8000 points or so (not sure about this) which is still very very easy to deal with, so there is absolutely no reason to get this "upgrade" as it will just ♥♥♥♥ you up.
- Platform speed modifier (slower/faster): well at least this one actually does something useful. The extra moving speed does help a bit, although it can also make it harder to control and make you ♥♥♥♥ up close dodges. If you ever played Osu! catch the beat, this is basically like having shift held on all the time at an easy map. In this game you don't really need the extra speed to get all the stars, so the function of it is just allowing a larger error window in your reaction time; basically another unecessary power-up. (a legit use of it is to get more of the extra items, but all items besides the extra life are pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥anyway)
- Extra life/life remover: self-explanatory. the +1 life spawns much less than the -1 life modifier, which is ok, otherwise the game would be even easier.
So in conclusion, the power-ups do not help much at all, they are all basically negative or not worth the risk.
Also, the way you are rewarded money is kinda weird. It keeps doubling your money reward after certain score milestones in a run, which is fine up until a certain number, but after you cross an amount of points (which isn't even that high) it basically gives you infinite money and you can buy everything in the game with no effort.
Does it have any positives, though?

The folks at chucklefish are at it again.
This time they made an 2D space exploration game that is very compelling yet it lacks actual dept. The game keeps itself challenging by making the controls floaty, not being able to change direction mid jump for instance, also giving your character weight, making it take time to fully speed up and slow down. They also make it so that you can't reliably get your hands on decent weapons, whilst you're amour will always be what you crafted. This makes it so that you have to gather a large amount of materials just to increase your defence whilst hoping your offence can keep up.
It definitely follows the saw tooth approach terraria held when it comes to difficulty curve. Giant wall only to lose its difficulty gradually until the next wall is reached. But with terraria the player did it for the loot/challenge. now we are stacked with this awful excuse for a main quest that just shows you how repetitive the progression curve is.
Aside from the flaws of the design the main quest also makes it very clear how limited the world generator is. Every other planet uses the same dungeon or town and you're just running through it frustrated it's not the kind you're looking for. It's a problem terraria got away with by only needing one world to live in. By the time you generated your second world you weren’t surprised that it's kind of the same but a bit different. Yet in starbound you're forced to explore similar worlds because of the main quest sets you out finding these artefacts of different species that you may or may not find on a specific planet type. Which is stupid because it's not incentivised to explore different planets of the same type (everything can be found on one planet of its type in terms of resources.) and if it didn’t make you do that you would just jump to the next type and be awed by all the cool new things you came across. Yet it's as if the games desperately want you to notice all the flaws in its design.
The game is also full of these design trails that lead to nowhere. They boast that survival mode is the medium of the difficulty modes and makes you have to think about eating food. But that is all it does. You can still eat food on casual mode and enjoy the benefits of it and food is so abundant that it never becomes a problem. It fails to have you create proper infrastructure and the process of collecting and making it is so menial it's nothing more than a chore. A set of actions you do once in a while because you otherwise might lose more time if you don't. If they would make food more fun to harvest, collect, preserve. Make cooking something to play around with, something that is worth experimenting with. Now you just cook whatever is available except for the mentally divergent then it's a tab on the collectables page.
The game has hover bikes and boats that do nothing. A mech that is a whole new saw tooth of a difficulty curve that they managed to completely separate from the main one. A colony builder that is there to make you money you already don't need any more because a colony deed costs more then you're willing to spend before money doesn't matter anymore. Ship crew that give you minor bonuses and mayor frustration as they stand in your way. You get these by doing multiple quests for them that come from a way to small side quest pool if you want to fully stock your ship on crew. There are pickaxes even though you have a magical item that can cut trees, dig soil and even place it back. You can change in an orb, double jump and even dash. These can be upgraded but only one upgrade can be applied at a time.
The building is fun though. There is a vast array of styles at your disposal, an endless amounts if you're creative enough. It just saddens me that the game doesn't know that and it can be happily ignored for the entirety of the game. I only expected to play Pixel Boy for a little while, but here I am three hours later hopelessly addicted and unable to contain my thoughts on it. The dungeon-crawling genre is one we've all come to know and love, but I can't even remember the last time one felt as fresh and unique as
. There are plenty of reasons why this stands out among the rest of the bunch on Steam;
My first moment with Pixel Boy is a relaxing one, with a slightly blurred image of the quaint little pixel town, Resolutia rolling by the title screen as I'm treated to the relaxing melodies of french electro artist Pyramid. I already feel like I'm in a most blissful state. However, this feeling of relaxation quickly ends, as I start the game and am thrown into the confines of a dark, dusty old dungeon and a glowing trail of blue light as my only guide in this confusion. The game eases you into the mechanics using a humorous narrator that reminded me a lot of Professor Frink from The Simpsons. The lines are delivered infrequently enough to not be a hindrance and are actually pretty damn funny.
The almost Minecraft-like graphics are extremely familiar and nostalgic and work exceptionally beautiful in tandem with it's mellow, almost cosmic sounding soundtrack. You're introduced to the armor and pixel power crafting system which are incredibly dynamic and massive in scope when it comes to the number of possibilities and the diversity shown in their execution. Fiddling around with the vast amount of powerups you come across to see which new powerful attacks you can come up with quickly becomes an obsession.
After finding the RGB keys and making it out of the first dungeon alive, you're brought back to the pixel-y town from the title-screen which you learn is your base of operations. This base will supply you with a multitude of features including shops for pixel powerups, armor, crafting, a monster museum to keep track of the enemies you've encountered, and doors leading to each of the main campaign dungeons. There is also a mysterious and colorful fountain in the center of the town which seems to be the source of the bliss enducing melody you hear.
Once you're done with your introduction to the the town, you will quickly return back to the depths of new dungeons where the pace really begins to pick up, with the music being kicked up a notch going from mellow ambiance to heavy, pulsating rhythms that pump you up for the oncoming journey. The action itself is fantastically solid and fast paced, with an array of stylish monsters and crazy bullet patterns there is a lot going on on the screen at once and it can become a serious sensory-overload in the best way possible. The top-down action combat here is very reminiscent of classics such as
or
combined with a weapon combo system similar to
and that is a *very* good thing for old school gamers or fans of the golden age of gaming.
The roguelike elements become strongly apparent here and are just right, with heavy randomized factors to the dungeon even involving a slot machine minigame to help decide the mobs for your current run (A really cool touch to the randomized aspect of these games!) and persistant stats and gold that will carry over between your deaths, making each consecutive and seemingly impossible run that much easier. The dungeons become extremely challenging and you'll be forced to utilize every item you find and every shop you happen to come across, as well as chestrooms which contain useful powerups for you to use (sometimes negative effects for the unlucky) if you're able to find or buy keys throughout the floor.
Pixel Boy really hits that rogue-lite sweet spot and will feel right at home with fans of games like Full Mojo Rampage or Binding of Isaac who want extreme replayability and even deeper, faster paced gameplay. This is an absolute must-have for any dungeon-crawler or rogue-lite collection.

For what it is, this is a decent little game. The combat has a surprising amount of nuance for the simplicity of the rules, and the visual effects, while being light enough for older systems, are nicely pretty.
The range of starting options also means that there's a lot of different approaches in the game, different starting conditions that you can control - as well as all the random variation that you can't control.
It's not a civ game, it's not MOO-like (or GalCiv-like, or SotS-like) - it's all about the adventure and tactical combat, with some light 4X-like elements to tie it all together.
And I'm having a lot of fun with it. There are some rough edges, like the lack of an 'exit game' control on the main menu, and no true-fullscreen (only fullscreen window, and that isn'r borderless), but then it's not a game to play for hours and hours on end, but 20-60 minutes here and there.
But I'm also going to have to go back to BE to get as much as I can out of it - some minor content elements are locked until you do something in BE to unlock them.

I'm a small fan of the Fate series and all, but I can't stand this game.
First off, the story isn't interesting at all. You can't even call the scene where Tamamo and Nero meet up a plot twist, because it's literally the beginning of the game. Most of the dialogue is skipable and if you wanna increase the bond level, you choose the skinship option--because it's all about that fanservice. So, unless you care about a plot that has nothing to do with the Fate series or doing lewd things with Nero, you'll skip the dialogue.
Supposedly, the games prior to this one were better in terms of story, so check those out if you want better story. Because I'm moving on to the gameplay, which is the main factor of this game and why you shouldn't buy it.
It's mindless. Absolutely mindless. You're only ever going to need two combos: Dash + Heavy for clearing out large waves so you can trigger minibosses, and Light 4x + Heavy, which shreds through the minibosses health. The actual bosses, which are enemy servants, are a joke; all you have to do is parry them, which is done by pressing any attack button the second they land a hit on you. But, maybe you wanna use special moves, so you run around to 3 nodes and get Noble Phantasm keycards, and then you use it. I skip the cutscene, because it's the same thing every time and that gets boring after a while. Same with transformation; you become more powerful, but your moveset gets EVEN SIMPLER. As for Extella maneuvers, it's basically a noble phantasm, but you use it more often. It has damage, it has a cutscene--except YOU CAN'T SKIP THIS ONE. You just have to sit through it, mashing the B button for that extra damage.
Overall, this game will waste your time. I"m just lucky enough that I could refund it with 2.8 hours played on it. So thank you for once, Steam.

Playing it in handheld mode alleviates this somewhat, and was my preferred method of play (I'm of the mind that all visual novels should be enjoyed in the comfort of one's own bed).
